Jewish judge overseeing Maduro's cocaine trafficking case dies at 92
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
23:13:40 UTC
08:13:40 KST

Just 13 days ago, he was still on the bench facing Nicolás Maduro, Venezuela's ousted leader, presiding over one of the most closely watched criminal cases in the United States. On Wednesday morning, federal Judge Alvin Hellerstein, an observant Jew who served for nearly three decades on the federal bench in Manhattan, died in New York at the age of 92. His death was confirmed by officials at the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York. The cause of death was not disclosed. The court must now appoint a new judge to oversee Maduro's trial, in which preliminary hearings have already begun, although the evidentiary phase is not scheduled until next year.
At his final hearing on October 15, Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, appeared before him. The couple were captured in January during a U.S. military operation in Venezuela, transferred to New York and charged with cocaine trafficking offenses. Appearing in prison uniforms and leg shackles, both pleaded not guilty to new charges of conspiring to torture opponents of the Venezuelan regime, including U.S. citizens. Maduro interrupted the judge, claiming the accusations were false, but Hellerstein cut him off and instructed that a not-guilty plea be entered on his behalf. Following the expansion of the indictment, the judge postponed the start of the trial by two weeks, to June 14, 2027. It remains unclear whether his death will lead to another delay.
The fact that a trial with such far-reaching international implications was being overseen by a 92-year-old judge had raised questions since Maduro's capture. But Hellerstein was not specially appointed to the case following the January operation. Its origins date back to a 2011 indictment against Hugo Carvajal, the former head of Venezuela's military intelligence service, over his alleged involvement in cocaine trafficking. Hellerstein had handled proceedings related to the case for years before Maduro's arrest. In 2020, the indictment was expanded to include the Venezuelan president himself, who was charged with conspiracy to commit narco-terrorism, cocaine trafficking and weapons offenses. Carvajal, who was extradited to the United States from Spain in 2023, pleaded guilty last year. When U.S. forces captured Maduro in January, the case simply continued before the same judge.
In the United States, federal judges are appointed for life and are not subject to a mandatory retirement age. Hellerstein was appointed by President Bill Clinton in 1998 and assumed senior status in 2011, allowing him to reduce his workload without retiring from the bench. Even at his advanced age, he continued to oversee complex trials and rule on cases of significant public interest.
However, reports published as early as January raised questions about his alertness. According to two people who attended a fraud trial he presided over every day in 2025, the judge sometimes appeared to doze off during testimony, with his aides waking him by passing notes or refilling his water glass. The daily court schedule in that trial was also relatively short. Following the reports, some called for Maduro's trial to be reassigned to another judge, citing concerns that the proceedings could last for years and that Hellerstein might have to be replaced midway through.
By contrast, attorneys who appeared before him described him as an alert and engaged jurist. Attorney Michael Hausfeld said Hellerstein was "sharper than many younger judges." Retired federal Judge Shira Scheindlin, who worked alongside him, said concerns about his age were legitimate but expressed confidence in his ability to assess for himself whether he was fit to continue serving. Legal experts noted that the federal judiciary has no uniform system for evaluating the competence of aging judges, leaving the decision of when to retire largely in their own hands.
Hellerstein was a familiar figure in New York's Jewish community and previously served as president of The Jewish Center, an Orthodox synagogue on Manhattan's Upper West Side. He strictly observed the Sabbath and played tennis with local rabbis for decades. During his judicial career, he presided over major lawsuits stemming from the September 11 terrorist attacks, including proceedings involving compensation for victims' families. He was also known for his independence in cases involving the administration. Among other rulings, he repeatedly rejected President Donald Trump's attempts to move the New York hush-money case in which he was convicted to federal court, and ruled against the deportation of Venezuelan migrants without due process.
Now, eight months before Maduro's trial is scheduled to begin, another judge will have to take over a complex criminal case that has developed over more than a decade. The new judge will face difficult legal questions, including anticipated arguments concerning the immunity of a former head of state and the circumstances under which Maduro was brought to the United States. For now, no announcement has been made about who will replace Hellerstein or whether the trial will proceed according to the existing schedule.

Wildfire smoke deaths in Canada now stand at 275%, a huge increase over the past two decades according to a new report, media reported Wednesday.
Published in The Lancelot, a leading international medical journal, the report found that there is an estimated 4,000 deaths annually in the four-year period to 2025.
That is a huge spike – there were 1,050 deaths annually from wildfire smoke for the period between 2003 and 2012, according to the report released Tuesday.
"For any individual, it might not be that [wildfire smoke] was the trigger," he said. "But on average across the population, we're seeing more death associated with those periods" said Ian Hamilton, co-author of the report in planetary health at the George Institute for Global Health at Imperial College in London, told CBC News.
Heat-related risks of wildfire smoke accelerated on hot days by simply going for an energetic walk.
It is particularly dangerous for young people who push through the heat, said Dr. Courtney Howard, chair of the Global Climate and Health Alliance.
"Young people are almost so strong, especially athletes, that they push through heat and heat related exhaustion," she said. 
"And unfortunately that can actually lead to mortality."
The exacerbation of climate change has a lot to do with the problem as wildfires in Canada increase each year.
The report found that 80% of heated days were the result of fossil fuel on climate.
"We need to know that this is going to keep getting worse year on year and year, unless we decrease greenhouse gas emissions," Howard said.

How Bedouin voters became a defining story of Israel's 2026 election - analysis
No one’s told you, and no one will. But we have a winner coming out of Election Day: The Israeli political system
Yesterday in the middle of the Negev Desert, something amazing happened. Negev Bedouin, the poorest people in our country, came out in the some of the highest numbers. The credit belongs to them. And also to the system.
https://x.com/i/web/status/2115573810833289637
This post can't be displayed because social networks cookies have been deactivated. You can activate them by clicking .
Israel’s system brings the splinters of this country real representation. These groups don’t get diluted by district lines for electing lawmakers.
They don’t get stuffed by being thrown into giant political parties that have to have to big tent.
No. They can put up parties, run candidates, and play politics on their own. With the big boys.
It works. And it renews the Israeli system time after time.
We've seen it with the Shas Party, forged by discrimination by Ashkenazi ultra-Orthodox against Sephardic counterparts. With immigrants from the former Soviet Union, especially in their early years in the country. Groups continue to try it, understanding that at first they may not succeed.
That happened in this cycle with a tiny party representing ultra-Orthodox who want change in their community on education, work, and military service.
So, yes, we have a lot of parties, and we have a lot of elections, and we have a lot of chaos. But our destruction is creative destruction. Creating a country where politics matter, where politics move forward. And where, with fits and starts, politics really and truly can include everyone.
Marginalized groups come out in the Israeli system because they know they come out of the polling place with members of Knesset who represent them. They don’t need to fight inside some big-tent party. Or make do with a representative of a district with lines on a map.
No. A party, in this the Raam Party, that represents them.
Israel’s system excels at that and has done it time after time. The wider public doesn’t always like the results. Narrow constituencies can be frustrating.
People hate our system. They say it has too many parties. Too many elections. And too much chaos.
What happened yesterday should put those arguments in the waste basket. As 77% of Israelis went to cast their ballots.

US President Donald Trump has demanded that Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola and a rival sharing the name of Alaska's Republican incumbent be removed from next week's election ballot, accusing Democrats of an illegal scheme to confuse voters.
His call followed a New York Times investigation reporting that Democratic operatives had secretly recruited so-called "spoiler" candidates, including another Dan Sullivan, in an effort to draw votes away from Republican Senator Dan Sullivan.
"It has just been determined that the Democrats in Alaska illegally searched for, and recruited, a man named Dan Sullivan," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
He alleged that Democrats had committed perjury by making false statements under oath in federal court, and demanded that the incumbent be allowed to run without either Peltola or the "FAKE Dan Sullivan" on the ballot.
And he told reporters later that Peltola and any other alleged accomplices should be prosecuted. "To me, that's voter fraud at the highest level," he said.
But the Times noted that recruiting candidates to split an opponent's vote, a practice known as ballot stacking, is generally legal and has been used by both parties.
As recently as 2024, little-known former Republican Anthony Frascone beat Democrat Mondaire Jones in a low-turnout Working Families Party primary in New York state.
Peltola 'definitely aware'
Among those it said were recruited was Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher from a remote Alaskan fishing community. He has said he entered the race of his own volition.
The newspaper identified Democratic operative Jerid Kurtz as a central figure, reporting that he travelled around Alaska under an assumed name to court potential candidates.
Peltola's former campaign manager Elisa Rios told the paper the candidate was "definitely aware" of the project but not directly involved.
Peltola's campaign has denied recruiting any candidates.
The revelations come days after Trump ordered the Justice Department to sue Alaska over the second Sullivan's presence on the ballot.
The lawsuit seeks to delay certification if Peltola narrowly defeats the incumbent and votes cast for his namesake could have changed the outcome.
On Wednesday, US Vice President JD Vance defended the Trump administration’s legal challenge to Alaska’s Senate election, describing the candidacy of a second candidate with a name nearly identical to that of the incumbent as a “big fraud” and arguing that it could confuse voters ahead of next week’s midterm elections.
He argued that many voters would recognise the alleged problem but said others might be confused because of competing demands on their time.

Historic Polish synagogue acquired through tender, to be restored after years of neglect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:57:24 UTC
07:57:24 KST

After years of neglect, the historic synagogue in Trzebinia, Poland, has been acquired through an international initiative aimed at restoring it to its original purpose and returning it to the Jewish community.
The plans include the restoration of the building, the establishment of a Jewish museum, and the creation of a hospitality center for visitors to the graves of revered rabbis and Hasidic leaders at the local Jewish cemetery.
The historic synagogue, located in Poland’s Silesian region, was returned to the Jewish people on Tuesday, after years of decay.
The Jewish community of Katowice relinquished its right to reclaim the building, after which the municipality put it up for sale through a tender process.
In response, a group of partners joined forces to prevent the property from being converted into a non-Jewish venue, and to ensure that it would be preserved as a site of Jewish historical significance.
The acquisition of the synagogue was made possible through cooperation among three parties: the Israeli delegation, led by Meir Bulka, known as the “Grave Hunter,” who heads J-NERATIONS, an organization dedicated to preserving Jewish heritage in Europe; Jacek Purski, director of Auschwitz Research Center on Hate, Extremism and Radicalisation; and Marcin Majchrowicz, a businessman and philanthropist committed to preserving Jewish heritage in Poland’s Silesian region.
Community history
The Jewish community in Trzebinia dates back to at least the 1500s, with a more prominent presence from the 1700s onward.
An independent Jewish community was established in the city in 1815, growing to its peak in 1921 when Jews accounted for 23% of Trzebinia's population.
Between the two World Wars, Trzebinia was home to four synagogues, a Talmud Torah, yeshivas, prayer houses, charitable institutions, and aid organizations.
Among the prominent rabbinical figures who served in the city were Rabbi Dov Berish Weidenfeld, known as the Gaon of Tchebinas, as well as Rabbi Ben Zion Halberstam, the second Rebbe of Bobov.
Adjacent to the synagogue is the Jewish cemetery, where rabbis and several spiritual leaders are buried.
However, the Holocaust destroyed the vibrant Jewish community. Many members of the community were deported to concentration camps and ghettos, and numerous residents of the city were murdered at Auschwitz.
The Jewish community’s properties were destroyed, leaving the surviving synagogue as the only remaining testimony to the city's Jewish heritage.
“The synagogue, located just a 40-minute drive from Kraków and now returned to the Jewish people, will soon become another destination for Jews visiting the region,” said Meir Bulka.
“I am deeply moved that we have succeeded in preventing the desecration of Jewish religious heritage and in making a meaningful mark on the history of the Jewish people in Poland."
"This is not merely about saving a synagogue; it is also about taking responsibility for preserving the memory of an entire community.”
Polish synagogue restoration aims to preserve Jewish heritage for future generations
Jacek Purski, director of Auschwitz Research Center on Hate, Extremism and Radicalization said that saving a synagogue is not purely about preserving a building, but about recognizing that Jewish life is "not only part of Poland’s past, but also part of its present and future."
Wherever possible, the partners said they will use historical documentation and archaeological evidence to recreate the site's appearance before the Holocaust.
In the coming days, a foundation will be established in Poland to manage the restoration of the synagogue, and it will be possible to participate through donations and investments.

The 2,000-Nit OLED in Apple’s New MacBook Is a Big Deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:54:16 UTC
07:54:16 KST

Laptops with OLED screens aren’t particularly special. They’ve been around for a decade. You can currently buy a touchscreen OLED machine for as little as $700, and even the iPad Pro has had an OLED screen since 2024.
So, why did Apple wait over a decade to release its own touchscreen OLED MacBook Pro? The simple answer for the long wait is that the company wanted to do it “the Apple way.” But in this case, “the Apple way” involves somehow cranking up the display to 2,000 nits, solving both the brightness and glare problems that OLED laptops have always suffered from.
Having seen the thing with my own eyes at a media event today in Los Angeles, I can tell you that this screen is the real deal.
Like No Other OLED
Apple is using a tandem OLED panel, the same layer-stacking technology used in the OLED iPad Pro. The real innovation here, however, is that the panel has been optimized to hit a new peak brightness of 2,000 nits, and that’s a result that matters.
That big number is meaningless on its own, but here’s the context. Nits are the standard measure of screen brightness used across the consumer tech industry. A cheap OLED laptop maxes out around 300 nits. A higher-end OLED laptop might get you up to 1,000 nits of brightness—but only in brighter and more colorful High Dynamic Range content like specific streaming apps, YouTube videos, and games. In other words, the vast majority of the time you’re using an OLED, it’ll feel like a dimmer screen than normal. The iPad Pro can get up to 1,600 nits for HDR content, and 1,000 nits for the less bright, less colorful Standard Dynamic Range content. That’s closer.
But this MacBook Pro’s screen is on an entirely different level. It’s a ground-up redesign of the tandem OLED layer arrangement in the iPad Pro, even down to the manufacturing process. And the result is that it can blast your eyes with 2,000 nits of brightness both in SDR and HDR. That means whether you’re looking at some generic wallpaper, a website, or a HDR-compatible movie, you’ll feel that extra brightness. That’s why, I assume, Apple gave it the name of PROLED XDR. In a world where the words “OLED” and “HDR” don’t necessarily indicate how good the experience is, more weighty jargon is needed.
As with all tech, bigger numbers don’t always add up to a noticeable difference for the user. But when it comes to HDR performance, we’ve been waiting a long time for OLED to catch up.
HDR, or High Dynamic Range, serves as a measure of color depth, brightness, and contrast—and in the past, this has always involved a trade-off. An OLED screen can turn each individual pixel any color, and it can turn off individual pixels in the display. This allows OLED to have great color control and unbeatable contrast, since when you turn a pixel off, it renders absolutely black.
But OLEDs couldn’t get super bright, and other screen tech like Mini-LED could get much brighter, which is why Apple stuck with Mini-LED for years, using it on the MacBook Pro and Studio Display XDR. This technology allowed Apple to have the laptops with the best HDR performance out there.
With the 2026 MacBook Pro, that compromise no longer exists. This OLED screen has both the brightness and contrast in its pocket, and you can see it.
An OLED panel has lots of more benefits over conventional backlighting beyond just contrast. Mini-LED struggles with an effect called blooming, where bright parts of images bleed light to the surrounding area, which is where lots of detail is lost in the image. OLED completely fixes that, giving each pixel a much wider range of control (up to completely turning off). As part of the Apple event I attended, we were shown a selection of HDR images with lots of contrast, a number of which had fields of darkness at the edges that made it look like the image simply disappeared into the bezel. Very pretty. We also watched a darker scene in the show Widow’s Bay in HDR, which was an excellent showcase of the range of detail this screen can show.
The new screen helps this MacBook stay exceedingly light, as well. Much of the savings in weight comes from the OLED design, since the screen uses thinner and lighter materials than screens past. Despite the computer using the same aluminum chassis as the previous MacBook Pro, the new 14-inch MacBook Pro weighs just three pounds, which is 12 percent lighter than before.
To put the new screen into context, we were also shown a comparison between Apple’s OLED and the OLED of a high-end competitive Windows laptop. The difference was striking, especially in off-axis viewing. At its worst, there were visible rainbow effects on the Windows machine’s screen.
There’s a catch, though. While Apple’s screen can get up to 2,000 nits, it’s normally capped at 1,000 nits. When the laptop’s built-in adaptive brightness sensor thinks you need a boost, the screen’s brightens increases up to 2,000 nits. So the brightness only hits the high end when you’re outside or working under really harsh lighting conditions. The previous-gen MacBook Pros also did this, but to a lesser degree. With this machine, you’re getting 400 more nits of SDR brightness right out of the box, with the ability to crank it up to twice as much.
Glare is another issue with conventional, low-brightness OLED laptops that the MacBook Pro improves. When deeper blacks are rendered on the screen, it often results in harsher reflections. Sometimes it can get so bad, it feels like you’re looking into a mirror. The brightness alone on the MacBook Pro goes a long way toward overpowering glare and reflections, but Apple is also using what it claims is a “state-of-the-art” anti-reflective coating. Almost every laptop screen uses some kind antireflective coating, so one can hope that Apple’s “state-of-the-art” coating is at least on par with those, but I can attest that this is the very best I’ve seen.
The ultimate solution to cutting glare and reflections is still the option for a nano-texture display, where the anti-reflective pattern is actually etched into the screen itself rather than layered on top. That’s available as an upgrade on both the 14-inch and 16-inch models.
Reach Out and Touch It
The other major innovation happening with the MacBook Pro’s screen is the introduction of touch. Like OLED itself, this is a feature we’ve seen on many other laptops for well over a decade. I came in hoping Apple would swing for the fences here, but its use of touch interaction feels much more modest. (Let us quickly forget the failure of the Touch Bar from 2016.)
The implementation itself is impressive. Interacting with elements on the screen feels every bit as fluid as it does on an iPad. The screen also supports many of the familiar trackpad gestures, such as pinch to zoom or a three-fingered swipe to switch Spaces.
The most natural feeling touch optimizations have been lifted directly from iPadOS. If you tap in the top left windows controls, they zoom in to let you select more precisely. You can even grab a window and flick it to the side to quickly get into Split View. My favorite optimization is the ability to tap, hold, and slide down to select an item within the Menu Bar. Very clever. And yet, I was still hoping for a stronger commitment on the software side. You can’t use an Apple Pencil on this screen, and nothing in the hardware of the MacBook Pro has been adjusted to make touching the screen feel any more ergonomic.
The bigger issue is with third-party apps though. While touch-to-click will work on all apps automatically, it’s up to developers to do any more than that. Even the third-party apps we were shown during demos had varying degrees of touch optimization.
The 3D modeling application ZBrush was a good example. While certain aspects were touch-enabled, none of the controls or menus had the useful optimizations that Apple’s first-party apps had. Hopefully this touch option will become more widely adopted, but I can foresee a future in which these fingers-first interactions are mostly forgotten outside of occasionally scrolling down a webpage with your thumb. And let me be clear: All of this is more than what Microsoft has ever done to optimize Windows 11 for touch. (And Microsoft even has Windows 2-in-1 tablets to support!)
With the 2026 MacBook Pro, Apple is doubling down on what’s working well for it: Leading the way in high-end hardware. There’s plenty more testing to do on the MacBook Pro in the coming weeks, but this OLED screen already looks like the one the entire industry will be chasing for years to come.

Cricket Australia has revealed the result of an MRI scan on Steve Smith's neck injury, which found a "cervical facet joint" injury.
Smith ruled himself out of playing the third and deciding Test against South Africa in Cape Town.
What's next?
Smith is expected to be back for the first Test against New Zealand in Perth on December 9, kicking off a run of 10 Tests in three months.
Australia expects to have Steve Smith back for the home summer after scans confirmed joint damage to the vice-captain's neck in South Africa.
Australian team officials said Smith had scans on Friday before failing in his bid to play in the third and deciding Test.
Those scans detected an injury to a "cervical facet joint", which connects to the spine and acts to guide and stabilise neck movement.
"Due to this and his limited range of motion, he was unfit to participate in the current Test," Cricket Australia said in a statement.
"Steve will continue to receive treatment and rehabilitation, with a full return to availability anticipated for the upcoming home Test series against New Zealand."
Smith has six weeks to recover for the first Test against New Zealand in Perth on December 9, which will begin a long run of virtually uninterrupted cricket through to mid-March, with a five-Test tour of India (January 21 to March 3) and the 150th anniversary Test against England at the MCG (March 11-15).
Australia will want Smith available for that stretch of 10 Tests in 14 weeks, just as they had hoped to have him for the return to Cape Town this week.
Even well after Friday's scans on arrival in Cape Town, Australia's coaching staff had been extremely confident Smith would be fit to face South Africa.
The 37-year-old batted in the nets for around 35 minutes on Sunday, two days out from the third Test, before sitting down and stretching his neck.
Loading Twitter content
He then briefly returned to batting, before growing increasingly frustrated and walking out of the nets.
Smith also attempted to bat on Tuesday morning just 90 minutes before the match, then determining he was not able to get his neck right.
"He is huge, one of the greatest batters we have ever had," Cummins said the day before the start of play.
"You don't play 100-odd Test matches without playing Test matches where you're not 100 per cent fit.
"Even though he is probably not going to be 100 per cent, hopefully he can compartmentalise that, like he has done 100 times before with other things, and come out and contribute like he does every week."
The injury means Smith is likely to never play another Test at Newlands, the venue of the ball-tampering scandal in 2018 that cost him the captaincy and a 12-month ban.

Yet to test legality of logical discrepancy in SIR: Supreme Court

SC said that while it upheld SIR in Bihar, it did not examine the legality of the ‘logical discrepancy’ criterion
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Wednesday said that even though the validity of SIR in Bihar was upheld, the court had no occasion to test the legality of the ‘logical discrepancy’ criterion as it was not used during the Bihar exercise.When EC’s counsel referred to smooth conduct of Bihar and West Bengal elections after SIR, the bench said, “Logical discrepancy (mode for deletion) was first resorted to in West Bengal. We are yet to examine its validity. We will go into logical discrepancy in detail later.”When petitioner Anjali Bhardwaj’s counsel claimed that lakhs of voters were deleted from the draft Delhi rolls on grounds of ‘logical discrepancy’, the bench asked how EC could reopen entries in the 2003 voter list and issue notices for logical discrepancy.“In a voter enumeration exercise like SIR, EC has taken the 2003 voter list as the base. If that is so, how could it classify those whose names figured in that list as ineligible on grounds of logical discrepancy? Can EC go beyond the list and reopen it?” the bench asked.During the last hearing, the bench had suggested that EC examine putting additional filters to avoid mechanical issuance of notices under ‘logical discrepancy’.
SC: Can EC go beyond 2003 list to scrutinise logical discrepancy?
In a voter enumeration exercise like SIR, EC has taken the 2003 voter list as the base. If that is so, how could it classify those whose names figured in that list as ineligible on grounds of logical discrepancy? Can EC go beyond the list and reopen it?” the bench asked.During the last hearing, the bench had suggested that EC examine putting additional filters to avoid mechanical issuance of notices under ‘logical discrepancy’.Opposition INDIA bloc functionaries, led by Rahul Gandhi, have filed a joint petition challenging many issues, including the SIR process, and questioned the allegedly arbitrary non-inclusion of names because of ‘logical discrepancy’.In its May 27 judgment, SC had examined the following questions — whether EC had the power to conduct SIR; whether SIR had a legitimate purpose and the process was proportionate to the object to be achieved; and whether the SIR procedure was contrary to Representation of the People Act, 1951, and Registration of Electors Act, 1960 — and found that there was nothing amiss in the conduct of SIR or the process adopted to achieve the object of weeding out voters who had died, shifted house or had duplicate entries.SC had categorically ruled that the SIR exercise “neither stands in direct conflict with RP Act and 1960 Rules, nor does it detract from the constitutional imperative of free and fair elections”. It had said, “The impugned SIR exercise, as conducted, satisfies the requirements of proportionality. The measures adopted bear a rational nexus to the objective sought to be achieved, are not manifestly excessive, and are accompanied by sufficient procedural safeguards to prevent arbitrary exclusion.
“We are equally satisfied that, in its object and design, the impugned SIR bears a direct nexus to the constitutional goal of free and fair elections. Free and fair elections do not rest merely upon the mechanics of polling. They equally depend upon the integrity, accuracy and purity of the electoral roll which forms the foundation of the democratic process.”

Microsoft gained billions of dollars in stock market value Wednesday afternoon after it reported better than expected revenue and profit, just days after it offered voluntary buyouts to some 60,000 employees.

The launch is part of a broader push by tech companies to release hardware that can handle more AI computing on-device and offline, so users do not have to rely solely on remote cloud datacenters, where running AI is slower and more expensive.

Turkey hosted Libya east-west reunification talks last week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:43:47 UTC
07:43:47 KST

Breadcrumb
Turkey hosted Libya east-west reunification talks last week
Turkey hosted talks between Libya's eastern and western administrations last week with the goal of reunifying them, a senior Turkish official familiar with the talks told AFP Wednesday.
Ankara is one of the rare countries that maintains ties with both sides in Libya, which has been divided between rival leaderships since 2014 following the 2011 downfall of longtime ruler Muammar Gaddafi.
"Discussions have so far focused primarily on military unification, while political unity is expected to be addressed at a later stage," the official said.
The talks, which took place in the capital Ankara, were attended by military officials from Libya's eastern and western administrations as well as diplomats, the source said, adding that Turkey was acting as a mediator between the two sides.
Beset by instability since the overthrow of Gaddafi in a NATO-backed uprising, Libya is divided between a UN-recognised government in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar.
Turkey strongly backed the Tripoli-based government during years of conflict in Libya, but ties with eastern authorities have warmed significantly in recent years.
On Friday, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said the time had come to reunify the eastern and western administrations, hinting that an announcement could come soon.
"We have now reached a stage where the conditions are ripe to permanently secure the reunification of the east and the west," Fidan said after hosting a meeting of top European diplomats and regional powers in Istanbul.
"One of the most important pillars of national unification is how the military units currently controlled separately by both sides will be brought together under a single umbrella," he added.
US 'backing'
The Turkish official who spoke to AFP on Wednesday said that no agreement had yet been reached, but the parties had agreed to continue the talks.
"Turkey is the priority to host the talks but they could also take place in Libya," he said.
"Given that Ankara now enjoys close ties with both Libya's eastern and western administrations, it is undoubtedly in a stronger position than any other external actor to negotiate a compromise on military and political reunification," Hamish Kinnear, an analyst at UK-based consulting group Verisk Maplecroft, told AFP.
Turkish mediation comes as Washington and the United Nations are also pushing for the reunification of the oil-rich country.
Asked whether Turkish and US plans conflicted, a foreign observer told AFP that Ankara and Washington's positions "are, in fact, aligned".
"If there is any significant friction, it is primarily with the Europeans, who are deeply divided on this issue, notably France and Italy, as well as Russia, which would see its influence diminish," the observer commented.
Kinnear agreed that Turkey's push for what he described as an "elite bargain" to reunify Libya "likely has the tacit backing of Washington".
Competition for power
Under the proposed US plan for Libya's reunification, Abdulhamid Dbeibah, who heads the Tripoli-based government, would remain prime minister, while Saddam Haftar, the eastern commander's son, would become head of the Presidential Council.
Kinnear suggested that the Turkish initiative might be "enough to secure a temporary reunification of Libya's governments", but warned that, in the longer term, destabilising competition for greater power and influence "is likely".
He said it was unlikely that these key figures would relinquish their direct influence over militias loyal to them and remain satisfied with their formal positions alone.
Last week, Libya's eastern-based parliament approved a maritime demarcation deal with Turkey, years after rejecting it when it was first signed.
The agreement has drawn anger from the European Union, Greece, Israel and Egypt, who denounced it as an infringement of their sovereign rights and a violation of international law.
Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan lashed out at the criticism, saying it had "no legitimate basis", speaking after a cabinet meeting on Monday.
Analysts say Libya's approval gives Turkey stronger political backing for offshore surveys and negotiations over exploration.

€100 million at stake: what Ukrainians could save by joining Europe’s euro-payment zone, if parliament votes before November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:38:16 UTC
07:38:16 KST

Ukraine should pass the bill to join Europe’s single euro-payment zone without delay, because it would save Ukrainians up to €100 million a year. For businesses that buy goods or equipment in the EU, the cost of a transfer would fall several-fold and settle in minutes or hours instead of five to seven days, says the country’s representative to the EU, Taras Kachka.
The bill, No. 14327-d, aligns Ukraine’s rules against money laundering and terrorism financing with EU standards and those of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), part of the commitments on its path to EU membership. It has to move soon: the simplified route into the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA) is open only until November 2026.
Ukraine must apply before November
If Ukraine misses that window, new stricter EU anti-money-laundering directives take effect, raising the bar and risking years of delay.
Even once parliament passes the bill, connecting Ukraine’s banks will take about another year and a half, with full launch set for 1 January 2028. In Kachka’s words: “Passing the European-integration legislation for Ukraine to join the Single Euro Payments Area is critically necessary, needed ‘yesterday.’”
He said he hopes lawmakers will use the opportunity to pass the changes.
Small business gains the most
Kachka expressed hope that Ukraine's parliament would vote in favor of the necessary amendments, using this important political moment to benefit society.
“This will truly help businesses of all sizes, traders, manufacturers, importers and, of course, ordinary people who have so many relatives and colleagues in Europe and interact with them regularly,” Kachka noted.
SEPA's greatest practical value lies with small and medium-sized firms, including limited liability companies and sole proprietors. Membership would allow them to make cross-border euro payments on the same day at minimal cost, with no need to provide founding or confirming documents for each transfer.
Additionally, Ukrainian producers who export to the EU would be paid on their invoices instantly, as easily as inside the country.
“It really is help for every small and large business, traders, producers, importers and, of course, ordinary people who have so many relatives and dealings with colleagues in Europe,” Kachka adds.

I’ve mailed off my vote in the US midterms. It will be a nail-biting watch, but easier from outside Trump’s America | Eleanor Limprecht
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:35:28 UTC
07:35:28 KST

Recently I made my own envelope out of a sheet of paper and sticky tape, signed it and affixed a sticker. Then I took it to my nearest Australia Post shop in Sydney and mailed it.
In other words, I voted from abroad in the US midterm elections. Because my last place of residence in the US was the state of Virginia, I can register to vote and request a ballot online, but the ballot still needs to be printed, signed, sealed in an envelope made of folded paper, signed again, placed inside another (store-bought) envelope and mailed in. There was no sausage sizzle or cake stall to reward me for my civic duty, and no spectre of a fine if I didn’t complete it.
I give a wide berth to anything resembling a craft project (haunted by the ghosts of Easter hat parades past) but I would cross-stitch a ballot if it lessened the power that President Trump wields over my country of birth. Hell, I would papier-mache an airplane and decoupage a pilot’s licence to deliver my vote in person.
Unfortunately, not everyone is as fervent: voter turnout in the midterm elections in the US is typically less than half the eligible voting population. The midterms are viewed as less important; in-person voting is arduous and inconvenient (with long queues, on a weekday rather than a Saturday) and some voters view state-based elections as secondary to the presidential election.
The current administration is trying to reduce voter turnout even more because things are not looking good for Republican candidates. They have gerrymandered, sued the state of California for refusing to disenfranchise 20,000 voters, tried to restrict mail-in voting (this was blocked by the supreme court) and already made a challenge to Alaska’s Senate election results if the incumbent Republican senator Dan Sullivan does not win.
Can you smell it from here? That’s not raw sewage overflow from the recent heavy rains, that’s Trump’s fear.
Democrats only need three seats to gain majority in the House of Representatives and four to gain majority in the Senate. If the Democrats control Congress it will be far more difficult for Trump to get his laws through. They could create committees to investigate the president and even begin an impeachment trial.
Trump’s egregiously named Operation Epic Fury has caused the price of fuel to skyrocket and most Americans (two-thirds) now view the ongoing war against Iran as a mistake. As the price of fuel goes up, Trump’s approval rating sinks. (His dismantling of democracy and campaign of disinformation didn’t seem to disturb voters in the same way that this hit to the hip pocket does.)
I am cautiously hopeful. I’ve spent the past two years wishing I was Canadian and rushing to turn off the radio or television at the sound of Trump’s hyperbole. Perfecting my simultaneous sigh and shrug when people hear my accent and ask me to explain how and why the bully-in-chief was re-elected.
But I keep recalling the awful events of 6 January 2021, when in the wake of a Trump rally, an angry rightwing mob attacked the US Capitol building after his defeat in the 2020 elections. Five people died and 174 police officers were injured while the rest of the world watched in horror. As a child in Arlington, Virginia, I visited those rotundas and chambers on field trips. As an adult here in Australia, I worried over friends and family who live and work in Washington DC. If the Republican candidates are defeated in these elections, will the administration accept the results?
There are three million Americans who live abroad and more than 110,000 here in Australia (around 60% of us have Australian citizenship). It will be nail-biting to watch the 3 November midterm elections, but easier from afar than from within Trump’s America: a country where immigrants are endangered, abortion rights have been eroded, artificial intelligence has grown without regulation and foreign aid, environmental protections and domestic social services have been gutted. Even Trump’s tariffs are backfiring for the United States, uniting the countries they are aimed against, such as Canada. Elbows up!
These midterms, I am hopeful it will be a win for democracy rather than dictatorship, for peace rather than war, and humanity rather than hubris.
Just please, whatever happens, don’t ask me to explain the electoral college come 2028.

New taxes in Russia fuel tensions between Kremlin and big business – intelligence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

New taxes in Russia fuel tensions between Kremlin and big business – intelligence
Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service reported this on Telegram, according to Ukrinform.
"Alexander Shokhin, president of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs (RSPP), has approached Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin with proposals to amend tax bills before their second reading. Businesses believe the new rules will increase the tax burden and break the promise to maintain stable tax conditions until 2030," the statement said.
The intelligence agency recalled that Russia had previously raised taxes on corporate profits, personal income, and value-added tax (VAT).
"The 'oligarchs' trade union' opposes a 30% tax on excess profits of mining companies. It is expected to bring approximately $8.3 billion into the state budget in 2027-2029. Instead, the RSPP proposes temporarily raising the corporate profit tax from 25% by 0.5-1 percentage point. This could generate between $5.9 billion and more than $11.9 billion in budget revenue," the agency said.
In addition, Russian businesses are demanding that the maximum federal investment tax deduction be increased from 3% to 10-12%, arguing that actual investment in the Russian economy fell by 4.6% in the first half of 2026.
The agency noted that the taxation of passive income is another particular concern for oligarchs.
"According to the RSPP, the combined tax on corporate profits and dividends paid out could reach 42%, reducing the attractiveness of Russian financial instruments and increasing the risk of capital outflows. Businesses propose limiting the higher rates to three years, retaining tax benefits for bank deposits and long-term investments, and indexing tax thresholds to inflation," the Foreign Intelligence Service said.
The agency also reported that the RSPP opposes taxing investment funds at a rate of 15%.
It noted that, with profit margins of 20-30%, taxes could absorb 50-75% of profits.
"Alternatives include taxing income at the investor level or postponing the introduction of the new rules. Businesses are also seeking tax breaks for companies protecting their property against drone attacks, including exemptions from property tax for the relevant facilities and permission to count mandatory spending on critical infrastructure protection twice for tax purposes," the intelligence agency said.
The agency explained that the RSPP's demands highlight the conflict between the state's need to replenish its budget and businesses' ability to finance growth.
"Additional taxes amid declining investment could slow the modernization of enterprises and shrink the future tax base. Unpredictable tax rules also undermine confidence in the government and force companies to postpone long-term projects," the statement said.

UN experts sound alarm at excessive use of force in French student protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:34:51 UTC
07:34:51 KST

UN experts sound alarm at excessive use of force in French student protests
UN experts have condemned police crackdowns, warning they deter demonstrators from exercising their rights.
United Nations experts have expressed alarm at the “excessive use of force” by French authorities in dispersing the recent nationwide student protests.
“The scale of the arrests and detention, affecting several thousand people, mainly minors, appears disproportionate and deters demonstrators from exercising their freedoms of expression and peaceful assembly,” the four experts, mandated by the UN Human Rights Council, said in a statement on Wednesday.
They included Gina Romero, special rapporteur on the freedom of peaceful assembly, and Farida Shaheed, the UN expert on cultural rights.
“Although authorities launched several initiatives to facilitate dialogue and respond to students’ demands in October, the priority given to a primarily security-focused response to the protests has led to the root causes of the mobilisation being sidelined,” the statement said.
France has seen ongoing student protests since mid-September, sparked initially over conditions in high schools, where young people complained about the deteriorating buildings, overcrowded classrooms and teacher absences. Students have also joined nationwide demonstrations to express anger over the rising cost of living, which led to riots and looting on the sidelines.
The French government deployed 70,000 security forces and arrested 1,000 people during demonstrations on Saturday, which drew 410,000 protesters nationwide, France’s Interior Ministry said. A week earlier, public buildings were vandalised, hundreds of businesses were looted and 2,700 people were arrested, with Interior Minister Laurent Nunez vowing to be “extremely vigilant, extremely firm” to quell future unrest.
“What we are seeing right now is a general outburst of resentment against [French President Emmanuel] Macron and his policies that have destroyed our rights, destroyed our living conditions,” Alice Cohen-Morzadec, a spokesperson for the Union Etudiante, told Al Jazeera.
Analysts say the French government has struggled to address students’ demands due to a severe fiscal crisis and planned budget cuts, which have led to a drop in the country’s education budget.
Police response to protests
French authorities have been criticised for their approach to security during some of the protests, and in one case a teenager in the northern city of Lille lost a hand when a grenade exploded as school protesters clashed with police.
“The serious and, in some cases, irreversible injuries sustained by underage demonstrators during law enforcement operations are unacceptable and unjustifiable,” the UN rapporteurs said.
The statement added: “The experts recalled past discussions urging French authorities to undertake a comprehensive review of their policing strategies and practices in order to enable demonstrators to express their concerns and to facilitate a peaceful resolution of social conflicts.”
“The experts are in contact with French authorities on the issue,” the statement concluded.

Libya’s eastern administration bars entry to Iranians, Afghans
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
23:32:35 CET
07:32:35 KST

TRIPOLI, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Libya’s eastern-based government banned the entry of Iranian and Afghan nationals through all land, sea and air ports, the government said late on Wednesday.
The move extends entry restrictions the eastern administration imposed on nationals of four African countries in June, in a country split between rival governments in the east and west since 2014.
The government did not give a reason for the decision.
“The nationals of both Iran and Afghanistan are prohibited from entering Libyan territory through all land, air, and sea ports of entry,” the government said in a statement posted on its verified Facebook page.
It added that the Ministry of Interior would be responsible for implementing the decision and for deporting Iranian and Afghan nationals who do not hold valid residence permits.
Libya has become a transit route for migrants fleeing conflict and poverty to Europe across the Mediterranean since the fall in 2011 of dictator Muammar Gaddafi to a NATO-backed uprising. Factional conflict has split the country since 2014.
The Benghazi-based government of Osama Hamad is allied to military commander Khalifa Haftar, who controls the east and large areas of southern Libya.
The internationally recognized government of Abdulhamid Dbeibah, who came to power through a UN-backed process in 2021, is based in Tripoli.
In June, Hamad’s government banned nationals of African countries – Sudan, Eritrea, Ethiopia and Somalia – citing a ”reorganization of foreign nationals’ entry to Libya”.
The members of accredited diplomatic and consular missions and family members are exempted, the statement said. The same applies to those working in medical and educational professions, provided they have obtained work authorizations.
Libya is home to more than 900,000 migrants, according to UN data collected in June.
(Reporting by Ahmed Elumami; Editing by Sanjeev Miglani)

From the U.S. sanctions list to the G20 table: Moscow says Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will attend talks in Atlanta
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will attend a meeting of G20 foreign ministers in the United States, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
Zakharova said Russia intends to use Lavrov’s visit to advance proposals to strengthen “the foundations of a multipolar world.”
The meeting will take place in Atlanta on October 30–31.
Lavrov has been under U.S. sanctions since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. He has nevertheless visited the United States several times since then to attend U.N. General Assembly sessions.
A summit of G20 heads of state will take place in Miami in mid-December. Russian President Vladimir Putin has been invited. Sources told The Atlantic that U.S. President Donald Trump wants Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to sign a peace agreement at the summit. The Kremlin has yet to confirm Putin’s attendance but has said it is “grateful” for the invitation.

Estonia to Build 150 Military Bunkers Near Russian Border for Baltic Defense Line

Estonia to Build 150 Military Bunkers Near Russian Border for Baltic Defense Line
Estonia’s Defense Minister, Martin Herem, revealed plans to construct roughly 150 military bunkers across the northeastern region of Ida-Viru County.
The construction forms part of the broader Baltic Defense Line initiative, according to ERR on October 28.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Under the current layout, 100 of these structures are designated for state-owned territory, while around 50 will stand on municipal or privately held land.
Placing installations on private real estate requires formal agreements with property owners. Government officials are considering various options to resolve property usage, including financial compensation for inconveniences, land leasing, or outright purchasing of the needed parcels.
“But, according to my information, currently there are no large-scale plans for the state to acquire a wider belt,” Herem added.
Estonia’s bunker project aligns with broader regional efforts, following Finland's completion of a major fencing project along its own border with Russia.
Finland completed roughly 200 kilometers of new fencing along selected sections of its border with Russia as part of a broader effort to harden NATO’s eastern frontier. Launched in 2023, the project cost approximately $413 million and featured a tall metal mesh fence equipped with surveillance cameras, lighting, loudspeakers, and an adjacent patrol road for border guards.
Finnish authorities originally initiated the construction to prevent unauthorized crossings, but the initiative ultimately became part of a wider regional push among northern and eastern European nations to fortify their borders facing Russia and Belarus.

Non-profit group leaks data of more than 40,000 homeland security workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:27:01 UTC
07:27:01 KST

Data identifying more than 41,000 employees and contractors for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) was released on Wednesday in an unprecedented leak that reveals how the agency is organized. The records, which were made public by the transpaency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets reference operation names, surveillance programs and information on undercover initiatives.
DHS did not immediately return a message seeking comment.
The leaked data unveils the names, phone numbers and email addresses of employees from various DHS agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border Protection, Homeland Security Investigations, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.
Most of the agents in the leak – more than 21,000 – work for CBP, and about 6,600 work for ICE.
The data also includes job titles, email groups and other details that show which agents were assigned to special operations, surveillance jobs, computer forensics and undercover work.
It was made public at a time when DHS, in turn, has aggressively sought to unmask critics on social media, and obtain records on protestors and journalists – even as it moves to keep its own agents anonymous, defending agents’ rights to hide their identities and faces while conducting enforcement.
In a statement, Emma Best, a Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder, said the hacktivist known as “maia arson crimew” developed a search tool for the data that would allow the public to browse it. Best said the tool would “replace anonymity with accountability” and empower journalists, guide public records requests and boost congressional oversight.
The Department of Peace did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but in a statement included with the data, it said that DHS employees “have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs” and that it hoped the data “can be used to limit further harm by the DHS and supports all efforts in that direction”.
The disclosure – which the non-profit data transparency group says draws on information obtained by an entity calling itself “Department of Peace” – is the third government data leak to have made headlines in the past month.
In September, the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed the theft of a massive trove of data from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, including sensitive job details and medical information from thousands of bureau employees. Last week, the defense department was hit with a class action lawsuit following a breach that exposed data on millions of current and former military personnel.
The Department of Peace in March claimed responsibility for hacking DHS and posting documents related to contracts with outside vendors.
Best’s statement said Department of Peace harvested the data from the Okta sign-on service used by DHS. Reuters could not immediately corroborate the claim. Okta said in response to a Reuters query: “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised.”
Reuters could not immediately verify the authenticity of the entire data trove but it was able to match personal information of about six DHS employees named in the leak to credit bureau records and breach data carried by the dark web intelligence platform District 4 Labs. In other cases, Reuters called three DHS employees directly and was able to confirm their phone numbers and other details. One said it was the first they had heard of a breach.
In several cases, the data tracked information available on DHS employees’ LinkedIn profiles. But in others, the data revealed nonpublic data about internal DHS organization charts or previously undisclosed programs or operations.

Darfur market strike killed civilians selling food to fighters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:25:56 UTC
07:25:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Strike on Darfur market killed civilians selling food to fighters, witnesses say
Multiple civilian vendors were among the dozens reportedly killed in an attack on a market earlier this week in a poverty-stricken Darfur city in southwestern Sudan, where they had gathered to sell goods to paramilitary fighters, witnesses said Wednesday.
More than 100 people were killed and 113 others were wounded on Monday in a Sudanese military drone strike on a busy market in Nyala, the capital of the South Darfur province, said Emergency Lawyers, a rights group tracking violence. The group said many of those killed and wounded were women and children.
A cigarette vendor told The Associated Press by phone on Wednesday that hundreds of Rapid Support Forces, or RSF, fighters had gathered at the market that evening. He said that he moved his stall between gatherings of the paramilitary fighters to sell cigarettes and that a drone struck around 8 p.m., killing dozens of fighters and women selling food. He spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of reprisals.
Mohamed Didan, the official spokesperson for the Special Operations Forces fighting with the army, wrote on Facebook that more than “150 militia recruits” were killed at the Dumaya camp, west of Nyala, in what he described as a “precise and targeted airstrike.”
The latest attack came as part of the ongoing war between the army and the RSF, which broke out in April 2023, triggering one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, according to aid organizations. The war has killed at least 59,000 people and displaced around 13 million people.
Another witness told the AP that the explosion was massive and killed many fighters. He estimated that around 14 civilians, including women and children, were also killed, most of them women selling tea and food.
The witness, who also spoke on condition of anonymity in fear of reprisals, said that civilians in Nyala often gather wherever fighters congregate to sell food and tea to earn a living amid widespread unemployment and few sources of income.
Final casualty figures from Monday’s attack in Nyala are unconfirmed amid limited information from the city.
Sudan Doctors Network, another group that tracks violence, gave a lower death toll and said that the attack was from shelling. It said in a statement Wednesday that at least 21 people were killed and more than 40 others were wounded. The toll includes civilians.
“The release of this statement was delayed due to difficulties in verifying the information, given the challenges of accessing field documentation sources within Nyala amid ongoing active military operations and security constraints that hinder efforts to monitor and verify the conditions of victims and the injured,” the group said. “The identities of all victims and the circumstances surrounding their presence at the site remain under verification, particularly in the absence of detailed and confirmed casualty lists.”
Doctors Without Borders, which is also known as Médecins Sans Frontières, or MSF, said Tuesday that 36 bodies arrived at its hospital in Nyala and reported seeing 150 wounded in an emergency room. It said 21 of them were wearing civilian clothing.
“Medical staff worked around the clock treating patients, including women and children. They’re all very shaken. The question everyone is asking is ‘Why are markets being targeted? The places where people need to access food, where a lot of civilians gather,’” said Dale Koninckx, MSF project coordinator in Nyala.
The war has pushed some parts of the country into famine. In RSF-controlled Nyala, the share of children seeking treatment for severe acute malnutrition more than doubled between January and August, from five to 11%, according to the latest figures by the United Nations released earlier this month.
Drone warfare has become the deadliest threat to civilians in Sudan’s conflict and both the military and the RSF are being supplied with drones by a number of countries in the Middle East and beyond, experts previously said.
Mubarak Bekheit, an aid worker in Darfur, told the AP by phone on Wednesday that many people remained missing and some bodies had yet to be recovered from homes in the area after the strike hit a civilian neighborhood.
“I personally know that war has no morality, but the reality we witness every day is that civilians are the ones paying the highest price. They lose their lives, their loved ones, and their homes, while living under the constant fear of further bombardment," he said.

Libya's eastern administration bars entry to Iranians, Afghans

Libya's eastern administration bars entry to Iranians, Afghans
TRIPOLI, Oct 28 - Libya’s eastern-based government banned the entry of Iranian and Afghan nationals through all land, sea and air ports, the government said late on Wednesday.
The move extends entry restrictions the eastern administration imposed on nationals of four African countries in June, in a country split between rival governments in the east and west since 2014.
The government did not give a reason for the decision.
"The nationals of both Iran and Afghanistan are prohibited from entering Libyan territory through all land, air, and sea ports of entry," the government said in a statement posted on its verified Facebook page.
It added that the Ministry of Interior would be responsible for implementing the decision and for deporting Iranian and Afghan nationals who do not hold valid residence permits.
Libya has become a transit route for migrants fleeing conflict and poverty to Europe across the Mediterranean since the fall in 2011 of dictator Muammar Gaddafi to a NATO-backed uprising. Factional conflict has split the country since 2014.
The Benghazi-based government of Osama Hamad is allied to military commander Khalifa Haftar, who controls the east and large areas of southern Libya.
The internationally recognized government of Abdulhamid Dbeibah, who came to power through a UN-backed process in 2021, is based in Tripoli.
In June, Hamad's government banned nationals of African countries – Sudan, Eritrea, Ethiopia and Somalia – citing a "reorganization of foreign nationals’ entry to Libya".
The members of accredited diplomatic and consular missions and family members are exempted, the statement said. The same applies to those working in medical and educational professions, provided they have obtained work authorizations.
Libya is home to more than 900,000 migrants, according to UN data collected in June. REUTERS

Proposed Air Canada-United deal likely to harm market competition: regulator
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:18:24 CST
07:18:24 KST

OTTAWA, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- A proposed deal between Air Canada and United Airlines to expand coordination would likely harm competition on key routes between Canada and the United States, Canada's antitrust watchdog warned Wednesday.
In a report submitted to the Minister of Transport, the Competition Bureau said the proposed arrangement between the two carriers would likely increase ticket prices on 10 cross-border routes, resulting in millions of dollars in consumer harm each year.
The proposal would allow Air Canada and United to coordinate on pricing and other operational aspects on these routes connecting four major Canadian hubs, Toronto, Montreal, Ottawa and Vancouver, with U.S. cities including Chicago, Cleveland, Denver, Houston, New York, San Francisco and Washington.
Cooperation on these specific routes is currently restricted under a 2012 consent agreement aimed at protecting market competition.
The regulator noted that Air Canada and United currently account for all non-stop passenger traffic on five of the 10 routes and hold significant combined market shares on the others. ■

UN condemns US embargo of Cuba, but more nations sit out after Trump pressure
The vote was 130-17, with 25 abstentions – a notable decrease in support from last year, when more than 160 nations supported the measure
The UN General Assembly condemned the US economic embargo of Cuba for the 34th year on Wednesday, even as Washington’s campaign to influence the outcome led to a number of countries voting against the resolution or sitting out the decision for the first time.
The vote was 130-17, with 25 abstentions – a notable decrease in support from last year, when more than 160 nations supported the measure and only 12 abstained. While such resolutions at the UN General Assembly are not legally binding, they do reflect world opinion.
For the first time in 34 years, Western countries like Germany, Italy and Latvia were among those that refrained from voting.

Trump’s deal with putin on the supply of Russian diesel did not help lower fuel prices in the US – WSJ
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
00:14:17 EET
07:14:17 KST

Trump’s deal with putin on the supply of Russian diesel did not help lower fuel prices in the US – WSJ
Kyiv • UNN
After Trump’s deal with putin, a gallon of diesel in the US rose to $6.35. Experts doubt its impact due to the small supply volumes.
The agreement between U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian dictator vladimir putin on the supply of Russian diesel fuel had virtually no impact on the American fuel market. Despite the announced deliveries, diesel prices in the United States continued to rise. The Wall Street Journal reports this, writes UNN.
Details
According to the publication, after the agreement was announced, the average price of a gallon of diesel fuel in the United States rose by 7 cents to $6.35.
On October 9, Trump said that russia had agreed to supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the American and global markets. In addition, he announced the delivery of another 500,000 tonnes in November and one million tonnes thereafter.
Analysts doubt the effectiveness of the agreements
Last week, a tanker carrying approximately 300,000 barrels of diesel fuel departed from the Russian port of Primorsk. The vessel was initially bound for New York, but later changed its destination to "for orders," meaning that no specific unloading port was indicated.
Experts doubt that the agreement between Washington and moscow will be able to significantly affect fuel prices. They cite the condition of Russian oil refineries and the existing restrictions on petroleum product exports among the main obstacles.
In addition, the planned delivery volumes remain relatively small. According to analysts' estimates, they will amount to slightly more than 100,000 barrels per day in October and about 125,000 in November.
By comparison, just a year ago, russia exported approximately 800,000 barrels of diesel fuel per day.
Thus, even the implementation of the agreements announced by Trump does not guarantee lower prices at American gas stations, as the volumes of Russian exports are significantly below previous levels.

Rail safety questioned after Spain suffers second fatal high-speed train crash in a year

Rail safety questioned after Spain suffers second fatal high-speed train crash in a year
Questions are being raised about Spain's rail safety as authorities launch an official investigation into the cause of Wednesday's high-speed train collision, which killed at least 68 people and wounded around 100 more, in the country's second fatal rail crash this year.
At least 68 people died when a Spanish high-speed express slammed into a stationary train on Wednesday, with rescuers scouring mangled carriages for more bodies after Spain's second fatal rail crash this year and Europe's deadliest since 2013.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said "all of Spain" was in mourning after the collision, which the transport minister said happened after a Renfe service was authorised to proceed despite an active red signal due to a stationary train ahead.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Oscar Puente told reporters in Madrid that the red signal was issued due to a computer communications failure, which automatically stopped traffic, but an erroneous decision was then taken to restart the Renfe train.
Sanchez said in a televised address from near the site south of Madrid that the "terrible tragedy" would be investigated and vowed to address any failures that came to light, adding that the causes of the two crashes appeared to be unrelated.
Read moreSpain to observe three days of mourning after scores killed in high-speed train collision
"If we need to further strengthen safety in order to rebuild confidence in our high-speed rail system, we will do so, because what is unacceptable for a country like Spain is to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year," Sanchez said.
Spain's opposition People's Party said it had cancelled all campaign events for the day, ahead of elections next month.
Trapped among seats
At the scene in rural Castilla-La Mancha, ambulances, funeral home vans and helicopters assembled beside one of the trains on an elevated stretch of track, while twisted metal and wreckage lay scattered down an embankment where at least three carriages had plunged.
The head of the regional government, Emiliano García-Page, said the death toll had risen to 68, while rescuers searching for other victims as darkness fell did not know if other fatalities would be discovered once the carriages were moved.
Passengers, some splattered with blood or bandaged, were evacuated along a nearby road after the crash, which Spain's health minister, Monica Garcia, said had injured 80 people, 15 of them very seriously. Salvador Arriza described the chaos in his carriage.
"I was very close to the door, but (other passengers) were breaking the windows to be able to get out. Some people practically couldn't move because they were trapped amongst the seats," said the 62-year-old.
Investigation under way
The disaster, the deadliest train accident in Europe since a 2013 derailment in Spain's Santiago de Compostela in which 80 people died, follows another fatal accident in January involving high-speed trains operated by the same companies on the same line, in which 46 people died.
In that collision, a train derailed and smashed into an oncoming train, prompting a debate over investment in railway maintenance.
Renfe said on Wednesday that after being authorised to continue its journey, its train had crashed into the Iryo train that had remained stationary "for reasons we don't know".
"The Renfe train continued on its way as instructed, and a collision occurred. The exact sequence of events, the traffic conditions and the circumstances of the impact will have to be established by the investigation," Renfe said in a statement.
Iryo, which said it had activated emergency protocols, and state-owned infrastructure operator Adif did not respond to requests for comment.
Passengers sent flying
A Castilla-La Mancha government spokesperson said 147 people were on board the Iryo train and 397 on the Renfe service when the collision occurred at about 9am (0800 GMT), derailing two Iryo carriages.
Passenger Rafael Barcelo said he felt lucky as he had stepped away from his seat for a coffee, adding there had been at least eight victims from his carriage.
"We were having breakfast, drinking a coffee when we felt a very strong impact and we were sent flying," he said.
At a school in Urda where relatives had been directed, a woman who gave her name as Ana fought back tears as she said there was still no news of her husband, Pepe. His name was not among those identified, although police had found their dog, Trece.
Renfe said it had opened a special line for families of victims. The railway operator said it had suspended ticket sales on the Madrid-Andalusia high-speed corridor until December 13.
Maintenance spending
A preliminary Civil Guard report in February pointed to defects in the track, rail or a weld between two sections of track as the leading theory behind January's accident, though investigators kept seven other possibilities open.
Spain's railway safety authority has reported that accidents, including derailments and collisions, increased from 45 in 2016 to 57 in 2024 and 69 last year.
A Reuters analysis of data from the Spanish competition authority showed some 25 million passengers used a high-speed train in Spain in the first half of 2026, a drop of around 14% compared with the same period last year.
Meanwhile, European Commission data shows Spain's maintenance investment in its roughly 4,000km (2,485 miles) of high-speed lines has lagged other large European countries.
Although Spain spent an average of about €1.5 billion a year on its high-speed network between 2018 and 2022, more than any other European country, most of that money went toward new construction. Only about 16% was earmarked for maintenance, renewals and upgrades.
Only recently did Spain open its rail network to private companies to compete against RENFE. The Italian-owned IRYO started operating in Spain in 2022.
A spokesperson for Spain’s train workers’ union, Joan Rodríguez, said increased traffic brought by privatization has put extra strain on rail infrastructure.
“We are not convinced that the liberalisation of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines,” Rodríguez told TVE on Wednesday. “I am not saying it was a determining factor (in the crashes), but yes, the increase in use of the network is a factor to keep in mind.”
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters and AP)

Police have completed the investigation into Hayden Panettiere’s death and named the official cause
Kyiv • UNN
Hayden Panettiere’s death was ruled an accident. Forensic experts detected the toxic effects of fentanyl and four other substances.
American police have completed an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the death of 36-year-old actress Hayden Panettiere, known for the series "Heroes" and "Nashville." Law enforcement concluded that her death was the result of an accident linked to the toxic effects of several substances. E! News reports this, citing the police department in Greenville, South Carolina, UNN writes.
Details
Police confirmed that the case was officially closed two months after the actress's death; she was found unconscious in a rented house on August 16.
Based on the medical examiner's findings and the results of the investigation, Hayden Panettiere's death was ruled an accident. The Greenville Police Department has concluded its investigation
What the medical examiners established
According to the Greenville County coroner's report, the actress's death was caused by the toxic effects of fentanyl and four other substances. These included 4-ANPP, alprazolam, methocarbamol, and quetiapine.
During a search of the house, investigators also found blue pills that mimicked prescription medications. Analysis confirmed that they contained fentanyl. In addition, law enforcement found a white powder in a sunglasses case.
According to police reports, on August 16, the actress's boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach called emergency services after finding Panettiere unconscious. Medics determined that she was in cardiac arrest, and at 2:32 p.m. officially confirmed her death.
The actress had previously spoken openly about her struggles with alcohol and opioid addiction. In her 2026 memoir "This Is Me: Reckoning," she recalled that a doctor had warned her of a serious threat to her life if she did not stop drinking alcohol.

Pentagon puts Iran war bill at $47B as midterm election pressure mounts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:06:18 UTC
07:06:18 KST

The cost of the Iran war to American taxpayers has grown to $47.1 billion, according to a fresh Pentagon assessment submitted to Congress, intensifying political fallout ahead of pivotal midterm elections as President Donald Trump leaves open the prospect of renewed hostilities.
The figures compiled by US Central Command, valid as of October 16, provide the most comprehensive accounting of expenditure since military offensives began in late February alongside Israel.
The sum reflects a $3.5 billion rise in spending since early September, when total costs stood at approximately $43.6 billion.
The economic strain of the conflict and its impact on domestic energy markets threaten Republican candidates facing voters on Tuesday to determine control of Congress.
Although Trump initially pledged an engagement lasting only weeks, he has flagged potential new strikes post-election while dispatching a third aircraft carrier and thousands of troops to the region.
Munitions depletion
The mounting expenditure has sparked sharp resistance on Capitol Hill, where the White House is seeking approval for a $1.5 trillion national defence budget alongside a $95 billion package supporting Middle East operations.
Replacing depleted munitions represents the single largest expenditure, absorbing roughly $29 billion.
Advanced defensive interceptors—principally for Patriot and THAAD batteries—account for the bulk of replenishment costs, with individual Patriot interceptors costing millions of dollars.
Direct operational activity totals $11.9 billion, whilst equipment destruction accounts for $6 billion.
Branch tallies list Air Force costs at $7.6 billion, Army expenses exceeding $2 billion, and Navy expenditure at $1.45 billion.
Official records list 21 American service personnel dead—18 from enemy strikes, aircraft crashes, or drone disposal—and 865 wounded, with the assessment omitting physical structural damage sustained across regional bases.
