NEW DELHI: Striking a discordant note among a clutch of petitions challenging the Transgender Amendment Act for denying right to gender self-determination, an all-women NGO Wednesday appealed to the Supreme Court not to confer trans-women, biological males identifying as females, the spectrum of constitutional rights guaranteed to biological women.‘Women’s Declaration International India’ through senior advocate Amit Sibal told a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana that “self-professed or socio-cultural gender identity or certificate or document cannot change a person’s biological sex or enable a biological male to access the entire spectrum of rights, protections and entitlements created specifically for biological females.” Differentiating between sex and gender, the petitioner said, “Sex and gender identity are distinct; gender identity concerns a person’s deeply felt internal experience, while sex is the stable immutable biological category on which numerous constitutional and statutory protections for women are premised.”SC asked Centre to respond to the petition with a comprehensive affidavit that also dealt with the other petitions challenging the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Act, 2026.
SG Tushar Mehta said a comprehensive affidavit is being drafted but gave an indication of what would be govt’s stand in defence of the erasure of gender self-determination clause, which was replaced by medically determined gender.He asked: “Can a transwoman be permitted to compete in a sporting event for women? Should a policewoman conduct physical search of a person with male genitals but perceives himself to be a woman? If a biologically male criminal perceives himself to be a woman, should police be barred from arresting him after sunset?”
Drawing the court’s attention to a recent incident in the US relating to a transgender inmate, who perceives himself to be a woman but impregnated two women inmates, Mehta said several aspects needed to be kept in mind while adjudicating the petitions.A male becoming a trans-woman will violate affirmative measures for women under the Constitution, equal opportunity to women in employment, women’s bodily privacy and personal security in sex-segregated spaces and criminal law safeguards, the petitioner said.

China Developing More On-Orbit Space Weapons: New Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:03:19 UTC
07:03:19 KST

China is expanding the arsenal of counter-space weapons it could use in a potential conflict with the U.S., to include on-orbit systems, according to a new report from the Defense Intelligence Agency.
The DIA released the third edition of its “Challenges to Security in Space” report Oct. 26, following on 2022 and 2019 versions. Among its findings, it noted that China “is developing space-based technology, including on-orbit counterspace weapons, capable of holding space systems at risk.”
Specifically, the report repeats previous warnings that China has ground-based laser weapons that can “disrupt, degrade, or destroy” satellites in low-Earth orbit but then goes further in adding that, by the late 2020s, “China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits.”
Directed energy weapons could include anything from microwaves to high-powered lasers—the most common at this point are lasers that can “dazzle” satellites with electro-optical sensors.
The new report also goes beyond previous versions in stating that the People’s Liberation Army’s electronic warfare jamming systems “include a combination of ground-based and on-orbit systems that enable it to leverage a variety of options during a conflict.” It’s the first time DIA has noted the existence of on-orbit jammers.
DIA also states definitively that Chinese firms are developing electronic jammers for the People’s Liberation Army to target synthetic aperture radar, “including military reconnaissance platforms.” The agency’s 2022 report only said China was “probably” developing such a capability, which may prove pivotal given the Space Force’s push to field hundreds of new targeting satellites to track objects on the ground and in the air.
The new report also notes that the Chinese military “probably intends to deploy additional [anti-satellite] missiles that can destroy satellites in low, medium, and high orbits”—previously, the agency had only said China “probably intends to pursue” such weapons. It highlights recent developments with mysterious Chinese satellites maneuvering within 10 kilometers of other nations’ satellites in geosynchronous orbit.
“These close approaches to foreign spacecraft are largely inconsistent with the stated mission of the satellites, suggesting China may have obfuscated their true mission,” the report states.
Taken together, the DIA’s findings reinforce what then-Chief of Space Operations Gen. B. Chance Saltzman told reporters in 2025: that China is pursuing new capabilities across what he calls the six types of counterspace weapons, three in orbit and three terrestrial:
- Kinetic, destructive weapons;
- Directed energy; and
- Radio frequency energy and jamming.
The new DIA report’s focus on on-orbit weapons follows closely on the Space Force’s own acknowledgement for the first time that it has on-orbit weapons for “space control,” something leaders revealed at this September’s AFA conference.
The report also includes a rare image of China’s experimental space plane, a mysterious system often compared to the Space Force’s X-37B orbital test vehicle. The image, captured by a commercial Maxar satellite, shows the Chinese spacecraft’s shape is not unlike the X-37.
“Spaceplanes are … reusable and feature enhanced maneuverability, making them more suitable for certain missions than traditional satellites,” the DIA report states, noting that the Chinese space plane has released, maneuvered around, and rendezvoused with other satellites during its time in orbit.
Besides China, the 2026 report also noted expanded counter-space activities by less advanced adversaries like Iran and North Korea.
Iran in particular has used jammers to disrupt satellite communications and navigation signals around the Strait of Hormuz, according to the report, and during Operation Epic Fury, both the U.S. and Iran “took offensive actions against each others’ space capabilities to degrade and disrupt military actions on both sides.” Pentagon and Space Force officials have claimed they have achieved “space superiority” in the conflict but have not detailed Iran’s efforts in space.
North Korea, meanwhile, managed to successfully launch a reconnaissance satellite into orbit in 2023, and “may also be developing jammers effective against military GPS signals,” according to the report.

Details
According to the publication, approximately 100 defensive structures are planned to be located on state-owned land, while another 50 will be placed on plots owned by municipalities or private individuals.

Estonia is also stepping up military training for young people
Alongside the development of defense infrastructure, the Estonian authorities plan to pay greater attention to preparing young people for national security issues.
As Martin Herem reported, Estonia’s Ministry of Defense has approved a new youth policy designed for the next four years.
The document provides for expanding the teaching of topics related to national defense in the school curriculum. In particular, students are to be taught the basics of operating drones.
Thus, Estonia intends to simultaneously strengthen its defensive positions on the border with Russia and raise the younger generation’s level of awareness in the areas of security and defense.

brazilian studio rótulo em branco turns oversized nails into sculptural steel tables
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:01:14 UTC

brazilian studio rótulo em branco turns oversized nails into sculptural steel tables
designed by ingrid sani lang, the prego collection reimagines construction nails as stainless-steel side, coffee, and bar tables with interchangeable heads.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
OVERSIZED NAILS BECOME SCULPTURAL FURNITURE
A nail is usually meant to hold things together, not become the center of attention. Brazilian design studio Rótulo em Branco turns that logic on its head with PREGO, a collection of sculptural stainless-steel tables inspired by the familiar construction fastener. Designed by architect Ingrid Sani Lang, the series translates the nail’s recognizable silhouette into three furniture typologies: a side table, a coffee table, and a bar table. Through an exaggerated shift in scale, an ordinary industrial component takes on an entirely different role in the domestic interior.
Founded in 2021 in Blumenau, southern Brazil, Rótulo em Branco approaches furniture as an opportunity to reconsider familiar objects and their functions. With PREGO, the studio explores what happens when an everyday element is removed from its original context and reimagined through proportion, material, and use. Rather than producing a literal oversized replica, the designer adapts the nail’s geometry to create functional surfaces with a sculptural presence. The collection retains the simplicity of its industrial reference while introducing an unexpected relationship between construction hardware and contemporary furniture.
INTERCHANGEABLE NAIL HEADS INTRODUCE PLAYFUL FUNCTIONALITY
Beyond its distinctive silhouette, PREGO incorporates a system of removable and interchangeable nail heads, allowing the tables to accommodate different uses. Two versions are available: a smooth surface designed to hold everyday objects and a sculpted alternative featuring recessed details. The latter can accommodate smaller items and introduce additional functions, including uses associated with incense. Both designs maintain the recognizable shape of the original object while giving the user a choice in how the furniture operates.
The interchangeable components introduce an element of interaction into what might otherwise remain a purely sculptural exercise. Users can switch between the two heads depending on their needs, allowing the same piece to move between different domestic arrangements. This flexibility challenges the idea of furniture as an object with one permanent configuration, while the familiar nail shape adds a small dose of visual irony. After all, the very component normally used to fix things in place becomes the part designed to be removed.
STAINLESS STEEL AND LOCAL PRODUCTION SHAPE PREGO COLLECTION
The collection is manufactured from AISI 304 stainless steel, combining a brushed finish on the main structure with polished surfaces on the nail-shaped elements. This contrast emphasizes the geometry of each piece, allowing the industrial material to take on a more expressive character. All three table typologies are developed and produced in southern Brazil, where Rótulo em Branco works with regional manufacturers. The studio’s involvement throughout fabrication, material selection, and finishing keeps the production process closely connected to its design practice.
PREGO was launched in collaboration with Nowdays, a Brazilian digital platform connected to contemporary internet culture, bringing the collection into a dialogue that extends beyond conventional furniture design. The partnership reflects Rótulo em Branco’s interest in objects that engage with visual culture and challenge familiar domestic conventions. Positioned somewhere between functional furniture and sculpture, the series finds new possibilities in one of construction’s most unassuming components. A nail may be a rather modest starting point, but here it has considerably bigger ambitions.

Beautiful landscapes may briefly put the brakes on the brain’s movement system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:00:53 UTC
07:00:53 KST

People tend to react slightly more slowly after viewing landscape photographs they find appealing, and their brains show weaker signs of getting ready to move, according to new research published in Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience. By recording electrical signals from the scalp while volunteers viewed nature scenes, the researchers found that images people liked more were linked to dampened movement-preparation signals alongside brain rhythms associated with heightened visual engagement. These findings suggest that experiencing beauty may prompt the brain to temporarily shift its resources away from physical action so it can focus more fully on taking in sensory details.
When people encounter an arresting view, such as a mountain range or a striking painting, they often feel momentarily transfixed. Psychologists refer to the mental and emotional evaluation of such sensory experiences as aesthetic appreciation. A central question in neuroscience is how this state of appreciation interacts with motor inhibition, which is the process the brain uses to suppress or hold back physical movement and the preparation to act.
Early brain-scanning research into how people respond to visual art pointed to an intriguing relationship between beauty and the brain regions that control body movement. For instance, a 2004 brain-imaging study found that looking at paintings rated as ugly triggered stronger activity in the motor cortex than looking at paintings rated as beautiful, which some researchers have interpreted as an urge to move away from unpleasant images. A few years later, the authors of a 2007 theoretical paper argued from a different angle that appreciating art actively engages the brain’s movement circuits, proposing that viewers mentally simulate the physical actions, gestures, or brushstrokes depicted in an artwork.
More recent neuroscientific frameworks have sought to reconcile how beauty affects the balance between perceiving the world and acting within it. In a 2020 review, researchers advanced what they call the “Stopping for Knowledge” hypothesis, arguing that the sense of beauty acts as a signal for the brain to temporarily halt physical action so it can redirect its limited processing power toward absorbing new information from the environment. Although earlier experiments using musical chords hinted that pleasant sounds can slow down button presses, researchers had not yet directly tested whether viewing preferred images suppresses the brain’s step-by-step preparation for physical movement.
To examine how visual appreciation affects physical readiness and brain activity, Paolo Barbieri and Irene Ronga of the BraIn Plasticity and behaviour changes Group in the Department of Psychology at the University of Turin and their colleagues, two of whom proposed the “Stopping for Knowledge” hypothesis, conducted two laboratory experiments to test it. The researchers examined whether looking at subjectively appealing photographs would slow down a person’s subsequent physical reactions and dampen the electrical brain signals that build up right before a movement takes place.
“The study was motivated by a theoretical hypothesis about motor inhibition that has received relatively little empirical attention, particularly in the visual domain,” study author Paolo Barbieri told PsyPost. “The idea is that temporarily inhibiting our tendency to act may allow us to focus more fully on a stimulus, giving us the time and resources needed to extract information and process it more thoroughly. We wanted to investigate whether aesthetic appreciation might be associated with this kind of temporary decoupling between perception and action.”
For their experiments, the researchers assembled a collection of 180 black-and-white photographs of natural landscapes, including mountains and seashores. They standardized all the photographs for brightness, contrast, resolution, dimensions, and color spectrum so that basic visual differences would not skew how participants reacted. In the first experiment, 30 right-handed young adults (17 women, with an average age of about 25) sat 80 centimeters from a computer monitor and viewed a random selection of 100 landscape photos one at a time.
Each trial in the first experiment began with a small cross in the center of the screen for 1.5 to 2.5 seconds, followed by a landscape photograph displayed for a random duration between 5 and 6 seconds. Varying the display time prevented participants from predicting the exact moment the image would vanish. Participants were instructed to look at the landscape and press the spacebar as fast as possible the instant the photograph disappeared, and then they had up to 3 seconds to rate how much they liked the image on a scale from 1 (least appreciated) to 9 (most appreciated). On 5 percent of the trials, a static white-noise image appeared instead of a landscape, serving as a check to ensure participants were paying attention and withholding their button presses when instructed.
Before analyzing reaction times, the researchers filtered out trials where participants failed to respond, pressed the key in less than 100 milliseconds, or reacted unusually slowly (removing about 8 percent of trials overall). For each participant, they compared reaction times following the roughly 25 highest-rated landscapes, which received an average score of 7.76 out of 9, against the 25 lowest-rated landscapes, which averaged a score of 3.06.
The results showed that participants reacted more slowly after viewing photographs they found appealing, taking an average of 297 milliseconds to press the spacebar after preferred images compared to 288 milliseconds after non-preferred images. This 9-millisecond slowdown represents roughly a 3.1 percent increase in reaction time, corresponding to a medium-sized statistical effect within participants.
To understand what happens in the brain during this brief delay, the researchers recruited a separate group of 20 right-handed young adults (10 women, with an average age of 25) for a second experiment using electroencephalography (EEG). This technique uses a cap fitted with small sensors on the scalp to measure electrical activity generated by the brain down to the millisecond. Participants completed four blocks of 80 trials, viewing the same set of 80 landscape images four times across the session, with each photo displayed for a fixed duration of 5 seconds.
Instead of reacting to the disappearance of the photograph, participants in the second experiment waited for a colored circle, acting like a traffic light, to appear on the screen right after the landscape vanished. When a green circle appeared, which happened on 75 percent of the trials (240 target trials per person), participants had to press the spacebar as quickly as possible and then rate the photograph on the 1-to-9 scale. When a red circle appeared on the remaining 25 percent of trials, they had to hold back their button press. Keeping the viewing time fixed at 5 seconds before the traffic light cue appeared allowed the scientists to track how the brain prepared to make a movement while the participant was still looking at the landscape.
The behavioral results of the second experiment echoed those of the first. Participants rated their top cluster of roughly 80 preferred trials at an average of 7.56 and their bottom cluster of 80 non-preferred trials at 3.54, and they were once again slower to press the spacebar after looking at preferred landscapes. Average reaction times were 504 milliseconds following preferred images compared to 497 milliseconds following non-preferred images, a 7-millisecond delay (or about 1.4 percent slower) that reflected a medium statistical effect. Overall reaction times were about 200 milliseconds longer in the second experiment than in the first, likely because participants had to identify the color of the traffic light before deciding whether to respond.
When the researchers examined the EEG recordings, they focused first on the readiness potential, a slow buildup of negative electrical voltage across the front and central areas of the scalp that naturally begins one to two seconds before a person performs a physical action. Larger readiness potentials generally indicate stronger preparation to move and tend to accompany faster reaction times. During the final moments of viewing preferred landscapes, specifically between 73 and 14 milliseconds before the traffic light cue appeared, this electrical buildup was noticeably smaller than when participants viewed non-preferred landscapes.
This dampening of movement-related brain activity continued even after the green traffic light appeared on the screen. Electrical brain responses linked to evaluating the green cue (occurring between 290 and 470 milliseconds after the light appeared) and physically executing the key press (between 660 and 1,010 milliseconds) were also reduced following preferred photographs. When the authors analyzed all trials individually without grouping them into categories, they found a consistent relationship across the entire rating scale: the higher a participant rated a specific landscape, the weaker their brain’s movement-preparation and execution signals tended to be.
“One of the reviewers suggested an additional analysis examining the relationship between aesthetic appreciation and neural responses on a trial-by-trial basis,” Barbieri explained. “Initially, I thought the effect might be driven mainly by the contrast between highly appreciated and poorly appreciated images, with intermediate ratings potentially obscuring the relationship. I was genuinely surprised to find that our brain responses were modulated so precisely and parametrically by our subjective preferences.”
In a final step, the team analyzed how the power of rhythmic brain waves, measured in cycles per second (hertz), shifted over time. They looked closely at alpha waves (8 to 12 hertz), which typically drop in power when the visual areas of the brain are actively focused on processing sights, and beta waves (roughly 20 to 33 hertz), which tend to surge in power when the brain is actively holding back physical movement. About two seconds before the traffic light cue appeared, viewing preferred landscapes produced both a steeper drop in alpha wave power and a stronger surge in beta wave power compared to viewing non-preferred landscapes, followed by another beta wave increase roughly 410 to 460 milliseconds after the cue. The authors interpret these rhythmic patterns as a sign that appealing images heighten visual attention while putting the brakes on motor planning.
“I think our findings offer an interesting perspective on how perception and the motor system bidirectionally interact,” Barbieri said. “They suggest that when we engage with something we appreciate, our tendency to act immediately may slow down, allowing us to focus on and explore what is in front of us. More broadly, this raises the possibility that a mindset oriented toward learning, exploration, and change may benefit from temporarily stepping away from more immediate, pragmatic goals.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. First, the reaction time delays observed after viewing preferred images were only 7 to 9 milliseconds on average. The effect is subtle, and the motor system is not shut off during aesthetic experiences. As the authors point out, holding back outward movement can happen at the same time that a viewer mentally simulates actions on the inside, and dynamic art forms like dance performances or energetic paintings may engage the motor system differently than calm black-and-white nature photographs.
“The differences in reaction times were small, amounting to fractions of a second,” Barbieri noted. “At first glance, this might seem to have little practical significance. However, perception–action cycles occur continuously throughout our daily lives, second after second. Even small shifts in how these cycles unfold may accumulate over time and reflect qualitatively different ways of engaging with the world.”
The laboratory setup also differs from how people usually experience art and nature in the real world. Viewing standardized grayscale photographs on a computer screen for five seconds at a time, and seeing the same images repeated four times across the second experiment, does not capture the complexity or emotional depth of walking through an art gallery or standing in front of a real landscape. In addition, the experiments tested relatively small groups of 30 and 20 young adults, so future studies with larger and more diverse samples will be helpful to confirm how broadly these patterns apply.
Because preference was based on participants’ own ratings rather than assigned by the researchers, the comparisons show how reactions varied alongside liking rather than proving that liking itself caused the slowdown. Other qualities of the favored images could also have played a role, despite the researchers’ efforts to standardize basic visual features.
“An important point is that aesthetic appreciation was measured through subjective ratings, independently of the images’ features,” Barbieri added. “In other words, we were interested in how much participants personally appreciated each image, rather than assuming that certain visual properties are inherently more beautiful than others. Our findings therefore concern the relationship between individual aesthetic preferences and motor responses, rather than a universal response to objectively beautiful images.”
Finally, although the brain wave recordings suggest that participants paid closer visual attention to preferred images while suppressing movement preparation, the experiments did not directly measure whether participants actually learned or remembered more information from those scenes. Alpha and beta brain waves are broad signals that can reflect several overlapping mental processes during a task, and future work will also need to explore how split-second, automatic impressions of beauty compare to deliberate ratings over longer periods of time.
“My next goal is to bring together different aspects of this framework within a single experiment,” Barbieri said. “In particular, I would like to investigate whether the decoupling between perception and action is accompanied by a greater predisposition to learn from and attend to the surrounding environment. This would help us understand whether motor inhibition is part of a broader state that facilitates exploration and information gathering.”
“More broadly, this study is part of a research program that views aesthetic experience as a possible way of navigating sensory uncertainty through curiosity rather than anxiety,” Barbieri concluded. “When we encounter something unfamiliar or unpredictable, we may experience uncertainty as a source of discomfort, or we may become curious and motivated to explore it. We are interested in understanding how aesthetic experiences might facilitate the latter response, fostering an openness to new information and learning. This perspective is also explored in our previous work.”
The study, “The gentle grip of beauty: Neural bases of motor inhibition during aesthetic appreciation,” was authored by Paolo Barbieri, Jacopo Frascaroli, Greta Varesio, Francesca Piovesan, Ludovico Bechis, Pietro Sarasso, and Irene Ronga.

Moscow and the Moscow region are under a massive drone attack; flights have been restricted at airports, and planes from Turkey have been turned back
Kyiv • UNN
Due to the massive drone attack, flights have been restricted at Moscow's airports. Two planes from Turkey returned to their departure airports.
On the evening of October 28, Moscow and the Moscow region came under a massive drone attack. Due to the threat of strikes, the Russian authorities imposed restrictions on the operation of the capital’s airports, while two passenger planes traveling from Turkey to Moscow were forced to turn back. This was reported by Russian media outlets, including TASS and ASTRA, UNN writes.
Details
According to TASS, citing air traffic control services, the Federal Air Transport Agency temporarily restricted the reception and departure of aircraft at Vnukovo, Domodedovo, and Zhukovsky airports. Approximately an hour later, the restrictions at Zhukovsky were lifted, while the other two airports continued to receive aircraft only with approval.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that Russian air defense had allegedly already shot down 57 drones heading toward the Russian capital. An air raid alert was declared in the Moscow region at approximately 10:00 p.m.
A series of explosions reported near Moscow
Meanwhile, readers of ASTRA reported at least three explosions near Naro-Fominsk, approximately 56 kilometers from the Moscow Ring Road.
According to local residents, they did not hear the characteristic sound of drones before the explosions. At the same time, they said that explosions were heard one after another from the direction of the neighboring Kaluga region.
Amid the attack, two passenger planes operating flights from Turkey to Moscow changed course and returned to their departure airports because of restrictions at Vnukovo.
There is currently no information about possible strikes, damage, or casualties. The Russian authorities’ statements regarding the number of drones shot down have not been independently confirmed.

Ukraine seeks European partners’ help with buses and generators, Bezgin says

Ukraine seeks European partners’ help with buses and generators, Bezgin says
Vitalii Bezgin, Ukraine’s Minister for Communities, Territories and Internally Displaced Persons, told an Ukrinform correspondent on the sidelines of the 51st session of the Council of Europe’s Congress of Local and Regional Authorities in Strasbourg.
“Representatives of Spain have already expressed their readiness to help under existing interregional agreements. We discussed buses, and they are ready to provide them. We also discussed generator deliveries. The basis for such assistance could be the agreements Catalonia signed with three Ukrainian regions earlier this autumn. These are memorandums with Zaporizhzhia, Dnipropetrovsk, and Lviv regions,” Bezgin said.
According to him, regional transport needs are growing because of continued Russian attacks. “In Kherson alone, losses of municipal vehicles amount to two per day,” he said.
The ministry also aims to expand direct partnerships between Ukrainian regions and regions in Council of Europe member states.
Bezgin identified French regions as active partners, highlighting their cooperation with Kharkiv region. In particular, the Kharkiv Regional Council has a partnership with France’s Grand Est region, through which communities receive generators among other assistance.
At the same time, Bezgin said eastern regions have fewer partnerships because of more complicated logistics.
“Our communities and regions have established the most ties with Poland, while cooperation with Czechia, Slovakia, and Austria needs to be intensified. Another effective mechanism we are proposing here is for partner countries to take responsibility for supporting the recovery of specific regions. There are already examples: Estonia’s support for Zhytomyr region, Denmark’s for Mykolaiv region, and Belgium’s for Chernihiv region,” he said.
In return, Ukraine offers partners its own expertise, particularly in defense technologies and the management of territories during combat operations.
According to Bezgin, European representatives are interested in meeting directly with Ukrainian manufacturers to discuss investment opportunities and business development.
There is also demand for practical experience in local self-government during wartime. Bezgin said a delegation of 16 Lithuanian mayors had recently sought information on legislative preparations, reserve formation, and the organization of community governance in the event of military threats. Other Baltic states, Finland, Poland, and Norway have shown similar interest, he added.
“We also plan to present a dedicated section on managing territories in active combat zones at the next Ukraine Recovery Conference, URC 2027, in Tallinn,” Bezgin said.
As Ukrinform previously reported, following the publication of Unbreakable Kherson, the Kherson Regional Military Administration plans to publish three more thematic guides compiling the experience of Ukraine’s regions and relevant ministries in keeping communities functioning during the war.

Promised discharge, but no trust: Why Ukraine’s new military contracts are struggling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:57:11 UTC
06:57:11 KST

Ukraine has offered its soldiers a fixed term and a guaranteed way home under new contracts to encourage more people to enlist. However, in more than four months, only about 8,600 have signed, a drop in the ocean for a force of around a million, Ukrainska Pravda reports.
The system, launched on 15 June 2026 as an experimental government project, lets soldiers sign for a fixed term for the first time: infantry-assault contracts of 6 to 14 months, and combat and base contracts of two years, each ending in a guaranteed discharge and a deferral from re-mobilization.
That guarantee was meant to draw people in, but many soldiers, even some who signed, do not believe the state will let them go when their term ends.
Soldiers don’t trust the way out
The most common answer soldiers give is flat: “I don’t believe that after the contract ends I will really be able to leave and get a deferral.”
The doubt has history: officials have promised fixed service terms since 2023 and kept pushing them back. About 2,000 had signed a month after enrollment opened, and the total has crept only to around 8,600 since.
Veterans have a second grievance: those who have served since 2022 can sign for the same terms as raw recruits and get the same deferral, which starts at six months, too short, many say, to rebuild a civilian life before the draft reaches them again.
The raises that split the ranks
Meanwhile, new pay is reaching the troops. Higher combat payments are going out after some early paperwork delays, commanders confirm.
“The guys are getting good money. Everyone is very satisfied,” says Oleksandr Nastenko, who commands the 475th separate assault regiment “Code 9.2” under the callsign Flint.
The increases, though, were uneven, now one of the sorest points in the ranks. Infantry and assault troops saw the biggest jump, from about $2,700 to between $6,700 and $10,300 a month, while drone operators and other combat specialists who often share the same trenches received no comparable raise.
Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara’s team is now weighing which parts of the experiment to carry into a future reform bill.

New book makes fiery claims about Jared Kushner’s finances in Trump’s first term
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:56:39 UTC
06:56:39 KST

A new book containing incendiary claims about Jared Kushner’s financial dealings during Donald Trump’s first term has ignited a political and media firestorm.
The book by author Matthew Cole is called Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East and was released in the US this week. An excerpt was published by Vanity Fair last Thursday, and immediately drew a furious response from Kushner, who called its claims “completely insane”. The book contains numerous allegations about Kushner, whose father-in-law is Trump and who has served as one of his top diplomatic envoys in the Middle East – the most explosive of which are claims linking him to huge bank accounts allegedly funded by Gulf states.
Kusher denounced the book on his site last week, and writing on X: “We denied every one of these claims on the record, yet the author failed to provide a single shred of evidence to substantiate any of them.” He has demanded that Vanity Fair retract the excerpt and has threatened legal action against the book’s publisher, Simon & Schuster.
He added: “During the period in question, I was one of the most scrutinized people in the world, subjected to intense media coverage, multiple congressional investigations, and a special counsel investigation. I voluntarily cooperated with these investigations, providing over 30 hours of testimony. None of these allegations ever surfaced, because none of these events ever happened.”
The Guardian contacted Kushner’s legal counsel from Clare Locke as well as Chad Mizelle for comment and received no response.
Cole’s sources are predominantly anonymous and he does not print images of emails or other documentation to support his reporting. Extensive footnotes indicate sources of information, including confidential interviews.
In the book, the top intelligence official in the United Arab Emirates, Ali Al Shamsi, is reported to have called Kushner “the most expensive employee we’ve ever had”. The book details alleged payments into two “slush fund” bank accounts allegedly set up for Kushner by Emirati prince Mohamed bin Zayed (MBZ) and Saudi Arabian prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) during Trump’s first term. The Guardian contacted the Saudi Arabian and Emirati embassies for comment and did not receive a response.
In the book, Cole claims the accounts were partially managed by Kushner on an iPhone hacked by Russian and Dutch intelligence.
But despite the Emirati spymaster’s opinion of Kushner, Cole alleges that the New Jersey real estate scion was not entirely trusted. Cole describes a dangerous world in which blackmail is as common a tool of statecraft as torture and murder, as in the cases of the Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, killed on the orders of MBS in Turkey in 2018, and the Emirati journalist and poet Habib Al Sayegh, whose killing by agents of MBZ in 2019 is described by Cole.
Kushner continues to steer US foreign policy despite having no official role, with questions about his business interests accompanying him as he travels the world with New York real estate magnate Steve Witkoff, this week seeking peace in Ukraine, if on terms favorable to Russia.
In response, an attorney “who has represented President Trump in multiple defamation lawsuits”, Alejandro Brito, told Cole that, “during his time working for President Trump, Kushner ‘always represented and sought the interests of the United States and the President of the United States and did not make any agreements or arrangements with leaders or officials in foreign countries that were not agreed by the President of the United States and in the best interests of the United States.’” He further said that “[a]ny allegation that Kushner knew of, had access to, had authorization for or engaged in or directed any conduct related to any government-funded or government-linked bank account is totally false and defamatory”.
Brito told Cole that “‘there are no accounts and never were.’” Cole writes that the Dutch government refused to comment in response to his questions about the alleged hacking of Kushner’s phone.
According to Cole, MBZ and MBS wanted Kushner to help achieve their “vision of a new Middle East, one in which Israel would become an integral part of the region, recognized diplomatically by Gulf Arabs today and eventually by the rest of the Arab world; the Palestinians would end their conflict with Israel and accept a peace built on prosperity; Islamic extremism would be defeated; and Iran’s expansionism and militancy would retreat, either by persuasion or force.”
Nearly 10 years later, the US and Israel are planning new strikes in their eight-month war with Iran; Saudi Arabia is at war with Houthi rebels in Yemen, and Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza since the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023.
Kushner entered Trump’s first administration with his wife, Ivanka Trump, as close presidential advisers. MBZ and MBS, Cole claims, saw a chance to secure the best access money could buy. Cole alleges that in early 2017 the two princes “proposed to give Kushner a fund, a bank account, which the two leaders, working with Jared, would use to identify and pay for projects and foreign policy goals to advance for President Trump’s benefit”.
According to Cole, an idea to fund Trump’s proposed wall on the US border with Mexico apparently did not work out but the author claims that “MBZ and MBS initially, and then MBZ alone, put at least $2bn into at least two banks for Kushner.” Classifying the accounts as “Alpha” and “Beta”, Cole claims the Alpha account was held at First Abu Dhabi Bank, the largest in UAE, and contained “roughly $750m” to be “used as a foreign policy fund” overseen by Kushner and MBZ and meant to help end the Israel-Palestine conflict.
Cole quotes a source who says he knew of the UAE’s alleged deal with Kushner as saying: “‘Jared was looking for shortcuts in his diplomacy.’” Cole writes: “This person held discussions with both senior UAE and Israeli officials about the secret financial arrangement between Kushner, the UAE, and, at least initially, Saudi Arabia. ‘Jared promised MBZ that he’d push their agenda with Trump if they participated in a fund. He wanted normalization with Israel so that business could take off,’” the source alleged.
The same source claimed that “a slush fund – a shared pool of money for off-the-books diplomatic objectives – was a common form of Gulf Arab government corruption … ‘The Emiratis and the Saudis do this once a year. A billion or two is nothing for them, and if it gets them what they want, it’s money well spent.’”
Citing “a person briefed on the Beta account”, Cole claims it contained “roughly $1bn” and at the suggestion of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, was moved by MBZ to the Israeli Central Bank via Azerbaijan, a favored conduit for laundering money.
“It is … unclear how Kushner used the money the UAE deposited into the Beta account for him,” Cole alleges, “but according to the person with knowledge of the money, its allocation was for Kushner’s personal benefit.”
Kushner’s attorney, Brito, told Cole his client “had no financial relationships with any foreign countries or leaders”, adding that his “complete financial disclosures are publicly available in his OGE [office of government ethics] form 278e filings during this period.”
Cole alleges that the “Alpha” account established for Kushner in Trump’s first term was drained by failed schemes and Kushner’s access was cut off. “It is unclear if the Israeli government allowed Kushner access to the Beta bank account” after the end of Trump’s first term, Cole writes.
Cole also examines the widely reported story about how Kushner ultimately secured Qatari investment in 666 Fifth Avenue, a marquee Manhattan property, thereby profiting from interests on both sides of a bitterly divided Middle East, given Saudi Arabia and UAE’s rivalry with Qatar. (Kushner has denied engaging in any conflicts of interest.)
In Trump’s second term, Kushner’s diplomatic work has been dogged by questions about another massive financial asset: a $2bn investment by the Saudi sovereign wealth fund in Kushner’s Affinity Partners private equity firm, made after Trump left power in 2021. Cole quotes an unnamed Arab official and Affinity investor who claimed: “We don’t pay Jared because he’s a savvy investor. We pay him to keep him happy. That keeps his father-in-law happy.”
Cole writes: “Deep relationships with MBZ, MBS, Emir Al Thani [of Qatar], and Bibi Netanyahu were useful as [Kushner] shuttled between capitals, trying to find a way to end the daily slaughter in Gaza. But as it had been when he was a government employee, there was little record of what his investors were negotiating with him.”
In his epilogue, Cole writes that Kushner “declined multiple requests for an on-the-record interview for the book”, adding that he “first contacted him with a list of questions in May 2026 and followed up via email twice more, asking additional questions.”
Through his lawyers, Kushner denounced all of Cole’s reporting. Also on X, Chad Mizelle, a Trump administration lawyer who identified himself as “Jared’s attorney”, said: “The central allegation in this book is categorically false. These are not questions of interpretation or competing recollections: there are no bank accounts. They don’t exist. These are egregious and defamatory claims without a shred of evidence to substantiate them.”

29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
Israel’s predominantly Arab Joint List political alliance said late Wednesday that mass participation by Arab voters had kept Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc short of a parliamentary majority, pledging to use its projected gains to help remove his government.
In a statement following Tuesday’s election, the alliance said preliminary figures showed that the Arab turnout had played a decisive role in preventing Netanyahu and his “fascist camp” from reaching the 61 seats needed for a governing majority.
Voters answered incitement and intimidation at the ballot box, it said, rejecting a “government of butchers” and its policies of home demolitions, racism and war crimes.
The Joint List said its electoral support reflected demands for political unity and a force capable of defending Arab citizens’ rights without concessions.
It pledged to work to remove Netanyahu’s government and prevent its return, saying it was ready to cooperate toward an alternative government.
Such cooperation, it said, required opposition figures willing to offer a genuine alternative to the government’s policies, reject the exclusion of Arab citizens and their representatives, and commit to their rights and demands.
The alliance cautioned that final election results had yet to be announced.
After all regular ballots were counted, Netanyahu’s bloc was projected to secure 53 seats compared with 48 for the opposition bloc led by former Army Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot and 19 for Arab parties, Channel 12 reported.
Neither main bloc was projected to reach the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.
The Joint List was projected to win 12 seats and the United Arab List (Ra’am) seven, bringing their combined representation to 19, up from 10 in the 2022 election.
More than 500,000 special double-envelope ballots remained to be counted, potentially changing the distribution of seats. These include votes cast by soldiers, diplomats and others voting away from their registered polling stations.
More than 7.3 million Israelis were eligible to vote in Tuesday’s election, the first since Israel launched its genocidal war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023.

Spain rail crash came after train ordered to go in error: Minister
A rail collision in Spain that claimed at least 68 lives on Oct 28 came after a train was ordered to go in “error” despite a technical failure that halted all services, the transport minister said.
Transport Minister Oscar Puente said 69km of track were affected by an outage of the automatic control system, which “caused all the trains that were running at that time to stop automatically”.
“The decision to resume traffic, while that system had not been restored, belongs to the control centre, and the control centre... took the decision to resume traffic in circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable,” Puente said.
92-year-old US judge handling Nicolas Maduro case dies
Alvin Hellerstein, the US judge overseeing the case against deposed Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro, has died aged 92, an official confirmed on Oct 28.
As one of the oldest US federal judges, questions had been raised about whether he was the right justice to preside over what could be a prolonged trial for Maduro on drug trafficking charges.
Hellerstein’s lengthy career included overseeing the civil cases arising from Al-Qaeda’s Sept 11, 2001 terrorist attacks on New York and Washington, often rejecting deals he saw as unfair to complainants.
Apple shows pricey touchscreen laptops

Ternus took the stage at an Apple event in Los Angeles and showed a MacBook Pro model with an organic light-emitting diode (OLED) display, playing up the display’s contrast, sharpness and brightness in front of an audience of content creators and creative professionals.
He also said the company would return to a glowing logo on the back of the laptops.
Bayern boss Vincent Kompany out of hospital
Bayern Munich sporting director Max Eberl said on Oct 28 that coach Vincent Kompany had been discharged from hospital, revealing the Belgian had been suffering from meningeal irritation.
Kompany was rushed to hospital after collapsing on the training pitch in Munich on Oct 23, with Bayern saying the coach was suffering from a virus.
Speaking minutes before Bayern’s last-32 German Cup tie with Magdeburg, Eberl told ARD the doctors had determined the cause of the illness and had discharged the 40-year-old Kompany.

US President Donald Trump has intensified pressure on Havana since the kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January. Trump has since repeatedly stated that Cuba would be “next” as his administration imposed a near-total energy blockade against the island nation.
The restrictions contributed to severe energy shortages on the island. Cuba has entered its worst economic crisis in decades, marked not only by prolonged blackouts but also food shortages. Last month, Trump described Cuba as an “absolutely failed state” and “a haven for foreign adversaries” on America’s doorstep.
Moscow and Beijing have expressed solidarity with Cuba in the face of American pressure. Russia has been among the countries providing relief to Cuba, delivering around 700,000 barrels of oil in March. China also said in late September it would support Cuba in “safeguarding its national sovereignty” and pursuing a “development path suited to its national conditions.”
In mid-October, the US issued an arrest warrant for former Cuban President Raul Castro, 95, accusing him of ordering an attack on two American planes operated by anti-Communist Cuban exiles off the island’s coast in 1996. The warrant followed a separate federal indictment brought against Castro and five others in May. Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel condemned the case as a “political maneuver, devoid of any legal foundation” and accused Washington of creating a pretext for a military intervention.
Moscow has condemned the accusations against the former Cuban leader as “groundless” and “contrived,” calling it a “revenge” by the anti-Cuban lobby.

Support for UN vote to end US embargo on Cuba falls to 30-year low
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:45:20 UTC
06:45:20 KST

Similar resolutions have been approved almost every year since 1992, but usually by overwhelming margins.
The UN General Assembly has again called for an end to the US embargo on Cuba, but support for the resolution fell to its lowest level in more than 30 years.
The resolution, which has been put forward and approved almost every year since 1992, passed with 130 countries in favour, 17 against and 25 abstentions. That's the lowest level of support since 1995.
Last year, more than 160 countries backed the proposal. Germany, Italy and Latvia abstained for the first time in 34 years.
Several countries, including Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Morocco, Slovenia and Bosnia, voted against the resolution, many for the first time.
The resolution, while not legally binding, is seen as a reflection of international opinion. It calls for the lifting of the economic, trade and financial embargo against the island.
Renewed US pressure campaign against Cuba
The US embargo dates back to 1960, after Fidel Castro’s revolution and the nationalisation of US-owned property. Tensions between the US and Cuba are currently running high, with a renewed pressure campaign by Washington including restrictions on oil supplies and broad sanctions that have severely damaged Cuba's economy.
Just minutes before the vote took place in New York, US ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz denied that Cuba was under a blockade and said "the plight of the Cuban people is exclusively the fault of this corrupt communist regime."
The Cuban government has in recent weeks accused the US of mounting a diplomatic offensive to pressure countries into withdrawing their support for the resolution.
Cuba's Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez accused Washington of seeking to "determine the nation's destiny" and "seize" its wealth.
There was also a heated confrontation between Rodríguez and Waltz, during which Rodríguez approached the US ambassador and accused him of lying, while Waltz shouted for him to back away.
During Tuesday's session, Waltz accused senior Cuban officials of enjoying luxury lifestyles while ordinary Cubans faced shortages. He held up pictures of Cuban leaders past and present, including President Miguel Díaz-Canel, wearing luxury watches, prompting members of the Cuban delegation to repeatedly bang on their desks in protest.
Writing on the social media platform X, Díaz-Canel accused the US of engaging in "gangster-like coercion."
"The world has once again spoken out overwhelmingly against the blockade, even despite the most blatant pressure and blackmail from the US to change the course of this vote," he wrote.
In January, President Trump threatened tariffs on countries supplying oil to Cuba, a move that has sharply reduced fuel deliveries and contributed to widespread power cuts and disruption to water, internet and telephone services.
Cuba is continuing to face severe economic hardship, with widespread shortages of fuel and other essentials, frequent power cuts and disruption to basic services including water, internet and telephone networks.

Ukraine seeks to present Carpathian strategy to EU by mid-2027, Bezgin says
Vitalii Bezgin, Ukraine’s Minister for Communities, Territories and Internally Displaced Persons, said this in comments to an Ukrinform correspondent on the sidelines of the 51st session of the Congress of Local and Regional Authorities of the Council of Europe in Strasbourg.
“Our next step is to develop a joint macro-regional strategy within the European Union framework. To this end, just two weeks ago, we secured the support of Raffaele Fitto, Executive Vice-President of the European Commission for Cohesion and Reforms. The Commission is now planning specific support for regions it refers to as the ‘eastern flank.’ As allies, we naturally want to be part of this process,” the minister explained.
According to Bezgin, the document must be prepared and discussed with European institutions in the first half of next year, as the EU’s next budget period begins in 2028.
“If we secure a dedicated strategy, we could qualify for specific funding under a transport cooperation program, primarily for infrastructure projects,” he added.
Bezgin said discussions at the Congress had been useful in examining how similar initiatives had been launched for the Alps and under the Danube Strategy, “because we want to do essentially the same things with the Carpathian Strategy.”
He said the Carpathian initiative was presented in Strasbourg on October 27 to the permanent representatives to the Council of Europe of countries in the Carpathian macro-region, as well as the heads of the relevant national delegations. It was also presented to the leadership of the European Committee of the Regions.
“At the local level, it is much easier to balance shared interests because the focus is on practical projects and their implementation, as well as on securing financial resources,” he said.
The initiative involves cooperation among eight countries: Ukraine, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, Hungary, Czechia, Austria, and Serbia. According to the minister, Hungary is currently the only country among them taking a cautious position. However, its representative also joined the discussions in Strasbourg.
On October 28, the Congress of the Council of Europe also decided to support the Carpathian integration initiative. As a next step, in early 2027, it is expected to facilitate a thematic meeting involving local and regional authorities from the Carpathian region and government institutions to agree on a concrete cooperation plan aimed at promoting cohesion, prosperity, and security.
As Ukrinform previously reported, following the first Carpathian Summit, held in Ukraine’s Ivano-Frankivsk region, leaders and representatives of Ukraine, Austria, Poland, Romania, Serbia, and Slovakia adopted a joint declaration.

WELLINGTON, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Nine days out from New Zealand’s general election on November 7, polls continue to show no clear winner or even coalition grouping.

High-speed train crash kills at least 68 people in Spain
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:38:54 GMT
06:38:54 KST

High-speed train crash kills at least 68 people in Spain
- Published
A high-speed train crash has killed at least 68 people and injured dozens more in central Spain.
It occurred when a train travelling from Madrid to Seville barrelled into another train - which was stationary on the tracks - on Wednesday morning. The force saw several carriages fall down an embankment.
The transport minister said a computer failure followed by human error caused the crash, which is one of the worst in Europe's modern history, and Spain's deadliest train disaster in 13 years.
Survivors described harrowing scenes of passengers being thrown into the air, trapped in the wreckage and smashing windows to get out.
The crash happened just after 09:00 (08:00 GMT) around 140km (87 miles) south of Madrid, between the municipalities of Mora and Orgaz.
The stationary train, run by private rail operator Iryo, had 147 passengers on board, and had stopped on the tracks because of a computer failure, Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said.
He explained that when there is a system failure, a 24-hour control centre in Madrid takes over, but it had made an "inexplicable" decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.
Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by another train, run by Spain's state-owned railway company, Renfe, which was carrying 397 passengers.
The force of the crash was "brutal", said 62-year-old passenger Salvador Arriza who was sitting in the Renfe-operated train.
Passengers started breaking the windows to get out, he told Reuters, adding that "some people couldn't move because they were trapped amongst the seats."
One of the carriages caught fire, and passengers described devastating scenes of trapped people crying and bleeding, with some buried under debris.
Pictures show that a long piece of railway track had speared through one of the carriages.
Tangui Binier, 22, was on the Iryo train and told the BBC that "suitcases started flying and people were screaming" when the train finally came to a halt.
There was a lot of smoke and confusion, he said, and described seeing the train "completely flipped over" when he stepped outside.
"It was hard to witness", Binier said, adding that his father carried a girl who had a broken hip out of the wreckage.
He also described seeing dead bodies and missing limbs: "I don't know if I'll ever recover."
Spanish journalist Antonio Jiménez Barca, who works for El Pais newspaper, was walking to the Renfe train's cafeteria when the crash happened.
"I felt like I was being pushed from behind, like I was being thrown to the ground," he described.
"I hit my head horribly... I was covered in blood. There were people on top of me. One person had an injured arm, and another had a head injury."
Another passenger, 46-year-old Sebastián Herrero, told El Mundo newspaper that he saw "many people with broken noses, broken arms."
"It was a terrible, terrible impact," he said, adding that he was "in the air for about four or five seconds," which felt like a lifetime.
Many of the passengers said they were in shock, and one sobbed during an interview with a local television station as he described a woman dying in his arms.
"She was very cold and she was all alone," he said, to which the show's presenter also started to cry.
Dozens of ambulances rushed to the scene, and a helicopter evacuated those with the most serious injuries.
Spain's Civil Guard said it would need DNA samples from relatives to identify some victims.
"The whole of Spain is grieving", Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said during a visit to the crash site. "Lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart, the pain is immense."
Most political parties in Spain cancelled their campaign events scheduled for Wednesday.
The exception was the far-right party Vox. Its leader, Santiago Abascal, said his party would not take part in what he described as attempts to "use mourning to silence criticism" of the country's rail infrastructure.
Spain was already reeling from a high-speed rail disaster near Córdoba in January that killed 46 people. It happened on the same rail line, but much further south.
The prime minister said it was "unacceptable" for Spain to have two serious train crashes in one year, and vowed to "get to the bottom of this" and determine if there was any negligence.
"Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure," said Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the the main opposition People's Party.
"If there have been failures in the security system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness."
Spanish trade union CSIF has demanded the transport minister resign, accusing him of "scapegoating" a traffic manager, by blaming human error in the control room, instead of "taking responsibility".
Wednesday's crash is the worst the country has seen since 2013, when when 80 people died on the outskirts of Santiago de Compostela in north-west Spain.

Russia Builds New Drone Base Near Ukraine Capable of Launching 100 Attack Drones Daily
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:38:14 UTC
06:38:14 KST

- Category
- World
Russia Builds New Drone Base Near Ukraine Capable of Launching 100 Attack Drones Daily
Russia is building a new drone launch facility near the Millerovo military airfield in the Rostov region, capable of supporting up to 100 attack drone launches per day, the Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine's Ministry of Defense (HUR) reported on October 28.
The facility's construction was confirmed through satellite imagery, according to Oboronka, citing an official statement by HUR. The site is located near Russia's border with Ukraine's temporarily occupied Luhansk region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"The facility's configuration indicates that it is designed to prepare and launch jet-powered attack drones, likely Geran-4 and Geran-5, as well as their modifications. Preliminary estimates suggest that once construction is complete, the site will be capable of supporting up to 100 launches per day," HUR stated.
According to the intelligence directorate, satellite imagery showed no visible signs of active construction at the site in late August 2026. By mid-October, Russian forces had established launch positions and supporting infrastructure.
HUR noted that the rapid construction could be explained by the use of standardized technical solutions and the concentration of resources on relatively simple launch infrastructure.
"The construction of a new UAV launch facility just 3.5 kilometers from Millerovo airfield means that the Russians intend to use the same air defense systems protecting the airfield to defend it," HUR explained.
The facility could also benefit from existing roads, communications networks, logistics infrastructure, and technical support systems associated with the military airfield.
However, HUR emphasized that the actual launch rate would depend on the availability of drones, fuel, warheads, trained crews, operational equipment, and assigned missions.
Meanwhile, Russia is modernizing its Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered attack drones, the intelligence directorate reported. The Geran-4 has a range of up to 770 kilometers and has received additional autonomous navigation capabilities, including an optical terrain-matching system.
HUR also reported that Russia has equipped the Geran-4 with a domestically produced jet engine and a new warhead designed to strike bridges and power transmission line supports.
The Geran-5 has a reported range of up to 950 kilometers. Its K5 modification is being fitted with a similar optical navigation system, potentially improving its ability to navigate without relying exclusively on satellite signals.
According to HUR, Russia currently operates at least 12 permanent attack drone launch facilities. The Millerovo site would expand this network and could form part of preparations to intensify drone strikes against Ukraine, particularly during the winter.
The Millerovo site is not an isolated expansion: the Tsymbulova drone base in the Oryol region has also been adding shelters and launchers for jet-powered drones as Russia ramps up output of the Gerans themselves.
As of early October, Russia was producing around 2,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones per month, though further growth hinges on turbojet engines largely supplied by China. Russian forces have also amassed roughly 10,000 piston-engine strike drones and launch both types together in successive waves to exhaust Ukrainian air defenses.
Ukraine has been developing interceptor drones in response, with a domestically produced P1-SUN JetKiller downing a Geran-5 on September 30.

F-22s, F-15s Rotate in at Kadena to Bolster Pacific Airpower
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:37:22 UTC
06:37:22 KST

Squadrons of F-22 Raptors and F-15C Eagles have arrived at Kadena Air Base, Japan, for temporary deployments as the critical Pacific base awaits its permanent F-15EX fighters.
Stars & Stripes reported Oct. 27 that a squadron of F-22s from Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Alaska, finished arriving Sept. 30. Another squadron of F-15s, from Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base New Orleans, La., also recently arrived, Stripes reported, citing a statement from the 18th Wing at Kadena.
The 18th Wing did not immediately respond to a query from Air & Space Forces Magazine. But independent aircraft trackers and photographs published by the military show those planes arriving at or operating from Kadena recently.
Kadena, located on Okinawa, is the U.S.’s closest air base to Taiwan and strategically vital.
The 18th Wing at Kadena flew squadrons of permanently assigned F-15C/D fighters for years. But those legacy fighters were rapidly aging, and in November 2022, the Air Force started withdrawing them. Those fighters will be replaced with 36 permanently assigned F-15EX Eagle II jets, beginning in fiscal 2027.
Until then, the service is rotating various fighters, including F-35s, F-22s, F-16s, and F-15 variants through Kadena on a temporary basis, to maintain the base’s ability to project airpower if necessary.
The first F-15EXs had been scheduled to arrive by now, but labor disputes and other challenges slowed Boeing’s deliveries and delayed plans. The first F-15EX earmarked for Kadena left Boeing’s St. Louis factory Aug. 28, and flew to Portland, Ore., for final systems integration, software updates, and other technical preparations. After that work is done, the jet will fly to Okinawa.
Photos posted by the 18th Wing on Oct. 27 show the Alaska F-22s at Tsuiki Air Base, Japan, taking part in Exercise Keen Sword 27, which aims to improve how U.S. and Japanese forces work together.
Aircraft trackers have also observed F-15 movements to Kadena in recent weeks.
Aviation enthusiast Aux OSINT on Oct. 24 and 25 posted flight tracker images on social media of KC-46 Pegasus tankers flying Coronet missions with F-15Cs from the 122nd, inbound to Kadena.
A Japan-based aviation photographer who posts online under the handle Okadna35 posted images Oct. 24 of F-15s arriving at Kadena, bearing markings of the New Orleans base’s 159th Fighter Wing, nicknamed the Bayou Militia.

Turkish engineer creates live 3D pixel map of adopted hometown Warsaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:36:45 UTC
06:36:45 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
A Turkish software engineer has, with the help of AI and vast quantities of Polish public data, created a precise digital replica of Warsaw, the city where he lives.
The map, which can be explored for free online, features almost 200,000 buildings, moving trams that match their real-life schedules, changing light and weather conditions, and over 45,000 accurately placed streetlamps that turn on at night. It is even possible to fly a virtual plane through the city.
The person behind the project, Bedirhan Yildirim, was inspired by recent efforts to produce similar maps of New York and London.
While he initially considered producing one of Istanbul, his hometown, he decided instead to pick the city he lives in, Warsaw. “It is smaller, mostly flat, and I walk its streets every day,” he explained of his choice.
Yildirim then used AI coding agents to create the map through a process of trial and error, constantly tweaking and improving the model.
The initial version took only two days to produce and was launched on 22 October, but it has been regularly improved since then based on feedback from users.
The work was made possible by what Yildirim says is the “incredible amount of data” Poland’s national mapping office, GUGiK, provides for free, including 3D building models, terrain scans, and even details of almost 2 million trees.
Further information, including on parks, streetlamps, and traffic lights, was taken from OpenStreetMap, a freely licensed database. Meanwhile, timetables from Warsaw’s public transport authority, ZTM, and Poland’s national rail operator, PKP, allowed the map to feature accurately timed trams and trains.
Current weather conditions are input from Open-Meteo, an open-source meteorological service. But users can also choose to manually adjust the time of day or year, with light and weather changing accordingly.
An observation deck at the top of the EU's tallest building, Varso Tower in Warsaw, has opened to the public.
Located 230m up on the tower's 53rd floor, the attraction offers a 360° panorama of Poland's capital.https://t.co/VeEapOmh4s
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 9, 2025
The result is an incredible level of explorable detail, from major landmarks, such as the communist-era Palace of Culture and Science and Varso Tower, the EU’s tallest building, down to the seating steps and bars along the Vistula River boulevards.
The map also features graveyards reflecting Warsaw and Poland’s diverse past, including Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Jewish and Tatar Muslim graves. Around 1 November, when Poles visit cemeteries around All Saints’ Day, candles glow around the graves.
A final touch Yildirim has added is a flight simulator, allowing users to travel over the city – and complete missions – in a Cessna aeroplane, an air ambulance, a flying car, or even a UFO that takes off from the Copernicus Science Centre and travels to the National Stadium.

Speaking to Notes from Poland, Yildirim says that he moved to Poland in 2022 to pursue a job in IT before starting his own business. Initially living in Kraków, the country’s second-largest city, he then moved to Warsaw in 2025.
Asked what his own personal favourite places in the city are, Yildirim points to Warsaw’s parks, such as Skaryszewski, Pole Mokotowskie and Łazienki. His favourite neighbourhood is Saska Kępa on the right bank of the Vistula.
The software engineer adds that his project is an example of how AI can be an “amazing tool to do 90% of the job very quickly”. The remaining 10% of human input “is what keeps it from being ‘AI slop'”.
Yildirim says that, without the use of AI, the map of Warsaw he created would have needed an entire team to build over a period of months.

Costa Rica’s mega-prison receives first inmates

Costa Rica’s mega-prison receives first inmates
President Laura Fernandez inaugurated the $35m mega-prison built to house up to 5,100 inmates near San Jose.
A newly opened maximum-security mega-prison in Costa Rica has received its first batch of inmates. The prison was built with the help of the Salvadoran government on the outskirts of the capital, San Jose, the country’s Justice Ministry announced.
The Costa Rican Justice Ministry shared images on Tuesday of 123 inmates dressed in orange, seated with their heads shaved and bowed and their hands behind their necks.
“Costa Rica is writing a new chapter in its penitentiary history,” Justice Minister Gabriel Aguilar said in a statement.
The new prison is called the High-Containment Center Against Organized Crime (CACCO) and constitutes a symbol of a new “tough on crime” approach championed by President Laura Fernandez’s administration. It has a capacity for 5,100 inmates.
The CACCO was built with the help of the Salvadoran government on the outskirts of Costa Rica’s capital, San Jose, at a cost of $35m. Fernandez inaugurated it on October 15.
“CACCO is a monument to national security, a forceful response to organized crime, and a guarantee that the state will exercise its authority without hesitation,” the statement added.
The new facility has a capacity equivalent to 20 percent of the country’s prison population and “will also help reduce overcrowding in the prison system”, according to Aguilar.
Costa Rica, long regarded as one of the safest countries in Latin America, has in recent years experienced a sharp rise in violence linked to drug trafficking and organised crime. It witnessed a record-setting 905 homicides in 2023, followed by 876 in 2024 and 873 in 2025.
Authorities attribute most killings to disputes between criminal groups over drug trafficking routes and markets.
Right-wing leaders in other Latin American countries have also sought to replicate the mega-prison model.

Putin's praise came after a series of sharp statements by Musk directed at the Ukrainian president. In particular, on October 11, the businessman wrote on the social network X that "Zelenskyy has gone too far," alluding to Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries.
In response, Zelenskyy said that Donald Trump and Elon Musk could not stop Putin, so they were trying to pressure others. After that, the American billionaire called on the Ukrainian president to resign and accused him of prolonging the bloodshed.
Amid the dispute, disruptions occurred in the operation of the Starlink and Starshield satellite systems used by the Ukrainian military. The communication problems became known on October 14.

Sumy Region Expands Underground Schooling, With 9 New Facilities Under Construction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:34:15 UTC
06:34:15 KST

Ukraine’s northeastern Sumy region is working on expanding its network of underground schools as Russian forces increasingly target civilians, with more than 4,200 Russian guided aerial bombs (KABs) launched during this year alone.
There are currently 13 functional underground schools in Sumy, with nine new facilities still under construction. Cost estimates and site plans had also been completed for another 14 facilities, head of the Sumy Regional Military Administration Oleh Hryhorov told Ukrinform in an exclusive interview on Wednesday, Oct. 28.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The process is ongoing and being scaled up as much as possible,” Hryhorov said, noting that the region was seeking international partners to help fund the construction.
Classrooms increasingly below ground
With the full-scale invasion now in its fifth year, Ukrainian authorities have continued working on giving children as normal a childhood as possible under such conditions.
When the school year began on Sept. 1, many students returned to in-person classes under new wartime rules, including restrictions on large gatherings that could put children at risk.
In the Sumy region, new underground schools are being built mainly in larger cities, where the number of students is highest.
The need is much lower in smaller communities, as some only have a single school, Hryhorov said. Of the region’s 280 schools, 225 have their own shelters. Although most are basic, more than 70 schools have radiation-proof shelters.
Russian Strike on Dnipro Industrial Site Injures 1 as Attacks Across Region Wound 5 Others
According to Hryhorov, such infrastructure allows the region to keep many students in physical classrooms. About 75,000 children are currently enrolled in the region’s schools, with 22 of them operating fully in person.
As most schools in other regions do as well, 193 are operating using a mix of in-person and remote classes.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in February 2022, 165 schools have been damaged in the region and 21 destroyed beyond repair, Hryhorov said.
Ukrinform reported that another underground school opened in the city of Sumy in October, able to accommodate up to 500 students.
A region under constant fire
The effort comes as Sumy, located about 20 kilometers from the frontline, (12 miles) continues facing near-daily Russian attacks.
Due to the proximity, Russian forces have increasingly begun relying on fiber-optic FPV drones, which can now reach almost 50 kilometers (31 miles) into the region. By October, more than 6,000 drone strikes of several types were recorded.
Since the beginning of the year, more than 4,200 guided aerial bombs were dropped on the region; about 500 targeted the Sumy community, including 192 that struck the regional capital itself.
The overall number of attacks is roughly the same as in 2025, Hryhorov said, although noting that their focus has changed. While Russian forces mostly struck military positions during the last year, they have concentrated on civilian infrastructure and the region’s residents in 2026.
To protect against drones, more than 450 kilometers (280 miles) of roads have been covered with anti-drone nets.
Hryhorov said each kilometer costs more than Hr. 1 million (roughly $22,000), rising to as much as Hr. 3 million ($66,000) when the work is done by private contractors.
The government has so far allocated Hr. 70 million ($1.5 million) for additional nets in Sumy, while regional authorities and local communities have provided a total of Hr. 1.35 billion ($30 billion) for overall security measures, including the netting.
Mandatory frontline evacuations
Meanwhile, in 213 settlements near the border, evacuations remain mandatory.
According to Hryhorov, more than 57,000 people, including 8,000 children, have already left. However, about 34,000 civilians still remain in the region.
Under mandatory evacuation orders, all children have been evacuated from the frontline communities.
On Oct. 22, regional authorities also extended mandatory evacuation of families with children to the entire Sloviansk community after Russian forces struck the settlements of the Donetsk region 42 times, injuring two boys.
Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv’s university district on Tuesday, Oct. 27, killing one person and injuring over 10, mostly students.
A Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv on Thursday, Oct. 1, while more than 100 children and over 60 teachers sheltered inside. The Geran-4 drone struck the wall of a stairwell between the school’s second and third floors without detonating.
Although deliberate attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are prohibited under international humanitarian law, they remain part of daily life for Ukrainian citizens.
