'There cannot be business as usual with Russia' — Dutch minister urges Europe to step up for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:11:12 UTC
05:11:12 KST

'There cannot be business as usual with Russia' — Dutch minister urges Europe to step up for Ukraine
Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, the Dutch Minister of Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation, in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 28, 2026. (Handout / Tetiana Bulhakova)
Ukraine is about to enter another harsh winter as Russian attacks continue crippling critical infrastructure, even before the coldest days set in.
In an attempt to relieve Kyiv, the Dutch government on Oct. 28 outlined a package of non-military aid worth 1.2 billion euros ($1.3 billion), to be disbursed over the next three years and directed toward the country's economic recovery.
The Netherlands will also provide 40 million euros ($45 million) to the Ukraine Energy Support Fund, as well as 55 million euros ($62 million) to fund energy equipment from Dutch companies via the Netherlands Enterprise Agency.
The Kyiv Independent walked through central Kyiv with Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, the Netherlands' minister for foreign trade, to discuss how Europe can help Ukraine withstand mounting pressure on its energy and water infrastructure amid ongoing Russian attacks.
Sjoerdsma explained the benefits of investing in Ukraine and commented on some countries' willingness to do business with Russia as its full-scale invasion of Ukraine continues.
The minister added that the EU must play a bigger political role in discussing how Russia’s war should end.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
The Kyiv Independent: How is the Netherlands coordinating assistance to Ukraine for the upcoming tough winter?
Sjoerdsma: The support package we are bringing, 1.2 billion euros ($1.3 billion), is mainly aimed at helping Ukrainians protect and restore energy and water facilities, but also at training people to prevent damage to and protect these facilities so they keep running.
We see that the urgency of the upcoming winter is to ensure that cities, whether it's Kyiv or small villages in the east, remain livable. We understand that the Russian strategy is to try to break the spirit of the Ukrainian people, to literally put you in the cold, and we're going to do anything we can to prevent that from happening.
The Kyiv Independent: Regarding the protection of these facilities, what is the Netherlands doing to aid Ukraine?
Sjoerdsma: Obviously, we have to make sure there's protection, and that they cannot be easily destroyed. We try, as best we can, to bring completed equipment, but this obviously cannot always happen, as we sometimes require Ukrainian expertise to help install and maintain it.
We try to make sure it's not just a one-off, but instead a complete, integrated process that helps Ukrainian energy and water facilities.
The Kyiv Independent: What potential do you see in investing in Ukraine during wartime?
Sjoerdsma: If you look at Dutch companies already present in Ukraine, their expertise varies a lot. Some are obviously defense companies that help Ukraine build missiles for military use.
Then there are companies like Philips that help supply essential medical materials. And then, there are many smaller companies helping Ukraine, for example, providing bakers with materials. So anything from a very small scale to a very large scale is already present. It's both a sign of solidarity and a business opportunity.
Kyiv Independent: What do Dutch businesses gain from investing in Ukraine?
Sjoerdsma: We are learning so much from Ukraine, just to give two examples. In the field of defense, the innovative way in which Ukraine's army operates and adjusts, changes material needs, and utilizes drones. These are huge lessons for how we organize our army.
But also, Ukraine's resistance against Russia, its ability to adapt and restore certain facilities, especially critical infrastructure, at such speed and ingenuity, is also crucial to us. If there are any problems with the Dutch electrical network or other facilities, we'll definitely call Kyiv first to ask how you do things.
Additionally, the day after the war ends and reconstruction begins, it's not only our duty to help Ukraine rebuild as soon as possible, but also a huge opportunity for Dutch companies. These can be some of their biggest assignments to date: rebuilding entire hospitals, schools, ports, and whatever else will help Ukraine flourish again.
Kyiv Independent: As some countries are showing willingness to trade and do business with the Kremlin and Russian companies, what is the Netherlands' stance on this matter?
Sjoerdsma: Let me be very clear, this war can end today if Russia decides to stop its aggression against Ukraine. For the Netherlands, this scenario is really quite clear. Looking at the way Russia is treating cities, not just Kyiv, and aiming to erase your cultural heritage, it's clear what Moscow's end goal is, and we cannot allow that to happen.
"There's no talk about Ukraine without Ukraine in the driver's seat of what's happening."
We love doing business with Ukraine and don't see any reason to do business with Russia at this time. So no, there cannot be business as usual with Russia. Our prime minister at the European Council was quite clear about this.
While the Dutch are very robust in their support, we also believe that other European countries really need to step up. And this is not a cliche — your security is our security. To treat it as something Ukraine can do on its own, I think, is ridiculous.
This is a partnership. We are doing what we can, but others need to increase their support, and they need to do so as soon as possible, before winter sets in.
The Kyiv Independent: How can the European Union help prevent the West's future deals with Russia?
Sjoerdsma: Obviously, we do not condone the diesel deal between the U.S. and Russia. We feel it not only legitimizes Russia’s government but also reinforces its position.
I think it's crucial that, since the bulk of Ukraine's assistance comes from the EU, the EU is also a political player.
We must use our political influence to ensure that whenever discussions about a ceasefire or peace agreement take place, Ukraine is at the table. There's no talk about Ukraine without Ukraine in the driver's seat of what's happening.
I think Europe's role is to support Ukraine in its resistance against Russia, but also to make sure you are in a position to determine your own future. We see how Russia is trying to erase your identity and history, and we are determined to prevent that from happening.

Chipotle earnings miss estimates, but same-store sales increase for third straight quarter

Chipotle Mexican Grill on Wednesday reported mixed quarterly results and said its restaurant-level operating margin shrank.
But the burrito chain saw traffic and same-store sales grow during the quarter as low-income consumers spent more, bucking industry trends, and CEO Scott Boatwright projected a strong finish to the year.
Shares of the company rose 7% in extended trading.
"Broader consumer and industry headwinds may continue, but initiatives across our recipe for growth strategy are building and giving us more tools to win in any environment," Boatwright said on the company's earnings conference call. "We are still in the early stages of this work, and it's gaining traction."
Like the broader restaurant industry, Chipotle saw trends soften in early October, although executives said its traffic has returned to growth since then. Boatwright said the company has "high confidence" in its performance for the rest of the fourth quarter.
"We feel very confident that November and December set up very well for us," Boatwright said.
Chief Financial Officer Adam Rymer said the company expects fourth-quarter same-store sales growth of about 2%.
Here's what the company reported for the period ended Sept. 30 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
- Earnings per share: 27 cents adjusted vs. 29 cents expected
- Revenue: $3.29 billion vs. $3.29 billion expected
Chipotle reported fiscal third-quarter net income of $339.9 million, or 27 cents per share, down from $382.1 million, or 29 cents per share, a year earlier. The company's restaurant-level operating margin fell from 24.5% to 23.3%.
Excluding restaurant asset impairment charges and stock-based compensation, the company earned 27 cents per share.
Net sales rose 9.6% to $3.29 billion, fueled by the chain's new restaurants. During the quarter, Chipotle opened 84 company-owned restaurants and five international locations run by licensees.
In the second half of July, Chipotle said it started to see sales pull back as diners grew concerned about consuming raw lettuce due to cyclospora, although its own supply was never tied to an outbreak. Then in August, the chain disclosed that it had temporarily pulled jalapenos from Minnesota restaurants after learning its supply was potentially linked to a salmonella outbreak.
Still, the chain was able to report same-store sales growth for its third straight quarter, shaking off last year's traffic woes.
Sales at stores open at least 13 months increased 2.1%, lifted by a 1.3% bump in average check.
For the first time this year, low-income consumers during the quarter outperformed the high-income cohort at its restaurants, Boatwright said. And discounts aren't the reason — low-income consumers spent the most in September, when promotions were at their low point during the quarter, he told analysts.
For the full year, Chipotle reiterated its previous forecast that its same-store sales will increase by a low-single-digit percentage.
Looking ahead to 2027, the company is projecting that it will open between 340 and 360 new company-owned locations in the U.S. and Canada and around 15 to 25 international restaurants.

The Peptide Rush Has Begun
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:09:42 UTC
05:09:42 KST

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) will not take action against licensed pharmacists who dispense certain unapproved peptides to consumers, according to a new policy published Oct. 28 in the Federal Register.
Peptides are short chains of amino acids that people inject into their bodies. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has said in the past that he is a “big fan” of the unapproved drugs, whose benefits are largely scientifically unproven.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) essentially banned peptides in 2023 because of safety concerns. But an FDA committee met in July to review the evidence on peptides and recommend whether or not to take the highly unusual step of allowing pharmacies to dispense them absent scientific review. The committee was made up of new appointees who consulted with or were employed by companies that were interested in promoting or dispensing peptides; it recommended allowing specialty pharmacies to dispense six peptides, despite FDA staff advising against the move.
The new policy—which was signed by Kennedy—says that after the July meetings, HHS believed there was “significant interest” in the use of obtaining these peptides from compounding pharmacies. “Therefore, to expand and improve patient access, HHS does not intend to take enforcement action against a State-licensed pharmacy, Federal facility, or licensed physician compounding a drug product using a peptide bulk drug substance found in Appendix A,” the notice said. The policy said that it was going to be published in the Federal Register on Oct. 30. The peptides listed in Appendix A were BPC-157, Epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax, and TB-500—the same ones the committee recommended allowing this summer.
A separate document posted on the HHS website says that after reviewing the recommendations of the committee that met in July, “the Secretary has determined that the policy advances patient choice and freedom while appropriately protecting patient safety.”
The decision to allow the compounding of peptides is a boon for companies like Hims & Hers, which had reportedly been preparing to offer peptides in 2026. Analysts have said the market for peptides could be as high as $3.3 billion. Hims stock shot up 5% after the Oct. 28 announcement.
The move “represents a vital step toward eliminating the unsafe gray and black markets, restoring safe patient access through legitimate, physician-supervised care,” said Lee Rosebush, chair of the American Academy of Peptide Medicine, a new advocacy group, in a statement.
Other public-health professionals raised alarm about the decision, which they say allows compounding pharmacies to dispense these medications absent scientific evidence. “American consumers should not be treated like guinea pigs,” said Fred Mills, chief policy officer for Americans for Safe and Effective Medicines, in a statement. “It is possible to advance both patient safety and access to legitimate medicines, but this is not it.”
At the July hearings, consumer advocacy groups including the Center for Science in the Public Interest had argued that allowing peptides to skip a rigorous evidence-based FDA approval process would be unprecedented and dangerous to consumers.
Many physicians have spoken up against allowing peptides to be compounded. “The peptides under consideration here are untested and poorly characterized experimental drugs that should not be allowed in compounded products,” said Dr. Adriane Fugh-Berman, a professor of pharmacology and physiology at Georgetown University Medical Center, at the public comment portion of the July meeting, reminding the committee that two women had required emergency treatment after receiving peptides at a Las Vegas festival.
Critics also expressed concern that people were turning to compounding pharmacies for untested drugs. Compounding pharmacies are often used to fill specific prescriptions from a doctor, but in recent years, they have mass-produced drugs like GLP-1s for patients looking to save money. The peptide boom will put even more pressure on compounding pharmacies to quickly make drugs for telehealth sites, said Annie Lambert, a pharmacist and clinical program manager for compliance solutions at Wolters Kluwer Health.
"Compounding can and should play a legitimate clinical role, from hospitals to home infusion to filling gaps during drug shortages. But it is not a substitute for FDA-approved manufacturing, and that distinction is where a lot of today's risk sits,” she said in a statement. “My concern is that pharmacies rushing into this space will move to make a dollar faster rather than make sure they meet every requirement, from ingredient sourcing and facilities to staff training and sterility testing.”
Shortly after the new notice was published, a number of telehealth websites were already marketing the six peptides, each for a price of anywhere from $199 to $249 a month.

Carriers from Delta Air Lines to Frontier have said customers are mostly continuing to book flights despite higher fares, but that record jet fuel prices, their biggest cost after labor, are eroding profits.
Frontier shares rose close to 12%.
Frontier had eclipsed Spirit Airlines as the biggest discount carrier in the country even before that airline collapsed in May.

UN fact-finding mission says external actors fuel Sudan war, backs nationwide arms embargo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:02:41 UTC
05:02:41 KST

Merve Aydogan, Aysu Bicer
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
The UN's Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan said Wednesday that foreign weapons, technology and personnel continue to fuel the war, as it urged stronger international action.
Speaking at a news conference at UN headquarters in New York, mission chair Mohamed Chande Othman said: "Our investigation found reasonable grounds to believe that external transfer of weapons, military technology, logistic support, and foreign personnel continue to sustain and intensify the conflict."
"We also found that external actors supplied both parties, and this helps sustain their military operations. The result is increasingly visible on the ground," he said.
Asked who is supplying the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the government, Othman said investigators found a cross-border network involving individuals and entities in Chad, Puntland in Somalia, southeast Libya and the United Arab Emirates, engaged in supplying weapons and training foreign fighters.
He said the mission is urging those states "to beef up their due diligence obligations" because of the direct consequences for civilians.
Stressing the distinction between governments and those operating from their territory, Othman said: "We have not yet, in terms of our evidence, linked any of the neighboring states as states. So, there’s a distinction there: individuals and entities in these states."
He said the mission is engaging with the UAE and Chad, noting that Chad denies using its territory and that the investigation into other states’ alleged roles is ongoing.
Mona Rishmawi, member of the mission, said both parties and their allies "are basically destroying a country of 56 million people."
"That’s really important to keep in mind," she said, adding that impunity from earlier conflicts is feeding the violence.
Asked about the Security Council's refusal in September and earlier this month to expand an arms embargo beyond Darfur, mission member Joy Ngozi Ezeilo said the report documents how surveillance and arbitrary detention are exposing civil society.
She said the mission’s role is to ensure "Sudanese civilians, whether women, children, or the displaced families, are not abandoned."
"This war, despite being the most atrocious war, is not getting the attraction it is supposed to get. And the international community is not responding in a way it should," said Ezeilo.
"We are for expansion of this arms embargo," she said, adding that the mission also supports extending the International Criminal Court’s mandate to all of Sudan.
The mission said civilians in the strategic city of El Obeid are exposed to grave risks as it remains partially encircled by RSF.
RSF-attributed drone strikes have also damaged schools and displacement sites, and disrupted access to healthcare, electricity and water, according to the report.
Meanwhile, security forces affiliated with the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have intensified surveillance and arbitrary arrests, further restricting civilian freedoms.
“The situation in and around El-Obeid remains grave and the risk of atrocities are high,” said Othman.
“The attacks reported in Blue Nile, Abyei and near the Sudan-Egypt border reinforce what we have been warning about for months: the conflict is becoming more geographically extensive, more technologically sophisticated and increasingly dangerous for civilians,” he added.
The army and the RSF have been fighting since April 2023, when disagreements about the integration of military forces escalated into war.
The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, amid worsening famine and a deepening humanitarian crisis.

Colombia’s lower house rejects changes to pension reform articles
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:00:20 CET
05:00:20 KST

BOGOTA, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Colombia’s lower house on Wednesday rejected changes to a package of specific articles from a pension reform bill that had been returned to the legislature by the Constitutional Court, which ordered lawmakers to remedy a procedural flaw in the bill.
In August, the Constitutional Court approved most of the 2024 pension system reform, championed by former President Gustavo Petro.
The rejection means the version of the bill approved by the Senate will stand and the court will now need to decide if the procedural flaw has been corrected.
The pension reform aims to strengthen the state-run pension administrator Colpensiones, reduce subsidies for high pensions, provide benefits to women with children, and expand coverage to protect older adults living in poverty.
The bill maintains the retirement age at 62 for men and 57 for women. The law requires all Colombians earning up to 2.3 times the monthly minimum wage — approximately 4 million pesos (about $1,300) — to make contributions to Colpensiones.
Those earning above that amount can choose a private pension fund for the surplus portion of their income.
The measure also stipulates that workers who failed to accumulate enough contribution weeks to qualify for a pension will receive aid, while those in poverty who did not contribute will receive a monthly payment of around $75.
The Petro government estimated more than 2.6 million older adults will benefit from the measures.
Men with 900 weeks of contributions and women with 750 will remain in the current system and will not be required to contribute to the state fund.
Some economic and social initiatives championed by Petro were rejected or faced difficulties gaining approval in Congress, where he lacked solid support. He left office in August and was replaced by right-wing President Abelardo De La Espriella, who has pledged to maintain some of Petro’s popular social reforms.
The reform is one of Colombia’s most significant social policy reforms in years, according to analysts, who note that it would expand the state’s role in the pension system while preserving a role for private funds—an issue that has long divided lawmakers, businesses, and unions.
(Reporting by Carlos Vargas and Nelson Bocanegra; Editing by Kylie Madry)

Early trauma may change how children’s cortisol responses relate to anxiety and behavior problems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:00:04 UTC
05:00:04 KST

Early trauma may shape how children’s stress responses relate to anxiety and behavioral problems, according to a study published in Development and Psychopathology. Among youth who experienced potentially traumatic events before age 6, a smaller cortisol increase during a social stress task predicted a shift over the next two years toward externalizing symptoms rather than anxiety, while a larger increase predicted a shift toward anxiety.
Cortisol is a hormone involved in the body’s response to stress. It can rise when someone faces a challenge, such as speaking in front of an audience. Researchers can measure the total amount of cortisol released across a task, which reflects starting levels, as well as how much cortisol rises during the task. These two measures may capture different aspects of the body’s stress response.
Anxiety and externalizing problems, such as aggression, anger, or rule-breaking, often overlap in children and adolescents. Previous studies have found mixed links between cortisol and these symptoms, with some tying externalizing problems to heightened cortisol responses and others to blunted ones.
Led by Gretchen R. Perhamus of the Medical University of South Carolina, the research team examined whether a history of early trauma helped explain those varying patterns. Their predictions were guided by the adaptive calibration model, a theory proposing that the stress system adjusts to the level of threat in a child’s environment, so that the same stress response may relate to symptoms differently depending on a child’s experiences. They also considered whether cortisol was related to overall symptom levels or to which type of problem was more prominent.
The study included 189 youth ages 8 to 15 (average age about 11; 99 girls and 89 boys) from a larger community study in Charleston, South Carolina. Caregivers and youth were separately interviewed about a wide range of potentially traumatic experiences, including serious accidents, violence, abuse, neglect, separation from a caregiver, and natural disasters.
The researchers classified 107 participants as having experienced at least one such event before age 6, based on either the youth’s or the caregiver’s report, and 82 as having never experienced one at any age, based on both reports. Youth in the early trauma group came from households with lower average incomes and were less likely to be white.
During a laboratory visit, each young person gave a three-minute speech to a camera, as if auditioning for a TV show about kids their age, while a judge watched. The researchers collected saliva samples before and after the speech and during the following recovery period to measure cortisol, and usable cortisol data were available for 145 participants. The youth reported their own anxiety and externalizing symptoms at that visit and again two years later.
For youth with early trauma exposure, higher overall cortisol output during the task was linked with more externalizing symptoms at the same time, and with externalizing problems being more prominent than anxiety. Unexpectedly, higher overall cortisol output was linked with less anxiety in both groups.
Over the following two years, among youth with early trauma, a smaller cortisol increase during the task predicted a shift toward externalizing problems relative to anxiety, while a larger increase predicted a shift toward anxiety. Among youth with no trauma history, a larger cortisol increase predicted a decrease in anxiety over time.
The findings depended on which cortisol measure and symptom comparison the researchers examined. Overall cortisol output was linked to current symptoms, while the rise in cortisol was more informative about later changes in symptom patterns. Several associations among trauma-exposed youth emerged only when the researchers looked at which type of problem was more prominent, rather than at anxiety and externalizing symptoms separately.
The two groups did not differ in their cortisol responses. Among youth with early trauma, the number of early traumatic experiences did not change the links between cortisol and symptoms, although most of these youth had experienced only one or two such events.
Perhamus and colleagues summarized: “the specific pattern of findings was complex and depended on whether models examined concurrent or longitudinal associations, and whether they examined symptom domains or directionality.” In other words, the results did not point to one simple relationship between cortisol and mental health.
Some limitations should be noted. Trauma histories were reported retrospectively, and the researchers did not examine whether youth in the early-trauma group experienced additional traumatic events later in childhood or during the study. Because of the study design, the researchers could not test whether early trauma altered stress responses, which in turn shaped symptoms.
Puberty can also affect the stress system, and although the researchers accounted for pubertal development, it may still have influenced the results. The study measured cortisol without examining other parts of the body’s stress response, used broad measures of anxiety and externalizing problems, and drew on a relatively small community sample, so the authors say the findings need to be replicated.
The study, “Early trauma exposure moderates associations between cortisol reactivity and youth anxiety and externalizing symptoms,” was authored by Gretchen R. Perhamus, Rachel E. Siciliano, Tiffany Phu, Christopher T. Sege, Zachary W. Adams, Jane E. Joseph, Jason E. Chapman, Colleen A. Halliday, Colin Bowyer, Donte L. Bernard, Benjamin L. Hankin, Lisa M. McTeague and Carla Kmett Danielson.

Massive Leak Exposes 41,000 Homeland Security Workers—Including Undercover ICE Agents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:00:00 UTC
05:00:00 KST

An unprecedented leak of Department of Homeland Security records has exposed details of more than 41,000 employees or contractors who work for the department and its constituent agencies. The records include email addresses, phone numbers, and office addresses, but also references to internal systems and sensitive information on undercover and surveillance programs. In all, the leak provides a map of how DHS is organized and how it operates.
The records, which span DHS itself as well as seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection, were last updated on August 19, 2026. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew previewed the data for WIRED, which they say they obtained from a group calling itself the Department of Peace.
DDoSecrets published the archive, which it calls “Icepick,” on Wednesday. In a press release, DDoSecrets says the data is from DHS's Okta login system. In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.”
An Okta spokesperson tells WIRED that it is unaware of any breach of its systems. “We are aware of this report. Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” the spokesperson says.
The leak comes as DHS has aggressively pursued its critics, seeking to unmask anonymous social media users, obtain customer records on protesters, and secure warrants for surveillance tools aimed at reporters. Since the start of the second Trump administration, DHS and the federal government have moved to hide DHS employees’ names and faces. The agency has also expanded its definition of “doxing”—a term that typically refers to publishing someone’s home address and other personal details for malicious purposes—to encompass the publication of basic facts about public employees, like their names and titles.
The leak follows a breach in which a group of hackers known as ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen personal information on nearly every FBI employee and their families. Law enforcement agencies have arrested several suspects and detained another who is alleged to be part of the group.
The DHS records are searchable on a website crimew built. “I don't think we should let them scare us into not looking into them,” she tells WIRED.
The DHS and DOJ did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. The FBI referred WIRED’s inquiry to DHS.
According to a WIRED analysis of the data, CBP staffers account for more than half of the records. ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing. Another 6,200 belong to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and nearly 1,000 are tied to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, more than half of them contractors. Altogether, the files cover about a seventh of DHS’s workforce, revealing how DHS is structured, from senior leadership down to individual immigration agents and detention contractors.
Like most large organizations, DHS uses permission groups to control access to internal systems, according to the leaked records. Nearly everyone named in the leak has access to at least some of these systems. At HSI, 39 employees across more than a dozen field offices belong to groups whose names include “CUC,” which government court filings say stands for “certified undercover operation.” Another group, apparently based in HSI's St. Paul, Minnesota, area of operations, references "Keyhole," which federal court filings describe as a certified undercover operation that recently funded HSI’s undercover surveillance of Minneapolis protest groups earlier this year. Others reference a “Communications Intercept Center TechOps (CICTO) Program,” a “Title III Intercept Program” for wiretaps, and an “Illicit Sensor Intercept Program (ISIP).”
The names of the groups—there are over 55,000 in all—appear to reference tools for accessing immigration court records, pulling data from seized phones, and conducting surveillance. These include Palantir’s Falcon investigative platform and PenLink, which analyzes phone records and social media.
Two permission groups, named “Executive Leadership” and “AI Access,” appear to list people given exceptions to DHS's web filter, which blocks some websites for employees. They contain the same 13 people, including former DHS head Kristi Noem; Antoine McCord, the recently departed DHS chief information officer who has returned to defense tech company Anduril; Philip Hegseth, listed as a senior adviser to the DHS secretary and the younger brother of defense secretary Pete Hegseth; and Jayce Krachenfels, listed as a policy adviser, who previously worked as a regional field director for Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment
Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot. One, called “Grok.com,” includes eight DHS technology officials, including the department’s former chief information officer and chief data officer.
“If authentic and current, this is an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS,” says Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at the threat intelligence company Recorded Future. “This dataset becomes way more valuable when correlated with previously compromised information, commercial data, and other intelligence collections. An adversary could spend months exploiting these relationships to identify vulnerable personnel, develop convincing impersonation attempts, or compromise ongoing investigations.”
More than 700 accounts are associated with a group apparently referencing Signal, the encrypted messaging app, nearly all belonging to CBP personnel. More than 200 CBP accounts belong to a group referencing Mobile Fortify, a face-recognition app that immigration agents use to identify people. The group includes field supervisors, special response team operators, and tactical and intelligence agents. About half are in Texas, California, and Arizona.
Roughly 1,300 ICE enforcement accounts have been created since July 4, 2025, when Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which funded the hiring of 10,000 new ICE Enforcement and Removal officers by the end of 2025.
Nearly 20 accounts appear to belong to personnel with the Department of Defense, which the administration styles as the Department of War; eight are in a group titled “ICE Tip Line DOW Surge.” About 170 accounts are listed as providing “military processing support” at ICE facilities, and 35 others explicitly identify National Guard members.
Dozens of accounts have job titles like “Designated Immigration Officer” and “287(g) Officer,” which mark local law enforcement personnel authorized to carry out some immigration enforcement duties. Many list county sheriff's offices and jails as their workplaces. The records also include roughly 4,400 “associates,” whose jobs range from IT developers and data scientists to nurses and detention officers. Of those, 145 are named as a “contractor” or “high risk contractor.”
More than 300 records reference senior titles associated with DHS headquarters, from Noem down through deputy undersecretaries, assistant secretaries, and chiefs of staff to officials overseeing intelligence, technology, biometrics, and privacy. Most records also name a supervisor, which could allow anyone analyzing the dataset to reconstruct reporting relationships across the department.
The Trump administration has prosecuted protesters for posting information about individual ICE officers and warned others for doing so. In June, 15 Minnesota residents were charged under laws related to stalking and threats of violence, which prosecutors linked to their participation in ICE-opposition activities. More than 100 HSI agents, including undercover operatives, took part in an operation that included widespread surveillance and infiltration of group chats.
Adam Steinbaugh, a senior attorney at the nonprofit civil liberties group FIRE, says that the Trump administration has taken an expansive view of 18 USC 119, a law that prohibits people from sharing “restricted personal information” about federal officers or their families with the intent to threaten them.
“This is information that would be on a business card,” says Steinbaugh of the names and basic work details included in the archive. “That’s not something the government can criminalize."
Despite the potential sensitivity of other records in the leaked data, the creators of Icepick do not consider it doxing. They see it as an accountability tool.
“The DHS especially as an agency completely lacks accountability, despite many parts of it being incredibly unpopular. The people who work there know this too; for example, some of their LinkedIn bios simply say ‘stuff at US Government,’” says crimew. “If they weren't hiding their involvement in the repressive arm of the US government, there would be no need for us to expose them in the first place.”

Costa Rica drops bid to join Pacific trade pact, sacks trade minister
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:59:59 CET
04:59:59 KST

SAN JOSE, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Costa Rica’s government has withdrawn its bid to join the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), a major trans-Pacific trade pact, and dismissed its foreign trade minister, president Laura Fernandez said on Wednesday.
Fernandez said the removal of foreign trade minister Indiana Trejos, who had participated in the negotiations as deputy minister during the previous administration, was due to lack of transparency. The president did not say who is due to replace Trejos.
The decision to scrap the application comes after protests from Costa Rica’s producer groups, especially from the agriculture sector.
The CPTPP is a free trade bloc of 12 nations across the Americas, Asia, Oceania and Europe that accounts for nearly 15% of global gross domestic product.
“Although it might seem like an excellent opportunity, its full content was declared secret by the negotiators to the point that almost no one knows what it entails,” Fernandez said in a video posted on social media.
Costa Rica submitted a request to join the CPTPP in 2022 and held more than 100 high-level meetings to build consensus among members. In November 2024 the bloc formally invited the Central American country form part of the CPTPP.
Since then, Costa Rica has reviewed its regulations against the agreement’s rules and negotiated market access for goods and services.
The CPTPP went into effect in 2018 as an offshoot of the Trans-Pacific Partnership, following the United States’ departure from that proposed trade bloc.
(Reporting by Alvaro Murillo; Writing by Raúl Cortés Fernández, Editing by Iñigo Alexander)

Spanish town rallies to help victims of deadly train crash

By David Latona
URDA, Spain, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Shocked residents of Urda swung into action to help as soon as they heard of Wednesday’s deadly train crash on the railway line a few kilometres from the normally sleepy Spanish town.
Urda’s 78-year-old pharmacist said he was one of the first on the scene, jumping into his car to try to help after his daughter told him of the crash involving two high-speed trains.
Antonio Garcia said that as he approached, the scale of the accident that has so far left at least 68 people dead became clear, with one carriage wedged inside another and scores of bodies.
“Just imagine what was inside,” said Garcia, who brought first aid materials, painkillers and tranquillisers from his pharmacy as well as blankets to help treat the injured.
Garcia described how one passenger who had lost an arm in the crash was calmly asking for an ambulance, while another was saying his final goodbyes to his family.
“His last words were ‘God is good’. For those of us who are believers, these are very beautiful words,” said Garcia.
Other locals brought bottles of water to give to passengers who were evacuated from the two trains.
‘DEVASTATING’
A few hours later, Urda was brimming with police, firefighters and emergency workers from across the region and its local sports hall was converted into a centre for survivors.
The local primary school was reserved for relatives of the victims, where a volunteer psychologist from Madrid called Carmen said she had been helping out since the morning.
“There were many mothers who found out their children had been killed. That was the worst of today. Telling a mother that her child has died in a train crash is devastating,” she said.
Some relatives made the two-hour trip from the Spanish capital Madrid to search for family members.
A woman who gave her name as Ana said she had travelled to Urda after a call from environmental police who had found their dog, Trece, who was on board a train with her husband Pepe.
Ana fought back tears as she described searching for her husband at the crash site, Urda’s sports hall and the primary school, adding that his name was not on any list.
(Reporting by David Latona; Writing by Charlie Devereux; Editing by Alexander Smith)

ULA says Vulcan Rocket Will Launch Again in November After Monthslong Pause
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:59:52 UTC
04:59:52 KST

United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket—sidelined since February after an anomaly—is scheduled to return to flight Nov. 13 to launch a batch of satellites for Amazon’s high-speed internet constellation in low-Earth orbit.
ULA revealed Vulcan’s highly anticipated return date Oct. 28, saying the launch vehicle will fly a redesigned solid rocket booster nozzle that it hopes will correct the issue that caused a Feb. 12 mishap, which the company characterized as a “significant performance anomaly.”
The anomaly occurred during the Space Force’s USSF-87 mission, which carried two satellites for the service’s Geosynchronous Space Situational Awareness Program and a training and demonstration satellite. While the launch was successful—the solid rocket booster anomaly occurred after liftoff—the fallout from the nozzle issue has left Vulcan grounded and has caused significant delays to the slate of military and commercial missions the rocket was scheduled to fly.
“The integrated team has made great strides in improving our understanding of the solid rocket booster anomaly that occurred on the previous Vulcan flight and have identified several potential contributors which have been mitigated through design and process improvements to the nozzle,” ULA said in a statement. “To support our customers, this upcoming launch will utilize the improved nozzle design, and additional testing and analysis will continue in parallel with the mission.”
While the Amazon LEO launch is a welcome step toward resuming regular Vulcan operations, it’s not clear when the rocket will once again carry U.S. military payloads. Brig. Gen. Eric Zarybnisky, the Space Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for space access, told reporters Oct. 21 that his team is “actively working with United Launch Alliance” to resolve the anomaly and understand what level or risk the service is willing to take on some key missions.
“We’re doing our due diligence to make sure that we’re understanding the real fundamental physics that are going on, and making sure we understand what happened and how we correct that,” he said.
The Space Force will collect data from Vulcan’s first few commercial flights and use that to craft a plan for future military missions, Zarybnisky said.
“It’ll depend a lot on what we see, not only on the engineering and tests that we’re doing on the ground, but also what we see from the flight data from the commercial missions they fly,” he said.
ULA and SpaceX are the only two launch providers with rockets currently certified to fly the most sensitive national security space missions, and Vulcan’s grounding has contributed to delays of several key Space Force missions, including the launch of the first Next-Generation Overhead Persistent Infrared missile warning and tracking satellite.
To mitigate those delays, the Space Force has shifted four missions originally scheduled to fly on Vulcan to SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets. According to Space Systems Command, those four include:
- The final GPS III satellite, which was launched on a Falcon 9 in April
- A Space Development Agency Tranche 1 tracking mission that is expected to launch on a Falcon 9 before the end of this year
- A payload stack that includes the Air Force Research Laboratory’s Oracle-M cislunar pathfinder satellite was moved from the USSF-112 mission to the USSF-63 mission, which is scheduled to launch on a Falcon Heavy this year
- A Next-Gen OPIR satellite previously manifested on a Vulcan mission, USSF-50, was moved to SpaceX’s USSF-174 mission, which will fly on a Falcon Heavy rocket
For the payload and full mission swaps, the Space Force will shift a future SpaceX mission back to ULA to launch at a later date rather than cancel the contracts it has in place with ULA.
Zarybnisky noted that while the service has been able to make some trades, not all missions or payloads can easily transfer from one vehicle to another. He said the Space Force meets with the NRO and NASA every two to three months to discuss the government’s manifest and determine how to balance priorities between civil, commercial, and national security missions.
“One of the challenges we see on some swaps is integration timelines and doing the work to understand loads and dynamics and all the analysis work it takes to do that,” he said. “If that work has been done ahead of time, they we can pretty rapidly execute the swaps. If it has not been done, that can drive some of the timelines. And then for some of my customers, there are really hard technical challenges they have, and they just can’t be swapped for specific reasons.”

“Homos‑masturbators” strike back.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:58:08 UTC
04:58:08 KST

Art: Maria Tolstova / Mediazona
What unites a Catholic priest from Kirov, a pensioner from Kurgan, and the author of a poem about a Porsche Cayenne? They all cheered Russia’s ban on the LGBTQ+ community—and then faced prosecution for posting rainbows.
“Right decision,” Vera Makeeva, a pensioner from Kurgan, commented on VK when the Justice Ministry first demanded the “LGBT movement” be banned as an “extremist organisation”.
Half a year later, a local court fined Makeeva 1,500 rubles ($18): a rainbow flag she had posted to her social media was now considered an “extremist symbol.” The administrative protocol was triggered by her repost of homophobic entries featuring the hashtag #YourFavoriteUnicorn and a photo captioned: “Welcome to the LGBT kindergarten! Who is QUEER? Maybe I should join LGBT too? Lesbians are so cool! Let’s draw a rainbow!”
“It’s my own fault—I hadn’t cleaned up my photo albums for 13 years, and people found it who were interested in checking,” Makeeva told Mediazona. “As for the photo, I took it from a Telegram channel and didn’t notice the trail of links. Why did I publish it at all? Because I am fiercely against this filth, and they were in Kurgan too.”
Following the Supreme Court ruling, LGBTQ+ mentions were completely outlawed in Russia. Books, films, and series face total censorship; at least 32 people across 14 regions are facing criminal charges for “LGBT extremism,” and administrative cases for “propaganda” or “extremist symbols” run into the hundreds.
Law enforcement operates on a well-worn track, and Makeeva’s case is far from unique: authorities are regularly charging the authors of overtly homophobic statements under laws meant to suppress the LGBTQ+ community.
Pyotr Voronin, a resident of Pyatigorsk, received one day of arrest for an image that featured both a swastika and a rainbow flag—both of which are considered “extremist symbolism” in Russia.
“I reposted a picture where Zelensky, Macron, and several other European leaders are shown with a fascist swastika and a rainbow. The FSB’s AI decided I was spreading propaganda,” he told Mediazona.
“In court, I asked the judge about patriotic films where actors do the Nazi salute and wear swastikas on their sleeves without being sent to prison,” Voronin said. “But they locked me up for a day, explaining that I considered Zelensky and Macron to be fascist and gay, which is openly advertised in the media. I asked if I should officially apologise to Zelensky. In short, the AI that reads our messages is a complete moron, and we mean nothing to it.”
Voronin’s outrage echoes the 2000s and 2010s, when Russians were routinely punished for publishing swastikas in historical or satirical contexts—from 1945 WWII Victory Parade photos to movie parodies. Only in 2019 was the law amended to allow extremist symbols, provided there is a “negative attitude” and no “propaganda”.
In some cases,courts are now applying this logic to homophobic statements in the context of prosecution for “LGBT extremism.”
Alimardan Ruziev,a host on Yamal’s Nashe Radio (apparently known there under the pseudonym Uncle Alik), published a post with a poem on his VK page in January 2023:
Three years later, an administrative case was opened against him.
Uncle Alik got lucky. He had originally added a disclaimer, so the court noted the illustrations were “placed precisely in a negative light”—and closed the case.
Vladimir Sugakov, a pensioner from Kuzbass, tried a similar defense. He was charged with “LGBT propaganda” for a slideshow of Pride photographs edited to a derogatory song by Sergei Trofimov.
“I created a video criticizing LGBT, but [the police officer] took screenshots and sent them without explanation. The court didn’t bother to figure it out and fined me,” Sugakov complained.
He was fined 100,000 rubles ($1240). According to his VK page, the pensioner is a committed homophobe who regularly uses the slur evropediki—something like “Eurofags”. But Russian courts rarely look into the specific brand of humour used by authors who subsequently claim they meant the exact opposite.
Georgy Rezankov, a 21-year-old teacher of history, social studies, and “fundamentals of homeland security” in Veliky Novgorod, was fined 1,500 rubles ($18) for demonstrating the rainbow flag.
One of his images featured German communists Clara Zetkin and Rosa Luxemburg next to a rainbow with the caption: “Aunt Clara and Aunt Rosa congratulate you on International Women’s Day. Kosher! Fashionable! Youthful!” Another image showed Honkler, a dogwhistling Pepe the Frog variety, wearing a rainbow wig. Following the police’s lead, the court deemed the wig an “extremist” symbol.
Rezankov asked Mediazona not to publish his comments, emphasising his “sincere negative attitude” toward “sodomites.” “And how did you even find me on Tel-agram?” the schoolteacher asked, further showing his antisemitism.
In St. Petersburg, a court blocked a poem titled “It’s Cool to Be Gay” by an anonymous author, despite its aggressively homophobic lyrics: “Let’s hit balls / Like billiard players / But we aren’t athletes / We are homos-masturbators.”
A Moscow resident was fined 100,000 rubles for a video equally homophobic and contemptuous of neo-Nazis. The two-minute clip, titled “Initiation into Nazis (boneheads),” showed a young man shaving his head, putting on skinhead clothing, and having sex with two similar-looking men, ending with a swastika and the phrase “Join our ranks!!!” The court considered this “LGBT propaganda.”
Other recent cases included a student in Karachay-Cherkessia fined 1,000 rubles for an image of Hitler with a rainbow flag, and a Kurgan man investigated for an image of Putin against a rainbow (the latter case was closed for lack of intent).
The court dealt most harshly with Father Grigory (Grzegorz Zwoliński), a Polish Catholic priest living in Kirov.
Father Grigory told Mediazona he has a long-standing public conflict with Paolo Pezzi, the metropolitan of the Moscow Catholic Archdiocese, whom the Polish priest criticizes for supporting the LGBTQ+ community. In February, he published a post about Pezzi, attaching a photo of the bishop next to a rainbow flag to “attract attention”.
“I was summoned to the migration service. It turns out there is a KGB office on the fourth floor,” Father Grigory recalled. “They immediately drew up a protocol saying I published an article. It was actually against LGBT, but there was a photo of Bishop Pezzi and a rainbow flag next to it.”
In court, he drew an analogy to swastikas: “Imagine I published a book about fascism, and on the cover is Hitler or a swastika, but it is against fascism!”
The court ignored the plea, fining him 1,000 rubles.
The priest’s problems did not end there. Because of the court-confirmed violation, Russian authorities annulled his residence permit and issued him a 50-year ban on entering the country. Having lived in Russia for 24 years, he is now unsuccessfully attempting to appeal his deportation from Poland, where he writes online about the revenge of the “rainbow church”.

Cam Green has fallen on the right side of a line-ball call and "that annoying number three" has collected another unwanted record as the Aussies sent Cape Town to sleep on a dominant second day.

1. Unwanted record for 'annoying number three'
The Aussies were cruising.

But things changed with Simon Harmer's entrance into the attack, with the off spinner promptly removing Travis Head for 41 and exposing the under-pressure Marnus Labuschagne.

But the hosts did not get much of an opportunity to enjoy Labuschagne's company, with the Queenslander spending four deliveries trying to work a single before edging to slip to be out for a five-ball duck.
Harmer wheeled away in celebration, joined by a horde of ravenous teammates, as Labuschagne's career crisis continued.

2. Green survives third umpire's Rorschach test
The Proteas were convinced they had their man.
Cam Green had made his way to 22 when he pushed tentatively to a Gerald Coetzee length ball, with his thick edge flying to a stooping Harmer at second slip.
At first glance, it looked to be a regulation grab, with the off-spinner rising then roaring in celebration, but Green was not going anywhere.
After a brief consultation, the umpires decided to send the decision upstairs, where the footage was combed over frame-by-frame.
It was close, with the two camera angles telling two different stories.
Straight on, it could be argued the ball had kissed turf as it nestled into Harmer's hands, but side on, the ball looked to have been collected cleanly.
It was something of a Rorschach Test for the third umpire, and unfortunately for the hosts, he saw the image that kept Green out in the middle.
Only a matter of moments later, it was Renshaw's turn to survive a very close call, with a line-ball LBW decision going the Aussies' way.
3. Sandpaper in the stands
The only remaining member of the trio that was punished for the Sandpapergate scandal in 2018, Steve Smith's 11th hour withdrawal robbed cricket fans of one of the most eagerly anticipated returns in Test history.
But if the Australians thought that meant they wouldn't be reminded of one of their darkest days, some in the Cape Town crowd have ensured they were mistaken.
Video emerged of Nathan Lyon taking his place on the boundary at fine leg on day one, with a cackling spectator leaning forward while holding out a sheet of what looked to be sandpaper.

Lyon declined the offer.
Another fan, wearing a shirt with Smith's sobbing face emblazoned across it, told the Herald Sun he was disappointed the batter wasn't playing, and that he had been looking forward to some "banter".

4. Magic Marco joins rare air
With both Renshaw and Green set and with the luck appearing to go their way, South Africa was in need of something special.
Marco Jansen provided it.
The world's number one ranked bowler provided a fearsome spell in the shadows of tea, dismissing both batters to swing the momentum once again.
Renshaw stood his ground as he just about middled one through to Ryan Rickelton behind the stumps, but was rightly given out for 74 on review, and Green (65) was caught — this time fairly — by Harmer at second slip.
With neither the ball nor pitch appearing to offer very much, it was a seriously impressive five-over spell, and one that saw the 26-year-old take his 100th Test wicket.
In terms of balls bowled, Jansen's 3,864 deliveries saw him become the fifth-fastest bowler to claim a century of scalps, and the third fastest since the 19th century.
5. Carey and Inglis put Cape Town to sleep
Coming together after that Jansen double strike and with Australia's innings at a crossroads at 4-185, Alex Carey and Josh Inglis were composed and circumspect in building their partnership.
The pair were for the most part untroubled in pushing their stand past 100, playing only the shots that were presented to them and offering up few opportunities to the increasingly desperate South Africans.
Not even the second new ball could interrupt their rhythm, with Jansen and Kagiso Rabada unable to emulate Mitchell Starc's stunning spell from late on day one.
But where Starc had low clouds and fading light, the South African spearheads had a placid pitch and still sparkling evening sun.
And in the dying embers of a taxing, 90-over day, some in the Newlands crowd couldn't help but nod off.
Carey (51*) and Inglis (85*) will resume on day three having batted the entire final session and with Australia one run in front.

Russia Equips Geran Drones With Magnetometers for Improved Navigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:57:32 UTC
04:57:32 KST

Russia has equipped its Geran strike drones with magnetometers to improve navigation.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the Ukrainian president’s commissioner for sanctions policy, reported this in a Facebook post, but did not specify the type of magnetometer.
The sensors were found in the drones’ tail sections and vertical stabilizers.
Vlasiuk also said specialists were examining the operating parameters of a new electronic jamming system found on the drones.
As is typical, all the new components and electronic modules are based on Western-made parts.
A magnetometer is an instrument used to measure the characteristics of a magnetic field and changes in that field across space. The device detects small variations in the magnetic background as it moves within Earth’s magnetic field or near large metal objects.
In military applications on drones, the sensor serves as an additional navigation aid. It measures the strength and direction of the natural magnetic field, functioning like an electronic compass.
The device’s primary purpose is to enable autonomous navigation when satellite navigation systems are being actively jammed. A magnetometer can help determine a drone’s heading and spatial orientation without relying on GPS or GLONASS signals.
In addition to magnetometers, Russian developers are equipping strike drones with new electronic jamming systems designed to counter Ukrainian electronic warfare measures.
Ukrainian specialists are already examining the operating parameters of the electronic equipment discovered on the drones.
Militarnyi previously reported that Chinese company Shenzhen Xingkai Technology supplies Russia with equipment for Geran and Gerbera drones, including mesh modems that allow the drones to maintain communications and be controlled during flight.
Journalists found that the manufacturer’s products had been shipped to Russia through the companies Atlant-Engineering and LT Global Forwarding. Customs declarations listed the equipment as antennas and remote-control devices.

US and Japan Finalize Agreement for AMRAAM Facility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:53:39 UTC
04:53:39 KST

At a high-profile meeting of defense ministers in the Philippines this week, U.S. and Japan leaders finalized an agreement to establish a production facility in Japan for the AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, following a massive $20.7 billion Pentagon contract to expand production of the missile over the next seven years.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi announced the agreement in an Oct. 28 press conference after meeting with U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations Defense Ministers’ Meeting.
The agreement is the culmination of an effort that began in July 2024 under both men’s predecessors.
“We finally reached an agreement on the establishment of a final assembly and inspection facility in Japan for the AMRAAM air-to-air missile, which is essential for the F-35,” Koizumi said, according to a translation of his remarks. “This is a groundbreaking agreement that will not only ensure the acquisition of equipment needed by both Japan and the United States, but will also strengthen Japan’s defense industry base.”
In a readout of the two leaders’ meeting, the Pentagon did not mention the AMRAAM facility but said Hegseth “welcomed Japan’s efforts to strengthen its defense industrial capacity, and both leaders committed to continue close coordination on critical munitions production.”
The location for the facility has not yet been announced.
The approval process took more than two years in part because Japan has severe constitutional restrictions on exporting lethal weapons or even coproducing offensive weaponry with allies, which date back to its peace-focused foreign policy following its devastating losses in World War II.
The AMRAAM also contains classified guidance systems and intellectual property that require key safeguards to prevent leaks of crucial information about the weapon.
U.S. and Japanese officials have said the agreement will diversify the AMRAAM industrial base and build regional stockpiles for both the U.S. and its allies at a time when President Donald Trump, and Hegseth and his leadership team at the Pentagon have urged allies to invest more in their own defenses.
AMRAAM has long been the U.S. military’s main dogfighting weapon—the first missiles were delivered in 1988. The latest variant is the AIM-120D, which features GPS guidance and improved range, lethality, and jam-resistance over its predecessors.
All legacy fighters, as well as fifth-generation fighters such as the F-22 Raptor and F-35 Lightning II, can carry the AMRAAM.
In late September, the Pentagon and contractor RTX announced a five-year production contract for AMRAAM with two additional option years valued at up to $20.7 billion. The two sides had previously agreed to a framework agreement in February for AMRAAM and other key munitions.
While the contract award—officially published by the Air Force on Oct. 23—does not specify quantities of missiles, the February framework agreement calls for RTX to increase production “to at least 1,900” per year.
Both the length and size of the new contract are far greater than previous deals. Those usually covered a single year, and demand could whipsaw depending on budgetary pressures or service priorities.
As recently as fiscal 2022, the Air Force budget request called for buying just 186 AMRAAMs and the Navy requested none. Those totals wound up changing through reprogramming requests and congressional adds, but generally speaking, procurement stayed at or below 400 missiles between the services from fiscal 2017 to 2022.
AMRAAM Procurement
Source: Department of Defense Program Acquisition Cost by Weapon System reports. 2026 totals not finalized.
This new award expands the Pentagon’s multiyear procurement authorities, covering Lots 41-47. Those lots include fifth-generation technology in AIM-120D-3 variants, such as modernized processors and software-defined measures for the electronic warfare threat.
The deal is part of a broader effort by President Donald Trump’s administration to secure multiyear deals for munitions and aircraft, aiming to break the stop-and-start funding cycles of the past few decades.
The contract also increases output to other countries, with foreign military sales to 16 international partners for additional procurement pipelines included.
“We are accelerating output to record levels to deliver this critical capability for the U.S. services and more than 40 allied nations,” an RTX spokesman told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email.
“We have invested heavily over the past several years to expand capacity, modernize manufacturing, and strengthen our supply chain,” the spokesman wrote. “RTX proactively sourced $80 million in test equipment before any award. These investments will ramp annual production over the coming years to at least 1,900 AMRAAM missiles.”
The company is currently delivering previously contracted AMRAAMs, but the new multiyear contract helps avoid delivery interruptions, the spokesman wrote.
AMRAAM production has faced bottlenecks from a variety of issues, including subcontractor component supply chain problems and solid rocket motor production lag times.
“Like many advanced defense systems, AMRAAM relies on complex components that have long lead times,” the spokesman wrote. “Through sustained investment, supplier partnerships, and efforts such as new U.S. rocket motor production lines coming online in 2027, we are building faster than ever before.”

Peltola campaign aides, DSCC officials helped recruit second Dan Sullivan in Alaska race: NYT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:52:06 UTC
04:52:06 KST

People working with Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola's campaign and senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee participated in efforts to recruit a man named Daniel J. Sullivan to enter the Alaska Senate contest, in a bid to draw votes away from incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, The New York Times reported Wednesday.
The Times — citing interviews, texts and documents prepared for a potential lawsuit against Peltola's campaign — reported that "not only did Ms. Peltola's team work with people trying to recruit Mr. Sullivan to run for Senate, but the effort was much broader."
"The group worked to coax other would-be spoilers into the race, to dilute the incumbent's support and help catapult the Democrat to victory," the newspaper reported.
Peltola's former campaign manager Elisa Rios told the Times that Peltola was not directly involved in the project, but she was "definitely aware," according to the report.
The Times noted Rios last week tried to retract comments she made confirming the effort to recruit spoilers.
Peltola's campaign and the DSCC "denied participating in efforts to recruit spoilers to the ballot in Alaska," The Times said.
The newspaper's report noted ballot-stacking tactics are "common in politics and generally considered legal — and have been employed by both parties in Alaska."
The report comes days after the Department of Justice filed a lawsuit allegingthe campaign by the non-incumbent Sullivan was geared toward him acting as a spoiler for the incumbent Sullivan because of voter confusion.
The DOJ has asked a federal judge in Alaska to block certification of any Senate race result "that may be impacted by voter confusion ... pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."
The winner of the election could determine whether Democrats regain a majority in the Senate, or if Republicans retain their current majority.
President Donald Trump has said he ordered the DOJ's lawsuit.
After the Times published its report, Trump demanded that Peltola and Daniel J. Sullivan both be removed from Alaska's election ballot.
Trump, in a Truth Social post, claimed the report showed Democrats "illegally" sought out the same-named man "in order to defraud, confuse, and obfuscate the Election, thereby taking votes away from the REAL Senator, Dan Sullivan."
Peltola's campaign, in a statement to CNBC on The Times article, said, "The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign. Like Mary, our campaign is focused on lowering costs and fixing the rigged system in DC."
A DSCC spokesperson in a statement to CNBC said, "The DSCC is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan."
"Republicans have a long history of recruiting and propping up candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns – including recruiting a prisoner with a New York address to run against Mary Peltola and spending nearly half a million dollars to secure a spot on the ballot in Alaska for an Arizona resident in the Senate race this cycle," the spokesperson said.
The spokesperson pointed to several examples of Republicans promoting third-party and dark horse candidates in the current election cycle and past ones to increase chances of a GOP candidate winning a race.
Peltola's campaign and DSCC, as well as Alaska's election officials, have asked the judge overseeing the DOJ's lawsuit, Sharon Gleason, to dismiss the suit before Election Day, Nov. 3. The League of Women Voters of Alaska and the advocacy group Common Cause have also sought to intervene in the case to oppose the DOJ's efforts.
Alaska officials said the DOJ "lacks authority to intervene in state elections at all, much less in support of a favored candidate," and that the lawsuit and "requested relief cast a cloud over Alaska's election."
State officials said in a court filing that Alaska's Division of Elections "has taken significant steps to distinguish" between the two Sullivans on the ballot, "so that voters can easily determine which candidate is which."
Gleason on Monday evening fast-tracked the case, increasing the chance she will decide whether to dismiss the case in U.S. District Court in Anchorage before Election Day.
Daniel J. Sullivan prevailed in a legal fight that ended with the Alaska Supreme Court allowing him on the nonpartisan primary ballot over the opposition of state election officials who argued his presence would confuse voters.
He won enough votes in that contest to win a place as one of four candidates on the general election ballot.
On that ballot, his name is spelled out "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr." with no other words next to it.
Directly below his name, Sen. Sullivan is listed as Sullivan, Dan. S. with the words "Registered Republican, incumbent" next to his name in parentheses.
Peltola, a former U.S. House member, is the only Democrat on the ballot.
Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, which allows voters to rank candidates by preference. That method could allow voters to rank both Sullivans as choices, allowing a vote for the non-incumbent to be transferred to the incumbent senator if the non-incumbent is eliminated in the first round of counting.
The Times quoted Peltola's former campaign manager Rios, who the newspaper reported was fired in August, as saying, "Alaskan voters need to know" about the effort to recruit others into the race.
"There was a lot of speculation, and voters should get the full picture when making their decisions," Rios was quoted as saying.
Rios told The Times last week that she wanted to retract her prior statements.
"As discussed on our call earlier today, I am confirming that I have retracted all statements made regarding the 2026 Alaska Senate Race in connection with any article you may or may not be writing," Rios wrote, according to The Times. "I am not willing to be a source for any story in any capacity."
The newspaper said it told Rios she would be part of its article, and noted her interviews "were consistent with The Times's other reporting."

UN human rights chief Volker Turk on Wednesday called sanctions imposed on UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese “not acceptable,” Anadolu reports.

Alliance response must be credible if Russia uses nuclear weapons, former NATO Director of Nuclear Policy says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:51:00 UTC
04:51:00 KST

Alliance response must be credible if Russia uses nuclear weapons, former NATO Director of Nuclear Policy says
Jim Stokes, a GLOBSEC expert and former NATO Director of Nuclear Policy (2023–2025), made the remarks in an interview with Ukrinform.
“In this hypothetical situation, if Russia uses nuclear weapons, NATO will have to respond... The response must be credible,” Stokes said.
He recalled NATO’s stated readiness to inflict damage far exceeding any potential gains. The response could involve nuclear weapons, conventional weapons, or a combination of both. The decision would be made at a later stage, as it would be unwise to reveal to an adversary where these red lines lie or exactly how a response might be formulated and carried out, the former NATO official emphasized.
Stokes said that in an emergency or during a crisis, the Alliance could make political decisions and implement them very quickly. He added that member states were also capable of acting independently and swiftly. The United States, the United Kingdom, and France could each independently employ their nuclear forces to deter aggression against the Alliance, not just a nuclear attack. Stokes described this as a major advantage for NATO.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and NATO’s designation of Russia as a threat to the Alliance, NATO has been adapting its nuclear deterrence posture, including by modernizing its nuclear forces. Exercises and preparations for a potential NATO nuclear operation demonstrate that the Alliance is capable of carrying one out effectively with its current capabilities and force posture, the former official said.
He noted that NATO aircraft could deliver free-fall nuclear bombs. Some advocate the option of launching missiles from sea-, land-, or air-based platforms. In Stokes’s view, all options should remain on the table.
As previously reported, British and French fighter jets conducted joint exercises over the Mediterranean for the first time in October, involving French nuclear forces and demonstrating deeper defense cooperation between the two countries amid tensions with Russia. In July 2025, the two countries agreed to deepen their cooperation on nuclear deterrence in response to growing threats to Europe and uncertainty over the role of the United States as an ally.

Ukraine Rolls Out Amphibious UGVs to Brave1 Market After 40-Km Combat Mission

Ukraine Rolls Out Amphibious UGVs to Brave1 Market After 40-Km Combat Mission
Ukraine has added a new category of amphibious unmanned ground vehicles to the Brave1 Market , allowing military units to order robotic systems capable of moving across both land and water, Ukraine’s Defence Ministry reported on October 28.
The ministry stated that three amphibious UGV models are already available on the platform, with additional systems expected to be added later. Military units will eventually be able to order them through Ukraine’s ePoints program .
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The deployment forms part of Ukraine’s growing use of unmanned ground systems for frontline logistics and other high-risk missions. By mid-August, Ukrainian UGVs had completed more than 100,000 missions in place of soldiers since the beginning of 2026.
Amphibious UGVs are designed for frontline logistics in areas where rivers, canals, wetlands, or damaged terrain can block conventional ground routes. The systems retain high mobility on land and can switch within seconds to moving through water, according to Ukraine’s Defence Ministry.
The ministry noted that Brave1 and the Defence Ministry have been developing the amphibious systems market to accelerate their deployment to Ukrainian units. Brave1 launched a dedicated grant program for amphibious UGVs in June 2026, while developers have continued refining the systems using feedback from frontline troops.
The technology has already been tested in combat. Soldiers from the Alter Ego unit of Ukraine’s 93rd Separate Mechanized Brigade recently completed what the ministry described as the world’s first combat logistics mission using an amphibious ground robot.
The vehicle traveled more than 40 kilometers across land and water before successfully delivering food and ammunition to Ukrainian positions.
Ukraine is also expanding unmanned aerial systems into battlefield casualty evacuation. UNITED24 Media previously reported that Ukrainian troops used the StarGate aerial CASEVAC drone to evacuate two seriously wounded soldiers in one week, including one mission covering nearly 60 kilometers round trip despite Russian GPS jamming.
