Lula’s victory once again showed Latin America is not US backyard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:17:21 UTC
04:17:21 KST

Lula’s victory once again showed Latin America is not US backyard
TEHRAN — History has a peculiar way of embarrassing those who believe political opponents can simply be imprisoned, exiled or erased. Nelson Mandela walked out of prison after 27 years and became South Africa’s first Black president. Juan Perón returned to Argentina after nearly two decades in exile and reclaimed the presidency.
In Brazil, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has written his own chapter in this tradition. A former factory worker and trade unionist who rose to the presidency, endured imprisonment and returned to power, Lula represents something that political establishments have repeatedly underestimated: the resilience of popular movements.
His political journey carries significance beyond Brazil’s borders. At a time when Washington seeks to consolidate its influence across Latin America and Israel faces growing international opposition over its treatment of Palestinians, Lula has refused to surrender Brazil’s independent political voice. His solidarity with Palestine is particularly significant.
Wearing a Palestinian keffiyeh, Lula publicly identified himself with the Palestinian people, turning a familiar symbol of resistance into a statement of political defiance. His criticism of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza has likewise challenged the Western assumption that solidarity with Palestinians must remain subordinate to Washington’s strategic preferences. For Lula, the Palestinian question is not separate from the broader struggle over sovereignty, dignity and the right of nations to determine their own future.
The October 25 presidential election demonstrated that this independence still commands substantial support at home. Brazil entered the final weeks of campaigning deeply polarized. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, led the first round by approximately 2.22 million votes. Most electoral calculations favored the challenger. Lula faced a deficit no candidate had previously overturned in 
 
Brazil’s modern presidential runoffs. Yet elections are not decided by opinion polls alone. 
Between October 4 and October 25, Lula's campaign transformed an apparent mathematical disadvantage into a nationwide mobilization. Workers, students, rural communities and social movements returned to the streets.
The Landless Rural Workers' Movement (MST) helped sustain the grassroots offensive, while an energetic digital campaign challenged the right's political narrative. The result was historic. Lula secured 51.79 percent of valid votes against Bolsonaro's 48.21 percent, winning by more than 4.43 million ballots.
The overall electoral margin shifted by approximately 6.66 million votes between the two rounds. For the first time in Brazil's modern presidential history, a candidate who finished second in the opening round emerged victorious in the runoff.
The victory also exposed the limitations of treating working-class voters as an electoral constituency to be courted every four years rather than an organized political force. Lula's achievements, including Bolsa Família, minimum-wage increases, expanded university access and support for family farming, established that poverty was not an unavoidable national condition.
Public policy could change millions of lives. But Brazil's economic contradictions remain unresolved. Wealth, land and financial power are still concentrated in relatively few hands. Conservative parliamentary forces, expensive credit and fiscal restrictions continue to constrain the government's ability to deliver deeper reforms.
Lula's fourth mandate will therefore demand more than preserving previous social achievements. Agrarian reform, industrial development, public investment and greater economic participation by ordinary Brazilians must become central priorities. The movements that rescued his electoral campaign must also have a meaningful role in shaping his government's direction.
Beyond Brazil, however, the election delivered an uncomfortable message to Washington. Donald Trump had considerable political reasons to prefer a Bolsonaro presidency. A right-wing government in Brasília would have strengthened his administration's attempt to consolidate a sympathetic regional bloc through the Shield of the Americas initiative, launched in Miami in March 2026.
Brazil is not an insignificant prize. It is Latin America's largest economy, a founding BRICS member and a country possessing enormous agricultural, energy and mineral resources. Its strategic independence complicates Washington's ambition to maintain the Western Hemisphere as an exclusive American sphere of influence.
Trump's reaction to the election was revealing. Rather than welcoming Brazil's democratic verdict, he publicly questioned the legitimacy of Lula's victory without substantiating his allegations. Bolsonaro initially challenged the outcome before his party acknowledged the result. There is a familiar contradiction here. Washington celebrates democracy when elections produce governments compatible with American interests, yet becomes considerably less enthusiastic when voters choose an independent political direction.
For Iran, this contradiction requires little explanation. From the 1953 Anglo-American coup against Mohammad Mossadegh to decades of sanctions and coercive diplomacy, Tehran has experienced the consequences of Washington's determination to shape other nations' political choices. Brazil and Iran have different political systems and national priorities, but both recognize the importance of a multipolar international order in which sovereignty is not conditional upon American approval. Their participation in BRICS provides an institutional platform for strengthening South-South cooperation and reducing excessive dependence on Western dominated economic structures.
Lula's position on Palestine gives this broader political argument an unmistakable moral dimension. In February 2026, he wore a Palestinian keffiyeh presented by Palestinian Ambassador Marwan Jebril during a diplomatic ceremony in Brasília. The image captured something that Western governments have increasingly attempted to suppress: public identification with Palestinians as a people entitled to dignity, freedom and statehood.
Lula has also challenged Israel's conduct in Gaza, refusing to accept that Palestinians’ suffering should be treated as an unfortunate footnote to Israeli security. His position exposes the double standards of a Western political establishment that invokes international law against its adversaries while repeatedly accommodating Israeli aggression. This does not make Lula an ideological counterpart of Iran, nor does it erase differences between their governments. It demonstrates something more important: opposition to Israeli policies and American unilateralism extends far beyond West Asia. It is increasingly part of a wider international demand for political independence and equal application of international law.
Brazil's election has not dismantled American influence in Latin America, nor has it eliminated the far right. Bolsonaro received nearly 60 million votes, demonstrating that the political forces behind his campaign remain formidable. Nevertheless, Lula's victory has disrupted Washington's preferred regional trajectory and given progressive movements across Latin America renewed political confidence.
Mandela's freedom did not automatically dismantle South Africa's economic inequalities. Perón's return did not resolve Argentina's political divisions. Lula's reelection will not, by itself, transform Brazil's entrenched economic structures. But history offers another lesson through these extraordinary political returns: powerful establishments may imprison leaders, manufacture political isolation and declare popular movements defeated. What they cannot always control is whether the people accept that verdict. On October 25, Brazil refused to accept it. And Washington was reminded, once again Latin America is not its backyard, the Strait of Hormuz is not its playground, and neither Brazil nor Iran needs America’s permission to defend their sovereignty.

The popular commander had been assigned to lead the pioneering new drone branch of Ukraine's military back in 2024, but was dismissed after less than a year in the job, amid reported disagreements with then-Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi.
Since then, Sukharevskyi has spent over a year in de facto wilderness as deputy commander of Ukraine's Eastern Group of Forces, a temporary command umbrella covering most of the eastern front line.
His return is part of a larger ongoing reshuffle of Ukraine's high command launched by Syrskyi's replacement, Mykhailo Drapatyi, in an effort to distance the military leadership from his predecessor's Soviet-style leadership culture.
Sukharevskyi etched his name in the history of Ukraine's resistance to Russian aggression in April 2014, when, as a senior lieutenant in the 80th Airborne Brigade, he ordered his troops to open fire on Russian proxy forces in Sloviansk, the first shots fired in Ukraine's effort to quash Moscow's fake "separatist" uprising in Donbas.
In the first years of the full-scale war, Sukharevskyi commanded the 59th Motorized Brigade, one of the key units which liberated the city of Kherson from Russian occupation.
Ukraine's Marine Corps — officially part of the country's navy — has traditionally specialized in amphibious warfare, similar to the Russian and U.S. equivalents.
Since the full-scale invasion, Ukrainian Marine brigades have fought in some of the most intense hotspots of the front line, from Mariupol, Pokrovsk, and Kostiantynivka in Donetsk Oblast, to the daring but costly Krynky offensive across the Dnipro River over 2023 and 2024.

US Fed Chair Warsh warns inflation remains too high as energy prices climb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:13:30 UTC
04:13:30 KST

Gökhan Ergöçün
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh warned on Wednesday that inflation remains too high after running above the central bank's 2% target for nearly six years, pledging readiness to act as needed to restore price stability.
Speaking at a news conference after the Federal Open Market Committee voted to keep the benchmark interest rate at 3.75% to 4%, Warsh said policymakers focused their two-day discussions mainly on curbing price pressures.
"Real activity is clearly pointing in the right direction; that's good news, but inflation is too high," Warsh said.
"Energy and related prices have moved higher again in recent weeks, and our job is to ensure that relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden out across the economy, and that inflation expectations remain as they are anchored," he added.
Warsh noted that US economic growth has strengthened, with gross domestic product expansion in the first half of 2026 revised up to 2.4% from an earlier estimate of 1.8%.
Third-quarter growth appears to have accelerated further, driven by consumer spending running above 3% and business investment rising at a double-digit pace, he said.
Capital expenditures have reached a historically high share of gross domestic product, led by high-tech investment alongside broader gains across other sectors, he added.
On the labor market, Warsh described employment conditions as "quite positive," pointing to a lower jobless rate compared to a year ago, faster payroll growth and a four-week moving average of unemployment claims near multi-decade lows.
Following the Fed's policy action in September, financial and credit conditions have tightened for some businesses and households as market participants become more selective in capital allocation, Warsh said.
"And while overall financial conditions are tighter, I'm unwilling and unable to call them tight," he said, adding that the shift supports longer, more durable economic growth and price stability.
Warsh also announced an institutional overhaul of the Federal Open Market Committee's meeting schedule starting in the fall of 2027.
While the committee will continue to hold eight meetings per year, one meeting in 2027 will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy without an interest rate vote or a policy statement, leaving seven regular rate-setting meetings.
In 2028, the central bank expects to dedicate two meetings to long-term strategy discussions and six to setting monetary policy, Warsh said.
"It's equally important we reserve time and space, as an intellectually diverse group, for strategic deliberations — for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons," he added.

US-Iran war bill reaches $47.1 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:06:56 UTC
04:06:56 KST

US-Iran war bill reaches $47.1 billion
TEHRAN — The cost of the US war against Iran reached an estimated $47.1 billion by October 16, with bombs, missiles and other munitions accounting for more than 60% of the total, according to figures the Pentagon provided to US lawmakers, The New York Times reported.
The estimate, disclosed to congressional national security committees last week, highlights the mounting financial burden of the military campaign launched by the United States and Israel against Iran on February 28, as well as the pressure on American weapons inventories and military resources.
Despite US President Donald Trump holding back, at least for the time being, from resuming major combat operations, the Pentagon incurred an additional $3.5 billion in costs over approximately six weeks, compared with the estimates previously shared with Congress.
The figures provide an unusual, unclassified breakdown of the expenses incurred by the US armed services, including the costs of deploying forces, maintaining military operations, replacing damaged equipment and transporting supplies.
However, congressional officials cautioned that the $47.1 billion estimate does not represent the full financial cost of the war, with several significant expenditures still excluded from the Pentagon’s accounting.
Munitions account for $29 billion
According to the figures cited by The New York Times, the US military has spent approximately $29 billion on munitions since the war began, making bombs, missiles and other weapons the largest component of the reported expenditure.
The extensive use of ammunition has depleted global inventories of several critical weapons, including Patriot air-defense interceptors, while supplies have also been diverted from US military commands in Europe and Asia to support operations related to the war.
The scale of the expenditure raises questions about the sustainability of prolonged high-intensity military operations and the resources required to replenish depleted stockpiles.
The Pentagon has also spent $6.1 billion replacing dozens of damaged or destroyed combat aircraft, weapons systems, and other military equipment.
These replacement costs illustrate how the financial burden extends beyond the direct expenditure on weapons used in combat to include the loss of valuable military assets.
Air Force, Navy and Army face mounting costs
The Pentagon’s breakdown shows that the US Air Force has spent approximately $7.6 billion operating dozens of fighter and bomber squadrons involved in the military mission.
The Navy has incurred around $1.5 billion in costs associated with deploying more than two dozen warships, including several aircraft carriers, while maintaining Army forces in the region has cost approximately $2.1 billion.
According to US Central Command, more than 50,000 American troops are assigned to the war mission.
The figures also reveal additional expenditures on specialized military operations and logistical support. The Pentagon has spent $645 million to deploy and sustain several thousand Special Operations personnel in the region.
US Transportation Command has incurred $92.2 million in costs for moving supplies and equipment, while US Cyber Command has spent $14 million on cyber support operations.
A congressional official, speaking anonymously to discuss information provided to lawmakers, also disclosed that $24.5 million had been spent on internal medical support for US service members.
The Pentagon has reported that 18 American service members have been killed and more than 860 injured in the war.
Official estimate excludes major expenses
Despite the scale of the reported spending, congressional officials said the actual cost of the war was almost certainly higher than the Pentagon’s estimate.
According to The New York Times, the administration’s calculations excluded $1.5 billion in fuel and other expenses that the Trump administration had requested through a supplemental funding proposal intended to cover the war’s costs.
The estimate also did not include the cost of repairing or rebuilding US military facilities damaged or destroyed by Iranian attacks, including the US Navy’s base in Manama, Bahrain.
The Pentagon has indicated that some damaged facilities could be closed permanently or left unreconstructed. However, if the US military or host countries decide to rebuild them, congressional officials estimate that the bill could reach tens of billions of dollars.
Such expenses could substantially increase the overall financial burden, particularly if Washington decides to restore damaged infrastructure while simultaneously replenishing weapons inventories and maintaining its regional military presence.
The extent of the additional costs remains uncertain, and the figures disclosed so far should therefore be treated as a partial accounting rather than a final assessment of the war’s financial consequences.
Washington seeks up to $70 billion in additional military funding
The disclosure comes as US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the Trump administration seek as much as $70 billion in emergency military spending to cover the costs of the war against Iran and finance additional weapons and personnel.
The request underscores the growing financial demands associated with the campaign, particularly as the Pentagon faces the dual challenge of sustaining military operations and replacing equipment and ammunition already expended or lost.
The unclassified figures provided to Congress offer a rare glimpse into the financial accounting of a war whose costs have largely remained undisclosed by the Pentagon’s senior leadership.
The reported $47.1 billion in spending, combined with excluded fuel costs, potential reconstruction expenses and the administration’s request for additional funding, indicates that the final bill could rise substantially beyond the amount currently acknowledged.
For Washington, the financial consequences extend beyond the immediate costs of military operations to the long-term task of replenishing strategic weapons reserves, restoring damaged facilities and maintaining military readiness across other regions.
The Pentagon has not immediately responded to The New York Times’ request for comment on the figures.
While the final cost of the war remains undetermined, the disclosed estimates highlight the considerable financial resources consumed by the US military campaign and the additional expenditures Washington may face as it addresses the consequences of the conflict.

Knesset stalemate plunges Israel into political paralysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:05:47 UTC
04:05:47 KST

Knesset stalemate plunges Israel into political paralysis
Netanyahu loses his majority, Eisenkot cannot win one, and the wars go on
TEHRAN — Israel voted in record numbers on October 27 and produced a parliament nobody can run.
With more than 85 percent of ballots counted as of writing this, Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc held 53 seats, down from the 68 his coalition controlled. Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's bloc had 48. Arab parties had 19. A government needs 61, and nobody is close.
Double-envelope ballots from soldiers, diplomats, and others away from home, more than half a million, are still being counted, and certified results are due by November 4.
This was Israel's sixth election since 2019, and like the other five, it delivered a verdict on Netanyahu and nothing else.
Turnout reached 77.7 percent, the highest since 1999, and more than seven points above 2022. Likud fell to roughly 27 seats from 32.
Eisenkot's Yashar took 21, Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid's joint list about 12, Yair Golan's Democrats 8, Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beiteinu 7.
On the other side, Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit kept seven and Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism six. Three years into the war, millions queued to pick its next manager.
Arab voters sink the right's majority
Palestinian "citizens" inside the Israeli regime, a fifth of the population, voted at an estimated 75 to 80 percent.
The Joint List and Ra'am nearly doubled their combined strength from 10 seats in 2022 to 19, the best "Arab" showing in Israeli history.
Netanyahu helped them along. All day Tuesday, he and Ben-Gvir warned followers about Arab turnout, and Likud paid crews to film Arab voters outside polling stations.
The legal center Adalah described stalled admissions and missing Arabic ballot slips. Joint List chair Yousef Jabareen said his voters had sent the fascist government "to the dustbin of history."
The arithmetic that sinks Netanyahu does nothing for his rival. Add the Arab seats to Eisenkot's 48, and the anti-Netanyahu side reaches 67.
But Eisenkot promised a "Zionist government," and Bennett, Lapid, and Liberman have ruled out the Arab parties outright. Eisenkot has said he would consider them only if they recognize Israel as "a Jewish state" and condemn Hamas. Golan alone broke ranks.
Four ways out, none of them open
After certification, President Isaac Herzog will pick a nominee. He is not obliged to choose the biggest party's leader.
That person gets 28 days, extendable by 14. If he fails, a second nominee gets a turn, and after that the Knesset heads for dissolution. Herzog has urged parties to keep an "open mind."
A Netanyahu coalition is the longest shot. He is eight seats short. Even if three of Eisenkot's lawmakers defected, he would reach 56 against 64.
Bennett and Liberman have both served in Netanyahu’s governments and walked out, and both campaigned on ousting him. Liberman also refuses to sit with the ultra-Orthodox parties over conscription.
A unity government is the option Washington has floated. The Washington Post reports Netanyahu's allies are pushing it, that Trump's envoys are receptive, and that it would let Netanyahu shed Ben-Gvir.
Eisenkot refuses to serve under him, rotation included. The only version that works on paper is Likud without Netanyahu, plus Yashar, Bennett, and Liberman: about 67 seats. Likud would have to dump its longtime leader.
Trump, who endorsed Netanyahu twice, claimed credit Wednesday for a "come-from-behind stalemate."
An Eisenkot minority government is the realistic alternative and the riskiest. He trails the Netanyahu bloc by five seats and needs at least six votes from outside his camp.
Jabareen says the Joint List will help remove Netanyahu, and Ra'am sat in the Bennett-Lapid government in 2021. But Eisenkot's own partners recoil from relying on Arab votes, and a handful of defections to Likud would sink it. Expect Netanyahu's operatives to work the phones.
A seventh election, likely in spring 2027, may suit both leaders better than compromise. Netanyahu would stay caretaker throughout, with a wartime premier's full powers.
On election night, he called this a "historic, one-time opportunity" to "finish Iran" alongside Trump. A new phase of hot war may freeze the political calendar in his favor.
Same wars, new cabinet
No outcome touches Israel's wars of aggression. Eisenkot, who laid out the Dahiyeh Doctrine of punishing civilian areas in 2008, promises to "destroy Hamas" within 18 months. Bennett calls a change of government in Iran "a must." Lapid wants Iranian energy facilities bombed.
Liberman has said Gaza holds no innocents. When five opposition leaders signed a September pact for a "Zionist, statesmanlike government," none of them even got close to accepting that the war on Gaza is a genocide, a conclusion a UN commission reached in 2025.
Israel holds about two-thirds of Gaza, and 1,493 Palestinians have been killed there since the ceasefire, by one count. Settlers beat a man in Burqa, near Nablus, as Israelis voted, while the army sealed every West Bank crossing.
Netanyahu enters the coming weeks as caretaker, under indictment, with his war powers intact. His possible successors have offered Palestinians, Lebanese, and Iranians the same wars with some changes in appearance.

Fed leaves interest rates unchanged despite inflation in the US
Rates will remain 3.75-4 percent even as inflation continues to rise.
The United States Federal Reserve is set to hold interest rates steady in its final monetary policy decision before the US midterm elections.
The central bank will maintain rates at 3.75-4 percent, following a 10-2 vote, in line with expectations.
CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, indicated that there was more than a 90 percent chance rates would remain unchanged.
“Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace,” the Fed said in its press release announcing the decision on Wednesday. “While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.”
The Fed noted how inflation continues to rise.
It also added, “The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 percent goal.”
The most recent Consumer Price Index (CPI) report showed the annual inflation rate increasing to 3.7 percent in September, up from 3.4 percent in August, with energy prices largely accounting for the monthly surge.
There were signs earlier this month that the central bank would maintain benchmark interest rates, with the Fed’s chair for supervision, Michelle Bowman, advocating a “wait and see” approach.
“I don’t feel any urgency for taking further action at this point,” she said at this month’s International Monetary Fund-World Bank meetings in Bangkok, Thailand. “We really need to take some time and understand how things will evolve.”
The decision comes before Thursday’s release of the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index report, which is used by the central bank to assess inflation and inform its decisions.
Today’s Fed announcement follows an interest-rate hike rise last month, amid surging inflation – the first increase by the central bank since July 2023. The move drew criticism from US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly pressed the Fed to cut rates since taking office. At the time, he wrote on Truth Social that “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less.”
The Fed’s next monetary policy meeting is scheduled for December 8-9, when it will give its final rate decision of the year.
Current forecasts point to a quarter-point interest rate increase.

Stoyanov announced the attack during a meeting with his counterparts from Romania and Türkiye in Sofia, Bulgarian National Television (BNT) reported on October 28.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"While this meeting was taking place, a container ship was struck by three naval drones in the adjacent waters. The distance is approximately 21 miles from Shabla," Stoyanov stated.
The vessel, identified as CONTSHIP JET, was traveling from Haifa, Israel, toward Constanța, Romania, when it was attacked near Cape Kaliakra, inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.

The three NATO members also agreed to establish a trilateral coordination mechanism for Black Sea security. The initiative will involve regular consultations, improved intelligence sharing, enhanced maritime surveillance, and stronger early-warning capabilities.
Stoyanov confirmed that the countries had adopted a joint statement and planned further political-level talks in Bucharest and military expert consultations in Ankara.

US jury convicts Rwandan American of lying about role in genocide
Jurors heard competing witness testimony on where Eric Nshimiye was and what he was doing in April 1994.
A federal jury in Boston, Massachusetts, has convicted a Rwandan American man of perjury and obstruction of justice for lying about his role in the 1994 Rwandan genocide.
Eric Nshimiye, a 55-year-old father of four and a United States citizen, was accused of lying in his testimony in a 2019 trial, also in Boston, for Jean Leonard Teganya, a former medical school roommate who was later convicted of helping to perpetrate the genocide. At the time, Nshimiye told the court neither he nor his friend had taken part in the killing and rape of Tutsis in Butare, where the pair were studying at a medical university.
Investigators from the US Department of Homeland Security arrested Nshimiye at his home in Ohio in 2024, alleging he had lied to them in an interview about his time in Rwanda during the genocide.
Nshimiye was originally charged with multiple counts of perjury, obstruction of justice and committing fraud on his immigration paperwork because prosecutors said he had told immigration officials he did not take part in the genocide when he moved to the US several years after the violence. He became a US citizen in 2009.
The immigration charge was dropped by prosecutors before the trial began. On Tuesday, the jury convicted Nshimiye on four counts of perjury and one count of obstruction of justice.
“For nearly three decades, this defendant concealed his involvement in the 1994 Rwandan genocide and the heinous acts of violence he committed, including clubbing people to death,” Assistant Attorney General A Tysen Duva in the Department of Justice’s Criminal Division said in a statement on Wednesday. “Then, he lied to immigration officials in order to become a US citizen, and he lied to a federal jury to protect himself and a fellow perpetrator of the Rwandan genocide.”
After the verdict, Nshimiye’s attorneys filed a request with the court to count the time he had already spent in prison before the trial towards any sentence. In a court filing, the attorneys argued Nshimiye should be set free because the two and a half years he had already spent in custody were longer than the usual sentence for the charges he was convicted of.
Nshimiye’s family, including his US-born children, were in attendance when the verdict was announced in court.
“It was quite shocking, difficult to process at first because we were expecting a different outcome. We were expecting to bring him home,” his son Tresor Nshimiye, told Al Jazeera.
Prosecutors brought a series of experts to help the jury understand the scope of the crimes in Rwanda, starting with academics who pointed out where the country was on a map of Africa.
Witnesses from Rwanda told jurors they recalled Nshimiye taking part in killings and other violence in Butare directed at minority Tutsis in 1994. They were part of a nationwide outbreak of genocidal violence by hardline majority Hutus that killed more than 800,000 people over about 100 days. Others said Nshimiye was part of the pro-Hutu National Revolutionary Movement for Development and the Interahamwe, the paramilitary group blamed for most of the killings during the genocide.
The defence argued Nshimiye had never been implicated in domestic and international tribunals after the genocide, including the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda as well as an informal transitional justice system inside Rwanda, called gacaca, which tried more than a million people for their roles in the atrocities.
Defence lawyers pointed out apparent inconsistencies in government witnesses’ testimonies and brought other witnesses who said Nshimiye was with them in the capital, Kigali, and other parts of the country during the genocide.
Nshimiye’s attorneys also argued in court that Rwandan authorities had interfered with the investigation because they had met with some witnesses before they testified in Boston.
“At the end of the day, it was just two competing stories, and so much is lost with this all happening 30 years or so ago. … I guess the jury was more convinced of the prosecutor’s witnesses because they victimised themselves in their stories,” Tresor Nshimiye said.
Nshimiye’s case is one of several currently under way in the US related to the Rwandan genocide.
In April 2025, prosecutors charged Faustin Nsabumukunzi, a 65-year-old beekeeper in Long Island, New York, who had applied for US citizenship, with similarly concealing his role in the violence. And in June 2025, authorities charged 65-year-old Vincent Nzigiyimfura of Dayton, Ohio, who had also applied for US citizenship, with concealing his role in the genocide.
Both men were previously listed publicly as fugitives by Rwandan authorities.

Putin tells African leaders Moscow will not pursue ‘neo-colonialism’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Putin tells African leaders Moscow will not pursue ‘neo-colonialism’
Speaking at the third Russia-Africa Summit, Putin frames Russia as an alternative partner to former colonial powers.
President Vladimir Putin has told African leaders visiting Moscow that Russia does not engage in “neo-colonial exploitation” of the continent, unlike former colonial powers.
Speaking at the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow on Wednesday, Putin said the West is still trying to exploit the continent’s resources and uses debt to hold back development.
“Africa is increasingly asserting itself as one of the key players in the global economy and politics. However, the emergence of a multipolar world is, of course, no easy task; it faces resistance from countries that are not prepared to accept this reality,” Putin told the summit.
Russian-backed government forces in a broad swath of North Africa are fighting armed rebellions as many countries in the region emerge from military coups that have shaken regional security.
Putin criticised “active attempts by Western countries” to drive Africans back into debt and to force them to accept much-needed financial resources on predatory terms, which he said slowed their long-term development.
“Our business does not engage in the predatory, neo-colonial exploitation of natural and human resources, but rather expands the processing of raw materials locally, thereby creating new jobs and generating tax revenue,” said Putin.
Disruptions to agriculture
Putin told delegations from 48 African countries, including 22 represented by their heads of state, that Russia was prepared to expand the geographical reach of agricultural product shipments.
Russia had supplied 13 million metric tonnes of agricultural products to Africa in the first nine months of this year alone, he added.
The remarks come as attacks in the Black Sea continue to disrupt exports of grain from both Russia and Ukraine, while the United States-Israel war on Iran has interrupted global fertiliser supplies.
Putin is due to hold one-on-one talks with individual African leaders who are attending on topics ranging from trade to security, grain supplies and arms deals.
The summit is expected to end with a final declaration on deepening cooperation between Russia and African nations.

Ground crews still excluded from nuclear test medal
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:00:08 GMT
04:00:08 KST

There are no plans to extend the Nuclear Test Medal to personnel of 543 and 27 Squadrons who recovered, washed, decontaminated and maintained aircraft used for nuclear cloud sampling between 1966 and 1980, because they did not deploy from the United Kingdom, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Lord Bourne of Aberystwyth, the Conservative peer, asked what progress has been made on extending eligibility to those personnel, in light of representations from nuclear test veterans involved in intelligence gathering of foreign nations’ atmospheric tests.
Lord Coaker, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “Nuclear Test Medal (NTM) eligibility has been broadened to include UK personnel who deployed in support of United States atmospheric nuclear tests, and UK personnel who were deployed from the UK in support of operations to monitor atmospheric nuclear tests conducted by France and China up to 1974 and 1980 respectively.
“Ministry of Defence officials will continue to keep the eligibility criteria under review to ensure that they are as comprehensive and inclusive as they can be given the current boundaries. There are no current plans to expand the criteria to include personnel who did not deploy from the UK in support of either UK or other nations atmospheric testing.
“Any formal proposal for the expansion of the NTM eligibility criteria would need to be endorsed by the Committee on the Grant of Honours, Decorations and Medals (HD Committee) and approved by His Majesty The King.”
Everything turns on deployment, because aircrew flown out to sample the clouds produced by French and Chinese tests qualify, while the people who met those aircraft on return and handled contaminated airframes do not, because they stayed at their home station.
Number 543 Squadron flew the Victor B2(SR) in the strategic reconnaissance role until 1974, and 27 Squadron took on the maritime radar reconnaissance and air sampling task with the Vulcan B2(MRR) thereafter. The Nuclear Test Medal was instituted in 2022 for veterans and civilian staff who took part in Britain’s atmospheric testing programme, after decades of campaigning.

Fed keeps interest rates steady despite 'high inflation' owing to US war on Iran

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:00:01 UTC
04:00:01 KST

The US Federal Reserve has held interest rates steady, in line with market expectations, days ahead of crucial midterm elections where surging inflation has been a key issue.
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh, meanwhile, said on Wednesday that political considerations had no bearing on the central bank’s decision.
"Politics played no role in the decision. I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics. I didn't hear a reference to politics, elections, what's happening in the next week," the Fed official said in a press conference.
The 12-member Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 to hold rates at a target range between 3.75 to 4.00 percent, citing the need for more data in the fight against inflation, after having hiked for the first time in three years at its previous meeting in September.
"The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's two percent goal," the Fed said in a statement announcing its decision.
Two members of the committee, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, calling instead for an immediate 0.25-percentage-point rate hike.
The central bank has missed its long-term two-percent target for inflation for more than five years, with households and businesses battered by sustained price increases.
US war on Iran
US war on Iran, launched in late February, has sent energy prices skyrocketing and fuelled domestic inflation, alongside his wide-ranging tariff policies.
Prices have also been driven by an investment boom in artificial intelligence (AI) technology and the build-out of huge data centres to support it.
The decision comes six days ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, in which the Democratic Party is seeking to wrest control of both houses of Congress from Trump's Republicans.
President Donald Trump's handling of the economy has been a key issue throughout the campaign, with working-class households across the country struggling to make ends meet despite largely stable overall economic growth.
US consumer inflation came in hotter than expected in September, clocking in at 3.7 percent, edging back towards a three-year high established in May.
Still, key policymakers at the Fed — including Warsh — have signaled that they did not see an urgency to raise rates again immediately.
On Wednesday, the Fed said economic activity in the United States was expanding at a "strong" pace, upgrading its language from the FOMC meeting six weeks prior.

Iran, Russia move toward joint construction of small modular nuclear reactors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:58:29 UTC
03:58:29 KST

Iran, Russia move toward joint construction of small modular nuclear reactors
TEHRAN — Iran is moving toward an agreement with Russia to accelerate the joint construction of small modular reactors (SMRs), as the country advances its domestic nuclear capabilities and seeks to expand the role of nuclear energy in meeting rising electricity demand, the spokesman for the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI) has said.
Behrouz Kamalvandi, who also serves as the AEOI’s deputy for International, Legal and Parliamentary Affairs, made the remarks in an interview with the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB) on Wednesday, discussing Iran’s participation in the Sixth Ministerial Conference on Nuclear Power in South Korea and the growing importance of nuclear energy worldwide.
Kamalvandi said Iran was in the process of signing a protocol with Russia aimed at accelerating cooperation on the joint construction of SMRs, a technology attracting increasing international attention for its potential to provide flexible, scalable sources of electricity.
“We are also in a good position in the field of small modular reactors,” he said, adding that the proposed protocol would help advance bilateral cooperation in their construction.
Unlike conventional nuclear power plants, SMRs are designed to be built in smaller units and can be deployed individually or in groups, offering countries an additional option for meeting growing energy needs. Their modular design also lends itself to standardized production and the deployment of multiple units.
Kamalvandi said global electricity demand was rising rapidly, driven in part by advances in artificial intelligence, digital technologies and the electrification of transport. These developments, he argued, were making the expansion of nuclear power an increasingly important consideration for countries seeking reliable electricity supplies.
Environmental challenges have also heightened international interest in nuclear energy, he said, as countries look for cleaner and more dependable sources of power.
According to Kamalvandi, the world currently generates around 400,000 megawatts of nuclear electricity, while Iran accounts for approximately 1,000 megawatts. He added that announced plans to triple global nuclear power capacity would require the construction of around 1,200 power plants comparable in size to the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant in southern Iran.
The AEOI spokesman underscored nuclear power’s capacity to provide a stable, continuous supply of electricity, distinguishing it from wind and solar generation, whose output fluctuates with weather conditions and the availability of sunlight and wind. Such reliability, he said, is particularly important as electricity consumption increases and modern economies become more dependent on advanced technologies.
Kamalvandi also highlighted the broader applications of nuclear technology beyond electricity generation, including nuclear medicine, agriculture and industry, emphasizing its potential contribution to scientific and technological development across multiple sectors.
Reflecting on Iran’s progress, he said his approximately 14 years of continuous service at the AEOI had given him a clear perspective on the country’s achievements in developing its nuclear industry.
“I can say with confidence that the country’s nuclear industry has reached full maturity, and we have now achieved self-sufficiency in the construction of nuclear power plants,” he said.
His remarks highlighted Iran’s emphasis on strengthening indigenous scientific, engineering and industrial capabilities, while pursuing international cooperation in emerging nuclear technologies.
The proposed Iran–Russia protocol on small modular reactors represents a further step in Tehran’s efforts to develop its nuclear power sector and broaden cooperation in a field that is gaining prominence as countries confront rising electricity demand, energy-security concerns and environmental challenges.

The New M6 MacBook Pro Has a Serious Price Problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:57:22 UTC
03:57:22 KST

Just yesterday, Apple refreshed its 14-inch MacBook Pro with the new M6 chip inside, and it’s currently available for preorder. This is the first MacBook to get the chip (but certainly not the last), and I look forward to testing this thing out myself. But I do already have a good sense of how well it’ll perform, as I already tested this same chip in the latest Mac Mini. And it points to an issue with the current state of the Mac lineup.
The 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro currently costs $1,999. That gets you 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage. Even for as good as these laptops are, that feels like too much money for those specs. Apple raised prices across all Macs earlier this year, but the base 14-inch MacBook Pro got hit the hardest, with a $300 bump. It was already an awkward configuration, as it used the same M5 chip as the much cheaper MacBook Air models. It was such bad pricing that it ended up on my “do not buy” list. The addition of the M6 seems like it’ll add some value, especially with the improvements to GPU performance I saw in the M6 Mac Mini. It also has the dual Neural Engine, which can speed up certain AI tasks in creative applications, especially for content creators. I won’t pretend to make a final evaluation until I’ve thoroughly tested the machine myself.
The Smarter Buy
But consider this. The M6 Mac Mini is on sale for $779 right now, $120 off its retail price. The 13-inch M5 MacBook Air is similarly $150 off its retail price right now. You could buy both for the same price as one M6 MacBook Pro. That’s kind of insane when you think about it. You miss out on the MacBook Pro’s excellent Mini-LED display and powerful speakers, but to me, it’s a tempting alternative for a $2,000 budget.
It’s even more compelling when you consider how many people are using Mac Minis these days—more as always-on AI agent boxes that you can control remotely with any old MacBook. Pairing the M6 Mac Mini and M5 MacBook air together is a recipe for AI goodness (especially if you configure the Mac Mini up to 32 GB or 64 GB of memory).
Another alternative is the M5 MacBook Pro with an M5 Pro chip inside for only $200 more. It looks identical on the outside, and has better performance on the inside.
I’m still interested to see how the new M6 MacBook Pro performs, but the price alone makes me wonder if there aren’t better ways of spending your money—even while staying within the Mac lineup.

‘We are a country divided’: Who will feel betrayed by Israel’s next government?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:56:43 UTC
03:56:43 KST

‘We are a country divided’: Who will feel betrayed by Israel’s next government?
Israel faces weeks of political uncertainty, as the parliamentary elections did not result in a majority for either side. A unity government could break the deadlock, but at what cost to domestic politics and regional stability?
After months of a fiercely contested race, Israelis are waking up to a political reality that offers little prospect of stability. The question is no longer who won the most seats in the Knesset, but who can form a government – and at what cost.
According to the preliminary results from the Central Elections Committee, which is responsible for counting the 7.3 million votes, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is leading with a projected 27 out of 120 seats. The former chief of staff and head of the Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, comes in second, securing 21 seats in the Knesset. These numbers will change as the counting continues.
Divided we stand
For some Israelis, the initial results have already proven disappointing.
“I really hoped that the victory of Eisenkot would be obvious and we could celebrate Bibi’s defeat. The country is tired of this man, we need a change but the results are not encouraging,” Miriam Hassan, a 40-year-old resident of Nazareth, said.
Others share her frustration. “The change bloc [a union of parties aligned against Netanyahu] did everything it could to end the rule of Netanyahu. Arab tried too. They went to the polling stations in their masses but now it is clear that the battle is not over yet. More work needs to be done for us to finally see this man handing down the keys to the premier’s office in Jerusalem,” according to Samer Nasrawi, another Nazareth resident in his 50s.
Ronen Attar, a voter of Yashar in his 30s, said:
“We voted for change, for hope, for the repair of this country. We wanted to see this government that was responsible for October 7 handing down power. Polls indicate our bloc can still form a government but everything is up in the air.”
On the other side of the political divide, Netanyahu’s supporters are celebrating.
“My entire family voted for Netanyahu,” Moshe Keif, a Jerusalem resident in his 50s, said. “He has done so much in these four years. The media and Israeli channels buried him politically, they said he will be crushed but now it is clear, Likud is still the strongest and the biggest party. Netanyahu is unsinkable.”
Itzik Dayan, another Jerusalem voter in his 50s, was less optimistic:
“I think Netanyahu should still be the PM despite his mistakes and vices. But the results show that half of the population doesn’t share these views. We are a country divided.”
Unity as a solution?
With polling stations closed and the count underway, it will take days for the final results to emerge. Even then, weeks may pass before Israel – and the world – learns who will become the country’s next prime minister.
Israel’s political system does not automatically award the premiership to the leader of the largest party. Instead, the president must nominate a candidate capable of assembling a coalition commanding at least 61 of the Knesset’s 120 seats.
The problem is that neither camp appears to have the numbers.
According to the Central Elections Committee, Eisenkot’s potential partners, the Together bloc led by former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu, and Yair Golan’s Democrats – are projected to win 12, 7, and 8 seats, respectively. Together, they would hold 48 seats, 13 short of a majority.
To bridge the gap and secure the premiership, Eisenkot could seek an alliance with the Arab parties: the Joint Arab List and Ra’am, which have won 13 and 6 seats, respectively.
“I voted for them,” Hassan said. “I support the idea of them joining forces with the change bloc to oust Netanyahu from power. Only this cooperation will bring the much needed change.”
Nasrawi agrees:
“It is time for the Arab parties to start cooperating with the Jewish ones. It has been long overdue. They have a chance now. Join forces and remove Netanyahu. Then start cooperating in other spheres, be it tackling high crime rates or the economy.”
Cooperation, however, may be easier said than done. Although Arab party leaders have repeatedly pledged to support initiatives aimed at ending Netanyahu’s premiership, their political priorities remain difficult to reconcile with those of the Change bloc.
The Israeli-Palestinian conflict is the clearest example. Arab parties advocate ending the occupation, withdrawing troops from Gaza, and establishing a Palestinian state. Eisenkot and his allies, with the exception of Golan, reject these positions and have pledged to take a tougher approach toward the Palestinians.
Israeli experts consider it unlikely that the Arab parties and the Eisenkot-led bloc will overcome these differences. Without their support, the former chief of staff may struggle to become prime minister. Even if he succeeds, his coalition could prove short-lived.
Netanyahu’s prospects are hardly brighter. Together with his traditional allies, including several religious parties, he commands 53 seats, 8 short of the 61 required for a majority.
To retain power, Netanyahu would need to persuade lawmakers from the opposing camp to defect or convince some members of the Change bloc to join a coalition under his leadership.
He has managed this before. On October 11, 2023, shortly after the Hamas-led attacks, he formed a unity government with Benny Gantz, who set aside his differences with Netanyahu to provide broad legislative support. This time, however, the task will be considerably harder. Several leaders in the Change bloc have already ruled out joining a Netanyahu-led coalition and pledged not to serve in ministerial positions under his leadership.
Yet neither side may ultimately have a viable alternative to a broad unity government.
According to a recent poll, around 60% of Israelis favor a unity government bringing Netanyahu and Eisenkot together; 33% want the former chief of staff to lead the government, 19% prefer Netanyahu, and 8% say they have no preference between the two.
Political pressure for unity is also mounting. President Isaac Herzog has indicated that he will work to establish a broad coalition between Netanyahu and Eisenkot. Netanyahu, too, has urged his opponents to consider the proposal, arguing that unity is the only way to address the pressing challenges facing Israel.
Voters, however, remain deeply divided over the prospect.
“Nobody trusts Netanyahu anymore,” Nasrawi said. “I don’t see how Eisenkot agrees to sit with the man who deceived all his coalition partners in the past.”
“This government needs to go. Striking an agreement with Netanyahu is criminal. If they do so, it basically means they betrayed our trust and threw all our votes out of the window,” Hassan said.
Dayan sees things differently: “I really don’t think there is an alternative but to have a unity government.”
“We still have Iran and Hezbollah on our borders, the situation in the West Bank and Gaza is not stable either, economy needs to be fixed, and all we are doing is dividing the country into pro and against Netanyahu. Only unity can bring a change.”
No bright future in sight
A government of national unity could have consequences far beyond Israel’s domestic politics. Netanyahu previously indicated that if he remains prime minister, he intends to complete what he considers unfinished business in Iran, Lebanon, the West Bank, and Gaza.
The groundwork for further military operations is already being laid. In Gaza, the IDF is conducting near-daily raids and targeted killings. In the West Bank, the military is pursuing a major campaign in the Hebron area aimed at dismantling Hamas infrastructure. These operations could intensify and expand if Netanyahu and Eisenkot join forces.
If they don’t, the future for the region doesn’t look bright either. In the event of a political deadlock, with neither side forming a government, Netanyahu will remain interim prime minister until another round of elections is held, typically within 90 days. Unless there is a war that can push it to a further date.
A war seems to be on the horizon. Reports suggest that Netanyahu planned an attack against Iran on October 10, but was blocked by US President Donald Trump at the last minute.
Experts suggest that he might resume his plans if he remains in office, even for a short period of time.
In the coming days, Herzog is expected to consult the leaders of the various parties before deciding which candidate to task with forming a government. Once given the mandate, the candidate will have 28 days to assemble a coalition, with the possibility of a two-week extension. If the attempt fails, another candidate may get the opportunity.
For now, the clouds of uncertainty hanging over Israel show little sign of lifting. A unity government could offer a way out of the immediate political deadlock, but it would not necessarily heal the divisions exposed by the election.
Israelis who went to the polls hoping for a clear direction may find themselves facing a familiar reality: a country still divided, a government still uncertain, and a future that remains difficult to predict.

Did UK pressure on Israel help Netanyahu, or bring his opponents closer to power? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:55:41 UTC
03:55:41 KST

Just weeks before Israel went to the polls, Britain and some of its allies imposed new sanctions and bans against Israeli settlements. Today’s election results may have exposed the limits of what outside pressure can achieve.
When British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced new measures against Israeli settlements on September 8, he insisted that Britain was not trying to influence Israel’s election.
“I do not want to, in any sense, interfere in that election. The election is for the Israeli people to make their own decisions about their future. I have set out the policy of the British government, and I have made it clear that our quarrel is not with the Israeli people but with the policies of the Netanyahu government,” he told parliament.
Miliband’s answer was in response to concerns expressed by various MPs, including Shadow Foreign Secretary Tom Tugendhat, that the sanctions and their timing would help the campaigns of Israel’s far Right.
He acknowledged the concern but said that the international community could not wait for an Israeli opposition government to change course.
The timing raised an obvious question. With Israelis due to vote on October 27, could sanctions announced by foreign governments help weaken the prime minister they were criticizing, or would they instead reinforce Netanyahu’s argument that Israel was being singled out by a hostile international community?
The answer we see today is not straightforward. Exit polls showed Netanyahu’s bloc falling short of the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority but with, nevertheless, more votes overall than the change bloc. Likud has far surpassed Eisenkot’s Yashar, which pre-election polls had suggested could perform much better.
Of course, neither outcome proves international pressure affected how Israelis voted.
But it does shine a light on a strategy that attempted to change Israeli policy through economic and diplomatic pressure.
The timing was not politically neutral
Britain’s September announcement was more than another expression of diplomatic disagreement. Its government announced measures targeting settlement expansion, including an import ban on settlement goods and restrictions targeting individuals and companies involved in settlement growth.
The British government maintains that these measures target settlement activity, not Israel within its internationally recognized borders.
Britain had already sanctioned National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich in June 2025, as did Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and Norway, citing their alleged incitement of violence against Palestinians in the West Bank. The September 2026 measures were therefore part of a more widespread deterioration in relations rather than an isolated attempt to intervene in an election campaign.
However, the proximity to election day made the political ramifications difficult to ignore. Miliband argued that the international community could not stand by as settlement expansion continued and that Netanyahu was making Israel “less secure.”
That distinction is notable: A government can legitimately seek to influence another country’s policies without explicitly seeking to change its leadership. But when it announces punitive measures just weeks before a significant election and publicly argues that the current leader’s policies are damaging the country’s security, the boundary between policy pressure and electoral pressure becomes more nebulous.
Were the warnings ignored?
A report by The Spectator, subsequently reported by Globes, alleged that British diplomats and intelligence officials had warned the UK government that announcing sanctions before the election risked affecting Israeli politics. According to the report, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar had asked Miliband to delay the measures until after the vote, and some British officials reportedly agreed that waiting was a favorable option.
The concern was reportedly that the announcement could give Netanyahu an opportunity to present himself as defending Israel against foreign pressure, potentially strengthening rather than weakening his position.
And this is indeed the narrative that Likud members peddled in response. On September 8, Sa’ar responded by accusing the UK of “blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and in its electoral process,” calling it a “completely unacceptable attempt by a foreign government to exert external influence in the midst of an election campaign.”
These allegations are worth taking seriously but do not constitute proof that the sanctions were designed to oust Netanyahu. There is a distinction between knowingly accepting a political risk and deliberately seeking a particular electoral outcome.
How might the pressure have played in Israel?
There were at least two plausible, and potentially concurrent, effects. For Netanyahu and his supporters, the measures could have reinforced an age-old argument that foreign governments are hostile to Israel regardless of its security concerns. Sanctions become evidence not of damaging government policy but of international actors attempting to dictate Israeli decisions. Netanyahu could present himself as defending national sovereignty against outside pressure.
His government could then present itself as the defender of national sovereignty against outside pressure.
For Netanyahu’s opponents, the same measures could reinforce the argument that it is his policies that have damaged Israel’s international standing and created consequences that a different government would have to rectify.
Diplomatic isolation may have been seen not as an external attack but as a cost of the current government’s approach to the Palestinians and to West Bank settlements.
Neither mechanism can be assumed to have determined votes. Israeli voters went into this election after years of war and profound security upheaval. The consequences of October 7, confidence in the government’s handling of national security, the future of military-service exemptions for haredi (ultra-Orthodox) men, and the cost of living all offered key incentives to support or reject the Netanyahu status quo.
The election’s high turnout and the weakness of his bloc in the exit polls cannot, on their own, establish which considerations mattered most to individual voters, or that sanctions shifted support between camps.
What, then, did the pressure achieve?
The British government said its measures were intended to restrict the economic activity supporting settlement expansion and preserve the possibility of a two-state solution. The success of those measures should ultimately be assessed against the objectives: whether the restrictions were implemented, whether they affected settlement activity, and whether they changed the calculations of those involved.
If the measures had little practical economic effect, their principal immediate consequences may have been diplomatic and symbolic. If they did impose meaningful costs, they may have influenced Israeli policy regardless of which government ultimately takes office. Neither outcome can be established simply by counting seats.
The broader question is: Can foreign governments apply pressure to Israel without strengthening the very political forces they hope to influence? The election has not supplied a definitive answer.
For now, the evidence supports a more muted conclusion: International pressure became part of Israel’s election debate, but the available electoral figures do not establish that it changed the result. Whether it altered Israeli voters’ calculations, or will ultimately alter Israeli government policy, remains a separate question.

Unidentified naval drones have attacked another merchant vessel in Bulgarian waters in the Black Sea.
Reuters reported the incident, citing a statement by Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov.
According to Stoyanov, three naval drones attacked a Liberian-flagged container ship in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, 20 nautical miles from the resort town of Shabla.
At the time of the attack, representatives of Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey were meeting in Sofia and calling for an end to attacks in the Black Sea that threaten commercial shipping.
The vessel’s crew was evacuated.
Another ship was dispatched to assist the damaged bulk carrier, which was sailing from the Israeli port of Haifa to Constanța, Romania.
The vessel’s owner, Contships Management, confirmed the attack. A company representative said all 18 crew members — 14 Filipinos and four Ukrainians — were safe and ashore.
In recent weeks, drone attacks on commercial vessels off the Bulgarian coast have killed about two dozen sailors.
At least six merchant vessels have been attacked.
On October 6, the bulk carrier Alfa Watan, owned by a Turkish company, sank off the country’s coast. Ten crew members were reported missing.
On October 13, the vessel HS Dignity sank in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone following a drone strike. Another 11 sailors were reported missing.
The bulk carriers Able and Chelsea-3 were also damaged. In addition, unidentified drones attacked several vessels off the Romanian coast.
Last week, NATO announced that it would send additional maritime reconnaissance aircraft, radar systems and drones to the Black Sea.

President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Prime Minister of the Netherlands Rob Jetten held a meeting in The Hague with representatives from the Ukrainian and Dutch business sectors, specifically in defense, energy, and software, to discuss joint technological and energy projects, as well as the development of satellite technologies and air defense systems.

During the meeting, key priorities and solutions were identified to strengthen practical economic cooperation. Discussions covered defense manufacturing, joint technological and energy projects, and industrial development. Particular attention was given to the advancement of satellite technologies and air defense. Both teams are tasked with developing the Bliksem air defense project; work on this initiative has already begun.
"We are elevating our cooperation to a level where it becomes clear that standing with Ukraine yields additional positive technological and social outcomes," Zelenskyy said.
Representatives of the Dutch business community described the areas in which they are already helping Ukrainians overcome the challenges of this war and proposed new forms of support. They expressed their full backing for Ukraine and extended their gratitude for the defense of shared European values.

Houthis say deadly Saudi strikes hit Yemen as they target Aden
Yemen's Houthis said Saudi strikes on a petrol station and a market killed more than a dozen people on Wednesday, while the Iran-backed group targeted the airport in government stronghold Aden, wounding several civilians.
The Houthis last month launched a lightning offensive in Yemen, reigniting a long frozen civil war against the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government there.
They have also launched sustained attacks on Saudi Arabia itself, the world's biggest crude exporter, rattling global markets already volatile from the wider Middle East war.
On Wednesday, Houthi broadcaster Almasirah reported 14 dead "and 15 wounded, including women and children in a preliminary toll", in attacks it blamed on Saudi Arabia in the northwestern Jawf province, where it reported strikes on a market and a petrol station.
In Aden, two ballistic missiles struck the perimeter of the airport, leaving several civilians wounded and causing damage, government forces spokesman Majed Abdullah Al-Nazili said on X.
He blamed the Houthis for the attack, describing it as "the sixth such attack on the airport".
A local police source told AFP that one missile fell inside the airport perimeter shortly before the Houthis issued a warning for people to evacuate the area.
"Our armed forces call on those present at Aden airport to immediately evacuate due to the presence of a military cargo plane belonging to the Saudi enemy transporting weapons to kill the sons of the Yemeni people," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Telegram.
The first strike happened while a Saudi military aircraft was at the airport, but the plane "was not hit and took off shortly afterward", the first police source said.
The second attack targeted an area "under Saudi forces' control inside the perimeter of Aden airport", the second Aden police official said.
Both sources spoke on condition of anonymity due to security concerns.

Wars, unhappiness, and loneliness frighten nearly 1 in 2 young people, survey finds
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:49:24 CET
03:49:24 KST

Wars, unhappiness, and loneliness
frighten nearly 1 in 2 young people in Italy, a new survey has
found.
                                    
International geopolitical tension has emerged this year as the
top fear among the younger generations, according to the
Observatory on Generational Fears—an initiative by the portal
Skuola.net—which surveyed 1,000 young men and women aged 11 to
29, asking them to identify which of the various "specters"
presented in the study they found most daunting.
                                    
The results paint a portrait of these generations—known as Gen Z
and Gen Alpha—caught in a double bind: on one hand, the terror
of rapidly escalating global catastrophes, and on the other, a
deep, personal sense of insecurity regarding their own futures
and romantic lives.
                                    
Only 13% of respondents felt confident—or fortunate—enough to
claim they had "none of these fears," with this sentiment being
significantly more common among males (20%) than females (8%).
                                    
Unlike similar surveys conducted in previous years, 2026 shows a
dramatic shift at the top of the list.
                                    
The fear of a nuclear or global war now ranks first, cited by
45% of young people.
                                    
This represents a sharp increase compared to the past, when this
fear stood at 34% (in 2025) and 33% (in 2024).
                                    
At the same time, young people continue to grapple with a
profound sense of inner distress.
                                    
Right behind the specter of war—in second place—is the fear of
never being happy or satisfied, cited by 43% of the sample (a
steady increase from 40% in 2025 and 38% in 2024).
                                    
Rounding out the top three is another concern closely tied to
one's personal life: the dread of never finding love, which has
seen a significant jump to 41%, up from 33% a year ago.
                                    
Further down the list, anxiety regarding financial independence
takes hold: 38% of young people fear not having enough money,
while 37% are frightened by the prospect of failing to build a
life of their own.
                                    
Also at 37%—tied with the previous concern—is a growing worry
about the rise in social violence, which has surged by 11
percentage points from 26% last year.
                                    
Just outside the top tier, at 35%, are the nightmare of being
unable to find work and the fear of climate change—an issue that
has once again begun to weigh on people's minds after remaining
relatively stable at 24% for the past two years.
                                    
Rounding out the list are the fear of having no friends (31%)
and the fear of being unable to travel (23%) to explore a world
that increasingly appears closed off and hostile.

====================================================================================================

The 'stigma' of being a non-disabled player in elite wheelchair sport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:49:00 UTC
03:49:00 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
Bayley McKenna to make history as Australia's first non-disabled captain at Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup
There are few athletes in world sport quite like Bayley McKenna.
Shaggy-haired and expressive, he is the kind of player highlights packages are built around, and at 26, he is the youngest-ever captain of Australia's wheelchair rugby league team.
But what really sets him apart is his status as a non-disabled athlete in elite wheelchair sport, with international wheelchair rugby league allowing participation from both people with disability and non-disabled players.
Leading out the Wheelaroos at the Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup, starting tomorrow in Wollongong, will undoubtedly be a pinch-me moment for the Townsville world-beater.
But it is also an occasion he approaches with some trepidation.
McKenna received a flood of online abuse during his breakout World Cup in 2022 and is now bracing for more negativity from outside the sport.
"There is such a f***ing stigma around able-bodied athletes playing in wheelchairs," McKenna told ABC Sport.
"It is ridiculous … I'd be lying to you if I said I was going into this World Cup not expecting it."
McKenna's journey as a non-disabled player
McKenna's journey towards the Wheelaroos began in 2006, when his father was involved in an accident and became a wheelchair user.
It was a tough period of transition for Darren McKenna, grappling with the realities of his disability and what it meant for his career, family and independence.
He was reluctant to accept assistance from anyone, but his six-year-old son gave him little choice.
"I pretty much said, 'I'm helping you no matter what,'" Bayley McKenna said.
"We did everything together. I was the only person allowed to push him in his wheelchair because I didn't really give him the option.
"I've been his little offsider ever since."
And it was not long before the father-son duo entered the sporting arena, first competing together in wheelchair basketball before finding wheelchair rugby league, which Darren McKenna was integral to growing in both Queensland and Australia-wide.
Participation from non-disabled players is vital to wheelchair sport at a grassroots level, allowing for more teams and competitions for disabled athletes, but wheelchair rugby league is unique in allowing international sides to field up to two non-disabled players at any given time.
This policy ensures that teams at every level of the sport can attract enough players to compete, while also fostering a unique kind of inclusion that flows from grassroots all the way to elite competition.
And the sport is full of stories like the McKennas' — including Australia's Cory Cannane, who shared the field with disabled father Craig at the 2022 World Cup, and non-disabled England legend Jack Brown, who only began playing the sport because of his disabled brother.
Having experienced the benefits of the policy firsthand, McKenna said it was that "inclusion" that provided the game much of its magic.
"I really, really didn't think that anything could have brought us closer together," McKenna said.
"But it did."
Wheelchair rugby league is also a mixed gender sport, although there are no women in the Wheelaroos' squad for the tournament.
Dealing with the 'stigma' of being a non-disabled player
McKenna burst onto the international scene at the 2022 World Cup in England, where his playmaking exploits earned him a spot in the team of the tournament as well as significant attention online.
Aged 22, McKenna's shaggy mullet, uncompromising hits and exceptional chair skills made for ideal social media fodder, with the Australian making regular appearances across the tournament's official channels.
McKenna was taken aback by the vitriol in the online correspondence he received as a result.
"I would have copped about a dozen messages from people all around the world saying, 'you're a fraud, you shouldn't even be in the chair, this is a sport for disabled people,'" McKenna said.
"These guys were coming at me, like, 'you're lucky you're not out there on the street by yourself.'"
It was only after an early-morning conversation with teammate and longtime friend Pete Arbuckle that McKenna began to feel at peace with the abuse.
"Me and Pete were at the gym over in the UK and I got one of these messages and Pete said, 'Don't worry about that bud, don't even stress. You're here representing your country and he's probably at home on the couch,'" McKenna said.
"That put me back in my stride a bit, and it helped me out a lot."
Recalling the conversation, Arbuckle said he reassured McKenna his journey to international competition was a "natural progression" from his early years playing alongside his amputee father.
"I said, 'You don't have to justify anything, you only have to justify yourself to us, your teammates. You don't have to justify yourself to anyone else on the planet,'" Arbuckle said.
"And he didn't let it affect him, and he had a really good World Cup."
Arbuckle, who lost a leg in an accident in 2016, said the contributions of non-disabled players have been vital to the growth of the sport in Australia.
"If it wasn't for the able-bodied players, I don't think we'd have the game here in Australia," Arbuckle said.
"We just wouldn't be feasible … there'd be no Wheelaroos to speak of, or certainly not at the level we're at currently."
McKenna said the rules of the game ensure it is a "level playing field" for all athletes, while both he and Arbuckle described their wheelchairs as equipment needed for the sport, analogous to cricket bats or baseball mitts.
"What people don't realise is this is a wheelchair sport; it's not a disability sport as such," Arbuckle said.
"We play a sport in wheelchairs, and our rules define what can and can't happen."
Wheelchair rugby league's looming watershed moment
The upcoming tournament will provide wheelchair rugby league the kind of exposure most non-mainstream sports could only dream of.
Bundling the wheelchair competition with the men's, women's and physical disability events allows for the World Cups to be marketed as one cohesive product, and for the Wheelaroos to benefit with free-to-air, prime-time coverage.
Well aware of the looming watershed moment, Arbuckle said he hoped the attention would bring more disabled players into the fold.
"It's really going to open our game to people that haven't heard of it before and people that want to choose a physical sport," Arbuckle said.
"I think there's an untapped resource out there."
But the Wheelaroos, and McKenna in particular, are also bracing for the spotlight's burn.
The Australian captain is certain his inbox will once again turn ugly.
But this time, knowing he can call on the support of his teammates and loved ones, he said he will be ready.
"It's just going to be one of those things we move past and move forward, and don't let it get in the camp," McKenna said.
"I've got some f***ing damn good mates, bud.
"And they will support me until the cows come home."
