Water tariffs will be reviewed under new rules: will Ukrainians’ bills decrease?
Kyiv • UNN
Tariffs will be set by local authorities, while the NEURC will remotely verify their calculations. There will be no automatic reduction in bills.
Ukraine is introducing a new mechanism for monitoring tariffs for centralized water supply and wastewater services. On October 27, the National Energy and Utilities Regulatory Commission (NEURC) approved a procedure for reviewing decisions on the cost of these services. The regulator will analyze whether the tariffs were calculated correctly and whether the expenses included in consumers’ bills are substantiated.
UNN examined who is now responsible for setting them, how the monitoring will work, and what consumers who doubt the fairness of the charges can do.
Who sets water tariffs in Ukraine
In March 2026, the division of powers in the field of centralized water supply and wastewater services changed in Ukraine. Law No. 4777-IX, which entered into force on March 11, transferred tariff-setting powers to local self-government bodies. Where they have the relevant powers, decisions may be adopted by military administrations of settlements. In turn, the licensing of water utilities and oversight of compliance with licensing conditions were transferred to authorized local state administrations. The NEURC retained responsibility for developing tariff-setting methodologies and verifying the correctness of tariff decisions.
As we can see, the new mechanism does not return to the regulator the right to directly determine the cost of water in each city. Local authorities will continue to adopt tariff decisions, while the NEURC may verify whether a decision complies with legislation and approved methodologies.
Water prices in Ukraine are set by local authorities — Shmyhal21.08.26, 12:55 • 3382 views
How inspections of water supply tariffs will be carried out
The NEURC reported that inspections will be scheduled and unscheduled. Both types of oversight will be conducted remotely: officials will not visit enterprises or local authorities. The basis will be the tariff calculations, documents, and explanations used when the relevant decisions were adopted.
Scheduled inspections will be conducted according to an annual plan published on the NEURC website. Unscheduled inspections may be carried out, in particular, if monitoring reveals inconsistencies in the documents, questionable figures, or grounds for examining a sharp tariff increase.
The oversight process will begin with a request to the body that set the tariff. It must provide the decision, the tariff structure, the water utility’s calculations, and supporting materials. The draft procedure stipulated at least ten working days to respond to a request and no more than twenty working days for the inspection after the documents were received. If the necessary information is insufficient, the deadlines will be suspended in accordance with the procedure.
In addition, the regulator will compare the approved tariff with the calculation data. The result will be a written conclusion. It will serve as the basis for replacing the tariff, but it will not automatically cancel it on the day the document is issued.
What will be examined in the cost of water
The water supply tariff covers the costs of extracting, treating, and delivering water to consumers. The wastewater tariff concerns the collection, transportation, and treatment of wastewater. They are calculated separately, although the vast majority of Ukrainians see a single item on their bills covering payment for water supply and wastewater services.
During the oversight process, authorized officials will verify whether the calculations comply with the established methodology, whether there are sufficient documents to substantiate the expenses, and whether the tariff approval procedure was followed. Particular attention will be paid to the cost of electricity for pumps and treatment facilities, labor costs, network repairs, the purchase of materials, and other economically justified components.
Investment expenses, planned service volumes, and the consideration of the results of previous inspections are separate issues. For example, if an enterprise included certain modernization expenses, it is necessary to determine whether their inclusion in the tariff meets the established requirements.
What will happen if the regulator finds violations
Based on the inspections, the NEURC will draw up conclusions. If the calculations are incorrect or the expenses are unsubstantiated, the conclusion will indicate the violations identified and recommendations for remedying them. They may be taken into account when reviewing, adjusting, or setting tariffs in the future. Once approved, the results must be published on the regulator’s website.
At the same time, local authorities have the right to express their objections to the conclusion.
When discussing the regulator’s recommendations, one more important point should be understood. The NEURC’s conclusions will not mean the automatic cancellation of a tariff or the return of money for services already paid for. A subsequent decision to change the price must be made by the authorized body in accordance with the procedure established by law. The new procedure itself does not establish a separate mechanism for compensating the public for overpayments.
Will water bills become lower, and how can they be challenged?
For household consumers, the new measure will provide an opportunity for additional oversight. If an inspection identifies inflated or incorrectly accounted-for expenses and the local authorities subsequently adjust the tariff, this may affect future charges. However, the regulator does not promise an overall reduction in tariffs.
Consumers should first check the current tariff decision on the website of the city or town council or the service provider. After that, they should determine the date the tariff was introduced, the separate costs of water supply and wastewater services, the consumer category, and whether the bill includes other charges not directly related to the price per cubic meter.
If there are doubts about the calculations, a written request may be submitted to the body that approved the tariff, asking it to provide the decision and an accessible justification. If there are indications of a violation, an appeal may be submitted to the NEURC, including through the "Citizens’ Appeals" section on the regulator’s official website or by writing to [email protected].
The application should indicate the locality, the name of the water utility, the details of the tariff decision, and the specific facts that raise doubts, attaching any available documents.
When the new rules will take effect
The NEURC approved the procedure on October 27, 2026. The text of the resolution prepared for the meeting states that it will enter into force on the day after its official publication on the regulator’s website.
It should also be emphasized that the mechanism is designed to operate during martial law and for twelve months after its termination or repeal. It is connected with the temporary redistribution of powers between the NEURC and local authorities.
Will NEURC oversight make water tariffs for households fairer?
The new inspections make it possible to compare local authorities’ decisions with economic calculations and make identified violations public. However, the effectiveness of the system will nevertheless depend on how fully the authorities provide information and whether they take the regulator’s recommendations into account.
As a reminder
Earlier, UNN reported that Ukrainians and businesses are being offered the option of paying to change their electricity consumption schedule. For example, they could shift the operation of appliances from peak-demand hours to another time. To participate, it will be necessary to conclude an agreement with an aggregator—a company that represents consumers in the energy market.

Constitutional Court rules on conditional early release of life prisoners for military service
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:07:40 EET
03:07:40 KST

The Constitutional Court of Ukraine (CCU) on October 28 ruled that provisions of the Criminal Code, which do not provide for the possibility of conditional early release for contract military service for individuals serving life sentences, are constitutional, the CCU's communications department said.
"On October 28, 2026, the Second Senate, at a plenary session, considered the case based on a constitutional complaint filed by Anatoliy Oleksandrovych Luzhynetsky and adopted Decision No. 13-r(II)/2026," according to a statement from the CCU Communications Department, which was received by Interfax-Ukraine on Wednesday.
It is reported that, after reviewing the case, the court concluded that the mechanism for conditional early release from serving a sentence for the purpose of performing military service, established by Article 81-1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, is temporary in nature (applicable during mobilization and/or martial law), and its application entails specific consequences due to the possession and use of weapons and military equipment.
Thus, in the court's view, "the conscription of individuals who have committed violent (intentional murder of two or more persons) and other particularly serious criminal offenses entails additional risks to military discipline, subordination, the proper execution of combat missions, as well as the lives and health of other military personnel and civilians."
"In light of the foregoing, the Court has found the provisions of the first part of Article 811 of the Code to be consistent with the Constitution of Ukraine, in that they do not provide for the possibility of applying conditional early release from serving a sentence for the purpose of performing military service under a contract to persons who are serving a sentence of life imprisonment, and exclude the possibility of applying such release to persons convicted of the intentional murder of two or more persons," the court said in its announcement.
The decision and its summary will be published on the court's official website on October 29, 2026.

New city project for Ukraine's reconstruction to be presented at Davos, URC2027 in Tallinn
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:07:09 EET
03:07:09 KST

Ukraine's Alternative Executive Director at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) Vladyslav Rashkovan, Presidential Advisor on Reconstruction and Investment Attraction Oksana Markarova, and Executive Director of the New City innovative urban initiative Viktoria Trotska are working on a new city project as part of preparations for Ukraine's recovery.
"For now, I'm mostly providing inspiration, while Oksana Markarova and Viktoria Trotska are already developing the new city project and plan to present the initiative at the World Economic Forum in Davos and at the URC in Tallinn – and perhaps even display a physical model of the city," Rashkovan said in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine on the sidelines of the Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group, held in Bangkok on October 12-18.
According to him, following the example of the construction of the city of Slavutych in 1986-1988, the new city project envisages various districts – conventionally Italian, French, German, Eastern, and others: an international team of German, Italian, French, and Japanese architects is working on the city's design, with weekly coordination meetings.
"So far, they're all working for free. To professionalize the project and anchor it to a specific territory, funding from international organizations is needed. The European Commission likes this idea as a showcase project, since Europe also lacks modern experience in building such new cities," Rashkovan said.
He added that over the next year, with the support of international partners, he wants to prepare a kind of blueprint – a book on the principles of building new cities after the war.
"It doesn't matter whether we're talking about a new city or the reconstruction of districts in Kharkiv, Odesa, Kyiv, or Trostianets. What's important is to establish these principles. Such a resource could be useful not only for Ukraine but also for Syria, Lebanon, and other countries that have suffered war damage. It will also be of interest to European partners, who also need to undertake significant construction projects," Ukraine's representative to the IMF said.
He said that since reconstruction takes place at the local level, the idea of building new cities seems promising, as 95% of what exists at the state level is already present at the local level.
According to Rashkovan, at the city level, for example, it is possible to implement green, distributed energy systems and inclusivity, put digital democracy tools into practice, and lay the technological foundation from the ground up for the city's effective functioning: rational use of water and electricity, waste management, and transportation organization.
"We would also like to create a self-sufficient city that will not require additional funding from Kyiv, that will itself create jobs and become a magnet for talent and business, serving as a model of deregulation and a favorable investment climate," Ukraine's representative to the IMF said.
According to him, as part of this project, there is ongoing collaboration with Jenny Roe, former former Director of the Center for Design & Health in the School of Architecture, University of Virginia – who is the author of the book "Restorative Cities" about cities capable of helping people heal – as well as with Finnish and Korean experts on the concept of a two-tier safe city, since Finland leads the Shelter Coalition and has one of the best track records in this field.
Rashkovan is optimistic about the prospects for implementing such a project: it must be supported by the government, but 80-85% of it will be financed by private capital, investments, commercial loans, private equity funds, and so on.
Read the full second part of the interview with Vladyslav Rashkovan, Ukraine's Alternative Executive Director at the IMF, on Interfax-Ukraine website at https://interfax.com.ua/news/interview/1227277.html.

Gokhan Ergocun
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
The US Federal Reserve kept its benchmark interest rate unchanged at a range of 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday as policymakers weighed elevated inflation against strong economic growth.
The Federal Open Market Committee approved the decision in a 10-2 vote to support the central bank's dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices, the Fed said in a statement.
Policymakers Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack dissented, preferring to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points at the meeting.
"Inflation remains elevated," the committee said, pledging that it "will deliver price stability."
"The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal," it added.
The central bank noted that US economic activity is expanding at a strong pace, supported by resilient domestic spending, strong productivity growth and robust capital investment despite elevated uncertainty linked partly to geopolitical developments.
Job gains have kept pace with the workforce and the unemployment rate has changed little, the Fed said, adding that it is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.

Expert: Russia must accept reality of NATO’s 32 member countries
Jim Stokes, a senior expert with GLOBSEC’s “Future of Security” program and former director of nuclear policy at NATO (2023–2025), said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
“Russia will therefore have to accept the reality: NATO now has 32 members. Russia can continue talking about this, and NATO can simply respond: “Noted. We are not going to change,” Stokes said in response to a question about whether the Alliance would be willing to agree to the Kremlin’s demands to roll back its military presence to pre-1997 levels.
According to the expert, this seems “absolutely impossible.” He was referring to the new members—Finland and Sweden—not to mention the 16 countries that joined after the end of the Cold War.
“They are not going to agree to leave the Alliance, and the other Allies are not going to agree simply to let them go. That has never happened in NATO’s 77-year history,” Stokes noted.
However, he acknowledged that another question is whether NATO will ever allow new allies to join. Such a decision is made by consensus among all 32 countries, Stokes reminded.
At the same time, the expert emphasized that the main problem right now is that this Russian war is shaping the perception of the threat, and it is precisely because of this war that Finland and Sweden decided to join the Alliance rather than remain mere partners.
“Much of the responsibility therefore lies with Russia. It can blame NATO for expanding closer to Russian borders, and I understand that it is unhappy about it. But Russia had no problem with this in the late 1990s and early 2000s. It turned the issue into a political one, and now it will have to come to terms with it,” Stokes concluded.
As reported, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that Ukraine expects a trilateral format of negotiations involving Ukrainian, American, and Russian representatives in November, and that Europe must be involved in the diplomatic process and participate in decisions regarding the end of the war.

The German brigade in Lithuania will monitor Kaliningrad and Belarus using electronic warfare equipment
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:02:31 EET
03:02:31 KST

The German brigade in Lithuania will monitor Kaliningrad and Belarus using electronic warfare equipment
Kyiv • UNN
The German brigade in Lithuania will use electronic warfare to detect the military activity of Russia and Belarus. The data will update the allies’ databases.
The German brigade being stationed in Lithuania will use electronic warfare systems for the early detection of military activity in the Kaliningrad region and Belarus. This was reported by the head of Germany’s cyber forces, Vice Admiral Thomas Daum, Reuters reported, according to UNN.
Details
The German brigade, whose full deployment is scheduled for next year, will also collect data on Russian and Belarusian military transmitters and radar systems to update electronic warfare databases used by German and allied forces.
"We will enter (the data) into electronic warfare databases, which will then notify all our systems if a new radar appears on the Belarusian side," Daum said.
He noted that Russia’s activities in some regions of Europe had reached what he called a "second phase, whose aim is to cause harm," but which does not cross the threshold of armed conflict.
"There is not yet a war in the cyber-information sphere, but it is no longer peace," said the head of the Bundeswehr’s military cyber unit.
The German army is currently testing electronic warfare systems in Lithuania, including drone detection equipment, signal interceptors, jammers, and sensors designed to transmit battlefield data to analysts.
"Before the war in Ukraine, German military personnel could barely persuade commercial companies to supply them with such systems," said Patrick Jeschke, who heads the Bundeswehr’s cyber innovation center.
According to him, the task has changed: now it is necessary not merely to find suppliers, but to select the most promising technologies from a multitude of offers.
"Over the past decades, we did not invest very much in new capabilities. We used what we had because we were focused on missions abroad—in Afghanistan and elsewhere. Now there is a need to improve our capabilities," Daum said.

Economic freedom should become the foundation of Ukraine's post-war reconstruction – ILI experts
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:02:09 EET
03:02:09 KST

The International Liberty Institute (ILI) presented Ukrainian editions of three books by German historian and sociologist Rainer Zitelmann and Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises in Kyiv, and also announced preparations for the publication of another work by Zitelmann. Participants in the presentation emphasized that private property, entrepreneurship, competition and limiting excessive government regulation should become important components of Ukraine's economic recovery.
The books in question are Zitelmann's "In Defense of Capitalism: Debunking the Myths" and "Capitalism Is Not the Problem, but the Solution: A Journey Through the Recent History of Five Continents," as well as Mises' "Bureaucracy." The fourth book, "How Nations Escape Poverty? Vietnam, Poland and the Origins of Prosperity," is currently being edited and prepared for printing, according to the organizers.
In particular, the author of "In Defense of Capitalism" examines ten common accusations against the market economy: from worsening poverty and inequality to environmental problems, monopolies, economic crises and wars. Separate chapters are devoted to the historical experience of socialist economies and the attitudes of citizens in different countries toward entrepreneurship and private property.
"The main idea of this book is to defend an economic system based on freedom, private property, competition and entrepreneurship. Any book that promotes the ideas of economic freedom will have an impact on the improvement and development of our society," Volodymyr Popereshniuk, co-founder of Nova Poshta and the International Liberty Institute (ILI), emphasized at a press conference at the Interfax-Ukraine news agency on Wednesday.
According to him, entrepreneurship creates goods, jobs and prosperity, while excessive government intervention and regulatory restrictions restrain business activity. Popereshniuk also outlined the author's arguments regarding economic inequality, environmental protection, monopolies and the causes of crises.
He separately focused on the sociological part of the publication. According to the presentation materials, Chapter 12 contains a study of Ukrainians' attitudes toward capitalism, while Chapter 13 presents the results of surveys in another 35 countries. According to the results cited by the organizers, pro-capitalist sentiments prevail in Ukraine, Poland, the United States, South Korea, Japan, Nigeria and the Czech Republic.
"Ukrainians perceive economic freedom as their own freedom. These studies give us hope that the ideas of entrepreneurship and competition will prevail in Ukraine," the Nova Poshta co-founder noted, commenting on the results presented in the publication.
Dmytro Dusheiko, PhD in Economics and an expert at the International Liberty Institute (ILI), who served as the academic editor of the Ukrainian edition of "Capitalism Is Not the Problem, but the Solution," in turn emphasized that Zitelmann analyzes the history of countries that chose different economic models under similar initial circumstances. The examples include North and South Korea, the Federal Republic of Germany and the German Democratic Republic, Chile and Venezuela, as well as China before and after the beginning of market reforms in the late 1970s.
The expert drew attention to the differences in the development of West Germany following Ludwig Erhard's reforms and the command-and-administrative system of East Germany. He also cited the experience of market transformations in China and Vietnam after periods of centralized planning.
"We have no right to win the first war for independence and lose the second war — for economic freedom. This very book demonstrates through specific historical examples why reforms will be of decisive importance for the country's development," Dusheiko stressed.
He also pointed out that Zitelmann wrote a special foreword to the Ukrainian edition, in which he emphasized the need for economic transformations after victory in the war for independence.
Dusheiko paid particular attention to the book "How Nations Escape Poverty? Vietnam, Poland and the Origins of Prosperity," on which publishing work is ongoing. In it, the author compares the experiences of two countries that had low levels of personal income at the end of the 20th century but subsequently demonstrated substantial economic growth thanks to reforms.
The economist described the adoption of the Wilczek Act at the end of 1988, which introduced the principle of freedom of entrepreneurship, as an important step in Poland. According to the data presented, the subsequent reforms of Leszek Balcerowicz contributed to 25 years of uninterrupted economic growth in the country between 1992 and 2017. The expert also compared the results of Polish reforms with Ukraine's experience.
"The law did not build anything; it merely allowed people to engage in free enterprise. War and poverty are not a sentence; they are an opportunity for reforms," Dusheiko noted, summarizing the conclusions that, in his opinion, Ukraine can draw from the experiences of these countries.
ILI Director Mykhailo Kamchatnyi presented Ludwig von Mises' work "Bureaucracy," first published in 1944. He recalled that the prominent representative of the Austrian School of Economics was born in Lviv in 1881. According to the institute's director, the first Ukrainian edition of "Bureaucracy" was published in a limited print run in 2021, while the current edition is the second; Mykola Bunyk served as the book's academic editor and translator.
Kamchatnyi explained that Mises distinguishes between management oriented toward profit and consumer needs and bureaucratic management based on compliance with laws, procedures and directives. In his opinion, the problem arises not from the very existence of the administrative apparatus, but when bureaucratic methods are extended to areas where market mechanisms can operate.
"Bureaucracy in itself is neither good nor bad — it is simply a method of management. The most important question is the extent to which bureaucrats interfere in people's lives and in the economy. The main thing we need to do before starting reconstruction is to clearly distinguish the functions of entrepreneurs and bureaucrats. When a former entrepreneur becomes a government official, he begins to act according to laws and regulations rather than the logic of profit," Kamchatnyi emphasized.
According to him, the effectiveness of government bodies should be assessed primarily by how they perform their statutory functions. For example, the amount of tax revenue also depends on the economic situation of a region, particularly its proximity to hostilities.
During the question-and-answer session, participants also addressed the role of private business in the country's defense. Volodymyr Popereshniuk stated that enterprises could participate more effectively in protecting critical facilities, particularly in air defense, but the current procedures, in his opinion, remain excessively bureaucratic.
"This is not a private military company. We do this on a voluntary basis, and the relevant units are subordinate to the military. Companies purchase the necessary equipment at their own expense and allocate personnel, but they operate within the military chain of command," he explained, speaking about business participation in air defense measures.
According to the organizers, the publishing projects presented are intended to encourage discussion about Ukraine's development model, the limits of government intervention and the role of business in reconstruction.

New study explores how money influences interpretations of the Bible
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:00:03 UTC
03:00:03 KST

A new large study reveals that a person’s household income shapes how they interpret the Bible’s teachings on poverty and charity, with wealthier and lower-income believers drawing starkly different conclusions. The research, published in the Journal for the Scientific Study of Religion, shows that highly religious low-income Americans tend to view biblical charity as a call for societal transformation. Highly religious affluent Americans tend to view it as a call for individual philanthropy. These patterns suggest that religious belief often amplifies the economic interests of a person’s social group rather than uniformly justifying economic inequality across all classes.
Sociologists have debated the fundamental nature of religion and its relationship to economic inequality for more than a century. One prominent theory originated with the 19th-century philosopher Karl Marx, who proposed that religion acts as an opiate for the masses. In this view, religious ideas offer a set of comforting illusions that persuade lower-income groups to accept their disadvantaged position.
By framing the current economic system as normal or divinely ordained, religion supposedly drains the motivation to fight for a fairer society. Modern scholars building on this idea argue that religion offers psychological compensators, promising eternal rewards that make present-day inequalities seem less important.
A competing theory takes a different perspective, viewing religion primarily as a tool for binding groups together. Rooted in the work of early sociologist Émile Durkheim, this concept suggests that religious norms and practices serve to unite an in-group and validate that specific group’s interests. Under this framework, religious beliefs do not automatically make people accept the economic status quo. Instead, believers might project their own group’s economic needs onto their theology.
Samuel L. Perry, a sociologist at the University of Oklahoma, wanted to test these two competing frameworks. He designed a study to see if high levels of religious commitment are associated with justifying the current economic system regardless of a person’s own wealth. Alternatively, he wanted to see if religious commitment amplifies different biblical interpretations based on how much money a person makes.
To answer this question, Perry analyzed data from the 2022 Public Religion Research Institute and Brookings Christian Nationalism Survey. This provided a large, nationally representative sample of 5,701 adults living in the United States. The survey included a question asking respondents what they thought Jesus and the prophets primarily meant when speaking about taking care of the poor in the Bible.
Respondents had to choose between two interpretations. The first option stated that biblical teachings on the poor primarily refer to charitable acts by individuals. This represents a more individualized approach to social issues, focusing on personal generosity without challenging the underlying economic system. The second option stated that these teachings primarily refer to an obligation to create a more just society. Scholars often refer to this as structural transformation, which involves altering systemic inequalities.
The researcher looked at two different measures of religious commitment. The first was a private expression of faith, measured by how often the respondents attended religious services. The second was a more public and ideological expression, measured by a person’s adherence to Christian nationalism. Christian nationalism is an ideology that seeks to closely merge Christian identity with American civic life and government policy.
The survey categorized respondents by their annual household income. Perry grouped the participants into three broad economic brackets. These included households earning less than $50,000, those earning between $50,000 and $99,999, and those earning $100,000 or more.
To ensure the results were not skewed by other variables, the statistical models controlled for a wide array of demographic and ideological factors. These included political ideology, political party affiliation, age, race, gender, educational attainment, religious denomination, and geographic region. The control variables performed as expected, with self-identified conservatives and Republicans being less likely to favor the structural-transformation reading of the Bible. In contrast, atheists, non-evangelical Protestants, and highly educated individuals were more likely to affirm the structural reading.
By analyzing these variables together, the study revealed distinct patterns that contradicted the idea of religion acting as a universal opiate. Among Americans in the lowest income bracket, greater religious commitment was linked to a higher likelihood of choosing the structural-transformation interpretation. Highly religious people in this group were more inclined to believe the Bible demands the creation of a just society.
The opposite pattern emerged among Americans in the highest income bracket. For those earning $100,000 or more, high levels of religious attendance and high levels of Christian nationalism were linked to the individualized charity interpretation. As religiosity increased for these affluent earners, they were much more likely to say the Bible teaches that helping the poor is a matter of individual charitable acts.
Middle-income earners fell somewhere in between, though they trended slightly toward the individualized interpretation as their Christian nationalism increased. As their religious attendance increased, they moved toward the individualized interpretation at a pace similar to the highest earners. Overall, the statistical models showed a distinct divide across income groups that widened alongside religious devotion.
The gap in biblical interpretation was widest among the most devout participants. For Americans who rarely attended religious services or scored very low on measures of Christian nationalism, household income was not associated with differing views on biblical charity. Less religious people across all income brackets were about equally split between the two interpretations of poor relief. It was only among highly religious individuals that economic position became strongly associated with a specific theological view.
The author suggests that these results support the in-group cohesion theory over the opiate theory. Instead of deadening the political desires of lower-income people with promises of future rewards, religion seems to amplify the economic interests of whatever class a person belongs to. Wealthy believers favor an interpretation that protects their assets while encouraging personal generosity, while lower-income believers favor an interpretation that demands systemic fairness.
These results come with a few methodological limitations. The survey data is cross-sectional, meaning it captures a single snapshot in time. Because of this design, the study cannot definitively prove that a combination of income and religion directly causes a specific interpretation of the Bible. It is theoretically possible that a person’s theological views might influence their economic position or religious attendance, though the researcher notes this is a less plausible explanation.
Additionally, the study relies on household income as a stand-in for social class. A person’s class is often defined by a combination of factors, including educational background, occupational prestige, and subjective feelings about their own social standing. Future research might incorporate these broader measures to see if the patterns hold up across different definitions of economic status.
The survey also used a single question to measure attitudes about biblical teachings on poverty. Researchers could build on these findings by incorporating multiple questions that ask how participants understand the Bible’s views on getting ahead in life or economic inequality more broadly. Identifying similar trends across a wider variety of questions would provide additional support for the current results.
The study, “Opiate or In-Group Amphetamine? Religion, Economic Position, and the Bible’s Teaching on Charity,” was authored by Samuel L. Perry.

Unregulated peptides contributed to actor's death, coroner finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Coroner recommends TGA review peptide restrictions after Australian actor's death
In short:
Actor Richard Norton's death last year is believed to be the first in Australia known to have been triggered by unapproved peptide use.
A coroner found he suffered a cardiac arrest after injecting CJC1295 and Ipamorelin, which had been prescribed to him by a doctor.
The coroner has recommended the TGA consider tougher restrictions on the use of unapproved peptides.
A coroner has found the death of Australian actor Richard Norton was "triggered by" his injection of unapproved peptides, and has recommended the medicines regulator consider tougher restrictions.
Norton's death is believed to be the first confirmed fatality in Australia from unapproved peptide use.
Norton, 75, was an experienced martial artist who worked in the film and television industry as an actor, stuntman, and instructor.
Coroner David Ryan found Norton's death in March last year was a result of complications that arose from his use of unapproved peptide products CJC1295 and Ipamorelin.
He collapsed and suffered a cardiac arrest after injecting the products, which a doctor had prescribed to him.
In findings delivered on Wednesday, Mr Ryan said Norton "had been taking amounts of the medication in excess of the dose prescribed by his medical practitioner".
The coroner recommended the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) review the therapeutic benefits and safety risks of peptides such as CJC1295 and Ipamorelin and "consider whether further restrictions ought to be imposed on their use".
Doctor prescribed unapproved peptides
Norton was "interested in peptide therapy" and he approached medical practitioner Jerzy Muchnicki, according to the coroner's report.
Norton, who had asthma, osteoarthritis and previous bilateral shoulder reconstructions, told Dr Muchnicki he had been previously prescribed peptides by another practitioner to treat symptoms relating to fatigue, reduced physical recovery, shoulder pain and the loss of lean muscle mass.
The coronial findings noted Dr Muchnicki reviewed Norton's medical history and "discussed in detail what was involved with peptide therapy, including the experimental nature of the treatment".
"They also discussed the potential risks and the lack of other alternative treatment options currently approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA)," the coroner wrote.
Norton also signed an "Informed Consent Form for Peptide Therapy" outlining the treatment, benefits and risks.
"Dr Muchnicki also arranged a series of blood tests 'to confirm baseline health parameters and assess for any contraindications or underlying conditions that may influence treatment decisions'," the report stated.
Norton was prescribed unapproved peptide products CJC1295 and Ipamorelin in injection form which were compounded for him by a licensed compounding pharmacy in Queensland.
The ABC has contacted Dr Muchnicki for comment.
Martial artist taking 'double the dose' of unapproved peptides
In the days before his death Norton reported to Dr Muchnicki that he was "feeling good and the peptide therapy was improving his symptoms".
The coroner noted Norton disclosed to a nurse at Dr Muchnicki's clinic that he had been administering double the prescribed dose of CJC1295 & Ipamorelin.
"The nurse advised Richard that from the following week he ought to only administer the prescribed dose."
Hours after that conversation, Norton became unresponsive after injecting a dose of CJC-1295 and Ipamorelin.
Norton died at Melbourne's Alfred Hospital on March 30, 2025.
Medical board investigation
The coroner's report said the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency received a notification "raising concerns" about Dr Muchnicki's treatment of Norton.
The Medical Board of Australia (MBA) then conducted an investigation which included a report from clinical professor Alistair Vickery.
Professor Vickery stated: "There is insufficient evidence that CJC1295/Ipamorelin is safe, effective or beneficial for human use."
He said taking into account Dr Muchnicki's training and experience and the history of written consent obtained from Norton, including his prior use of peptides without adverse effects, "the clinical care provided by Dr Muchnicki was at a standard reasonably expected".
However, he considered that the notes taken by Dr Muchnicki were "sparse, inadequate and perfunctory" and that his "performance as a medical practitioner was below the standard expected in regards to this issue".
The board's investigation noted that Dr Muchnicki acknowledged these criticisms, accepted accountability for his actions and apologised for his errors in judgement and lapses in record keeping.
"And [he] expressed sorrow for the impact on Richard and his family," the report stated.
He said he had reflected on the circumstances and was committed to improving his practice and professional standards and had engaged an educator to provide one-on-one education in clinical record keeping and management.
In its decision in July this year the MBA found Dr Muchnicki's practice, "is or may be unsatisfactory" however regulatory action was not warranted. He received a caution and conditions were imposed.
The coroner's report noted the TGA said various pathways existed which enabled medical practitioners to access unapproved peptides.
In a statement after the coronial finding was handed down, the TGA said it "continues to warn consumers about the risks of unapproved peptides which have not been assessed by the TGA for safety, quality or effectiveness".
The medicines regulator said it had also communicated those risks to health practitioners.
"We are continuing to assess the risks associated with these products and considering whether further regulatory or other measures may be appropriate," the statement said.

CSIRO criticised for lack of transparency over gas leak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

CSIRO shared draft media release with Santos over Darwin tank leak, documents show
In short:
Internal emails and messages obtained under Freedom of Information (FOI) laws reveal CSIRO staffers were uncomfortable about scrutiny of the agency.
The correspondence followed reporting by the ABC about a secret 18-year leak from Santos's Darwin LNG plant.
What's next?
CSIRO has been called on to open its books on the scale and impact of the leak for public consideration.
Australia's national science agency scrambled to spin its role in helping fossil fuel giant Santos investigate a secret 18-year leak from its Darwin LNG plant, internal CSIRO messages have revealed.
The ABC exposed the leak and government agencies' knowledge of it last year.
CSIRO was engaged by Santos for a range of services in 2021 and 2024 including to advise on methods used to monitor emissions at the Darwin site.
The science agency staffers sent emails and internal messages revealing how uncomfortable they were with scrutiny of the agency, following the ABC's reporting, noting it made things "difficult and tricky" with the minister, documents released to the Environment Centre NT (ECNT) under Freedom of Information (FOI) laws show.
The staffers openly discussed how some of their responses to questions could be more "fulsome" and went to lengths to note the agency's work did not include direct monitoring of the leak — while also acknowledging internally CSIRO's contract with Santos allowed for direct monitoring.
"These documents suggest to us an ongoing and frankly unacceptable reluctance on behalf of CSIRO to be transparent with the public," said Bree Ahrens, CEO of the ECNT.
Former NSW Supreme Court judge Anthony Whealy said there was a "distinct impression given that CSIRO have not been entirely frank and open in relation to their dealings in this matter".
"They are a public agency and we should expect them to be open with us. I think the public expect that and the media expect that as well," he said.
Leak that helped scuttle Australia's largest ever foreign takeover bid
In September 2025, the ABC revealed the LNG storage tank at Santos's Darwin LNG plant had been leaking methane into the atmosphere following damage it incurred during commissioning in 2006.
The amount of methane released was estimated to be nearly 100 kilograms per hour — just shy of what would count as a "super-emitter" under US regulations.
The revelations were widely reported as contributing to the collapse of a $36 billion takeover bid for Santos.
The reporting also revealed a number of state and federal agencies had knowledge of the leak, including CSIRO, which was engaged by Santos to help validate emissions measurement methods.
None of those agencies made the leak public, or informed other government agencies that were considering approving Santos's application to use the damaged LNG tank for decades beyond its planned life.
Santos has since been approved to continue using the tank for another 20 years — an outcome that played a crucial role in the company's development of the controversial Barossa gas field off the north coast of Australia.
'Your mate': Draft CSIRO statement shared with Santos
The documents show how scrutiny played out inside the agency, and between CSIRO, the minister and the Department of Industry, Science and Resources (DISR), which oversees it.
In one explanation about CSIRO's work to DISR, CSIRO said: "In 2024, CSIRO was engaged by Santos to undertake monitoring of the Darwin LNG project site."
Across multiple messages, CSIRO staffers explained the agency also assessed methodology used by Santos to measure the leak, and assessed options for ongoing monitoring.
But internal discussions show the agency was at pains to minimise any impression CSIRO was involved in monitoring of the tank leak. At one point a draft response was edited, with a staffer noting: "I suggest adding wording to reinforce it was 3rd party methods we reviewed to be crystal clear we didn't do any monitoring."
As staff drafted a public statement responding to the ABC story, one staffer shared the agency's contract with Santos. A reply read "perfect — that's pretty clear… says we can do monitoring… but we didn't".
One staffer then asked the other if they had checked the draft public statement about the ABC report with Santos, asking "are you going to send our statement to your mate?".
A staffer responds, "All good — I sent to their media chap this morning", noting that Santos would be busy with another story about the leak that day in the Australian Financial Review.
A spokesperson for CSIRO told the ABC: "CSIRO developed and approved its own media response. A copy of the statement was provided to Santos as a courtesy."
In the published statement, CSIRO said the work "did not involve monitoring, prevention or remediation advice related to the leak".
CSIRO staff squirm following ABC investigation
As questions mounted, one staffer working on a response to the ABC wrote in an internal message "difficult and tricky — for us too with the minister. god damn it".
The final CSIRO published response said it was correcting "errors" in the ABC report, but no errors were identified in the statement.
The reporting from September last year focused on revelations CSIRO knew about the leak and did not tell other agencies or the public. The FOI documents confirmed the agency knew the size of the leak, with staffers noting it was estimated to be 97.6kg per hour.
The CSIRO spokesperson said the agency's concern was "that the article conflated CSIRO's work assessing background methane concentrations and a desktop review of third-party methane measurement methods with advice relating to management of the reported leak. CSIRO did not provide monitoring, remediation or leak-management advice".
Ms Ahrens called on CSIRO to open its books on the issue.
"We've had various claims about what the volume of the leak from the Santos facility is, and little to substantiate claims that there is no reason to be concerned about its impact on air quality," she said.
"The only way to resolve these unanswered questions is to put the full set of data and the review on the table for the public to consider."
The possibility of making the data available was raised when CSIRO staffers discussed how to respond to questions from then-Greens leader Senator Larissa Waters.
"Do we take the opportunity to be a bit more fulsome and include the work?" one staffer asked.
The CSIRO spokesperson said: "As is normal when developing responses, different levels of detail and draft formulations were considered. The final statement reflected the information considered necessary to accurately explain the nature and scope of CSIRO's work."
A Santos spokesperson told the ABC the company developed a "leak detection and repair program” in 2025.
"This program is aimed at finding and mitigating any potential fugitives within the facility. This measurement and monitoring will further enhance reporting of fugitive emissions."

Bad inflation result lays bare the ugly truth: there is no easy way out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Bad inflation result lays bare the ugly truth: There is no easy way out
It is hard to imagine after nearly five years of economic pain, but the grim truth revealed by yesterday's batch of high inflation numbers is inescapable: the worst is yet to come.
Most observers now think the Reserve Bank will hike rates again on Tuesday. That would take the cash rate to 4.85 per cent, its highest level in 18 years. By now, we know this means a tighter financial squeeze for all borrowers.
Few will want to spare a thought for the politicians, but the news also piled on the agony for Treasurer Jim Chalmers, who had to front up once again for a stony-faced press conference and a Question Time laden with jeers from the opposition benches.
As he has done countless times, Chalmers acknowledged those "doing it tough" and solemnly swore the government would continue to be "responsible". And, as always, he snarled at "commentators" who say public spending is the root cause of the problem.
He might have a point. The role of global events is obvious. They are driving up inflation worldwide. And a private sector investment boom, propelled by the rush to build data centres, hasn't helped either. They're excuses, but they're real ones.
Still, how many times can you reassure people that you're doing everything you can and that you're sensitive to the difficulty they're enduring before your words lose weight?
The answer: you can keep it up for as long as you can sell hope. And that's getting tough.
The demise of the narrow path to a soft landing
Rewind to 2022, when this inflation episode began, and hope was a carefully calibrated part of the message. The government and the Reserve Bank were singing from the same song sheet, promising a relatively painless route out of trouble.
They called it "the narrow path to a soft landing". Interest rates would rise, but not as sharply as in other countries. They might stay high a little longer, but without doing excessive damage to the jobs market or the broader economy.
There were always those who said this sounded too good to be true. Inflation has wrought havoc whenever it has taken hold in history, and it has rarely been possible to banish it without a recession, such as the one Paul Keating said we "had to have" in 1990.
But it was an admirable ambition, and it's not entirely anyone's fault that it didn't work out. Yes, the "narrow path" strategy probably was the reason why Australia had more heat left in inflation when the war hit. But that's why it was called "narrow".
And the war, coupled with the AI investment boom, have made for a perfect storm not just in Australia but in other countries, too. The boom pushed up demand, and the war constrained what could be supplied, stretching out the gap where inflation thrives.
The inflation game
That is inflation's simple, ruthless logic. When demand in an economy outstrips what can be supplied, inflation is the result, because the excess demand has nowhere to go other than to bid prices up.
To stamp that out, all that can be done is to slash demand or expand our capacity for supply. The latter option is what economists mean when they talk about productivity. Sluggish productivity growth is what Michele Bullock calls our "fundamental challenge".
But, in the meantime, the only other option is to slash demand, from anywhere. Rate hikes do this by slugging borrowers. Critics who say they do not address the root cause of inflation misunderstand the aim; it might be unfair, but it can be effective.
The government can also reduce demand, either by cutting spending or hiking taxes. These can be more targeted approaches, but the political difficulties are obvious.
That is why economists like Chris Richardson tend not to ask governments to slash and burn, and instead judge them by the precautionary principle: at the very least, don't make things worse by spending more or handing out large tax cuts.
Loading
The wide path to a deep landing
Of course, that is exactly what governments are tempted to do when voters are worn down by all those high prices. And, as Chalmers put it on Tuesday, helping people with the cost of living can be legitimate and necessary. It's an exercise in "balance".
As the opposition has pointed out, the government could have been a little braver if it wanted to. Spending like the EV discount and the home batteries discount might have achieved a climate goal but has put billions into the pockets of high-income earners.
But these are small in the grand scheme of things. And as the government points out, nobody in politics wants to identify acceptable spending cuts on a grander scale. It's hard to argue that a subsidy here or there is the main reason we are where we are.
Anyway, that sort of quibbling dodges the ugly truth about what lies ahead. The Reserve Bank, with the government's support, tried to get rid of inflation without triggering job losses and a recession. The soft approach didn't work.
That means that narrow path, and that soft landing, are likely beyond us. We have escaped the worst until now, with minimal change in the jobs market and minimal business closures or distressed housing sales.
Absent a productivity boom, which nobody can clearly articulate how to create, we will be going harder for longer, suppressing demand well into 2027.
Higher rates will do that, and it will probably happen on the budget balance sheet too. For all his defensiveness about the role of government spending, Chalmers has promised further savings and poured cold water on calls for cost-of-living relief.
Around the cabinet table and the RBA board table is a shared recognition: that inflation is destructive, that it is making people angry, but that the only way is through.

In response, the NABU and the SAPO stated that they view such actions as a continuation of a systematic attack on independent anti-corruption agencies. On the evening of September 14, the PGO reported that no such charges had been filed.
Kravchenko, for his part, stated that he had left Ukraine, claiming he had gone on a business trip. According to unconfirmed reports, Kravchenko and his wife may be in Vienna (Austria) and are in talks with local law firms regarding asylum.
Acting Prosecutor General Anton Kovalsky announced in October that an internal investigation into the departure abroad of former Ukrainian Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko is ongoing; the circumstances surrounding the organization of his business trip are being examined, and, in total, eight individuals mentioned in connection with operation "Carthage" have been dismissed from the prosecutor's office.

Switzerland adopts new climate adaptation plan as temperatures rise

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Switzerland has adopted a revised climate adaptation strategy and action plan, the Federal Council announced Wednesday, as temperatures continue to rise across the country.
According to the council, Switzerland's average annual temperature has risen by around 3 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, making the country particularly vulnerable to climate change.
The council said heat waves, summer droughts and heavy rainfall have become more frequent and intense.
The strategy for 2026-2031 identifies 30 areas for action aimed at protecting the population, infrastructure and natural resources from worsening climate impacts.
According to the council, key priorities include reducing heat exposure in urban areas, safeguarding water supplies, strengthening protection against natural hazards and improving the resilience of agriculture, forests, ecosystems and transport infrastructure.
The plan also outlines measures to improve workplace safety during extreme heat, protect water quality, develop climate-resilient forests and adapt navigation on the Rhine River to increasingly dry summers, the council said.
The government said the strategy draws on Switzerland's 2025 climate risk assessment and updated national climate scenarios, including the possibility of continued increases in greenhouse gas emissions.
The action plan also includes 12 cross-sector measures aimed at improving scientific knowledge, coordination and implementation, according to the council.
The Federal Council said the strategy seeks to minimize climate-related risks, strengthen society's ability to adapt and take advantage of potential opportunities arising from changing climatic conditions.

He said that "the tyrannical America's condition is no better," noting that Iran and its great people stood firm, and Iran offered martyrs, foremost among them the Sayyid, the leader of its march and the march of the Ummah, the martyr Imam Ali Khamenei and his family, and martyrs from the leadership and the people, but it foiled America's and Israel's objectives of overthrowing the Islamic system and dividing the country.
He added: "It has become clear that it is impossible for America to control Iran, at a time when America is experiencing turmoil in its political decisions, a severe economic crisis, and has lost its global standing, and is preparing to exit the region."
Sheikh Qassem affirmed that all of this was achieved thanks to the steadfastness of the great Iranian people and the wise and courageous leadership of Sayyid Mojtaba Khamenei.

Reporter's notebook: Visiting a POW camp is the best possible antidote to sympathy for Russian soldiers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:57:43 UTC
02:57:43 KST

Reporter's notebook: Visiting a POW camp is the best possible antidote to sympathy for Russian soldiers
Russian soldiers, enticed by lucrative payouts, continue to sign up voluntarily in droves to attack and kill in Ukraine.
Captive soldiers of the Russian military eating lunch at a Ukrainian prisoner of war camp in western Ukraine on June 25, 2026. (Francis Farrell / The Kyiv Independent)
Once our eyes adjusted to the aggressive glare of the freshly painted white walls around the yard, we began to make out figures, dozens of them dressed in navy blue, clinging to the inner walls of this surreal space.
It was a scorching June day in western Ukraine, and we had just been released, like kids in a petting zoo, into a courtyard full of prisoners of war from the Russian military.
Who we decided to walk up to and talk to, and what we wanted to talk about, was up to us.
Whether these men, captives of the country they had attacked with rifle in hand, wanted to speak to us was up to them.
And so we began our work.
Looking one's enemy in the eye and trying one's best to see their human face is a strange place to put oneself in.
Standing opposite a man who, in some ways, is the living embodiment of all the suffering and death brought to your home and the people living in it, and trying to have a normal, civilized conversation is especially strange.
That was my goal when I signed up this summer to visit one of the Ukrainian prisoner-of-war camps where Russian soldiers were being held captive.
This wasn't exclusive access. Trips like this for the press are organized by Ukrainian authorities at the same facility every month.
But I wasn't there just for the shock and awe of seeing Russian POWs and asking them gotcha questions.
In the fifth year of full-scale war, Vladimir Putin is still doing his best to continue his quest to destroy independent Ukraine without needing to announce large-scale forced mobilization at home.
But Russia's offensives continue, with hundreds — often upwards of a thousand — Russian single-use soldiers killed or badly wounded on the battlefield every day.
Moscow can sustain this because, somewhere, all across the depths of that huge country, tens of thousands of men every month continue to sign up voluntarily to fight in Ukraine.
For there to be any chance of Putin considering winding his war down, this flow of warm bodies needs to dry up. But for now, they just keep coming.
I wanted to understand why. I wanted to understand who these people are, and why they decide to leave their civilian lives and join a war of aggression.
Fast forward four months, and not only is this basic fact about Russia's wartime military still not understood, but the question of whether or not one should have sympathy for these invaders has once again become a popular topic of discussion.
Deep into autumn, the weather has turned, the first blackouts have begun, and a nation of tens of millions is bracing itself for a winter humanitarian crisis unlike anything seen before, all thanks to Russia's escalating strike campaign against critical infrastructure.
But as if this time wasn't going to be difficult enough as it is, openly showing contempt for Ukraine and directly assisting Russia's war effort through waived sanctions, diesel deals and the throttling of Starlink is now in vogue among two of the most powerful men in the world, Donald Trump and Elon Musk.
Reading it from Kyiv, Musk's post on X about feeling sympathy for the poor young Russian soldiers forced to fight crosses into the domain of the absurd.
And yet here we are.
More than anything, this moment in time back to that summer day at the POW camp and what I heard from the Russian soldiers themselves about why they ended up in Ukraine, fighting for the aggressor's army.
This was my second time speaking to Russian prisoners of war.
The first time, ironically, was probably the only scenario in which Musk's comment really applied: when Ukrainian forces captured hundreds of young Russians doing mandatory military service as they broke across the border in Kursk Oblast in the summer of 2024.
This time, all four Russians were, unsurprisingly, contract soldiers. And, by coincidence, they all happened to hail from the depths of Siberia, from the regions around Lake Baikal.
This is what they had to say.
Pavel Malikov was the first man I approached in the yard. He seemed aloof at first, but after I asked him if we could speak, he replied, “Well, we're already speaking, aren't we?” At which point, we pressed the record button.
A factory worker from the remote Altai Krai, Malikov had joined Russia's Spetsnaz, Moscow's once-feared special forces.
But by the time he first saw the battlefield in Ukraine, his mission barely differed from that of the average assault infantryman: move forward to his designated point, dig in and wait for orders.
He was captured on his second mission.
Looking me in the eye, Malikov spoke confidently with an air of pride, the basis of which I couldn't quite understand.
"I signed the contract because… well, you know… there was seemingly nothing bad in my life, but not much good either, I was kind of stuck. My decision wasn't so much about changing my life as it was about changing myself.
"I went and signed the contract. Many people regret it after they sign it, they think, 'why the hell did I do this,' and so on. I don't have any such thoughts. I signed the contract, that means it was meant to be.
"I had an idea of what was going on here, but I only gained a full understanding after I came here. Yes, war is bad, but nonetheless, I am a patriot of my country, my Russia, and I still stand by my country, no matter what."
Next was 41-year-old Oleg Krasikov from Buryatia, captured that summer after suffering light wounds to his leg, who told a commonplace story of being deceived and forced into the assault infantry.
Now a prisoner, his position on the war had suddenly been imbued with a performative moral clarity.
"It's not clear yet when it will all end. I hope that Moscow will come up with something, because as I understand it, comrade Zelensky is ready to negotiate."
But beyond the facade of remorse lay Krasikov's real story, and his motivations for joining up in the first place couldn't have been more banal.
"I had an ordinary life, home work, traveling for work.
"At one point, work stopped, and I stayed at home for half a year, doing odd jobs. I saw the advertisement, and honestly, I had financial problems, I needed to do renovations (to my home). Maybe that's what pushed me, the urgent need for money. So I signed the contract.
"They offered something different, not the front line, not shooting, nothing like that. I had a picture of what it might be, but it wasn't like that.
"I went to a recruitment center, they explained everything there, and gave me a contract to sign.
"I signed the contract, got the money, and did the renovation."
At a conference in Europe last year, I had a rare conversation with an exiled journalist from Russia's Arctic region.
In his grim appraisal of Russia's manpower situation, he predicted that Putin would not have to announce forced mobilization.
After years of war, the pervasive militarization and wholesale brainwashing in Russia's school system, he argued, would ensure a consistent flow of young voluntary recruits joining up after school for years to come.
After a bland but nutritious lunch shared with the POWs, we had time for two more interviews. I specifically requested to speak with younger soldiers who had been captured this year.
The first was 21-year-old Dmitry Nefedov, who had spent the entirety of Ukraine's most recent brutal winter in a basement in the gray zone, surrounded by Ukrainian soldiers and abandoned by his commanders, until he was finally captured.
Nefedov spoke with a blankness in his eyes and a passive naivety that I still think about to this day.
Nothing in his words or mannerisms suggested that any part of this ordeal had been a lesson to him.
"I didn't have enough money, and I wanted to hang out, have fun. First my friends signed up, for a while I thought about it, and I signed a contract."
I asked if he didn't think that this war and the deaths of so many countrymen was pointless.
"I don't even know what to say… I know that only presidents can solve this.
"If I'm released and all of this is over, I don't know what I will do. If I don't find a normal job, I'll sign another contract. Otherwise, I might try to become a welder or a builder."
The last Russian soldier was even younger. Eighteen-year-old Maksim Alechko, had barely started school when Russia first invaded Ukraine.
He seemed more mentally proactive and switched on than any of the other POWs I spoke to.
But even then, Alechko's worldview seemed defined by a complete disconnect from the reality of the war, let alone any moral framework for understanding what his country was doing when he volunteered to join.
In his hometown, the industrial city of Chita, the Russian military and service in it carried only positive associations, he said.
"I liked the army, I joined the army, and stayed there. That's it, an order is an order.
"I only ever saw myself in this field. It's prestigious, it's beautiful, something to be proud of, to be a soldier.
"I wasn't interested in the war in Ukraine, I was interested in being a soldier. For my country.
"I didn't think anything bad about Ukraine, but when the war started, this whole information war began. Future generations are being turned against each other.
"What they are saying in Russia now, the reasons to join the military… The last time I watched, they were saying 'We are winning, come join the ranks of the victorious!' or something like that.
"People think the war will end soon, so they can sign up, earn some money, and that will be it."
Note from the author:
Hi, this is Francis Farrell, the author of this piece. We are entering a new phase of the war, where once again the daily, brutal fight on the front line to hold Russia back is drowned out by geopolitical noise. Despite the difficult winter ahead of us and the effect that will have on the work of our newsroom, we will continue to report from the field wherever necessary. China Tests Trimaran Submarine Designed to Carry Missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:56:42 UTC
02:56:42 KST

China is developing a trimaran submarine that combines the concept of a semi-submersible missile carrier with an uncrewed platform.
The vessel is undergoing tests in Huludao, in the Bohai Bay area. It was transported there from the southern city of Guangzhou via the port of Dalian, according to Naval News.
The vessel is designed to carry a large number of missiles and launch them using targeting data from other ships, aircraft or satellites.
The central hull houses two missile compartments containing launch canisters. The total number of missile launch cells is estimated at 16 to 18.
To launch its weapons, the submarine must surface, open the compartment doors and raise the launchers into a vertical position.
The vessel may carry anti-ship missiles or land-attack cruise missiles. Possible options include YJ-20 missiles, which are used on Type 055 destroyers.
The hull design, with additional side floats at the stern, provides stability while underway and when stationary on the surface. These elements compensate for shifts in the center of gravity as the missile canisters are raised.
The vessel is equipped with a snorkel to allow its diesel engines to operate while submerged. Its propulsion system consists of main propellers or waterjets for diesel-powered operation, along with electric propellers on the side floats.
The trimaran has a submerged displacement of approximately 900 metric tons. The weapons compartment occupies most of the vessel’s internal space.
Due to the lack of available interior space, the vessel is believed to be uncrewed. The bridge at the top is intended only for control during port entry and maneuvering in roadsteads.
Its operating concept resembles that of diesel-powered submarines from the Cold War era, which surfaced to launch missiles.
Militarnyi previously reported that Russia had transferred technical documentation and materials to China for submarine testing.

Govt targets $220 bn investment in RE during 2027-30
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:56:41 UTC
02:56:41 KST

New Delhi: Govt is targeting to mobilise $220 billion in investment in the renewable energy sector by 2030 to expand manufacturing, transmission infrastructure and green hydrogen production, as it prepares to host the four-day Bharat Renewable Energy Summit & Expo (BRESE) in the capital from Nov 2 to 5.While solar energy projects would require an investment of nearly $70 billion, wind projects would need $25-30 billion, energy storage deployment $20 billion, transmission networks $40-45 billion, hydropower $12-15 billion and green hydrogen offtake $20-25 billion. India aims to achieve 500 GW of installed non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030.The summit will be inaugurated by PM Narendra Modi at Bharat Mandapam on Nov 2 and is likely to be attended by energy ministers from 30 countries, including Australia, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom, as well as representatives of the European Union, with the aim of exploring cooperation in renewable energy financing, green hydrogen, energy storage, clean energy manufacturing and technology development.Santosh Sarangi, secretary in Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE), said India had secured $64 billion in private investment between June 2024, when the previous RE-Invest Summit was held, and June 2026, including $6.2 billion in foreign direct investment (FDI).“With 308 GW of installed non-fossil fuel capacity, we are firmly on course to reach our 500 GW target by 2030. Realising this ambition will require approximately $220 billion in investment between 2027 and 2030, alongside accelerated deployment of energy storage, stronger transmission networks and expanded domestic manufacturing capabilities,” Sarangi said, adding that financial investors, private equity firms, pension funds and mutual funds were expected to play a key role in it.
Ministry is also developing a framework to assign exploration rights for geothermal energy, similar to the guidelines on petroleum exploration, which is expected to be ready within a month or two.BRESE 2026 will be held alongside the 9th Session of International Solar Alliance (ISA) Assembly and 4th International Conference on Green Hydrogen (ICGH).
Sarangi said Indian green hydrogen developers have so far secured orders for about 5.5 lakh tonnes per annum (MTPA), including 4.5 lakh MTPA secured in 2026 alone. Japan, South Korea and the EU were looking at greater sourcing of green ammonia and green methanol.He said green hydrogen had huge potential, with several pilot projects already under way in the direct reduced iron (DRI) steel and transportation sectors. India is also conducting an experiment across 10,000 acres in six states, covering 10 different crops, to inject ammonia directly into the soil instead of applying urea, a move that could improve efficiency and reduce costs and losses due to volatilisation and irrigation, Sarangi said.

Atul is known for investigative depth and strong human-interest narratives as he strives to bring clarity and context to complex issues. He currently tracks the energy sector, writing on power, renewable energy, coal and mines.

Ethiopia receives 12 Russian Su-35 fighter jets, plans to acquire S-400 air defenses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:56:19 UTC
02:56:19 KST

Andrew Wasike 
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced Wednesday that Ethiopia has received 12 advanced Russian-made Su-35 fighter jets and plans to acquire four S-400 air defense systems.
The announcement comes as tensions with neighboring Eritrea and renewed fighting in the northern Tigray region raise fears of a wider conflict in the Horn of Africa.
"Ethiopia's newly deployed military jets will remain more ready than ever to defend the airspace!" Abiy wrote on US social media platform X.
He said the fighter jets were delivered under an earlier agreement with Moscow, and the S-400 air defense systems are expected to arrive later.
"I would like to express my gratitude to my friend, Russian President Vladimir Putin, for his dedication in ensuring we received these warplanes a year ahead of our agreed schedule," said Abiy.
He described the acquisitions as a major step toward strengthening Ethiopia's military capabilities and protecting its sovereignty.
The Russian multirole combat aircraft is designed for air superiority and ground attack missions. The S-400 is a long-range surface-to-air missile system that can engage aircraft and other aerial threats.
Tensions have heightened between Ethiopia and Eritrea, former allies whose relations have deteriorated because of Addis Ababa's demand for access to the Red Sea and disagreements on security in northern Ethiopia.
Ethiopia has been landlocked since Eritrea gained independence in 1993, and Abiy has repeatedly described maritime access as essential to the country's economic and security interests.
Renewed fighting in Tigray, where Ethiopian federal forces and rival Tigrayan factions have been engaged in hostilities, has also raised concerns about instability along the Ethiopian-Eritrean border.
The two countries fought a border war from 1998 to 2000 before restoring diplomatic relations in 2018. Eritrean troops later fought alongside Ethiopian government forces during the 2020-2022 Tigray conflict, but relations have since deteriorated.
