Balad leader blasts ‘racist’ exclusion of Arab parties in Israel
Elections have yielded no clear winner but opposition bloc refuses to ally with Arab parties.
The leader of Israel’s Balad party has condemned the country’s main political leaders for refusing to form a coalition with Arab parties, even after a record showing in polls could make them kingmakers for the next parliament after no clear winner emerged.
Sami Abu Shehadeh told Al Jazeera that Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about a fifth of the population, are being treated as illegitimate partners despite their turnout.
“This is racism,” he said. “We are a legitimate elected leadership of the national minority. The vast majority of our people decided that we are their leadership.”
Arab parties are on course to win a record 19 seats, giving them potentially decisive leverage over the main political blocs. With 85 percent of the vote counted, Israel’s Central Elections Committee has Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc ahead with at least 53 seats, and the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot on 48.
Both are short of the 61 needed to govern. Netanyahu says Israelis chose a strong right-wing government, while Eisenkot says they voted for change.
Abu Shehadeh, who leads Balad, one of the Joint List’s three parties, was not a candidate.
Israel’s elections committee voted to disqualify him at the request of far-right Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who accused him of supporting the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack due to an article issued the following day in which Abu Shehadeh called it an “important historical event”.
Abu Shehadeh subsequently told the Supreme Court he did not support “armed struggle” but acknowledged that a paragraph in the article had been incorrectly worded. He said his intention was to call for moving the conflict towards a political process.
He withdrew in October after a majority of the Supreme Court panel appeared willing to approve the disqualification. He rejects the grounds and said the court had made clear that Israel has “two different judicial systems, one for the Jews and one for the Arabs”.
“We are very proud of the Arab Palestinian minority in Israel that went in this very high percentage of voting,” he told Al Jazeera. The community’s first promise to voters, he said, was to prevent “this gang of criminals” from returning to power, naming Netanyahu and far-right ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Ben-Gvir. “So our first promise, we can keep it from now .”
Numbers point to Arab parties but opposition bloc resistant
Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, said Netanyahu “has scared off everybody from talking to the Palestinian Israeli parties”, leaving him best placed to “call the shots”. She said that Eisenkot and his allies have indicated that they want a Zionist government and “do not want to form a government” with the Arab parties, leaving them few options.
Danny Ayalon, a former Israeli ambassador to the United States, told Al Jazeera that turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel came in “really unprecedented numbers” and that the parties “are going to have some significant clout”.
Mathematically, he said, Eisenkot’s bloc could join forces with the two Arab parties and pass the threshold, though it would take “political wizardry”. Yousef Jabareen, who leads the Joint List, has said his alliance’s “hands are extended” to oust Netanyahu.
Abu Shehadeh set out what Palestinian citizens want from the next government.
“We are against genocide and we are against apartheid. We want to promote a different political alternative, one which is based on the values of freedom, justice and equality for both people who are living between the river and the sea.”
Of Netanyahu, he said: “Our problem … is that he is a war criminal.”
A UN commission said in a report published on Monday that Israel has continued to commit genocide in Gaza after last October’s US-brokered ceasefire in the enclave.
The Hague-based International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu in 2024 for war crimes during the Gaza war.

Activist Dolores Huerta Dies at 96. Here's What To Know About Her Trailblazing Life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:52:43 UTC
02:52:43 KST

Dolores Huerta, an internationally renowned activist, community organizer, and political force who co-founded what is now known as the United Farm Workers of America (UFW) alongside Cesar Chavez, died Wednesday at her home in Bakersfield, California. She was 96.
News of Huerta’s death was shared by family members through her Instagram account, though the post did not disclose a cause of death. The New York Times reported that the cause of death was cancer, citing a spokesperson for Huerta.
"We know that many of you around the world share in our mourning, and we will be following up on plans to recognize and celebrate her incredible life and legacy," the post said.
Huerta dedicated her career to fighting a variety of causes, including labor rights, women's rights and immigrants’ rights. She is also credited with coining the phrase "Yes we can"—"Sí se puede"—which was later adopted by Barack Obama.
In March 2026, Huerta publicly accused Chavez of sexually abusing her decades earlier, breaking a silence she said she had maintained to protect the farmworker movement. Her disclosure accompanied a New York Times investigation into allegations that Chavez sexually abused women and girls.
"I think she kind of radiates empowerment not only for herself, but for others," Mario Garcia, a professor of Chicano Studies and History at the University of California, Santa Barbara, told TIME in an interview before Huerta's death. "She's really quite an electrifying person."
Indeed, when Huerta received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012, Obama noted that she "does not play."
"Without any negotiating experience, Dolores helped lead a worldwide grape boycott that forced growers to agree to some of the country's first farmworker contracts," Obama said during the ceremony. "And ever since she has fought to give more people a seat at the table. 'Don't wait to be invited,' she says. 'Step in there.'"
"On a personal note, Dolores was very gracious when I told her I had stolen her slogan, Sí se puede, Yes we can," Obama added. "Knowing her, I'm pleased that she let me off easy."
How Huerta's early life shaped her activism
Huerta was born on April 10, 1930, in Dawson, New Mexico, to Alicia Chávez and Juan Fernández, who both played a major role in her views on justice.
Her father was a miner and farmworker who went on to join the New Mexico state legislature. After her parents' divorce, her mother opened up her own hotel in Stockton, California, and often offered affordable or free rooms to low-wage workers, according to a biography by the Dolores Huerta Foundation (DHF). Huerta often said she became a feminist because of her mother. As a girl, Huerta was a high-achieving student, an active member of several school clubs, and a member of the Girl Scouts. Huerta now has a Scouts patch dedicated to her.
In 1945, one of her two brothers was beaten for wearing a zoot suit, an ensemble then popular with Black and Mexican-American men who were often unfairly labeled as delinquents. She has said that her brother's beating further influenced her activism.
After Huerta graduated from high school, she obtained a provisional teaching credential at the University of the Pacific’s Stockton College, which later became San Joaquin Delta College, and began teaching at an area elementary school. She also got married and had two children with her husband at the time, Ralph Head. She has repeatedly said that her students, many of whom were children of farmworkers, inspired her activism.
"I think the one thing that really kind of hooked me for life was going to the homes of some workers who did not have linoleum or wood on their floor, only dirt," Huerta told MAKERS, a documentary project featuring influential women, in 2012. "And yet, these are people who are working, they're working very hard and you know that this is wrong."
Huerta decided to pursue a career in community organizing in 1955 when she met Fred Ross Sr., founder of the Community Service Organization (CSO) and a nationally influential community organizer who began his career fighting for the rights of Dust Bowl-era farmworkers.
Dolores Huerta accepts TIME100 Impact Award
Finding her voice
At a November 2018 TED Talk, Huerta told an audience she found her voice while volunteering at the Stockton chapter of CSO, which she co-founded.
She described a day she was volunteering there when she was 25 years old and a disabled farmworker walked in asking if someone could help him apply for disability benefits. She went to a welfare office with the man, but she was not allowed to submit an application on his behalf. Defeated, she returned to CSO, where Ross told her to go back and demand that a supervisor allow the man to submit an application.
"I kind of overcame my anxieties and my fears. I went down to the welfare office and I demanded to see the supervisor," Huerta said. "That taught me a lesson. That taught me that I had a voice."
Ross taught Huerta to make demands of people, she said, especially public officials. He also instilled the importance of voting.
While at CSO, Huerta founded the Agricultural Workers Association, led voter registration drives and met Cesar Chavez in 1955, while he was an organizer with CSO. Chavez would later become CSO's executive director in 1959.
Ross died in 1992, but Huerta described Ross as her "spiritual father" for the rest of her life, and the first person to teach her and Chavez community-organizing techniques.
Founding the United Farm Workers
In 1962, Huerta and Chavez left CSO to found the National Farm Workers Association, which would later become UFW, a union that continues to advocate for the rights of agricultural workers.
They were motivated to found the association after hearing from scores of California farmworkers working under harsh conditions: no benefits, low wages, and no access to bathrooms or water while in the fields. The Bracero Program, established through a 1942 agreement between the U.S. and Mexico, recruited Mexican workers to address wartime agricultural labor shortages and continued until 1964.
Chavez and Huerta believed the Bracero Program allowed for farmworker abuses and lobbied to end it. They lobbied against the program, which ended in 1964.
Huerta and Chavez continued their fight for workers' rights, including leading protests, worker strikes, hunger strikes, and arguably their most famous tactic, national boycotts. Huerta helped organize the nationwide grape boycott that supported the Delano grape strike of 1965-1970. The strike began with Filipino farmworkers affiliated with the Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee; Huerta and Chavez’s National Farm Workers Association subsequently joined them. The Delano Grape Strike and Boycott convinced grocery store chains to stop selling the fruit until industry labor standards were set.
Huerta’s boycotts were effective in forcing industries to guarantee better working conditions for their employees.
"I think one of the things about when people are oppressed is that they start accepting their condition and they often kind of blame themselves," Huerta said during a 2015 Q&A with the National Portrait Gallery. "Our job was to convince them again that they could make a difference and that they had the power to do it."
In 1975, California passed the Agricultural Labor Relations Act, which gave farmworkers the right to unionize. The state credited Huerta as instrumental in establishing those rights. Though Chavez often receives national accolades for the achievements of the farmworker movement, historians say Huerta played an equally essential role through every success—but historically received far less credit.
"[Chavez] didn't win you over with his rhetoric, [Chavez] was always soft spoken, but he also radiated strong internal leadership qualities," Garcia said. "[Huerta], by contrast, was always much more verbal, a much better speaker than [Chavez]."
In a 2018 interview with TIME, Huerta said she didn't expect recognition.
"I think that’s very typical of women," she said. "I had been acculturated to be supportive, to be accommodating, to support men in the work they do. We never think of getting credit or recognition or even taking the power. We didn’t think in those terms."
She added that she believed times were changing. "That could make an incredible amount of difference in our world,” she said. “We will never have peace in the world until feminists take power."
In March 2026, Huerta disclosed that Chavez had sexually abused her in the 1960s. She alleged that he pressured her into sex on one occasion and raped her on another. Both encounters resulted in pregnancies, she said, and she arranged for the children to be raised by other families. She said she later developed close relationships with them.
Huerta said she had remained silent for decades because she feared damaging the movement to which she had devoted her life. Coming forward after a New York Times investigation into allegations that Chavez abused other women and girls, she emphasized that the movement’s achievements belonged to thousands of people.
Balancing activism and motherhood
Huerta was a change-maker while also raising 11 children, which gave her kids a front-row seat to her activism.
During the five-year Delano grape boycott, Huerta said she and her family encountered violence.
"There were times when my home was terrorized in the middle of the night, my windows broken when I'm there alone with my children," she told MAKERS. "We had shotguns and rifles aimed at us."
In order to start the farmworkers union, Huerta had to move most of her family—by then she had seven children—to Delano, while leaving two of her children behind in Stockton, California. Huerta credited the women of the movement, including Cesar Chavez's wife, Helen Chavez, and his sisters-in-law, for organizing childcare in Delano.
"I had a lot of criticism from family and friends for years until huelga [the strike] became famous and now they all like me," Huerta jokingly said during the 2015 National Portrait Gallery Q&A. "But it was difficult. We were pretty much living like the farmworkers."
Huerta's family and Chavez's family relied on assistance from a food bank and were organizing the union without a steady source of income of their own.
"In the strike, women were always on the picket lines with the children," Huerta said.
It was also not lost on Huerta that Chavez and other male activists were not asked about how they managed their important work with their parental duties.
"The thing about that is that every single mother in every single working family has that question every single day. Who am I going to leave my children with? Are they going to be safe? Are they going to be protected? That’s something women have to deal with all the time," she told TIME in 2018.
Huerta had 14 children, 24 grandchildren, 23 great-grandchildren, and seven great-great-grandchildren, a spokesperson tells TIME.
“Dolores was a deeply private person when it came to her family, and while all 14 of her children were part of her life, some parts of that story were never shared publicly,” according to the spokesperson.
Her lasting legacy
Over the course of her career, Huerta was arrested more than 20 times. In 1988, she was severely beaten by a police officer in San Francisco at a rally against presidential candidate George H. W. Bush. She was 58 years old at the time, and suffered broken ribs and a ruptured spleen.
Despite those types of encounters, Huerta continued to mobilize and fight for causes through her Dolores Huerta Foundation. She established her foundation in 2003 after receiving a $100,000 prize from the Puffin/Nation Prize for Creative Citizenship in 2002. Her youngest daughter, Camila Chávez, helped run the foundation as the executive director.
In the course of her career, Huerta was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the Eleanor Roosevelt Human Rights Award, and the Mexican Government's Ohtli Award. She also received at least nine honorary doctorates from universities across the country. In 2026, TIME named Huerta one of the world’s 100 most influential people, with a tribute by Gloria Steinem recognizing her decades of organizing and her courage in speaking publicly about Chavez. She received the TIME100 Impact Award at the TIME100 Gala in New York City on April 23, 2026.
Huerta endorsed presidential candidates, including speaking at the 2016 Democratic National Convention in support of Hillary Clinton. She was also the subject of a PBS documentary, Dolores, which won a Peabody Award in 2018.
"She was not afraid to speak truth to power," Clinton said of her in the Dolores documentary.
In July 2018, California Governor Jerry Brown signed a bill declaring April 10 Dolores Huerta Day. "Dolores Huerta deserves proper recognition for her numerous sacrifices in the name of justice and the amelioration of severely inadequate working conditions," the bill’s text said.
"Change comes from the bottom," Huerta said during a May 2012 interview. "But you've got to be able to organize those folks at the bottom to be able to get out there and make the changes that they need. And of course, if you don't have organization, then you don't have a democracy."

Oman, Pakistan and Qatar have maintained diplomatic contacts aimed at resolving differences between Tehran and Washington.

Apple unveiled the MacBook Pro with a touch-sensitive OLED display
Kyiv • UNN
The new MacBook Pro features a touch-sensitive OLED display, M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, and up to 24 hours of battery life. Sales begin on November 6.
Apple unveiled a new MacBook Pro with a touch OLED display, M5 Pro and M5 Max processors, and support for Dynamic Island. The laptop features a display with a refresh rate of up to 120 Hz, up to 24 hours of battery life, and the ability to connect up to four external displays. Preorders are already available, and sales will begin on November 6. The Verge reports, writes UNN.
Details
The presentation took place on Wednesday during the “Pro and tell” event. The new MacBook Pro is equipped with a PROLED XDR display featuring a tandem OLED structure. It supports peak SDR brightness of up to 2,000 nits and has a contrast ratio of 10,000,000:1.
The screen features Dynamic Island, which can display Live Activities—interactive notifications similar to those available on the iPhone. In addition, Apple has brought back the illuminated logo on the laptop lid.
According to the company, the touch sensor is built directly into the display panel rather than placed on top of it. This design is intended to reduce latency when interacting with the screen.
Touch controls can be used to scroll through web pages, zoom in on photos, test apps for iOS and iPadOS, and work with software musical instruments. Apple also said that its apps are optimized for touch input, while an updated API will allow third-party developers to add touch support to their own applications.
The laptop is available in two sizes. The 14-inch model weighs approximately 1.36 kg, while the 16-inch model weighs 1.81 kg. The displays’ actual diagonals are 14.2 and 16.3 inches, respectively. Both models are thinner thanks to a redesigned construction.
According to Apple, the MacBook Pro provides up to 24 hours of battery life. The ports include MagSafe 3, a headphone jack, an SD card reader, HDMI, and three Thunderbolt 5 ports. The laptop supports connecting up to three external displays simultaneously, while the M5 Max version supports up to four.
Apple also highlights a six-speaker audio system that, according to the company, delivers 50% deeper bass and clear sound. In addition, the device features a newly designed hinge for improved stability.
The 14-inch MacBook Pro starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch model starts at $3,399. Preorders can be placed now, and official sales are scheduled to begin on November 6.
Apple did not support the idea of touchscreens in laptops for a long time. In 2016, the company began equipping the MacBook Pro with a Touch Bar instead of traditional function keys. However, in 2021 it brought back physical keys, and in 2023 it completely discontinued the Touch Bar.

Europe must finally hold Russia accountable for hybrid attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:50:35 UTC
02:50:35 KST

Europe must finally hold Russia accountable for hybrid attacks
A soldier patrols outside the building hosting the NATO summit of heads of state and government in The Hague, Netherlands, on June 24, 2025. (John Thys/AFP via Getty Images)
Marek Zenisek
Czech politician and academic
Europe has already learned to better recognize hybrid threats, which is definitely a good thing, but recognition alone is not enough and doesn't serve as sufficient deterrence.
European officials have grown accustomed to scenarios where a cyberattack disrupts public services and critical infrastructure, drones appear over sensitive sites, and a flood of misinformation on social media exploits societal uncertainty.
European governments then investigate, share information, release statements, and sometimes announce new security measures until another incident elsewhere grabs the headlines again.
This approach is obviously not enough. Up until today, it appears that Russia is pretty confident that the cost of these hybrid attacks is a bargain — it costs little, and consequences look spectacular in Russian intelligence reports.
And this is exactly where Europe still has a problem. Resilience and deterrence are not the same thing. Europe must become a harder and, above all, much more expensive target for Russia.
Europeans must ensure that deterrence is a priority, as resilience is an unlikely tool to actually change the cost of a Russian attack.
Let's stop treating every incident as an isolated case and add them all up
A single attack may seem too small to justify a major response.
We've seen it many times.
In July 2024, an incendiary package caught fire at Leipzig airport on July 20, followed by similar incidents in Poland and the U.K. over the next two days.
German security authorities did not issue a wider warning to the aviation and logistics sectors until Aug. 28, more than five weeks after the first incident.
The subsequent investigation established links between the incidents and a broader Russian sabotage campaign. The response eventually came, but the delay illustrates the advantage Russia gains when individual incidents are treated separately rather than as parts of a broader campaign.
Determining responsibility can take weeks, and governments may differ in their assessment of the available evidence as well as their opinion on the appropriate reaction. Before responsibility is confirmed, political attention may shift elsewhere, giving Russia a strategic advantage in this gray zone.
This creates an asymmetry that favors the aggressor. Moscow can carry out a long-term campaign while European states deal with individual incidents one by one.
European governments, therefore, need to evaluate individual incidents in a broader context and together.
A cyberattack, sabotage, or an attempt to infiltrate an intelligence network is a full-blown hybrid campaign targeted against European countries.
Repeated operations also consume European resources, reveal weaknesses, create uncertainty, and above all, test how far Europe is willing to go.
So every new investigation shouldn't start from scratch, and instead should take into account what came before it.
Deterrence can't start only after an attack
The central objective of Europe's deterrence strategy should be to change Moscow's calculus and make further aggression an unacceptable gamble. European governments can rise above the Kremlin's dirty tricks by pursuing a constructive, systemic approach that addresses the threat at its roots.
To develop that, European governments should prepare a credible set of possible consequences before another serious incident occurs. Russia doesn't need to know exactly what Europe will do in every situation; strategic ambiguity has its value, but Moscow must believe that Europe will respond and that the consequences will matter.
That's the foundation of credible deterrence.
There's also a broader reason why this is important. If we add up the various forms of pressure Russia has exerted on European countries in recent years, future generations could rightfully ask why Europe tolerated so many things without developing a more systematic response.
It will be especially hard to explain to our children and grandchildren why a group of countries with much greater economic resources than Russia repeatedly allowed Moscow to set the pace of the confrontation.
Europe needs to be much better prepared. European countries should have a set of possible responses ready that can be adapted to specific cases, instead of having to come up with a reaction from scratch after every new attack.
That way, deterrence becomes more than just a statement made after the damage has already been done.
Got an opinion on anything you've read in the Kyiv Independent so far?
and it may appear in our Letters section.
Europe needs to change the calculation
Everyone understands that Europe cannot prevent every hostile operation. It can't know where the next test will come from, just like it can't rule out the possibility that Russia or another adversary will take advantage of Europe's openness. It can, however, make such operations more difficult.
Europe can better protect its societies. It can improve the ability of its intelligence and security services to identify hostile networks. It can coordinate accountability better. It can remove unnecessary legal and institutional obstacles. And it can make it clear that repeated aggression will not go unpunished.
The main goal, as mentioned before, has to be to change the adversary's calculation.
Russia must not only ask whether a certain operation can be carried out successfully. It also has to ask how much it will cost if Europe uncovers it and holds Moscow responsible.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

Herzog urges Israeli parties to avert fresh election as neither bloc secures majority

Unknown Publisher

02:49:45 KST

Israeli President Isaac Herzog has urged political parties to make every effort to avoid another election after preliminary results left neither main bloc with a parliamentary majority.
“Everything must be done, especially after yesterday, to avoid repeating another election,” Herzog told reporters on Wednesday in remarks carried by Israeli public broadcaster KAN.
He said he would begin consultations with parliamentary factions next week after receiving the official election results from the Central Elections Committee.
“I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind,” Herzog said.
He said he would listen to each faction, ask questions and hold discussions before deciding which lawmaker to task with forming a government.
Under Israel's basic law governing government formation, the president must consult parliamentary factions and assign a Knesset member the task of forming a government within seven days of the official publication of election results.
The selected lawmaker receives 28 days to form a government, with the possibility of extensions totalling up to 14 additional days.
If the first candidate fails, the president may appoint another lawmaker. At a later stage, at least 61 lawmakers can nominate a candidate to form a government.
Failure to establish a government could ultimately trigger another election.
Although coalitions generally seek support from at least 61 lawmakers, Israeli law allows minority governments to take office if more lawmakers vote in favour than against in a parliamentary confidence vote.
Until a new government wins the Knesset's confidence and takes office, Netanyahu's outgoing government will continue performing its duties.
According to Israeli Channel 12, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc was projected to win 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset after all regular ballots were counted on Wednesday.
The opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot was projected to secure 48 seats, while predominantly Arab parties were expected to win 19 seats, the broadcaster reported.
More than 500,000 special ballots remained to be counted.
Neither main bloc has been projected to reach the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.

Israeli exit polls show deadlock in apparent setback for Netanyahu

02:48:08 KST

JERUSALEM (Reuters) -- Israel's wartime election was deadlocked on Tuesday, exit polls showed, with Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc running neck and neck with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's camp, leaving neither side with a clear path to power.
The projections pointed to a setback for Netanyahu's coalition, though the deadlock could allow Israel's longest-serving prime minister to remain in power as caretaker during coalition negotiations.
"The Israeli public has voted against Netanyahu's service as Israel's prime minister ... a worthy leader would have accepted the people's nonconfidence and announced today his retirement from politics," Eisenkot told cheering supporters in Tel Aviv.
Turnout was 77.7%, Israel's Central Elections Committee said, the highest in more than two decades and around 7 percentage points higher than in 2022.
Kan 11 and Channel 13 showed the two blocs level, while Channel 12 gave Eisenkot a narrow edge over Netanyahu's Likud-led camp. None gave either side the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Far-right religious parties led by Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich were projected to take a combined 13 seats within Netanyahu's bloc.
Arab parties outside the two main blocs could hold the balance of power. But Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party and a former military chief, has all but ruled out forming a government with them, complicating his path to power.
Final results could take days, and Israel's fragmented political system leaves smaller parties potential kingmakers.
It was the first election since the Hamas-led attack of Oct. 7, 2023, and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute, called the exit polls a major defeat for Netanyahu's coalition, but cautioned that Eisenkot had not emerged as a clear winner and much could change as votes were counted.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid said in a statement: "Don't let anyone confuse you: the Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat. This is a total collapse and the public has told them to go home."
Eisenkot, 66, who lost a son and two nephews in the Gaza war, emerged as Netanyahu's strongest challenger, stressing his security credentials while positioning himself as a centrist domestically.
He entered politics only four years ago and joined Netanyahu's war cabinet after the 2023 Hamas attack, but quit eight months later, criticizing the prime minister's leadership.
Eisenkot offers a break with Netanyahu's leadership and far-right allies, but not with the hardline approach to security that has become more entrenched since the 2023 Hamas attack. He opposes Palestinian statehood and says Hamas' military wing must be destroyed or dismantled.
Eisenkot says Israel's response -- a war that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza health authorities -- was a failure because Hamas remains in charge.
The headquarters of the Joint List, an alliance of several Arab parties, burst into whistles and applause when exit polls were released, on a historic night for turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.
"We refuse the occupation and racism, and we will remain here," Faten Gattas, a candidate in the Joint List, said in a speech at the alliance's headquarters in Nazareth. Candidates hoped high Arab turnout would allow them to play a decisive role in blocking Netanyahu's coalition from returning to power.
Voters grappled with the trauma of Israel's deadliest day, when Hamas killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostage, and the wars in Gaza and with Lebanon's Hezbollah and Iran that followed.
While Netanyahu was criticized for the country's biggest security failure, he argued that he had made Israel and the world safer by killing top leaders of Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran.
The policies of Netanyahu's right-wing coalition have been divisive at home and deepened Israel's international isolation, but he has portrayed himself as the leader with the mettle to face down Israel's foes.
Netanyahu, 77, has served as prime minister for nearly 19 of the past 30 years and has repeatedly survived political crises. His opponents have managed to wrest the premiership from him only once since 2009, after four inconclusive elections in two years. Eighteen months later, he was back.
He entered the election facing long-standing corruption charges, which he denies, and criticism over intelligence failures that allowed Hamas-led militants to carry out their attack.
Netanyahu campaigned on an endorsement from U.S. President Donald Trump, his ally in the war against Iran.

In Ukraine's Kherson, brief ceasefire brings rare respite

In Ukraine’s Kherson, brief ceasefire brings rare respite
KHERSON, Ukraine, Oct 28 - Years of near-daily Russian drone and artillery attacks have turned the southern Ukrainian city of Kherson into a battered urban landscape where death is never far away.
On Wednesday, however, the residents who remain ventured cautiously into sun-drenched streets after a US-brokered ceasefire around the nearby frontline town of Oleshky put a temporary pause to the aerial threat.
"Honestly, I can't put it into words," kiosk owner Oleksandra Kosenko told Reuters during a visit on Wednesday. "If it stays this way, it would be really wonderful."
Ukraine said on Wednesday that the six-day ceasefire, brokered by US first lady Melania Trump, was holding, providing a rare moment of relief in the fifth year of grinding war.
The pause in fighting is aimed at paving the way for humanitarian relief for Oleshky, where residents face acute shortages of food and medicine.
CRITICAL RESPITE
For Kherson, a regional capital across the Dnipro River from Oleshky, the ceasefire - which took effect early on Tuesday - brings a brief window of respite.
Since Ukrainian troops recaptured the city from Russian occupation in November 2022, Moscow's forces stationed on the opposite bank have shelled it regularly and hunted residents with deadly drones, officials say. Both Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians.
As the attacks continued, residents fled and businesses closed, making daily life increasingly dangerous.
The city still functions, with buses ferrying people around and shops and cafes serving customers. But the scars of the war are plain to see. Some buildings are in ruins, the pavements are largely empty and anti-drone nets are draped over the main roads.
On Wednesday, residents walked their dogs without glancing toward the sky. Elderly men sipped coffee on a bench without the din of distant explosions.
"Kherson, which was constantly under fire, literally came to life," said Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, on the Telegram messaging app.
"People are calmly going out, walking, enjoying the autumn sun. What for some is ordinary everyday life, for residents of the Kherson region today is the greatest desire."
Kosenko, the kiosk owner, said she had seen a near-doubling in the number of clients: around 50 in total. She was relieved to no longer be dashing for cover on the way to work.
ATMOSPHERE OF TENSION
On Tuesday, top Ukrainian officials described the ceasefire as a major de-escalation that could build confidence for future agreements.
Yet beneath the relief, Kosenko and others expressed wariness that fighting could erupt again at any moment. Many residents approached by Reuters declined to speak, appearing tense.
Anti-personnel mines dropped by the Russians still pose a danger even when hostilities are paused.
Battles are also raging elsewhere along the 1,200-km (750 mile) front line, where Russia remains intent on capturing the parts of the eastern Donetsk region still outside its control.
Moscow is also continuing its bombing campaign of Ukrainian cities, which has damaged critical infrastructure including in Kherson.
Locals like Olha Chyupikova, who lived through Russia's occupation of her city, said they had learned to prepare for the worst.
"The Russians have proven that they can't be trusted," said the 52-year-old municipal worker.
"So I think everyone subconsciously feels like there could be some sort of provocation at any moment." REUTERS

The day after: Opposition moves to oust Knesset speaker before Netanyahu forms government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:44:17 UTC
02:44:17 KST

On the Change bloc agenda for the day after: replace Knesset speaker as Eisenkot, Bennett and Liberman discuss alliance
With neither political bloc securing a majority, opposition leaders are exploring a coordinated effort to oust Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana before a new government is formed; the move would require support from Arab parties, raising political concerns as coalition negotiations begin.
Ahead of the inauguration of the 26th Knesset, scheduled for November 10, parties in Israel's change bloc are beginning to prepare for the political and parliamentary maneuvers that will follow the election. Since Wednesday morning, senior figures in Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar! party, representatives of Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu and members of Naftali Bennett's Beyachad party have been holding talks aimed at coordinating strategic moves against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
At the center of the discussions is the possibility of replacing incumbent Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana of Likud as soon as the new parliament is sworn in, even before a government is formed. The speaker is one of the most influential figures in the Knesset, wielding considerable power over the parliamentary agenda and the advancement of legislation.
Under a 2020 Supreme Court ruling, a demand by 61 Knesset members to hold a vote on electing a new speaker requires the matter to be brought to a vote, even before a government is formed. However, securing a majority for such a move would also require support from lawmakers representing the Arab parties, a politically sensitive issue for the change bloc.
Some figures within the bloc are seeking to distinguish between forming a coalition or government dependent on Arab parties and cooperating with them on specific parliamentary initiatives. Even those who support the proposal recognize the public sensitivity surrounding such cooperation and are weighing its potential impact on support for the bloc.
Netanyahu's associates, meanwhile, intend to work to block the move and challenge its public legitimacy through an extensive political campaign.
Alongside discussions about replacing the Knesset speaker, senior figures in the change bloc are attempting to establish a center-right alliance comprising Bennett, Liberman and Eisenkot's three parties. The goal is to create a coordinated political framework that would allow the three leaders to present a united front against Likud and strengthen their bargaining power in the expected coalition negotiations.
The discussions also include whether to bring Yair Golan's Democrats into the alliance. Some participants oppose the idea because of the party's identification with the left and concerns that its inclusion could make it harder for the three parties to appeal to center-right voters and broaden their support.
Political observers believe Eisenkot could begin exploring the possibility of forming a government together with Bennett and Liberman in the coming days. One option under consideration would see the three parties operate as a single bloc in negotiations with Likud, maximizing their leverage and influencing the composition of the next government. Such an arrangement could also reduce the bargaining power of Otzma Yehudit chairman Itamar Ben-Gvir and potentially weaken the influence of the ultra-Orthodox parties.
Members of Eisenkot's Yashar! list met to discuss the election results reported so far. They thanked the hundreds of thousands of voters, thousands of activists, campaign headquarters officials and grassroots volunteers "who worked over recent months and helped deliver an unprecedented achievement in public support for a new party established only a year ago, attracting large and diverse groups across Israeli society."
The moves under consideration come against the backdrop of the 26th Knesset election results, which have so far failed to give either political bloc a governing majority. According to the latest interim results, with 85.6% of votes counted, Netanyahu's bloc holds 53 seats, the change bloc 48 and the Arab parties 19.
Likud is the largest party with 26 seats, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar! with 21. The Joint List and Bennett and Yair Lapid's Beyachad each hold 12 seats, while the Democrats have eight. Yisrael Beytenu, Ra'am, United Torah Judaism, Shas and Otzma Yehudit each have seven seats, while the Religious Zionism-Identity list has six.
The picture remains incomplete, however. The counting of double-envelope ballots, estimated at between 430,000 and 480,000, has not yet been completed and could alter the distribution of Knesset seats.
With neither bloc holding the 61-seat majority required to form a government, the Arab parties are in a pivotal position regarding any attempt to replace the Knesset speaker, as well as potential scenarios for forming the next coalition.
Amid the emerging political deadlock, President Isaac Herzog called on the parties Wednesday to approach consultations at the President's Residence with an open mind and do everything possible to avoid another election.
Herzog said he expects to receive the official results next week, after which he will begin consultations with parliamentary factions before deciding which candidate to task with forming the next government.

He said Sudan was seeking to join a maritime coalition established to ensure collective protection of the Red Sea.
“Sudan cannot remain outside efforts to secure the Red Sea, which represents a strategic depth for the country,” he said.
Kabroun noted that Sudan has a coastline stretching approximately 800 kilometers (497 miles) along the Red Sea.
Saudi Arabia announced the establishment of a maritime coalition on July 30, 2026, to protect navigation, trade and energy supplies in the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden and Bab al-Mandab Strait.
On Aug. 13, the Saudi Defense Ministry announced that 15 countries signed the coalition’s founding declaration, while 13 had completed their national procedures to join.
Kabroun also said Sudan was surrounded by African countries facing multiple security challenges, including the proliferation of weapons, smuggling, human trafficking and the presence of rebel movements.

The minister added that security coordination had previously been carried out through joint forces with neighboring countries, but the ongoing war had disrupted their operations on the ground.

Iran war costs US taxpayers $47.1 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:40:00 UTC
02:40:00 KST

The U.S. war with Iran has cost American taxpayers an estimated $47.1 billion, according to new Pentagon figures submitted to Congress, as the conflict's financial toll fuels debate ahead of the midterm elections and President Donald Trump signals that further military action remains possible.
The figure from U.S. Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, is as of Oct. 16 and offers the most up-to-date cost for the conflict since it was launched in late February by the United States and Israel. The latest price tag, obtained by The Associated Press this week, shows a $3.5 billion bump in U.S. spending since early September, when that figure stood at about $43.6 billion.
The growing cost of the unpopular war and its economic ripple effects on energy prices could hurt Republicans in next week's midterm elections. Voters on Tuesday will decide which political party controls Congress during Trump's last two years in office.
The Republican president has said new strikes on Iran are an option after the midterms and is sending more military resources to the Middle East, despite initially promising Americans a military campaign that would last only a matter of weeks. As the war’s costs in lives, tax dollars and economic impact grow, most voters say they want Congress to prioritize ending the conflict, according to a recent AP-NORC poll.
The expense of the conflict and military spending in general are already a contentious issue on Capitol Hill, where the Trump administration is pushing for the passage of a historic $1.5 trillion military budget proposal. The White House is also asking lawmakers to approve a $95 billion package that would help fund the Iran war and other priorities.
Wednesday marks eight months of the war, which Democrats have been trying to end through legislation that has failed to pass the Republican-controlled Congress.
"Trump and his ego led us into this war with no plan, no authority, and no exit strategy," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said in a news release. "Senate Democrats will continue to do everything in our power to end this disaster of a war and stop the costs, chaos, and corruption seeping from the White House.”
In the latest estimate, the bulk of the war's costs are for replacing munitions, at about $29 billion. The advanced weapons most in demand and whose stockpiles have been drawn down are defensive missile interceptors, such as those launched by the Army’s Patriot and THAAD systems, with a single Patriot interceptor costing millions of dollars.
The Pentagon says about $11.9 billion is related to costs of operations, while an additional $6 billion is tied to equipment losses. The Air Force's costs are now $7.6 billion, and the Army's are more than $2 billion. The Navy's costs were listed at $1.45 billion, which is a significant drop from the $2.2 billion listed in early September.
When asked why the Navy’s cost estimates decreased over the roughly six-week period, both the Navy and U.S. Central Command referred the questions to the Pentagon, which did not immediately respond to emails requesting comment on the new cost estimates.
The latest estimate does not include damage to U.S. bases in the Middle East, which the Islamic Republic has attacked with ballistic missiles and drones. A report from the Pentagon inspector general released last month said Iranian strikes have damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.
The Pentagon’s official tally lists 21 service members killed and 865 wounded in the conflict. That count includes troops who died in medical events and other situations that do not have a direct connection to the conflict, with 18 service members having been killed from Iranian strikes, combat aircraft crashes or the disposal of Iranian drones.
While Trump has mused repeatedly about whether to make a deal with Iran or "finish them off,” a third aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are making their way to the region. The Trump administration also has reduced staffing at some U.S. Embassies after receiving intelligence that Iran has stepped up efforts to target American personnel.

The ‘Change Bloc’ is dead. Israel’s opposition to Netanyahu had their chance, and blew it - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:39:58 UTC
02:39:58 KST

The ‘Change Bloc’ is dead. Israel’s opposition to Netanyahu had their chance, and blew it - analysis
The election results do not have a clear path for the opposition bloc to form a stable government to unseat the Israeli Prime Minister. This was the best opportunity they will ever have to do so
After the 2022 election, the 5th cycle in just over three years, the ‘Change Bloc’ of Zionist parties disgruntled by Benjamin Netanyahu faced a reckoning; after a brief term governing with a coalition cobbled together from across the political spectrum, the Israeli public overwhelmingly rejected them in favor of the one issue, or person, around which they had united.
That government failed because they lacked cohesion. The left, the right and center were pulling from different directions, and the inclusion of the Arab party Ra’am as a voting partner exacerbated tensions with the right wing of the bloc. They were determined not to make the same mistakes this time.
The new Change Bloc ran an efficient campaign. Left-wing Meretz, which was 0.09% below the threshold in 2022, merged with Labor, who narrowly crossed the threshold, to form The Democrats. Yair Lapid’s Yesh Atid, which was the largest party in the opposition, joined forces with Naftali Bennett to form B’yachad, after polls showed a huge and continuous decline in support for Yesh Atid. Those two, along with Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party and Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu, agreed to fight alongside each other; not to disparage and siphon votes off one another. And, barring the occasional blip of egotism, they managed this.
Working together is one thing. Removing Netanyahu from office is another thing entirely. But over the last four years, everything had seemingly fallen into place for an opposition to seize power.
Starting with the unpopular proposed judicial reforms, to the failures on October 7th and the subsequent lack of accountability, the endless wars fought by reservists while the ultra-orthodox can evade the burden of military service, the international reputational damage caused by government ministers, Netanyahu’s alleged links with Qatar and his ongoing corruption trial, and a cost of living crisis; the ground was as fertile as it ever has been, and ever could be, to unseat the government.
Yet they did not.
The results have a glass half full/half empty picture. On the one hand, the majority of Israelis voted against the Netanyahu government.
But on the other hand, the government’s bloc was larger than the Eisenkot-led Change Bloc. Netanyahu won and lost simultaneously. The Change Bloc lost. Their most plausible path to a majority would be to bring in Ra’am, which served in the previous anti-Netanyahu coalition, and the Joint List, which holds more extremist views. This would take them back to where they started.
Speaking to government voters in the days and weeks leading up to Tuesday’s vote, they fall into several categories. The first is the ultra-orthodox, who vote based on who their rabbis tell them to vote for.
The second is security hawks, who feel that some aspects of the opposition are too diplomatic (or as they would say, pacifist) for a country constantly under attack, especially regarding the West Bank, which many fear will be the next major war arena without intervention and deterrence. The third category is ‘Bibists’, immovable supporters of Netanyahu who approve of his pragmatism, experience, and his security successes in the form of targeted assassinations.
Where can the Change Bloc get votes from? The Haredim and the Bibists are highly unlikely to ever vote for the opposition. The right-wing hawks were supposed to be enticed by the policies of Liberman, Bennett and former IDF Chief of Staff Eisenkot. But not enough people made that jump.
Israel’s demographics are changing too. The religious, right-leaning population is growing exponentially, while secular liberals leave the country. Furthermore, most other democratic countries have a youth population that is overwhelmingly left-wing. In Israel, it is the opposite. Polls before the election indicated that the far-right Otzma Yehudit was among the most popular for first time voters. This is why many opposition supporters viewed this election as a sliding doors moment. And the door is closing.
Policy-wise there is a lot of overlap between the likes of Yashar, B’yachad and Netanyahu’s Likud. They are Zionist, security-focused, free market parties and, without Likud having to rely on extremist and ultra-orthodox parties, could see eye-to-eye more on issues pertaining to social liberalism and Haredi enlistment to the IDF.
And crucially, those three parties could form a strong government. But it will not happen as long as Netanyahu is at the helm. He has alienated too many voters and politicians from the Change Bloc for any stable government alongside them to work. It would also be political suicide for those politicians who join forces with him - just ask Benny Gantz.
If there are more elections, they will need to expand their reach in order to form a government. Whether this is with the Arabs or from the Netanyahu coalition, they will have to decide. But until then, or until Netanyahu leaves party politics, the Change Bloc is dead. May its memory be a blessing.

Trump is using tariffs as a 'tool for grift,' Raskin says in demand for donor records
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:39:43 UTC
02:39:43 KST

A top House Democrat on Wednesday accused President Donald Trump of using tariffs as a "tool for grift and self-enrichment," pointing to what he says are suspicious import-tax exemptions for industries whose leaders have curried Trump's favor with gifts and donations.
"You took care to cut lots of sweetheart deals with corporations and industries that won carve-outs from your tariffs when you saw you could get something good in return," Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., told Trump in a fiery letter obtained first by CNBC.
Raskin, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee and the former top Democrat on the House oversight committee, highlighted three such tariff carve-outs — for Brazilian meat, diamonds and smartphones — that he says "make little to no sense" under the criteria set by the Trump administration.
"They do, however, make sense when factoring in the now world famous Trump Tariff Discount," Raskin wrote, coining a term to describe the president's alleged willingness to cut breaks for his allies and benefactors "when the price is right."
The letter asks Trump to hand over multiple categories of records spanning his second term, including communications between the White House and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, or USTR, related to any form of tariff relief for more than a dozen industries.
It makes a similar request for communications involving private-sector representatives, including Apple executive chairman Tim Cook and Rolex CEO Jean-Frederic Dufour. Raskin asked for those records by Nov. 11.
Raskin's pugnacious letter directly accuses Trump of "profound corruption," asserting that his heavy-handed use of tariffs is really about clinching "levers of power that you could maliciously pull to extract exciting concessions for yourself."
The missive — which cites the Judiciary Committee's "jurisdiction over corruption, conflicts of interest, and effective enforcement of criminal and civil laws" — could offer a preview of how Democrats will flex their oversight powers against Trump should they win majority control of the House or Senate in the midterm election.
Raskin also drew a link between Trump's alleged misuse of tariffs and Americans' affordability concerns, connecting two of voters' top concerns in the final stretch of the election cycle.
"While you have protected your personal investments and crocodile skin connoisseurs from the giant bite of your tariffs, the American people are suffering. Independent analysts expect that your latest round of tariffs will cost an average of $820 per U.S. household this year," he wrote, citing data from the nonpartisan Tax Foundation.
The most recent CNBC All-America Economic Survey found voters are most concerned about government corruption, followed by high grocery and gas prices. Democratic candidates have deliberately tailored their campaign messaging to make connections between corruption and high costs.
"The only special interest guiding the Trump administration's decision-making is the best interest of the American people," a White House official told CNBC on condition of anonymity to respond to Raskin's letter.
The USTR did not respond to CNBC's request for comment.
Raskin homed in on the far-reaching tariffs the U.S. imposed in July using Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.
The Trump administration says those duties, which apply to more than 80 countries and cover nearly all U.S. imports, are meant to crack down on foreign forced-labor practices. But Raskin and other critics, including plaintiffs in a major lawsuit challenging the tariffs, argue they are actually intended to replace the sweeping "liberation day" duties the Supreme Court struck down in February.
"One could be forgiven for doubting the sincerity of your Administration's sudden concern for the victims of forced labor," Raskin wrote.
He pointed to Trump's decision last year to lift forced-labor-related restrictions on Dominican sugar producer Central Romana, despite allegations that the company's abusive practices persisted.
Central Romana's owner, José Francisco "Pepe" Fanjul, reportedly hosted a $50 million fundraiser for Trump in 2024, and his family corporation that year donated $1 million to a pro-Trump PAC. He has also been listed as a donor to Trump's White House ballroom project.
The USTR only offers exemptions to the Section 301 tariffs in certain cases, including where additional duties would not help reduce forced-labor practices. But the trade office's exemption list "contains conspicuous —and suspicious — carve-outs for a few industries," Raskin wrote.
Raskin referenced tariff exemptions for beef and bovine products, which took effect despite opposition from U.S. cattle producers who strongly opposed the move, citing "the well-documented use of forced labor in the Brazilian cattle sector and the documented surge of Brazilian beef."
In late August, Trump reportedly met in the Oval Office with Brazilian billionaire Joesley Batista, co-owner of JBS, the world's largest meat processor. The next day, Trump announced the U.S. would allow the import of up to 300,000 metric tons of "product for ground beef" below market prices.
"Coincidentally, JBS's U.S. subsidiary, Pilgrim's Pride, made a $5 million donation to your 2024 inaugural fund, the largest donation of any single company!" Raskin wrote.
Diamond jewelry is also exempt from the Section 301 tariffs, which Raskin called "laughably indefensible" because the precious stones are identified by the U.S. Labor Department as a good produced using forced or child labor.
Raskin suggested the exemption was the result of Belgium's Antwerp World Diamond Centre gifting Trump an opulent gold ring — studded with 321 natural diamonds and 75 other gemstones — in June. The company's press release about the ring said it was given to Trump as a symbol of "the historic trade relationship between Antwerp and the United States" and in honor of the 250th birthday of the U.S.
"A diamond is truly the President's best friend!" Raskin quipped in his letter.
He also wrote that USTR exempted Chinese smartphones from the Section 301 tariffs, even though "abusive working conditions are a hallmark of smartphone manufacturing, including the Apple iPhone."
He listed multiple examples of Cook's flattery toward Trump, including reportedly donating $1 million to Trump's inaugural committee in 2025 and gifting Trump a gold plaque in the Oval Office. Raskin also noted Apple's donation of $25 million to Trump's White House ballroom project, a tie for the largest contribution.
"The exemptions above only scratch the surface of your profound corruption," Raskin wrote.

How could double-envelope votes change Israeli election results?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:39:31 UTC
02:39:31 KST

Breadcrumb
How could double-envelope votes change Israel's election results?
Israel's election results could still change as officials count hundreds of thousands of special ballots known as "double envelopes", potentially affecting the parliamentary gains made by Arab parties and the balance of power between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the opposition, led by Gadi Eisenkot.
Preliminary results gave Netanyahu's bloc 53 seats, compared with 48 for Eisenkot's bloc and 19 for Arab-led parties, leaving neither major bloc with the 61 seats required for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.
However, between 600,000 and 650,000 special ballots could influence the final distribution of seats, particularly for smaller parties hovering around the electoral threshold.
What are double-envelope ballots?
Double-envelope voting is a mechanism used in Israeli elections to allow people who cannot vote at their registered polling stations to cast ballots elsewhere.
The system protects voter anonymity while preventing duplicate voting.
Unlike ordinary ballots, which are counted locally, double-envelope votes undergo additional verification and are processed during the final stages of the election.
Who can vote using double envelopes?
The system covers voters whose professional, medical or geographical circumstances prevent them from reaching their designated polling stations.
They include Israeli soldiers and military officers, diplomats serving abroad, hospital patients, medical personnel on duty, prisoners and detainees, and people with disabilities.
Israeli military personnel account for the largest proportion of these ballots, making their voting preferences particularly significant.
How does the system work?
Voters place their chosen party's ballot paper inside a standard blue envelope containing no identifying information.
That sealed envelope is then placed inside a larger outer envelope bearing the voter's personal details.
Election officials transfer the ballots to the Central Elections Committee, where they check the information against the national voter register to ensure the individual has not voted elsewhere.
Once verified, the anonymous inner envelope is separated from the identifying outer envelope and mixed with other ballots before counting.
If a duplicate vote is detected, the special ballot is invalidated and the case may be referred for legal proceedings.
Why could these votes change the results?
The large number of outstanding ballots could affect the allocation of Knesset seats, particularly among smaller parties close to the electoral threshold.
With each parliamentary seat requiring approximately 40,000 votes, shifts in party support could determine whether some parties enter parliament or lose representation.
The final count could therefore alter coalition calculations, although it would not necessarily resolve the political deadlock.
Could Arab parties lose seats?
Arab-led parties could see their parliamentary representation reduced despite the high turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Because Israeli soldiers account for a substantial share of double-envelope voters, and Palestinian citizens are largely exempt from compulsory military service, Arab parties traditionally receive a smaller proportion of these votes.
As the outstanding ballots are added to the national total, their overall vote share could decline, potentially costing them seats.
Ultra-Orthodox parties also tend to perform less strongly among double-envelope voters because of lower military participation.
However, the large number of Israeli reservists voting this year could make traditional patterns less reliable, complicating predictions about which parties might benefit.
When will the final results be known?
The double-envelope count might not be completed until Friday, 30 October.
Acting Central Elections Committee director Dean Livne warned that high turnout could mean more special ballots than initially anticipated, potentially delaying the count.
Until those votes are processed, the final parliamentary balance remains uncertain, including the extent of Arab parties' gains and their potential influence over the formation of Israel's next government.

Yemeni army claims 239 Houthis neutralized in 749 operations over 24 hours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:37:23 UTC
02:37:23 KST

Şahin Demir
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Yemen’s armed forces said they neutralized 239 Houthi commanders and fighters in 749 operations targeting the group’s military positions across several fronts during 24 hours as part of Operation Dawn of Yemen. 
Col. Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili, spokesman for the armed forces, said on US social media company X that the operations targeted Houthi command centers, fortifications, firing positions, reinforcements and supply routes. 
He said the attacks disrupted Houthi field command operations, suppressed firing positions and prevented frontline units from receiving reinforcements and supplies. 
The operations resulted in the neutralization of 239 Houthi commanders and fighters, while 117 military vehicles and pieces of combat equipment were destroyed or damaged, according to the spokesman. 
Army units and allied Popular Resistance forces continued consolidating their gains and increasing pressure on Houthi positions in southwestern Taiz province, he said.  
Al-Nuzaili added that operations continued along the fronts in Al-Jawf, Marib and Al-Bayda provinces, as well as the southern and southwestern fronts. 
He said the armed forces would continue operations in accordance with military plans while taking precautions to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure. 
Meanwhile, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed on X that Saudi warplanes and missiles carried out 101 strikes over 24 hours, targeting civilian sites in the capital, Sanaa, and several provinces. 
He said the attacks targeted Al-Jawf, Taiz, Amran, Hajjah, Saada, Al-Dhale, Al-Mahwit and Lahj provinces, in addition to the capital. 
Saree claimed the strikes involved F-15 and Typhoon fighter jets that took off from Saudi Arabia's Khamis Mushait and Taif air bases, as well as missiles launched from Najran. 
He also claimed the attacks killed and injured dozens of people, including women and children, but did not provide an exact casualty toll. 
According to Saree, the total number of Saudi airstrikes and missile attacks since the beginning of the latest escalation has reached 3,480. 
Neither side's battlefield claims could be independently verified. 
The statement comes amid intensified fighting between government forces and the Houthis, who have controlled the capital, Sanaa, and large parts of northern Yemen since 2014. 
The latest escalation has seen government forces and their allies launch Operation Dawn of Yemen against Houthi positions across multiple fronts, including Taiz, Marib and Al-Jawf.  
A Saudi-led coalition has also conducted airstrikes against Houthi military targets amid renewed cross-border missile and drone attacks. 
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government. 
The prolonged conflict has caused one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, leaving millions dependent on humanitarian assistance.

====================================================================================================

Election deadlock leaves political leaders silent. Who will break their promise?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:31:15 UTC
02:31:15 KST

The parliamentary election, which ended Tuesday at 10 p.m. when polling stations closed, revealed several unexpected developments: high overall voter turnout, exceptionally strong participation among Arab voters and liberal strongholds where turnout approached its potential maximum but still failed to bring about a change in government.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu survived the election campaign but did not win a clear victory, leaving him at the center of a political deadlock.
Since addressing their supporters Tuesday evening, the political party leaders have largely disappeared from public view.
Netanyahu broke with his usual practice of calling the leaders of his political bloc on election night after the exit polls were released. He also spent Wednesday dealing with matters unrelated to his coalition partners.
The prime minister issued no statements to the media apart from two social media posts, one of which was addressed to the general public and simply read: "Thank you very much."
However, the office of United Torah Judaism Chairman Yaakov Asher said it had received a message from Netanyahu's representatives.
"In response to journalists' inquiries, we wish to clarify that there have been no approaches from party leaders, apart from a message conveyed by people close to Prime Minister Netanyahu indicating that he intends to keep the coalition parties together," Asher's office said.
But Netanyahu's unusual silence toward his political allies is not the only development attracting attention. The leaders of the rival pro-change bloc have also largely remained silent.
Apart from Joint List Chairman Yousef Jabareen, who called Wednesday morning on the pro-change parties not to ignore the Arab parties, none of the main political figures has appeared publicly to assess the election results, outline their next steps or explain how they intend to proceed.
Democrats Chairman Yair Golan limited his response to a post on social media.
"There is an opportunity to form a government in partnership with the Arabs. Netanyahu has no business lecturing anyone about Zionism," he wrote.
The silence may partly reflect the fact that the official election results have yet to be finalized.
But senior political figures believe it also reflects shock and disappointment on both sides over the realization that virtually any scenario other than another election would require at least one major political player to break a fundamental campaign promise.
For the pro-change bloc, that could mean considering a unity government with Netanyahu despite pledges not to serve under him.
For Netanyahu, it could mean abandoning some of his longstanding political allies, despite promising that all would remain part of his governing bloc.
For now, it remains unclear which direction Israel's political leaders intend to take or which options they consider realistic.
Most are holding closed-door consultations, weighing their public messages and, above all, developing strategies for the next stage.
In Eisenkot's Yashar! party, for example, members of the electoral list met and thanked the hundreds of thousands of voters who supported them, along with thousands of campaign activists, local campaign leaders and field organizers.
Hundreds of thousands of ballots could change the outcome
As of the latest count, 93% of polling stations had been tallied, representing 85.6% of all votes cast.
Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc was projected to win 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for the pro-change bloc and 19 for the predominantly Arab parties.
Neither major bloc had reached the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority.
The results could still change significantly, however, with an estimated 430,000 to 480,000 so-called double-envelope ballots yet to be counted.
These ballots are cast by soldiers, reservists and other eligible voters who vote outside their regular polling stations. Counting was expected to begin Wednesday evening.
Under the current circumstances, the only electoral list still below the 3.25% threshold for entering the Knesset that appears to have a possible path into parliament is the joint Reservists-Economic Party list led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha.
With 85.6% of votes counted, nearly 128,000 ballots had been cast for the list, which runs under the Hebrew ballot letters Dalet-Yod.
That means the alliance needs approximately 57,500 additional votes to cross the electoral threshold, estimated at around 185,000 votes.
If the joint list manages to overcome the odds and enter the Knesset, the consequences could extend well beyond its own parliamentary representation.
Based on the count of 93% of regular polling stations, before the double-envelope ballots are included, the parties currently positioned to lose seats would be Shas, Beyachad, the Joint List and Yashar!.
Politically, that would reduce Eisenkot's pro-change bloc to 46 seats and Netanyahu's bloc to 52.
The Arab parties would hold 18 seats, although that figure could decline further depending on the distribution of the outstanding double-envelope ballots.
Such an outcome would further complicate coalition negotiations and potentially give Hendel and Zelekha a significant role in determining the composition of Israel's next government.
Likud alleges Arab parties 'stole the election'
While Netanyahu himself has remained relatively quiet, his Likud party has already approached the Central Elections Committee with allegations of widespread election fraud involving Arab political parties.
Likud claimed that "the elections were stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the destruction of the Jewish state through serious criminal offenses involving bribery, threats, violence, forgery and the use of prohibited voter-mobilization software."
In its statement, Likud said it had submitted hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence to the Israel Police and Shin Bet domestic security agency concerning alleged irregularities at numerous polling stations in Arab communities.
The party cited "thousands of envelopes containing cash and Ra'am ballot slips, threats and violence against polling station officials, multiple voters behind voting booth curtains, voting under duplicate identities, discrepancies between the number of envelopes and the number of voters, the use of prohibited voter-mobilization software and more."
Ra'am is an Islamist party led by Mansour Abbas that draws much of its support from Israel's Arab population.
The allegations come after unusually high Arab voter turnout helped the predominantly Arab parties make substantial electoral gains, with their combined representation projected at 19 seats in the latest count.
That increase has become particularly significant because neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the rival pro-change bloc appears capable of securing a parliamentary majority on its own.
Likud demanded a thorough investigation into the alleged irregularities.
With the final vote count still underway, Israel's political leaders face an uncertain parliamentary landscape in which forming a government may require difficult compromises, broken campaign promises or another election.

A group of former US government officials who resigned because of Washington’s policy in the Gaza Strip has urged candidates seeking the 2028 presidential nomination to pledge not to appoint officials they said enabled Israel’s genocide in the enclave, Anadolu reports.
“Senior Biden Administration officials who were architects of the Gaza policy are now actively white-washing their own roles in enabling genocide,” Gaza Resignees said in a statement signed by 12 former officials.
“They violated U.S. and international law by providing U.S. weapons while Israel indiscriminately and disproportionately attacked civilians and civilian infrastructure, and as Israel arbitrarily blocked humanitarian assistance to Gaza,” it said.
The signatories include former State Department officials Josh Paul, Annelle Sheline and Stacy Gilbert, former diplomats Hala Rharrit and Mike Casey, former White House official Anna Del Castillo and former USAID senior adviser Alexander Smith. Also among them are former Army officer and Defense Intelligence Agency official Harrison Mann, former Air Force Maj. Riley Livermore, former Navy Lt. Cmdr. Hani Z. Nofal and former political appointees Tariq Habash of the Education Department and Lily Greenberg Call of the Interior Department.
“Not even two years since the end of their disastrous time in office, many of these same officials appear to be pursuing a path back into the halls of power,” they said.
“The most basic level of accountability, the most minimal level of consequences, is to ensure that those who have wreaked so much harm from within the highest levels of our Government cannot return to it,” according to the statement.
The group said that “Gaza has become a litmus test for the credibility of American politicians and the viability, in particular, of Democratic candidates.”

“We have watched as elite institutions have welcomed these officials,” said Mann, as the video showed former White House Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk, who is now with venture capital firm Lux Capital and a CNN commentator. It also showed former National Security Adviser Jake Sullivan and former USAID Administrator Samantha Power, who both joined Harvard Kennedy School after leaving office.

“And we say, enough,” the former officials said in the video. “Enough with the culture of impunity in Washington. Enough with policies that break our laws and defy our values.”
“They have blood on their hands,” they added.
Top Biden administration officials at that time acknowledged civilian suffering in Gaza but defended Israel’s right to defend itself following the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack.
