Feature: Chinese firm helps upgrade Africa's first geothermal power plant in Kenya
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:47:12 CST
23:47:12 KST

Staff members inspect the equipment at Olkaria I Geothermal Power Plant at Hell's Gate National Park in Nakuru County, Kenya, Oct. 19, 2026. (Xinhua/Xie Jianfei)
NAIROBI, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Plumes of steam rise above the Olkaria I Geothermal Power Plant in Kenya's Hell's Gate National Park, as a network of pipes channels steam from deep underground to the plant's generating units, where the earth's heat is converted into electricity.
Commissioned in the 1980s as Africa's first geothermal power station, Olkaria I faced growing challenges in maintaining its generating capacity and efficiency as its equipment aged over more than four decades of operation.
Following a rehabilitation project undertaken by SEPCOIII Electric Power Construction Co., Ltd., a subsidiary of Power Construction Corporation of China, the plant's total installed capacity increased from 45 megawatts (MW) to 63 MW, while the amount of steam available for power generation remained unchanged.
Located along the Great Rift Valley, Kenya has substantial geothermal potential. Data from Kenya's Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority show that geothermal power accounts for around 40 percent of national electricity generation, making it the country's leading source of electricity.
Under the Kenya National Energy Compact 2025-2030, the country aims to increase its installed geothermal capacity to 1,681 MW by 2030 and achieve 100 percent clean electricity generation.
Upgrading an existing plant can be more challenging than building a new one, said Zhang Yang, deputy project manager of the rehabilitation project.
"Building a new plant is like painting on a blank canvas, where you can plan everything from scratch. With a rehabilitation project, much of the existing structure has to remain, so you have to find solutions within the space and layout already available," he said.
The project, which began in August 2023, involved upgrading all three generating units within the constraints of the decades-old facility. Engineers had to ensure that new equipment was compatible with existing systems while coordinating mechanical and electrical components within the plant's original layout, Zhang said.
The team also redesigned the steam-field pipeline layout based on steam parameters and optimized several components, including separators, exhaust stations, control valves and cooling systems. These adjustments helped increase the plant's generating capacity without requiring additional steam, Zhang added.
Maurice Awuor, electrical engineering manager at the Kenya Electricity Generating Company (KenGen), said the rehabilitation had raised the plant's installed capacity to 63 MW, equivalent to about 2 percent of Kenya's total installed electricity generation capacity.
"This is the only geothermal rehabilitation project in Kenya over the past three years that has been commissioned and added installed capacity to the national grid," Awuor said.
The rehabilitation also saw the installation of Chinese-made equipment, including condensers, circulating water pumps and cooling towers, to replace aging machinery.
Zhang said that after KenGen personnel visited Chinese factories and exchanged views with manufacturers, they gained a better understanding of the performance of Chinese equipment and its manufacturing processes, paving the way for its adoption in the geothermal project.
"This time, we have introduced Chinese-made equipment into a geothermal project in Kenya, and I believe more projects will adopt Chinese equipment in the future," Zhang said.
Awuor said Chinese companies had strengths in technology and equipment, and cooperation with them was important for Kenya as it seeks to develop its geothermal resources.
Beyond equipment, the project has also facilitated knowledge-sharing between Chinese engineers and their Kenyan counterparts.
Perry Karuri, a Kenyan quality assurance and control engineer responsible for construction inspections, said it was her first time working with Chinese engineers.
During equipment installation and commissioning, she discussed technical parameters, construction quality and on-site challenges with her Chinese colleagues. The teams jointly examined problems and worked out solutions to ensure that construction met the required standards, she said.
"We not only share knowledge and exchange experience, but also learn from each other's different working methods. I have learned a more rigorous approach to work from the Chinese engineers," Karuri said, adding that the cooperation had provided opportunities to develop practical skills and gain experience in operating and maintaining the upgraded equipment.
Zhang Liang, the project manager, said some areas around the plant had previously experienced rotational power cuts due to electricity shortages, and additional installed capacity at Olkaria I has helped strengthen the local power supply.
He added that geothermal power can also complement other renewable sources. While wind and solar generation fluctuate with weather conditions and the time of day, geothermal plants can provide a relatively stable supply of electricity, helping balance the grid when wind generation is low or solar output falls after sunset.
"Geothermal resources are an important domestic energy source for Kenya. Their relatively low generation costs can help reduce the electricity sector's sensitivity to fluctuations in international oil and gas prices," Awuor said.
He noted that the additional capacity at the upgraded plant could help Kenya meet rising electricity demand, support industrial production and manufacturing, and advance efforts to diversify its energy mix and transition toward cleaner energy. ■

Economic Watch: Chinese design gives exports new edge at Canton Fair
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:46:59 CST
23:46:59 KST

GUANGZHOU, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Stainless steel has long endured a rather understated existence. It can be found in kitchen sinks, saucepans and rubbish bins, having proved durable and practical but unglamorous. At the 140th China Import and Export Fair in Guangzhou in south China's Guangdong Province, however, a Chinese jewelry maker is giving this metal a different purpose.
Its display of gold-toned, silver-colored and brightly hued ornaments has drawn crowds of overseas buyers at this fair, which is also known as the Canton Fair. These pieces look like fine jewelry, but most are made of stainless steel, offering a polished finish without the price tag of precious metals.
For consumers, the proposition is timely, with gold and silver prices soaring globally. "Some jewelry customers are turning to new product lines," said Chen Danping, deputy general manager of Guangzhou-based Justop Jewelry.
Stainless steel ornaments, Chen explained, combine jewelry-making techniques and appearance with the cost advantage of a much cheaper material.
For Jacob Ruiz Palomo, a buyer from Spain, the appeal is straightforward: the jewelry pulls off a commercial trick, making an inexpensive material look anything but cheap. "Its competitive prices need not come at the expense of good design," Palomo noted.
This trick points to a broader change in Chinese manufacturing. For decades, China's exporters built their strength on scale, speed and cost. These advantages still matter today, but many manufacturers are aiming higher and trying to win the competition via smarter technologies and better designs.
The Canton Fair, China's vast twice-yearly trading floor, offers a snapshot of this transition. Serving as a barometer and wind vane of China's foreign trade, this year's fair, marking its 70th anniversary, has brought together products that seek to compete not only on function and price, but also on intelligence, appearance and design.
The fair's 2026 design innovation award, known as the CF Award, offers a glimpse of where Chinese manufacturing design is heading. This year, 222 products from 174 companies made the cut, with AI-powered products accounting for 32 percent of entries and green, low-carbon products for 44 percent. The top award winners included the ZXMOTO 820RR motorcycle and an intelligent capsule robot for gastric endoscopy.
Yet the value of design is not confined to high-end products. It can also transform the most ordinary household items, making them more functional and distinctive.
At the stand of Guangdong-based brand EKO, a range of stainless-steel rubbish bins showed how thoughtful design can elevate an everyday household item. One model, equipped with an automatic sensor, caught the attention of many buyers.
"The company pays attention to details as small as the angle of a corner and the curve of a lid," said Pan Libin, a representative.
"Thoughtful design can expand a product's uses," Pan added. "A rubbish bin can fit into different settings, from living rooms and kitchens to bathrooms and bedrooms. We can tailor designs to different needs in terms of size, shape, color and available space."
EKO began as an original-equipment manufacturer, making products for other companies. In 2007, it started developing its own brand, betting that design could give it a more distinctive place in the market. One of its products became a Red Dot winner this year, adding international recognition to its effort.
For other Chinese companies, drawing on domestic cultural heritage is another way to differentiate a product.
Zhu Bingren copper art, based in Hangzhou in east China's Zhejiang Province, is a business featuring craftsmanship spanning multiple generations, and has drawn strong interest from overseas buyers at this year's fair. The business incorporates copper carving techniques, recognized as part of China's national intangible cultural heritage, into products ranging from home ornaments to tea sets, thus transforming centuries-old craftsmanship into contemporary designs for global consumers.
"Foreign customers are showing particular interest in traditional Chinese elements," said Gu Dawei, the company's sales manager. "While staying true to our cultural roots, we also pay close attention to the needs and preferences of different markets so that our products can better appeal to consumers around the world."
More than 700 samples brought to the fair have been snapped up by buyers, according to the company.
Industry insiders said the increased presence of Chinese design in consumer products worldwide is underpinned by the strengths of China's manufacturing ecosystem. Its comprehensive industrial chains allow creative ideas to be turned into tangible products quickly, while efficient supply chains enable manufacturers to respond swiftly to changing market demands.
Michael Schjerbeck Jensen, general manager of F&H Asia, told Xinhua that the Danish group's joint product development with Chinese partners has repeatedly turned ideas into reality. In an uncertain world, Jensen said, China's comprehensive, stable and efficient supply chains offer a particularly valuable source of certainty.
"The growing international reach of Chinese design is increasingly evident," said Luo Weiyu, business director of 3&1 Industrial Design. "Backed by China's complete industrial chains, domestic designers can also update their concepts and bring new products to market quickly, making them more responsive to consumer demand. More buyers from countries including Italy and Japan are now seeking partnerships with Chinese designers." ■

LONDON, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- British Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey on Wednesday announced measures to reduce the costs of energy for households in the 2026 Budget to help families ease cost of living pressures.
The government will introduce a scheme worth 2.6 billion pounds (about 3.5 billion U.S. dollars) to take the energy pressure off for families this winter. Some 100 pounds (about 133 dollars) will be paid directly into the bank accounts of each of the 20 million qualified households, Healey said in his budget statement in the House of Commons.
He also announced the measure of extending the value-added-tax cut on electricity bills to July 2027.
Earlier Wednesday, Healey abolished standing charges on household gas bills, a fixed daily fee added on top of a household gas bill regardless of how much gas has been used, according to a statement on the government's official website.
Instead, these fixed costs will be paid on the unit rate, which could save 60 percent of account-holding households around an average of 45 pounds (about 60 dollars) off their annual bill, it said. ■

Syria, Jordan agree on joint security committee as border crossing reopens after deadly airstrikes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:46:52 CST
23:46:52 KST

Vehicles and trucks are seen at the Nasib border crossing between Syria and Jordan in Daraa province, southern Syria, Oct. 28, 2026. Syria and Jordan have agreed to establish a joint security committee to investigate recent Jordanian airstrikes on southern Syria, as the Nasib border crossing between the two countries reopened Wednesday following a temporary closure, Syrian state media reported. (Str/Xinhua)
DAMASCUS, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Syria and Jordan have agreed to establish a joint security committee to investigate recent Jordanian airstrikes on southern Syria, as the Nasib border crossing between the two countries reopened Wednesday following a temporary closure, Syrian state media reported.
The agreement was reached during a telephone conversation between Syrian foreign affairs chief Asaad al-Shaibani and Ayman Safadi, Jordan's minister of foreign affairs and expatriates, according to a joint statement carried by the Syrian state news agency SANA early Wednesday.
Jordanian air force struck several locations in Syria's southern Daraa province on Monday evening, killing seven civilians, including three children, and injuring three others.
During the conversation, Safadi expressed deep regret over civilian casualties resulting from the airstrikes and extended condolences to the victims' families.
The two officials stressed the importance of direct security coordination in combating terrorism and cross-border drug and arms smuggling, while reaffirming their commitment to maintaining close bilateral relations.
The agreement to establish a joint committee comes as Damascus and Amman seek to clarify the circumstances of the strikes and strengthen coordination along the shared border.
Meanwhile, Syria announced that passenger and commercial traffic through the Nasib border crossing with Jordan had returned to normal on Wednesday morning following its closure on Tuesday.
The Jordanian Armed Forces said earlier that the strikes were launched in retaliation for a deadly attack during a church funeral in Karak governorate last Friday, alleging that those responsible were linked to militant organizations operating in southern Syria.
The Jordanian military stated that the operation targeted Islamic State militants and was conducted in coordination with Damascus, while the Syrian government denied that any prior coordination had taken place and expressed its objection to military operations inside Syrian territory without advance consultation. ■

Senators Demand to Know if Dr. Oz Collaborated With Election Denial Groups
Unknown

2026-10-28
14:46:35 UTC
23:46:35 KST

With a week to go before the midterms, a group of Democratic senators are demanding that Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), share communications his department may have had with far-right groups promoting a baseless conspiracy theory about left-wing groups stealing votes from residents of nursing homes.
In July, Oz’s agency issued a memo rescinding previous guidance on how staff at nursing homes could help residents to vote by assisting with mail-in voting or transporting residents to polling locations. The memo replaced that guidance with threats of prosecution if staff “engage in inappropriate coercion or other violations of residents’ rights.” Referring to this memo, election denial groups last month began to boost claims that voter fraud was happening inside care facilities.
That campaign was spearheaded by the Election Integrity Network, a group led by Cleta Mitchell, a former adviser to president Donald Trump. “These left-wing groups go into the nursing homes, and they go into the group homes, and they basically steal the votes of these most vulnerable,” Mitchell said in a recent appearance on Steve Bannon’s War Room show.
Now, citing WIRED’s reporting on the nursing home conspiracy theories, a group of senators that includes Elizabeth Warren, Richard Blumenthal, Alex Padilla, Mazie Hirono, Ron Wyden, Kirsten Gillibrand, Jeff Merkley, and Cory Booker wrote in a letter to CMS to ”urgently request that CMS rescind its July 2026 memorandum and reinstate its 2020 and 2024 nursing home voting guidance.”
“This is as low as it gets,” Warren tells WIRED. “The Trump administration’s unfounded allegations of election fraud are inspiring election denial groups to harass nursing home residents and staff. With less than a week until Election Day, every lawmaker in America should be standing up for fair elections and pushing back on this attack on seniors’ voting rights.”
A CMS spokesperson did not respond to questions about the agency’s communications with election denial groups but instead referred WIRED to the July 2026 memo.
In the letter, Warren and her colleagues specifically ask Oz about communications between CMS and Mitchell, the Election Integrity Network, and Project Civica, a New York–based election-denial group. The senators demand Oz “identify each organization and individual involved, the dates and nature of those communications, and any recommendations provided to CMS.”
Mitchell and EIN did not respond to a request for comment. "[We] had no communications or interactions with CMS regarding its memorandum or our Adopt a Care Facility initiative," Kim Hermance, president of Project Civica, tells WIRED. "Our only engagement with the agency's guidance has been reviewing the publicly available information on its website."
In August, Warren sent a letter to Oz questioning the July memo and asking him to reverse the changes. In September, Oz responded in a letter to Warren directly addressing the guidance that was removed from the CMS website in relation to helping nursing home residents with voting.
“Providing neutral logistical assistance, such as helping a resident request a mail-in ballot, completing a ballot per the resident's own expressed wishes, or arranging transportation to a polling location, is not the type of conduct that would give rise to a voter fraud investigation,” Oz writes.
Addressing the apparent contradiction in this response, the senators in their letter to Oz asked: “Why has CMS not reinstated its previous guidance clarifying nursing homes’ responsibilities to facilitate residents’ voting rights?”
With just days to go to the midterms, efforts to boost baseless conspiracy theories about voter fraud continue to gain traction. On Tuesday, Trump said he is willing to accept the outcome of the midterms if they are “honest elections.” But his administration has spent months pushing conspiracy theories about mail-in voting and noncitizen voting, while actively trying to disenfranchise voters.

Montreux Convention helped contain fallout from Russia-Ukraine war in Black Sea: Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:41:26 UTC
23:41:26 KST

Türkiye has strictly implemented the Montreux Convention since Russia launched its war against Ukraine in 2022, helping prevent the conflict from spreading to a wider region and limiting its impact on the Black Sea, Turkish Defence Minister Yasar Guler has said.
Speaking on Wednesday at a joint news conference in Sofia after a meeting of defence ministers and chiefs of general staff from Türkiye, Bulgaria and Romania, Guler said Ankara remained committed to Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity while maintaining channels of dialogue with Russia to prevent further escalation.
Chief of General Staff General Selcuk Bayraktaroglu also attended the meeting.
Türkiye warns over attacks on commercial vessels
Guler said the war had significantly affected Black Sea security, with commercial vessels coming under attack and threats emerging from drifting mines, unmanned surface vehicles, drones and missile fragments.
He expressed concern over repeated attacks on commercial shipping and said Türkiye had urged both sides to exercise restraint and respect freedom of navigation in international waters.
“We learned today that another commercial vessel was struck by three drones in Bulgaria’s maritime jurisdiction,” Guler said, calling for greater caution from both parties.
He added that Türkiye reserved all legal rights in response to attacks on Turkish-flagged and Turkish-operated vessels and was closely monitoring developments.
Although Türkiye, Bulgaria and Romania had the military capabilities to respond to threats, Guler stressed that decisions must account for timing and regional circumstances.
He called for careful diplomacy and rational decisions at both tactical and strategic levels to avoid increasing tensions.
Regional cooperation to counter mines and protect infrastructure
Guler said Türkiye, which has the longest coastline on the Black Sea, considers regional stability and maritime security essential.
He highlighted mine-countermeasure operations conducted by Türkiye’s naval and naval aviation forces to reduce risks to shipping.
He also pointed to the Black Sea Mine Countermeasures Task Group, known as MCM Black Sea, established by the three coastal countries to tackle the threat posed by drifting mines.
Other countries can contribute to the initiative without deploying vessels, in line with an agreement among its members, he said.
Guler also emphasised the importance of protecting critical underwater infrastructure, noting that amendments to a related memorandum of understanding were signed on July 7 on the sidelines of the NATO Summit.
Türkiye has further demonstrated its commitment to regional cooperation by assuming leadership of the Maritime Component Command under the Ukraine Volunteer Coalition, he added.
Ankara calls civilian shipping a red line
Guler said Türkiye continued to use diplomatic channels to create opportunities for dialogue between Russia and Ukraine, with the aim of protecting maritime trade routes and ensuring freedom of navigation.
Both sides were being repeatedly warned that commercial shipping must remain outside the conflict zone and that attacks on civilian vessels must stop immediately, he said.
He described the coordinated position adopted by Türkiye, Bulgaria and Romania as a clear message that the safety of commercial routes and the security of Black Sea coastal countries must not be compromised.
The three countries have taken joint steps to limit the war’s impact on their security and citizens’ well-being, while maintaining safe navigation, Guler said.
He pledged that Türkiye would continue taking necessary measures to support maritime safety, guided by regional cooperation and the capabilities available to the countries involved.
The joint text agreed upon at Wednesday’s meeting, he added, reaffirmed the three countries’ firm stance on Black Sea security.

Newborn immunisation against respiratory virus could cut infant winter hospitalisations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:39:25 UTC
23:39:25 KST

As the cold season nears, immunisation of newborns against universal RSV could significantly reduce infant hospitalisations across Europe
As the season for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and other respiratory diseases approaches, a new report from the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) indicates that universal immunisation of newborns against RSV could substantially reduce hospitalisations among infants linked to the disease during the winter season.
‘Protecting infants from RSV in the first months of their life is particularly important,’ said Bruno Ciancio, ECDC Head of Unit. ‘And we have a tool to do just that. Universal immunisation of newborns against RSV can reduce the risk of hospitalisation due to respiratory infections in young children by more than half.’
The models assessed the potential of providing vaccination to expectant mothers, or immunising infants directly with antibodies. Assuming 90% of newborns are immunised with long-acting monoclonal antibodies at birth, models project that 61% of RSV-related hospitalisations in infants can be prevented in the first two months of life. In the same assessment, ECDC estimates that universal vaccination of pregnant mothers would also lead to substantial reductions in RSV hospitalisation among infants in the first two months of life (52%).
As Europe enters the autumn and winter months, RSV, influenza and other respiratory infections can put children at risk of serious illness, while also placing additional pressure on healthcare systems across the region. This makes it all the more important to ensure that newborns are immunised against RSV.

====================================================================================================

Can Singapore Help Europe Rethink Its Indo-Pacific Strategy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:38:00 UTC
23:38:00 KST

On October 27, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Singapore with a message that Europe needs closer partnerships in the Indo-Pacific. Trade, underwater infrastructure, and industrial artificial intelligence may seem like separate policy areas. In fact, they expose the same problem: Europe’s prosperity depends on networks that it cannot secure or shape alone.
Singapore has spent decades making itself indispensable to a global economy in which it has little control over the behavior of the major powers. Germany might be seeking to learn from that example.
At his meeting with Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, Merz proposed an interregional trade agreement between the European Union and the 12 members of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP). Together, the two groups account for more than a third of global trade. Wong and Merz also agreed to deepen defense cooperation and industrial AI collaboration under an updated strategic partnership, building on their original agreement from 2024.
The EU already has trade agreements with CPTPP members Singapore and Vietnam in Southeast Asia, as well as with other CPTPP members, including Japan, Canada and New Zealand. Singapore specifically has had a free-trade agreement with the EU since 2019, followed by a digital trade agreement that took effect in February 2026. According to the European Commission, bilateral trade in goods between the EU and Singapore reached 47.8 billion euros in 2025.
Merz’s proposal to link the EU more closely with the CPTPP would therefore need to do more than connect markets that already have bilateral FTAs. Its value would lie in addressing gaps between existing agreements, aligning trade rules where possible, and making it easier for businesses to operate across countries with different regulatory systems. But an interregional agreement would be politically difficult to negotiate.
In the realm of security, Merz and Wong focused on undersea cables, which carry more than 99 percent of international data traffic. These cables support financial transactions, cloud services and government communications, yet they are vulnerable to both accidental damage and purposeful sabotage.
Singapore has taken a leading role in efforts to improve cooperation on critical underwater infrastructure. In May 2026, on the sidelines of the Singapore-hosted Shangri-La Dialogue, 17 countries launched the Guiding Principles for Underwater Infrastructure Defense Exchanges (GUIDE), a voluntary framework for sharing information and exploring practical defense cooperation. Singapore was one of the founding members; European countries, among them France and Italy, accounted for over half of the 17 states that joined at the launch. Germany joined GUIDE during Merz’s visit.
Much underwater infrastructure is built, maintained, and repaired by private operators, making coordination between governments and industry essential. GUIDE provides a framework for countries to share information and improve their response to disruptions that cross national borders. The damage to five undersea cables in the Gulf of Finland in December 2024 illustrated the stakes. Such incidents can disrupt communications, incur substantial repair costs, and leave governments struggling to establish responsibility. For Singapore, a major hub for international data routes, and Germany, whose economy depends on secure digital connectivity, closer cooperation is therefore a practical necessity.
Industrial AI offers a third example of why EU-Singapore connections matter. Germany has deep manufacturing and engineering expertise; Singapore has invested in digital infrastructure and the application of AI.
At their joint press conference, Wong said Singapore was focusing less on building frontier models than on deploying AI in areas such as logistics, healthcare, finance, and advanced manufacturing. The National AI Strategy 2.0, launched in 2023, aims to make the city-state a leading center for AI solutions by 2030. It emphasizes adoption across industry, government and research.
That focus complements Germany’s industrial base. Cooperation could help manufacturers introduce robotics and automation, improve productivity, and bring AI into existing production systems. But the test will be whether cooperation produces systems that businesses actually use.
The EU has spent years declaring the Indo-Pacific a strategic priority. Europe cannot eliminate its dependence on international markets, digital infrastructure, or foreign technology, and it cannot expect Singapore to become an alternative to the United States or China. Singapore’s strength lies in maintaining connections across competing centers of power, not in choosing one at the expense of the others. Europe could learn from that approach. Singapore cannot solve Europe’s strategic problems, but it already has the trade agreements, security partnerships, and technological ambitions that Europe says it wants to build on.
Merz has put forward a vision for closer transregional cooperation, but he has yet to explain how the EU would turn closer CPTPP ties into a workable trade framework. GUIDE remains a voluntary platform, and industrial AI cooperation has yet to demonstrate its economic impact. Merz’s Singapore visit set out the ambition, but the work of implementation has barely begun.

====================================================================================================

INTERVIEW - Former Caribbean leader urges slavery apology as Britain’s king visits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:36:26 UTC
23:36:26 KST

- Former Saint Vincent and the Grenadines premier calls for ‘full, unequivocal apology’ as palace aides say king will not apologize during Caribbean tour
- ‘They don't want to help to finance any of the matters because they feel that it will cost them a great deal of money,’ says Ralph Gonsalves
- Gonsalves sees Commonwealth summit as potential ‘watershed moment’ for reparations
As King Charles III arrived in the Bahamas for a Caribbean tour, former Saint Vincent and the Grenadines Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves said expressions of sorrow over slavery were no longer enough.
"The starting point is for a full, unequivocal apology," Gonsalves told Anadolu in an interview Tuesday.
“They don't want to do an apology. They don't want to help to finance any of the matters because they feel that it will cost them a great deal of money,” he added.
Gonsalves, now a senior adviser to The Repair Campaign and a leading figure in the Caribbean’s reparatory justice movement, argued that the consequences of slavery remain visible in Caribbean societies’ health, education, housing and access to land.
An apology must lead to measures addressing those inequalities, he added.
His appeal comes ahead of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda on Nov. 1-4, which Charles will attend during his nine-day regional tour.
Speaking in the Bahamian capital Nassau on Tuesday, Charles acknowledged the “great suffering and injustices of the past” and said leaders of affected Commonwealth countries would discuss those issues at the summit.
However, Buckingham Palace has made clear that no formal apology is expected. 
A ‘watershed moment’?
Despite that resistance, Gonsalves sees Charles as someone who could help advance the discussion.
He said he raised reparations directly with Charles during a 2019 visit to Saint Vincent, when the monarch was still Prince of Wales, and again after his accession to the throne.
“I have a sense that the king would be supportive of that conversation,” he said.
Gonsalves acknowledged that Charles acts on government advice but argued that he could seek the British prime minister’s approval for an apology.
“He can apologize certainly for his own family's role in the enslavement of African bodies,” he added.
He pointed to the Netherlands, where then-Prime Minister Mark Rutte apologized for the Dutch state’s role in slavery in December 2022, followed by King Willem-Alexander in July 2023.
For Gonsalves, the upcoming summit offers an opportunity to begin “a mature, honest, respectful conversation” about the consequences of Indigenous genocide and the enslavement of Africans.
“This Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting is likely to be a watershed moment for reparations in the Commonwealth,” he said. 
Slavery’s lasting consequences
Gonsalves said generations of exploitation had left Caribbean societies confronting deep inequalities in education, health, housing, land ownership and economic development.
"For us on this issue, the present is the past," he said. "When the British say they don't want to go to the past, we say we don't want to live in the past. But the contemporary legacies are consequences of these grave historical wrongs."
He said formerly enslaved people emerged from slavery without the resources to build secure livelihoods.
"They had no education. They were in a terrible health situation. No housing. They had no land. No property of any kind," he said.
Britain, meanwhile, paid slave owners £20 million in compensation following abolition in the 1830s, Gonsalves noted.
“In today's money, that is over $100 billion,” he said.
Those who had been enslaved received no comparable compensation for generations of forced labor. Many were required to continue working without pay under an apprenticeship system that lasted until 1838.
"This free labor built the wealth of Britain," he said, arguing that slavery helped finance the country's commercial and industrial development, including its banking system.
Gonsalves argued that addressing those injustices would also help Britain confront racial tensions at home.
"It is in the interest of Britain," he said. “British society has a lot of dissonance on ethnic issues.” 
10-point reparation plan
The Caribbean Community established its reparations commission in 2013. Regional leaders approved a revised 10-point reparatory justice plan in July, which was relaunched at a conference in Barbados in September.
The plan addresses the legacies of Indigenous genocide and the enslavement of Africans. Its proposals include a full formal apology, debt cancellation, monetary compensation, health and education initiatives, infrastructure development, the return of cultural artifacts, memorialization and psychological rehabilitation.
Gonsalves said an apology and financial redress were parts of the same process.
“All 10 are interconnected, they form a composite of all,” he said. “So it's not a question of you're doing one and you don't do the other.”
He called for a structured program of compensation and development initiatives, with deadlines and milestones to measure progress.
“We have to have a repair. A compensation, among the repair items,” he said.
For Gonsalves, reparations are "a matter of international justice," extending beyond Britain and its former Caribbean colonies to Africa and the wider diaspora.
He rejected suggestions that institutions and cultural practices introduced under British rule could offset the harm of colonialism.
“Did you have to carry out native genocide and enslave African bodies to take us out of our own developmental path?”  
The monarchy’s future in the Caribbean
Alongside demands for reparations, Gonsalves predicted that more Caribbean countries would remove the British monarch as their head of state.
“More and more Caribbean countries will become republics in the future,” he said.
Barbados became a republic in 2021, following Guyana in 1970 and Trinidad and Tobago in 1976. Dominica became a republic upon independence in 1978.
Gonsalves said constitutional requirements, including referendums in some countries, could slow the process.
He said he "strongly" supports a republic in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines while retaining respect for Charles and the royal family.
Whether Britain itself should become a republic was a question for the British people, he added.
As Charles continues his tour from the Bahamas to Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda, Gonsalves said he expected protests but believed they would remain peaceful.
Around a dozen demonstrators gathered outside Tuesday's youth event in Nassau carrying placards demanding reparations, according to the BBC.
Gonsalves said he did not anticipate a security threat to the king and stressed that Caribbean leaders wanted their demands addressed through respectful dialogue rather than confrontation.
"The standing of Britain in the world would improve if they address this question honestly, maturely, once and for all with us, and with Africa," he said.

Putin woos African leaders at showcase summit, says Russia is better partner than 'colonial' West
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:36:09 UTC
23:36:09 KST

Putin woos African leaders, says Russia a better partner than 'colonial' West
MOSCOW, Oct 28 - President Vladimir Putin told African leaders on Wednesday that Russia was their best partner, accusing what he cast as a colonial West of still trying to exploit the continent's resources and using debt to hold back development.
Putin was speaking at the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, a two-day event attended by African leaders and government delegations from 48 countries, and will hold one-on-one talks with many of the 22 individual African leaders attending on issues such as trade, security, arms and grain.
The event, first held in 2019, is part of a concerted push for Russian political, economic and military influence on a continent where paramilitary fighters from Russia's Africa Corps remain active.
Russian state media and cultural institutions are also trying to expand their footprint in Africa, and Russian state companies are trying to expand their interests in areas from mining to power generation.
Wooing African leaders and others from the Global South has also been part of Moscow's strategy to counterbalance pressure on the world stage from the West over Russia's war in Ukraine.
"Africa is increasingly asserting itself as one of the key players in the global economy and politics," Putin said.
"However, the emergence of a multipolar world is, of course, no easy task; it faces resistance from countries that are not prepared to accept this reality: those who are accustomed to thinking in terms of their colonial past and to enriching themselves fabulously."
Putin, whom Western critics accuse of trying to leverage Africa's colonial past to Moscow's benefit, did not name the countries he had in mind.
But he spoke of what he called "active attempts by Western countries" to drive Africans back into debt bondage and to force them to accept much-needed financial resources on predatory terms, which he said slowed their long-term development.
RUSSIA READY TO SHARE
By contrast, Putin said Russia was ready to share its know-how, including digital know-how, and localise production rather than just buy raw materials, creating jobs and generating tax revenue.
Russian paramilitary forces have been accused by Western governments of propping up military juntas such as the one in Mali to try to shore up Moscow's geopolitical influence and squeeze out former colonial powers such as France. Moscow rejects these assertions.
Burkina Faso's prime minister, Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouedraogo, said cooperation with Russia was transparent and ensured both parties' interests, and that Moscow was not trying to erase African languages and cultures.
"This is completely different from what we had with imperialist France," he told Russia's state RT television channel.
Putin told the summit that Russia championed greater African influence in the IMF and World Bank, was ready to embark on joint transport and agricultural infrastructure projects and that Moscow stood ready to supply grain and fertiliser to more African countries. REUTERS

Farhangsara-ye Khorasan, a cultural hub rooted in Tehran’s history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:36:08 UTC
23:36:08 KST

Farhangsara-ye Khorasan, a cultural hub rooted in Tehran’s history
TEHRAN – Farhangsara-ye Khorasan, or Khorasan Cultural Center, in southern Tehran is a place where people can take part in cultural activities, enjoy artistic programs and attend educational and social events. But what makes it especially interesting is its location in an area with a rich history.
The center stands near the site of Iran’s first Mashin Doodi railway station, linking its present-day cultural activities with an important part of Tehran’s past.
There is usually a variety of programs to choose from, ranging from art and educational activities to local celebrations and community gatherings. These events give people living in the area a chance to meet, learn something new and take part in the cultural life of their neighborhood.
The center also has an amphitheater with audio and visual equipment and seating for 80 people. It can be used for performances, presentations, meetings and other events, making it a useful space for local cultural activities.
Yet a visit to Farhangsara-ye Khorasan is about more than what happens inside the building. Its surroundings have a story of their own, closely tied to the early days of railway travel in Iran.
A cultural center with a historic legacy
The Mashin Doodi railway began operating in 1882, during the reign of Qajar king Naser al-Din Shah. Its name, which refers to the smoke and steam produced by its locomotives, became familiar to people in Tehran. The railway connected the capital with the historic city of Rey along a route of about eight kilometers.
Before the railway arrived, people mainly travelled by horse-drawn carriage or used camel caravans to move goods. Such journeys could be slow and expensive. The new railway made travelling between Tehran and Rey easier and helped trade and everyday interactions grow.
It also played a part in changing the face of Tehran. Shops and businesses sprang up around railway facilities, more people settled in the area, and construction gradually spread. As the city grew, streets and public services also developed.
The Mashin Doodi railway remained in operation for decades, until regular services ended in 1962, when more modern forms of transport began to take its place. Its story did not end there, however. In 2018, sections of the old railway were rediscovered during construction work in Rey. Restoration efforts later helped preserve parts of this heritage, including a Qajar-era locomotive, which now attracts visitors interested in Iran’s early railway history.
The story of Khorasan station is part of this wider period of change. Historical accounts describe how French specialists studied possible railway routes and locations for the station before the project received approval from the Qajar court. Building the railway was not easy. Workers and engineers faced financial problems, shortages of materials and equipment, and technical difficulties in laying tracks and constructing bridges and small tunnels.
The station building itself reflected a mix of Iranian and European influences. Brickwork, high arches, spacious halls and decorative details gave it a distinctive character, while its design served the practical needs of a modern railway.
As Tehran expanded and passenger numbers grew, the railway facilities changed over the years. Eventually, after railway services ended, the historic site found a new purpose as a cultural venue.
Connecting Tehran’s past with its cultural present
Today, Farhangsara-ye Khorasan gives the historic area a new lease on life. Instead of being just a reminder of an earlier era, it has become a place where people can gather for cultural events, learn new skills and enjoy artistic activities.
For an ordinary visitor, that combination is what makes the center worth discovering: it is a place to take part in cultural life today while getting a glimpse of Tehran’s past.

Wendy's shares jump 15% as Nelson Peltz's Trian offers $1.4 billion to buy burger chain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:35:51 UTC
23:35:51 KST

A group of investors led by Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management has offered $1.4 billion to buy Wendy's, according to a regulatory filing Wednesday.
The group has offered $7.35 per share in cash to take the burger chain private, paying a 20% premium to Tuesday's closing price. In addition to Trian, it includes investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners, plus Flynn Group, one of Wendy's largest franchisees.
Wendy's shares spiked about 15% in morning trading following the offer. The Wall Street Journal first reported Peltz's proposal.
Wendy's did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC. Trian declined to comment beyond the filing.
The take-private deal offer comes after a tough two-year stretch for the burger chain. Wendy's stock has tumbled 65% over that period, including Wednesday's gains. For six straight quarters, the company has reported same-store sales declines.
Wendy's is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings before the bell on Nov. 5.
Wendy's challenges have made the company a cheaper acquisition target for Peltz, whose history with the brand dates back to an activist campaign he led more than two decades ago.
Budget-conscious diners have been eating out less often, and Wendy's and its rivals have leaned into discounts to lure consumers into restaurants. Wendy's has also dealt with a revolving door of chief executives, who have had different ideas about turnaround strategies for the struggling chain.
"In our view, a take private makes sense as Wendy's turnaround is likely to be prolonged given the challenged state of the lower income consumer and soft state of the quick service burger category," TD Cowen analyst Andrew Charles wrote in a note to clients on Wednesday.
In May, former Potbelly CEO Bob Wright joined Wendy's as its latest chief executive, after his former employer went private. In his first earnings conference call with analysts in August, he was candid about what he views as the chain's biggest issues, like muddled value offerings, inconsistent execution at its restaurants and too many one-off promotions.
Trian previously explored a takeover of Wendy's in 2022, but later decided against it. The firm and affiliated parties own a 16.25% stake in Wendy's, according to the regulatory filing, making them the company's largest shareholder.

US warns Gulf of 'intense' return to Iran war after midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:33:28 UTC
23:33:28 KST

Breadcrumb
US warns Gulf states to brace for 'intense' Iran war after midterms
The US has warned several Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a possible short but intense military campaign against Iran following next week's US midterm elections, according to a report published by The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday.
The warnings, delivered through diplomatic and military channels, come as the US and Israel make preparations for renewed strikes against Iran, potentially targeting the country's nuclear facilities and other critical infrastructure.
US President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on launching another military operation, but is leaning towards a major attack after the 3 November elections, the newspaper reported, citing people familiar with his thinking.
The preparations are intended to give Trump military options while Washington continues to pursue an agreement with Tehran.
The US military is transferring an additional Patriot missile defence system from Texas to Israel, according to flight-tracking data and officials familiar with the deployment.
American forces have also relocated personnel from vulnerable military bases across the Middle East, replenished ammunition stockpiles and prepared bombers and fighter aircraft for potential operations.
An additional aircraft carrier strike group and Marine expeditionary unit are expected to join approximately 20 American warships already operating in the region next month, although some vessels could be withdrawn.
Israel has also reportedly identified targets and prepared plans for another military offensive, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu continuing to advocate further strikes against Iran.
The White House declined to discuss the reported preparations.
"President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon," it said.
Trump has previously said he would not attack Iran before the midterm elections.
Speaking at a campaign rally in Texas on Tuesday, he suggested that further developments involving Iran could follow within weeks.
"You'll see Iran in a couple of weeks, if you don't mind," Trump said.
Gulf states face renewed threat
The reported preparations come as Gulf governments attempt to prevent another regional war while confronting the prospect of Iranian retaliation against their territory.
Iran has warned that further American or Israeli attacks would provoke strikes against economic and military targets across the region.
During the previous phase of the war, Iranian missiles and drones targeted American military facilities, diplomatic installations, energy infrastructure and airports in Gulf countries.
Another confrontation could expose Gulf states to renewed attacks at a time when Washington and its regional allies are attempting to replenish missile defence systems depleted during earlier fighting.
Despite extensive American and Israeli bombardment, Iran retains substantial missile capabilities and has reportedly been rebuilding its military arsenal and air defences.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on 28 February, with Iranian responding with attacks on what it said were US facilities in the region and closing the Strait of Hormuz.
Washington subsequently intensified economic pressure through sanctions and a naval blockade that have severely restricted Iranian oil exports and international trade.
Renewed diplomatic efforts
The prospect of renewed attacks comes amid diplomatic efforts by regional governments to secure an agreement between Washington and Tehran.
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have recently participated in high-level consultations with Iranian officials, while other regional mediators have attempted to revive negotiations over Iran's nuclear programme.
However, the talks have made little progress, with Washington insisting on restrictions on Iran's nuclear activities and Tehran maintaining its own conditions for negotiations.
The International Atomic Energy Agency said on Tuesday that it had identified no evidence of reconstruction at Iranian nuclear facilities damaged during previous American and Israeli attacks.
However, agency chief Rafael Grossi warned that inspectors had been unable to access the damaged sites or verify the status of Iran's nuclear material.
Analysts have also questioned whether further military action would compel Tehran to make concessions, warning that renewed attacks could instead strengthen Iran's determination to rebuild its military capabilities.
The reported American preparations therefore leave Gulf governments confronting the possibility of another major regional conflict, even as diplomatic efforts to prevent renewed fighting continue.

The UK, the Netherlands, Finland and Poland will begin treaty negotiations as part of a joint defense procurement scheme, with the initiative expected to become operational in 2027, according to a statement Wednesday.
In a joint statement, the four European countries said they had stepped up efforts to begin treaty negotiations as part of the Multilateral Defense Mechanism (MDM) partnership, which aims to accelerate defense investment and joint procurement.

Flavio Bolsonaro lands in Miami after losing Brazil’s presidential election
Bolsonaro and his family have fled to the US amid a Brazilian Supreme Court order to surrender his passports.
Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has issued a statement hours after arriving in Miami, in the United States, with his family, days after losing a presidential election to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, and claimed he was “the true elected president of Brazil”.
The far-right politician thanked US President Donald Trump. Bolsonaro said the allegations of embezzlement and money laundering against him were “a politically motivated witch-hunt, intended to hold me hostage”. He also claimed without evidence that the election results were fraudulent.
“Faced with the politicization of the justice system in Brazil, I brought my family to the US. I did not flee Brazil; I left for Brazil’s sake. I left a state of exception so that I could be the leader my people deserve,” he said.
Bolsonaro asked the international community “not to normalize what is happening in Brazil” and said he would lead the country’s opposition from the US.
Dressed casually in a dark polo shirt and flanked by his wife and two daughters, Bolsonaro stepped out of the plane shortly after it landed at about 9:30am local time (13:30 GMT). Florida, where Miami is located, is home to the largest population of Brazilians in the United States.
Al Jazeera’s John Holman, reporting from outside Opa-Locka executive airport, where the family landed on Wednesday morning, said the group was “whisked away in an SUV” from the airport soon after arriving.
Brazil‘s Supreme Court had ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports shortly after the election, in an attempt to make sure the right-wing senator did not flee the country before he could be investigated for embezzlement and money laundering.
As a senator, Bolsonaro had immunity from potential criminal prosecution, but he would lose that protection in January, since he gave up his seat to run for president.
Holman said the Bolsonaro family’s flight from Brazil was a dramatic escape, starting with crossing into neighbouring Argentina “on a rope bridge, on foot”.
Argentine immigration authorities said the senator and his family entered the country late on Tuesday night, and less than an hour later boarded a private plane operated by Baires Fly destined for Guayaquil, Ecuador.
That plane arrived in Ecuador, and later took off for Miami, Florida, with Bolsonaro and his family on board.
Both Ecuador and Argentina are run by right-wing leaders who are close allies of US President Donald Trump, said Holman. The countries provided “stepping stones among allies”, and the US Department of State issued visas for the family.
Brazil and the US do have an extradition treaty, but Holman said it is expected Bolsonaro will be protected by Trump, who said yesterday the Bolsonaro family were “fine people”.
“The signs are, with the State Department issuing him a visa, with the comments coming from President Trump, that they’re not gonna be in any hurry to hand him back to Brazil,” Holman said.
Flavio’s father, Brazil’s former President Jair Bolsonaro, undertook a very similar journey to Florida after he lost his bid for re-election in 2022. While he was in the US, the elder Bolsonaro’s supporters attempted to orchestrate a coup. He later returned to Brazil and is currently under house arrest there.

US imposes sanctions on Rwanda's defense ministry over Congo conflict
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 - The US imposed sanctions on Rwanda's ministry of defense on Wednesday over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, as Washington seeks to increase pressure on Kigali and bring an end to the fighting.
Clashes have continued in eastern Congo, where rebels, who the UN says are backed by Rwanda, are fighting Congolese forces and the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), a Hutu militia rooted in the 1994 genocide.
Rwanda denies backing the Refoundation of the Nation rebels, formerly known as AFC-M23.
"Rwanda must halt its support for M23 and withdraw its troops from eastern DRC," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.
US President Donald Trump's administration has sought to broker peace between the two countries, which signed a deal in 2025 to end fighting. So far those efforts have brought little change on the ground.
Rwandan government spokesperson Yolande Makolo said the Washington Accords contain commitments on the neutralization of the FDLR that are unmet.
"Rwanda remains ready to fully implement the Washington Accords, concurrently with the willingness of the DRC to fulfill those commitments, and with the mediator holding all parties accountable," she added.
Congo's ministry of foreign affairs welcomed the sanctions in a statement.
"These sanctions send a clear message that Rwanda cannot act with impunity... Rwanda must honor its commitments under the Washington Accords, respect the UN Charter, and withdraw its tens of thousands of troops from the DRC," the statement read.
The US Treasury Department in the statement said that the Rwandan ministry of defense directed the Rwanda Defense Force, which was previously sanctioned by Washington, to deploy thousands of troops across eastern Congo's North and South Kivu provinces, where they conducted operations alongside the rebels and provided the armed group with military equipment and other support.
The US on Wednesday also imposed Congo-related sanctions on Zigama Credit and Savings Society, which it said was a Rwandan financial institution operating on behalf of the country's security services. The Treasury accused it of playing a key role in facilitating Rwanda's support for the rebels.
The Treasury said the financial institution had facilitated payments to entities in China and other countries for weapons, ammunition and other military equipment for the Rwanda Defense Force. A Zigama branch also enabled the transportation of gold from rebel-controlled territory in Congo to Rwanda, the Treasury added.
Zigama's CEO did not immediately respond to a request for comment. REUTERS

Sweden sends four Saildrones into the Baltic
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:30:54 GMT
23:30:54 KST

Sweden has begun a year-long maritime surveillance mission using four Saildrone Voyager uncrewed surface vessels to support Swedish Navy maritime domain awareness in the Baltic Sea, according to the company.
The Voyager is a ten metre wind and solar powered vessel that carries radar, cameras and acoustic sensors and can stay at sea for months without refuelling or a crew, which makes it suited to the persistent watch over shipping lanes and seabed infrastructure that Baltic states have been trying to establish.
The deployment follows a run of damage to cables and pipelines on the Baltic seabed, which has drawn NATO’s Baltic Sentry activity and a series of national responses. The Swedish Defence Materiel Administration announced the programme alongside the company.
Saildrone vessels have been used by the United States Navy in the Gulf and the Caribbean and by NATO in European waters, and the Royal Navy has run its own trials of uncrewed surface vessels for maritime surveillance.
Ministers told Parliament last week that up to £330 million is going into improving Britain’s ability to deter, detect and respond to threats against critical undersea infrastructure.

What do young Europeans think about democracy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:30:25 UTC
23:30:25 KST

What matters to young people in Europe? How do they see democracy, and how would they like their voices to be heard?
The latest Eurobarometer on Youth and Democracy explores the views, concerns and expectations of young Europeans in 2026. The findings offer insights into how young people see democracy and their role in shaping Europe's future.
What are the main takeaways?
- Youth policies: Young people most often want youth policies to address real issues they face (40%). They also emphasise having a stronger say in decisions and greater financial support for youth programmes (32% each).
- Intergenerational fairness: Around one third consider that policymakers take long-term consequences into account. Similarly, 33% think young people have the same chances as 30 years ago or will have the same chances in 30 years' time.
- Civic engagement and societal change: Over half young Europeans have already participated in societal change actions (e.g. signing a petition, joining a rally, contacting a politician). Voting and social media are seen as the top levers to make young people's voice heard.
- Impact of EU actions and priorities for the future: Three in four young Europeans feel the EU has an impact on their daily lives. Young Europeans expect the EU to preserve peace, fight poverty and create jobs.
- Digital education: Young Europeans overall feel very confident in their ability to use AI safely but less confident when it comes to using it to deliver intended results.
Young people's perspectives matter. As the European Commission works to strengthen youth participation in policymaking and prepares for the next EU Youth Strategy beyond 2027, these findings can help inform efforts to ensure young people's voices are heard.

Why Arab parties may not be the ‘kingmakers’ in this Israeli election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:30:17 UTC
23:30:17 KST

Why Arab parties may not be the ‘kingmakers’ in this Israeli election
Exit poll projections show that if Eisenkot’s bloc teamed up with Arab parties, they could unseat Netanyahu. But observers don’t believe that will happen.
Israel’s Arab-led parties are projected to win a record number of seats in the Israeli parliament, exit polls indicate, making them increasingly hard to ignore by the leading blocs.
“Probably the most important phenomenon of this election is the rise and the revival of the Arab vote,” Daniel Shek, a former Israeli ambassador, said. “The statement is clear: You cannot disregard such a large portion of the electorate in the calculations for Israeli politics.”
The latest projections from Tuesday’s voting showed that the Arab parties – the Joint List and Ra’am – could hold a record combined 17 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
So far, no clear winner has emerged as partial results give Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc 54 seats and the opposition alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot 49.
While Arab parties might theoretically wield influence as the two main blocs fail to win majorities in the Knesset, they are not “kingmakers”, observers said, pointing to what amounts to a political veto that limits Arab parties’ ability to turn electoral gains into influence.
“This veto is rooted in a racist structure that regards the Arab citizen as illegitimate and as an unwanted partner,” Honaida Ghanam, director general of the Palestinian Forum for Israeli Studies in Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, told Al Jazeera, alluding to the resistance by the majority of Israeli parties to form any government with Arab-led lists.
Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have rejected the idea of partnering with them, citing a lack of shared values.
What do the numbers say?
The numbers from exit poll projections thus far are looking clear: If Eisenkot’s bloc teams up with Arab parties, they could secure the 61 seats needed for a majority in parliament and depose Netanyahu.
According to The Times of Israel, the latest partial results would give a partnership between Eisenkot’s opposition alliance and Arab-led parties 66 seats.
According to Palestinian political analyst Ahmed Najar, the unwillingness by the opposition bloc to join forces is purely “ideological”.
“Eisenkot has imposed loyalty tests on Arab parties and ruled out relying on them even as the electoral arithmetic makes their support indispensable,” Najar told Al Jazeera.
How politically feasible is such a partnership?
Observers are divided on this.
According to Najar, a partnership with the Arab parties is not only feasible, it may be the only “realistic” route for Eisenkot to remove Netanyahu.
Omar Shaban, director of Palthink for Strategic Studies, pointed to the fact that Mansour Abbas, the leader of Ra’am, has already shown a willingness to join Eisenkot’s government if the Israeli candidate is elected, based on the condition that internal security matters will be handled by the Arab party.
Abbas has even appointed Jewish lawmaker Yoav Segalovitz to the number two spot on Ra’am’s electoral slate for the elections, Shaban explained.
Such a collaboration, if it came to fruition, could help foster better relations between Palestinian citizens and Jewish Israelis, he said.
Meanwhile, on Wednesday, Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen said his party is prepared to take responsibility for bringing Netanyahu’s far-right coalition down.
“The government has made the lives of every Arab citizen miserable,” Jabareen was quoted by the Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper as saying.
His movement “will know how to leverage” its political strength to advance its values, he added.
Ahmad Tibi, also a Joint List leader, on Wednesday said the bloc was extending its hand to the opposition alliance to oust Netanyahu, according to Israeli media reports. It was far from clear, however, that the bloc would formally join a governing coalition.
A roadblock to such a partnership is the more “radical” elements in Israeli society that Eisenkot would have to face who “don’t want the Israeli government to be supported or dependent on Arab votes”, Shabaan said.
Najar said Eisenkot would also have to persuade his prospective partners, including Naftali Bennett from the Together alliance and Avigdor Liberman, who heads the Yisrael Beytenu party.
“Politically, however, it would require him and his prospective partners, particularly Bennett and Lieberman, to abandon the longstanding Zionist consensus that Palestinian citizens of Israel may vote but that the parties representing them are not legitimate partners in governing the country,” he said.
Ghanam outlined four possible outcomes: another election, an opposition minority government supported from outside by Arab parties, defections from the opposition to Netanyahu’s bloc or a national unity government.
“Beyond the arithmetic, the most telling result of this election is the resilience of Netanyahu’s camp, which has proven deeply entrenched and cohesive,” she added.
What are the terms Eisenkot has laid out for a partnership with Arab parties?
According to The Times of Israel, Eisenkot has said he would consider partnering with any party that recognises Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, endorses the values of the Declaration of Independence and commits to all Israelis performing national service.
He hasn’t, however, expressed whether Ra’am, with or without Jewish lawmaker Segalovitz, would meet those criteria, the outlet also reported.
Have Jewish and Arab parties teamed up before?
Yes, there is precedent for such a move.
Most recently, after the 2021 elections, Ra’am emerged as a possible kingmaker, and its support was vital for the formation of the short-lived Bennett-Yair Lapid government at the time.
“Ra’am participated in the 2021-2022 coalition while Arab parties have previously supported governments from outside, most notably during the Rabin period,” Najar said, referring to Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, who served in the country’s top post in the 1970s and 1990s.
“The obstacle is, therefore, neither constitutional nor practical but ideological.”
What have other party leaders said about partnering?
Netanyahu said on Tuesday that a coalition with Arab-led parties to form a government would be “a shame and a disgrace”.
“It is forbidden – simply forbidden – to endanger Israel and to establish a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties,” he told supporters.
Bennett, meanwhile, who is currently in third place, has reversed course from the past: He has made clear that he now only wants “Zionist” parties in government and wants to exclude Arab parties.
By contrast, Yair Golan, leader of the centre-left Democrats party, which is part of the opposition bloc led by Eisenkot, has urged his allies to abandon their refusal to cooperate with Arab parties.
“We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” Golan wrote on X.
What does the reluctance to partner say about Israeli democracy?
The reluctance of Jewish-led opposition parties to work with Arab parties “reveals the fundamentally racist structure of the Israeli political system”, Najar said.
“Jewish opposition leaders describe Netanyahu and the far right as an existential danger to democracy, yet many would apparently prefer Netanyahu to remain in power rather than share political power with Palestinian citizens of Israel,” he said.
Their objection is not only to a particular Arab party or programme but to the very idea that Palestinian representatives could possess genuine governing power, Najar added.
“A state cannot credibly call itself democratic when more than one-fifth of its citizens are permitted to vote but the representatives they elect are treated as inherently illegitimate,” he said.
Palestinian citizens of Israel, he pointed out, are accepted as voters when their participation serves the system but rejected as political actors when they seek the power to shape it, Najar added.
“This is not an accidental failure of Israeli democracy; it is the consequence of a system built to preserve Jewish political supremacy,” Najar said.
“If Eisenkot is serious about replacing Netanyahu, he must decide whether he is prepared to challenge that racist political order or remain confined by the same exclusionary logic that Netanyahu has spent years exploiting.”

France planning new riot crackdown law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:28:38 UTC
23:28:38 KST

France planning new riot crackdown law
France’s Senate has backed a sweeping “vandals pay” bill that could force people involved in violent gatherings to cover up to €10,000 ($11,100) in damage caused not only by them, but also by other members of the group. The vote follows weeks of nationwide protests which spiraled into looting, arson attacks, and clashes with police.
The bill was initially drafted by the government over the summer after violence following Paris Saint-Germain’s Champions League victory, but it gained urgency after a new wave of mass public disorder. Demonstrations against soaring living costs and worsening quality of education turned violent in several cities this month, with rioters looting shops, torching vehicles, and destroying the 19th-century city hall in Limoges. Thousands of people were arrested during the unrest, with hundreds injured.
Senators passed the measure by 229 votes to 105 on Wednesday, backed by conservatives, centrists, and Marine Le Pen’s right-wing National Rally despite fierce objections from the left.
While presenting the legislation, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez argued that it seeks “to deter vandals and looters who burden taxpayers and demonstrators with their misdeeds, and… to better compensate the victims of this damage.”
He added that the bill is also “firmly based on fault; fault exists when one participates in a group formed with the intention of committing violence.” Meanwhile, centrist Senator Olivier Bitz reassured that “it should not be assumed that this text would allow for the prosecution of passersby or peaceful demonstrators.”
The bill – which included around 20 additional provisions compared to its original version – establishes joint civil liability for people who knowingly join a group formed to commit violence or vandalism, or remain in a crowd after police dispersal warnings while aware of ongoing attacks. Those found liable could owe up to €10,000 for destruction committed by others, although the final sum is to be determined in court, and peaceful participation alone would not trigger the measure.
To recover court-ordered compensation, the legislation would also allow deductions from social benefits, including family allowances, housing assistance, and minimum-income payments. The bill would also exempt people who remain in a gathering for legitimate reasons, potentially including journalists and medical volunteers.
While centrists and right-wing supporters portrayed the bill as a more just measure to extract damages from those involved in vandalism and protect law-abiding taxpayers, socialist Senator Marie-Pierre de La Gontrie warned that the welfare measures risk penalizing entire families.
Nathalie Godard, Director of the Action Department at Amnesty International France, also argued that the bill “threatens to further deter people from taking to the streets to exercise their rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly,” adding that it comes on the heels of the government’s push to crack down on protests.
The Senate passed the bill ahead of the 2027 presidential race, with two key contenders taking contrasting positions over the unrest. Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner in recent polls, has championed the “vandals pay” principle, accusing President Emmanuel Macron’s government of failing to control the violence.
Her left-wing rival Jean-Luc Melenchon has backed the protests while condemning looting and vandalism and accusing the authorities of inflaming tensions through police brutality.
While the bill sailed through the right-dominated Senate, it now faces a much tougher test in the fractured National Assembly, where centrist and right-wing lawmakers together hold enough seats to outvote the left but remain divided over the proposed crackdown.
