A mirror trick that adds a sixth finger also changes what people think their hand can grab
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:00:56 UTC
23:00:56 KST

Tricking the brain into feeling an invisible sixth finger can quickly change how people judge what their hands are physically capable of doing, according to new research published in Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance. After experiencing a brief mirror-based illusion of having an extra digit beside their pinky, volunteers estimated that they could grasp wider blocks and needed larger openings to fit their hand through. The shift in opening-size judgments appeared even among participants who did not consciously feel the extra finger, suggesting that the brain may update its sense of the hand’s physical boundaries partly outside conscious awareness.
Whenever a person reaches through a narrow gap or picks up a wide glass with one hand, the brain automatically calculates how the physical dimensions of the body match up with the surrounding environment. Psychologists refer to these perceived possibilities for action as affordances. Rather than measuring spaces in inches or centimeters, people use their own bodies as a built-in ruler, and this internal gauge adapts rapidly when physical dimensions change. For instance, a 2008 study on movement decisions found that when adults wore a prosthetic that widened their hand by one centimeter, they recalibrated their judgments and selected wider openings as the smallest gap their hand could pass through.
Beyond adapting to physical prosthetics or tools, the brain can also adopt nonexistent extra body parts, known as supernumerary limbs or digits, when visual and touch signals are manipulated in unison. In a 2016 paper describing what is known as the Anne Boleyn illusion, researchers showed that sitting at a mirror and receiving synchronized strokes on both hands alongside a stroke in empty space could trick volunteers into feeling a sixth finger beside their pinky. Building on this technique, a 2025 study on extra-finger illusions indicated that people can experience this phantom sixth digit even when it is angled at biologically impossible postures up to 180 degrees away from the palm, while still feeling their real pinky in its normal spot.
Knowing that an illusory sixth finger can feel independent from the rest of the hand raised an unresolved question: does the brain treat this invisible digit as an isolated sensory quirk, or does it integrate the extra finger into the whole hand when sizing up physical actions? To test whether an illusory sixth finger alters perceived action boundaries, Denise Cadete and her colleagues designed an experiment combining the mirror-box setup with tests of hand width and grasping span. Cadete is an associate lecturer in the School of Psychological Sciences at Birkbeck, University of London, a researcher in the university’s Body Representation Lab and Vestibular×Space Neuroscience Lab, and the lead author of the 2025 posture study. The team preregistered the study’s design, hypotheses, and main analyses before collecting data.
“I first wanted to find a way of having an implicit measure for the experience of having a sixth finger, to overcome the limitations of having self-reported data,” Cadete told PsyPost. “I was interested in the illusory perception of an extra finger beyond the conscious interpretation of that phenomenon. Later, I was very intrigued by using an action perception task that would unravel whether the illusion of having an extra finger would update action representations too.”
The researchers recruited 50 healthy adults, including 32 women, with an average age of 31.4 years. All but one of the participants were right-handed, and every volunteer completed the experiment using their left hand as the target hand across both an illusion condition and a control condition in a counterbalanced order. During each session, participants sat at a table with an upright mirror aligned down the center of their body, placing their left hand out of sight behind the mirror and their right hand in front of it. Looking into the glass created the visual impression that the reflection of their right hand was actually their hidden left hand.
To induce the illusion, a researcher stroked the matching fingers of both hands at the exact same time, brushing back and forth twice from the thumbs to the little fingers. After touching the inner side of the hidden left pinky alongside the top of the visible right pinky, the researcher delivered 20 synchronized strokes to the outer edge of the hidden left pinky while simultaneously stroking the empty table space just outside the reflected right pinky. Because participants saw the stroke land on empty space at the moment they felt touch on the side of their hidden hand, many experienced the sensation of a sixth finger. In the control condition, the researcher followed the same one-minute routine, except the final 20 strokes were applied directly onto both pinky fingers rather than empty air.
Immediately after the one-minute stimulation, the researcher covered the participant’s hands with a box to block visual inspection, and participants kept their hands still so that muscle and joint feedback, known as proprioception, would not disrupt the illusion. Across eight trials per condition, participants first judged aperture passing by watching a wooden frame fitted with black plastic triangles that opened and closed like a camera shutter (from 2.7 to 18 centimeters), calling out when the opening matched the smallest gap their closed left hand could pass through without touching the edges.
Across another eight trials per condition, they judged grasping ability by looking at 16 square foam-board blocks (ranging from 4 to 25 centimeters wide in 1.4-centimeter steps) and stating whether they could stretch their left thumb and fingers across opposite edges to hold each block. Brief top-up strokes were delivered after every two estimates, and at the end of each block, participants rated their conscious sensations on a 0-to-10 scale. At the end of the session, participants physically placed their left hand inside the shutter and grasped the foam blocks so the researchers could calculate an accuracy ratio dividing each person’s estimated size by their actual physical limit, where 1.00 is an exact match, above 1.00 is an overestimation, and below 1.00 is an underestimation.
Questionnaire ratings confirmed that the mirror procedure worked as intended: on the 0-to-10 scale, average scores for feeling six fingers rose from 1.13 in the control condition to 4.36 in the illusion condition. Participants also gave higher ratings during the illusion for feeling two little fingers (3.96 versus 1.24), touch in an unusual place (4.92 versus 1.86), touch off the body (3.55 versus 0.93), and a larger little finger (3.06 versus 1.80). By contrast, a control prompt about feeling an entire extra hand showed no statistically significant difference between the illusion (1.35) and control (1.10) conditions. Ratings across the full group averaged below the scale’s midpoint, in part because 22 of the 50 participants reported little or no sixth finger.
“The illusion is not imaginary, is not a weak sensation or a delusion; it is a vivid sensation of having a sixth finger, created by a trick using visual-tactile stimulation that will map a real touch onto empty space next to the hand,” Cadete explained.
In the action-judgment tasks, experiencing the sixth-finger illusion shifted how participants sized up both their hand width and their grip reach. In the aperture task, the average ratio of estimated-to-actual opening size increased from 0.92 in the control condition to 0.97 after the sixth-finger stimulation, reducing the proportion of participants who underestimated their needed space from 72 percent (36 of 50 people) in the control session to 58 percent (29 of 50 people) during the illusion.
Similarly, though more modestly, in the grasping task, the average ratio of estimated-to-actual grasp width rose from 0.98 in the control condition to 1.01 in the illusion condition, indicating that participants believed they could span wider blocks after the illusion. Participants who showed a larger increase between the control and illusion sessions on the aperture task also tended to show a larger increase on the grasping task.
“These findings point to a flexibility of the mind, not only in perceiving extra body parts that they never had, but also in integrating them immediately into their action perception,” Cadete said. “People change the perception of the action abilities of their hand when experiencing an invisible and illusory sixth finger, as if their hand had indeed six fingers to move and grasp objects.”
Unexpectedly, statistical analyses showed no significant correlation between how strongly participants reported feeling a sixth finger on the questionnaire and how much they adjusted their aperture or grasping estimates. In an exploratory analysis that was not preregistered, the researchers split the sample into 28 participants who consciously felt a sixth finger (scoring between 4 and 10) and 22 participants who did not (scoring between 0 and 2), finding that both subgroups still selected wider openings in the aperture task after the sixth-finger stimulation.
The average aperture ratio climbed from 0.90 to 0.97 among those who consciously felt the extra digit and rose from 0.95 to 0.98 among those who did not, though the shift was roughly twice as large for those who felt the illusion (an average change of 0.07 versus 0.03). In the grasping task, the within-group shifts from 0.97 to 1.00 among those who felt the finger and from 1.00 to 1.01 among those who did not were not statistically significant, possibly because splitting the sample into smaller subgroups reduced statistical power.
The aperture result among participants who did not feel the extra finger surprised Cadete. “This shows that the illusion is updating the perception of action abilities of the hand, regardless of its conscious experience of it,” she noted.
The authors interpret this disconnect between conscious reports and spatial judgments as a sign that the illusion works on two partly distinct levels. In their view, synchronized touch and visual cues beside the hand may update the body schema, the brain’s unconscious working map of body size and posture used to plan actions, even when a person does not consciously experience a sixth finger.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these results. Participants estimated their physical limits by looking at the apparatus and imagining the actions while their hands stayed motionless under a cover, rather than physically reaching out during the illusion. Because imagining a movement and physically executing it rely on partly separate neural pathways, actually moving the hand might produce different results than imagined estimates. In addition, whereas people in prior aperture studies typically overestimated the space their hidden hand needed, participants here underestimated their required opening in both conditions (ratios below 1.00), which the authors suggest may stem from participants watching their hand in the mirror during the stroking routine.
Because spatial judgments shifted even among volunteers who reported little or no sensation of an extra digit, the changes in action perception may reflect a broader effect of mapping touch onto nearby empty space rather than the specific mental image of a sixth finger. Future work will need to examine how this sensory remapping affects real-time physical movement and whether the findings generalize beyond healthy adults in laboratory settings. Even so, the results suggest that passive touch and vision alone can begin reshaping perceived hand capabilities in just 60 seconds, without requiring active movement or mechanical control.
“These findings can help design supernumerary robotics and prosthetics, in a way that updates their body perception but also their action perception,” Cadete added. “At the same time, this shows the flexibility of our mind in the way our bodies are perceived, allowing for additions and including them into a new and extended representation of the acting body.”
“I wish to understand the mechanisms for representing extra body parts and why they seem to have different constraints from real body parts,” she continued. “Ultimately, I want to explore why would humans have this ability, and extend this research into supernumerary robotics, so that they can be better integrated into one’s body representation, overcoming motor limitations due to injury or neurological disorders.”
The study, “Beyond Five: How the Experience of a Supernumerary Sixth Finger Alters Action Perception,” was authored by Denise Cadete, Harriet Morris, Megan Rose Readman, Sally A. Linkenauger, Elisa R. Ferrè, and Matthew R. Longo.

Tale of Brazil's Bolsonaros: Father jailed, mother in senate, sons in congress, third flees to US

23:00:32 KST

The patriarch is under house arrest, his wife is a senator, two sons are in Congress, and a third, who just lost the presidential race to Lula da Silva, started a self-imposed exile in the US.
As Brazil's preeminent new political dynasty, the Bolsonaros are serving up the kind of drama, infighting and ambition.
Many had written off Bolsonarism when former president Jair Bolsonaro was convicted of mounting a failed coup bid after he lost a 2022 election bid to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
But, family fortunes surged again as Flavio Bolsonaro briefly appeared a shoo-in to become president of Brazil, and four other family members were elected to Congress.
But then Flavio Bolsonaro lost in the second round and amid accusations of corruption and money laundering fled into self-imposed exile in the United States.
The patriarch and the coup
Jair Bolsonaro, 71, won a devoted following for his combative style and defense of "God, Homeland, and Family", while drawing criticism for comments demeaning women and others.
The former army officer is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for plotting ways to stop Lula from taking power in January 2023.
Flavio had vowed to free his father if he won, leaving the patriarch's future uncertain.
Flavio, the 'moderate' who fled
The eldest of Jair's five children, the 45-year-old fired up his father's conservative base and less ideological voters, pitching himself as more moderate than his father.
He won a first-round vote and was seen as the favorite ahead of the runoff, before being trounced by President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
Flavio Bolsonaro is being investigated in several cases, including for alleged corruption and money laundering linked to the financing of a biopic, "Dark Horse," about his father, bankrolled by Daniel Vorcaro.
Flavio at first denied having contact with Vorcaro, but was forced to backtrack after audio leaked of him imploring the banker to make overdue payments.
He arrived in Florida on Wednesday after avoiding Brazilian authorities who demanded his passports.
Michelle, the step-mother
Michelle Bolsonaro, 44, is around the same age as three of her stepsons.
A devout evangelical Christian and devoted wife, she has become a political powerhouse in her own right, and was elected senator representing the capital Brasilia.
During the campaign she aired a public feud with Flavio, accusing him of mistreating her.
In February, after another stepson, Eduardo Bolsonaro accused her of not doing enough to support Flavio's campaign, she shared a picture of fried bananas she was making for her husband.
This was perceived as a dig against Eduardo.
Eduardo then shared a supporter's post saying she should keep frying bananas while he and Flavio worked to "rescue the country."
Eduardo: guns and Trump
Eduardo, 42, moved to the United States in March 2025 where he has met with President Donald Trump and addressed conservative conferences in his push for US pressure on Brasilia.
He lost his lawmaker seat due to his long absence and was sentenced to four years and two months in prison in absentia in June, for his lobbying for US sanctions and tariffs against Brazil.
Seen as the most radical of the Bolsonaro sons, he has shared videos of rifles and guns he has bought, arguing for relaxed gun laws in Brazil.
Carlos, the strategist
Jair's second-eldest son Carlos, 43, entered into politics at age 17 after his father pushed him to run against his mother Rogeria on the Rio de Janeiro city council, a year after his parents divorced.
He won the seat, in an episode he described as "traumatic" and later became his father's social media strategist.
This year he was elected senator for the southern city of Santa Catarina.
His youngest brother, Jair Renan, 28, was elected a lawmaker for the same city.
Jair's brother, 62-year-old Renato Bolsonaro, a retired military officer was elected as a deputy for Sao Paulo state.

Thai central bank holds policy rate at 1 pct
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:58:27 CST
22:58:27 KST

BANGKOK, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's central bank kept its key interest rate unchanged for a fourth consecutive meeting on Wednesday as policymakers maintain an accommodative stance and targeted financial measures to support an uneven economic recovery.
The Bank of Thailand's monetary policy committee voted unanimously, with one member absent, to hold the one-day repurchase rate steady at 1 percent, marking its longest pause since the current easing cycle began in October 2024.
"The committee views that the current policy rate is appropriate to support economic recovery," the central bank said in a statement, adding that it would keep watching the inflation outlook and the effects of low interest rates on long-term macro-financial stability.
The bank now expects the Thai economy to grow 2.4 percent this year and 2.1 percent in 2027, up from June forecasts of 2.3 percent and 1.8 percent, citing stronger-than-expected merchandise exports and private investment tied to the global tech and artificial intelligence cycle.
However, growth remains below potential, and the gains are concentrated among businesses and workers in related manufacturing and service industries with limited spillovers to the broader economy, said Don Nakornthab, secretary of the monetary policy committee.
He said private consumption growth was cut to 2.3 percent for this year from 2.6 percent, as high household debt, a fragile labor market, and weak purchasing power weigh on spending.
The central bank also expects foreign tourist arrivals to slip to 32 million this year from 33 million in 2025, partly due to higher oil prices.
Headline inflation is forecast to average 2.1 percent in 2026, down from the 2.8 percent projected in June, and 1.3 percent in 2027, within the bank's 1 percent to 3 percent target range.
Inflation is projected to rise through the rest of this year and into early 2027, driven by energy prices and El Nino, before easing due to base effects and weak domestic demand, the bank said. ■

An aerial drone photo taken on Oct. 27, 2026 shows a night view of a smart greenhouse at an agricultural science and technology industrial park in Jindong District of Jinhua City, east China's Zhejiang Province. The agricultural science and technology industrial park was established in September 2023 as a designated benchmark project for modern agriculture in Jindong District of Jinhua City.
The park covers an area of 198.2 mu (about 13.2 hectares), including modern agricultural smart greenhouses, outdoor standardized planting areas, as well as supporting facilities such as water sources and parking lots. It aims to create an intelligent agricultural comprehensive industrial park integrating seedling research and development, ecological planting, deep processing, brand sales, tourism, and agricultural technology demonstration.
The park has introduced specialty fruit and vegetable varieties of pineapples, dragon fruits, and blueberries to build a demonstration model for high-end tropical fruit and vegetable planting. It has revitalized the idle land resources in the area, optimized the regional agricultural industrial structure. (Xinhua/Xu Yu)

Feature: South Sudanese farmers turn floodwater into rice harvests
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:58:06 CST
22:58:06 KST

JUBA, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- For years, seasonal flooding has threatened the livelihoods of farmers in South Sudan's Northern Bahr el Ghazal, destroying sorghum crops and undermining household food supplies.
But in Aweil, the capital of Northern Bahr el Ghazal, some farmers are learning to capitalize on the waterlogged land by cultivating rice.
Santino Akech, a 45-year-old farmer, said rice cultivation had offered his community an alternative to traditional crops that struggle to survive in flooded lowlands.
"When flooding came, it affected sorghum, but the rice succeeded," Akech said during a recent interview in Aweil.
Haileselassie Berhanu, head of program at the World Food Program (WFP) Aweil Field Office, said, "We have tried to consider the flood as a potential opportunity, not as a threat," explaining that the WFP and local communities began exploring rice cultivation in waterlogged areas several years ago.
This year, more than 2,100 households were participating in rice cultivation, with approximately 1,000 hectares under cultivation across the wider initiative, according to Berhanu.
Farmers previously cultivated individually but had limited capacity to expand production, said Akech. Through group farming, they pooled resources, expanded their cultivated land and received training in rice-growing techniques from a local partner. In 2025, Akech said that farmers harvested 42 bags of rice weighing 90 kg each from about 1.68 hectares of land.
However, he also identified weeding and harvesting as major challenges, noting that rice cultivation was still a relatively new practice for many community members. Farmers need machinery to prepare waterlogged land, training in improved cultivation methods and access to rice varieties suited to local conditions as well.
In a recent field trip to Aweil, Mutinta Chimuka, WFP country representative for South Sudan, said helping communities produce their own food was an important part of the agency's work to improve food security, alongside the distribution of food assistance.
She described the crop observed as promising, saying the location had retained water despite a dry spell that had affected agricultural production elsewhere.
The crop was flowering and expected to be ready for harvesting soon, Chimuka said.
Chimuka urged closer cooperation with state and national authorities to identify the most suitable locations for rice cultivation and varieties that could perform well under local conditions.
Chinese Ambassador to South Sudan Ma Qiang, who also joined the field visit, said the rice initiative demonstrated the potential to leverage natural conditions, strengthen agricultural production and improve resilience to climate-related shocks.
Ma said that China's experience and agricultural technologies could provide opportunities for further cooperation with South Sudan, including through engagement with national and local governments and other partners.
China has previously donated agricultural machinery to local communities, he added.
Martha Abuk, a 40-year-old farmer who also cultivates rice in Aweil, said that farming and participation in group savings activities had helped her household meet some of its needs, including school fees for the children.
As the WFP and its partners explore ways to expand rice cultivation, the experiences of farmers in Aweil illustrate both the opportunities and the constraints involved in adapting agriculture to climate-related challenges.
Sustaining that progress, however, will depend on farmers' access to suitable equipment, technical knowledge and resources to increase production. ■

KAMPALA, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Mbale City in eastern Uganda and Guiyang City in southwest China have signed a letter of intent to establish friendly exchange and cooperation relations, laying the groundwork for a future sister-city partnership, Uganda's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Wednesday.
The agreement, signed on Monday in Guiyang by Mbale City Mayor Joyce Matuka Kidulu and Wang Hong, mayor of Guiyang, outlines five priority areas for cooperation: smart city development and digital governance, industrial development and investment, agriculture and value addition, tourism and cultural exchange, and environmental sustainability, according to a ministry statement issued in Kampala.
The two cities agreed to establish a joint working group within two months and arrange a technical visit to Mbale to explore investment opportunities in industrial development, coffee processing and tourism, the statement said.
The proposed partnership aims to link Mbale's strengths in Arabica coffee production with Guiyang's expanding coffee industry and expertise in digital technology and green development.
Located near Mount Elgon in eastern Uganda, Mbale is a major coffee-producing area and an important industrial hub. Guiyang, the capital of China's Guizhou Province, has developed a strong presence in big data and digital industries.
The signing took place during a working visit to Guiyang by a Ugandan delegation, which also participated in a coffee trade promotion and business-matching session with the Guiyang Coffee Industry Association.
Uganda's coffee exports to China increased by 224 percent in the 2025/2026 financial year, the statement said, pointing to opportunities to expand market access and promote value addition through the cooperation framework. ■

The gendarmerie will continue operations to prevent drug production and trafficking, identify illegal cultivation sites and apprehend street-level drug dealers, the statement added. ■

MADRID, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- The World Health Organization (WHO) has postponed a high-level event scheduled for Wednesday as part of the 2026 Madrid Global Obesity Summit following a collision between two high-speed trains in central Spain that left dozens dead and many others injured.
The summit, co-hosted by the WHO and Spain's Ministry of Health, began on Monday and was due to conclude on Wednesday with a high-level session at the ministry's headquarters in Madrid.
Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia described the train collision, which occurred near Urda in the province of Toledo, about 120 km south of Madrid, as a "major tragedy" and called for blood donations to help those injured.
Garcia said the ministry was mobilizing all available resources in coordination with the relevant authorities to assist.
Pedro Gullon, director-general of Public Health at the Spanish Ministry of Health, announced the cancellation of Wednesday's event.
"We do not yet know the full extent of the accident, but it is undoubtedly a human tragedy," Gullon said, explaining that the Spanish government had suspended its official agenda for the day.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus expressed his deepest condolences to the victims and their families.
"Out of respect for the deceased, their families, and the government and people of Spain, we have decided to postpone today's event," Tedros said, adding that a new date would be announced in due course.
Meanwhile, the Royal Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) announced the postponement of all 24 Copa del Rey first-round matches scheduled for Wednesday as a mark of respect for the victims. ■

====================================================================================================

Why are three of the UK’s four nuclear deterrent submarines at sea?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:56:41 UTC
22:56:41 KST

Why are three of the UK’s four nuclear deterrent submarines at sea?
The deployment marks the first time in years that three Vanguard-class vessels have been at sea at the same time.
The United Kingdom has simultaneously deployed three of its four nuclear deterrent submarines at sea for the first time in five years, The Times reported on Wednesday.
At least one of the vessels – known as Vanguard-class submarines – was said to be armed with ballistic missiles which carry nuclear warheads.
The report named the three submarines at sea as HMS Vanguard, HMS Vigilant and HMS Vengeance, with the fourth, HMS Victorious, currently undergoing maintenance.
A navy source quoted by The Times described the deployment as “unusual”, without elaborating.
The UK continuously deploys at least one of the four submarines as a security guarantee.
The deployment has raised questions over whether the UK has changed its defence posture after Defence Secretary Wes Streeting warned last week that Britain should be prepared for war.
Here’s what we know:
Has this happened before?
The last time three submarines were at sea was more than five years ago, according to The Times.
Navy Lookout, the UK’s leading independent publication on the Royal Navy, says one submarine carrying ballistic missiles has been at sea without interruption since 1969.
It said the second vessel was believed to be preparing to relieve a patrol boat, while the third was likely conducting sea trials or work-up activity.
Last year HMS Vanguard patrolled the seas for 200 days, just a week shy of the longest known submarine deployment of 207 days, carried out by HMS Victorious in 2021.
What has the UK government said?
According to Sky News, a spokesperson for the defence ministry said the country’s nuclear deterrent is the “cornerstone of our national security, protecting the UK and our NATO allies every moment of every day”.
“We remain the only European ally to commit its nuclear deterrent to the defence of NATO. This means that all NATO allies already benefit from the protection of our nuclear deterrent,” the spokesperson added.
Last week, British and French fighter jets flew together in their first joint exercise involving France’s airborne nuclear capability.
The French armed forces ministry said British RAF Typhoon fighters escorted the French jets, simulating a nuclear strike.
France’s Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin said that having “independent nuclear forces does not preclude coordination”.
“Our nuclear cooperation with the United Kingdom continues to deepen,” she added.
The UK’s Streeting said that in an “increasingly dangerous world, our adversaries should be in no doubt”.
“The United Kingdom and France stand together in their commitment to European security and to maintaining the deterrence that has helped preserve peace for generations,” he added.
What are the UK’s ‘war readiness’ plans?
On Saturday, Streeting wrote in the Telegraph newspaper that Britain must be ready for war within 1,000 days.
“Our adversaries’ willingness to harm us is not new. What has changed is their capacity. By 2030, their force strength and war economy could put them in a position to attack,” Streeting wrote.
“That gives us a little over 1,000 days to complete our mission: to be ready with our allies to fight and win. This Government will make sure it is mission accomplished,” he said.
His message followed last week’s launch of the government’s “Be Ready” campaign, which called on households to store three days’ supply of tinned food and water bottles, cash and a wind-up radio in case of a cyberattack or a weather event which disrupts infrastructure.
The warning also followed reports that Russia has been using fishing trawlers to track and spy on the UK’s undersea cables.

Finland buys German RGW110 anti-tank weapon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:47:07 UTC
22:47:07 KST

- Finland will buy the RGW110 heavy disposable anti-tank weapon from Dynamit Nobel Defence for about $94 million, excluding value-added tax.
- The weapon will replace the APILAS launcher bought in the 1980s, with deliveries and training starting in 2027.
Finland will buy the RGW110 heavy disposable anti-tank weapon from Germany’s Dynamit Nobel Defence to replace the APILAS launcher its soldiers have carried since the 1980s, the Finnish Army said on Oct. 28.
The purchase is worth about €84.5 million (about $94 million) excluding value-added tax, and deliveries of the weapons, training equipment and instruction will begin in 2027, Finland’s government said after Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen authorized the deal. The Finnish Defence Forces did not say how many launchers it is ordering.
“The main battle tank will remain a threat on the battlefield in the future as well. The new disposable launcher system is intended for destroying tanks at close range and will replace the APILAS system acquired in the 1980s as the troops’ heavy close-range anti-tank weapon,” said Col. Ari Mure, inspector of infantry at Finnish Army Command.
The RGW110 is a shoulder-fired, single-use weapon that a soldier fires once and throws away, so units can carry it like ammunition and spread it across many fighting positions without the support crews that guided missile systems need. The Finnish Army said this lets several soldiers fire at the same tank from different positions at once, while keeping the logistics burden and the load on each soldier lighter. The rocket is unguided, so it cannot be jammed, and the army said it works in any light or weather, from towns to forest and in both attack and defense.
The trade-off is range. The army acknowledged that the unguided round has a relatively short reach, but said Finland’s broken, heavily wooded terrain makes up for it by letting soldiers get close to enemy armor unseen. Dynamit Nobel Defence lists an effective range of up to 800 m (2,600 feet), roughly twice that of the Panzerfaust 3 it was designed to succeed, European Security & Defence reported.
Penetration drove the choice. The Finnish Army said a modern anti-tank weapon must first clear a tank’s explosive reactive armor, the boxes of explosive bolted to the outside of the hull to disrupt incoming warheads, and then carry a large enough caliber to punch through the main armor behind it. The RGW110 uses a 110 mm tandem warhead, in which a small lead charge sets off the reactive armor before the main charge strikes, and its maker says it can penetrate about 1,000 mm of armor steel behind reactive armor. Finland compared the systems on the market, tested the one that met its criteria against a target with realistic armor protection, and then worked with the manufacturer to further improve the warhead. The army said observations from the war in Ukraine confirmed its earlier assessments of how well an adversary’s tanks are protected.
The RGW110 is the larger, 110 mm member of Dynamit Nobel Defence’s RGW family, whose 90 mm RGW90, known as MATADOR, has been used in combat in Ukraine since Germany cleared exports and Ukraine received more of the German-made anti-armor weapons from the company’s stocks in 2022. Hungary became the first customer for the RGW110 in 2022 and has set up a joint venture with Dynamit Nobel Defence to build parts of the weapon locally, while the warheads are still made at the company’s plant in Burbach, Germany.
Hungary became the RGW110’s first customer in 2022 and has set up a joint venture with Dynamit Nobel Defence to build parts of the weapon locally, while the warheads are still made at the company’s plant in Burbach, Germany.

Supreme Court says legality of EC's 'logical discrepancy' checks in SIR remains undecided
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:47:04 UTC
22:47:04 KST

The clarification came during a hearing on a petition alleging a lack of transparency in notices.
The Supreme Court on Wednesday clarified that it has not yet delivered a final ruling on the Election Commission of India’s (ECI) use of the “logical discrepancy” category to flag voters’ details during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said its earlier decision allowing the Election Commission to use the category in West Bengal was only an interim measure. It also clarified that the court’s ruling on the SIR exercise in Bihar had not settled every legal question surrounding the revision process.The clarification came during a hearing on a petition alleging a lack of transparency in notices issued to voters during the ongoing SIR exercise in Delhi. Senior advocate D S Naidu, appearing for the Election Commission, had argued that the court had examined all stages of the SIR process and upheld its validity.Justice Bagchi rejected the suggestion that the earlier proceedings had conclusively settled the legality of the logical discrepancy category.“Bihar is not a final determination of every question arising in these proceedings. In Bihar, the Election Commission had not initially undertaken logical discrepancy as a category.
We permitted it as an interim arrangement in West Bengal. We have not finally adjudicated upon the legality of the logical discrepancy exercise,” Justice Bagchi was quoted as saying by the news agency PTI.The judge also cautioned against treating oral observations made during hearings as final judicial decisions, particularly in sensitive cases.
"We do not wish to make further comments because observations in sensitive matters are sometimes taken out of context. These observations are not conclusive. There is a difficulty when judicial observations are repeatedly cited out of context as if every issue has already been decided," he said.
What is the ‘logical discrepancy’ category
During the SIR exercise, the Election Commission uses the “logical discrepancy” category to flag inconsistencies in voters’ records. These discrepancies are identified through ERONet, the poll panel’s centralised technology platform, which uses automated checks to examine electoral data.Such flags can arise when information in a voter’s profile or details linking family members appear inconsistent with mathematical, biological or clerical records. The category is intended to identify entries that require scrutiny.

MILAN, Oct 28 - An Italian judge has ordered the release of a university researcher accused by police of helping orchestrate violent protests this month, infuriating Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who denounced the decision as "shameful".
Youssef Siher, a 30-year-old Italian freelance journalist and geopolitics graduate of Moroccan origin, was detained by Milan prosecutors on October 24 on charges of incitement to commit crimes, aggravated by alleged terrorist purposes.
But in a sharp rebuke to prosecutors who had portrayed him as a dangerous militant, Milan judge Tiziana Landoni said the investigation appeared deeply flawed.
"There are no serious grounds for believing that (Siher) committed the offences with which he has been charged, nor is there a risk of flight," Landoni wrote in her ruling.
Siher himself always denied any wrongdoing. Prosecutors did not immediately comment, but Meloni was swift to denounce the decision.
"I think this is an unbearable humiliation of the work of the police and investigators," she said in a video posted on social media.
"I really don't know how a normal state can defend decent people in the face of these decisions by certain sections of the judiciary," she added.
Italian police had identified Siher as the administrator of the Telegram group "October 17 Movement", which was created following violent protests in Milan.
According to the detention order, Siher published what investigators described as "subversive content" and messages calling on protesters to gather on October 24 with the aim of carrying out offences against public order.
However, Landoni said such comments were posted by other group members, not Siher himself. "Siher was not found to have encouraged or in any way supported the violent actions advocated by those users," she wrote.
The case is notable because prosecutors cited a new offence introduced under a security decree enacted by Meloni's government this month as part of its latest law-and-order crackdown.
The newly defined crime carries prison terms of between four and 12 years for organisers of groups that, while taking part in public demonstrations, endanger public safety or cause damage.
Siher's arrest has sparked concern among legal observers and members of the Italian Bar Association.
Critics also questioned the extensive media coverage of the case, with some Italian newspapers portraying him as guilty and revealing detailed descriptions of his life and family. REUTERS

Kyrgyzstan Temporarily Bans Imports of Apples (and More)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:41:00 UTC
22:41:00 KST

In early October, Kyrgyzstan’s Cabinet of Ministers proposed imposing a temporary ban on the import of apples into the country until February 2027. The proposal was up for public discussion until October 23, with the European Union weighing in against the measure. On October 27 local media reported that Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers Adylbek Kasymaliev had signed the resolution.
Kyrgyzstan’s Cabinet of Ministers explained the temporary import ban as necessary to support the country’s agricultural sector and ensure the “timely sale of the 2026 apple harvest.”
Kyrgyzstan has more than 26,000 hectares of apple orchards, and expects a harvest of more than 179,000 tons this year. In justifying the temporary ban, the Cabinet of Ministers pointed to growing imports of foreign apples and declining exports of Kyrgyz apples.
In 2024, the Cabinet stated, apple imports totaled more than 14,000 tons; in 2025 they amounted to just over 2,900 tons. But in the first eight months of 2026, from January to August, Kyrgyzstan had imported nearly 6,500 tons of apples, more than twice the 2025 total. These apples originated mostly in Poland (3,554 tons), China (1,696 tons), and Uzbekistan (860 tons).
At the same time, Kyrgyz apple exports were down 13 percent in the first eight months of 2026, over the 2025 data. “The decline in export shipments increases the importance of the domestic market for the sale of apples grown within the country,” the Cabinet argued in its justification for the resolution. “An influx of imported apples during the season when domestic supply is at its peak can intensify competition within the domestic market.”
The European Union submitted a comment on the resolution, expressing “serious concerns” regarding the proposed ban. “It is all the more concerning that the import ban appears to be intended as a measure to support the domestic producers during the harvest, whereas under World Trade Organization (WTO) rules such measures are to be invoked only in exceptional circumstances and subject to very strict criteria.”
Kyrgyzstan has been a member of the WTO since December 1998. It was the first Central Asian country to join, followed by Tajikistan in 2013 and Kazakhstan in 2015. Uzbekistan started down the WTO path in 1994 but dithered for decades before resuming talks in 2020. Last year Uzbek officials laid out 2026 as the target to finally accede, but a March 2026 goal post passed quietly by. Uzbek officials reaffirmed their goal to accede in 2026 during a Working Party meeting in July.
In its comment on the then-draft Kyrgyz resolution, the EU argued that “the sudden introduction of import restrictions would send a negative signal not only to EU apple exporters, but to all EU traders potentially interested in the market of the Kyrgyz Republic.”
The EU noted that it is among Kyrgyzstan’s largest trade and investment partners, “with our Partnership and Cooperation Agreement (PCA) underpinning this relationship.” The PCA, the EU comment continued, “provides that goods originating in the EU shall be imported into the Kyrgyz Republic free of all quantitative restrictions…”
While apples hold special significant in Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan – the name of Kazakhstan’s largest city, Almaty, comes from the Kazakh word for apple, алма – it’s not just apples Bishkek is worried about. On October 16, First Deputy Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers Daniyar Amangeldiev signed a resolution banning the import of potatoes for six months.
It’s not clear whether the EU will take its complaints to the WTO, though that threat certainly is conveyed by its comments on the apple ban.

Nshimiye, 54, is scheduled to be sentenced on January 26, according to a spokesperson for US Attorney Leah Foley, whose office prosecuted the case.
"We are obviously very disappointed with the verdict, but we will continue to pursue all avenues of relief on Eric's behalf," Kurt Kerns, Nshimiye's lawyer, said in a statement.
Nshimiye has lived in the United States since 1995, when he gained admission as a refugee. He became a US citizen in 2003. At the time of his arrest in 2024, he was working as an engineer for Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co while living in Uniontown, Ohio.
Prosecutors said Nshimiye falsified and concealed information about himself to hide that he participated in the massacre by the hard-line Hutu regime of an estimated 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and moderate Hutus during three months of slaughter in his native Rwanda.
Citing witnesses, prosecutors alleged that when the violence broke out, Nshimiye was in Butare, where he had been attending university as a medical student along with his classmate Jean Leonard Teganya.
Prosecutors said both men belonged to the political party that helped perpetrate the genocide, and that Nshimiye during the violence attacked Tutsis and handed Tutsis over to be raped or killed.
Yet when called as a defense witness in Teganya's 2019 trial, Nshimiye denied participating in the genocide or being a member of the ruling Hutu-dominated party, the National Revolutionary Movement for Development.
Teganya was convicted of perjury and visa fraud charges and was sentenced later in 2019 to more than eight years in prison.
Kerns, Nshimiye's lawyer, told jurors in his opening statement on October 13 that the charges against Nshimiye were based on "fabricated accusations" and that he was not even in Butare when the violence began. Kerns argued that prosecutors charged Nshimiye only after he stepped up to help a friend by testifying as a character witness in Teganya's case. REUTERS

Why Are Russia and China Cooperating on ‘Patriotic Education’?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:40:00 UTC
22:40:00 KST

On October 21, China’s Premier Li Qiang traveled from Beijing to St. Petersburg to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin. The Li-Mishustin summit – the 31st such encounter between the Chinese and Russian heads of government – culminated in a long communiqué outlining a great number of collaborative initiatives in areas ranging from artificial intelligence to space exploration and nuclear energy.
Nestled among these, a commitment to “enhancing patriotic education for youth” toward the end of the communiqué could easily be overlooked. But this item deserves greater scrutiny. Often portrayed as simply a matter of convenience or unsentimental realpolitik, China and Russia’s collaboration on patriotic education helps to reveal how the two countries’ “no limits” friendship is, in reality, rooted in a shared obsession with revenging national humiliation and “Western influence.”
The term “patriotic education” is used broadly across the post-Communist world, from Belarus to Vietnam, part of an inherited Leninist approach to “thought work” and propaganda. In all cases, it refers to top-down efforts to suppress criticism and promote loyalty to the state throughout the education system, drilling school children in correct “moral-ideological” standpoints. In many cases, the rollout of “patriotic education” measures is a direct response to a moment of political crisis. In Belarus, for example, a new patriotic education program was approved by the Council of Ministers as a response to the 2020 anti-government protest movement.
China is the archetype of this trend. The term “patriotic education” was first discussed by China’s leadership in June 1989, a mere two weeks after the massacre of student protesters in Tiananmen Square. Facing a serious legitimacy crisis, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) assumed the garb of patriotism to deflect overseas criticism. As part of the new “patriotic education campaign” rolled out across Chinese schools, students were exhorted to be loyal to the state and to distrust Western influences, with a dire reminder of Europe’s colonial exploitation of China during the 19th century. Schools held flag-raising ceremonies, instructed students in a new “patriotic” curriculum, and organized visits to historic sites, such as the remains of the Summer Palace razed by British and French forces in 1860. A new generation of Chinese students would be sternly exhorted, at every step, biewang guochi: “never forget national humiliation.” It worked: the Tiananmen crisis abated and the CCP recast itself as the righters of historical wrongs suffered by China.
Both Putin and Xi Jinping appear to have taken this lesson to heart. In 2001, with Russia still reeling from the disintegration of the USSR, Putin – then newly-elected president – unveiled a new five-year plan for “the Patriotic Education of the Citizens of the Russian Federation.” Originally, Russian patriotic education stressed national pride in Russian culture and history, as well as instructing students in conservative moral teachings. However, successive iterations of patriotic education became more explicitly militaristic and resentful of foreign influence, particularly after Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014. Patriotic education became a crucial medium through which to promulgate an image of Russia locked in an existential struggle against external threats, and to valorize military service for the glory of Russia.
Under Xi’s rule, meanwhile, the Chinese state has elevated the patriotic education campaign into a whole-of-society effort to enforce ideological compliance with the CCP and combat “historical nihilism,” the party’s preferred term for public criticism of its record or skepticism about official historical narratives.
This effort culminated in the 2023 Patriotic Education Law, which created a legal obligation for a wide range of institutions, not just schools and universities, to inculcate loyalty to the nation and the CCP. Professionals and organisations are expected to demonstrate “patriotic feelings and behavior that bring glory to the country.” The message – to be repeated continuously across Chinese society – is that under Xi, China has now overcome its historic humiliations and resumed its proper role as the regional superpower.
Why the intensifying need for patriotic feelings among Chinese youth? China has keenly followed the developments of Russia’s patriotic education system, noting its success in cultivating nationalist feeling amongst Russia’s youth – and its role in boosting support for Putin’s military operations via military ceremonies and training sessions in Russian schools. Concerningly, patriotic education in China similarly appears to lay the groundwork for promoting the annexation of Taiwan, the self-governing island that the CCP claims as its territory.
The Patriotic Education Law, which speaks of “the sacred duty to complete the great undertaking of uniting the motherland,” is explicitly aimed at increasing popular support for the forcible unification of Taiwan and China, including via covert influence operations in Taiwan itself. When CCP apparatchiks claim that the goal of patriotic education is to “gather the strength of the people for the great cause of building a strong country and national rejuvenation,” this is party-speak for Taiwanese unification, peaceful or otherwise.
“Patriotism is the last refuge of a scoundrel,” observed Samuel Johnson, famously, in 1775. Just over 250 years later, having staked their legacies on grand promises of expanded territory and renewed national pride, Putin and Xi alike find themselves under pressure to deliver or be exposed as weak and illegitimate in the eyes of the public. A commitment to boost cooperation on patriotic education suggests that these leaders are doubling down on a shared narrative of existential struggle against “the West.” The implications for the inhabitants of Eastern Europe and Taiwan, and for all of us, are sobering indeed.

Japanese football association vice president resigns over actions surrounding FIFA World Cup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28

Saadet Gökce
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Japan Football Association Vice President Takeshi Okada resigned Wednesday, citing a "significant gap" between his principles and how the organization is handling issues surrounding the upcoming FIFA World Cup.
"Throughout my career, I have valued the social significance of sports guided by my conviction that sports must be conducted with integrity," he said in a statement. "However, the series of responses to the issues surrounding the upcoming FIFA World Cup has revealed a significant gap between those responses and my own convictions. As a sportsman, I cannot accept them.”
The resignation comes one week after Asian Football Confederation (AFC) President Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa pledged the AFC’s support for Gianni Infantino’s bid for another term as FIFA president.
Okada said he understood that aligning with the AFC was a practical option, given Japan's relationship with the body and the potential effect on Japanese soccer.
Infantino faced mounting calls to stand down two months ago following the controversy surrounding the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal.
The proposal would have involved transferring a portion of FIFA's commercial rights to a private investment firm through a new commercial entity, including rights linked to FIFA competitions such as the World Cup.
It was abandoned within days of details emerging, prompting criticism from several confederation presidents and major European leagues.
Infantino has led FIFA since 2016 and is seeking another term in the March 2027 election.

Pakistan restored overflight rights to Taiwanese airlines after banning them from using its airspace in line with its One-China policy, local newspaper Dawn has reported.
The Pakistan Civil Aviation Authority authorised China Airlines Ltd. and EVA Airways Corp. to use the country's airspace from Oct. 28 to March 27, 2027, according to documents seen by Dawn on Wednesday.
Bloomberg earlier reported that Pakistani Defence Minister Khawaja Asif told Bloomberg News that aviation authorities had followed "the One China policy — only mainland China is allowed."
He had said that Islamabad only allowed airlines from the People’s Republic of China to fly over Pakistan, excluding Taiwan.
Taiwanese carriers reroute flights
According to flight-tracking data, Taiwanese carriers began rerouting flights over the weekend, with China Airlines Ltd. and EVA Airways Corp. no longer flying over Pakistan since Sunday.
The two carriers declined to comment to Bloomberg, while Taiwan’s Civil Aviation Administration did not address the rerouting.
Islamabad's restrictions were even stricter than those imposed by China, which allows Taiwanese airlines to fly over its territory.
Beijing considers Taiwan a breakaway province, while Taipei insists on its independence.
Pakistan severed official relations with Taiwan in 1951 in support of the One-China policy.
Islamabad and Beijing have bolstered ties under Beijing's ambitious Belt and Road Initiative, through the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, which has channelled billions of dollars into Pakistan.
China is also Pakistan’s largest supplier of weapons and launched the China-Pakistan Information Corridor on Tuesday.

Earlier mediation efforts helped produce an interim peace agreement in June, but the deal quickly unravelled.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Hsinchu Mayor Kao Hung-an (高虹安), who is seeking reelection, signed a pledge addressing eight education policy demands at a forum on Wednesday.
The forum was jointly organized by Hsinchu City Teachers Association and Hsinchu City Teachers’ Union, with representatives of teachers’ and parents’ groups invited to discuss education policy, per CNA.
The eight demands cover smaller classes and adequate staffing, lighter administrative workloads, special education, school safety, teachers’ professional dignity, a friendly school environment, teachers' well-being and labor rights, and stable education funding.
The mayor said the city’s education budget had risen from NT$9.67 billion (US$298.33 million) in 2023 to NT$14.1 billion this year, and is projected to reach NT$15.68 billion in 2027, per UDN. She said the city plans to spend NT$60 billion on education over the next four years, with annual spending of at least NT$15 billion.
The city had introduced full-academic-year contracts for substitute teachers and invested nearly NT$60 million in salary improvements, Kao explained. Previous work experience now counts toward salary placement, allowing eligible teachers to advance on the seniority-based pay scale.
The city will allocate NT$24 million in the 2026-27 school year to hire 30 additional elementary school substitute teachers, according to Kao. It also plans to reduce elementary school class sizes in three phases, targeting 28 students per class by 2028-29, and cut weekly teaching loads for junior high school teachers in certain subjects from 20 to 18 periods.

Turkey warns against further attacks by Russia, Ukraine on Black Sea vessels

Turkey warns against further attacks by Russia, Ukraine on Black Sea vessels
ANKARA, Oct 28 - Turkish Defence Minister Yasar Guler on Wednesday warned Russia and Ukraine against further attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea, saying Ankara reserved the right to take legal action against the strikes, in Turkey's most direct intervention to date.
NATO member Turkey, which has maintained good ties with both Moscow and Kyiv since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, has repeatedly called on both sides to halt attacks in the Black Sea that have also struck Turkish-flagged and Turkish-owned commercial vessels.
Ankara says it is waiting for responses to a proposal it conveyed to Russia and Ukraine aimed at stopping the intensifying attacks and ensuring the safe shipment of grain from the region.
Speaking in Sofia after a security meeting between defence ministers and military chiefs of Black Sea littoral states Turkey, Romania and Bulgaria, Guler said commercial vessels sailing and operating in the Black Sea had been affected by drone attacks, stray mines and missiles during the conflict.
"We follow with concern the intense attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea and call on the sides to act with common sense, in line with the principle of navigational safety in open seas," he said, adding that another commercial vessel had been struck by three drones inside Bulgaria's maritime jurisdiction on Wednesday.
It was not clear who carried out the attack on a Greek container ship that was sailing under the Liberian flag in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
"We also reserve every legal right regarding attacks on Turkish-flagged or Turkish-owned vessels and follow developments very closely... The necessary warnings are constantly being conveyed to both sides to keep commercial navigational out of the conflict zone and immediately halt attacks on civilian vessels," Guler added.
Ukraine has stepped up attacks on ships and infrastructure facilitating Russian oil and grain exports since July, when Russia intensified its missile and drone strikes on the main Ukrainian grain export hubs of Odesa, Chornomorsk and Pivdennyi.
In a late September meeting, Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan told Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskiy that attacks by Russia and Ukraine on commercial vessels in the Black Sea were inexplicable and steps must be taken to stop them.
Guler also said Turkey, Romania and Bulgaria — which operate a de-mining operation in the Black Sea — agreed it was important to also focus on protecting critical subsea infrastructure. REUTERS

UK defence spending target of 3 percent by 2030
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:31:23 GMT
22:31:23 KST

The Chancellor has set a target date of 2030 for defence spending to reach three per cent of gross domestic product, and will set out at next year’s spending review how Britain meets its NATO commitment of three and a half per cent by 2035, according to the Budget statement.
John Healey, who held the defence portfolio before moving to the Treasury, told the Commons: “At the spending review next year, I confirm that I will set out the details of how we will meet our NATO commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, with a target date for 3% in 2030.”
On how it will be paid for, he said: “Today, I am getting work underway to get there in a fiscally sustainable way, that will include looking hard at public spending, as I have done today, to fund the defence investment plan. But I am also determined to use more innovative financing alongside the private sector and our international allies.”
A new innovative defence finance task force will lead the work ahead of the spending review, the first of four measures announced. Treaty negotiations will begin on a multilateral defence mechanism, which Healey also called a bank, with Finland, Poland and the Netherlands, intended to boost defence investment and joint procurement across NATO allies. The government will seek the maximum private investment into the defence industrial base, including through public-private partnerships. And the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank will launch a new focus on defence, dual-use technology and sovereign capability, deploying up to £5 billion of investment and lending over the next four years.
Healey said: “I will ensure this record defence investment works twice: once for our national security, and once for British jobs and British business. Places across all four nations: Barrow, Rosyth, Aldershot, Plymouth, Glascoed, and Belfast, reindustrialised and transformed.”
On Ukraine, the Chancellor said he and the Prime Minister had called President Zelensky that morning to tell him what the Budget contained, and that the response was “you’ve made my day”. The package is £10 billion of additional economic and military support based on loans and export finance guarantees, together with urgent military funding for this winter.
Healey said: “The whole house, the whole country, is united for Ukraine, and today we send a clear message to Moscow: Britain will stand with Ukraine for as long as it takes.”
The Chancellor made the case personally, drawing on his own family: “I say this as Chancellor. I say this as former Defence Secretary. And I say this as a dad whose son is an army reservist, a reservist that came back four years ago from early training to say they had no kit and they had no bullets to fire. That’s the truth.”
He said that for fourteen years Conservative governments had hollowed out and underfunded the armed forces, and that the defence budget this year is £14 billion higher than in the final year of the last government, which he described as the biggest increase in defence spending since the end of the Cold War.
Britain signed up at the NATO summit in The Hague to three and a half per cent of gross domestic product on core defence by 2035, with a further one and a half per cent on defence-related resilience and infrastructure making up the alliance’s headline five per cent. Ministers had previously described three per cent as an ambition for the next Parliament, and attaching a target date of 2030 to it is firmer than the language used before.
Industry witnesses told the Defence Committee this month that the Defence Investment Plan is not investable as it stands, that most defence technology firms report a declining market, and that the department’s small business office has four staff. The finance task force and the £5 billion through the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank are the Treasury’s answer to that.

MOD appoints its first Director General Innovation
The UK’s commitment to be a leader in innovative defence technologies will be strengthened as Anthony Reeves takes up DG Innovation role.
- Anthony Reeves appointed as the first Director General Innovation, bringing extensive military, government and industry experience.
- Role oversees 4,800 innovation experts and scientists and a £3.7 billion science, technology and innovation budget over the next four years to ensure the UK remains at the cutting edge of warfighting.
- National Armaments Innovation harnesses UK ingenuity and boosts military technology, as part of a drive to turbocharge innovation.
After an external competition, Anthony will become the newest 3* senior civil servant within National Armaments, part of the organisation’s Executive Committee, and the Ministry of Defence’s first Director General (DG) Innovation.
Taking up the role this Autumn, Anthony will lead the newly designed National Armaments Innovation area, which includes some 4,800 experts and scientists working in the Defence Investment Unit (DIU), the Defence Science & Technology Laboratory (Dstl), the Defence Uncrewed Systems Centre (DUSC) and UK Defence Innovation (UKDI).
Anthony will oversee a ringfenced £1.6 billion defence innovation budget over the next four years, as well as supporting £2.1 billion investment in core science and technology.
He will play a pivotal role in accelerating the adoption of cutting-edge technologies, fostering collaboration with industry, academia and government departments, and embedding innovation as a core military capability.
Rupert Pearce, the National Armaments Director, said:
  Anthony’s appointment marks a gear shift for UK Defence as we place innovation at the heart of the way we maintain war-fighting readiness, become an engine for economic growth and learn from the lessons of Ukraine to deter our adversaries.
As a leader, Tony brings a rare combination of frontline military experience, deep technical expertise and a proven track record of delivering transformation across Defence, government and industry.
His leadership will be instrumental as we strengthen Defence’s innovation ecosystem, accelerate the adoption of emerging technologies and deliver the capabilities our Armed Forces need, now and in the future.
Anthony joins National Armaments from Deloitte, where he led the UK and NATO Digital Defence section and was National Armaments Practice Head and Global AI Leader for Defence and Security.
He has worked extensively across UK Defence, NATO, AUKUS partners and defence industry organisations and his experience spans operational military service, national security, emerging technologies, AI and large-scale transformation programmes.
Commenting on his appointment, Tony said:
  Innovation in Defence must be about mindset before toolset. I look forward to working with brilliant colleagues across Defence, industry, academia and our international partners to make innovation everyone’s business, bring new technologies into military service at pace, and deliver tangible growth for the UK.
Under Anthony’s leadership, National Armaments Innovation will identify, mature and exploit emerging capabilities, strengthen collaboration with industry, academia and allies, and help ensure the Armed Forces can access the technologies and capabilities needed to maintain operational advantage.
Anthony’s earlier career included responsibility for delivering critical communications, networks and information capabilities for military operations and specialist users, alongside operational deployments as an infantry officer in the British Army, which included Northern Ireland, Bosnia, Kosovo and Sierra Leone.
Before joining Deloitte in 2020, Anthony advised defence organisations on digital transformation and technology adoption at Microsoft, and led major defence and national security programmes within PA Consulting and Detica.
He is a regular speaker on defence innovation, digital transformation and artificial intelligence, and serves as a Board member of the AI Institute UK, and mentor to future leaders through King’s College London and the Common Mission Project.

Construction of a new radar facility in Kaliningrad has been under way for some time and forms part of wider Russian investment in military capability that Britain and NATO allies are monitoring, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Gregory Campbell, the Democratic Unionist Party member for East Londonderry, asked whether the government would raise the construction of the radar at Gvardeysk, close to the Polish border, with NATO partners.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The Government remains in close consultation with NATO Allies on developments that may affect the security environment in the Euro-Atlantic area, including monitoring and assessing Russia’s investment in its military capabilities.
“Construction of the radar facility in Kaliningrad has been underway for some time and forms part of this wider investment. The UK and NATO Allies routinely monitor relevant Russian military developments and share information and assessments where appropriate.
“NATO continues to maintain an effective deterrence and defence posture, including on its Eastern Flank.”
Gvardeysk lies around thirty miles east of Kaliningrad city and has hosted Russian early warning radar infrastructure for years, including a Voronezh-DM site that watches across central and western Europe. The exclave has no land connection to the rest of Russia, hosts the headquarters of the Baltic Fleet at Baltiysk, and carries air defence and missile systems whose reach extends well into allied airspace.
Kaliningrad borders Poland to the south and Lithuania to the north and east, and the stretch of frontier between them, the Suwalki gap, is the only land route between the Baltic states and the rest of the alliance.

European parcel tax: Millions in revenue and far fewer cheap parcels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:27:01 UTC
22:27:01 KST

Over the past three months, 65 per cent fewer cheap parcels from countries including China have been declared than in the same period last year, according to Belgian customs authorities. This sharp decline is entirely due to the introduction of the European parcel tax of 3 euros per item. Moreover, in just a few months, the tax has generated tens of millions of euros.
European parcel tax: Millions in revenue and far fewer cheap parcels
The European Union – including Belgium – has for years been grappling with the massive influx of cheap parcels, the vast majority of which come from China. Think of the Sheins, Temus and AliExpresses of this world. Last year, 1.3 billion such parcels arrived via Liège Airport (Belgium).
It is not uncommon for these to contain counterfeit goods or products that do not meet European safety standards, but the customs service simply cannot manage to check them all.
More revenue
To bring this under better control, the EU introduced a temporary parcel tax of 3 euros per item from 1 July this year. This applies to parcels worth less than 150 euros that do not originate from the EU. On top of that, from 1 November – this coming Sunday – a fixed European handling fee of 2 euros per item will also apply.
The parcel tax is already proving to be a great success, as customs figures show. In total, it has raised 364 million euros in European taxes since July – or around 28 million euros per week. Belgium is entitled to keep a quarter of that sum.
Kristian Vanderwaeren from the Belgian customs service does, however, warn of an increase in attempts at fraud. “For example, people are now trying to declare the value of parcels as over 150 euros in order to pay less tax. Sometimes they also declare fewer items than are actually in the parcel, just to pay the parcel tax only once. But my team is working on ways to detect this.”
The business organisation Unizo is pleased with the results. “This is a victory for us, but above all for our businesses and the economy, as the measures are clearly delivering results,” says CEO Bart Buysse.
He believes the government should reinvest the millions generated by the tax. “For us, it is essential that this revenue is actually invested in additional customs officers, better technology and stricter checks. Because as long as foreign online shops can sell products that aren’t even allowed on shop shelves here, competition remains unfair.”
And the government must go even further, Buysse adds. “We must also close the loopholes. Anyone who repeatedly sells unsafe products must be dealt with much more strictly. And if a single dangerous product is found during an inspection, the rest of the consignment must not simply be allowed to pass through unchecked.”

Blind Ukrainian man faced conscription – court papers

Blind Ukrainian man faced conscription – court papers
A blind Ukrainian man was allegedly held for days at a conscription center despite being clearly unfit for military service, according to court papers.
The case, reported by Ukrainian media on Wednesday, stems from a complaint filed by the unidentified man with a district court in Odessa seeking an official investigation. A judge ruled in his favor last week, ordering the authorities to look into the allegations, a decision that was made public shortly afterward.
According to the complaint, the man has been visually impaired since childhood and was exempted from military service as early as 1994, with his status reaffirmed in 2020 and 2023. Despite this, he says draft officials refused to recognize his condition and held him for almost five days.
He was allegedly seized on a street in Odessa in March, held incommunicado without being formally booked, and released only after intervention by his lawyer.
The regional branch of the State Bureau of Investigation, which had earlier refused to register his complaint, was ordered by the court to reverse that decision. The man had separately secured a court ruling ordering his removal from a list of people wanted for draft evasion.
Kiev relies on compulsory mobilization of fighting-age men to sustain its war effort against Russia, but the campaign has been marred by widespread corruption among draft officials and public perceptions that the system is deeply unfair. The government has responded to draft evasion with heavy-handed enforcement that has repeatedly involved the illegal use of force by military officials.
Illegal detention at recruitment centers has become a recurring problem, according to the office of Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmitry Lubinets.
In one high-profile case reported by Lubinets in June, 21 men were found to have been illegally held in poor conditions at a conscription center in Uzhgorod, some for more than 50 days.
In another case, the three-day detention of 39-year-old Aleksey Ivanko at a Kharkov recruitment center in May 2025 ended with him jumping from a third-floor window to his death. Lubinets said in his annual report that his office found no evidence Ivanko had been physically abused by draft officials, but concluded there had been no legal grounds to restrict his freedom and that the prolonged confinement had contributed to the circumstances of his death.
