====================================================================================================

Toward a New ‘Normal’: The Recalibration of the Japan-US Alliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:36:00 UTC
21:36:00 KST

The United States has never been a “normal country” – although it is difficult to find or define what that actually means – and has always, since its founding, been proud of its “exceptionalism.” The righteousness that has been one of the driving motivators of the republic has led it to take a moral stance on issues that are not directly related to its own material needs and to fight for values and principles rather than focusing purely on the defense of the homeland. However, if this way of behavioral instincts were to face a reckoning, the year 1991 provided the right opportunity to change course.
The Soviet Union, once an “evil empire,” and by then far less menacing, was gone, ending a half-century standoff between the two superpowers that had faced each other at the brink of nuclear Armageddon. The successful campaign and diplomatic coordination that defeated Iraqi aggression against Kuwait revived hopes for international governance and for multilateralism as a means of maintaining peace. The U.S. role of global policeman – a role Washington had concluded it needed to fill after Pearl Harbor in order to deter threats before they reached its shores – now seemed unnecessary, with the monsters abroad gone.
While triumphalism had taken hold in the United States, and Europe was still buoyed by German unification and held high hopes for the regional integration that proceeded during the decade, for Japan the 1990s were a different story. Many Americans saw Japan as the real victor of the Cold War and a graver threat than the Soviets had ever been. Among Japanese, there was dread, disappointment, and disbelief that the country’s cherished pacifism went unrecognized – and so did its contribution to the Gulf War.
Japan had sent no troops but had given billions of dollars, including funds for humanitarian purposes. Yet many dismissed Japan’s contributions entirely – including the Kuwaiti government, which omitted Japan from a newspaper advertisement thanking the countries that had sent troops to liberate it. Economic prowess was one of Japan’s proudest post-war achievements, and the rejection of that power’s use deepened Japan’s disillusionment with its own altruism.
The experience of 1991 was vastly different for the United States and Japan. However, at the same time calls for normalcy in both countries began to gain momentum. In the United States, both mainstream and marginal figures began calling for the U.S. to become a “normal” country – one that does not feel required to right every international problem, regardless of the distance and resources at its disposal.
The previous year, former U.S. ambassador to the U.N. Jeane Kirkpatrick, an archetype of Cold War foreign policy thinking, published an essay titled “A Normal Country in a Normal Time,” in which she urged the governing elites to adopt a foreign policy more attuned to domestic needs, with the end of the Cold War in sight.
“The time when Americans should bear such unusual burdens is past,” she wrote. “With a return to ‘normal’ times, we can again become a normal nation – and take care of pressing problems of education, family, industry, and technology. We can be an independent nation in a world of independent nations.”
On the other side of the spectrum, Pat Buchanan, who declared his bid to challenge the sitting president in December 1991, called for a reversal of the post-Cold War consensus, advocating trade protectionism and immigration restriction under the slogan “America First.”
However, for the vast majority of mainstream policy elites, a new world order was in sight, and the “unipolar moment” had arrived for the United States. In the following decades, U.S. foreign policy was guided by missionary zeal for exporting democracy and liberalized markets, ultimately leading to nation-building projects. Yet these prolonged, ambitious undertakings abroad gradually eroded the popular support that had initially sustained them, and the resulting frustration culminated in the rise of the anti-elite populist Donald Trump.
In contrast, while a debate over “normalcy” was ignited in Japan, 1991 turned out to be the moment when the country realized that it was not truly “normal” after all. The debate over troop deployment during the Gulf War highlighted the domestic nature of Japan’s definition of pacifism, as well as the lack of international understanding of how it put pacifism into practice.
In 1993, Ozawa Ichiro, then a rising star in the Liberal Democratic Party, laid out the case for “normalcy” in his best-selling book “Nihon Kaizō Keikaku,” later translated into English as “Blueprint for a New Japan.” For Ozawa, being a “normal country” meant doing what is taken for granted in the international community, and cooperating to the fullest extent with “countries striving to build prosperous and stable lives for their citizens” and on the common challenges facing humanity.
He also challenged what he saw as a “misunderstanding” of the so-called Yoshida Doctrine, a grand strategy, coined by scholars, that praised the genius of former Prime Minister Yoshida Shigeru’s decision to put the economy first and outsource the main burden of deterrence to the United States, which laid the foundation for postwar development. In Ozawa’s view, Yoshida’s decision was only tentative. In his book, he quoted at length from the former prime minister’s own 1963 writing, in which Yoshida argued that Japan should reduce its security dependence on the United States and instead bear responsibility for contributing to world peace.
Ozawa left the LDP shortly after the book’s publication, as it sold hundreds of thousands of copies. He remained an influential power broker in opposition politics for the rest of his career, with little direct influence on foreign policy. Nevertheless, his foreign policy vision largely defined the course the Japanese government charted over the following three decades.
In 1992, Japan dispatched Self-Defense Forces personnel to Cambodia for a peacekeeping operation, the first such overseas deployment since the SDF’s founding. The SDF went on to participate in missions in other regions across the globe. In the following decades, Japan became an advocate for global issues such as “human security” and environmental action. In terms of international security, Japan has used its alliance with the United States as a platform for contributing to global security. Japan’s championing of free trade agreements that span the globe is also compatible with Ozawa’s vision of the dual pursuit of national and international interests.
At the present, Japan and the United States seem to hold different notions of what a “normalized” foreign policy entails. For the United States under Trump, it rests on the idea, similar to Kirkpatrick’s, that the national interest, narrowly and unambiguously defined, should be the guiding principle, and that the United States should not lecture other powers or dictate how they govern themselves, so long as they do not interfere with U.S. interests. For Japan, becoming a “normal country” means shouldering a greater burden for regional and international security and committing itself to being a facilitator of international cooperation. This resembles the “exceptional” path the United States took after 1991, albeit in a quieter and more modest fashion.
However, the two “normalcies” are converging. The United States is pursuing an offshore balancing approach that delegates primary responsibility for defense to allies, while Japan shows greater willingness to shoulder the burden, driven by an independent-minded prime minister, a public concerned about regional stability, and a coalition partner that wants to truly normalize the Japan-U.S. alliance by revising it into a mutual defense pact.
The roots of this ongoing trend lie in the 1991 moment and the lessons both countries drew from it. These different but aligning conceptions of “normalcy” are likely to reinforce the Japan-U.S. alliance going forward, as the roles within it need to be redefined and reconstructed.

Defense Minister Yaşar Güler attended the Türkiye-Bulgaria-Romania Meeting of Defense Ministers and Chiefs of Staff, held in Sofia, alongside General Selçuk Bayraktaroğlu, Chief of the General Staff. (AA Photo)
Turkish Defense Minister Yaşar Güler met with his Bulgarian and Romanian counterparts in Sofia on Oct. 28, for a security meeting amid a surge in attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea.
Güler was accompanied by Turkish Chief of General Staff Selçuk Bayraktaroğlu. Following a family photo, the three countries’ defense ministers and chiefs of general staff began their meeting.
More than 200 civilian and commercial vessels have come under attack in the Black Sea since the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine war in February 2022, with the vast majority of incidents occurring this year, according to the Turkish Chamber of Shipping (IMEAK DTO).
Black Sea littoral states have recently stepped up security measures following a series of deadly attacks on commercial vessels, with Bulgaria announcing plans to hold urgent consultations with Türkiye and Romania to ensure the safety of navigation.
Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova said on Oct. 7 that Sofia would propose urgent consultations with Türkiye and Romania to develop joint measures to prevent further attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea and safeguard freedom of navigation.
Iotova also proposed that Bulgaria launch a diplomatic initiative involving all six Black Sea littoral states, Bulgaria, Türkiye, Romania, Ukraine, Russia and Georgia, to seek an agreement on a moratorium aimed at halting hostilities in the Black Sea.
The initiative aims to transform the Black Sea into a “common security area,” according to proposals outlined after the meeting.
Bulgaria will also push for the establishment of a framework mechanism under the European Union’s Black Sea strategy to ensure free and secure maritime traffic in the region.
Sofia is additionally expected to call for increased NATO air and maritime surveillance capabilities in the Black Sea, stronger coastal defenses and the deployment of additional anti-drone systems.

From Morocco to Poland: The roots of Israel's political leaders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:31:32 UTC
21:31:32 KST

Breadcrumb
From Morocco to Poland: The ancestral roots of Israel's political leaders
As Israel's election results leave the country's political future uncertain, the backgrounds of the politicians competing for power reveal a history of migration from Europe, North Africa and other parts of the Middle East.
While many of Israel's leading political figures were born in Israel, their native origins trace back to countries including Poland, Lithuania, Morocco, Iraq, Germany and Moldova.
These backgrounds reflect successive waves of Jewish migration to Palestine encouraged by the Zionist movement, both before and after the establishment of Israel in 1948, and the historical divisions between Ashkenazi Jews of European descent and Mizrahi Jews with actual links in the Middle East and North Africa.
Among the politicians are Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose family came from Eastern Europe, and his main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, whose parents emigrated from Morocco.
Other figures, including far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, and Palestinian politician Mansour Abbas, represent different backgrounds within Israel's political landscape.
Here is a closer look at their family histories and political careers.
Benjamin Netanyahu: Polish and Lithuanian
Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister and leader of the right-wing Likud party, was born in Tel Aviv in 1949 and grew up in Jerusalem.
His paternal family traces its roots to Poland and Lithuania. His father, historian and political activist Benzion Netanyahu, was born Benzion Mileikowsky in Warsaw in 1910.
Netanyahu's grandfather, Rabbi Nathan Mileikowsky, emigrated with his family to British-ruled Palestine in 1920. The family subsequently adopted the surname Netanyahu, which Nathan had previously used when publishing articles.
His paternal grandmother, Sarah Lurie, was born in Lithuania in 1885.
Politically, Netanyahu has dominated Israeli politics for decades, serving multiple terms as prime minister since 1996.
He faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. He is also on trial in Israel on corruption charges.
Gadi Eisenkot: Moroccan
Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main challenger in the 2026 election and leader of the centrist Yashar party, comes from a Moroccan Jewish family.
Born in Tiberias in 1960, Eisenkot is the son of Moroccan immigrants. His father, Meir Eisenkot, was born in Marrakesh, while his mother, Esther, was born in Casablanca.
The family name is associated with Morocco's Jewish community, with members of the Azencot family historically holding leadership positions in Marrakesh.
Eisenkot spent approximately four decades in the Israeli military, eventually becoming chief of staff before entering politics.
His military background has been central to his political career, particularly as he seeks to challenge Netanyahu on questions of security and leadership.
Eisenkot's Moroccan ancestry also distinguishes him from many previous Israeli prime ministers, who have predominantly come from Ashkenazi Jewish backgrounds.
Naftali Bennett: American and Polish
Former Israeli Prime Minister Naftali Bennett was born in Haifa in 1972 to American Jewish parents who had emigrated from San Francisco.
His parents, Jim Bennett and Myrna Lefko Bennett, moved to Israel in 1967, following the June Arab-Israeli war.
Bennett's ancestors had previously migrated from Europe to the United States during the 19th century.
His family history includes roots in Poland, the Netherlands and Germany, according to genealogical research highlighted during a visit to the Museum of the Jewish People in Tel Aviv in 2017.
Bennett served as prime minister between 2021 and 2022, heading a coalition that brought together parties from across Israel's political spectrum.
A right-wing politician, he opposes Palestinian statehood and supports the expansion of Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
In the 2026 election, Bennett has been politically aligned with former prime minister Yair Lapid in efforts to challenge Netanyahu.
Yair Lapid: Hungarian and Yugoslavian
Yair Lapid, leader of the centrist Yesh Atid party and a former Israeli prime minister, comes from a Jewish family with Hungarian roots.
His father, journalist and politician Yosef "Tommy" Lapid, was born in Novi Sad in 1931, when the city was part of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. It is now in Serbia.
Tommy Lapid survived the Holocaust as a child before emigrating to Israel in 1948.
His experiences during the Second World War and his subsequent career in journalism and politics became an important part of the family's public history.
Yair Lapid worked as a journalist and television presenter before entering politics, eventually serving as prime minister in 2022.
He has remained a prominent figure in the opposition to Netanyahu and has worked with Bennett in efforts to form an alternative government.
Avigdor Lieberman: Moldavian
Unlike many of Israel's other leading politicians, Avigdor Lieberman was born outside Israel.
The leader of the nationalist Yisrael Beiteinu party was born on 5 June 1958 in Chisinau, then part of the Soviet Union's Moldavian Republic.
His parents, Lev and Esther Lieberman, belonged to the city's Russian-speaking Jewish community.
Lieberman emigrated to Israel in June 1978, aged 20.
His political career has been closely associated with Russian-speaking Israelis, many of whom arrived during successive waves of immigration from the former Soviet Union.
He has served in several senior government positions, including defence minister and finance minister, and has been a prominent critic of Netanyahu despite previously serving in his governments.
Yair Golan: German and Ukrainian
Yair Golan, a former Israeli military general and leader of the Democrats party, was born in Rishon LeZion in 1962.
His father's family originated in Germany, while his maternal grandfather came from Ukraine.
His father, Gershon, fled Nazi Germany with his family in 1935, when he was four years old, and settled in British-ruled Palestine.
Golan spent decades in the Israeli military, eventually becoming deputy chief of staff, before entering politics.
He leads the Democrats, a left-wing Zionist party that forms part of the broader opposition to Netanyahu.
Itamar Ben-Gvir: Iraqi and Kurdish
Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir traces his family roots to Iraq and Kurdistan. Ben-Gvir, who leads the Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party, has spoken publicly about his family's origins.
In an interview with the Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth, he said his father was of Iraqi Jewish descent, while his mother's family came from Kurdistan.
He also revealed that his family's original surname was Hanan before his father changed it to Ben-Gvir.
His mother was reportedly active in Irgun, a Zionist paramilitary organisation that operated in British-ruled Palestine before Israel's establishment in 1948.
Ben-Gvir built his public profile as a lawyer representing Jewish extremists accused of violence against Palestinians.
He has previous criminal convictions, including for supporting a terrorist organisation.
As national security minister, he has advocated policies including the expansion of Israeli settlements and the displacement of Palestinians from Gaza, which he has described as "voluntary migration".
Bezalel Smotrich: Ukrainian and Lithuanian
Bezalel Smotrich, Israel's far-right finance minister and leader of the Religious Zionism party, traces his family roots to Ukraine, Lithuania and other parts of Eastern Europe.
He was born in 1980 in the Haspin settlement in the Israeli-occupied Syrian Golan Heights and grew up in the Beit El settlement in the occupied West Bank.
His surname is associated with the Ukrainian town of Smotrych, where his ancestors lived.
His maternal grandfather, Chaim Moshe Fein, was born in Panevezys, Lithuania, while another relative on his mother's side was born in Riga, Latvia, according to biographical information reported by Israel's Knesset Channel.
Smotrich has become one of the most prominent advocates of Israeli annexation of the occupied West Bank.
His Religious Zionism party supports settlement expansion and policies strengthening the Jewish religious character of the Israeli state.
Mansour Abbas: Palestinian roots
Unlike the Jewish Israeli politicians competing for influence in the next government, Mansour Abbas was among Palestinians who managed to remain on their land following the Nakba of 1948.
Abbas, a dentist by profession, leads Ra'am, also known as the United Arab List, an Islamist party representing Palestinian citizens of Israel.
He has served in the Knesset since 2019 and became a prominent figure in Israeli coalition politics when Ra'am joined the government formed by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid in 2021.
It was the first time an independent Arab-led party had formally joined an Israeli governing coalition.
Abbas has focused much of his political programme on issues affecting Palestinian citizens of Israel, including organised crime, housing, public services and economic inequalities.
His approach has differed from that of other Palestinian political leaders who place greater emphasis on the Israeli's restrictive policies on Palestinians throughout Palestine.
Ahead of the 2026 election, Abbas included former police commander and centrist politician Yoav Segalovitz in second place on Ra'am's electoral list.

Italy puts Ukraine weapons package on hold – media
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has put a major new weapons package for Ukraine on hold until after the US midterm elections, according to La Repubblica. The move comes as her ruling coalition faces mounting resistance to arming Kiev.
The long-delayed 13th military aid package remains stuck despite repeated assurances that Rome will continue to support Ukraine, the Italian outlet reported on Tuesday. Initially expected in July, the shipment was pushed back to September, then delayed again, with a decision now potentially postponed until after the November 3 US congressional elections.
La Repubblica noted that the delay has cast doubt on whether Meloni will deliver on promises made to French President Emmanuel Macron and Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky to send more Aster 30 interceptor missiles for Kiev’s SAMP/T air defense systems by the end of October.
The Italian parliamentary intelligence committee has yet to review the decree authorizing the shipment, while Rome continues to declare its support for Ukraine without specifying when the weapons will be delivered.
Earlier this week, Italian media reported that Meloni’s government is split over further arms supplies to Kiev. Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, leader of the League party, has opposed further weapons deliveries, while Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti, also from the League, has reportedly resisted signing off on the package. In December 2025, Tajani rejected Italy’s immediate participation in the US-led PURL scheme, under which NATO members bankroll American weapons for Kiev, citing ongoing peace talks. “If we reach an agreement and the fighting stops, weapons will no longer be needed,” he said.
Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani and Defense Minister Guido Crosetto, meanwhile, have pushed for continued military assistance, leaving Meloni caught between her government’s commitments to Kiev and opposition from a key coalition partner.
According to La Repubblica, Rome is also holding off on further arms deliveries until the US midterms, which could strip President Donald Trump’s Republicans of their control of Congress. The November 3 vote will determine control of both chambers, with Democrats leading Republicans 53% to 44% in an October 22-26 Reuters/Ipsos poll. The delay could stretch even further as Italy heads toward its own elections in 2027. Silver Bulletin’s October 27 forecast also indicated that Democrats were strongly positioned to retake the House, while the Senate remained less certain.
Public opposition to arming Kiev is growing in Italy. A September Termometro Politico poll found that 55.4% of Italians opposed further weapons shipments, against 38.8% in favor. Ukraine’s EU membership bid has also split opinion, with a May survey showing 32% backing eastward enlargement and 26% opposed.
Russia has warned that Western weapons deliveries to Ukraine prolong the conflict and obstruct peace efforts. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has accused European countries of fueling the fighting, while Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has warned that any shipments carrying foreign arms into Ukraine would be considered legitimate military targets.

Not so in the United States. There, the budget and borrowing authorisation are two separate legislative processes. Congress approves the budget in one decision, and in a second it sets a ceiling up to which the administration is entitled to borrow.
Don’t ask me what the point of this convoluted and slightly illogical process is; that’s just the way it is. Before 1917, it was even worse: Congress had to approve every instance of government borrowing separately. Traditionally, raising the debt ceiling has happened quietly. Since World War II, the debt ceiling has been raised over a hundred times, usually without any fuss.

BAE tests deck launcher that can reload at sea
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:29:19 GMT
21:29:19 KST

BAE Systems has completed the first live firing of the Adaptable Deck Launcher, a missile launcher that bolts onto a ship’s deck and can be replenished at sea without the vessel returning to port, according to the company.
The launcher was developed under a United States Department of War contract for the NATO Seasparrow Project Office. It uses the logistics and electronics suite of the Mk 41 vertical launching system already in service, which the company says gives it the reliability of that system at lower operating cost.
Jason Casciotti, vice president of weapons systems at BAE Systems, said: “The successful demonstration of the Adaptable Deck Launcher is a major milestone in our commitment to enhancing the Navy’s combat effectiveness and readiness. The ADL complements the Mk 41 VLS, the foundation of naval missile integration, by providing a capability for rapid replenishment, using standard shipboard equipment and offering the fleet additional flexibility in how it sustains combat loads at sea.”
Replenishment is where the real significance lies, I’d argue, because after a warship empties its vertical launch cells, it must go back to a port with the right facilities to reload them, which in a sustained campaign takes the ship off station for days or weeks. Royal Navy and United States Navy ships firing interceptors at Houthi drones and missiles in the Red Sea ran into exactly that constraint, and the United States Navy has spent several years working on ways to rearm cells while under way.
The launcher is designed for anti-air defence and can go on aircraft carriers, amphibious ships and other surface combatants. BAE Systems said it is also optimised for uncrewed warfare, with compact configurations suited to medium uncrewed surface vessels, which is where a deck-mounted launcher has an obvious advantage over cells built into a hull.
As mechanical design agent for the Mk 41 family, the company built the launcher to take Evolved SeaSparrow Missile Mk 25 quad-pack canisters, which hold four missiles in the space of one cell and provide defence against supersonic anti-ship missiles, aircraft and other aerial threats.

- Panahi is a major Iranian director and Cannes winner. He has long faced bans, arrests and charges over films seen as critical of Iran.
AI generated
TEHRAN – An Iranian court has sentenced renowned filmmaker Jafar Panahi in absentia to over five years in prison, Iranian media said quoting his lawyer, although the latest charges remain unclear.
“The Tehran Revolutionary Court sentenced my client to five years and one month in prison and ordered the confiscation of all his moveable and immoveable property,” the ISNA news agency reported, citing his lawyer, Mostafa Nili, on Oct 27.
“The court also imposed a two-year ban on social media activity and a two-year travel ban,” he added.
The ISNA report did not specify the charges.
Nili said he discovered the conviction after Panahi told him last week that his bank accounts had been frozen, prompting the lawyer to visit the sentence enforcement office of the Culture and Media Prosecutor’s Office.
The lawyer said Panahi returned to Iran during the war with Israel and the United States that broke out on Feb 28.
It remains unclear if Panahi has remained in Iran.
Panahi currently has three pending cases, Nili said, adding that his client has not been notified of the hearing date in the latest case.
In June, an Iranian court rejected Panahi’s appeal against a one-year sentence in one of the cases, which was handed down in December on charges of “propaganda” against Iran.
Panahi, 66, won the top prize in the 2025 Cannes film festival for It Was Just An Accident, a film in which five former inmates contemplate whether to exact revenge on a man they believe to be their former jailer.
He has won a host of prizes at European film festivals since showcasing his debut film, The White Balloon, in Cannes in 1995, which won an award for best first feature.
In 2010, Panahi was banned from making movies for 20 years and from leaving Iran after he supported mass anti-government protests a year earlier and made a series of films that critiqued the state of modern Iran.
Convicted of “propaganda against the system”, he was sentenced to six years in jail but served only two months behind bars before being released on bail.
A year later, he dispatched a documentary with the title This Is Not A Film to the Cannes festival on a flash drive stashed in a cake.
His 2015 movie Taxi featured him acting as a taxi driver and was shot entirely in a car.
In 2022, he was arrested in connection with protests by a group of filmmakers but was released nearly seven months later.
Iranian filmmakers, prominent media figures and celebrities are closely monitored in Iran, and their work reviewed for content deemed critical of the Islamic republic. AFP

ICRC praises Iranian rescuers, pledges support for Red Crescent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:25:31 UTC
21:25:31 KST

ICRC praises Iranian rescuers, pledges support for Red Crescent
TEHRAN – The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has expressed readiness to strengthen cooperation with the Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) and provide it with the necessary equipment, praising Iranian rescuers for their efforts during crises.
Nicolas Von Arx, the ICRC’s regional director for Near and Middle East, made the remarks during a meeting with Pirhossein Kolivand, head of the IRCS, in Tehran on Tuesday, Mehr News Agency reported.
Referring to the ongoing conflicts in different parts of the world, the official said wars are cruel, violent, and destructive. Still, the presence of first responders and aid workers who risk their lives on the front lines to help people, clear debris, and provide psychological support and mental health services makes them seem a bit less horrific.
“From a distance, we observed how relief workers and even the head of the Iranian Red Crescent Society arrived at the scenes of explosions and conflicts on motorcycles to reach those who were injured and in need of assistance; a truly extraordinary effort,” he emphasized.
The official referred to the expansion of cooperation in specialized fields between the two organizations since June, saying that “the joint efforts can further expand. Our team is ready to boost ties with your team and provide the essential items and support needed by the society.”
He went on to say that the ICRC is following up on regional issues like reopening IRCS hospitals in the UAE.
For his part, Kolivand presented a report on the activities of the IRCS during the imposed 40-day war.
Lauding the ICRC's support and assistance, Kolivand underlined the necessity of promoting collaborations in relief, humanitarian, legal, and rehabilitation sectors, the IRCS website reported.
“Given the extensive scope of humanitarian missions and the specific conditions in the region, we expect this cooperation to be strengthened further, particularly in protecting civilians, developing specialized services, and addressing violations of international humanitarian law,” he stressed.
Elaborating on the IRCS capacities, he said the IRCS benefited from quick response teams, consisting of some 120,000 trained rescuers, to provide relief services during the recent conflicts. They managed to rescue 7,215 individuals alive from under the rubble.
The IRCS rescue teams carried out thousands of relief missions on a daily basis, reaching affected locations in less than four minutes. Some relief operations lasted one single day, while some others extended up to 25 days. The complexity of these operations showcases the operational capabilities, preparedness, and the spirit of self-sacrifice of the aid workers, Kolivand noted.
Beside rescue operations, 2,388 experts affiliated with the IRCS also provided free psychological support, some took an hour or more, to some 25,000 callers. The service played a crucial role in helping those affected by warfare recover.
The official also expounded on the US-Israel attacks targeting civilians and rescue centers, including residential areas, universities, hospitals, clinics, pharmacies, and research centers, which were directly targeted. The IRCS sent over 40 letters and legal documents elaborating on the violations of human rights by US-Israeli attacks on Iran.
He urged the ICRC to help facilitate the reopening of the IRCS medical branch in Dubai.
The official called for strengthening joint efforts through training and equipping teams and providing technical expertise and support in locating and clearing landmines and explosive remnants of war from conflict-affected areas and managing the health effects from blast and toxins.
Recent joint efforts
The IRCS and the ICRC held the second and third training courses on the Application of Personal Protective Equipment during Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) incidents.
The first round of the course was held in Tehran from June 7 to 21. The second and third courses were held from October 4-8 and 11-15, separately. The courses aimed to improve preparedness and the operational capacity of relief teams and have been attended by a total of 150 members of rapid response teams from different provinces in the country, the ICRC website announced in a press release on October 15.
During the closing ceremony, the attendees and instructors reviewed achievements, strengths, and grounds for improvement. Stressing the need to repeat the exercises, organize the course in provincial levels, and to provide complementary equipment required, the attendees emphasized that the experience was different from previous maneuvers.
The instructors also expressed gratitude for the participants’ active involvement, reiterating their positive performance during practical simulation exercises in applying the learning points and following the decontamination process suited to each type of contamination.
Speaking on the sidelines of the ceremony, the head of ICRC’s Tehran Delegation, Marisela Silva Chau, highlighted the close collaboration between ICRC and the Iranian Red Crescent Society, citing the workshop as a concrete example, putting together IRCS’ operational experience and ICRC’s academic expertise and technical and equipment support. She reiterated the ICRC’s readiness to throw support behind similar courses to be held at a provincial level, while stressing the importance of transferring learnings to operational teams and their application in daily activities.
The IRCS Deputy Director for Education, Research and Technology, Rouzbeh Rajaei, also stressed continued training, teacher training, and planning for similar courses to be held for female participants, noting the participation of experts from different scientific institutions and centers.
The continued collaboration and transfer of knowledge and experience to operational teams is an important step in strengthening the incident preparedness and response capacity.
The first training course targeted basic health care unit (BHCU) team leaders from five high-risk provinces, namely Tehran, Qom, Markazi, Isfahan, and Bushehr, as well as passive defense trainers.
In September, IRCS, in cooperation with the ICRC, held the first three-day training workshop on ‘Trauma for First Responders’ for selected IRCS personnel, with a focus on trauma and pre-hospital care.
The training aims to enhance the emergency response and pre-hospital care capacities of the IRCS personnel, particularly in mass-casualty incidents, to provide timely and effective lifesaving services and ensure the safe evacuation and transfer of injured and sick people, the ICRC website announced in a press release on September 26.
The recent escalation of hostilities has created significant operational challenges for the IRCS Relief and Rescue Organization, one of the key actors at the forefront of emergency response. Its teams are often among the first responders at the scene of mass-casualty incidents and, in high-risk environments, are responsible for evacuating casualties, stabilizing patients and carrying out emergency transfers. This has further highlighted the importance of strengthening technical preparedness through specialized training in mass-casualty management.
The training brought together eight IRCS personnel from the Training, Relief and Rescue, and Emergency Health departments from Tehran and Alborz provinces.
In the opening ceremony, IRCS Under-Secretary-General for Education, Research and Technology, Dr. Rajaei, said the course aims to improve staff knowledge and skill levels, bring education closer to global standards, and eventually form a specialized team for pre-hospital trauma.
“The planning for the course began last year after the first hostilities.” Explained Navid Dadbin, Health Program Manager at the ICRC. “It will be implemented with three 3-day training courses followed by selection of a group of participants to be trained as trainers. A road map for continuation will be drawn up in the end,” he added.
The courses include theoretical and practical sessions, group work, scenario-based exercises covering different types of incidents, and simulation exercises.

EXPLAINER - Israel’s election reflects shifting political trends
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:24:47 UTC
21:24:47 KST

Israel’s Oct. 27 parliamentary election has highlighted several shifts in the country’s political landscape, from record voter participation and renewed mobilization among Palestinian citizens to changes in the balance between right-wing parties and the opposition.
With vote counting still ongoing, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc was projected to win 54 seats in the 120-member Knesset, seven short of a governing majority, with 84.5% of votes counted in Israel’s parliamentary elections, according to Israeli media.
The opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot was projected to secure 49 seats, while predominantly Arab parties were projected to win 17 seats, according to The Times of Israel newspaper, citing the Central Elections Committee.
The election is seen as pivotal in determining the country’s political direction amid the Gaza genocide and the war with Iran.
It also came after years of political instability, including five parliamentary elections between April 2019 and November 2022, and tested whether Netanyahu could maintain the coalition arrangements that returned him to office four years ago.
The most striking developments so far are the highest turnout in decades, a potential record for Arab-led parties, a reorganization of opposition alliances and signs of pressure on some of Netanyahu’s ultra-Orthodox and far-right partners.
As vote counting continues, the results remain uncertain, but several key trends have emerged.
Voter participation reached 77.7%, with around 5.7 million voters casting ballots, according to Israel’s Central Elections Committee, the highest level since the 1999 parliamentary election.
The figure was 7.1 percentage points above the 70.6% recorded in 2022 and exceeded turnout in each of the five elections held between 2019 and 2022.
Historical figures show turnout of 68.5% in April 2019, 69.8% in September 2019, 71.5% in 2020 and 67.4% in 2021.
The military separately reported turnout of 79.9% among soldiers, higher than in 2022.
The rise comes after a period of repeated elections, political deadlock and growing divisions over the government’s policies. The Gaza war, security concerns, military service exemptions and disputes over democratic institutions have all featured in the campaign.
According to latest reports, the predominantly Arab Joint List was projected to win 11 seats, while the United Arab List (Ra’am) was expected to secure six.
If confirmed, the result would exceed the 15 seats won by the Joint List in 2020, when Ra’am was part of the alliance. The two parties hold 10 seats in the outgoing Knesset.
Turnout rose sharply in several Arab communities. Ynet reported participation of 86.8% in Sakhnin and 82% in Rahat, a Bedouin city in southern Israel. These are local figures, not a final nationwide turnout rate for Arab voters.
Channel 12 separately reported participation of around 80% among Arab voters.
For comparison, Israel Democracy Institute research puts participation in Arab and Druze localities at 44.6% in 2021 and 53.2% in 2022.
The mobilization comes amid concerns over occupier violence, housing demolitions and the extremist policies of far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Jewish voters supporting Arab-led parties is an established phenomenon, particularly around Hadash, which has long included Jewish politicians and supporters. The more distinctive development this year is within Ra’am, Israel’s Islamic party.
Ra’am placed Yoav Segalovitz, a Jewish former lawmaker from the centrist Yesh Atid party, a Zionist and a former senior police official, second on its candidate list. His prominence represents a significant effort to broaden the party’s constituency and its acceptance as a governing partner.
The Joint List also sought Jewish support through a Hebrew-language campaign launched in Tel Aviv on Oct. 5. Chairman Yousef Jabareen estimated it could attract 10,000-15,000 Jewish voters, while Ahmad Tibi appealed to voters opposing Israel’s wars and occupation.
Another important comparison concerns Shas and United Torah Judaism, the two principal ultra-Orthodox parties and longstanding partners of Netanyahu.
They won 18 seats between them in 2022: 11 for Shas and seven for United Torah Judaism. Early Wednesday exit poll updates reported by The Jerusalem Post put their combined strength at 12-13 seats, suggesting a potentially substantial reduction.
The forecasts come amid a dispute over military service by ultra-Orthodox men.
These parties have resisted efforts to expand conscription, while other Israelis have demanded a wider sharing of service obligations during years of war.
The election reflects a transformation that began well before 2022: the traditional left no longer dominates Israeli politics as it once did, while centrist parties and leaders have become important alternatives for voters who oppose Netanyahu without necessarily identifying with the left.
The 1999 election illustrates that fragmentation is not new. Fifteen lists entered the Knesset, and Ehud Barak’s One Israel won 26 seats. His success in the direct prime ministerial vote did not translate into a unified parliamentary bloc, requiring cooperation among parties with differing interests.
In the latest election, former Prime Ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid contested the election on a joint list, Together, while former military chief Gadi Eisenkot led Yashar. Labor and Meretz, meanwhile, joined forces under Yair Golan’s Democrats.
These arrangements seek to reduce the risk of votes being wasted when small parties fail to cross Israel’s 3.25% electoral threshold. In 2022, Meretz and Balad failed to enter parliament despite receiving a combined total of nearly 290,000 votes.
More than half a million young Israelis became eligible to vote for the first time in this election, according to pre-election reporting by The Times of Israel. Their political experiences include the coronavirus pandemic, protests against the judicial overhaul and the Gaza war.
A Channel 12 survey published on Sept. 23 found that 74% of young respondents identified as right-wing or center-right. Yet 16% said they would vote for Eisenkot’s Yashar, compared with 14% for Likud, according to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency and The Times of Israel.
The findings suggest that identifying with the right does not necessarily translate into support for Netanyahu personally. Security, the cost of living and concerns about the country’s future also featured among young voters’ priorities, local media reported.

Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a majority; a unity coalition may prevent another election - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:23:39 UTC
21:23:39 KST

- i24NEWS
- Analysis & Opinion
- Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a majority; a unity coalition may prevent another election - analysis
Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a majority; a unity coalition may prevent another election - analysis
A deal could see Eisenkot serve as prime minister in the second half of the term, with Netanyahu positioned as the government’s candidate to succeed Herzog as president in July 2028
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot both delivered victory speeches to their constituents early Wednesday morning.
In Eisenkot's speech, he prematurely eulogized Netanyahu and declared that the public had voted to end his tenure. Had he waited half an hour to start his speech when more results were in, perhaps he would have been more careful.
Netanyahu defiantly defended all his current coalition partners, mercilessly mocked the rival camp, and called for a right-wing nationalist government. Had he waited, perhaps it would have become clearer that he lost his 64-MK majority in this election.
The truth is that neither side won. Simple math: Neither of them have the 61 MKs out of 120 needed for a stable government.
So what happens now? Is Israel doomed to go to perpetual elections?
The answer is it depends on the success of the president. Which president? Three of them, actually.
President Isaac Herzog can try to condition granting Netanyahu a mandate on him making a serious effort to draft a national unity government with Eizenkot as defense minister, Naftali Bennett as foreign minister, and Itamar Ben-Gvir and Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties as spectators in the opposition.
President Donald Trump can do the same, knowing that a unity government in Israel can help him advance his foreign policy at a time when his domestic agenda could be handcuffed by Congress.
And Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian can continue to reject compromises and bring about another round of war with Israel and the United States.
Wars are good excuses to break campaign promises, which Eizenkot must do to prevent an election in which he would likely no longer be his bloc's candidate for prime minister. He could be prime minister in the second half of the term, without taking the risk of another race.
It is, of course, a risk to trust Netanyahu to hand over power after he did not honor an agreement with Benny Gantz. But Netanyahu could be made the government’s candidate to replace Herzog as president in July 2028, shortly before Trump's term ends, perhaps replaced by a president less friendly to Israel.
Netanyahu’s criminal trial, which was the initial reason for boycotting him, has been petering out anyway.
Such a government would enable Eizenkot to keep his promise about forming g a coalition without the haredim that could pass a tougher draft law.
And what about the Arabs, whose impressive showing in the election cannot be ignored? Banishing Ben-Gvir would be a victory for them. They would not join the government or the coalition, but vast initiatives to fight inter-Arab crime and poverty could be initiated and well-funded, overseen by the Knesset Interior and Public Security committees, led by Arab MKs.
This scenario is not what Netanyahu or Eizenkot called for in their victory speeches. But it could bring the stability and reconciliation needed at a time of war.

Israel’s election: The battle between change and anti-Palestinian sentiment
With both blocs short of a majority, parties face a choice: to break the taboo on Arab allies or return to the polls.
With Israel’s governing and opposition blocs failing to secure a majority in Israel’s election, and neither appearing ready to ally with Arab parties that could allow them to form a coalition, speculation is growing over the future shape of the government.
The vote on Tuesday, billed as one of the most important in Israel’s history, saw turnout reach 77.7 percent of eligible voters – the highest level since 1999.
With nearly 80 percent of votes counted by Wednesday afternoon, the outgoing coalition led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, centred around his Likud party, had secured 54 seats, short of the 61 needed to establish a governing coalition.
Former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot’s self-styled Zionist opposition, drawing from parties as diverse as Yair Golan’s relatively left-wing Democrats and Avigdor Lieberman’s hard-right Yisrael Beiteinu, had 49 seats, also short of a governing majority in the 120-strong Knesset.
Holding the balance of power, in theory at least, are the Arab-dominated Ra’am and Joint List, with 17 seats, more than enough to give either bloc a majority with which to appoint a speaker, pass legislation and form a working government.
Those figures are not final, however, with the final tally expected by Friday and official results formally published on November 4 .
What happens next is a matter of procedure as much as politics.
President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders on who they want as prime minister, before tasking the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government. That candidate has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension. If they fail, the mandate can pass to another member of parliament, and if that also fails, the Knesset is dissolved and Israelis return to the polls, with the current cabinet staying on as caretaker.
Turnout
Turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel, who account for one-fifth of the total population, reached about 80 percent, according to some estimates, also above the 1999 figures.
Analysts said the surge was propelled by the harsh treatment of the Israeli-Palestinian minority by the Likud-led government, which increased significantly following the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023 that triggered Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza. Netanyahu’s outgoing government is the most right-wing in Israeli history, featuring far-right figures such as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, whose policies and rhetoric against Palestinians have essentially made him a recruiting sergeant for the pro-Arab parties.
Analysts also attributed the strong performance to a well-organised campaign that targeted the demands of Israel’s Palestinian community and the opportunity for a greater voice in the Knesset.
“Having just two well-organised lists significantly improved their vote-collecting efficiency and ground-level mobilisation – particularly for Ra’am, the Islamist party, which ran a much more efficient campaign than usual,” Roi Zur, a lecturer at Essex University and specialist in Israeli voting behaviour and election strategies, told Al Jazeera.
“The broader shift, however, comes down to how voters view their place in Israeli politics,” he added, “especially following October 7 and the subsequent war,” Zur added.
“On one hand, many voters feel more integrated into Israeli society, driven by shifts in how the public processed both the October 7 attacks and the government’s subsequent policies, making them feel more invested in the political system.”
Polarised puzzle
However, both blocs ran campaigns that critics have described as profoundly racist. Likud spent much of the election race making unsubstantiated claims that the opposition was planning to form a government reliant on Arab parties after the vote, while petitioning to bar the Joint List from running.
On the opposition side, Lieberman ruled out a coalition with either Arab or ultra-Orthodox (Haredi) parties, while Together’s Naftali Bennett, whose 2021-22 coalition included Ra’am, told an activists’ conference there was “no mandate” to form a government with Arab parties after the October 7 attack.
“The ‘opposition’ bloc continues to think you beat Bibi by being Bibi-lite, offering no substantive alternative or hope,” said former government adviser Daniel Levy, using a common nickname for the Israeli prime minister. “Really, the opposition got what they deserved,” he added, arguing it would have won the election if its members’ commitment to removing Netanyahu had outweighed their “commitment to a racist ethno-centric version of Zionism”.
Levy sees four possible scenarios ahead for either bloc, listed in no particular order: the possibility of a new election; Likud drawing enough defectors from the right of the opposition to form a government; a so-called “unity government” led by Netanyahu that draws on the right across the Knesset; and “Eisenkot and company biting the bullet and using the anti-Netanyahu majority to form a minority government with Arab support,” he said.
“Even if they announce it’s time-limited before another election, the Arab parties’ asking price will not be particularly high,” he said, with the caveat that he considered such a coalition unlikely.
Wheeling and dealing
The chance of defection amidst what is seen as a highly polarised society remains unclear.
Much of the Eisenkot bloc’s campaign, and by extension its vote, rested upon opposition to the de facto exemption from military service offered by the Likud-led government to the Haredi parties in return for their support in the Knesset. Rivalling the pressure to extend the draft to Israel’s ultra-Orthodox youth were the calls for an independent inquiry into the government’s alleged security failings before the October 7 attack, calls rendered more pressing in light of the reports of the alleged advance warnings given by the United Arab Emirates and Egypt.
“I think it would be very hard to see Eisenkot working with anyone in Netanyahu’s camp because of the ultra-Orthodox draft issue and because of October 7,” said Mairav Zonszein, an analyst with the Crisis Group. “His main demands are a state commission of inquiry and a universal draft for everyone, so he couldn’t work with a lot of the partners there, including Netanyahu,” she added.
“However, Bennett and Lieberman are different stories. Bennett has swerved once before,” she said, referring to him reneging on election promises and working with Ra’am in 2021.
“Lieberman, as much as he hates Netanyahu, is also a very hard-right politician,” she said of the likelihood of Yisrael Beiteinu allying with Likud to prevent any liberal-leaning politics.
For now, though, speculation continues. For some, including Levy, that includes the possibility of the Netanyahu government seeking a military escalation, potentially against Iran, as a pretext to establish an emergency government.
For others, such as Israeli political psychologist Daniel Bar Tal of Tel Aviv University, the future rests upon the more prosaic mathematics of a government coalition.
“It is a very challenging moment in the history of Israel,” he said, reflecting on the many opportunities to gain power missed by the opposition.
“It is hard to know [what will happen] because the majority of Israelis are rightists, racists, religious and nationalists,” he said, before cutting to the heart of the dilemma faced by many in Israel on the day after the election: “They want change but do not want to cooperate with Arab parties.”

Iranians cut essentials and put dreams on hold as war-hit economy bites

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28

21:21:19 KST

Iranians cut essentials and put dreams on hold as war-hit economy bites
DUBAI, Oct 28 - Iranian families are cutting back on food, housing and education as the eight-month-old war with the United States fuels one of the country's worst inflation surges in decades, eroding incomes and pushing households to the brink.
The strain is being felt far beyond the country's major cities. Workers say wages no longer cover basic expenses, while businesses face rising costs and weakening demand as families spend most of their budgets on food, rent and other necessities.
The conflict, triggered by US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28 and followed by Tehran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz and a US blockade of Iranian ports in the Gulf, has disrupted oil exports, trade and government revenues. The turmoil has compounded the impact of decades of sanctions and economic mismanagement.
Reuters spoke to more than two dozen people across Iran from different social and economic backgrounds who said worsening conditions had left them struggling to afford food, housing, healthcare and education.
"We have no money, no future and no hope. We're tired of living in fear, fear of another US attack and fear of not being able to make ends meet at the end of every month," said Mohammadali, a 47-year-old shopkeeper and father of two in the northeastern city of Mashhad.
Iran's Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh on Tuesday apologised for the mounting cost-of-living pressures facing Iranians, state media reported, saying pensioners, workers and civil servants were bearing the brunt of soaring prices and high inflation.
Iran's inflation surge has shown little sign of easing. Consumer prices in September were nearly 90% higher than a year earlier, while annual inflation accelerated to 73.6%, according to official data and figures reported by state media.
Food prices have risen even faster. The cost of food and beverages was 121.8% higher than a year ago, forcing many families to cut spending elsewhere.
PRICES OUTPACE PAYCHECKS, JOBS DRY UP
For Mahmoud, a 44-year-old government employee in the central city of Isfahan, the gap between wages and living costs widens every month.
"With my salary of less than $100, you can survive only for 10 days ... My wife and I lie to our daughters all the time when they ask for a toy or new clothes," he said.
Official estimates put the minimum monthly cost of living for a three-person working-class family at around $336, more than three times the average monthly wage of roughly $92 at the free-market exchange rate.
As wages fail to keep pace with inflation, many families have exhausted savings, cut consumption or borrowed money to cover daily expenses. Government-mandated pay increases have been swiftly overtaken by rising prices.
For many Iranians, the challenge is no longer preserving their standard of living but avoiding financial collapse.
"We had to move to my parents' house last month because my husband got laid off from a small tile factory in May. We spent all our savings. But my husband is still jobless and we could no longer afford rent," said Hamideh, a 39-year-old mother of two in the northern city of Rasht.
Rising housing costs have added to the squeeze on family budgets. Rents in September were 32.8% higher than a year earlier, while housing, utilities and fuel costs were up nearly 38%, according to official data.
The pressure extends to the labour market. The official unemployment rate climbed to 9.1% in the spring, up 1.8 percentage points from a year earlier. The economic participation rate fell to 40.7%, indicating fewer working-age Iranians were employed or actively seeking work. Nearly a quarter of young people aged 15 to 24 are unemployed.
"I have been looking for work since graduating in advertising, but after months of searching I've started to lose hope. Companies are cutting budgets, not hiring. Most of my classmates are either unemployed or working in fields unrelated to what they studied," said 23-year-old Firouzeh, who lives with her parents in the northwestern city of Urmia.
STUDYING ABROAD A DISTANT DREAM
The weakening rial is also closing off opportunities once seen as pathways to upward mobility. Iran's currency has lost more than half its value over the past year, putting overseas education beyond the reach of many families.
"Both my parents are government employees. Their dream was to send me abroad to become a medical doctor. But after two years studying in Turkey, I could not pay the tuition for this year and I am returning home," said Shahriyar, 25, in Istanbul. He said several of his friends were in the same situation.
Washington's expanded sanctions, announced on August 24 as part of "Operation Economic Outcast" and aimed at cutting Tehran's funding for the war, have added to the economic strain on ordinary Iranians, analysts said.
Businesses are under pressure. Sanctions and war-related disruptions have increased the cost of imports and restricted access to foreign currency and raw materials, while retailers and small businesses face higher operating costs just as demand weakens, threatening revenues and jobs.
For Iran's rulers, the challenge is maintaining essential imports and public services while financing a costly conflict. Central Bank Governor Abdolnasser Hemmati said in mid-October that US claims Iran's economy was collapsing were "an illusion".
The deterioration in living standards also presents a growing political challenge for the authorities, who remain wary that worsening economic conditions could reignite nationwide unrest.
Economic grievances have fuelled repeated waves of protests in recent years, leaving officials sensitive to signs that war, inflation and rising unemployment are further eroding public patience.
The clerical establishment responded to previous outbreaks of unrest with a sweeping crackdown that, according to Iranian officials and rights groups, killed thousands in January. REUTERS

The Army will procure a Heavy Wheeled Recovery Vehicle to recover Boxer in the field, the order remains at 623 vehicles with more than five hundred being built in Britain, and seventy two Boxer RCH artillery vehicles are being bought, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked how Boxer will be repaired in the field given that no repair and recovery variant has been ordered.
Luke Pollard MP said: “Boxer is a world-class vehicle that will boost our soldiers in a variety of military missions and scenarios across the globe. As I said in Parliament on 19 October 2026, the programme is hugely successful, delivering important capability and national benefit.
“The Army will absolutely have the ability to recover and support Boxer vehicles on the battlefield, such as through the Boxer support variants and the wider force, including the Heavy Wheeled Recovery Vehicle which we will procure.

“The work in Telford, Stockport and plenty of other locations across the country is backing more than 1,000 British jobs.”
The commitment to buy the recovery vehicle firms up an answer given the day before, in which Pollard said the Flensburger Fahrzeugbau Gesellschaft armoured recovery module had been assessed for the role and rejected, the department concluding that a generic heavy wheeled recovery vehicle would offer greater utility and affordability across the force. He also set out that Boxers currently recover one another peer to peer, backed where needed by the Support Vehicle (Recovery) and the Challenger Armoured Repair and Recovery Vehicle.
The RCH 155 is the wheeled self-propelled gun built on the Boxer drive module, pairing the artillery turret developed by Krauss-Maffei Wegmann with the vehicle already in British service. Seventy two of them will replace the AS90 in the close support artillery role.
All 623 Mechanised Infantry Vehicle Boxers are being delivered to a common build standard, and ministers confirmed last week that a planned third batch is no longer being pursued through the Boxer programme, a decision that cannot be tied to a single date because it was taken as part of the work on the Defence Investment Plan.

South Korea and the US have delayed a key bilateral security dialogue to next year amid Seoul’s demand that the Pentagon return wartime operational control of South Korean forces.
The decision to postpone the annual Security Consultative Meeting (SCM) came during a maiden meeting between US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and South Korean Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul, who met in Cebu City of the Philippines.

The annual SCM is usually held in late October or early November.
"Seoul seeks to regain wartime OPCON (operational control) before the Lee Jae Myung administration's five-year term ends in 2030, pushing to announce a target year for the OPCON transfer at the upcoming SCM," Yonhap News reported.
South Korea hosts around 39,000 American soldiers under a mutual defense treaty, and the administration of South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has committed to restoring command over the forces by the end of his term in 2030.
Hegseth “reaffirmed the United States' commitment to the wartime operational control transition, and both ministers agreed to closely cooperate to ensure the transition proceeds smoothly at the right time,” said the statement.

Hegseth and Koizumi agree on new Japanese missile production line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:18:24 UTC
21:18:24 KST

- Japan and the United States agreed on Oct. 28 to build an AMRAAM air-to-air missile final assembly plant in Japan.
- Defense chiefs Shinjiro Koizumi and Pete Hegseth also agreed to share technical data to expand SM-3 Block IIA interceptor production.
Japan will host a final assembly plant for the AIM-120 AMRAAM air-to-air missile after Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth agreed on Oct. 28 to build the facility as part of joint U.S.-Japanese missile production, Nikkei reported.
The two met for about 30 minutes in Cebu, the Philippines, on the sidelines of an expanded meeting of Southeast Asian defense ministers. The facility, known as a final assembly and check-out plant, or FACO, is where completed components are put together into finished missiles and tested before delivery, Financial News reported, citing the Asahi Shimbun and NHK. Hegseth welcomed Japan’s work to strengthen its defense production base, and the two sides also agreed to expand joint exercises, including live-fire drills.
The ministers also agreed to share technical information to expand production of the SM-3 Block IIA, a ship-launched interceptor that destroys ballistic missiles in space, Nikkei reported. The Japanese side said Hegseth did not press for a specific increase in Japan’s defense budget, and the Defense Ministry said the talks were not held with any particular amount or outcome in mind.
The AMRAAM is a radar-guided missile that fighters fire at enemy aircraft beyond visual range, and it guides itself to the target after launch, so the pilot can turn away or engage another threat. It arms U.S. and allied F-15, F-16, F/A-18, F-22 and F-35 fighters, including the F-35s that Japan is buying, and it also serves as the main interceptor for the ground-based NASAMS air defense system. Raytheon builds the missile in the United States and in February agreed with the U.S. Department of War to raise annual AMRAAM production to at least 1,900.
The plant would take a years-long effort a step further. The United States and Japan first agreed in July 2024 to explore joint production of the AMRAAM and the PAC-3 MSE Patriot interceptor, and Japan’s Acquisition, Technology and Logistics Agency then ran a feasibility study with Mitsubishi Electric and Raytheon. In April, the two governments identified circuit card assembly, the production of the missile’s electronic boards, as part of Japan’s share, with a final assembly plant in Japan raised as a possibility, Mitsubishi Electric said. Japan is also a major AMRAAM customer: in January 2025, the U.S. State Department approved the sale of up to 1,200 AIM-120D-3 and AIM-120C-8 missiles to Japan, valued at an estimated $3.64 billion.
The SM-3 Block IIA has a longer history as a shared program. Raytheon and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries developed it jointly, and it entered full-rate production in 2024. In March, the two governments agreed to quadruple production of the interceptor in Japan, and Japan now pays for a large share of new orders, covering nearly half the immediate funding in a $745 million contract for SM-3 Block IIA missiles awarded this summer.
During the meeting, Koizumi briefed Hegseth on Japan’s plan to revise its three main national security documents by the end of 2026. He said Japan would strengthen what it calls denial defense, the ability to stop an invading force from succeeding, along with deterrence intended to discourage an attack in the first place. The ministers also agreed to step up cooperation against cyberattacks, The Japan Times reported.

Thinking a possible Netanyahu departure changes anything? Think again.

The prospect of seeing the architect of Israel’s genocide of the Palestinian people, Benjamin Netanyahu, ousted from political office would be a small, albeit completely pyrrhic, ‘victory’. This is a politician who has spent the past three years justifying industrial-scale levels of civilian slaughter, the enforced starvation of an entire civilian population and the complete levelling of the Gaza Strip. He has been the public face of Israel on the global stage for the best part of 20 years, rubbing shoulders with world leaders and garnering support for the expansion of Israel’s settler colonial mission in historic Palestine.
As something of a political cockroach, he has managed to survive various high-profile scandals. These include criminal proceedings brought against him on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust, and a (largely symbolic) arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court, one that he and leaders in the West have completely ignored. Nevertheless, it seems that Netanyahu has become increasingly awakened to the fact that his time may well be running out. He turned to his X account to post an AI-generated image of a nuclear bomb hitting downtown Tel Aviv in an ever so subtle effort to stir up feelings of existential dread amongst an Israeli public who have fully drunk the anti-Iranian Kool-Aid.
Waiting in the wings to take over could be former Israeli army chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot. He is a man said to be fervently against Palestinian statehood and fully committed to the destruction of Hamas. His ‘achievements’ include the creation of the ‘Dahiya Doctrine’, a policy born of the 2006 Lebanon war that promotes the use of extraordinary and excessive military force against civilians and civilian infrastructure.
Whilst there can be no doubt that the Zionist project of expansion and the associated erasure of Palestinians have been moving at warp speed since 2023, those who are watching the Israeli elections from afar (including many in the activist community) and hoping for change would do well to adopt a longer gaze.
It has never really mattered who is in charge in Israel. The policies that undergird decades of relentless genocide and ethnic cleansing of the Palestinians have, over the years, largely remained the same. Political commentators euphemistically throw around terms like ‘hawk’ and ‘dove’ to provide the illusion that there is even the slightest possibility an Israeli leader is remotely interested in ‘peace’. But the terms are meaningless, and as with everything in the region, Israeli leaders’ actions speak louder than hollow words.
READ: Trump claims his endorsement helped Netanyahu perform better than expected in Israeli election
Take, for example, the tenure of Yitzhak Rabin: winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, architect of the ‘break their bones’ policy (sounds peaceful, right?) and the person responsible for signing the Oslo Accords. Under his watch, Palestine continued to be subjected to the scourge of relentless settlement expansion and the house demolitions that went with it. ‘Peace’ for Rabin was far removed from ending the occupation. Instead, it meant managing and containing the Palestinian population and their legitimate demands for self-determination, whilst subscribing to a ‘peace’ plan that outsourced responsibility for the occupation to a subservient Palestinian Authority and willing accomplices in the West.
Then there is the chameleonic Shimon Peres, a man who enjoyed adulation amongst many in the West. They would do well to google the Qana massacre in southern Lebanon, an abhorrent act of barbarity that he once famously said he was at ‘peace’ with (no pun intended). See also Ehud Olmert, who, whilst being relatively outspoken against the ongoing genocide in Gaza (not using that language, of course), oversaw the targeted assassination of Palestinian leaders, the 2006 war in Lebanon and the continued expansion of illegal Israeli settlements. Former Prime Minister Ehud Barak was threatened with arrest whilst visiting the UK in 2009 over allegations of war crimes committed in Gaza while he was defence minister. Others, including Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, have made it very clear that they have little to no interest in making ‘peace’ with Palestinians, nor even in countenancing the notion that there would ever be a Palestinian state.
What should be abundantly clear, therefore, is that for Palestinians, as Elaine Bradley and I have previously argued, the passing of time can be mapped on to a series of failed ‘peace’ processes, from Madrid to Oslo to Wye River to Camp David. The consistent theme has been the creeping erasure of Palestine and a doubling down of the West’s support for Israel’s expansive settler colonial aims.
I don’t say any of this whimsically, but those who are advocating for Palestine must be far more critical in their analysis than simply hoping for change based on the possible downfall of Netanyahu.
If you are committed to Palestinian liberation, you must shun any false ‘hope’ that comes with the appointment of a new political leader in Israel. It is a mirage and an unhelpful distraction. No matter who is in charge, without a fundamental reckoning with the racist ideology that undergirds the Zionist state-building project and a full dismantling of the architectures of militarisation and apartheid, things will continue along the same path. Our role, therefore, is not to place any false hope in a change of leadership inside Israel, but to double down on our efforts to ensure we do all at our disposal to support inevitable Palestinian liberation.

Factbox-Spain’s deadliest train disasters
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:16:23 CET
21:16:23 KST

Oct 28 (Reuters) - At least 30 people were killed when two high-speed trains collided south of Toledo in Spain on Wednesday, regional authorities said.
It is the second deadly accident in less than a year on the line and will likely raise further questions over the country’s train infrastructure ahead of November’s snap election.
Here are some of Spain’s deadliest train disasters, starting from the most recent:
ADAMUZ (2026)
Forty six people died and more than 120 were injured in southern Spain after a high-speed train derailed and collided with an oncoming one on January 18 near Adamuz, in the province of Cordoba.
The accident is still under investigation. A preliminary report by Spain’s Civil Guard in February pointed to defects in the track, rail or weld between two sections of track as the main hypothesis for the accident, but kept seven other theories open.
SANTIAGO DE COMPOSTELA (2013)
A railway accident in the summer of 2013 left 80 people dead and 145 injured when an eight-carriage high-speed train veered off the track on a sharp bend near the northwestern city of Santiago de Compostela, slamming into a concrete wall and bursting into flames.
A Transport Ministry commission concluded that the accident was caused by speeding and the driver being distracted by a call from a superior, but a victims’ association blamed the accident not only on human error but also on the railway’s security systems.
MADRID COMMUTER TRAIN BOMBINGS (2004)
On March 11, 2004, 10 backpack bombs detonated on four Cercanias commuter trains, killing 193 people and injuring thousands of others during Madrid’s rush hour. The attacks were carried out by Islamists opposing Spain’s participation in the Iraq war.
EL CUERVO (1972)
An accident caused by a head-on collision between two trains on the Cadiz-Seville route left 86 people dead and more than 150 injured near the southern town of El Cuervo in 1972. The accident was caused by a driver’s failure to stop at a red light at El Cuervo station, according to an investigation by state-owned rail operator Renfe.
URDULIZ (1970)
A head-on collision of two trains killed 33 people in the town of Urduliz, near the northern city of Bilbao, in the summer of 1970. A stationmaster was initially blamed for the accident, but it later emerged that he had been working 16-hour shifts for the previous four days.
GRISEN (1965)
A train on the Madrid-Barcelona route caught fire in 1965 in the town of Grisen, near northeastern Zaragoza, killing dozens of passengers. Though the train operator said at the time that 30 people died, later reports have said the real death toll was up to 80 and that the Francoist leadership tried to play it down.
TORRE DEL BIERZO (1944)
The 1944 crash of three trains in the El Bierzo region of León province is considered one of the deadliest railway disasters in Spain, with the estimated death toll of 78 still being debated due to censorship under Francisco Franco.
A train travelling from Madrid to A Coruña suffered a brake failure and collided with a locomotive inside a tunnel, just before a third train entered the same gallery and crashed into the wreckage.
(Compiled by Mirko Miorelli and Javi West Larrañaga in Gdansk; Editing by Milla Nissi-Prussak and Alison Williams)

Reuters, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Sea drones struck a container ship off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast on Wednesday, the ship’s owner and the government said, the latest in a string of attacks that have raised concerns about the growing scope of Russia’s war in Ukraine.
It was not clear who carried out the attack on the Greek ship that was sailing under the Liberian flag in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ), or what the vessel’s 421 containers were carrying.

A maritime security source with knowledge of the matter said the ship had been badly damaged and was listing.
INTERNATIONAL CONCERN
Drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria have likely killed some two dozen international seafarers in recent weeks, according to government statements on missing crew members. At least six merchant vessels have been attacked.
The strikes have been in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, an area that stretches beyond Bulgaria’s waters but where the country holds sole rights to explore and manage resources.
The attacks have prompted international condemnation and concern about the growing reach of the war in Ukraine. Bulgaria, a member of the European Union and NATO, has sought allied assistance to bolster maritime security.
Ukraine has blamed the attacks on Russia and Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said the attacks appear to benefit Russia, but Moscow has denied involvement.
In a sign of the international concern, Turkish Defence Minister Yasar Guler warned Russia and Ukraine on Wednesday against carrying out attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea. He said Ankara reserved the right to take legal action against the strikes.
