====================================================================================================

Men and women report similar levels of “duty sex,” and similar reasons behind it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:00:50 UTC
20:00:50 KST

People have sex for many reasons beyond physical pleasure or having children, and sometimes those reasons involve a sense of obligation. A new study published in Evolutionary Psychology suggests that individuals who worry their partner might cheat, who see their partner as a more desirable catch than themselves, or who experience higher levels of emotional instability tend to report having sex out of duty more often. The findings are consistent with the idea that obligation-based sex may function as a strategy to keep a romantic relationship intact when people sense it might be at risk.
“Duty sex” refers to consensual sexual activity motivated by a feeling of obligation rather than personal desire. People typically engage in duty sex to maintain their romantic relationship, protect their partner’s feelings, avoid an argument, or prevent their partner from leaving. While this behavior is related to the broader psychological concept of sexual compliance, which covers any consensual sex that a person does not actively desire, duty sex specifically describes encounters driven by a sense of duty to one’s partner.
Although engaging in sex out of obligation is relatively common in romantic relationships, it often comes with emotional drawbacks. Prior research has linked duty sex to lower sexual satisfaction among women, and sexual satisfaction tends to go hand in hand with relationship satisfaction and well-being. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 found that women with a history of nonconsensual sexual experiences were 35 percent more likely to report frequent duty sex and experienced higher levels of sexual pain and lower sexual satisfaction than women without such histories.
To better understand what drives people to have sex out of obligation, F. Sid Dougan, a doctoral candidate in evolutionary psychology in the Buss Evolutionary Psychology Lab at the University of Texas at Austin, teamed up with Kate B. Metcalfe and Cindy M. Meston, who conducted that 2024 study, to examine the behavior from an evolutionary perspective.
“My colleagues, Kate Metcalfe and Dr. Cindy Meston, were already doing great work investigating Duty Sex from a clinical perspective, and they kindly invited me to share my thoughts on the subject,” Dougan told PsyPost. “Some past research had looked at certain factors that are associated with greater engagement in Duty Sex, but what I thought was missing from the puzzle was ‘why’ people engage in Duty Sex. To an Evolutionary Biologist/Psychologist like me, this means asking questions about ultimate evolutionary function – that is, what reproductive advantages might this behavior have provided over our evolutionary history? I wanted to know if Duty Sex serves an ultimate function, and if so, what that function is.”
From an evolutionary perspective, losing a partner would have carried steep costs for our ancestors’ chances of passing on their genes. Evolutionary psychologists argue that this pressure favored what they call mate retention tactics, which are behaviors aimed at keeping a partner invested in the relationship and preventing a breakup.
These relationship-preserving tactics generally fall into two categories. Cost-inflicting behaviors attempt to stop a partner from leaving by lowering their self-esteem or limiting their social options through tactics such as insults, putting down rivals, or even violence. Benefit-provisioning behaviors, on the other hand, aim to make the relationship more rewarding by showering a partner with gifts, affection, or compliments. The authors of the new study proposed that duty sex acts as a benefit-provisioning tactic, using sexual access to keep a partner satisfied and committed when the relationship feels threatened.
If duty sex is a tool for holding onto a mate, people should be more inclined to use it when they sense their relationship is in danger. One major threat to any romantic partnership is infidelity, which frequently leads to breakups. Another potential threat is a mismatch in what psychologists call mate value, which is a person’s overall desirability as a romantic or sexual partner based on traits like attractiveness, status, and personality. When someone believes their partner has a higher mate value than they do, they may worry that their partner will eventually leave them for a more desirable alternative.
Individual personality traits can also shape how people respond to relationship insecurities. Neuroticism is a core personality trait characterized by emotional instability, anxiety, and a tendency to experience negative emotions. People who score high in neuroticism tend to be especially sensitive to signs of rejection and worry more about losing their partners. Because prior work on duty sex focused mostly on women, Dougan and his team wanted to test whether infidelity fears, mate value gaps, and neuroticism predict duty sex across both men and women.
To test these predictions, the researchers recruited 252 sexually active university students between the ages of 18 and 24, with an average age of about 19. The sample included 176 women and 76 men who were all currently dating at least one partner and had engaged in vaginal, anal, or oral sex within the past four weeks. About three-quarters of the participants were in committed relationships, while the rest were casually dating, and the average relationship length was just under 15 months.
Participants completed a 45-minute online survey that measured their sexual motives, relationship perceptions, and personality traits. To measure duty sex, the researchers used a four-item questionnaire asking how often participants had sex out of fear that their partner would stop loving them, get angry with them, not want to be with them, or leave them. Responses were totaled on a scale ranging from 4 to 20, where a score of 4 meant the participant almost never or never had sex for any of those obligation-based reasons.
To gauge infidelity concerns, participants estimated the percentage likelihood, from 0 to 100 percent, that their partner would engage in five behaviors with someone else: going on a romantic date, kissing, having a one-night stand, having a brief affair, or having a long-term affair. Participants also rated their own overall desirability as a partner and their partner’s desirability on a 7-point scale, allowing the researchers to calculate the discrepancy between the two scores. Finally, participants completed a brief personality assessment to measure their levels of neuroticism.
Overall, most participants reported engaging in duty sex rarely. On the 4-to-20 scale, women averaged a score of 5.24 and men averaged 4.76, and the researchers found no statistically significant difference between men and women in how frequently they engaged in duty sex overall.
That lack of a gap between men and women was unexpected for Dougan. “A big difference between men and women across cultures is that men have much higher sex drives than women on average,” he explained. “Therefore, engaging in sex with a male romantic partner might be an especially effective mate retention tactic for women, but less so for men with female romantic partners, given women’s lower sex drives. For this reason, I thought that women might engage in more Duty Sex than men on average.”
When looking at the combined sample of men and women, all three of the researchers’ main predictions were supported. Participants who perceived a higher probability that their partner might cheat reported engaging in more duty sex, a pattern that held true when analyzing women and men separately. On average, women estimated an 11 percent chance of partner infidelity, while men estimated just under 10 percent, and higher estimates tracked with higher duty sex scores.
“Sex isn’t always motivated by desires for physical and emotional pleasure,” Dougan said. “People have sex for all sorts of reasons, and our findings suggest that one of these reasons is to prevent their romantic partners from straying elsewhere.”
These findings align with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which found that experimentally triggering fears of a partner cheating increased jealousy and made people more likely to use both affectionate and controlling mate retention behaviors over the following month. While that earlier study examined broad relationship maintenance behaviors following an experimentally induced threat rather than obligation-based sex specifically, both studies link concerns about unfaithfulness to efforts to preserve a relationship.
Perceiving oneself as less desirable than one’s partner was also associated with higher duty sex scores across the combined sample. When the researchers analyzed the sexes separately, this link was statistically detectable among women, with duty sex increasing most noticeably among women who viewed themselves as substantially less desirable than their partners. While the association was not statistically significant within the male group alone, a direct statistical comparison between men and women showed no significant difference in how mate value gaps related to duty sex across the sexes.
This pattern is consistent with recent work on how desirability gaps shape sexual behavior. A study covered by PsyPost earlier this year found that women who view their partner as more desirable than themselves report a stronger drive to sexually satisfy them, which was indirectly linked to initiating sex more often, performing oral sex, and faking orgasms.
Similarly, a 2025 study covered by PsyPost found that men who see themselves as having lower mate value than their partners perform oral sex more frequently, a link explained by a stronger motivation to keep their partners sexually satisfied. Although those two studies focused on specific sexual acts driven by a desire to please a partner rather than sex motivated by obligation, they similarly suggest that feeling outmatched by a partner is linked to using sex as a relationship maintenance strategy.
Personality also played a role in the new study, as both men and women who scored higher in neuroticism reported engaging in more duty sex. This association remained present even when accounting for infidelity fears and mate value discrepancies, suggesting that neuroticism is linked to duty sex beyond what those relationship worries explain. However, the researchers noted that the size of this effect was modest, meaning that duty sex scores rose only slightly across the spectrum of neuroticism when other factors were held constant.
The researchers also looked at whether relationship length and commitment level were linked to duty sex. How long a couple had been together was not statistically related to duty sex for either men or women. Being in a committed relationship rather than casually dating was linked to more duty sex in the combined sample and among men, which the authors suggest may reflect the higher stakes of losing a partner when people have more invested. However, the difference between men and women on this measure was not statistically significant, and far fewer participants were casually dating, so the authors advise caution in interpreting this pattern.
Together, the main statistical model accounted for about 29 percent of the variation in duty sex scores across the sample.
“I think the practical significance of our findings is that Duty Sex shouldn’t automatically be viewed as something negative or dysfunctional,” Dougan noted. “We often assume that people should only engage in sex when they’re experiencing sexual desire, but sexual behavior can serve functions beyond immediate sexual gratification. Consensually engaging in sex to strengthen bonds within a romantic relationship might be a perfectly understandable response to the possibility of losing a valued partner. Our findings will hopefully encourage people to think about this behavior in terms of what motivates it, rather than simply assuming it’s always a problem.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. Average duty sex scores sat very close to the minimum possible score of 4, so most participants rarely had sex out of obligation. The results indicate that when duty sex does occur, it tends to show up among people experiencing heightened relationship insecurities or emotional instability.
Dougan also cautioned against reading the findings as advice. “Natural selection works in the currency of reproductive success, not happiness or ethical conduct,” he told PsyPost. “Therefore, I really want to emphasize that explaining why a behavior might have evolved is not the same as saying that people ought to engage in it. Our study does not imply that people who aren’t experiencing sexual desire should still have sex with their romantic partners simply because doing so might help maintain their relationships.”
Because the study surveyed participants at a single point in time, it cannot establish cause and effect. For example, while worrying about infidelity might lead someone to have sex out of obligation, it is also possible that preexisting relationship problems cause both infidelity fears and duty sex simultaneously. In addition, the sample included only 76 men compared to 176 women, which gave the researchers less statistical power to detect smaller effects among men and makes it harder to draw firm conclusions about potential differences between the sexes.
The reliance on young university students in relatively new relationships also means the findings might not apply to older adults or married couples who have been together for decades. Nor did the researchers measure whether participants were experiencing emotional manipulation or relationship abuse. If an abusive partner intentionally insults someone to make them feel undesirable and replaceable, that manipulation could artificially inflate the gap in perceived mate value and pressure the victim into having sex out of fear or obligation.
Some of the measures were also fairly limited. Neuroticism was assessed with only two questions, which showed modest statistical reliability. The four duty sex questions focused entirely on fear-based motives, such as worrying a partner will get angry, lose feelings, or leave. That focus means the measure does not capture sex driven by a calmer, proactive sense of duty, and its overlap with worries about a partner straying could strengthen the apparent link between the two.
Future studies could track couples over time to see whether duty sex actually works as a strategy to prevent breakups, or if it breeds resentment and lowers satisfaction in the long run. The authors also suggest that future work should separate passive duty sex, where someone goes along with a partner’s request for sex to avoid a fight, from active duty sex, where someone intentionally initiates sex to keep their partner happy and secure.
“Looking forward, I’d like to conduct studies that distinguish between what I call ‘active’ and ‘passive’ Duty Sex,” Dougan said. “These two forms likely have very different motivations and consequences, in terms of individual wellbeing and relationship stability. Exploring this could provide valuable insights into understanding when Duty Sex might be beneficial or harmful to individuals and their relationships, and how best to address it in clinical settings.”
The study, “Who Engages in Duty Sex?—Infidelity Concerns and Mate Value Discrepancies,” was authored by F. Sid Dougan, Kate B. Metcalfe, and Cindy M. Meston.

How Trump Could Interfere With the Midterms on Election Day, and the Days After
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

With less than a week until Election Day, the Trump administration is ramping up efforts to shape the outcomes, prompting concerns that the midterm elections could face unprecedented interference by federal authorities.
In recent days, Trump officials have sued to potentially block the certification of a Senate race in Alaska, threatened election officials in California with jail time, and implied that the outcome in a Senate race in Minnesota couldn’t be trusted if the Republican didn’t win. Trump’s allies have also been urging the President to potentially take drastic measures, including declaring martial law to seize ballots.
Election officials in dozens of states are preparing for a wide range of possible interference on Tuesday when millions of voters will cast ballots, as well as in the days that follow as the votes are counted, the final batches of mail-in ballots come in and the election outcomes are certified.
The prospect of so many challenges has led to intense efforts by voting rights groups, election officials and teams of lawyers to be ready to respond to election meddling anywhere in the country.
Here’s how the Trump Administration could potentially interfere in each step of the election process—and how state and local officials, and various outside groups, are preparing for each scenario:
Polls open for in-person voting
Election workers are preparing for possible federal interference both inside and outside polling places on Tuesday.
Over the past few months, officials from the Trump Administration have given vague answers when asked if the Administration might try to deploy federal agents to the polls. Federal laws explicitly prohibit military or federal officials from stationing troops or armed men where elections are held in an attempt to interfere with a federal election. Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine assured a Democratic senator in late August that the military had “no plan” to be deployed to polling locations during the midterm elections. Yet Trump has declined to rule out measures such as declaring a federal emergency on Election Day or sending ICE agents to the polls, telling TIME in an interview in September that he didn’t “rule anything out” at this point.
At least three lawsuits have been filed to preemptively block ICE agents from being deployed to polling sites on Election Day. According to one of the lawsuits, at least one county sheriffs’ office in Colorado has already been cooperating with ICE and conducted “warrant checks at polling locations” this year.
Along with the prospect of ICE agents conducting immigration enforcement, election officials have also expressed concern that the federal government might try other ways to disrupt polling places, citing voter fraud allegations as a premise. For months, the Administration has been involved in a legal fight with dozens of states over allegations that noncitizens are on their voter rolls. Election experts say voter fraud is incredibly rare. 
In some local communities, there are indications that federal agents showing up at polling locations could sow chaos at the polls. Virginia’s Arlington County stated in its preemptive legal filing against federal agents at the polls that the county had developed plans regarding “whether and how to make arrests, and any prosecutorial response or civil legal actions that might be necessary.”
“Arlington has never before needed to prepare for these threat scenarios,” the filing adds. When reached for a statement, the Arlington County government says the local police department remains in contact with election officials and is prepared to respond to any reported incidents.
Polls close and ballot counting begins
As polling stations close Tuesday evening, local election officials and voting rights groups are bracing for the prospect of federal officials possibly seizing election materials and voting machines. In January, the FBI raided the Fulton County election office in Georgia and seized election materials in connection with the 2020 election. In May, a federal judge ruled that the federal government could continue to retain the ballots. The FBI has not announced any wrongdoing stemming from the investigation.
“The lesson of Fulton County was that you have to be ready to be in court literally in minutes,” Norm Eisen, co-founder and executive chair of Democracy Defenders Action, tells TIME. Eisen has been working closely with voting rights groups as well as local and state election officials in multiple states to prepare for any federal interference in next week’s elections. That includes being ready to immediately file lawsuits as soon as any federal officials try to seize any ballots or voting machines.
Other legal scholars are also encouraging judges to consider alternative solutions if federal authorities seek to retain election materials. Rick Hasen, a law professor and director of UCLA’s Safeguarding Democracy Project, published a white paper urging judges who might see warrant applications for ballot seizure to consider ordering copies of the ballot to allow the election certification process to continue.
Waiting for the last batches of mail-in ballots
Many mail-in votes won’t arrive until days after Election Day. Some will be from members of the military stationed overseas. The fight over who can receive mail-in ballots, and which mail-in ballots should be counted, has been underway for most of Trump’s second term.
In March, President Trump signed an executive order requiring states to work with the United States Postal Services to establish lists of verified voters and asking USPS to withhold mail ballots from anyone not on the lists. The executive order was quickly met with a flurry of lawsuits, which resulted in a preliminary injunction blocking the USPS from enforcing any new rules in response to Trump’s order.
But election officials are still preparing for the possibility that some federal officials may try to get in the way of mail-in ballots being counted. On Monday, the DOJ asked the state of Washington to not count ballots from more than 400 voters whom it suspects to be noncitizens, as more than 1 million ballots have already been cast.
Even with the federal effort on hold, state governments have pressed ahead with new rules that are already pushing ballot rejection rates higher. In North Carolina, the State Board of Elections implemented a new rule that requires voters to use at least three different envelopes to deliver their ballots and copies of their ID. Failure to seal any of the three envelopes would result in the ballot being rejected. So far, the state is already seeing an uptick in the ballot rejection rate compared to the previous election cycle, from 2.6% to 3.1% statewide, according to local media outlets.
Certifying the election results
After all the votes are tabulated, county officials will begin certifying the election results. Although each state has its own rules on raising and resolving a challenge from county officials, certifying the election results is a mandatory duty. According to the Campaign Legal Center, if an official delays or refuses to certify results, state officials and courts can step in to compel certification. State officials can also pursue criminal or civil penalties to hold local officials accountable. 
On Thursday, the Justice Department preemptively sued the state government of Alaska to block the certification of its closely-watched Senate race if Republican incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses to Democrat Mary Peltola. The department accused the state of failing to “protect the integrity of the election” by allowing independent candidate Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot.
“The DOJ attempting to intervene at this late stage is entirely against department policy, as there is no legitimate enforcement of federal law here, and it raises serious concerns about political interference,” said David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation and Research. “I cannot recall an administration ever attempting to stop the certification of an election — and certainly not 11 days before polls close.”
Various election officials expect that Alaska won’t be the only state that says a certification challenge. During the 2020 election, President Trump sought to pressure Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to undo the state’s certification of Joe Biden’s win and “find 11,780 votes”—the number needed to overturn his loss in Georgia. Trump’s allies also led a pressure campaign, meeting with lawmakers in Michigan, Pennsylvania, Georgia, and Arizona in an attempt to overturn the election results, according to the investigation by the bipartisan January 6 committee.
Correction, Oct. 28
The original version of this story misstated Norm Eisen's title. He is the co-founder and executive chair of Democracy Defenders Action, not its executive director.

Underrepresentation of Non-Native English Speakers in Philosophy: Findings from over 100,000 Papers (guest post)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

The “largest and most systematic study of linguistic inequity in academic philosophy to date” was recently published.
Its authors are Neri Marsili (University of Turin) and Paul Rehren (Max Planck Institute).
In the following guest post, they share some of their findings.
Underrepresentation of Non-Native English Speakers in Analytic Philosophy: Findings from over 100,000 Papers
by Neri Marsili and Paul Rehren
It’s no secret that a good command of English is a prerequisite for a successful career in analytic philosophy. But what if English isn’t your first language? As many non-native English speakers (“non-natives”, for short) can attest, having learnt English as a second language can create friction at every stage of your academic career, from your first days as a student to tenure and beyond. Yet while obstacles tied to gender or race have long been recognised in the profession (and rightly so), disadvantages due to native language have only recently begun to attract attention and research.
So, for example, a recent survey of more than 1,600 philosophers (discussed on this very blog last year) found that non-native English speaking scholars on average need twice as long to read a paper in English and nearly twice as long to prepare a talk (even controlling for proficiency). The hurdles, however, don’t stop at manuscript preparation. Getting published isn’t easy either: non-native authors only accounted for 31% of the authors in 18 philosophy journals between 2013 and 2017—not much, considering philosophy is done all over the world. Those who are lucky enough to get published still get comparatively little attention. Among the 500 most cited works in four leading generalist journals, only 5.8% were by non-native philosophers.
While this research offers valuable insights, it has important limitations—perhaps inevitably so, given how new this area of study still is. The papers and blog posts just cited looked at relatively narrow samples, covering relatively short periods of time; they reported only raw percentages (which say little about representation) and did little to pin down what causes the gap between native and non-native speakers.
Our Study
At a workshop on corpus methods back in 2021, it struck me (Neri) that most of these limitations could be overcome by studying the problem at scale. Paul Rehren turned out to have exactly the data we needed. Our study, just published in Research Integrity and Peer Review, covers over 100,000 English-language articles published in more than 200 philosophy journals between 1975 and 2021.
Here’s how we did it. Since we obviously couldn’t check every author’s native language one by one, we used two proxies: whether the author works in an English-speaking country, and whether they got their PhD in one. This method is inexact, of course. Still, when we checked a random sample by hand, both proxies were right about nine times out of ten: imprecise, but not too bad.
Next, we needed a baseline: to quantify underrepresentation, we needed to establish the percentage of non-native philosophers in the profession. To estimate this, we turned to PhilPeople. Using the country for current academic staff as a proxy, we estimated this share at just over half (53%). We suspect, however, that the real share is substantially higher, since PhilPeople, by its own account, has “heavier coverage in Anglophone countries”. This matters for what you’re about to read: our estimates of underrepresentation are likely very conservative.
What does the data say? Overall, non-native authors come fairly close to “parity”—having a share of publications proportional to their share of the professional population—on one proxy (where they work, about 9/10 of what one would expect if they were equally well represented), and less close on the other (where they got their PhD, just over half). Before concluding that their underrepresentation is overstated, though, consider what this means. Nobody ever suggested that non-native philosophers struggle to publish anywhere. Surely you can place a paper in the least selective journal of your discipline even if your English prose doesn’t display the “flair, elegance, or vivacity” of a native speaker. What matters, by any reasonable standard, are the journals at the top: these are the publications that get you a decent readership, and that matter for hiring, funding and professional recognition.
We defined top journals in two ways: broadly, as the thirty or so journals ranked in the Leiter Reports polls, and narrowly, as the “Big Four”: Philosophical Review, Mind, Noûs and Journal of Philosophy. Once we focus on these subsets, the picture changes. In the broader group, non-native authors publish either half as much or a quarter as much as their numbers would predict (depending on the proxy, see Figure 2). In the Big Four, they publish between 12% and 38% of what you would expect. (We also looked at a third definition of top journals based on citation impact, which produced similar results).
One cool feature of our dataset is that it covers almost five decades, so we can look at how differences evolve over time. Things are improving, but it doesn’t look great where it matters. Since 1975, representation in lower-ranked journals has improved a lot, to the point of near parity (classifying authors by where they work). Representation in the top journals has improved, too, but that change has been quite a bit slower. As a result, since 1975 the gap between the top and bottom journals has become much wider.
What explains the gap?
With our data, we could test three potential explanations for the gap between top journals and other journals.
The first hypothesis is a familiar story, which some readers of this blog have suggested in other discussions as an innocent explanation of the gap. Maybe non-native authors simply write less polished English, and top journals are pickier about style. If so, the gap should be larger for authors whose first language is very different from English and who consequently have a harder time learning it, such as Japanese or Korean, and smaller for closer languages like Dutch. There is a slight trend in that direction, but it is weak, and it is driven almost entirely by a few outliers closest to English (mostly Norwegian and Swedish authors). Language quality doesn’t seem to be a major driver of underrepresentation, at least by our (admittedly crude) measure of linguistic distance.
The second hypothesis is that non-native authors face active discrimination from reviewers. We tested this through a natural experiment. Over the past few decades, some top journals switched from open or single-anonymous review to double- or triple-anonymous review. If reviewers were penalizing authors for their non-native background, non-native representation should go up after the switch. Which is exactly what we found. Classified by where authors work, representation jumped from around a fifth to around a third of what parity requires. Classified by PhD institution, the change, though also positive, is much smaller and statistically uncertain. (On the assumption of active discrimination, this pattern would be somewhat unsurprising, since unblinded manuscripts show authors’ affiliations, but not where authors got their PhDs.)
Let’s keep in mind, too, that anonymous review hides a bunch of things at once: the author’s name, their institution, its prestige, the country where it’s based. To call this discrimination against non-natives (as opposed to discrimination that affects non-natives) might be a bit of a stretch, as the effect might be driven by a few compounding factors (we discuss more limitations in the paper). Still, what we detected is certainly consistent with some form of discrimination.
The third hypothesis is that non-native English speakers simply have different interests. Top journals are quite particular about the topics they deem worthy of their attention: they publish mostly metaphysics and epistemology, and very little from what PhilPapers calls “philosophical traditions” (continental and non-Western philosophy, for instance). Perhaps this mix of subfields caters better to the interests of native authors than to those of non-natives, and this contributes to the gap. According to our data, this conjecture is not far off: the work of non-native authors is comparatively more concentrated in the areas top journals publish least, and less concentrated in the areas they publish most.
It would be naive, however, to read this as an indication that non-native authors and their idiosyncratic interests are to blame for the gap. What a journal publishes is in large part an editorial choice. What seems like poor strategy from the native’s side might equally be read as self-serving topic selection by editorial boards whose interests reflect the Anglophone institutions in which they are based.
What this Shows and What Can Be Done
Our study has significant limitations. Our proxies are noisy. We have no data on books. Above all, we don’t have submission data, so we can’t measure how much of the gap comes from non-native philosophers submitting fewer papers to top journals. Even so, this is the largest and most systematic study of linguistic inequity in academic philosophy to date. With all its limitations, it confirms the picture painted by earlier work: non-native philosophers are underrepresented in the journals that matter most, and the gap is getting wider.
What can be done to improve the situation? Our data suggest that increasing anonymity on top journals that haven’t yet transitioned to triple blind could help. More anonymity would be a good idea anyway, given our profession’s problem with prestige bias. Top journals could also appoint more people from outside the English-speaking world to their editorial boards: currently, only about 4% of the editors of fifteen prominent journals work at institutions outside Anglophone countries. If boards better reflected the actual composition of the profession, there’s a chance that their editorial choices (which subfields they focus on, which level of English they deem stylistically acceptable) might too, giving non-native scholars a fairer shot at publishing. Finally, the Barcelona Principles for a Globally Inclusive Philosophy ask very little of journals and institutions: it wouldn’t hurt if more journals signed up. We’d get an extra perk, too: since the Principles recommend collecting statistics on submissions by non-native speakers, we’d finally get the data we need to settle some of the questions that our study left open.

Why do flamingos dance while they eat? This scientist found out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Why do flamingos dance while they eat? This scientist found out
On a family trip to Atlanta, Víctor Ortega Jiménez spent time taking pictures and videos of flamingos as they fed in their pond. It wasn’t to admire their long legs or flamboyant pink color. Instead, he noticed the “beautiful” ripples spreading across the water as the birds ate under the surface. But he didn’t know why the waves were happening.
It took “more than four years to answer that question,” says Ortega Jiménez, of the University of California, Berkeley. “But I think the answer was fascinating.”
Ortega Jiménez’s focus is biomechanics, or the study of how mechanics applies to animal movement and structure. His goal is to understand how animal behaviors might lead to human-made engineering feats.
He discovered that, by retracting their heads, flamingos produce vortexlike traps with water to scoop up algae. They stomp around — or dance, if you will — amplifying the vortex. The series of motions brings the food to their crooked beaks. The beaks then filter in food, releasing silt and mud.
The impressive process can weed out particles the size of a single cell. This kind of self-cleaning filter for extremely small particles can be applied to remove microplastics and so-called forever chemicals called PFAS from water, Ortega Jiménez says.
“Nature is always full of secrets,” he says. “And I think that’s the riddle that keeps me going, trying to understand nature. That’s my way to see science: by observation and trying to be inspired and trying to solve a problem.”

Sauerkraut at Every Meal? These Fermentation Fanatics Tried That Long Before MAHA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Waking early, I put a small jar of my sauerkraut into my messenger bag, hop on my bicycle, ride to Seattle's King Street Station, and board a train heading to the Portland Fermentation Festival, the yearly gathering affectionately nicknamed “Stinkfest.”
Usually the sheer existence of a festival like this is enough to get people revved up to come together and talk about their favorite ferments, but in an interesting twist, fermented foods are enjoying a popularity boost from a different crowd. The MAHA movement, and particularly the Donald Trump cabinet, are big into fermented food, eating meat, usually steak, with fermented sides like kimchi or sauerkraut at every meal.
I've come to Portland, Oregon, wondering if there was going to be any overlap in the Venn diagram between festival attendees and the MAHA steak-and-ferment crowd. I mentioned this to my cousin-in-law Erick, who's been part of the Portland food scene for years, and he laughed out loud.
“It'll be more like a Venn dumbbell,” he said, making a pair of thumb-and-forefinger circles and tracing a line in the air between them. “No overlap, but food will be the bridge.”
Still, I was curious. I’d check.
The festival is almost exactly what the fermentation-friendly might hope to find. Right inside the main door next to the check-in desk is a bacterial petting zoo—pure festival charm—and a table where attendees can drop off their own ferments to share. Further on, lining every wall of the main room, are exhibitors who have paid a grand total of 25 bucks for a table, handing out free samples of fermented foods.
The space quickly fills up–several hundred people flow through over the course of the evening–and it appears that there's both a line in front of each exhibitor and perhaps a more organic continuous line with people flowing clockwise from one exhibitor to the next. People are notably excited and happy. There's a kid walking around with a tray of handmade pickle pins he's giving people to wear and there's a collective gasp when 20 or 30 minutes in, Dillon T. Pickle, the mascot of the Portland Pickles West Coast League baseball team, walks into the room. At one point, a big baby crawls across most of the main floor, unhindered and happy.
In the middle of it all is festival co-organizer, journalist, and cookbook author Liz Crain. She explains that the Fest, now in its 14th installment, was started in 2009 by friends who love to ferment. There were members of a little company called Picklopolis and a club called The Kraut Collective, and, with some help from author and fermentation rockstar Sandor Katz, they launched a Portland tradition.
When I ask how the festival has evolved since its first year, she gets a little philosophical.
“Keep Portland Weird. People get excited,” she says in a tone where several punctuation options would be in the spirit of the festival. “People lined up on the sidewalk all the way around the building for the first one. I poured hard cider that I made from a tree in my backyard.”
“There's nothing for sale, and that gives it a potluck-y party style. Most big festivals have consumers and purveyors, but without those distinctions here, it makes conversations a bit deeper, a bit more personal,” she says. “There's no gatekeeping, no secret recipes. It's always been wacky and fun.”
She isn't sure how much MAHA crossover I'll encounter, but she has an openness to it.
“RFK is certainly infatuated with sauerkraut and steak. There's some good to be found in the overall MAHA tenets, but so much of it has been muddied by the anti-vax stance and ludicrous conspiracy theories,” she says, though she believes it's important to “look closely and critically at pesticides and favor less-processed foods.”
“But a diet that's based solely on meat, particularly beef, animal fats, and sauerkraut … well that's not a very diverse diet,” she says. “Let's just say I wouldn't want to sit next to that person on a plane or be stuck in an elevator with them.”
I pick up on these ideas with Chris Curtin, a fermentation microbiology researcher at Oregon State University.
“Historically, everything has shown that narrowing the scope of your diet misses some things. They don't turn out to be the best in the long run,” he says. An Australian living in the US for the last decade, he can clearly see the way trends are moving and notes that registered dietitians have consistently put fermented foods at the top of their superfood lists for the past decade.
Curtin describes his work as caring about what happens when we mess around with microbes to see what happens to the raw material. As he puts it, "I'm interested in tinkering if it involves microbe wrangling." He also gets the festival's popularity among those who ferment.
“Fermenting is such a readily accessible scientific experiment that you can do in your kitchen. People go, find foods they like and want to make in their own kitchens. It's accessible and tactile.”
This plays out at the festival as I begin to sample the merchandise. The first thing I taste is an “orange whey Julius” that includes whey and OJ and is pleasingly reminiscent of the Orange Julius I'd get as a treat as a kid at the Mall of New Hampshire.
Next to that is Nat West's booth with Peruvian corn beer called chicha. West has run a cider company, dabbled in politics, driven a TriMet city bus in Portland, and now runs the Vancouver, Washington, farmers’ market. In a chicha, the fermentation starts by the brewer chewing ground field corn. At the festival, attendees are drinking what West has chewed. As people in line joke about drinking this guy's spit, or at least the byproducts of it, West interjects, “nobody's died yet!”
“The ptyalin enzymes in the saliva kickstart the starch-to-sugar process,” he explains as I take a sip and gaze longingly at the draft beer in the hands of someone who's wandered into the show from the Hotlips pizza next door.
Further along, Portland's Jorinji Miso has a double booth with samples of miso soup with bonito flakes along with koji (rice fermented with Aspergillus oryzae spores) and amazake, a koji-based drink.
The couple who run Maypop Wine Co. have their hands full at the Fest. The company’s cofounder Vince Kelsea explains that they make “anything but pinot” in the Willamette Valley—a lush north-south valley in Oregon renowned for its pinot noir. Making unfiltered, low-intervention wines like Maypop in a region famous for its pinot sounds like they're making things hard for themselves, but the attendees maintain a several-deep line at the booth all night long.
In one corner is Kiyomi Hasagewa, a third-generation Japanese bean purveyor. She’s sharing tastes of a 15-year-old miso she dehydrated and ground so she could bring it from Hokkaido to the festival. She sprinkles it over the rice and tops it with a wedge of sun-dried daikon which her elderly mother fermented in a mashed pumpkin paste. It is easily the most interesting bite in the room.
Back in the entry hall are my personal favorites, the ferments that attendees have brought to share. Liz Crain has brought along plum and dandelion wines, pickle brine, a blackberry-blueberry-lemon water kefir, and a monster jar of sour dills. I note with pride that the jar of sauerkraut I brought is next to Liz’s pickles, near-empty. Nearby is another giant jar of “fermented carrot coins, cherry bomb, garlic, ginger, horseradish,” which I anticipate as a pleasant assault on my senses, but it's really just pleasant. A garlic blast for sure, but one with all of the harsh edges smoothed by time and beneficial bacteria into something lovely.
Also at the community table are Portland occupational therapist Eva Ortega and her fermentation buddy Letti Kittel who drove down from Seattle.
“I've only made unsuccessful ferments so far,” says Ortega, undeterred. “I'm here to learn.”
Kittel says she's been nerding out on fermenting for about a year and has brought a kombucha starter with its bacteria-and-yeast scoby for others to bring home and try. And while both of them have no comment about the MAHA connection, Ortega puts some of Kittel's starter in a little jar and drops it into her purse.
I'm expecting another round of “no comment” when the MAHA diet comes up with three other fermenting friends, Megan Andricos, Josh Monifi, and Desiré Demarest, but Andricos, aka DJ Sappho, followed a similar diet 20 years ago in what they call their “fermented-pickled food and protein phase,” which consisted of “mostly kimchi and meat.”
They're off that diet now, but they liked being on it. “Kimchi evens out my gut biome. I felt better. Not superhuman, but better.”
Also on the community table is something called “Higgins Kraut,” made with Napa cabbage, carrots, garlic, and ginger, which, with a lovely melding of flavors, won my personal Best-in-Show award.
Turns out it's made by one of the show’s other founders, George Winborn, who was involved for the first 10 years. He'd been farming in Dallas when he moved to Portland, to a place that had no yard and nowhere to farm.
“Doing the Fest helped scratch the itch,” he says. He's now getting Wellspring Farm in Gresham, Oregon, off the ground and noted how the festival has become a bit more commercial, a bit less homemade. But all that's relative, considering we're standing here over our jars of sauerkraut, and the exhibitors are very small businesses, if they're businesses at all.
“I still love the DIY and starter tables,” he says. “It reminds you that everyone can do this.”
Update, Wednesday October 28 at 3:30 pm: The original version of this story misquoted one sentence attributed to Liz Crain. When asked about the enduring popularity of the festival, she said “Keep Portland Weird,” which is an unofficial motto of the city that speaks to its countercultural enthusiasm. The story was updated to correct that quote.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP Kaohsiung mayoral candidate Lai Jui-lung (賴瑞隆) defended campaign donations from renewable energy firm J&V Energy Technology Co. on Wednesday, stressing that the contributions were legal.
KMT Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) questioned Lai’s ties to the renewable energy firm, per KNews. She pointed out that during the 2020 election cycle, J&V Energy Technology and New Green Power each contributed NT$1 million (US$30,800) to Lai’s campaign, along with 10 separate NT$100,000 donations from senior executives at the two companies.
Hsu noted that J&V Energy Technology subsidiary Jin Chen Energy Co. worked with New Green Power to install solar panels at the Legislative Yuan — at Lai’s recommendation. The legislature later removed the panels after discovering that key components contained Chinese-made parts.
Hsu also highlighted Lai’s efforts to organize renewable energy-related hearings at the legislature, often inviting specific companies. KMT lawmaker Wang Hung-wei (王鴻薇) added that after J&V Energy Technology began investing in wind power in 2020, Lai helped organize six offshore wind power-related hearings between 2021 and 2023.
Lai said he would address any legal issues over the donations if they arose, per CNA. He emphasized that politicians must comply with the Political Donations Act.
Lai’s rival, KMT lawmaker Ko Chih-en (柯志恩), called on him to explain his relationship with J&V Energy Technology in detail, per UDN. She said the two companies' pattern of making multiple smaller donations was unusual and urged Lai to hold himself to the same standards applied to other politicians facing controversy.
J&V Energy Technology’s relationship with the DPP has long been a focus of opposition criticism. Political commentator Huang Yang-ming (黃揚明) pointed out in 2023 that the company directed approximately 80% of its political donations to DPP-affiliated candidates, per Newtalk.
The DPP pushed back against the criticism. Then-Vice Premier Cheng Wen-tsan (鄭文燦) challenged the KMT to identify any misconduct related to J&V Energy Technology’s political donations, per Liberty Times. Then-DPP Spokesperson Chang Chih-hao (張志豪) accused the KMT of applying a double standard, noting that several KMT politicians, including Wang, had also received donations from the industry, per Liberty Times.
Chang also pointed out that many senior KMT figures had investments in the renewable energy sector.
Then-KMT Legislative Caucus Deputy Secretary-General Lee Te-wei (李德維) rejected Chang’s argument, saying KMT figures were associated with long-established companies, unlike J&V Energy Technology, which was founded in 2016, per Liberty Times. KMT Taipei City Councilor Yu Shu-hui (游淑慧) said J&V Energy Technology had regularly secured government projects and that its gross profit had grown by 919% over several years.

Mercedes to cut more jobs as Chinese competition bites
- Mercedes-Benz will restart its Germany severance programme in December and discuss more cost cuts with unions, as it tries to lower fixed costs and protect profits.
- The company warned on full-year profits after weak demand and fierce competition in China, where sales have collapsed and more than 100 carmakers are fighting a price war.
- Mercedes said Germany has 15% of sales but two-thirds of staff, and it cannot leave China because it is vital for a global carmaker, despite lower costs elsewhere.
AI generated
FRANKFURT – Premium German carmaker Mercedes-Benz will restart a voluntary redundancy programme and is in discussion with unions over further cost-cuts, its chief executive Ola Kaellenius said on Oct 28 after the firm warned on full-year profits.
“Germany accounts for roughly 15% of our sales, but two-thirds of our employees and structures are based here,” Kaellenius told reporters and investors on an earnings call to present third-quarter results.
“To reduce our fixed costs further, we have decided to restart the Germany severance programme in December,” he added, without giving a target number of job cuts.
German carmakers have struggled with cutthroat competition and falling demand in China, the world’s largest car market, leading to painful adjustments at home.
Mercedes-Benz on Oct 27 became the third of the big three German carmakers – alongside Volkswagen and BMW – to have issued a profit warning for 2026, citing difficulties in China.
BMW aims to cut 8,000 jobs by the end of 2027 with its own voluntary redundancy programme, and the Volkswagen Group plans to have cut 120,000 jobs globally by the end of the decade across its brands, which include Porsche and Audi.
Kaellenius said Mercedes-Benz could not give more detail since discussions were ongoing, adding that he was nevertheless pressing hard to get costs down.
“We will continue with determination to adjust the structures of the company to fit the revenue position of the company,” he said.
Labour costs in China, Hungary, Romania and the United States are all lower than in Germany, Kaellenius said, adding that “eastern Europe as a whole is open to any industrialist looking to expand”.
Net profit for the third quarter rose almost 30% to 1.52 billion euros (S$2.16 billion) even as overall sales declined 4.5% to 30.7 billion euros, largely the result of a collapse in China.
But Kaellenius said the company could not afford to abandon the Chinese market despite an intense price war driven by over 100 competing carmakers.
“If you’re a global car company like Mercedes, there’s not a play where you put China aside,” he said. AFP

Kazakhstan sees Turkic world integration as foreign policy priority: FM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:57:22 UTC
19:57:22 KST

Kazakhstan attaches importance to developing comprehensive cooperation with Türkiye and strengthening ties within the Organization of Turkic States (OTS), with the integration of the Turkic world among the country’s key foreign policy priorities, Kazakh Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi said.
Tileuberdi spoke to Anadolu ahead of Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s official visit to Ankara on Wednesday and the 13th Summit of the Organization of Turkic States, to be hosted by Türkiye.
Noting that the current international environment is shaped by profound geopolitical changes, transformations in the global economy, and intensifying technological competition, Tileuberdi stressed the growing importance of relations based on mutual trust, respect for national interests, and a willingness to act jointly.
“Kazakhstan and Türkiye are united by centuries-old historical ties, spiritual affinity, shared cultural traditions, and the rich linguistic heritage of the Turkic world,” he said.
“Today, bilateral relations have acquired the character of an expanded strategic partnership covering political dialogue, trade, investment, energy, transport, industry, education, digital technologies, and other areas. At the current stage, the most important task is to resolutely continue transforming the accumulated political capital into tangible economic results, new production facilities, employment opportunities, and long-term projects,” he added.
More than 100 joint projects implemented
Describing Türkiye as one of Kazakhstan’s main trade, economic, and investment partners, Tileuberdi said bilateral trade volume rose 66.5 percent in the first eight months of 2026 from the same period last year, reaching $5.66 billion.
Kazakhstan’s exports to Türkiye nearly doubled during the period to $4.75 billion, he said, adding that the figures demonstrated significant potential for further expanding economic ties.
Tileuberdi stressed the importance of diversifying products, removing non-tariff barriers, and facilitating trade procedures to increase bilateral trade volume. He also said investment cooperation between the two countries is developing actively.
Turkish investments in Kazakhstan have exceeded $6 billion, while Kazakh investments in Türkiye have surpassed $2.5 billion, he said.
More than 100 joint projects have been implemented in Kazakhstan, while over 50 projects are being implemented and negotiations are ongoing for another 70, he added.
Over 4,000 companies with Turkish capital operate in Kazakhstan, which Tileuberdi described as an important indicator of Turkish investors’ confidence in the country.
He said Kazakhstan will continue developing mechanisms to support investors, protect their rights, and establish a predictable, long-term business environment. The country provides support throughout the investment process, from identifying suitable locations for production facilities to implementing projects, he added.
‘We view Ankara summit from a broad perspective’
Tileuberdi said Turkic integration should be developed on the basis of pragmatism, mutual respect, and equal consideration of the interests of all participating states.
He also shared Kazakhstan’s expectations for the upcoming OTS summit in Ankara.
“We view the Ankara summit from a broad perspective. We hope that the summit will not only reaffirm the determination of the states to deepen cooperation, but also provide an opportunity to set concrete goals for joint work in the future,” he said.

Alm. Brand to lay off 55 employees as it reports record insurance result
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:56:33 UTC
19:56:33 KST

Danish insurance group Alm. Brand has decided to lay off 55 employees and has eliminated 30 other positions as part of efforts to reduce costs, even as it reported its highest quarterly insurance result to date.
The group’s insurance result reached 755 million DKK in the third quarter, according to financial statements released Wednesday. The measure reflects earnings from its core insurance business, taking account of premium income, claims and operating expenses.
Chief Executive Officer Andreas Ruben Madsen said the job cuts were needed to improve efficiency and support the company’s previously announced strategy.
“It is a difficult decision because it affects colleagues, but it is at the same time a necessary step to realize the efficiencies that support the strategic direction we have already announced,” he said in a stock exchange announcement.
Lower claims costs were the main factor behind the record insurance result. Claims expenses fell by 165 million DKK from the same period last year to approximately 1.7 billion DKK. Insurance income rose slightly to more than 3 billion DKK.
The group reported a third-quarter profit after tax of 397 million DKK.
Madsen attributed the insurance result mainly to fewer major claims, fewer weather-related claims and positive run-off results. Run-off results arise when an insurer adjusts its estimates for claims from previous periods.
He cautioned that those factors might not provide the same boost in future quarters.
“This contributes significantly to earnings in the quarter, but at the same time these are conditions that we cannot expect will contribute at the same level going forward.”
Copenhagen Airport says tighter security checks and staffing shortfalls contributed to long queues
An order from the Danish Transport Authority led to additional baggage checks from October 8. Some passengers missed flights, and SAS reported rebooking 352 travelers.
Copenhagen Airport introduced additional security checks following an order from the Danish Transport Authority and underestimated staffing needs on some days in October, the airport said Wednesday after long queues caused passengers to miss flights.
The airport received the order on October 6 and introduced the measures two days later. The changes meant more passengers had their baggage checked manually, it said in a press release.
The airport did not explain why the authority issued the order or give details of its requirements.
There were periods of long waits on October 8, October 22 and October 23, the airport said. Passengers also faced waits of up to an hour early on Saturday, October 24.
Danish media have reported lengthy queues, particularly over the past five days, with some passengers reaching their flights too late to depart as booked.
The airport acknowledged that it had underestimated staffing needs on some days during October. It said “it is naturally not satisfactory” that some passengers had had “a bad experience”.
SAS said on October 23 that it had rebooked 352 passengers because of the long waits. Passengers were also urged to arrive earlier than usual and allow extra time for security.
Norwegian also offered affected customers rebooking.

Danish tax agency faces further scrutiny over identity theft cases
Denmark’s Parliamentary Ombudsman has demanded further explanations from the Danish Tax Agency over its handling of cases involving citizens who were wrongly pursued for millions in taxes after becoming victims of identity theft.
Ombudsman Christian Britten Lundblad said the agency’s report, submitted on August 31, did not adequately address concerns raised about the cases.
“After reviewing the report and the complaint that I previously received from a lawyer on behalf of a citizen in the complex of cases, I have found reason to ask the Danish Tax Agency for a statement,” Lundblad wrote.
The investigation concerns 126 people involved in tax cases linked to money transfers through five businesses. The agency began examining the transfers in 2021.
In June, TV 2’s investigative programme Operation X highlighted how citizens had faced incorrect tax claims worth millions following suspected identity theft connected to money laundering cases.
The agency’s own report found that it should have acted in 2023, when police provided information suggesting widespread identity theft.
In August, Danish Tax Agency Director Thomas Hjortenberg acknowledged the mistakes and apologised to those affected.
“Our mistakes have had major personal consequences for the affected citizens,” he said.
Hjortenberg also admitted that the agency should have responded much earlier to the police’s warnings.
The ombudsman now wants to establish what information the agency possessed before issuing its tax assessments.
He has also requested clarification on whether evidence in each case supported the information obtained from the money transfer businesses.
The Danish Tax Agency has until November 7 to provide its response.

Study finds problematic social media use more common among girls
More than one in five girls aged 15 to 21 in a Danish study show signs of problematic social media use, compared with fewer than one in 10 boys, according to research from the Rockwool Foundation, a Danish research foundation.
The study surveyed 8,239 young people about their use of platforms such as Snapchat, TikTok, Instagram and Facebook. Researchers also asked about their well-being and the amount of time they spend on social media.
Based on their answers, participants were classified using an internationally recognized scale for problematic social media use.
The results show that 22.2 percent of the girls surveyed fell into the category, compared with 9.6 percent of the boys.
Nadja Eifler, a PhD student at the Rockwool Foundation, said part of the difference could be explained by the activities young people choose online.
“In the study, we asked specifically about social media such as Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat, so part of the difference between girls and boys may lie in the fact that many boys spend more time on computer games, which is also for many a social activity where you can be in dialogue with friends,” she said.
The study also found a link between problematic social media use and poor well-being, particularly among girls.
“We can clearly see that poor well-being is most widespread among young people with problematic social media use, especially for the girls, where more than half of these young women have low well-being,” Eifler said.
Among girls who did not have problems with social media use, just under four in 10 reported low well-being.
The report recommends looking beyond the number of hours young people spend on social media when assessing whether their use is problematic.
Other warning signs include difficulty reducing use, feeling restless or uneasy when a phone is out of reach, and social media having a negative effect on school or education.
The findings suggest that how young people use social media, and how it affects their daily lives, may be important factors alongside the time they spend online.
ATP’s investment return falls to 1.5 percent after weak quarter
Danish pension provider ATP recorded a negative investment result in the third quarter, reducing its total return for the first nine months of the year to 1.5 percent.
The company announced the figures in a press release on its website but did not disclose the size of the investment loss during the third quarter alone.
ATP’s return stood at 14.5 percent when it published its half-year report a few months earlier. The latest figures show that much of the return earned during the first half of the year was lost in the following three months.
ATP Chief Executive Officer Martin Præstegaard described the period as difficult, pointing to rising interest rates as a key factor behind the weaker result.
“We have had a challenging third quarter, where rising interest rates have affected the result negatively,” he said.
He added that the company had delivered a good investment return during the first half of the year, leaving the overall return positive for the first nine months.

ATP is Denmark’s statutory supplementary pension scheme. Employees who work at least nine hours a week and their employers pay contributions into the scheme. People receiving certain public benefits also contribute to ATP.
Around 5.8 million people are members of the scheme.
ATP provides a guaranteed, lifelong monthly pension payment that supplements the Danish state pension after people stop working.
The company’s investment portfolio accounts for approximately 20 percent of its total assets.
The latest figures cover the first nine months of the year, including the period from July through September, when rising interest rates weighed on investment performance. Despite the decline in the third quarter, ATP said its overall return for the year remained positive.
Viking-era Danish coin sells for 136,000 DKK at Copenhagen auction
A Danish coin dating back more than 1,000 years has sold for 18,300 euros, approximately 136,000 DKK, at an auction in Copenhagen.
The coin, associated with Viking king Svend Tveskæg, fetched more than twice its estimated price of 6,000 to 8,000 euros, or roughly 45,000 to 60,000 DKK.
Auction house Stack’s Bowers confirmed the sale on its website following Tuesday’s auction.
The coin is considered the first official Danish coin to feature both the name of a Danish ruler and the country’s name.
Svend Tveskæg was the first ruler to have his name appear on a Danish coin.
“This coin type is considered the first official Danish coin and has an exceptionally great historical significance because it was the first Danish coin that bore both the king’s and the country’s name,” the auction house stated.
However, archaeological discoveries indicate that coins were used in Denmark long before this particular type was produced.
The coin weighs just 1.95 grams and had previously been broken into several pieces before being repaired, according to the auction house.
It belonged to a collection assembled by Danish businessman Lars Emil Bruun, who died in 1923.
Bruun made his fortune as a butter wholesaler, exporting canned butter to markets around the world.
In his will, he stipulated that his extensive coin collection could not be sold until 100 years after his death.
Several other coins from Bruun’s collection were also sold during Tuesday’s auction in Copenhagen.
The auction is scheduled to continue Wednesday, October 28.

Danish company Epiq ApS has recalled four electrical products sold at Bilka and Føtex supermarkets because they pose a risk of electric shock.
The recall covers power strips, extension cord sets and a double-socket adapter sold between June 2 and September 18, 2026, the company announced in a press release.
According to Epiq ApS, the affected products lack child safety protection covering the socket openings, creating a potential electric shock hazard.
The company has urged customers to “immediately stop using the products” and return them to the store where they were purchased.
Customers will receive a full refund even if they no longer have their receipt.
The recall covers the following four products:
Scoop ledningssæt med tre stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with three sockets. EAN code: 5713359129661.
Basis ledningssæt med fire stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with four sockets. EAN code: 5713359131749.
Scoop ledningssæt med fem stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with five sockets. EAN code: 5713359129692.
Scoop dobbeltstik: A double-socket adapter. EAN code: 5713359129685.
An EAN code is a product identification number commonly found on packaging or labels. Epiq ApS says the codes for the recalled items can be found on the back of the products.
Consumers can use these numbers to check whether an electrical product they purchased is affected by the recall.
The company has instructed customers to return affected products to their original Bilka or Føtex store for a refund without requiring proof of purchase.

Danish parties move toward majority support for ban on fast-growing chickens
Several Danish political parties are backing a ban on breeding fast-growing chickens, commonly called “turbo chickens,” amid concerns about animal welfare.
Around 70 million of these chickens are produced annually in Denmark, according to Berlingske.
The Ross 308 breed, widely used in Danish poultry farming, grows from approximately 50 grams to two kilograms in just 33 days.
Their rapid growth can put considerable strain on their legs, leaving many chickens sitting for much of their final weeks before slaughter, Berlingske reports.
The Alternative, the Red-Green Alliance, the Socialist People’s Party, the Social Liberal Party, Liberal Alliance and the Conservative People’s Party support a ban. The Denmark Democrats have also expressed support for its aims.
The Moderates, a centrist party, have changed their position since 2024, when parliament rejected a proposal to ban the production, sale and import of Ross 308 chickens.
At the time, the governing coalition preferred pursuing a European Union-wide solution.
“When you say A regarding the pigs, then I also think you have to say B regarding the chickens,” Moderates animal welfare spokesperson Ellen Emilie Mindegaard-Müllertz told Berlingske.
An EU-wide agreement could take time, while a Danish production ban would not prevent imports from other countries.
Animal welfare organization Anima recently reported that fast-growing chickens account for two-thirds of chicken sales at Salling Group’s Netto, Bilka and Føtex supermarkets.
At Rema 1000, the figure is 15 percent.
Social Democratic animal welfare spokesperson Birgitte Vind also told Berlingske that the chickens’ conditions were unacceptable and should be examined.

The European Commission proposed Tuesday expanding the personnel available to Frontex, the EU’s border agency, to 30,000 and giving it a larger role in deportations.
The plan would create a reserve of 17,000 personnel who could be deployed when needed. According to AFP, these would be national border guards made available by member states.
Frontex’s own workforce would grow from 3,000 to 6,000, alongside 7,000 personnel already on loan from EU countries. The proposal also includes a rapid reaction force.
“Europe decides who comes to our union – and under what circumstances,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.
“Therefore, we are proposing today to strengthen Frontex so that it can support the member states when and where it is needed.”
The proposal follows an incident in July when thousands of migrants entered Ceuta, a Spanish territory on the African continent, within a short period.
Established in 2004, Frontex helps EU countries protect the external borders of Europe’s free-movement area. Its responsibilities expanded in 2016, following the previous year’s refugee and migration crisis, to include broader border management and a greater role in fighting cross-border crime.
The agency frequently faces criticism from migrant rights groups. Melissa Camara, a member of the European Parliament’s Greens group, criticized the direction of EU policy.
“Ever more oppression, dehumanization of displaced people, and an increasing tendency to mimic the rhetoric of the far right,” she said, according to AFP.
The proposal requires approval from the European Parliament and the Council, which represents EU member governments.

Danish tax minister seeks pause in court cases over triple taxation
Denmark’s tax minister, Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates party, wants to put court cases involving so-called triple taxation on hold while he prepares legislation to end the practice.
The disputes arise when tax authorities decide that someone working through their own company should instead be treated as an employee, resulting in corporate income tax, personal income tax and dividend tax being charged on the same earnings. Media reports have described people facing tax bills totaling as much as 110% of their income.
Engel-Schmidt, who considers the practice unfair, has asked the state’s legal counsel, Kammeradvokaten, to examine whether the cases can be paused pending the change.
He said the separation of powers prevents him from deciding which individual cases should be brought or appealed, but argued that a general pause while the law is being changed would be appropriate. According to the minister, “a small handful” of cases are currently before the courts.

A new Danish news outlet, Projekt Y, launches today at 1 p.m. with an approach that combines artificial intelligence-generated articles with traditional editorial oversight.

Coverage could eventually expand to sports and culture.

Two-thirds of Danes believe artificial intelligence will benefit Danish companies, while only about half as many expect employees to gain from the technology.
The findings come from a new survey by TrygFonden, a Danish foundation supporting safety and social initiatives.
Frederik Olsen, a senior analyst at Arbejderbevægelsens Erhvervsråd, an economic institute linked to the labor movement, said there was not yet evidence that AI benefited companies more than workers.
Even in occupations expected to face job losses, employment is developing similarly to the broader labor market, he said.
Olsen described AI as a productivity improvement but said investment in continuing education and skills development was necessary for both workers and employers to benefit.
The survey also found concern about young people entering the labor market.
Six in 10 respondents ages 18 to 35 feared that AI would make it harder for young people and recent graduates to find jobs. Across the full population, 46 percent shared that concern.
A September analysis from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank, found that youth employment grew more slowly at companies using AI than at companies that did not.
However, young workers who might previously have joined AI-using businesses generally found employment elsewhere.
Nationalbanken expects companies to introduce AI gradually enough for affected workers to find other jobs.
It nevertheless said uncertainty remained high and could not rule out AI reducing Danish employment over the longer term.
Danish publisher bans AI tools for work on manuscripts
Danish publisher Lindhardt og Ringhof has prohibited employees and external partners from using artificial intelligence to complete work for the company.
The ban applies to proofreaders, editors, manuscript readers and consultants, according to a letter distributed by the publisher.
“It is not permitted for any purpose to use AI tools for tasks that one as an external partner solves for Lindhardt og Ringhof,” the letter states.
Manuscripts and other documents provided by the publisher must not be uploaded to AI systems under any circumstances.
The company said even apparently harmless uses, such as asking AI to summarize a manuscript, could create legal and copyright risks.
“Texts that are uploaded into AI tools can subsequently be copied and data mined, even if the provider claims otherwise,” the publisher said.
Literary director Sune de Souza Schmidt-Madsen told Danish public broadcaster DR that Lindhardt og Ringhof was not aware of external partners already using AI for its assignments.
However, he said the publisher expected the issue to emerge eventually and wanted to establish its rules in advance.
The restrictions also apply to the publisher’s own employees, Schmidt-Madsen said.
Denmark issues safety guidance for vulnerable people after CPR data leak
The Agency for Societal Security has published new guidance for people who may face increased risks following the leak of 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers and other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The advice is aimed at people who have previously experienced harassment, hold jobs that could attract criminal attention or are publicly known and at risk of having their names misused.
It also covers people whose names may expose them to harassment or identify them as members of vulnerable social, ethnic or religious minorities.
“The leak means that persons among these exposed or vulnerable groups of people must have a greater awareness of, among other things, their surroundings, behavior on social media and the security of their homes,” the agency said.
People who believe they face physical danger because a specific person may now know their address can consider applying for name and address protection.
The agency also recommends considering contact with police, a crisis center, the Danish Stalking Center or another specialized counseling service.
People can additionally request a hidden, secret or unlisted telephone number.
A hidden number prevents the recipient of a call from seeing the caller’s number.
Secret and unlisted numbers are also excluded from public telecommunications services, directory assistance and online telephone directories.
