====================================================================================================

Horror isn’t just intense fear, new psychology study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:50 UTC
19:00:50 KST

Reading a news headline about a violent tragedy can provoke an unsettled, sickening jolt that feels very different from the anxiety of facing a personal threat. A new study published in Cognition and Emotion suggests that when descriptions of harm involve extreme outcomes or vivid, gory details, they tend to heighten horror much more than fear, in part because they make the event seem more abnormal. The findings provide evidence that horror is not merely an intense version of fear, but a distinct emotional reaction to events that violate our basic expectations of how the world works.
In everyday conversation and dictionary definitions, horror is often treated as a synonym for extreme fear. In psychology, however, the two terms can represent different ways of interpreting and categorizing a harmful event. Fear functions as a threat-detection system that alerts a person to potential danger and motivates self-defense or escape. Some emotion researchers define real-world horror, by contrast, as an emotional and mental shock experienced when witnessing or learning about actual harm that contradicts a person’s fundamental assumptions about human safety and how the world operates.
“‘Horror’ is one of dozens of English words we have to label our emotional responses to harm, but it remains largely unstudied,” study author Pamela Marie Taylor, an assistant professor in the Faculty of Global Connectivity at Akita International University, told PsyPost. “This neglect might be because research in the 1980s categorized horror as a subtype of fear, or because it has become closely associated with the fictional genre of horror films. However, people use the word ‘horror’ to describe their responses to real events, and do so in a way that is meaningfully different from how they use the word ‘fear’.”
“For example, ‘horrified’ is often paired with verbs like ‘learn’, ‘realize’ and ‘discover’ that indicate a response to extreme novelty or abnormality (e.g., ‘I was horrified to learn’),” Taylor explained. “In contrast, people typically use the word ‘fear’ to describe the anticipation of some possible harm (e.g., ‘fear the worst’, ‘fear of snakes’). This study was done to test if horror can be differentiated from fear based on how abnormal a harmful event is seen to be.”
How people evaluate unusual events plays a central role in shaping their emotional reactions. In a 1986 theoretical paper, psychologists proposed that people judge how unusual an event is by comparing it against their mental norms, and that bad outcomes preceded by abnormal circumstances provoke amplified emotional responses. Building on this idea, a 2022 experimental study by Taylor and a colleague found that people reported greater fear when facing common, mild, or personally relevant threats, whereas they reported greater horror when learning about extreme or abnormal harm that had already happened, even when the victims were strangers.
Encountering accounts of bizarre or extreme harm often leaves people struggling to reconcile the event with their worldview. Some research suggests this tension can shape how people seek explanations. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2023 indicated that individuals with higher morbid curiosity about unsettling events and dangerous people are more likely to seek out and believe conspiracy theories as explanations for threatening occurrences.
Although the 2022 research linked horror to abnormal harm, its experimental scenarios blended together the severity of the injury and the graphicness of the wording, leaving it uncertain which feature actually made the harm feel abnormal. To isolate these factors, Taylor designed two experiments examining how harm severity and graphic language independently shape perceptions of abnormality. She defined graphicness through the distinction between abstract and concrete language.
Taylor reasoned that abstract descriptions use broad, familiar categories, such as stating that “a person was murdered,” which allows the mind to file the event into existing mental frameworks, whereas concrete descriptions include specific sensory details, such as “a camper was slaughtered by his friend who sliced into his chest with a rusty axe,” which are harder to fit into normal expectations.
Taylor also wanted to test whether perceived abnormality is what truly separates horror from fear, or if the difference comes down to physical arousal. In psychology, arousal refers to the level of physical activation or agitation in the body’s nervous system. If horror is simply an intense form of fear, then heightened physical arousal alone should explain why people label their reaction to gruesome news as horror rather than fear.
In the first study, Taylor recruited 60 adult native English speakers in the United States through the online platform Prolific. The participants had an average age of 35.5 years, ranging from 21 to 69, and the sample was 70 percent female and 71.1 percent White. Each participant read four text stimuli presented as real news headlines adapted from The Daily Mail tabloid describing a person being harmed, with each headline remaining on the screen for seven seconds before rating questions appeared. Taylor preregistered the main prediction that severe harm and graphic descriptions would increase horror more than fear.
The headlines were systematically varied across two dimensions: the severity of the harm (moderate injuries that heal versus extreme, permanent harm such as death) and the graphicness of the description (abstract, general wording versus concrete, tangible details). After reading each headline, participants rated the perceived abnormality of the harm on a 5-point scale from 1 (“not at all”) to 5 (“extremely”) using four items assessing how unusual, abnormal, or unheard-of the event seemed.
They also rated their emotional reactions on the same 5-point scale, where scores for “horrified” and “shocked” were combined to measure horror, and scores for “scared” and “afraid” were combined to measure fear. To measure physical arousal, participants selected one of five illustrated figures ranging from a calm, closed-eyed figure to a wide-eyed figure with jagged lines depicting intense bodily activation.
To account for individual tendencies to score higher or lower on rating scales, Taylor analyzed the repeated measurements while statistically controlling for baseline differences between participants. Across the 5-point scale, where the overall average abnormality rating was 3.40, shifting from moderate to extreme harm increased perceived abnormality by 0.89 points, and shifting from abstract to concrete language increased it by 0.88 points.
Both factors also elevated horror much more strongly than fear. Across all conditions, the overall average emotion rating was 2.69, with horror averaging 0.98 points higher than fear; describing extreme rather than moderate harm boosted horror by 1.09 points compared to a 0.45-point increase in fear, while concrete rather than abstract descriptions raised horror by 0.70 points compared to a 0.22-point increase in fear.
Participants also rated the general harmfulness of each event based on whether someone suffered bodily pain or injury, and in the first study, these general harmfulness ratings predicted horror and fear equally, as the difference between the two emotions was not statistically significant. Taylor then used mediation analysis, a statistical technique that estimates how much of a relationship between an experimental condition and an outcome passes through an intermediate step, to test whether perceived abnormality explained the rise in horror.
Perceived abnormality accounted for 39 percent of the total effect of harm severity on horror and 76 percent of the effect of graphic language on horror, while explaining 63 percent and 83 percent of why severity and graphicness increased horror more than fear. In one Study 1 model, the effect of graphic language on horror over fear was no longer statistically significant once physical arousal was taken into account, and when physical arousal and perceived abnormality were tested side by side as parallel pathways, both independently explained a portion of the shift toward horror.
To verify whether these patterns would hold up in an independent sample, Taylor conducted a second study with another 60 adult native English speakers in the United States recruited via Prolific. Participants in the second group had an average age of 42.57 years, ranging from 21 to 75, and the sample was 70 percent female, 30 percent male, and 75 percent White. The procedure and rating scales were identical to the first experiment, except that one headline from Study 1 involving an animal attack was replaced with an interpersonal attack so that all four headlines depicted one human harming another.
The second study closely replicated the core findings regarding abnormality and horror. Around an average abnormality rating of 3.42 on the 5-point scale, extreme harm raised perceived abnormality by 0.85 points and concrete graphic descriptions raised it by 0.89 points. Extreme harm increased horror ratings by 1.01 points compared to 0.39 points for fear, making the effect on horror more than 2.5 times larger, while concrete descriptions increased horror by 0.62 points compared to 0.14 points for fear, an effect more than four times larger.
Unlike the first study, general ratings of bodily harmfulness in Study 2 showed a stronger association with horror than fear, though the author noted that because every headline involved harm, 12 percent of participants in Study 1 and 22 percent in Study 2 gave identical harmfulness ratings across all four headlines, limiting the precision of that specific measure.
Where the second study diverged most notably from the first was in the role of physical arousal. When arousal was tested on its own in Study 2, it again helped explain the shift toward horror, but once abnormality was added to the model, the arousal pathway was no longer statistically significant, with indirect effects of 0.11 for harm severity and 0.06 for graphicness. Perceived abnormality, by contrast, remained a strong, consistent pathway in both studies even after controlling for self-reported bodily activation. Taylor argues that whereas fear tends to arise from uncertainty about potential danger, horror arises from an excess of concrete information about severe harm that is hard to square with a person’s understanding of a safe world.
For everyday news consumers, the findings highlight how subtle shifts in phrasing can alter how a story lands emotionally. “When the same harmful event in a news headline was described using concrete language, it was rated as more abnormal than when it was described using abstract language, and caused an increase in horror that was three-to-four times greater than the increase in fear,” Taylor noted. “In other words, a person’s emotional reaction to a news event is influenced by the language with which it is told.”
“In terms of practical significance, it seems that a lot of online and political rhetoric uses abnormality to capture attention, shape discourse and influence interpretations,” Taylor said. “Therefore, people should be aware of how their emotional responses to events can be shaped by how events are described. We are increasingly aware of the dangers of online misinformation, but that focuses on the factuality of what is described. These results indicate that even in factually accurate descriptions, the language with which the event is described can influence our perception of how normal or abnormal it is, and consequently our emotional response to it.”
“We would not argue that using concrete language is bad or that headlines that use it are necessarily manipulative,” Taylor added. “The current findings examined how concrete and abstract language elicit different emotional responses without investigating the appropriateness of the language. Another way to read this study’s findings is that describing harm with abstract language can normalize it, which also has consequences when reporting on harmful events.”
There are a few additional caveats to keep in mind when interpreting these results. Because adding vivid sensory details requires extra words, the concrete headlines were naturally longer than the abstract ones, meaning word count could have contributed to the impact of the graphic descriptions. In addition, the experiments only examined short tabloid headlines about harm happening to strangers in ordinary, everyday settings, without a non-harmful baseline condition. It remains an open question whether severe harm in settings where danger is already expected, such as a combat zone, would feel less abnormal and elicit less horror.
Perceived abnormality was measured rather than manipulated, and the analyses testing it as a pathway were exploratory, added after the main results were known. The horror measure also combined “horrified” with “shocked,” a feeling that may overlap with judging an event as unusual. Both studies used nearly the same set of headlines and newly created two-item emotion scales, so it remains to be seen whether the results hold with other materials and measures.
Methodologically, participants rated perceived abnormality, physical arousal, and their emotions at the exact same time after each headline, so the statistical models cannot establish a strict chronological sequence of events. Physical arousal was also assessed through a single visual self-report scale rather than biological measures like heart rate or skin conductance.
Additionally, both study samples were 70 percent female and restricted to native English speakers in the United States. Because not all languages separate horror and fear into distinct everyday words, such as Japanese, which uses the term osore for both, future research could explore whether horror functions as a culturally specific emotion concept.
“Because many conspiracy theories seem to involve attempts to make sense of a horrifying event, I am interested in investigating if feelings of horror play a role in conspiratorial thinking,” Taylor said. “For example, can conspiracy theories act as a form of emotion regulation that people use to turn the helplessness of horror into anger, with the latter associated with a greater sense of control?”
The study, “Gruesome Details: Graphic Descriptions and Extreme Harm Differentially Elicit Horror (vs Fear) via Increased Perceptions of Abnormality,” was authored by Pamela Marie Taylor.

The cause of the collision remained under investigation, and the number of injured was not immediately confirmed.

Netanyahu or Eisenkot? Can you form Israel’s next coalition government?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:11 UTC
19:00:11 KST

Netanyahu or Eisenkot? Can you form Israel’s next coalition government?
Israel has only ever been governed by coalitions. Can you put one together that reaches 61 of the Knesset’s 120 seats?
Israelis voted on October 27, but there appears to be no clear winner.
The next government, like every government in Israel’s history, will have to be a coalition.
The question now is who can secure at least 61 of the Knesset’s 120 seats to form a government and become Israel’s next prime minister.
Al Jazeera has built an interactive tool that lets you test different combinations of parties. Start with any of the four exit polls or enter your own seat numbers. Then add parties until your coalition reaches 61 seats. You can add an entire bloc at once or select parties individually.
Who is ahead?
Initial counting by the Central Elections Committee put Likud ahead as the largest single party, with 27 seats.
Netanyahu’s bloc was projected to win 54 seats, against 50 for Eisenkot’s.
Four exit polls published on election night showed how close the race is.
Kan 11 and Channel 13 put Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc and Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc level at 51 seats each. Channel 12 gave Netanyahu 52 seats to Eisenkot’s 49, while Channel 15 was most favourable to the incumbent, projecting 55 seats for Netanyahu’s bloc against 49 for the opposition.
How many seats are needed?
Israel’s parliament, the Knesset, has 120 seats. Parties win seats in proportion to their share of the national vote, provided they clear the 3.25 percent threshold to enter parliament.
A government needs the support of at least 61 politicians to secure a majority.
Neither of the main blocs has reached that number in the exit polls or the initial count. The next step is to find enough parties willing to join forces to make up the difference.
Why is forming a government so difficult?
The Arab-led parties Ra’am and the Joint List could hold the balance of power, with exit polls putting their combined support at between 16 and 19 seats.
But the political obstacles are considerable. Netanyahu has described a coalition with Arab parties as “shameful”, while leading figures in the Jewish-led opposition have also ruled out governing with them.
That leaves potential coalitions that may work on paper but face serious political barriers.
Which parties belong to each bloc?
Netanyahu’s bloc spans Likud, the ultra-Orthodox parties Shas and United Torah Judaism, and the far-right parties Religious Zionism, led by Bezalel Smotrich, and Otzma Yehudit, led by Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Eisenkot’s opposition bloc includes his Yashar party, the Together list associated with former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu and Yair Golan’s Democrats.
What happens next?
Once the results are certified, the president gives the mandate to the member of the Knesset considered most likely to assemble a majority.
That politician has 28 days to form a government, with a possible extension of up to 14 days. If they fail, another lawmaker can be given a chance. If no one can form a government, Israel may have to hold another election, as it did repeatedly between 2019 and 2022.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, with 19 years in office across three stints, remains caretaker prime minister while coalition negotiations unfold. He is also standing trial on corruption charges, which he denies.
Official results are due on November 4. Negotiations to form a government could take considerably longer.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will host a meeting of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) in Ankara on October 29 2026.
The meeting will be hosted as part of the organisation’s 13th summit, scheduled for October 29-30.
The meeting will bring OTS foreign ministers together for the fifth time this year, following one regular and four informal council meetings.
Ministers are expected to discuss cooperation within the organisation and efforts to strengthen its institutional structure. Several administrative and financial documents related to the organisation’s functioning are also expected to be approved.
In addition, Fidan is scheduled to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts on the sidelines of the meeting.
In his address, Fidan is expected to highlight the strengthening of political dialogue and joint action among Turkic states, as well as efforts to turn shared history, language, culture and fraternal ties into concrete cooperation.
He is also expected to outline Türkiye’s priorities during its OTS chairmanship, including strengthening the organisation’s institutional capacity, developing the Secretariat’s human and financial resources, and improving coordination among Turkic cooperation organisations.
Fidan is expected to emphasise the importance of translating economic and strategic cooperation into tangible outcomes, particularly in energy, trade, investment, digital transformation and defence industry.
He is also expected to underline the importance of strengthening the Trans-Caspian Middle Corridor to improve connectivity between Asia and Europe and enhance economic resilience.
The foreign minister is expected to draw attention to developments in Afghanistan and their implications for regional security, stability and connectivity, calling for greater consultation and coordination among OTS member and observer states.
The OTS was established as the Cooperation Council of Turkic-Speaking States under the Nakhchivan Agreement, signed on October 3 2009, by Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. Its name was changed to the Organization of Turkic States at the Istanbul summit in 2021.

I Thought Running Would Make Me Worthy of Love
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:02 UTC
19:00:02 KST

Endurance sports are having a moment. Run clubs, marathons, and ultramarathons have never been more popular. In North America, ultramarathon finishes have roughly tripled since 2010, exceeding 150,000 runners last year, according to UltraRunning magazine.
I understand the appeal. I spent years competing in some of the world’s most difficult endurance races, finding satisfaction and eventually a professional career in seeing how far I could push myself. But as more runners test their limits, I hope they’ll also ask themselves what they need those achievements to prove. For me, winning became a way to feel worthy of love. Every finish line offered reassurance that lasted only until I started worrying about the next race.
It took losing my professional running career to understand why I needed that reassurance so badly. The story began long before I laced up a pair of shoes and entered a race.
Divorce and my parents’ own troubled upbringings made my childhood difficult. As an adult, I can now see that my parents were unable to provide the safe, nurturing, and stable environment a kid deserves.
My young mind came to a conclusion that many children do: I must not be good enough the way that I am. Love, attention, and care, I believed, were all things that you had to earn.
As a teenager, I was desperate for the attention I rarely received at home. My grades were good, but not scholarship level; I was on the cross-country team and acted in school plays, but was never the standout star in either.
Despite my best efforts, nothing worked. That is, until I found success in ultrarunning.
At 15 years old, I watched my mother train and complete her first marathon. I was mesmerized. Maybe I could win her affection by doing what I’d seen her do.
Later that year, I crossed the finish line of the San Diego Rock n’ Roll Marathon. I loved the challenge, but I wanted more. Within a few years, I was running my first 50-mile ultramarathon. As part of my senior project, I pledged to run 100 miles around my high school track while fundraising money for the Leukemia & Lymphoma Society in honor of a friend who was battling cancer.
The ensuing media coverage was much more than I expected. To be honest, I loved the attention. Suddenly I felt seen by my mom. Again, I wanted more.
At 19, I finished Badwater, a 135-mile race across Death Valley in July. A year later, I flew out to Minnesota and completed the Arrowhead 135, in which I pulled a sled across the frozen landscape for nearly 54 hours. By age 20, I had attempted the Barkley Marathons for the first time, a race so difficult that in its 40-year history, only 20 people had ever officially finished. It would take me two more attempts navigating heinous trails through the hillsides of Tennessee to ultimately finish the race in 2013, becoming finisher 13.
Soon I was flying across the world, competing in 200-mile races, and living the life of a professional trail runner. It was everything I could have hoped for: the attention, the praise, the pre-race interviews, and the post-race adulation. And yet a part of me knew that if I didn’t win every race I entered, the worthlessness that I’d kept at bay for so long would drown me.
In 2018, that tidal wave finally came crashing over me. I had been diagnosed with a congenital bicuspid valve in my heart, and the resulting aortic aneurysm meant open-heart surgery.
Just like that, my professional running career was over, and with it went my path to validation. I had lived my whole life up to that point working for my worth; it was never inherent. If I couldn’t achieve results, who was I? Did I even exist? How could I be loved without having earned anything?
I spent the next five years dismantling my own self-worth from sport through therapy. The first and most pressing thing I had to face was the threat of suicide and self-harm. Running, it turns out, was protective of the deep-seated worthlessness I had developed from childhood.
Through intensive dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), medication, and an inpatient program, I curbed the more life-threatening aspects. DBT taught me awareness and the skills of emotional regulation. Later, lifespan integration and internal family systems therapy helped bring the roots of my childhood trauma to light and ultimately helped me place the hurt and shame back to their origin with my parents.
Slowly, I began to develop the understanding that I could be enough without having to achieve.
This lesson was never screamed at me. I was never explicitly told that I wasn’t enough. Instead, this anxiety whispered, quietly and convincingly, within me. It was the shaking hands of my 15-year-old self racing his heart out for the love of an absent parent. It was my 19-year-old self, slapping himself to keep going and push harder up the climb because some nebulous time or position would merit the love I never felt.
Through therapy, I came to realize I’d been fighting the wrong fight all along, and my relationship with running changed. After a full recovery from my heart surgery, I was able to begin running again, though not at the same level as I’d done before. In spite of the slower times, I was still able to get out into nature and, more importantly, spend time with my wife, whose running career was taking off.
I could hear my internal voices more clearly than ever and separate myself from it all a bit more. Eventually, I hired a running coach who, in addition to my wife, helped support me entering into shorter distance events that I’d eschewed early in my career. Not being a short-distance specialist, I’d been afraid to enter races I probably couldn’t win. Now I tried them anyway, and I had fun.
I realized I didn’t have to win a race to enjoy it or find value in it. I was finally enjoying running without needing it to be directly tied to my success.
Looking back on my career and with the perspective of both age and a tremendous amount of work, I’ve asked myself if I could have reached the same heights without that feeling that I need to win to be worthy of love.
Perhaps, and perhaps not; I’m less interested in that answer.
What I’d like to do is go back to my younger self and be there for every track meet, every race, no matter how well I performed. I’d tell myself, “I love you no matter what happens here today. There is nothing to prove. This is just a race.”
If you or someone you know may be experiencing a mental-health crisis or contemplating suicide, call or text 988.

Musk's PAC lawyer runs in Texas House district that is home to billionaire's business interests

Two years ago, Chris Gober was leading Elon Musk's political operation. Now, the former director and top lawyer for Musk's America PAC wants a seat in Congress representing Texas' 10th District, which is home to part of the Tesla and SpaceX CEO's growing business empire.
With less than a week until Election Day, Gober isn't exactly touting his connection to the world's richest person, as he tries to secure a Republican victory in an open seat considered a safe GOP win.
The 10th District is home to the Terafab, a sprawling artificial intelligence chip factory being built by Musk's companies Tesla and SpaceX. The district also cuts through Pflugerville, which houses offices for Musk's tunneling venture, The Boring Co.
While Gober is not talking about his work for Musk as a key pillar of his campaign, his Democratic opponent Caitlin Rourk scathingly highlighted it in a new ad.
"Elon Musk already had MAGA extremist Chris Gober as his lawyer. Now he wants him in Congress," a voice on the ad says. "It's clear who Chris Gober would serve in Congress, and it's not us."
Gober's campaign website touts an endorsement from President Donald Trump, and in the "key issues" section, the candidate says he will be "standing strong for President Trump and delivering his America First Agenda" if elected.
But neither Musk's name nor that of America PAC appeared on the campaign's site as of Tuesday.
Gober, in an email from campaign manager Zach Gregory, told CNBC, "My work with America PAC has been widely reported and is no secret."
"I've discussed it throughout this campaign as one of the many examples of taking on the toughest fights at the highest levels," he said.
Gober said Musk and America PAC are not mentioned on his campaign site because it was updated in the final weeks of the election "to focus on the priorities I'm running to deliver for the people of Texas's 10th Congressional District."
SpaceX PAC is supporting Gober
SpaceX's political action committee has donated $10,000 to Gober's campaign this election cycle, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Axios first reported the filing Monday.
SpaceX has expanded aggressively into AI in 2026.
The segment has become the company's largest business unit, with third-quarter revenue surging ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million a year earlier, according to its Oct. 20 earnings update.
Gober's campaign website deleted a section that had been titled "Ensuring America's AI Dominance," Axios reported in its article Monday, amid opposition to data centers used for AI.
Gober told CNBC the section's removal does not reflect a shift in his position.
"I believe Texas should lead the country in AI and innovation, and that growth has to work for the communities that make it possible," he said. "That means protecting our water and power supply, building the infrastructure to support it, and making sure rural communities share in the benefits."
Rourk criticized Gober's coziness with the AI industry and Musk, saying "There's just so much to his background that is really concerning."
"I think he's trying to bury his head in the sand, and just kind of wait until Election Day, hope that people won't notice," Rourk, a U.S. Army veteran and former Dell Technologies employee, told CNBC.
"If he wins a seat in Congress, he can sit there for the next 10, 20, 30 years where he is going to vote to tether taxpayer dollars in defense to SpaceX, in transportation to Tesla and vote against anything like a subpoena of Elon Musk," she said, alluding to bipartisan worries over SpaceX's dealings in Ukraine and Democrats' calls to investigate Musk over his Department of Government Efficiency work slashing the federal workforce.
Musk did not respond to an email seeking comment.
Attacks over AI go both ways in the campaigns. Gober's campaign in a YouTube ad and in an email to CNBC claimed Rourk makes a majority of her household income from investments in data centers.
Rourk called that accusation laughable.
She said she owns some Dell stock she acquired through employee equity grants when she worked there from 2021 to 2025. Rourk said she would sell those shares, which are not a source of household income for her, if she is elected to Congress.
If elected, she said her focus would include "ending forever wars including President Trump's reckless war in Iran," and on "fighting special interests."
Gober says he is 'proud' of his career
Asked about his opponent's accusation that he would work for Musk more than the people of Texas, Gober told CNBC, "I will make decisions based on what is best for my constituents. Period."
"I'm proud of my career and I'm not going to hide from it," he said. "I've worked at the highest levels of politics and public policy, and I intend to turn that experience into an asset for the people of Texas' 10th Congressional District."
Gober's law firm, Lex Politica, is representing Musk and his America PAC in two would-be class action lawsuits in Austin federal court that alleged Musk and the PAC defrauded people in swing states during the 2024 election by promising a daily $1 million prize for randomly selected people who signed a petition to support the U.S. Constitution and conservative causes.
Gober, during a Nov. 4, 2024 hearing in a Philadelphia courtroom held on the eve of Election Day, revealed that the 18 prizewinners were "not chosen by random, as in a lottery drawing, but that the super PAC instead selects the winners based on who it believes would be effective political spokespeople," NBC News reported at the time.
Lex Politica and other attorneys for Musk and America PAC and lawyers for the plaintiffs on Oct. 15 told the Texas judges overseeing the cases in Austin that they had agreed to settle the civil suits.
Terms of the settlement were not revealed, and Musk's PAC had denied any wrongdoing.
Gober told CNBC on Tuesday that he's "proactively working" with the House Ethics Committee to comply with all their rules, and if elected, he will "withdraw from all ongoing representations" since members of Congress are banned from practicing law outside of limited pro bono work.
Musk factor in race could cut either way
Whether Musk will be a boon or detriment to Gober's campaign remains to be seen.
Ben Leff, CEO of the survey company Verasight, told CNBC in an email that his firm found that Musk is "judged by Americans through a partisan lens."
In an April survey of 2,000 U.S. adults, Verasight found that 74% of Democrats have a somewhat or very unfavorable view toward Musk, compared to 53% of Independents and 17% of Republicans.
Among Americans who identify as members of Trump's MAGA movement, 85% believe that Musk represents the movement.
"In close races, candidates who are backed by or associated with Musk might face additional challenges in an already weak election cycle for Republicans," Leff said.

Comets probably didn’t deliver life’s building blocks to Earth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

The chemical building blocks that gave rise to life on Earth probably didn’t come from comets.
Most comets would have been traveling too fast and at too steep an angle to Earth for prebiotic compounds to survive impact with the planet, researchers contend October 28 in Scientific Reports. While the study doesn’t completely rule out the possibility that comets brought these molecules to Earth, it contradicts the long-standing idea that comets seeded Earth with the chemicals necessary for life to arise.
“Even though we see that comets contain all of these molecules in really high concentrations, it’s not straightforward to go from there to saying we’re going to have all of these available for prebiotic chemistry on the surface of the Earth,” says Richard Anslow, a planetary scientist at the Met Office, the national meteorological service for the United Kingdom in Exeter.
Comets carry carbon- and nitrogen-containing molecules left over from early in the solar system’s formation. These molecules can react to form biologically important compounds like sugars and DNA. Scientists have long thought that comets could have delivered these building blocks to Earth when they collided with the planet during its first billion years.
But it’s important to revisit these ideas as our understanding of both comets and the early solar system improves, says Nicolle Zellner, a physicist at Albion College in Michigan who was not involved in the study.
In the new work, Anslow and colleagues used computer simulations to predict the likelihood that a chemical called hydrogen cyanide would survive a comet’s journey through Earth’s present atmosphere and its impact with the planet’s surface. The early Earth’s atmosphere was probably much denser, so would have been even more destructive.
The strong chemical bond between the carbon and nitrogen atoms in hydrogen cyanide can release energy that drives later chemical reactions necessary for life. It also makes the molecule particularly stable compared to other carbon-based chemicals.
“It’s probably one of the more robust molecules to surviving impacts,” Anslow says. “So if things look bad for hydrogen cyanide, then we think it’s going to be much harder for other, more complicated molecules that are more likely to be broken down during these impacts.”
Based on the simulations, a comet impact that kept hydrogen cyanide intact would be extremely unlikely, the team found. On average, the simulations suggest that only one impact would have been able to deliver a meaningful amount of hydrogen cyanide to the planet’s surface over more than a billion years. For hydrogen cyanide to survive the crash, the comet would have to be larger than 100 meters across, slow moving and traveling at an oblique angle to Earth.
A comet that met those narrow criteria would also have had to crash into land, rather than an ocean, to kick off any biologically useful chemistry. If the comet landed in the ocean, any hydrogen cyanide that survived would be diluted too quickly to trigger those reactions.
While still improbable, comets may have been more likely to deliver carbon-based molecules to Mars than to Earth, the simulations showed. Mars’ thinner atmosphere and smaller size meant that comets would impact at lower speeds. That could mean that more compounds could survive the collision.
If Earth’s carbon-based chemicals didn’t come from comets, they may have come from carbon-rich asteroids called carbonaceous chondrites, says Gordon Osinski, a planetary geologist at Western University in London, Canada, who was not involved in the study. Other sources might have included volcanoes and hydrothermal vents.
The study “definitely will make people think twice about comets being the originator for the delivery of organics,” Osinski says. “I hope other people will try to reproduce these results [and] then potentially try something similar with carbonaceous chondrites as well.”

Please Let the Internet Die
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

The internet must be put out of its misery.
Any rational observer can admit that the current iteration of the web—and the social fabric woven there—is not what they signed up for. Symptoms of advanced cultural decay can no longer be ignored. This thing is eating itself.
Giants including Meta and Google have been forced to settle massive consumer lawsuits brought over privacy violations and mental health harms allegedly caused by the addictive mechanisms of their platforms. Schools are banning smartphones as multiple countries institute social media restrictions for under-16s. Parents are in a panic about their kids aspiring to careers as social media celebrities, losing themselves in a vast ecosystem of online casinos, or joining extremist movements.
Generative AI, briefly considered an amusing novelty, is now a turbocharged slop engine for the web, filling feeds and comment sections with useless, grotesque content. As humans scroll past headlines about AI taking their jobs, confusing fantasy for reality, and contributing to cognitive decline, any consumer appeal the technology might have is turning to anguish. The data centers that power it have become increasingly unpopular, and politically radioactive.
To be online, many now admit, is to be endlessly manipulated and exploited. In December, Oxford University Press declared rage bait to be the word of the year, noting that use of the term had tripled over the previous 12 months. The lexical spike represented a heightened awareness that monetized social accounts churn out bad-faith takes and extremist content, automating this abusive behavior with generative AI, simply to profit off hostile engagement. Billionaire oligarchs have opened the floodgates to such inauthentic activity, conspiracy-mongering, and hate speech by rolling back moderation.
In short, when you hang around online in 2026, you see little worth saving. Perhaps a decade ago, you felt that the glimmers of community and joy, of artistic and intellectual exchange, were enough to balance out the toxic junk. No longer.
It’s not necessarily that people have gotten worse. “Dead Internet Theory”—the proposition that a vast majority of the interactions on the web are fake, bots talking to other bots—has accrued more supporting evidence recently. One cybersecurity firm concluded this spring that agents already outnumber human users, their traffic surging by 8,000 percent through 2025. No wonder seemingly everyone has at some point caught themselves scrolling through a wasteland of brainrot and asked, “What the hell am I even looking at?” Underlying that question is another: “Is it always going to be like this?”
With this anxiety hammering at my prefrontal cortex day in and out, I was more than intrigued by the absolutist title of technologist and Pulitzer-winning journalist John West’s new book, The Internet Will Die, and So Will You: On Learning to Live in Our Digital Age. In his discerning treatise, West confirms what many have suspected for a good while now: The platforms once seen as enduring archives of knowledge and communication are being cannibalized by ideological warfare and basic greed.
But that’s not the whole story. For one, West argues, people misperceive the “vastness” of the internet, which really amounts to “a vanishing fraction, a rounding error, of the human experience.” Moreover, it is remarkably fragile—West opens with the story of how a 2001 train derailment in a Baltimore tunnel took out a major bundle of fiber-optic cables, leading to internet slowdowns nationwide—and continually undergoes cycles of death and rebirth as a result of this natural instability.
If the internet is much smaller and less solid than imagined, West’s book suggests, then it’s crucial to recognize the forces that determine how those deaths unfold, or which pieces are preserved while others crumble. Because the market has falsely sold us the web as a comprehensive library of accumulated wisdom, each transient phase of this global network comes to define the present, for better and worse. Today we witness a dismal paralysis brought on by algorithmic incentives to churn out inflammatory garbage: Full-time influencers are in a losing arms race for attention with low-effort, high-volume channels that streamline production by delegating the creative process to bleeding-edge software.
West draws a sharp contrast between this holographic environment of monetization and a passionate, personalized internet that spanned from the primordial GeoCities to Tumblr, describing how these innovative communities have been gradually erased. While some endure in half-dead and highly corrupted form, others are lost. In middle school, West maintained a web page devoted to his love of anime; later, he kept a blog documenting his college years. Looking back as an adult, he’s vexed by the fates that have befallen each.
“I really wanted to delete my anime site,” West tells WIRED. “I don't have access to the AOL account anymore, and I couldn't do it.” Instead, it lives on as a zombie page, cluttered with spam ads and dead-end links. As for the college blog, he had neglected to pay domain fees toward the end of his time writing it, and so the final year of posts disappeared. “I kind of got obsessed with this idea that the things we want to last really don't, and then oftentimes the things that we kind of wish would go away hang on for way too long,” West says.
These shifting sands are a far cry from the flawless, collective, permanent memory that internet users originally believed they were building. “‘Forever’ is such a strong word, and it's the wrong word,” West says. Online spaces are memento mori, the same as individuals who self-promote across them (and that includes certain longevity-obsessed biohackers). Sure, there was a time when a celebrity could be “canceled” for tasteless posts unearthed years later, but in 2026, it’s not so easy to surface specific messages when you go hunting for them in your AI-powered Gmail account. Zeitgeist-defining platforms like Vine can be vaporized in an instant, a fact reinforced in January 2025, when Americans posted farewell TikTok videos ahead of an expected US ban on the app.
This random ephemerality, West points out, has eroded any confidence in claims previously backed up by hypertext cross-references, and thus any kind of consensus truth. An analysis of hyperlinks in articles on The New York Times website between 1996 and mid-2019 found that 25 percent of all links were inaccessible. According to a 2016 study, “three out of four citations in scholarly articles have drifted—the websites they purport to cite no longer say what they once did,” he writes. “Over half of Wikipedia’s entries contain at least one link in its references section that goes nowhere, a Pew report found.”
The impulse to drive engagement spreads to users themselves: West noticed, for instance, that when he recently reread a favorite book, Marilynne Robinson’s Gilead, he had the nagging thought that while he loved returning to the novel for the fourth or fifth time, he wouldn’t be able to count it toward his annual Goodreads stats. West says this fixation on the internet’s hollow validations creates “the exact conditions for a space to be filled by something that isn't human.”
Wouldn’t it be liberating, then, to actually deny our attention to astroturfed outrage, engineered virality, and influencer sponcon? To let the mainstream digital economies propped up by AI-enabled surveillance finally fall to ruin? If what the titans of the industry have to offer us these days are “pervert glasses” and the suppression of ads for a probably unflattering documentary, why are we helping them stay in business? Leaving their platforms for dead might be the last lever of power available to the masses.
Doing so could free people to explore dormant corners. West notes that some of the most interesting parts of the internet are the ones that nobody sees, like web portals to streams of YouTube videos that have almost no views. “Some of it’s fucking weird and creepy, but a lot of it’s just people singing a song and having a blast,” he says. West also cites the bustling, zero-revenue, circulation of poetry in web journals as proof that “you can find meaning and make meaning online all the time,” provided there is no financial motivation.
When you eliminate what the platforms want you to fixate on, it’s clear what you’ve been missing, and how you were steered away from it. Your opinions are shaped in a bubble by avatars you’ve never met, weaponized against equally hermetic rival camps. The internet doesn’t really have winners, unless you count the few without the sense to stop chasing relevance at any cost. That’s why the main characters are so malleable in their beliefs; never afraid to pivot, betray, and discard what they once held to be the core of their identity. And that’s when they stood for anything to begin with.
Absent a sudden, lasting outage due to a fresh and severe catastrophe, the internet as it exists won’t perish anytime soon. There are, however, splintering cracks in its facade, which may create room for emergent and strangely evolved life-forms. There’s no reason to assume that the present tech empire will rule the century to come; the organic and anarchic web stands to mount a triumphant renaissance if (or when) it falls.
“Look, the internet is rotting,” West says. “The question is, where are we going to put our energy?” A metaphor he often turns to in his book is compost. “Compost is just rot harnessed for a purpose,” he says. Can a decaying internet be fertilizer for something better? It’s a rosy notion, but speaking as a perennially failed composter—it’s just too gross, and I’m too lazy—I have my doubts about whether enough hardy, patient gardeners can be mobilized to make our digital landscape bloom once more.
Then again, as West’s book sought to remind me, I am destined to die as well. Maybe I’ll be mixed in with the soil.

As missiles hit Saudi Arabia, residents insist life goes on — and the show does too
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

As missiles hit Saudi Arabia, residents insist life goes on — and the show does too
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Despite missile strikes that killed people, disrupted air travel and postponed major events, Riyadh Season opened with thousands attending concerts, comedy and attractions in the Saudi capital.
- Residents say daily life feels largely normal, but renewed Houthi attacks and the Iran war are weighing on the kingdom.
- Government messaging which once touted economic and cultural development, promotes patriotic themes.
RIYADH, Saudi Arabia — The lineup was announced months ago, with top-flight stars in tennis, DJing, comedy and more set to descend on the Saudi capital for a 10-week run of events known as Riyadh Season.
But after successive missile strikes hit Riyadh’s airport this month, killing more than a dozen people, shuttering parts of the country’s airspace and setting off a flurry of cancellations, many wondered if audiences would show up, or if there would be anything to show up for at all.
The answer to both questions came this past weekend, when crowds gathered for Riyadh Season’s opener at Boulevard City, a car-free district in the capital that’s part open-air mall, part amusement park and part entertainment venue.
By the time sunset had turned to dusk, families were milling about a replica of Times Square. Patrons assembled for a sold-out comedy play at one of two theaters, while others went to a 7,000-seat arena, where a famous Lebanese pop star was debuting his comeback tour. It too was sold out.
This is a twilight moment for the Saudi capital. In normal times, October is when the convection-bake temperatures of Riyadh’s ferocious summer give way to a bearable, even pleasant heat, and the city hosts dozens of large-scale events aimed at showcasing Vision 2030, the kingdom’s all-out drive to transform itself into a sporting and entertainment powerhouse.
But between the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and Riyadh’s escalating grudge match with the Iran-backed Yemeni rebels known as the Houthis, these are hardly normal times.
For years, the war with the Houthis — whose official name is Ansar Allah, or Partisans of God — had ebbed and flowed between campaign and ceasefire, but for most Saudis, it had remained background noise. That changed in recent months, with a truce breaking down, and the Houthis lobbing drones, ballistic and cruise missiles across Saudi Arabia.
All of a sudden, the war took on a more present form, unsettling a kingdom unused to conflicts playing out on home turf. Almost every night in Riyadh brings the bass-drum booms and thuds of interceptors launching to destroy incoming projectiles.
Government messaging has turned pugilistic, replacing paeans to Vision 2030 and the country’s leadership with images of Saudi F-15s en route to do battle over Yemen, or commercial billboards declaring “Our bravery brings us together” or “Stable home, reassured hearts.”
In October alone, Houthi missile strikes on Saudi airports have killed at least 21 people and wounded hundreds, forcing authorities to shut down operations in the country’s main international airport in Riyadh and curtailing travel in others. (On Sunday, officials announced some flights at the Riyadh airport had resumed.)
Schools shifted to online-only learning, while many businesses — including Saudi Aramco, the country’s state-owned oil company — were ordered to evacuate headquarters and have all staff work remotely. The U.S. Embassy ordered “non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members” in Saudi Arabia to leave.
The attacks come at an inopportune juncture. Many of the kingdom’s marquee, international-facing gatherings have been affected, including the World Petroleum Congress, a summit between the European Union and Persian Gulf nations, and the government’s flagship investment conference, the Future Investment Initiative.
Though the congress went ahead — with many top oil executives attending virtually — the summit and investment conference were shelved till next year. Also postponed were some of Riyadh Season’s major sporting events, such as the Six Kings Slam tennis tournament.
But other events — including boxing and UFC championships and the WWE Crown Jewel event — remain stubbornly on the calendar. The first few days of Riyadh Season have gone ahead with little incident, even if participants were forced to divert to other cities or even neighboring Bahrain or Kuwait before being ferried back to the Saudi capital.
That shrugging off of the war was a common attitude among visitors to Boulevard City, organizers say.
In the replica Times Square, building-sized screens cast windows of light as people grabbed elaborate drinks made with iced tea, coffee or hibiscus. Trackless trains, their carriages mocked up as reindeer, ferried kids around a giant illuminated orb.
“Between foot traffic in Boulevard City, audiences for the plays and the concerts, we had something like 27,000 people coming in,” said Hassan Albar, Boulevard City’s director, a note of pride — and some relief — creeping into his voice.
“And we’re still at the beginning of the season.”
Despite the daily cellphone alerts that warn residents to remain indoors until danger passes, people interviewed emphasized a show-must-go-on disposition.
“We like to keep it positive, so we’re not going to be staying inside. It’s human nature to feel afraid if you don’t have control, but the situation is fine,” said Neetika Malotra, 33, who was taking pictures of Ankid Abishaikh, 34, before a Boulevard City sign.
Abishaikh said conditions in Saudi Arabia are different from how they’re portrayed online.
“Our parents are outside in India, so when they see news channels or social media, it looks very scary. But we tell them that what they see there is not always right,” he said.
“When you’re here, everything feels normal and we’re doing well.”
Both the U.S.-Israel war on Iran and the Houthis’ campaign have harmed Saudi Arabia’s oil production, with closures of the Strait of Hormuz denying the kingdom its main energy export corridor. In addition to missiles at Riyadh‘s airport, the Houthis over the weekend targeted crude oil pumping stations, an oil refinery, an Aramco facility in Yanbu and the East-West Pipeline, which transports oil to terminals on the Red Sea coast.
The Saudi military has struggled to defend against Houthi missiles, hampered by the sheer size of the country — Saudi Arabia’s territory is more than five times the size of California — and a fast-depleting supply of interceptors.
The fighting with the Houthis is compounding the economic headwinds forced on the kingdom by the Iran war and a general economic slowdown; Saudi officials already have had to reassess some of the grander ambitions underpinning Vision 2030.
Contractors, all of whom spoke on condition of anonymity so as not to jeopardize future professional prospects, say that staff working on so-called gigaprojects have been drawn down, reassigned or let go. Ancillary businesses — catering and events organizers — have endured losses of up to two thirds of revenues amid a cost-cutting pullback.
Yet despite those complaints, the consensus among many residents is that the war hasn’t had a drastic impact on their lives, at least in terms of their sense of safety.
“It’s very secure here. I don’t feel anything like what’s said on the news,” said Abdul Rahman Al-Hassan, 38, a dentist who moved to Riyadh nine months ago from Moscow.
He compared the situation here to the Russian capital, which has been the frequent target of a Ukrainian drone campaign.
“Journalists say the same sort of thing about Moscow: That it’s very dangerous and that people are hiding in their basements from the drones,” he said.
“But it’s not true there, and it’s not true here. You can have an attack in one area, but people are still going out normally.”
That may hint at a head-in-the-sand mentality, and it’s hard to gauge public sentiment in a country where openly expressing dissatisfaction with government policies can land you in jail or have you deported. But among Saudis, the conflict with the Houthis appears to have spurred a rally-round-the-flag moment.
“We fully trust the government and the leadership in charge,” said Awatef Mohammad, a 31-year-old English teacher strolling with her partner through Boulevard City.
Similar sentiments emerge even in places more directly in the line of fire. Over the weekend, spectators gathered at Riyadh’s King Abdulaziz Racecourse for an evening of horse racing, despite the fact that the track is barely three miles from the airport.
Jamil Mohammad, a 42-year-old occupational therapist, had his children Jad and Joury in tow. He propped up Joury on a railing to watch the horses saunter past as they prepared for the race. His eyes on his daughter, he expressed a belief in God’s protection that, to many outsiders, can sound like fatalism.
“Look, whether I’m here near the airport, or anywhere else in the world, if God says it’s my time to die, then it’s my time to die. It won’t matter,” he said.
“Death only comes once. I’m not going to let it stop me living my life.”

Paris braces for more unrest as riots reshape the city's streets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Riots across France have left more than 3,000 businesses attacked or looted. Paris shopkeepers have boarded up windows and bought pepper spray and tear gas.
- The unrest has left Paris a city of contrasts: Daily life continues alongside shattered windows, police helicopters and residents’ fear of renewed violence.
- Many residents of Paris, Marseille and other major cities beset by riots still feel under siege, much like Los Angeles after the 1992 riots.
PARIS — Business is up tenfold at a weapons store near Place de l’Opéra in Paris: Shopkeepers from all over the city have been stocking up on pepper spray and tear gas.
In the nine days since riots erupted in cities across France, thousands of merchants have also boarded up their storefronts, radically altering the Paris streetscape. The screech of electric saws and pounding of nails into plywood are now background noise in the French capital.
“They’re afraid their stores will be attacked and looted,” Yves Gollety, owner of the weapons store, explained.
Adding to the dark mood are police helicopters hovering, with searchlights blazing, to enforce a late-night curfew in the Les Halles and République sections of Paris.
And the city has removed many of the huge street-corner bins where Parisians are accustomed to dropping their empty wine and beer bottles. Rioters had been knocking them over to get glass ammunition against police.
Yet daily life has barely changed in much of Paris, where it can seem like normal times amid the chaos. Friends chat in cafés with shattered windows. Customers ignore plywood covering the front doors of shops.
But the social and economic grievances that boiled over so violently have not gone away, and nobody can escape the dreaded question: What’s next?
More demonstrations, for sure, and a strike planned for Nov. 5, which has left many resigned to toggling, for now, between upheaval and ordinary life.
The contrasts can be jarring.
At Cycles Laurent, a bike store on Boulevard Voltaire, a makeshift wooden window doubles as a spray-painted sign urging people to come on in.
“We remain open,” it says.
The bike shop is one of more than 3,000 businesses attacked or pillaged in France in the aftermath of giant protests against the government of President Emmanuel Macron the weekend of Oct. 17.
Although a tense urban peace has taken hold since then, many residents of Paris, Toulouse, Marseille and other cities beset by riots still feel under siege, much like Los Angeles after the 1992 riots.
“This whole climate is horrible,” said Yolande Montagnac, a retiree who has lived for 45 years near the Gare de Lyon in Paris and was heartbroken by the damage to the city.
Scattered curfews and a police surge to keep nationwide protests under control have helped to stop the looting. More than 400,000 protesters returned to the streets on Saturday, by the police count; closer to double that number, according to unions. Apart from a few tear-gas skirmishes, the demonstrations ended peacefully.
The unrest began after high school students took to the streets last month to denounce poor conditions and resources at their campuses. On Monday, Macron said the government would take “concrete measures” to address those concerns.
As the turmoil has grown, Paris has been the setting of odd contrasts.
As boulevard barricades were burning Oct. 17 in Les Halles, the lilting harmonies of a roving choir singing a peace ballad were soothing passersby shopping for cheese and wine a few blocks away.
Hours later, vandals smashed scores of windows around the corner and ransacked stores as neighbors watched in horror from apartments above. Unchecked by police, looters returned the next night.
Not a week had gone by before a gaggle of fashionistas, testing the limits of decency and humor, gathered on the same stretch of the Rue Étienne Marcel for a riot-porn glamour shot in a wrecked ad-poster frame.
In the distance was a bronze statue of Louis XIV on a rearing horse in the majestic Place des Victoires, its stone pedestal stained by protesters’ splashes of red paint.
On Place de la République, the scene of violent clashes between police and protesters on Oct. 17, the usual skateboarders were back on Sunday morning. By then, graffiti had been scrubbed from the central monument that pays tribute to the French Republic, including its tradition of insurrection.
At Gollety’s weapons store, Armurerie de la Bourse, dozens of guns are on display, but firearm restrictions are so tight in France that merchants were not trying to buy any.
“In France, nobody shoots a robber,” he said. “You go to prison.”
Arnaud, 24, a pastry chef who works at a bakery and declined to share his last name, bought tear gas Friday “to neutralize someone if need be.”
“It’s incredible that it’s come to this,” he said as he left Gollety’s shop. “I think we’ve reached that limit where the French are saying, ‘OK, the state isn’t protecting me, I’m going to try to protect myself until the state protects me.’”
Arnaud supports France’s far right. “There’s no center anymore, no core that can bring everyone together. It’s a loss of bearings, and it’s a mess,” he said.
In the run-up to the protests on Saturday, the Paris police commissioner, Patrice Faure, heightened anxieties by advising merchants to hire security guards, saying police alone could not “guarantee the protection of every business.”
Florence Portelli, the mayor of Taverny, a Paris suburb, was mortified by the call for self-defense.
“The day we start opening the door to that, we end up with what sometimes happens in the United States, in countries where things go absolutely, completely crazy,” she told BFM television.
Since the protests started, they have expanded to cover the high cost of living, aggressive police tactics and other grievances. French police have arrested about 12,000 people.
At the Paris protest on Saturday, a row of police in riot gear led the crowd along the authorized route down boulevards on the city’s outskirts. Just behind them was a group of “black bloc” militants yelling ACAB, the international slogan for “all cops are bastards.”
The sea of 100,000 people marching behind them was a wide mix of union members, students, leftists and others unhappy with Macron.
Chloé Brani, a 21-year-old student from the suburbs, carried a sign that summed it up: “We’re all fed up.”
She blamed inequalities in France on “elites who don’t care.”
If military and police money “were simply put back into the causes we’re asking for — a normal salary, normal living conditions for workers in every possible profession, and high schools in good condition — there actually wouldn’t be a problem,” she said as she marched. “It’s the distribution of wealth that’s unjust.”
Montagnac, a retired executive assistant, sees France’s political leadership in a state of collapse, most evident in its loss of control during the riots. But she also thinks the turmoil is rooted in the decline of human contact in the digital age.
“Everyone is on their phone all the time,” she lamented Sunday morning at the bustling Aligre outdoor produce market, where neighbors were, just like before the riots, buying fruit, vegetables, meat and fish. “There’s no more friendliness. People don’t take the time to stop and chat. It’s always a rush.”
For Montagnac, 69, it was especially painful to see the owner of a furniture store on Boulevard Diderot hauling his sofas and chairs into the back of the shop to deter looters.
“He can’t sleep at night, he’s so scared,” she said.

Commentary: Agitating for attention, Trump and Bill Maher get into it, again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Agitating for attention, Trump and Bill Maher get into it, again
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Soaring gas prices and a war with Iran. Historically low approval ratings. A potential blue tsunami. A new rape allegation.
President Trump has a lot on his plate, and so too does the nation. Sunday, he took to Truth Social to address the people.
“Let’s talk about this COMPLETE AND TOTAL LOSER, Bill Maher,” the president wrote at the top of his longest post ever.
A fireside chat it was not.
The 1,300-word-plus screed was triggered by Friday’s episode of “Real Time With Bill Maher,” a mainstay on HBO since 2003. The comedian referred to Trump as a “lame duck” president with low approval ratings during a segment with his guest, former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt.
Trump, 80, likely expected praise from his fellow curmudgeon Maher, 70, since the men had recently dined together at the White House. It was their second such date following a controversial get-together in March 2025, which Maher juiced for all it was worth in an effort to stand out from his fellow late-night hosts.
When Colbert was named the new host of ‘The Late Show’ in 2015, he was considered an unusual choice, but he turned out to be the right fit for these times.
Maher’s chummy relationship with Trump has made him an outlier among his peers, many of whom have been in the president’s crosshairs.
CBS canceled Stephen Colbert’s show after decades on the air following pressure from Trump’s Federal Communications Commission chair. Trump has bitterly complained about being treated unfairly by Jimmy Kimmel and Seth Meyers. They, too, now have targets on their backs.
Maher has avoided the same fate by railing on Trump only half as much as his late-night peers, leaning into various MAGA grievances about the “woke” left and forging a fair-weather friendship with the second-term president.
If the Maher of 2003 could see himself now, he’d likely dedicate a searing monologue to the hypocrisy. The host was once positioned as an irreverent comedian whose political satire was guided by his no-BS take on Capitol Hill and American culture. Common sense over party fealty. Political correctness be damned.
But as the political landscape has shifted, so too has Maher’s approach.
Now he plays the role of a staunchly nonpartisan crank on TV while dining with the president in person.
“Yeah, I did it again, b—!” Maher said to his audience Friday. “I know. I’m the bad guy because I go and say face-to-face to the man the things you write in articles that he’ll never read, but OK. You know what? F— you. I like these dinners.”
So brave. So calculated.
Maher was dipping back into the attention he received in 2025, when he first dined with Trump and described the president as “gracious and measured.”
Their rendezvous was just the sort of thing the comedian would have mercilessly lampooned if he wasn’t in fact part of the joke. Fellow comedians such as Patton Oswalt have criticized the HBO host for placating Trump, while Larry David satirized Maher’s first date with the president in a New York Times essay titled “My Dinner With Adolf.”
The controversy was a boon for “Real Time,” boosting its waning relevance by putting Maher back in the news and reinforcing the tired charade that his fearlessness knows no bounds.
This week’s public skirmish was a repeat performance, if not a somewhat pathetic display of both men’s need to agitate for attention.
Maher told his audience on Friday’s episode that he spoke with the president about deadly ICE incidents, Ukraine and how Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was “dragging” Trump down. In closing, he assured the audience he was no pushover by poking at the president’s recent favorable dealings with Russia (a diesel deal, lifting sanctions), then saying, “I could not have been treated better if I was Russian.”
Given the president’s delicate psyche, Maher knew anything short of absolute praise would be perceived as an insult. As for the knock about Trump’s slumping approval numbers? A sure trigger.
In Sunday’s Truth Social manifesto, Trump referred to Maher as a “biased, dumb SLEAZEBAG” whose program is plagued by low ratings. The president also alleged that the comedian was drunk and had a drink in hand as he toured the White House on Oct. 15, and that Maher is a “major POTHEAD” who “looked like hell this time.”
So much for Trump’s initial comments about their meeting. He had told reporters that it was “a great dinner.”
“Bill Maher, I tell you what, he likes me a lot more than people understand,” Trump said. “And I actually like him.”
Not unlike Trump, Maher also enjoys praise, and blames the “woke left” when he doesn’t get it.
The typically smug host appeared upset earlier this year at the Golden Globes when presenter Wanda Sykes roasted him and another nominee up for best performance in stand-up comedy on television, Ricky Gervais.
“There’s some people pissed off that a queer Black woman is up here doing the job of two mediocre white guys,” Sykes said. “... But first, I want to give them some love.” Addressing Maher directly, she said, “You give us so much. But I would love a little less. Just try less.” The camera panned to a stone-faced Maher, who appeared “butthurt” (a term he likes using to dismiss the gripes of folks he gripes about).
The bruised feelings didn’t stop there. Later, on Maher’s “Club Random” podcast, he vented about being passed over by Hollywood.
“I’ve been nominated for 33 Emmys, and they would never give it to me,” he told his guest Joel Edgerton. “I speak freely, and this woke town f— hates that. That’s OK. I’ve made my peace with that, so I know how this goes.”
If Maher has been “soft-canceled” by the industry, as he claims, then Hollywood has a funny way of showing its disdain: HBO renewed “Real Time” through 2028.
Perhaps he learned from his frenemy Trump that grievance politics sells, and it’s time to cash in.

Almost 3 in 10 machines in Belgian factories stand idle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:57:56 UTC
18:57:56 KST

Belgian industry is in the doldrums. Nearly 30% of all the machines in Belgian factories currently stand idle, according to financial dailies De Tijd and L’Echo. The metal and technology federation Agoria describes the industrial slump as “unprecedented”. Sector federations are therefore calling for measures to tackle high costs and are warning of further job losses.
Almost 3 in 10 machines in Belgian factories stand idle
‘In our sector, we have been struggling with a capacity utilisation rate below 80 per cent for four years now. That is unprecedented,’ Patrick Slaets, chief economist at the metal and technology federation Agoria, told VRT NEWS.
“The cause lies in a lack of demand. There is too little investment, due to the high interest rates brought about by inflation and excessively high energy costs resulting from the geopolitical situation.” This is why energy-intensive companies are suffering the most.
A fall in capacity utilisation also means a greater risk of job losses, warns Slaets. “If the machines aren’t running, there’s no need for people to work there. In the technology sector, 20,000 jobs have already been lost over the past three years. That represents a 6 to 7 per cent reduction in capacity compared with pre-crisis levels.”
Chemical sector also reeling from high energy costs
The chemical sector is also facing tough times. According to a study by consultancy firm Roland Berger, European capacity fell by 9 per cent between 2022 and 2025. On top of that, only 69 to 70 per cent of that (reduced) capacity is being utilised.
It’s been announced that chemical company Vynova in Tessenderlo-Ham is temporarily halting production due to high energy prices. 600 employees are at risk of temporary unemployment.
“It is gradually becoming clear that this crisis is more severe than the previous one,” says Gert Verreth, spokesperson for the chemicals’ federation Essenscia.
It is being argued that urgent action is needed to address issues such as high energy costs and bureaucracy. This applies not only to Belgium, as the rest of Europe is also grappling with similar problems.
‘There is political awareness, but progress at European political level is too slow,’ says Verreth. On the one hand, the high costs must be tackled, but on the other, Europe must also send a strong signal on the geopolitical stage.
There is the context of increasingly aggressive industrial policies, with Trump’s tariff war and the mass production being encouraged by the Chinese government. “Europe must act more swiftly and urgently show its teeth.”
It’s being argued that in Belgium, in particular, labour costs must be kept under control. They are already higher than in neighbouring countries and are threatening to rise even further. “If they are not kept in line with our neighbours, we could end up in an industrial recession next year,” Slaets also fears.

Israel’s stock market drops as exit polls show no clear election winner
Benchmark Tel Aviv 125 index drops more than 3 percent amid uncertainty over who will lead the next government.
Israel’s stock market has fallen sharply amid exit polls showing no clear winner in the country’s parliamentary elections.
The benchmark Tel Aviv 125 index dropped as much as 3.5 percent in early trading on Wednesday as investors weighed the unclear results of Israel’s first election since the start of its genocidal war on Gaza.
Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition nor the opposition bloc headed by Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot appeared on track to gain a parliamentary majority in the 26th Knesset.
With more than 84 percent of votes counted as of 11 GMT, Netanyahu’s coalition was on course to win 54 seats, while Eisenkot’s opposition bloc was headed for 49 seats, according to tallies published by Israeli media.
Sixty-one seats are needed to form a majority in the unicameral parliament.
Israel’s economy has been running hot despite being on a war footing for the past three years amid an influx of investment in the local tech sector.
Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 2.9 percent in 2025 and 3.2 percent in the first half of 2026, according to government figures.
The Bank of Israel last week raised its GDP growth forecast for all of 2026 to 5.6 percent, up from 4 percent, citing ramped-up production by Israeli firms overseas.
The central bank has forecast that GDP growth for 2027 would reach 7.5 percent, far surpassing estimates for advanced economies such as the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany and Japan.

Media groups urge EU Commission transparency as Gaza documents probe unfolds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:54:15 UTC
18:54:15 KST

A group of 15 media outlets, journalist associations and press freedom organizations urged European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday to improve journalists’ access to public documents, as an inquiry by the EU Ombudswoman into the commission’s refusal to release documents concerning Gaza unfolds, Anadolu reports.
In an open letter to von der Leyen, the organizations called on the EU executive to address what they described as a “silent crisis” that has hampered journalists’ efforts to obtain information needed to scrutinize matters of public importance.
The appeal comes after European Ombudswoman Teresa Anjinho last week opened an inquiry into a news outlet’s complaint over the commission’s refusal to release 17 documents concerning EU-funded infrastructure projects in the Gaza Strip.
EUobserver first requested the documents in February as part of an investigation examining the extent to which Israeli attacks had destroyed infrastructure financed by the EU in the Palestinian territory.
The commission refused to release the material, arguing that there was no overriding public interest justifying disclosure. EUobserver’s subsequent appeal went unanswered.
As a first step in her inquiry, Anjinho has asked the commission to respond to the appeal by Nov. 4 at the latest. If the EU executive fails to provide a satisfactory response, she will examine the documents herself.
Against this backdrop, the 15 organizations urged the commission to commit to greater transparency, saying journalists routinely face severe delays in obtaining documents, questionable refusals and extensive redactions that render released material largely meaningless.
In some cases, they said, the commission also fails to retain and properly archive crucial documents.
The restrictions have hindered reporting on issues of major public interest, including how EU member states spent billions of euros in post-COVID recovery funds and cooperation with Israel on arms research, the letter said.
“Around Europe, public debate is being harmed. Stories which should emerge do not. Citizens cannot make important political judgements at critical moments,” it said.
The signatories called on the commission to revoke its December 2024 internal rules of procedure, which they said had made access to documents more difficult, and ensure strict implementation of the regulation on public access to EU documents.
The groups also called for a renewed action plan to improve journalists’ access to information, including implementing recommendations from the European Ombudsman, fully complying with European Court of Justice rulings and strengthening internal procedures for filing and archiving documents.
“The European Commission’s reputation for safeguarding EU democratic values is in peril. At a time when democratic norms are under attack around the world, now is the time to uphold these values,” the letter warned.
The signatories included the Committee to Protect Journalists, EUobserver, the European Federation of Journalists, Follow the Money, Forbidden Stories, the International Federation of Journalists, the International Press Institute, Investigate Europe and PEN International.
