Harassed by Russian drones, Ukraine’s trains keep on rolling
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:54:06 CET
18:54:06 KST

By Yurii Kovalenko
ON A TRAIN BETWEEN DNIPRO AND ODESA, Ukraine, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Ukrainian beauty salon owner Antonina Viter is getting used to having her travel plans disrupted by the threat of Russian drone attacks, as she criss-crosses the country by rail to keep her business going.
“Every third trip, we end up evacuating once, twice or even three times,” she explained on board a train from the southeastern city of Dnipro to Odesa on the Black Sea.
“What can you do? How else do you get to your client?”
Kyiv has set new rules for rail passengers during air-raid alerts and, sure enough, soon after she spoke, the 36-year-old was standing outside under a pitch-black October sky, wrapped in a blanket, waiting for the “all-clear”.
In a country long reliant on its vast rail network, hours-long delays and repeat evacuations when air-raid sirens sound are another way in which Russia’s escalating missile and drone attacks are wrecking everyday life for civilians.
New Russian jet-powered drones that are hard to shoot down have attacked everything from shopping centres and filling stations to power plants and other critical infrastructure. And the railways are no exception.
UKRAINIAN RAILWAYS ATTACKED 1,700 TIMES THIS YEAR
The state operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, says Russia has attacked more than 1,700 rail facilities this year, including stations, locomotives and passenger wagons. Russia says its targets are objects used by Kyiv’s military.
A trip on the line from Dnipro to Odesa, some 400 km (250 miles) to the southwest, showed how Ukrainians are coping with those disruptions.
The outward journey featured eight evacuations of roughly 30 minutes each, the return journey - one more.
Direct attacks, like the drone strike that killed two train drivers on the Dnipro-Odesa line on August 13, are an ever-present threat.
But air-raid alerts can unexpectedly double the travel time on any route, and some stations in the east and south have been shut indefinitely as fighting creeps closer.
The prospect of being hit is one that 41-year-old IT worker Larysa Konstantynova - who was travelling from Dnipro to Odesa with her teenage son at the start of a holiday trip to Europe - prefers not to think about.
Like Viter, who travels at least six times a month to manage two salons in Kyiv and Dnipro, she says she is adapting.
“It’s how your mind works: you just try to be positive and survive with the way things are.”
Other attacks have included a strike on a Warsaw-bound train near the Polish border in September.
For some, overnight rail journeys - once opportunities to unwind with few distractions - are now spent in anxious anticipation.
During air raid alerts, passengers can be jolted awake and forced to scramble into fields or up and down embankments, sometimes with children or pets in tow. In the winter, temperatures are often below freezing.
RAILWAY JOURNEYS HAUNTED BY RISK OF RANDOM DEATH
Huddled outside her train with a colleague, Viter tracked a nearby drone on a cell-phone app after hearing its distinctive ‘whoosh’ overhead.
It was the third evacuation in two hours.
“Better to stand in a field for an hour than to risk never getting to see the next hour,” she said, knowing she had to teach a beauty workshop in Odesa the next day.
In fact, although delays of 5 to 12 hours are not unusual on the Dnipro-Odesa route, this train arrived just an hour and 20 minutes late.
Nevertheless, the risk of random death has soared as Russia has broadened its drone and ballistic-missile campaign, exploiting Kyiv’s shortage of air defence missiles.
More than 50 railway workers have died on duty this year alone, according to Ukraine’s infrastructure minister, and dedicated staff have had to adapt their routines to maintain a network that appears to be close to their hearts.
At the beginning of each journey, conductors sweep through the carriages closing curtains to block out light that might alert a Russian drone.
“They can see us, so we have to hide a bit,” said train attendant Olha Boniuk, 49, with the air of a mother soothing her child.
After each evacuation, chief conductor Mykola Zakharchenko, 47, sits in his cramped booth diligently recording the interruption.
All the same, he smiles recalling conversations with passengers, and still enjoys watching dawn break through the carriage window: “Train work, as they say, is romance.”
Locomotive driver Mykola Kovalenko put it another way.
“If I quit,” he said, “who will drive the trains?”
(Additional reporting by Thomas Peter; Writing by Dan Peleschuk; Editing by Mike Collett-White and Kevin Liffey)

MADRID/BEIJING, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Real Madrid issued an apology on Wednesday after their French forward Kylian Mbappe sparked a fierce backlash over his comments referring to the former Chinese leader Mao Zedong as a dictator.

China’s state-owned broadcasting platform Migu is not showing Real Madrid’s LaLiga game against Racing Santander on Sunday, and Chinese brands including dairy companies Mengniu and Shanghai Milkground Food Tech as well as Eastroc Beverage ceased all cooperation with Mbappe.
REAL MADRID GAME NOT ON TV
Migu is scheduled to show nine of LaLiga’s 10 games this weekend, with Real Madrid’s match the only one not covered. Migu did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
LaLiga moved quickly to set up a crisis unit and reached out to Real Madrid, a significant move following years of strained relations between Tebas and the club due to a power struggle within Spanish football. Real Madrid recently called for Tebas’ resignation.
Both parties put aside their differences, however, acknowledging the potential immediate and long-term financial repercussions of Mbappe’s comments. Following Real’s statement, people at LaLiga said Tebas was considering travelling to China to neutralise the threat of a massive financial loss for Spanish football.
LaLiga will also consider strengthening its institutional engagement with Beijing amid serious concerns about a sharp drop in revenue, as Chinese state television awaits further gestures of reconciliation.
In a video on a French podcast that has since been taken down, Mbappe is heard discussing a humorous meme where his face had been photoshopped on to that of “some guy — I think he’s a Chinese dictator”.
Fans have previously created memes superimposing Mbappe’s face on images of military and political leaders to suggest that he has the power to influence decisions at the teams he plays for. Mbappe has been nicknamed “the dictator” in the European press.
On Wednesday, when asked what China thought of Mbappe’s apology, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said: “We take seriously the apology that the person has made.”

By Andrew Mills and Parisa Hafezi
Oct 28 (Reuters) - Qatari mediators have presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war with the US and Israel, an official briefed on the negotiations said, but a senior Iranian official said Doha had only put forward unacceptable ideas that did not amount to an offer.
The official briefed on the negotiations, who is not from Iran, said a new draft peace proposal for the eight-month-old conflict was presented on Sunday and was being considered by Tehran, with a response expected by the end of the week.
Qatar, along with Pakistan, has led mediation to end the war, which has disrupted global shipping and oil supplies and recently spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
The proposal presented by Qatar sets a seven-day timeline addressing both Tehran’s and Washington’s concerns, laying out daily confidence-building steps that each side must take, the official briefed on the negotiations said. The timeline could begin early next week and several countries would act as guarantors of the deal, the official added.
Shortly afterwards, a senior Iranian official involved in the talks said Qatar had presented only “unacceptable ideas and not an offer”, and that Tehran’s policy on showing no flexibility over the nuclear issue remained unchanged.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Wednesday that Tehran remained in close contact with intermediaries to review ideas that could ensure the implementation of its own seven-day proposal aimed at ending the war in the Middle East.
He said Iran continued to give diplomacy a chance to succeed, adding that Tehran’s seven-day plan could be implemented in less than a week.
Washington wants Iran’s decades-long nuclear programme to be part of negotiations to end the war from the outset, while Iran says its conditions — which include an end to the US blockade of Iranian ports and the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil exports — must be met first. Iran rejects Western concerns that its nuclear programme is military in nature.
ATTACK ON SAUDI OIL REFINERY
In late September, Iran presented its seven-day proposal under which Araqchi said the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy shipping channels, could be reopened if certain conditions were met. US President Donald Trump rejected it, prompting further Qatari mediation.
The draft discussed in Tehran on Sunday was different from that proposal, the official briefed on the negotiations said, though the details of the latest plan were not immediately clear. The official had previously told Reuters that the Qatari mediators had coordinated with Washington before going to Tehran.
Earlier mediation efforts to end the war that the US and Israel launched on February 28 helped produce an interim peace agreement in June, but it quickly unravelled.
In recent weeks, Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi forces have launched repeated attacks against Saudi Arabia — a key US ally and the world’s largest crude exporter — opening a new front in the eight-month-old war.
Oil prices rose more than 1% to more than $115 per barrel on Wednesday after a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s largest oil refinery, Ras Tanura, stoking concerns over supply risks.
Fighting with the Houthis intensified last month as the militant group advanced against Saudi-backed forces towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another important shipping lane on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula from Hormuz.
CONCERNS ABOUT RISK OF NEW STRIKES
The official briefed on the negotiations said there were concerns ahead of Sunday’s meeting in Tehran that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, fighting for another term in a general election, could resume attacks on the Islamic Republic this week.
On Friday, Trump repeated threats to strike Iran again, while Iranian security officials told Reuters Tehran had drawn up detailed plans to attack Gulf undersea cables if the US and Israel resumed attacks.
On Monday, top officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan also met Iranian officials in Tehran as part of de-escalation efforts. Qatar said on Tuesday that Iran needs to stop threats against Arab Gulf states and open the Strait of Hormuz to show good intentions for mediation efforts to succeed.
Gulf states came under sustained bombardment earlier in the war.
The war also reignited fighting between Israel and the Iran-backed Lebanese armed group Hezbollah. It has eroded Trump’s approval ratings ahead of the US midterm elections that decide control of Congress.

The BJP came to power in the state for the first time, ending the TMC’s 15-year rule.
Turning to the murder of Chandranath Rath, Adhikari alleged that his aide was killed because of his association with him, describing it as a “supari”, or contract killing.“Chandranath was murdered simply because he was my aide. The CBI has arrested seven people, including the shooters and contract killers. What remains to be established is where the Rs 2 crore ‘supari’ for the contract killing came from. Was it Camac Street, Kalighat or Diamond Harbour? Once that is known, the investigation will be complete,” he said.Adhikari appeared to be referring to Camac Street, associated with the office of Trinamool Congress national general secretary and Mamata's nephew Abhishek Banerjee; Kalighat, where Mamata Banerjee resides; and Diamond Harbour, the Lok Sabha constituency represented by Abhishek Banerjee.

Dozens killed in Spanish high-speed train collision (VIDEOS)
At least 68 people have been killed after two high-speed trains collided near Toledo, Spain, Castilla-La Mancha regional President Emiliano Garcia-Page has said, according to Spanish newspaper ABC. More than 179 people have reportedly been injured.
The crash occurred at 8:54 AM local time on Wednesday between the towns of Los Yebenes and Urda, around 120 km south of Madrid, on the high-speed line linking the Spanish capital with Andalusia. A Renfe AVE train reportedly struck an Iryo train from behind, sending two carriages off the tracks and down an embankment, according to rail infrastructure operator Adif.

The two trains were carrying a combined total of more than 500 passengers, according to Spanish media reports.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has announced three days of national mourning and pledged a thorough investigation into the disaster. Speaking at the crash site, he vowed to establish the cause of the collision and hold anyone responsible for negligence accountable.
Former Spanish Labor Minister Fatima Banez, 59, was among those killed, according to several Spanish media outlets. Banez served under Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy from 2011 to 2018 and was reportedly travelling aboard the Iryo train to attend a business event in Seville.
Spain’s Transport Ministry has identified human error by an operator at rail infrastructure manager Adif as the leading preliminary explanation for the crash. An operator reportedly authorized the Renfe train to pass a red signal despite the Iryo service remaining stationary on the same track.

Wednesday’s disaster is the latest in a series of serious railway accidents in Spain this year, raising concerns over the safety of the country’s rail network. On January 18, two high-speed trains collided near Adamuz in the southern province of Cordoba, killing 46 people and injuring more than 150. Just two days later, a commuter train struck a collapsed retaining wall near Barcelona, killing the driver and injuring dozens. Another passenger train collided with a crane near Cartagena on January 22, injuring six, and a collision at a level crossing in February reportedly left one person dead.
The incidents have fueled concerns over railway infrastructure and maintenance standards, prompting demands for stronger safety measures. The Spanish train drivers’ union (SEMAF) has called a nationwide strike for Thursday, October 29, accusing Renfe and the Transport Ministry of failing to implement safety improvements promised after the disasters in January. Renfe dismissed the accusations, insisting it has fulfilled its commitments.

Japan flags 3 reasons for ‘deteriorating’ security environment in Southeast Asia, vows support to regional bloc
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:48:08 UTC
18:48:08 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Japan on Wednesday flagged “three reasons” for the “rapidly deteriorating” security environment in Southeast Asia, pledging support to the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
“Disasters are growing more severe, striking communications, medical care, and transport at once. Conflicts worldwide are reaching our supply chains and energy supplies, and the military balance is shifting fast, raising the risk of collision against a vulnerable and of dangerous miscalculations,” Shinjiro Koizumi, Japan’s defense minister, told a joint meeting of ASEAN defense chiefs in Cebu City, the Philippines, current chair of the Southeast Asian bloc.
“These crises do not merely adapt; they overlap and amplify one another,” said Koizumi, stressing ASEAN’s “unity, centrality, and resilience.”
“Japan values all three” as they “are international public goods, safeguarding peace, prosperity, and every nation's freedom to choose,” he said.
Koizumi said the ASEAN members “are strengthening their own ability to respond and deter.”
“ASEAN as a whole is tackling shared challenges from disaster response to maritime security. These efforts complement each other, and Japan … will support both,” he said.
“Our aim is simple: to widen the options for ASEAN and for each member to understand, decide, and act on its own,” said the Japanese defense chief, urging ASEAN and Japan to “update our areas of cooperation.”
He pledged that Japan “will do everything it can” to turn ASEAN “choices into real strength.”
The meetings in Cebu City mark the 20th ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting and 13th ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting Plus, which also brings together the defense chiefs of US, China, South Korea, Japan, Australia, and India, although China this year did not send its defense minister.

Iran hasn't tried to repair damaged nuclear facilities: IAEA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:47:50 UTC
18:47:50 KST

Breadcrumb
Iran hasn't tried to repair nuclear facilities damaged in US strikes: IAEA chief
The head of the UN nuclear agency said Tuesday there has been no indication Iran has tried to repair or reconstruct its nuclear facilities damaged in US and Israeli military strikes this year or last year.
President Donald Trump has said one of the major reasons the US went to war with Iran on 28 February was to deny Tehran the ability to develop nuclear weapons, even as he has insisted that strikes the US carried out on Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025 "obliterated" the country’s atomic program.
During a UN Security Council meeting, International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi urged Iran to give inspectors access to all nuclear sites, including those damaged in the military attacks. The IAEA has not been able to verify the status of Iran's stockpile of near weapons-grade uranium since the US bombed its sites last year.
Grossi said that "since June 2025, we have not identified any activity to repair or reconstruct any of the facilities damaged in the military attacks of 2025 and 2026."
Trump has consistently downplayed the economic impact of the Iran war, which has emerged as a liability for Republicans heading into next week’s midterm elections, and has argued that higher fuel prices are worth paying to prevent a nuclear-armed Iran. The White House didn’t immediately respond Tuesday evening to a request for comment on Grossi's remarks.
Iran insists its nuclear program is peaceful. Meanwhile, the IAEA says the country has a stockpile of 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium enriched up to 60% purity—a short, technical step away from weapons-grade levels of 90%.
The UN meeting on Tuesday was called by Bahrain, Denmark, Latvia, France, the United Kingdom and United States after the IAEA referred Iran to the Security Council for failing to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation obligations. Russia and China, allies of Iran, tried unsuccessfully to prevent the meeting.
Under those obligations, which are part of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, Iran is legally bound to declare all nuclear material and activities and allow IAEA inspectors to verify that none of it is being diverted from peaceful uses.
Iran's UN deputy ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi attacked the council for its silence after the US-Israeli attacks, denouncing their "wars of aggression against Iran" and noted the US is committing war crimes against the Iranian people.
He added that "Israel possesses nuclear weapons, yet your concern is the absence of inspectors in Iran."
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz called Iran a "brutal dictatorship" and asked if the Iranian ambassador wanted to apologise to Bahrain's envoy, a council member, for attacking his country.
"We've heard tireless allegations against the United States," he said. "What we have not heard today is an explanation for Iran's continued failure to satisfy its safeguard obligations."
The IAEA asked Iran for answers, Waltz said, and it would be smart for the Iranian representative to start providing some answers.
"Your lies are no good here," he said.

Trump says Putin-Zelenskyy meeting to be arranged 'very soon'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:47:47 UTC
18:47:47 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday that a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy could be arranged soon, as Moscow offered to host direct talks in the Russian capital and diplomatic efforts intensified to end the war.
Trump expressed optimism about progress in negotiations but gave no date or location for a potential summit. His remarks came as Russian officials discussed resuming trilateral talks with Ukraine and the United States in Abu Dhabi, while European leaders stepped up contacts with Moscow and Kyiv.
“I think with Russia, we’re making a lot of progress with Russia-Ukraine. There’ll be a meeting set up here soon,” Trump told reporters after returning from Texas, where he had attended midterm election campaign rallies.
Asked about the timing, Trump said the meeting would happen “over the next not too long.” He added that progress could be achieved without a face-to-face meeting between the two leaders.
The comments offered no confirmation that Putin and Zelenskyy had agreed to meet. Neither Kyiv nor Moscow had publicly confirmed an arrangement for a leaders' summit following Trump's remarks.
The latest diplomatic push comes as the war, launched by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, continues to exact a heavy human and economic toll. Trump's administration has pursued negotiations since he returned to the White House in January 2025, but efforts to secure a settlement have yet to produce a breakthrough.
Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said Tuesday that Putin had invited Zelenskyy to Moscow for direct negotiations, promising that security arrangements would be made for the Ukrainian leader.
According to Russia's state-run TASS news agency, Ushakov said Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb had informed Putin during a recent telephone conversation that Zelenskyy was interested in meeting him directly.
“Our boss reiterated that if Zelenskyy truly wishes to hold direct negotiations, he should come to Moscow, where all necessary conditions, including those regarding his safety, will be provided for him,” Ushakov said, according to TASS.
The invitation leaves a major question unresolved: whether Zelenskyy would accept Moscow as the venue for negotiations with a leader whose forces continue to occupy Ukrainian territory.
Zelenskyy has repeatedly called for direct talks with Putin, arguing that territorial disputes and other fundamental questions about the war's future require decisions at the highest level. He has also insisted that Ukraine must participate in any negotiations affecting its sovereignty and future security.
There was no immediate indication that Kyiv had accepted the Moscow invitation.
Ushakov said the recent 90-minute telephone conversation between Putin, Stubb and Støre focused largely on plans to resume negotiations involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States.
The discussions could take place in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, in the first half of November, although a final date and venue had not been confirmed.
“There were many questions on this matter and requests for clarification from our side,” Ushakov said, describing the call as thorough and substantive.
He added that the parties had agreed to speak again if necessary.
Ushakov also said the question of European representation in future negotiations had not yet been addressed, suggesting that Moscow was not currently considering who might represent the continent at the negotiating table.
The position highlights a potential point of friction between Russia and European governments, which have sought a role in shaping any settlement because of its implications for European security.
The latest diplomatic activity follows meetings between U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Ukrainian and European officials in Oslo on Oct. 20, followed by discussions with Putin in St. Petersburg the next day.
Those contacts covered possible peace arrangements, security guarantees and postwar economic issues.
Russian officials subsequently indicated that Moscow was prepared in principle to resume technical-level negotiations with Ukraine and the United States.
Zelenskyy has supported restarting the talks, while arguing that working groups should address technical matters and prepare the ground for a meeting between the leaders.
He has also maintained that any agreement affecting Ukraine must involve Kyiv directly.
Despite renewed diplomatic activity, the prospects for a breakthrough remain uncertain because Moscow and Kyiv continue to disagree over the fundamental terms of a settlement.
Putin has demanded Russian control over occupied Ukrainian territories, including areas Moscow claims but does not fully control. Russia has also opposed a broad cease-fire before an agreement on the main terms of a settlement, arguing that a pause in fighting could allow Ukraine to strengthen its military.
Ukraine has rejected demands to surrender territory and insists that any peace agreement must protect its sovereignty and provide credible security guarantees against another Russian invasion.
Zelenskyy has argued that territorial disputes cannot be resolved by treating occupied land as a matter of geography alone, pointing to the lives lost defending Ukrainian communities.
The Ukrainian president has also warned against easing sanctions on Russia before meaningful progress is made, arguing that doing so would weaken Kyiv's negotiating position.
Relations between Trump and Zelenskyy have been strained by disagreements over the pace and terms of negotiations. Trump has pressed Ukraine to reach a settlement, while Zelenskyy has resisted proposals that could compromise the country's territorial integrity or leave it vulnerable to renewed Russian aggression.
The prospect of a meeting in Moscow could prove particularly difficult given the ongoing war and the two governments' competing demands. Although Ushakov said Russia would guarantee Zelenskyy's safety, no agreement on a venue has been announced.
The renewed push for negotiations comes as fighting and attacks continue across Ukraine, with both countries facing mounting military and economic costs.
Trump's administration has pursued several diplomatic channels, while European leaders have sought to ensure that any settlement accounts for the security of Ukraine and its neighbors.
A separate, limited cease-fire around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson region has also offered a narrow opening for humanitarian cooperation. The arrangement, reached with the involvement of U.S. First Lady Melania Trump, is intended to facilitate aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
However, local humanitarian arrangements have yet to translate into a broader halt to hostilities.
Trump's latest remarks signal Washington's continued effort to bring the Russian and Ukrainian leaders into direct negotiations. But his prediction that a meeting will take place “very soon” remains an expectation rather than a confirmed diplomatic agreement.

Dozens killed as high-speed trains collide in Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:47:00 UTC
18:47:00 KST

The scene of a collision between two trains in Urda, Spain on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. (Europa Press via AP)
A collision between two high-speed trains south of Madrid killed 30 people on Oct. 28 and the toll could rise, regional authorities said in Spain’s second such disaster this year.
Images shared by local media showed the wreckage of two trains strewn on the tracks and an embankment as emergency services rushed to the scene, while shocked travellers dragged away their suitcases as they escaped.
The accident in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha comes one month before Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who faced heavy criticism for the first disaster, seeks to overturn unfavourable polls in an early general election.
Sources from authorities in Castilla-La Mancha told AFP “at least 30” people had died, raising a previous toll of 10. Authorities have not yet given a toll for any wounded.
Esther Padilla, spokeswoman for the government of Castilla-La Mancha, had told local media CMM that “it is possible that the number will increase.”
State railway operator Renfe confirmed in a statement that the main high-speed line from Madrid to southern Spain had been suspended after one of its services suffered an accident with a train from private Spanish company Iryo.
A spokesperson for the Spanish emergency services told AFP the trains collided just before 9 a.m. (0800 GMT) in the municipality of Urda, around 130 kilometres (80 miles) south of Madrid.
“All resources are currently being deployed,” the emergency services spokesperson said, including “several fire crews, three helicopters, and two mobile intensive care units.”
Sanchez, who is seeking to extend his eight-year premiership in the Nov. 29 vote, said on X that he was “shocked” by the accident and sent “my love, solidarity and support to all the victims and their families.”
He cancelled his participation in a summit in Madrid after the news broke, while his Socialist party suspended all its campaign activities.
Condolences flooded in from across Spain and Europe. The Spanish royal household said on X it was “shocked and concerned” by the accident, conveying its support to the victims, their loved ones and the emergency services.
European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen said “Europe mourns” with the victims after the “devastating news,” while French President Emmanuel Macron expressed his country’s “solidarity.”
Spain’s high-speed rail network has received huge investment in recent years, growing to become the world’s second-largest after China and a source of national pride.
But Oct. 28's accident comes after another collision between two high-speed trains outside the southern village of Adamuz in January left 46 dead, which raised major questions about safety on the country’s railways.
That crash was Spain’s deadliest train accident since 2013, when 80 people died after a train veered off a curved section of track outside the northwestern city of Santiago de Compostela.
Both of this year’s accidents happened on the line linking Madrid to Seville.

The Men Spending $50,000 Just to Reserve a Tesla Roadster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:45:00 UTC
18:45:00 KST

In mid-October, CEO Elon Musk sort of made good on a long-standing promise: Tesla’s new second-gen Roadster flew through the air. Technically, the vehicle used compressed air to “thrust” itself—the “flying” lasted mere seconds, and the system takes six to seven hours to refill.
Never mind, though—some buyers were eager to unsheath their credit cards to reserve one of the cars. “I was freaking out,” says Alex Lawrence, the owner of used-electric-vehicle dealership EVAuto, who already had one reservation for a second-gen Roadster and watched the demonstration live online. “I placed another one.”
It’s not a decision most would make lightly. Tesla took years to get the sports car even close to production. The automaker first introduced the vehicle, a successor to its first car ever, as a surprise at a 2017 event, and immediately began taking $50,000 reservations. At the time, the plan was to deliver the cars in 2020; Musk and company now say the vehicle will enter production in 2028, with delivery dates unclear. (If reservation holders had put that money into Tesla stock, they would be up nearly $1 million today.)
The Roadster is also expensive to reserve—and will likely get pricier to buy. The vehicle’s base model, which doesn’t include acceleration thrusters or the flight system, still costs $50,000 to reserve. The second-tier Thrust variant, which comes with the thrusters, requires a $250,000 deposit. The actual flying car, called Rocket, is listed as “invite-only,” and even Musk has acknowledged the vehicle won’t be street legal. Meanwhile, the automaker’s reservation terms note that purchase prices are “only an estimate”—and those estimates don’t even exist yet.
Whatever! “I’m going to do everything in my power to get the flying one,” Lawrence says. When he sees the Roadster, after all, he sees money signs. His EV dealership has a large and growing social media following, and the business, not the man, technically put down the money for the Roadster reservations. “We’re going to put it on the track and use it for marketing content,” he says.
Utah-based tech founder Travis Cook upped his nearly 10-year-old reservation for the base Roadster variant to the Thrust because he actually wants to live with the thing. He calls himself a “car aficionado” and has a dealer’s license so he can buy and sell fun cars. He loves little more than driving an unusual vehicle, he told WIRED from behind the wheel of a Cybertruck as he used the company’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised) feature.
“When I roll up somewhere, all the other car aficionados come out, and they're so excited,” he says. “I just get a buzz from that.”
Cook says he has no regrets about his years-old reservation, though he may get frustrated if the price shoots up closer to half a million. “I’m not sure I’m willing to drop too much money on the car—but I probably would,” he says. Close family tolerates his obsession, though his wife doesn’t enjoy going 0 to 60 in his other cars and probably won’t in the Roadster, either. “She’s not going to want to go in it,” he says.
The tech founder has faith in Musk and Tesla. The October demonstration was even crazier than he had expected. “When it launched off the top of the ramp and went and landed, my jaw was on the floor,” Cook says.
Despite the Roadster’s memeable debut, the vehicle doesn’t seem to be a top priority for Tesla. Musk has said for years now that the automaker isn’t really in the business of making cars anymore and instead is focused on robotics, artificial intelligence, and autonomy. He has touted the new Roadster as the company’s last human-driven car ever. The supercar garnered just two mentions in Tesla’s hourlong earnings call with investors this month, with Musk calling it “arguably the coolest demo of any product ever.” Musk, meanwhile, has other preoccupations—he has donated at least $445 million to Republican candidates ahead of the US midterms.
But Lawrence believes Musk will pull off what he says he will and that his own business’s investment in the Roadster will be worth it in the end. The looping, wedge-shaped car demo left him a little nostalgic, a little existential.
“We don’t do crazy stuff like this anymore, like going to the moon. There’s not a lot today that will stop you in your tracks,” he says. “I felt like I was 15, watching that.”

social-security-contributions relief for working mothers with at
least three children, could be extended to those with two.

bonuses for lower-income earners.

their state pension at 64, three years before the current
retirement age, advocated by Deputy Premier, Transport Minister
and League leader Matteo Salvini looks set to be postponed.

used for this mechanism January, sources said.

like to bring before the cabinet with the goal of balancing the
budget and honouring our commitments, while continuing to pursue
the priorities we have set for ourselves in recent years,"
Meloni told the Moneta Economic Forum on Tuesday.

From Leonardo to Galileo, from Dante to Boccaccio, right up to the challenges of contemporary communication and creation: Italian is not merely a language, but a tool for conceiving, designing, and creating. This is the message that emerged from “Lingua geniale: ideare, progettare, creare con l’italiano” (Brilliant Language: Conceiving, Designing, and Creating with Italian), the event hosted by the Consulate General of Italy in Paris in collaboration with the International Alumni Committee of the Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore in Milan (UCSC) in Paris. Launched on the occasion of the presentation of the book *Lingua gentile, lingua geniale: Conceive, Design, Create with Italian,” produced by the Accademia della Crusca together with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation on the occasion of the 26th Week of the Italian Language in the World, under the High Patronage of the President of the Republic, the event featured presentations by Grazia Quaroni, Director of Collections at the Fondation Cartier pour l’Art Contemporain, and Thierry Guérin, Vice President of Business Development at Dedar Milano, who offered a concrete and unconventional perspective on the connection between the Italian language and Italian craftsmanship. From art to craftsmanship to design, the Italian language accompanies the creative process and helps express its quality, precision, and attention to detail. Moderated by Maria Teresa Zanola, a member of the Accademia della Crusca and professor at the Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore, the discussion highlighted the flexibility of our language and its ability to interpret contemporary transformations. This is a calling that spans the centuries—a living heritage that continues to generate ideas and forge connections.

Mapping the siege of Yemen’s Taiz, and the price families are paying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:43:09 UTC
18:43:09 KST

Mapping the siege of Yemen’s Taiz, and the price families are paying
Three weeks into the siege of Yemen’s third-largest city, prices have doubled, and families are down to the basics.
Taiz, Yemen – In the besieged city of Taiz, Yousef Farhan’s family has run out of choices at mealtime.
“The whole day, we either eat rice or beans, whether in the morning or in the evening,” the 39-year-old father of four told Al Jazeera.
Shelling forced the family from their home years ago, and they have lived in a school in Taiz’s Wadi al-Qadi zone ever since.
Farhan used to sell cucumbers from a small cart in front of the school, earning between 4,000 and 5,000 Yemeni riyals (roughly $2.50 to $3.20) a day. The money was never steady, but it bought a gas cylinder each month and, now and then, a meal with some variety.
Then the siege closed the school, and his trade went with it. The family now cooks over firewood.
“With the suspension of the school due to the shelling and the siege, my source of income stopped, and I was unable to find alternative work since the siege caused many people’s jobs to come to a halt,” he said.
His children, aged five months to five years, depend on whatever he can find. So do his sister and her child, who joined him after their neighbourhood came under fire.
Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, is home to about 1 million of the country’s roughly 43 million people.
The city has been cut off since early October, when it lost both of its land routes. The Houthis took the town of al-Turbah by October 4, severing the Taiz-Al-Turbah-Aden Road, the main artery for goods.
A day earlier, forces loyal to the internationally recognised government closed the eastern al-Houban crossing into Houthi-held territory, citing attempted Houthi incursions.
On October 20, the United Nations warned that road closures and lack of security were blocking vital supplies.
Prices of the food and fuel still available had more than doubled, and Taiz’s water production had dropped by half.
Across Taiz, families like Farhan’s are working out what to eat and whether they can afford to cook it.
The map below shows the main Taiz-Al-Turbah-Aden Road and three other routes out of the city, all now closed.
One day at a time
For weeks, 40-year-old Sayyun Burhan has looked no further ahead than tomorrow.
“We barely live day-to-day, waiting to see how the next day will pass,” she said.
Work is no longer available at the local store where Sayyun’s husband was employed, and his failing health makes it harder for him to find anything else. Meanwhile, the family still needs money for rent, food, water and cooking gas.
Across the city, the cost of water delivered by tankers has roughly tripled since the fighting escalated, according to UN officials.
The strain reaches beyond the kitchen. For Burhan’s children, the siege means missed lessons and long days inside, as she is afraid to let them out.
“They have been deprived of schooling and play,” she said.
Keeping both children safe and fed is becoming harder.
A city running on fumes
Fuel is behind many of Taiz’s civilian emergencies. Diesel keeps water pumps working, hospital generators running and ambulances moving. Petrol enables people can get to work, and patients to treatment. Cooking gas lets families and restaurants prepare food.
But the city’s fuel stations have been closed since October 5.
Prices gathered by Al Jazeera in Taiz show how sharply fuel costs have risen. A 20-litre (5.3-gallon) container of petrol now costs 120,000 riyals ($77), four times last year’s price of 30,000 riyals ($19).
The price of 20 litres of diesel has nearly doubled, from 46,000 riyals ($29) to 90,000 riyals ($58). A cooking gas cylinder has risen from 11,400 riyals ($7) to 40,000 riyals ($26).
Bus fares have risen from 200 riyals (13 cents) to 500 riyals (32 cents), an increase of 150 percent. Every ride now takes a bigger share of household budgets already stretched by rising food prices.
For Farhan, the move to firewood shows how far his family’s spending power has fallen. He once managed with a gas cylinder each month. Now, even a pot of rice or beans depends on what he can burn.
Water shortages are not new in Taiz, but the siege has made them worse. Diesel shortages have disrupted the pumps.
Local authorities say access restrictions are also stopping tankers from the Al-Dhabab basin, an important source of drinking water, from entering the city.
A hospital hall for a home
Fatima Khaled, 55, has kidney failure. She cannot afford repeated trips from her village west of the city to the hospital for treatment, or a room closer to the hospital. She sleeps on the floor of the dialysis hall at Al-Jumhuri General Hospital.
Closed roads and long mountain detours have made every journey for treatment exhausting and expensive.
The hospital itself is under strain. On October 22, the World Health Organization warned that 42 health facilities in Taiz were reporting severe shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicine and medical supplies.
“I feel like I am imprisoned here. We have no housing or shelter here. This hall is our shelter,” Fatima says.

Services producer prices rise 0.17 pct in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:41:27 UTC
18:41:27 KST

Türkiye’s services producer price index rose 0.17 percent in September from the previous month and 33.23 percent from a year earlier, the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) said on Oct. 28.
The index was 32.88 percent above its level at the end of 2025.
The 12-month average rise stood at 34.31 percent.
All six main service groups recorded price increases compared with September last year.
Transportation and storage posted the largest annual increase, at 39.99 percent.
Prices in the sector also rose 1.78 percent from August.
Annual increases were 32.44 percent in professional, scientific and technical services, 30.17 percent in administrative and support services, 28.09 percent in accommodation and food services and 28.03 percent in information and communication.
Real estate services recorded the smallest annual rise, at 21.93 percent.
On a monthly basis, prices fell 2.53 percent in administrative and support services, 2.51 percent in real estate and 1.16 percent in accommodation and food services.
Professional, scientific and technical services prices rose 0.84 percent from August, while information and communication prices increased 0.37 percent.

Export growth narrows September trade deficit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:39:00 UTC
18:39:00 KST

Türkiye’s trade deficit narrowed 25.8 percent year-on-year in September to $5.16 billion as exports grew faster than imports, official data showed on Oct. 28.
Exports rose 15.3 percent to $25.97 billion, while imports increased 5.6 percent to $31.13 billion, according to provisional foreign trade figures compiled jointly by the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) and the Trade Ministry.
Exports covered 83.4 percent of imports, up from 76.4 percent in September last year, when the trade deficit stood at $6.96 billion.
For the first nine months of 2026, the deficit widened 5.7 percent to $70.97 billion from $67.16 billion a year earlier.
Exports increased 5.2 percent to $210.95 billion, while imports rose 5.3 percent to $281.92 billion.
The export-to-import coverage ratio for January-September stood at 74.8 percent, slightly below the 74.9 percent recorded in the same period of 2025.
Excluding energy products and non-monetary gold, September exports rose 10.5 percent from a year earlier, increasing from $21.17 billion to $23.39 billion.
Imports on the same basis grew 6.7 percent, from $22.43 billion to $23.93 billion.
On that basis, the trade deficit stood at $541 million, with exports covering 97.7 percent of imports.
Combined exports and imports excluding energy and gold increased 8.5 percent to $47.31 billion.

Sports events to mark Türkiye’s 103rd Republic Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:37:35 UTC
18:37:35 KST

(AA Photo)
Türkiye will mark the 103rd anniversary of the founding of the republic with cycling events across its 81 provinces, a horseback ride along a historic independence route and an international race on the Osmangazi Bridge, bringing together sports enthusiasts to celebrate the national holiday.
Republic Day, observed on Oct. 29, commemorates the proclamation of the Republic of Türkiye by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk in 1923, following the collapse of the Ottoman Empire and the Turkish War of Independence.
The Turkish Cycling Federation’s “Türkiye Pedals” initiative will run from Oct. 29 to Nov. 1, combining Republic Day celebrations with efforts to raise awareness of climate change ahead of the U.N. climate summit COP31, scheduled to take place in the southwestern city of Antalya on Nov. 9-20. The events will be open to licensed athletes, cycling clubs, students, families and other enthusiasts, encouraging bicycle use as a low-emission alternative to motorized transport. In Istanbul, participants will set off from Beşiktaş Square at 10 a.m. on Oct. 31 for a ride covering approximately 10 kilometers.
Meanwhile, 45 riders from across Türkiye have embarked on a two-day horseback journey along the 95-kilometer İstiklal Road, a historic route used during the War of Independence to transport weapons and ammunition from the Black Sea port of İnebolu into Anatolia. Organized for the third time by the Equestrian and Culture Association, the ride commemorates those who supported the independence struggle.
Another major event, the International Osmangazi-Türkiye Century Run, will take place on Oct. 29 on the Osmangazi Bridge, which connects the two sides of the Gulf of İzmit. Organized by Kocaeli Municipality in cooperation with national and local institutions, the event has attracted nearly 8,000 applications, with athletes from 19 countries expected to participate. It will feature a 10-kilometer elite race and a five-kilometer public run.
Kocaeli Mayor Tahir Büyükakın said organizers hope to make the race an annual tradition and eventually establish it as an internationally recognized sporting event, linking the republic’s historical legacy with a vision of a more sustainable future.

Radev Seeks European-Level Food Markups in Bulgaria as Budget Talks Continue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:36:13 UTC
18:36:13 KST

Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the government aims to bring Bulgarian food price markups in line with those in other developed European countries, maintain household electricity and heating prices until July 1, 2027, and preserve planned income increases in the 2027 budget as negotiations with the European Commission continue.
Speaking at the start of a cabinet meeting, Radev welcomed the energy regulator’s announcement that electricity and district heating prices for households would remain unchanged throughout the current heating season and until July 1, 2027, despite a sharp increase in international natural gas prices.
He said the government would ensure that consumer protection mechanisms had sufficient funding, particularly through the Security of the Electricity System Fund, to prevent household energy bills from rising.
On food prices, Radev stressed that the government would not impose prices in Bulgaria’s free-market economy but would strengthen oversight through a clear legal and regulatory framework. He said the administration and its parliamentary group had made the Consumer Protection Act and the Protection of Competition Act two of their first legislative priorities and had secured their adoption.
The government subsequently developed secondary legislation establishing procedures and formulas for regulatory action, allowing authorities to carry out structured inspections of prices, unfair commercial practices and product quality.
Radev said the aim was to bring Bulgarian markups closer to levels in developed European countries, adding that the regulatory framework was now in place and inspections would continue.
The prime minister also addressed the arrests of the mayors of Sungurlare and Belitsa last week, insisting that the cases were unrelated to ethnicity, politics or the election campaign and urging people not to speculate about their motives.
He said law enforcement was operating without political interference and that investigations into the misuse of public funds were leading to legal proceedings where prosecutors were functioning effectively. Radev cited the murders in Plovdiv and Sofia, including the killing of Slavi Binev, as well as the October 9 arson attack on Starlink antennas, saying the perpetrators in these cases had been identified rapidly.
Regarding the Starlink incident, Radev said the suspects had already left Bulgaria when their identities were established, preventing authorities from immediately disclosing their names. Bulgarian services alerted international partners, but securing their arrests required the lengthy procedure for issuing a European Arrest Warrant. The suspects have since been taken into custody.
Radev warned those who had already begun organizing vote-buying schemes or intended to participate in them that the Interior Ministry would respond firmly.
“Do not do it. The Ministry of Interior will act uncompromisingly and strictly within the bounds of the law,” Radev said, calling for transparent, fair and responsible elections. He urged Bulgarians not to fear threats or give in to pressure and to vote according to their conscience and convictions.
Speaking to reporters outside the National Assembly, Radev said the government was negotiating with the European Commission over several disputed elements of the 2027 state budget, with the aim of preserving planned increases in wages, pensions and social benefits.
Asked whether submitting the budget to Parliament after the elections would violate the Public Finance Act, he did not give a specific date or a definitive answer on the legal deadline. He said the government was seeking to balance higher incomes, deficit reduction and continued capital spending on priority infrastructure projects.
“For us, the most important thing is to achieve a crucial balance: between the policies we have planned to raise people's incomes and the reduction of the deficit, while simultaneously maintaining capital expenditures for priority projects within the country,” Radev said.
He noted that Bulgaria was preparing its state budget in euros for the first time, requiring specific coordination procedures with the European Commission. Several points of disagreement remained under discussion, he said, and the government wanted to resolve them before proceeding.
“We must succeed in fully discussing and negotiating this with the European Commission. Bear in mind that, for the first time, we are drafting a budget in euros,” Radev said, adding that he did not want to rush the process.
He warned that failure to reach an agreement could affect citizens’ incomes, an outcome he wanted to avoid. The prime minister did not specify which budget parameters remained contentious.
Radev said the government intended to retain all previously announced social measures and was negotiating the details of how to finance them. Planned increases include salaries, pensions, maternity benefits, child allowances, scholarships for school and university students, and pay for young doctors.
He said preserving these measures was among the main reasons the cabinet was taking its time with the budget.
The prime minister also discussed the need to update property tax valuations, describing the current figures as significantly outdated. He said mayors, businesses and other groups had called for a gradual adjustment to bring the valuations closer to actual market levels.
Radev said more realistic property tax valuations could help limit manipulation in real estate transactions, but did not specify when an update might begin or how large the adjustments would be.
Asked about the government’s position on election-related issues following his expression of support for Iliana Yotova’s candidacy, which was publicized by the government press office the day after the first round of voting, Radev declined to repeat the cabinet’s position.
“Our press office has already issued a clear statement. I do not wish to repeat it. You are well aware of what it says,” he told reporters.
Radev also questioned whether the timing of the election campaign had been considered when assessing the government’s actions.
“And when does the campaign actually begin? What period were we in at that time? Did you take that into consideration?” the prime minister asked.

Iran’s Greco-Roman wrestler Esmaeili wins gold at World Championships
TEHRAN – Iran’s Greco-Roman wrestler Saeid Esmaeili from Iran won gold at the 2026 World Wrestling Championships Tuesday night.
The Paris Olympic champion completed a successful defense of his 67kg crown with a crushing victory by fall over Aytjan Khalmakhanov from Uzbekistan on Tuesday, giving Iran its fourth champion as the Greco-Roman competition wrapped up at the World Championships in Astana.

Israeli right makes provocative statements as election votes are counted

Israeli right makes provocative statements as election votes are counted
Netanyahu and Smotrich incite against Arab voters as rival political camps face an uncertain path to power.
Senior figures on Israel’s right have made a series of provocative statements about Arab voters, alleged attempts to steal the election and plans to establish Jewish settlements in Gaza.
The remarks came during Tuesday’s election and after exit polls suggested Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing alliance had suffered a setback.
With neither major political camp securing a clear majority, Arab-led parties could play an important role in deciding who forms the next government.
Speaking early on Wednesday at his far-right Religious Zionism party’s election headquarters in Jerusalem, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich dismissed opposition celebrations and promised to preserve the expansion of settlements in the occupied West Bank, which are considered illegal under international law.
He said his political opponents would not reverse the government’s settlement “revolution”, declaring: “Jewish settlements will be established in Gaza.”
Israel dismantled its settlements in Gaza in 2005.
Earlier on Tuesday, Smotrich warned on Facebook that voter turnout was unusually high in Arab communities and left-wing strongholds, without providing supporting figures.
He claimed that failing to mobilise right-wing voters could allow “terror supporters” to enter government.
Netanyahu, who leads the right-wing Likud party, made similar appeals during voting, warning that Arab voters were rushing to polling stations and that an opposition victory would threaten Israel’s Jewish character.
He also accused three senior figures from Ra’am, an Arab-majority party, of attempting to steal the election.
Police confirmed they arrested three people on suspicion of voter bribery, but there was no indication they held senior positions in Ra’am.
Transportation Minister Miri Regev, also from Likud, echoed the unsubstantiated election theft allegations in a post on X on Tuesday. “They’re trying to steal the elections and the country from us,” she said. “It’s either the right or Palestine.”
British-American political scientist Dov Waxman told Al Jazeera that Netanyahu’s plan after the inconclusive election result will likely be to “hammer home the message” to the Israeli public that a governing coalition that consists of Arab parties is “illegitimate”.
Arab political leaders condemned Netanyahu’s election-day messages as racist and inflammatory.
Al Jazeera correspondent Nida Ibrahim, reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, said Netanyahu’s bloc of right-wing and religious parties was projected to win 56 seats, with 84 percent of ballots counted, short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel’s 120-seat parliament.
She said Mansour Abbas, the leader of Ra’am, claimed he had received approaches from both Netanyahu’s Likud and the opposition camp led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who heads the Yashar party.

ICE Is Running One of the Largest Anti-Left Surveillance Operations in US History
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Attorneys for 15 Minnesota residents facing federal conspiracy charges have obtained evidence of a sweeping, possibly unconstitutional spying operation carried out by Immigration and Customs Enforcement against left-wing social movements in Minnesota and beyond.
The high-profile Minnesota 15 prosecution makes clear that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), flush with federal funds and newly hired personnel, is now President Donald Trump’s primary tool against dissent, with a powerful array of post-9/11 investigative authorities brought to bear against everyday Americans organizing their communities.
Nothing of this scale has been seen in the United States, experts say, since the federal government’s counterinsurgency against the New Left and the anti-war movement in the 1960s and 1970s.
Among the records revealed during the discovery process in these cases are dozens of reports, audio transcripts, emails, intercepted Signal chats, photographs, database queries, and more. They reveal the inner workings of the domestic terrorism investigations, running under the names Project Whipple Shield and Operation Puppet Master, authorized by the controversial National Security Presidential Memorandum 7.
Published following Charlie Kirk’s assassination in September of last year, NSPM 7 instructs federal law enforcement to use every tool available against organizations and people who criticize the administration's policies and espouse "anti-Christian" ideas. The full scope and extent of the investigations it authorizes remains unknown.
Defense attorneys for the Minnesota 15 claim that the prosecution stems from a broader nationwide surveillance operation aimed at opponents of the Trump administration’s immigration policies. One attorney in the case directly compares the DHS-run campaign to the FBI’s infamous Counterintelligence Program, or COINTELPRO, which unconstitutionally surveilled, infiltrated, and blackmailed racial justice, civil rights, and anti-war movements from the 1950s through the early 1970s.
Three former law enforcement officials who reviewed filings concur, telling WIRED that the case is almost certainly part of a wider intelligence-gathering operation that began long before the administration invaded Minnesota in December 2025.
Dueling motions in the case over discovery of DHS’s surveillance program reveal that personnel with Homeland Security Investigations—one of ICE’s two components—repurposed funding mechanisms and investigative tools for serious criminal probes and turned them on domestic dissenters. Operation Keyhole, the HSI undercover program that bankrolled the Minnesota 15 prosecution, dates back to 2008. As of June 2026, it was underwriting a half dozen active undercover investigations in the Minneapolis–Saint Paul area.
Around 120 HSI agents, many drawn from specialized units across the country that have served as the leading edge of the administration’s militarized immigration enforcement operations, were assigned to the case—including 11 undercovers. They used highly invasive surveillance techniques, including the deployment of Reaper drones and Patriot Act tools usually restricted to money laundering and terrorism investigations. Undercover operatives also infiltrated churches in apparent violation of a court order.
The Minnesota 15 indictment stems from the Trump administration’s demand that the Justice Department “go big and go loud” to crack down on community response networks during last winter’s Operation Metro Surge. Twin Cities activists organized volunteers to monitor DHS agents and their vehicles using encrypted Signal groups, homebuilt vehicle databases, and a centralized dispatch system. Government prosecutors claim that this amounts to a criminal conspiracy to block immigration enforcement, unlawfully identify and stalk federal agents, and even assault them.
Their defense attorneys say the heavy charges filed against the Minnesota 15 don’t align with their alleged conduct. “This is the first time I’ve had a client who’s accused of a conspiracy and went on a speaking tour,” says Kevin Riach, who represents defendant Isaac Sant.
Peeking Through the Keyhole
An internal ICE document laying out the scope of Operation Puppet Master—which led to the indictment of the Minneapolis 15—ends by noting, “This case has also been accepted under CUC Op Keyhole.” According to prosecutors, Operation Keyhole is a long-standing program created by HSI’s Saint Paul office to fund “undercover activity”—primarily equipment purchases and personnel costs—in a region covering Minnesota, North and South Dakota, Iowa, and Nebraska. The program has funded at least 77 investigations into “narcotics trafficking, child sexual abuse, financial investigations, and counter-proliferation” since it started in December 2008.
The CUC prefix, per an internal 2008 DHS handbook unearthed by the independent media outlet Unicorn Riot, refers to Certified Undercover Operations, a formal designation with clearly defined oversight mechanisms, procedures, and reporting requirements. Operation Keyhole’s parameters are reviewed every six months by a committee comprising senior DOJ and DHS officials. As of June 2026, when it was last renewed, Keyhole funded six active investigations, including Project Whipple Shield, which was initiated in February to probe claims of assault, stalking, and doxing of DHS agents and other federal employees, and underpins the Minnesota 15 indictment.
At least 11 undercover agents working under Operation Keyhole infiltrated Twin Cities anti-ICE activists, participating in martial arts and know-your-rights trainings, marches, general strikes, and community meetings. They also infiltrated activists’ communications network for identifying possible undercover ICE vehicles and dispatching activists to tail them through the Twin Cities, and penetrated several activist group chats on Signal, transmitting their contents back to other HSI colleagues for analysis and eventual inclusion in the indictment.
Activist conferences as far away as Seattle, Michigan, Chicago, and New York City were placed under surveillance as part of the investigation, and HSI teams photographed and ran the license plates of every car parked in the lot of a meeting location or seen transporting activists. There is also drone footage from unarmed Customs and Border Protection Reaper drones of the activists moving around the Twin Cities area.
The undercovers were part of a much broader group of more than 50 HSI agents, including at least two dozen from HSI’s little-known Special Operations Group, that took part in the investigation and surveillance of the defendants, both digital and in-person. Feds with decades of experience on complex financial crimes, drug cartel investigations, human trafficking, and organized crime were pulled into the Minnesota 15 investigation.
Several of the Minnesota 15 case agents are from out of state and appear in court records for the prosecutions of anti-ICE activists in other cities. This includes Los Angeles–based HSI agents Robert Kurtz III, who specializes in financial fraud, and Ryan Ribner, who allegedly assaulted SEIU California president David Huerta at a June 2025 protest of an ICE enforcement operation, arrested him, and then claimed the then 58-year-old Huerta attacked federal law enforcement. (Huerta’s charges were dropped in July after videos contradicting Ribner’s account surfaced.) HSI records show Ribner was also involved in at least two prosecutions of Southern California residents who physically confronted ICE and Border Patrol agents last year.
Other agents from the conspiracy investigation have also been involved in recent high-profile incidents. Tim Gerber, the “team leader” of an HSI Special Operations Group squad, led the investigation of former CNN host Don Lemon for reporting on a protest at a Minneapolis Church where an ICE agent was a pastor. Fellow SOG agent Yue Her was present at the scene of a 2025 incident when Renee Good’s killer, ICE Special Response Team agent Johnathan Ross, was dragged by the car of a man he tried to apprehend.
“This operation does not seem in any way limited to Minnesota,” says Spencer Reynolds, a former DHS attorney and counterterrorism lawyer who now works at the NAACP Legal Defense Fund. “As we saw with the boots on the ground in the streets, with Greg Bovino leading CBP and Border Patrol special forces units on sweeping raids across the country, this is the intelligence and undercover investigative apparatus that is running in parallel to the door-kicking.”
Follow the Money
Mike German, a retired FBI agent who worked undercover domestic terrorism cases for years before becoming a sharp critic of post-9/11 federal law enforcement, likens the Minnesota 15 case to federal law enforcement’s long history of suppressing left-wing social movements, including the CIA’s Operation MH/Chaos, which surveilled the anti-war movement during the Vietnam War for evidence of foreign influence. One difference is the sheer scale—this time, it’s bigger.
According to a 2011 book by former CIA officer Frank Rafalko, the CIA secret investigation into suspected foreign influence on the New Left and anti-Vietnam War movement had 42 officers working the case at its peak. Court records show 119 HSI agents worked on the Minnesota 15 case alone.
“Broad monitoring of social media, communications, and financial transactions are used to link an ever increasing number of people as potential subjects of investigation and prosecution,” German says. “These are exactly the kind of intelligence activities J. Edgar Hoover adopted to suppress the Civil Rights and anti-war movements in the 1960s.”
The key difference today, German says, is the vast pool of data available to the feds.
HSI used highly invasive measures—including scrutiny of wire transfers, PayPal reimbursements, and other financial transactions; forensic digital analysis of website traffic; 15 terabytes worth of infiltrated Signal chats; and information from a commercial data broker—to identify individuals under investigation.
After a local activist uploaded a license-plate search tool on Fly.io, a developer-focused public cloud platform, to an infiltrated Signal chat, HSI agents reviewed website DNS queries and Stripe data along with data purchased from a commercial broker. This gave HSI access to SSH session logs, outbound connection records, the Fly.io account’s signup IP, and a Stripe card fingerprint on an account that had never completed a payment. Agents fused that with Minnesota DVS records and commercial data from the Thomson-Reuters CLEAR platform to produce a driver's license number, Social Security number summary, years of address history, phone numbers, property records, and jointly registered vehicles.
Documents concerning financial records requested through the Treasury Department’s 314(a) suspicious activity reporting program—created by the Patriot Act to enable speedy tracking of finances for terrorism and money-laundering investigations—show that the feds targeted records of 29 “subjects” during queries conducted on March 31, 2026. Emails viewed by WIRED between several HSI agents based in Los Angeles and Arizona show that batches of records were turned over pursuant to those inquiries, including some dealing with SEIU that a senior Minnesota HSI agent sent to a LA-based colleague to be filed “wherever these records are stored.”
HSI investigators used similar workarounds to warrants and grand jury subpoenas to obtain phone records for several journalists who covered Operation Metro Surge, as first reported by The Guardian. Court records show the feds used an administrative summons request reserved for violations of customs and taxation requirements, which does not fit the activity that made up the criminal charges filed by the Minnesota US attorney against former CNN anchor Don Lemon and others.
The Minnesota 15 case is the clearest example yet of DHS pursuing the Trump administration’s efforts to crack down on what have long been upheld as First Amendment–protected activities. But it’s unlikely alone.
Riach, the defense attorney, says the HSI reports show the agency is complicit in what he called “the new COINTELPRO.”
“What we saw during the immigration surges last year was that ICE is the administration’s paramilitary force, the projector of strength,” Riach says. “Here, we see that HSI are taking the FBI’s place as the investigative secret police—it’s the classic one-two punch of authoritarian regimes around the world.”

Bulgargaz will revise its proposed natural gas price for November, while Prime Minister Rumen Radev said household electricity and heating prices would remain unchanged through July 1, 2027, and pledged measures to protect consumers from rising energy costs.
Bulgargaz Executive Director Georgi Tatarski announced the revised proposal during a meeting of the Energy and Water Regulatory Commission (EWRC), Nova TV reported.
The company initially proposed a November natural gas price of 59.08 euros per megawatt-hour (MWh), a 34% increase from the regulator-approved October rate of 44.09 euros per MWh.
Tatarski said the company had explored ways to limit the increase, including participating in a tender for additional gas volumes to be stored at the Chiren facility. The projected volumes have increased, allowing Bulgargaz to revise its original proposal.
“We looked for ways to mitigate the increase. We participated in a tender for additional gas volumes to be stored at the Chiren facility; since the projected volumes have increased, we are able to adjust our initial proposal,” Tatarski said.
He added that the company would submit the revised proposal in writing at the end of the month. According to Tatarski, the proposed price remains more than 40 euros per MWh below the price on the exchange.
Speaking at the beginning of the regular Council of Ministers meeting, Radev said household electricity and heating prices would not rise during the current heating season or before July 1, 2027. He pledged that the government would secure the funding needed to maintain mechanisms protecting households against price increases.
“Despite the increase in the price of natural gas, prices will not change this season - nor until July 1, 2027,” Radev said, referring to the energy regulator’s intentions.
The prime minister said the government would focus on ensuring that compensation mechanisms across the energy sector remained financially sustainable. The cabinet would take steps to provide sufficient liquidity, including for the Security of the Electricity System Fund, so that higher costs for energy companies would not translate into larger household electricity and heating bills.
Radev also addressed rising food prices, saying the government would not impose administratively set prices but would increase oversight of unfair commercial practices.
“We are a free market economy; we have stated categorically that we will not dictate prices, we are not going back to the old days, and that is not the policy of our government,” Radev said.
He argued that effective market supervision required transparent pricing, clear rules and action against unfair commercial practices. A clear legal and regulatory framework, he said, would provide the basis for objective pricing, effective oversight and greater transparency.
The government is establishing a central electronic register of food prices, while inspections are being carried out into pricing, commercial practices and product quality.
Radev recalled that consumer protection and competition legislation were among the administration’s first legislative initiatives. He said the resulting framework allowed regulators to conduct inspections using defined criteria and methodologies rather than through ad hoc campaigns.
“Based on these laws, we have managed to develop a comprehensive regulatory framework, establishing clear mechanisms and formulas for our actions,” Radev said. “We have now begun operations in accordance with these methodologies - conducting structured, legally grounded inspections covering pricing, unfair commercial practices, and product quality.”
The prime minister stressed that the quality of goods was as important as their prices. He said Bulgaria needed to achieve the same level of consumer protection and oversight as other developed European countries.
