10:19:49 KST

Diyar Güldoğan
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
 The US is likely to face continued fiscal pressures regardless of the outcome of the upcoming midterm elections, with rising entitlement spending and debt-servicing costs threatening to push government debt higher, Fitch Ratings said Wednesday.
In a report, the credit rating agency warned that Democratic control of one or both chambers of Congress could increase the likelihood of political brinkmanship over the federal debt ceiling and government funding, potentially putting further pressure on the country's already-large fiscal deficit.
However, Fitch said the underlying drivers of the US fiscal outlook would persist regardless of which party controls Congress, pointing to rising entitlement expenditures and debt-servicing costs as key challenges.
Without policy changes, these structural pressures are likely to lead to a further deterioration in the country's debt-to-gross domestic product (GDP) ratio, the agency said.
The US federal budget deficit reached nearly $2 trillion, equivalent to 6.1% of GDP, in fiscal 2026, according to Fitch.
The agency forecasts that the general government deficit, which includes the balances of state and local governments, will widen to 7.5% of GDP in 2026 and 7.6% in 2027. State and local government balances account for around 1% of GDP.
Such a deficit would be the highest among sovereigns rated in the 'AA' category, Fitch said.
The agency also warned that the fiscal priorities of both major political parties could add to budgetary pressures unless offset by other measures.

US costs of Iran war rise to over $47 billion: Pentagon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:25:48 UTC
17:25:48 KST

Breadcrumb
US costs of Iran war rise to over $47 billion, according to Pentagon estimate
The US military has spent over $47 billion so far for the war on Iran, more than 25% higher than the Defense Department's estimate in July, according to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters.
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on its estimate, which has not been shared publicly.
The disclosure about the rising cost of the Iran war comes as Republicans wrestle with the political fallout of the unpopular conflict ahead of the 3 November midterm election that will determine control of Congress for the next two years.
The war's impact on global energy costs has weighed on support for Republican candidates and hurt President Donald Trump's approval ratings. Trump's Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress.
The Pentagon's latest estimate was tied to the operational costs of carrying out the war, with a projected cost of more than $29 billion to replace expended munitions used in the conflict.
More than $6 billion would be needed to replace military equipment and so-called "platform losses," which include the loss of aircraft including many drones lost during the war.
Trump launched the Iran war jointly with Israel in February, predicting that the conflict would last a short time.
Trump's initial strategy in the Iran war focused on first using expensive, high-end precision missiles to bomb Iran's defenses so it could later use less expensive munitions, including gravity bombs like the air-launched JDAMs, which are plentiful.
But an April ceasefire gave time for Iran to dig out underground storage facilities, bringing back online some Iranian defenses, as well as missiles and drones that had been inaccessible.
Trump has since imposed a naval blockade on Iran to starve it of oil export revenue and held out the possibility of restarting combat operations after the midterm elections. US officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, say the Pentagon has been planning to restart heavy fighting if ordered to do so.
The latest Pentagon estimate compares to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's July estimate of $37.5 billion for the cost of the war.
While the figures include a host of operational costs, from flight operations to cyber support, the US military's Iran war cost estimates did not clearly account for the massive expense expected to repair damage to US bases sustained by Iranian missile and drone attacks.

Lawyers frame India's Kashmir rule as 'settler-colonial', like Israeli occupation of Palestine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:25:28 UTC
17:25:28 KST

The Worldwide Lawyers Association (WOLAS) has accused India of implementing a dangerous plan of "assimilation, dispossession, and settler colonialism" in India-administered Kashmir, likening it to Israeli occupation practices in Palestine and announcing the initiation of legal proceedings under universal jurisdiction in foreign courts against Indian officials linked to rights abuses in the region.
Members of WOLAS, who released their damning report titled "Longest Siege: Settler Colonialism and Structural Violence in Indian Occupied Jammu Kashmir" to mark the 79th anniversary of landing of Indian troops in Jammu and Kashmir following 73 days of Kashmir's independence — an occasion commemorated by many Kashmiris and Pakistan as "Black Day" — said they aim to bring human rights violations in Kashmir before courts worldwide under universal jurisdiction.
During a press conference in Istanbul on Monday, WOLAS Chairman Enes Kafadar stressed that although Kashmir is geographically distant from Türkiye, it is "historically, culturally, and strategically close."
Kashmir was introduced to Islam in the 14th century by Turkic Sufi Bulbul Shah, Kafadar noted, recalling support of subcontinent Muslims to Türkiye during the War of Independence.
He highlighted parallels between Kashmir and Palestine, arguing, "The drones in the skies of Kashmir are Israeli-made Herons. The weapons pointed at the people in the streets are Israeli-made Tavor rifles. Lawyers, human rights defenders, and journalists are being wiretapped with Israeli-made Pegasus spyware."
"The suffering experienced by the Palestinian people and the Kashmiri people is very interconnected," the WOLAS chairman added.
Kafadar stated that WOLAS aims to activate international legal mechanisms through the reports it prepares, adding, "This report is not actually an end result, but the beginning of a legal operation."
"It is precisely at this point that we, as the Lawyers of the World Association, aim with this report to bring the human rights violations in Kashmir to many courts around the world under universal jurisdiction and to ensure that those responsible are held accountable."
'Israeli officials were present in torture centres in Kashmir'
Kafadar stated the report shows events in India-administered Kashmir are "planned assimilation and settler colonialism" by New Delhi breaching international law, not a mere security or border dispute.
He stated that several UNSC resolutions mandate Kashmir's status be decided via plebiscite, adding India's 2019 revocation of Article 370 and annexation of the region breached UN resolutions and the right to self-determination.
He said the new residency laws imposed by India in the disputed region breach the Fourth Geneva Convention, "granting outsiders rights to reduce Kashmiris to a minority in their own homeland."
"The colonial methods of repression in the occupied West Bank and Gaza are being transferred to [India-administered] Kashmir," Kafadar added.
He said that an information blackout persists in Kashmir, with journalists detained, their passports revoked, civil society organisations shut down, and books seized.
"While the Indian administration uses Bollywood productions and media manipulation to present the occupation to the world public as an 'internal security' issue, it is simultaneously implementing the colonial repression methods that Israel uses in the West Bank and Gaza in Kashmir," he added.
Kafadar said while Indian diplomats openly declare that they are basing their operations in the region on Israel's illegal settlement model, "witness statements in files submitted to the UK Metropolitan Police War Crimes Unit indicate that Israeli officials were present in interrogation and torture centres in Kashmir."
During the Israeli genocide in Gaza, the WOLAS chairman said they identified Israeli soldiers guilty of war crimes and sought Interpol Red Notices against them under universal jurisdiction, vowing to pursue Indian officials next.
"Today, we publicly announce that we are also pursuing the same legal mechanism against Indian military and civilian officials who committed crimes of torture, demolition with explosives, arbitrary executions, and demographic displacement in Kashmir," he promised.
Seven concrete steps
Hasan Basri Bulbul, a member of the WOLAS Board of Directors who presented the key issues highlighted in the 95-page report, said New Delhi has been rapidly changing the demographic structure in India-administered Kashmir since 2019.
Bulbul revealed that India had imposed 890 federal laws on the region, repealed 205 local laws, and amended 130 others, calling for the establishment of a UN Commission of Inquiry to investigate human rights violations and for those responsible to be prosecuted under universal jurisdiction.
In August 2022, he said, approximately 2.5 million new voters (a 30 percent increase) were added to the electoral rolls by granting voting rights to Indian citizens temporarily residing in the disputed region. 
Bulbul said that India-administered Kashmir has the highest military-to-civilian ratio in the world "with over 900,000-armed Indian personnel", adding "not a single military officer has been allowed to be prosecuted in civilian courts for 36 years under the Special Powers of the Armed Forces Act (AFSPA)."
Between 2019 and 2026, he said, 26,129 arbitrary detentions were recorded under draconian laws such as Public Safety Act (PSA) and the Prevention of Unlawful Activities Act (UAPA). With convictions below 1 percent, he said, massive indictments and prolonged detention serve as punishment before any verdict. 
The WOLAS official accused India of violating privacy of Kashmiris through household-level biometric registration and digital identity applications, "while the archives of local newspapers and human rights monitoring organisations are seized."
"As of September 2026, 4,249 books have been removed from circulation from universities and libraries; journalists, lawyers, and academics have had their passports revoked, systematically restricting their freedom of travel. Eid prayers at the central Friday Mosque and Eid Prayer Ground (Eidgah) in Srinagar have been blocked for eight consecutive years, including May 2026," he added.
Bulbul said the international community and legal institutions could implement seven concrete steps without requiring India’s consent or approval — implementation of UN Special Procedures and the establishment of an independent commission of inquiry, making legal applications in third states under universal jurisdiction based on documented concrete facts, implementing targeted sanctions against officials responsible for violations committed under AFSPA protection, and observance of human rights conditionality in international trade relations and defence transfers.
The steps he suggested also include continuous independent field and evidence documentation activities in accordance with international verification standards, requesting an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice via the UN General Assembly on the repeal of Article 370 and the conformity of the settlement regime with Article 49(6) of the Fourth Geneva Convention, and establishing a permanent Peoples' Tribunal that will convene at regular intervals to challenge the policy of invisibility. 
New Delhi has not responded to the report yet.
India and Pakistan each administer a part of Kashmir, but both claim the territory in its entirety. The neighbouring rivals have fought two of their three wars over the territory since they gained independence in 1947. China also administers a portion of Kashmir, known as Aksai Chin, following the defeat of India in the 1962 Sino-Indian War — making the Himalayan region the world's only nuclear tri-junction.
Rebel Kashmiris in the New Delhi-administered portion of Kashmir have been fighting Indian rule since 1989. The majority of Muslim Kashmiris support deciding the future of the region through a UN-mandated plebiscite.
India claims the Kashmir revolt is funded by Pakistan. Islamabad denies the charge and insists it only lends Kashmiris moral, political and diplomatic support. Many Kashmiris consider it a legitimate freedom struggle. Tens of thousands of civilians, rebels and Indian troops have been killed in the conflict.
India has deployed more than 500,000 troops to the region, making it one of the planet's most militarised zones.

Bulgaria’s Food Price Row Escalates as Retail Chains Face Inspections and Fines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:22:00 UTC
17:22:00 KST

Bulgaria Has EU’s Highest Road Death Rate
Bulgaria recorded the European Union’s highest road fatality rate in 2025, with 71 deaths per million inhabitants, according to final figures released by the European Commission
Maya Manolova, chair of Bulgaria’s Consumer Protection Commission (CPCo), said on BNT that basic food products cost more in Sofia than in Vienna and Berlin, accusing major retail chains of imposing excessive markups and unfair charges on Bulgarian suppliers.
Manolova said the CPCo’s inspections focus primarily on food prices in retail chains because they account for the largest share of the market. While the chains claim to hold up to 60% of the market, figures from other experts put their share of food retail at 70%.
Comparisons conducted during the inspections showed that basic food items were more expensive in Sofia than in the two European capitals. Manolova also said the difference between wholesale and retail prices was sometimes several times greater in Bulgaria than in Germany, where the owners of the country’s two largest retail chains operating in Bulgaria are based.
She accused the chains of exploiting Bulgarian consumers through high profit margins, leaving them at a greater disadvantage than German shoppers.
Manolova brought a plastic crate into the studio to demonstrate what she described as an unfair commercial practice used by four major retail chains, which she said adds costs for producers, particularly fruit and vegetable growers.
She said the crate costs 3.50 euros, but producers must pay a rental fee of 1 euro excluding VAT, or 1.20 euros including VAT, every time they deliver goods to a retail chain using it. Suppliers must also pay an annual deposit equal to the crate’s value.
According to Manolova, a company affiliated with a retail chain receives 365 euros in annual revenue from the arrangement. She called the container a “cash-cow” crate, arguing that the rental fees are ultimately passed on to consumers through higher product prices.
She said four major retail chains use similar practices through affiliated companies. One chain has explained that the crates are taken to Romania for washing and disinfection.
“ Naturally, this remains to be verified, but regardless of how you look at it, the cost is 3.50 euros. The daily rental fee for a single delivery to a store is 1 euro, excluding VAT. That is excessive,” Manolova said.
A formal complaint about the practice has been submitted to the Commission for Protection of Competition (CPC).
Manolova said the CPC should protect retail-chain suppliers and regulate relations between retailers and food producers. She added that penalties for unfair commercial practices can reach 10% of a chain’s turnover and called for a substantial fine against the retailer involved.
Regarding violations found at a central kitchen in Plovdiv that prepares ready-to-eat meals for a major chain’s hot food counters, Manolova said state institutions had begun inspections to protect consumers.
The Bulgarian Food Safety Agency identified several problems at the facility, including extremely poor hygiene in the premises and on food-processing equipment. Documentation establishing the traceability of ingredients was also missing.
Manolova said inspectors could not verify the origin, expiration dates or quality of the products used to prepare the meals, stressing that all such information must be supported by documentation.
A warehouse belonging to a major retail chain was also found to contain products past their expiration dates, in breach of the law. The products were meat items, and authorities are reviewing records to establish how they were removed from storage and whether they were destroyed.
Two hot food counters in supermarkets operated by another chain have also been closed, including one in Sofia. Manolova said inspections were taking place across the sector and that the CPCo was investigating unfair commercial practices, adding that the law should be applied consistently whenever violations are found.
Manolova said she had signed four penalty decrees the previous day, imposing a total of 110,000 euros in fines for misleading commercial practices.
The violations included discrepancies between shelf-label prices and the amounts charged at checkout, promotions that advertised discounts without actually lowering prices, and insufficient stocks of goods promoted as being on sale. In one case, only six units of an advertised product were available on the first day of the promotion.
Manolova said retailers might rely on promotional advertising to attract customers who then buy other products, and stressed that such practices should be sanctioned.
She also warned about so-called “miracle” dietary supplements, which she said frequently deceive elderly consumers. Some products claim to treat gastrointestinal problems, calm the nervous system and cure autoimmune diseases, while others are advertised as cancer treatments using ingredients such as dandelion or turmeric.
Manolova said such products were often marketed as remedies for almost any condition, particularly through online pharmacies, although similar practices also occurred in physical stores. Sellers are required to substantiate claims about a supplement’s effects with official documentation, laboratory analyses and scientific research.
The CPCo has not yet investigated the specific cases she mentioned, but Manolova said such schemes typically involve selling an allegedly miraculous remedy, usually an unregistered dietary supplement, for about a month before the seller disappears.
Asen Vassilev, leader of We Continue the Change (PP) and a former finance minister, criticized the government’s response to rising prices, budget policy and household incomes during an appearance on Nova TV, bringing a basket labeled “Care” into the studio. He also discussed the presidential runoff, pardons for people convicted of drug-related offenses and the war in Ukraine.
Vasilev argued that imposing administrative limits on commercial markups would not resolve rising prices. “The question is: what is the ultimate effect of the government's actions? Will there be lower prices for Bulgarian citizens? Will fines be imposed if excessive markups are actually found? Or will this 'care' be just like this basket - somewhat empty? Ultimately, prices will continue to rise,” he said.
Under the headline “They are reaching into people's pockets to cover up thefts,” Vassilev argued that the government should instead focus on electricity, natural gas and fuel prices because they affect the cost of producing other goods.
“When you attempt to restrict market players using non-market mechanisms, things usually don't work. Setting a maximum markup on a product in a functioning market implies that you would subsequently have to audit every single cost,” Vassilev said.
He maintained that incomes should rise faster than inflation and accused the government of preparing a budget that would reverse the trend seen in previous years.
“If you look at the overall picture for 2022, 2023, and 2024, incomes have grown faster than inflation - twice as fast, in fact. In other words, people are not becoming poorer. Yet, the current budget has been carefully designed to ensure that incomes grow more slowly than inflation. For the first time, a budget explicitly accounts for the impoverishment of Bulgarian citizens,” the PP leader said.
Vassilev also criticized the distribution of public spending, saying administrative operating costs were increasing much faster than salaries.
“Why are you raising operating costs by 35% while increasing salaries by only 5%? It comes down to priorities and how money is being spent. Operating costs cover things like electricity and water bills, minor repairs, and the purchase of supplies. These costs have risen by 1.5 billion euros. There is money for operating expenses, but none for salaries,” he said.
He questioned capital spending and called for greater transparency in the use of public money. Regarding the 2027 budget, Vassilev said he suspected it would be less favorable than the 2026 framework, although he said it was better to wait for the details.
“I suspect the budget will be much worse than the 2026 budget. But rather than speculating, it is better to wait and see. We need to know what the money of Bulgarian citizens will be spent on,” he said.
Vassilev also discussed the upcoming second round of the presidential election between Iliana Yotova and Andrey Gyurov, arguing that turnout, rather than agreements between parties, would determine the result.
“With a 22% voter turnout, nothing is decided. It is unclear how many people will turn out for the next round, or who exactly will show up. Everything will depend on the Bulgarian citizens, not on deals made in party headquarters,” he said.
He rejected the idea that party leaders should negotiate support for a particular candidate, saying the president should be chosen by voters rather than through behind-the-scenes agreements between political parties.
Vassilev accused the ruling authorities of using fears of war for political purposes and diverting public attention from economic problems.
He also questioned pardons granted to people convicted of drug-related offenses during Iliana Yotova’s tenure as vice president, saying five cases required clear explanations.
“If someone is caught with drugs, released to undergo treatment, caught a second time while undergoing that treatment, and subsequently convicted a second time—you simply cannot pardon such a person. Regardless of their state of health,” Vassilev said.
On Ukraine and relations with Europe, Vassilev said he did not expect a direct military confrontation between NATO and Russia.
“I do not believe it will come to a direct clash between NATO and Russia. This is precisely where all these layers of fear come into play. Currently, the discussion centers on providing financial support to Ukraine and selling weapons to the country,” he said.
He argued that Bulgaria should pursue its national interests through active cooperation with European partners rather than confrontational rhetoric.
Vassilev also responded to claims that he had demanded that GERB leader Boyko Borisov be handcuffed during his arrest in 2022.
“Let me tell you right now: put handcuffs on the cameraman. What does that tell you? How could a Finance Minister order someone to apply handcuffs?” he said.
Regarding the upcoming election of members of the Supreme Judicial Council, Vassilev said PP would decide its position after the candidates’ hearings.
He also said arrests of mayors must be based on sufficient evidence rather than political considerations.
“I am opposed to the arrest of individuals against whom there is insufficient evidence. You cannot detain a person without having sufficient evidence - regardless of who that person is,” Vassilev said.
Nikolay Valkanov, executive director of the Association for Modern Trade, rejected claims that retail chains alone were responsible for rising food prices in Bulgaria.
Valkanov acknowledged that retail prices had increased between August of last year and August of this year, but said retailers were not to blame in nine out of 10 cases.
He said Bulgarian suppliers had increased their domestic prices by more than 70% since 2021, arguing that producers and processors were the main drivers of the increases.
Despite the rises, Valkanov said prices on the Bulgarian market remained among the lowest in Europe, with fresh milk as the exception.
He added that retailers selling certain goods at prices substantially below the European Union average had to raise the prices of other products to compensate for the losses.
On products whose quality was in question, Valkanov said manufacturers were responsible for ensuring that the actual composition matched the information on the label.
“If a retail chain discovers a discrepancy, it immediately terminates its contract with the supplier,” Valkanov said.
He added that the industry had requested three meetings with the prime minister to discuss specific proposals and measures to ease prices and improve production, but the Council of Ministers had shown no willingness to engage in dialogue.

Burials in nature are growing in popularity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:15:34 UTC
17:15:34 KST

In the Vinderhoutse Bossen in Ghent, a new site is being created to allow people to have their ashes buried in a natural way, without an urn. Funeral directors are also receiving more enquiries about this kind of option, notes funeral director Gerrit Cispa from Drongen: “The demand for new forms of burial in Ghent, closer to nature, is gradually increasing.”
Burials in nature are growing in popularity
The new natural burial site forms part of the Vinderhoutse Bossen woodland area. Unlike in a traditional cemetery, no urns are buried here. The ashes are buried in the natural environment, without an urn or any other container.
“It is not actually a cemetery, but a nature site that forms part of a nature reserve,” says Gerrit Cispa of the Cispa funeral home. “That is why no urns are buried here. In Drongen, however, an urn is required at the burial site. We are seeing an increase in the number of enquiries we receive for that location, but the whole thing is still in its infancy.”
Drongen is Ghent’s first natural burial ground and opened in 2021. Over the first four years, ashes were scattered on 46 occasions, and 67 biodegradable urns were buried. No memorials are permitted, and a plot is granted for 25 years.
Growing interest in natural burials
According to Gerrit Cispa, interest in natural burials has grown in recent years. “People are increasingly opting for a farewell ceremony in which nature plays a central role. This can be achieved by burying an urn, but also by having the ashes buried directly in nature or by choosing to scatter them.”
“There is an increasing demand for urns to be buried in a natural way, returning them to nature. It is a trend that is gradually gaining ground,” says Gerrit Cispa. “Ash scattering is also more frequently taking place at natural burial grounds.”
According to the funeral director, the traditional burial in a coffin at a conventional cemetery has been losing popularity for some time. “Those figures have been falling for quite a while. There are more new forms that are also in greater demand. People want to say their goodbyes in a more environmentally friendly way.”
Information session on Vinderhoutse Bossen
During an information session organised by the City of Ghent, Gerrit Cispa was briefed on the new site. The city has laid out new paths to guide visitors to the nature reserve. The funeral director has already visited the site himself and describes it as a beautiful, newly developed area.
However, the space available for natural burials is limited. “For the time being, part of the nature reserve has been set aside for this purpose. I believe there is currently a limit of 1,250 plots. But further expansion may be possible in the future, although that depends on the city’s future plans.”

U.S. Army pilots test MV-75 tiltrotor in simulators before its first flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:15:07 UTC
17:15:07 KST

- U.S. Army aviators and National Guard officers took part in the sixth MV-75 Cheyenne II Special User Evaluation at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, Aug. 24–28, 2026.
- Participants flew a virtual prototype, compared Chinook and Black Hawk cockpits, and practiced maintenance in virtual reality to inform the tiltrotor’s design.
U.S. Army aviators and National Guard aviation officers spent a week this summer flying a virtual MV-75 Cheyenne II, critiquing cockpits and rehearsing maintenance in virtual reality, as the service brings soldiers into the tiltrotor’s design before the first test aircraft has flown.
The sixth MV-75 Special User Evaluation ran Aug. 24 to 28 at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, according to an Army statement published Oct. 27 by the program’s acquisition office. Participants came from the MV-75 Operational Development Team, a group of aviators, crew chiefs and maintainers based at Fort Rucker, Alabama, and from a National Guard advisory working group with representatives from Colorado, Idaho, Kansas, Louisiana, Minnesota, New York and Pennsylvania. The Army has not released findings from the evaluation, and the account describes what participants did and how the program will use their feedback without saying whether any design changes resulted.
Special User Evaluations put the people who will fly and fix an aircraft into its development cycle early, so that problems with workload, human-systems integration and maintenance surface while they are still cheap to correct. For this session, crews worked through the MV-75 virtual prototype to learn the crew station and flew simulated missions over terrain to assess tiltrotor flight dynamics, vertical-lift controls and conversion from helicopter mode to high-speed airplane mode. At the Army’s Advanced Prototyping Engineering and Experimentation Laboratory, aviators compared the cockpit layouts of the CH-47 Chinook and UH-60 Black Hawk to identify features worth keeping and usability problems worth avoiding, and they flew familiarization sorties in an MD 530 helicopter with the Army Flight Test Directorate to assess its cockpit. The program office said it will consolidate that comparative feedback and use it in technical discussions with Bell, the aircraft’s builder.
Maintainers used virtual-reality interfaces to practice removing and replacing major components, and participants also reviewed cybersecurity, infrastructure and acquisition lifecycle requirements. Staff Sgt. Eric Lopez of the Operational Development Team said the aircraft’s upgraded electronics, maintenance packages and technical manuals would simplify sustainment for soldiers, an assessment that cannot yet be tested on real hardware.
The National Guard participants focused on how the aircraft would be used at home. CW4 Darren Frey of the Colorado National Guard and the High Altitude Army National Guard Aviation Training Site said the MV-75’s longer range and faster transit could let states centralize fleet maintenance at a single hub while still covering the whole state for rapid-response missions, potentially reducing infrastructure and maintenance requirements. Col. Jim Mandel of the Idaho National Guard said the officers in the working group advise their states’ adjutants general on positioning aviation assets for state and federal missions.
Maj. J.T. Hingey, deputy team chief of the Operational Development Team, said the evaluation was the team’s first in-person engagement with the project manager and the flight test directorate. He said flying the virtual prototype under the guidance of experimental test pilots with V-22 Osprey experience gave the Fort Rucker team insight it will use to improve its own simulator, refine tactics, techniques and procedures, and brief senior Army leaders. He also stressed the need for a shared understanding of the program baseline and the outside factors that affect it, so the aviation enterprise can stay aligned when funding, schedules or other variables change.
The MV-75 is the production version of Bell’s V-280 Valor demonstrator, which first flew on Dec. 18, 2017, and won the Future Long Range Assault Aircraft competition in December 2022. The program reached Milestone B, the formal start of engineering and manufacturing development, in August 2024, and in April 2026 the Army officially named the aircraft the Cheyenne II, the first all-new platform to enter its inventory since the 1980s. The 101st Airborne Division’s combat aviation brigade has been selected as the first unit to receive it.
The company completed the first MV-75 wing in February and said it took 90% fewer labor hours than the first V-22 wing, an efficiency it attributes to the aircraft’s digital design. By midsummer the first six test aircraft were in various stages of assembly, with final assembly at Amarillo, Texas, and fuselages built at a new center in Wichita, Kansas. The first gearbox has been completed, and testing on the first flight control computers has started in Bell’s weapon systems integration lab.
The schedule is less settled. The Army sharply accelerated the program in early 2026, pulling initial fielding forward to 2027 from a previous target of around 2031, but at the April naming ceremony officials declined to commit to first flight or production dates. Funding then interrupted the work: after fiscal 2026 money for the program ran out in July, the Army and Bell went through a three-month communications blackout under federal funding rules and only resumed program discussions in October. The Army’s fiscal 2027 request includes $2.1 billion in research and development funding for the MV-75, up from $350 million in fiscal 2026, and Bell said meetings with the government are planned to agree on a feasible baseline schedule.
The Operational Development Team’s work at Fort Rucker draws heavily on the V-22, the only tiltrotor in U.S. military service, which the U.S. Marine Corps and U.S. Air Force have operated since 2007. The MV-75 differs from the Osprey in a key respect: its engines stay fixed in the nacelles while only the rotors and driveshafts tilt, and a driveshaft through the wing lets one engine power both rotors. The Army has never flown a tiltrotor, so the team is using virtual prototypes and joint-service V-22 lessons to build tiltrotor expertise, streamline pilot training and prepare units before the first aircraft arrive.
The aircraft’s speed will also force changes around it. The Army has said the MV-75 is designed to fly roughly twice as far and twice as fast as its current helicopters, and Army officials have noted that the AH-64 Apache, which normally escorts assault helicopters, tops out at about 300 km/h (185 mph), well below the tiltrotor’s planned cruise of more than 480 km/h (300 mph). The Black Hawk, which the MV-75 is meant to partly replace, is expected to remain in service into the 2050s.

At least 3 dead after Cylone Arnab hits southern India
Authorities evacuate 180,000 people as severe storm causes flooding, disrupting flights and train schedules.
At least three people have been killed after Cyclone Arnab made landfall on India’s east coast, causing widespread damage and bringing heavy rainfall and wind speeds of up to 135 km/h (84mph).
Trees fell onto highways and power supplies were disrupted after Arnab crossed into Andhra Pradesh early on Wednesday morning.
Narendra Singh Bundela, a top official at the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), told reporters that three people lost their lives when the storm hit and confirmed Andhra Pradesh was the worst affected.
Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu said in a letter to federal Home Minister Amit Shah that at least 180 houses were destroyed, 220 trees were brought down and power supply in several areas was disrupted.
Officials in Naidu’s office told Reuters that two of the deaths were caused by a tree falling and electrocution.
At least 180,000 people were evacuated from Andhra Pradesh and Odisha states a day earlier. Flights and train services were cancelled, and some schools were forced to close.
Authorities say more than 12 million people live in the cyclone’s expected path.
One resident of Kakinada district in Andhra Pradesh, in Arnab’s path, said: “No one knew whose house the water would rush into next or whose home would be submerged.”
India’s Meteorological Department forecast a storm surge of up to 1.5m above the tide level, warning that it was likely to submerge low-lying areas in Andhra Pradesh.
‘Very severe cyclonic storm’
Arnab made landfall as a “very severe cyclonic storm” – the third-highest category on its scale, before being downgraded to “severe” after moving further inland.
In neighbouring Nepal, authorities warned tourists on Tuesday not to enter high-altitude areas over fears Arnab could trigger torrential downpours, snowstorms and avalanches from Thursday through to Saturday.
Reuters news agency reported that authorities suspended issuing trekking permits for three days.
This is peak hiking season in Nepal, with about 750 hikers receiving permits daily.
Nepal is still recovering from a catastrophic glacial mountain collapse in August, which killed more than 1,400 people and left at least 5,000 missing.
Sri Lanka has also closed schools, with its Department of Meteorology warning the storm could trigger flash floods and landslides.

Top U.S. general says AI will change how America fights its wars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:07:10 UTC
17:07:10 KST

- Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, called artificial intelligence one of his three strategic priorities, after the budget and ahead of operations.
- Caine used the term super intelligence, which a Sept. 29 executive order directs the executive branch to use in place of artificial intelligence.
Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, has named artificial intelligence as one of his three strategic priorities, ranking it behind only securing a budget and ahead of ongoing military operations.
Caine made the remarks on Oct. 26 during a fireside chat at the National Defense Transportation Association and U.S. Transportation Command fall meeting in Grapevine, Texas, moderated by Transcom commander Gen. Randall Reed of the U.S. Air Force, according to a Pentagon News account of the session. Throughout the discussion, Caine referred to the technology as “super intelligence,” or SI, the term President Donald Trump is trying to substitute for “artificial intelligence” across the federal government.
“I have sort of three strategic priorities right now, separate from [others]. No. 1 is making sure that we have a budget. … No. 2 is [super intelligence], and No. 3 is ongoing operations,” said Caine.
The wording follows a Sept. 29 executive order that directs the executive branch, to the extent the law allows, to use “Super Intelligence” and “SI” in place of “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI.” The order does not create a new category of technology. It defines super intelligence as the same systems already covered by the statutory definition of artificial intelligence in federal law, so when Caine says SI, he is describing the AI tools the military uses and develops today.
Trump first announced the change in his Sept. 22 speech to the United Nations General Assembly, saying all U.S. government documents would switch to the “much more accurate term.” The State Department has since ordered its staff to rename AI-related programs and systems, and military offices have started adopting the language as well; the U.S. Marine Corps aviation acquisition office this month described new maintenance tools it is pursuing as predictive super intelligence technologies.
The term already carries a different meaning in the technology field. Researchers and AI companies have long used superintelligence to describe a hypothetical future system that surpasses human intelligence, and the industry more often uses “artificial general intelligence” for AI that would match or exceed people across tasks. Critics have argued that the government’s branding blurs that distinction, and Trump has responded by calling anyone who uses the term “Artificial Intelligence” an enemy of the White House.
Caine told the Transcom audience that the technology will be essential for the joint force to win tactical engagements, run logistics and sustainment, and carry out command and control, the functions that let commanders direct forces in combat. He described a future conflict in which the number of kinetic and non-kinetic actions moving between the United States and an adversary, from missiles, rockets and bombs to cyberattacks, would be significant enough to require machine help.
“When I think of SI, …it’s going to be a game changer as we move forward,” said Caine.
The chairman stressed that the work involves training leaders as well as systems and models, so that future commanders get decision support while humans stay appropriately involved and the military balances the opportunities against the risks. He said the Joint Staff is already working on that effort.
“It’s going to be an important part of our future, [and] we need to lean in,” said Caine.
The Pentagon’s use of the technology has grown quickly over the past year. In May, Under Secretary of War Emil Michael said the number of department personnel using AI tools rose from about 80,000 to 1.5 million in a single year, spanning enterprise productivity software through classified intelligence analysis. The department is also applying AI to missile defense data fusion and has launched a pilot program that uses AI-assisted tools to manage security classification.
Transcom offers an obvious test case for the logistics side of Caine’s argument. The command moves troops, equipment and supplies worldwide by air, sea and land, and the forecasting, routing and maintenance planning behind that work are the kind of data-heavy tasks where the Pentagon has been most willing to put AI tools into daily use. Caine did not describe specific Transcom programs during the session, according to the Pentagon account.
He closed the point by saying the commercial sector is likely to set the pace if past experience holds, and that the military needs to keep up.
“And we need to match them at the same speed and tempo,” Caine said.

The banker, the basketball star, the cardiologist and the chemist: meet Serbia's potential new leaders
BELGRADE, Oct 28 - After a leaderless student-led protest movement swept Serbia's former President Aleksandar Vucic from power in a historic snap election on Sunday, the country is waiting to hear who it will appoint as prime minister and to other key ministerial positions as it forms a government.
Here are some of the prominent candidates on the students' list.
FORMER CENTRAL BANK GOVERNOR DEJAN SOSKIC, 59
Dejan Soskic, an economist and professor at the University of Belgrade's Faculty of Economics, served as governor of the central bank between 2010 and 2012, before resigning in protest at legislative amendments that he argued compromised the institution's independence. He has for years been a vocal opponent of Vucic's government.
Soskic, who was an avid biker in his youth but has mellowed into a softly spoken reformer, has frequently criticised the country’s institutional weaknesses under Vucic. In 2021, he said, pointing to Serbia's standing and declining scores on international transparency metrics, that systemic corruption in the Balkan state was more widespread than in neighbouring countries and that it was deterring domestic and foreign direct investment. Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party have repeatedly denied accusations of corruption.
Soskic says that prudent public finances will create a stable foundation for a permanent increase in wages and pensions.
Pro-government media have criticised Soskic’s central bank record, accusing him of triggering the depreciation of the dinar during his tenure. Soskic has defended the depreciation as a reflection of the mandatory monetary policy amendments of the time rather than a personal failure.
Nonetheless, during the election campaign, in order to increase export competitiveness, Soskic proposed correcting, or weakening, the exchange rate of the dinar - which is in a managed float against the euro - to make domestic goods cheaper in foreign currencies. An alternative, he suggested, would be to maintain a fixed, stronger exchange rate but lower costs by cutting wages.
CARDIOLOGIST AND PROFESSOR ILIJA SRDANOVIC, 55
Ilija Srdanovic, a practising cardiologist, professor at the University of Novi Sad Faculty of Medicine and a keen cyclist, became the student movement's lead candidate when the ballot list was finalised in September.
Srdanovic’s transition to frontline politics began during the student-led anti-corruption demonstrations, where he frequently appeared as a public speaker. The physician participated in the movement's "Guardians of the Constitution" bicycle tour across the northern Vojvodina province.
Srdanovic campaigned with the promise of a decentralised health system "at the service of citizens and based on equality for all patients". In an interview with the Belgrade-based FoNet news agency, Srdanovic said his political objective was building "a better Serbia, nothing else is important".
He declined an invitation from Vucic to participate in a televised debate during the campaign.
European Council President Antonio Costa on Tuesday wrote on X that he had held a "good" telephone conversation with Srdanovic, saying that the priority is to establish a new government without delay.
Some of Srdanovic's policies do not represent a sharp departure from some of those of the previous government. He stressed the Student List position that Kosovo, which declared independence from Serbia in 2008, remains an integral part of the country. During the campaign he also said that European Union integration is not a current priority and that the immediate focus for the incoming administration must remain on domestic anti-corruption reforms and national "existential survival".
FORMER BASKETBALL STAR DEJAN BODIROGA, 53
Dejan Bodiroga, the former captain of the Yugoslav national basketball team and current EuroLeague president, is one of the student movement's most prominent public speakers.
He described Sunday's election as a fight "for the return of a country that has been hijacked".
The step into politics is the latest chapter in a life that has gripped the basketball-mad nation - from capturing back-to-back FIBA World Championship gold medals in 1998 and 2002 and leading the then Yugoslav team to an Olympic silver medal at the 1996 Atlanta Games to entering senior sports administration upon his retirement as a player in 2007 and being appointed as EuroLeague president in 2022.
During the election campaign, Bodiroga appeared at student rallies and took part in open-air folk dancing in rural municipalities. His fans frequently cheered him with a 1990s slogan "We have our God, his name is Bodiroga."
CHEMISTRY PROFESSOR RADOMIR SAICIC, 64
Radomir Saicic, an organic chemistry professor and a member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts (SANU), was the face of the students' election win on Sunday, taking the podium at their headquarters after Vucic conceded defeat to hail the outcome as a "citizens' victory".
He is a specialist in medicinal chemistry whose research focuses on the synthesis of chemotherapy treatments and antiviral therapies, including a special COVID-19 project in collaboration with the Pasteur Institute.
Saicic joined the student-led anti-corruption protests that followed the 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in the northern Serbian city of Novi Sad. He became a target for pro-government tabloids after signing a petition with 24 other academics demanding Vucic's resignation, and in May 2026 he walked out of a SANU gallery exhibition to protest an appearance by Nikola Selakovic, the minister of culture.
During the campaign, he told crowds that Serbia was "occupied from within" and said he was ready to put "even his life" at the disposal of the student movement.
Saicic says Kosovo is a "temporarily occupied territory" and backs energy ties with Russia.
Political analysts and local media have tipped him as a contender in the presidential election which will also be triggered by Vucic's recent resignation from the post. REUTERS

Boeing gets nearly $500 million more for Apache support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:01:44 UTC
17:01:44 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Boeing a $499.8 million modification for AH-64 Apache engineering services and technical support, extending the contract to February 2031.
- The Army received one bid, and work locations and funding will be set with each order under the contract first awarded in 2021.
The U.S. Army has added nearly $500 million to a Boeing contract for engineering services and technical support on the AH-64 Apache attack helicopter, extending the work through February 2031.
Army Contracting Command at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, awarded the $499.8 million modification to Boeing’s Mesa, Arizona, operation on Feb. 21, 2026, according to the Department of War announcement. The Army solicited bids online and received one, and because work locations and funding will be set with each individual order, the announcement does not say how much money has been obligated so far or where the engineering will be done.
The modification extends a contract the Army first awarded in August 2021, when it gave Boeing a $487 million cost-plus-fixed-fee deal for the same Apache engineering and technical support, originally due to run until Feb. 6, 2026. The new action came about two weeks after that end date, adding a sum roughly equal to the original ceiling along with five more years of performance. Engineering support of this kind pays for the work that keeps an aircraft type flying and evolving after it leaves the factory, from investigating fleet problems and updating technical documentation to integrating new equipment, though the announcement does not list the specific tasks planned for the next five years.
The money arrives as the Army shrinks and reorganizes its Apache force. Under the Army Transformation Initiative announced in 2025, the service is retiring every remaining AH-64D, the older Longbow variant whose last new airframe was built in 2013, and deactivating 11 air cavalry squadrons, most of which flew the D model. The Army has been planning that drawdown for years, and as early as 2020 it sought contractors to dismantle hundreds of AH-64Ds. In April 2026, the Army’s director of aviation said the service had divested nearly 60% of its D models within a year, while procurement funding for Apaches in the fiscal 2027 budget request fell from $361.7 million to $1.5 million.
The newer AH-64E Guardian remains the Army’s only attack helicopter, but its numbers are also coming down. A Pentagon budget document reviewed by Aviation Week showed the service plans to retire some AH-64Es as well, culling the E-model fleet in greater numbers next year even as it completes the move to an all-E force.
Much of the remaining engineering effort is tied to upgrading the aircraft the Army keeps. The service’s priority is Version 6.5, an AH-64E software and hardware update that adds an open-systems interface for faster technology insertion, enhanced Link 16 data sharing for manned-unmanned teaming, and the groundwork for launched effects, the small drones an Apache can release to scout or strike ahead of it. Version 6.5 first flew in October 2023 and is meant to bring every E-model onto a single software baseline, and Boeing said in April that the Army was testing the configuration and that adding it to production would require only a modification to the existing contract.
In May 2026, the Army was investigating a newly discovered transmission problem affecting the AH-64E, at a time when funding shortfalls had forced some units to cut flight hours and speed up the retirement of their D models. The Army has not said whether any part of the new engineering modification is linked to that investigation.

‘Nobody heard us’ – why Gen Z are leading protests across Europe
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:00:21 CET
17:00:21 KST

By Fedja Grulovic , Alex Fraser , Bart Biesemans and Fatos Bytyci
BELGRADE/MILAN/BRUSSELS/TIRANA, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Maya Gourdel, a 19-year-old student in Brussels, sits at a desk writing slogans against those running her country: “If we burn, you burn with us!” The slogan, taken from the 2012 film “The Hunger Games” that has been adopted as a symbol by many youth movements globally, reflects the anger, frustration and desire for change driving Gen Z-led protests around Europe.
From the suburbs of Paris to the squares of Belgrade, thousands have taken to the streets.
The demands are various but often overlapping – frustrations with shabby schooling facilities, perceived lack of economic opportunity, cost of living, corruption, housing and a sense of not being listened to. At times those protests triggered violence – with thousands of shops in France alone being damaged or looted in recent weeks – and police firing stun grenades and water cannons.
This weekend they also brought real change – student-led protests culminated in the toppling in an election of Serbia’s long-time leader Aleksandar Vucic after nearly two years of demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism.
“Waking up, the first thing we felt was certainly a sense of relief and freedom,” said student protester Stasa Piletic. “Personally, I feel a sense of victory. I feel that we finally moved from protests to responsibility.”
‘AN EXPLOSION OF RAGE’
Chiara, a 21-year-old student in protest-hit Milan, believes “it’s vital to take part in people’s spontaneous movements born from an explosion of rage that made collective action possible.”
“I think the worst damage this ruling class has done to my generation is stealing even the ability to imagine a future, to dream,” she said.
She said Italian students were confronting a reality of schools without enough teachers and crumbling buildings.
“And all of this with the prospect of an underpaid job which we didn’t qualify for and the prospect of living in a tiny, overpriced house, probably away from our city, which we didn’t want to live in.”
Protests led by Gen Z have caused ructions globally as the generation born roughly between 1997 and 2012 found its voice, from Bangladesh in 2024 and Nepal in 2025, to India this year. Now Europe has become a focal point.
Rising prices and the cost of living are a concern for 40% of 16-30-year-olds, according to a European Union survey published in 2025.
Among the 92.7 million people in the EU who faced the risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2025, the highest risk was recorded for young adults aged 18-24 years, at 26.3%, while the lowest was recorded for adults aged 65 years or over, at 18.8%.
Younger people are also wary of shouldering the financial burden of an older generation that tends to vote in greater numbers. People over 60 in France make up a quarter of the population but own 60% of France’s wealth, according to the OFCE think tank.
French pensions are by far the biggest public expense, on track to reach 14% of economic output, as the population ages and voters resist raising the retirement age or reducing benefits. That is still less than Greece or Italy, which spend the largest proportion of national income on public pensions among OECD countries, at around 16% of GDP, according to OECD figures in 2025. But it is much more than Australia, Chile, Iceland, Ireland or South Korea, which spent less than 4% of GDP on public pensions, according to the OECD.
‘YOUNG PEOPLE IN EUROPE ARE UNITED’
Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris, has been protesting against “deplorable” conditions and staff shortages at his school. “There used to be rats,” he said. Students were evacuated last year when a roof collapsed on the courtyard, though no one was hurt, he said.
Protests showed “that young people in Europe are united”, he said, adding, “we all agree on one point: that young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren’t listened to enough.”
A French government report in October said pension spending had risen by 2.5 percentage points of GDP between 2000 and 2023 while that for education had declined 0.5. It also showed 32% of the education ministry’s budget went towards pensions, crowding out money for other areas.
Gourdel, too, has been protesting for better conditions in schools in Belgium.
“We tried to do it passively. Nobody heard us. It’s only when people started to burn trash or that kind of stuff that the media and cameras started showing us,” she said.
The protests are still spreading, with a demonstration planned in Germany this weekend over cost of living, inequality, war and the state of schools.
Unrest has also hit Albania, where student-led demonstrations against Prime Minister Edi Rama’s government, fuelled by anger over perceived corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, engulfed Tirana and spread to other cities.
“Our Prime Minister spent 130 days not listening to us,” said Xyke Kurti, a 19-year-old architecture student.
“If you ask a student in Albania, ‘where do you see your future?’ Everyone says ‘outside this country’,” she said, arguing that at home, even if you have talent, someone with “connections is always going to beat you”.
Serbia’s student movement did what demonstrators in other European capitals can only dream of.
Now, though, comes the gritty business of governing – something neither the students nor their candidates have any experience of. Luka Stojakovic, another protester, brushes that aside. “We have seen where people with political experience have brought us.”

A Fiat that converts from a family car into a pickup and a Peugeot with a glass-bubble roof were among six concept cars unveiled by Stellantis at the 2026 Paris Motor Show, as captured in this video carousel by Dezeen.
Automotive corporation Stellantis unveiled the six concepts at a preview event in Meudon, outside Paris, on the eve of the motor show, offering an early look at the designs before the exhibition opened to the public.
The concepts explored different approaches to future car design – from reworking historic models to experimenting with colour-changing paint and illuminated bodywork.
Among the cars presented was Fiat’s Multiplay, which combines the proportions of a family vehicle with the functionality of a pickup.
Measuring 4.45 metres long, the concept has a sliding rear section that converts its six-seat-plus-one configuration into a four-seat vehicle with an open cargo bed.
Inside, a front passenger seat called the Sunseat folds into a lounge-style position beneath the panoramic roof, while a modular Petsenger seat can accommodate a pet, a child seat or storage.
The concept was finished in bright green, with a pink floor and red and pink upholstery inspired by the colours of a watermelon.
Citroën revisited its 1948 2CV with a compact electric concept featuring an orange-red body, grey steel wheels and yellow accents.
Inside, yellow tartan upholstery echoes details of the original model, while a fabric sunroof and removable storage basket replaced some of the conventional fittings found in modern cars.
The concept also features a detachable radio called Radioën, which doubles as a portable speaker, as well as door compartments designed to hold eggs, echoing the practical requirements of the original car.
Peugeot presented its RCZ Vision concept, a low-slung coupe with a sculpted body and a glass roof with a distinctive double-bubble profile that extends from the bonnet towards the rear.
Slim horizontal headlights reinterpret the brand’s three-claw motif, while a rear spoiler deploys only when the car is moving, keeping the bodywork smooth when parked.
Inside, a square steering control called Hypersquare replaces a conventional steering wheel and transparent micro-LED displays provide driving information while reducing the visual prominence of screens.
DS Automobiles’ F3VER concept features a compact body finished in Cosmic Blue paint that changes from vivid blue to violet depending on the light.
Its two-tone finish wraps around the rear of the car, while vertical Y-shaped headlights frame the front emblem.
At the rear, 16 LED panels sit within a sculptural light assembly informed by the vaulted roof of Paris’s Grand Palais.
Opel’s STX Concept is an electric estate car with a low roofline, sharply creased bonnet and sloping rear. Its front grille, known as the Vizor, incorporates vertical animated lights around an illuminated Opel emblem.
The rear bumper features extendable aerodynamic elements, while glass light strips run from the rear side windows into the roof.
Cameras replace conventional wing mirrors and three-section alloy wheels are designed to improve aerodynamic efficiency.
Alfa Romeo’s Cuorerosso concept car explores the brand’s future sports-car design through a streamlined body, active air intakes and slim aerodynamic mirrors.
Its rear window echoes the shape of the brand’s triangular front grille, while the interior is organised around the driver, with controls concealed in the central console until needed.
Stellantis was formed in 2021 through the merger of Fiat Chrysler Automobiles and France’s PSA Group.
Its portfolio includes Alfa Romeo, Citroën, DS Automobiles, Fiat, Opel and Peugeot, among other automotive brands.

BAE to build thirty five thousand guidance kits a year
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:57:49 GMT
16:57:49 KST

BAE Systems has signed a framework agreement running up to seven years with the United States Department of War to lift production of APKWS laser guidance kits to as many as thirty five thousand a year, according to the company.
The kits turn unguided two point seven five inch rockets into precision guided munitions, and are in service with the United States Air Force, Army, Marine Corps and Navy. They are available to American allies and work in air-to-surface, surface-to-surface, surface-to-air and air-to-air engagements, including against drones.
Tom Arseneault, president and chief executive of BAE Systems, Inc., said: “APKWS delivers proven, reliable and affordable precision at scale to counter evolving threats and ensure our warfighters maintain a decisive advantage. This agreement highlights the importance of sustained investment in critical munitions to strengthen readiness and equip forces for evolving operational needs.”
Under the framework the company will increase production while negotiating a multi-year contract within it, which the company described as surge-ready support for evolving operational demands. BAE Systems said it has invested in manufacturing capacity, materials and expertise in line with the department’s Acquisition Transformation Strategy, and continues to develop upgrades, mission specific variants and new technologies.
The kits are built at BAE Systems facilities in Hudson, New Hampshire and Austin, Texas. The company delivered its hundred thousandth APKWS kit earlier, and the system is the United States government’s only programme of record for guided seventy millimetre rockets.
APKWS came to wider attention when American aircraft used the rockets against Houthi drones over the Red Sea, where a guidance kit costing a fraction of an air-to-air missile proved able to bring down one-way attack aircraft. The cost exchange problem that drove that use is the same one pushing European manufacturers towards cheaper interceptors.

Canada’s CH-148 Cyclone fleet gets radar warning software fix
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:55:22 UTC
16:55:22 KST

- Lockheed Martin received a $9.8 million contract to update AN/ALQ-230 radar warning software and a mission data tool for Canada’s CH-148 Cyclone helicopters.
- Canada is funding the work through Foreign Military Sales, with Naval Air Systems Command contracting and completion expected in October 2030.
Lockheed Martin will update the radar warning and electronic support software on Canada’s CH-148 Cyclone maritime helicopters under a $9.8 million contract awarded through the U.S. Navy, with work running until October 2030.
Naval Air Systems Command placed the contract with Lockheed’s Owego, New York, operation on behalf of the Canadian government, which is paying the full amount through Foreign Military Sales. It covers a new version of the operational flight program software for the helicopter’s AN/ALQ-230 electronic support measures and radar warning receiver, along with new Canadian Mission Data Load Tool software, and includes development, documentation, testing, installation and training aimed at fixing software and system trouble reports already logged against the equipment. Owego accounts for 97% of the work, with the remaining share split evenly between Ottawa, Halifax and Patuxent River, Maryland, and the contract was not competed.
The AN/ALQ-230 is the Cyclone’s passive electronic warfare sensor, a Lockheed system developed for Canada’s Maritime Helicopter Program that listens for radar emissions from ships, aircraft and air defense sites, identifies them and warns the crew when the helicopter is being tracked. The operational flight program is the software that runs the receiver itself, while the mission data load is the library of emitter signatures the system uses to recognize what it detects. A Canadian tool for building those mission data files lets the Royal Canadian Air Force prepare and update its own threat libraries, which have to change as new radars appear and as crews deploy to different regions.
The contract announcement does not describe the trouble reports or say how many have been recorded, and neither Lockheed nor the Canadian Department of National Defence has said whether the work will add capability or only correct existing faults.
The Cyclone is a militarized, fly-by-wire version of the Sikorsky S-92 built by Sikorsky, which Lockheed Martin owns, and it shares its basic airframe with the U.S. Marine Corps’ VH-92A presidential helicopter, which is also built on the S-92. Canada ordered 28 Cyclones in 2004 to replace the CH-124 Sea King, but development problems delayed deliveries until June 2015, and the helicopter did not reach initial operational capability until June 2018, the same year the last Sea Kings retired. The aircraft flies from Royal Canadian Navy Halifax-class frigates for anti-submarine and anti-surface warfare, search and rescue and utility missions, carrying a multi-mode radar, a HELRAS dipping sonar, two torpedoes and a mission system developed by General Dynamics Mission Systems-Canada in addition to the ESM suite.
National Defence puts the cost of acquiring the Cyclone, including project management, infrastructure and contingency, at C$3.75 billion, and the cost of major in-service support at C$11.17 billion. Its 2025 briefing notes set full operational capability for the fleet in September 2026 and the aircraft’s estimated life expectancy at 2043. One Cyclone was lost on April 29, 2020, while operating from HMCS Fredericton in the Ionian Sea, killing six Canadian Armed Forces members, which leaves 27 airframes from the original order.
The electronic support suite has been linked to an earlier fleet problem. Cracks found on almost all Cyclones in 2021 were caused by structural loads from the ESM and satellite communications antenna mounts in flight, according to National Defence, and Sikorsky repaired the aircraft. In April 2025, the fleet was briefly paused again after questions arose over whether some spare parts were in use beyond their service life.
Keeping the Cyclone’s mission systems current has been a recurring concern in Ottawa. Internal documents reported by CBC News in January 2024 showed the air force was worried about sustaining the helicopter’s weapon system over the medium and long term, partly because Canada is the only country flying the CH-148 and therefore bears the full cost of software and hardware updates unique to the type.
Lockheed’s Owego site also builds the AN/ALQ-210 electronic support system for the U.S. Navy’s MH-60R, and NAVAIR, which manages that work, is buying the Canadian update on Ottawa’s behalf, with part of the testing planned at Patuxent River.

Media groups urge EU Commission transparency as Gaza documents probe unfolds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:53:28 UTC
16:53:28 KST

Melike Pala
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
A group of 15 media outlets, journalist associations and press freedom organizations urged European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday to improve journalists’ access to public documents, as an inquiry by the EU Ombudswoman into the commission’s refusal to release documents concerning Gaza unfolds.
In an open letter to von der Leyen, the organizations called on the EU executive to address what they described as a “silent crisis” that has hampered journalists’ efforts to obtain information needed to scrutinize matters of public importance.
The appeal comes after European Ombudswoman Teresa Anjinho last week opened an inquiry into a news outlet’s complaint over the commission’s refusal to release 17 documents concerning EU-funded infrastructure projects in the Gaza Strip.
EUobserver first requested the documents in February as part of an investigation examining the extent to which Israeli attacks had destroyed infrastructure financed by the EU in the Palestinian territory.
The commission refused to release the material, arguing that there was no overriding public interest justifying disclosure. EUobserver’s subsequent appeal went unanswered.
As a first step in her inquiry, Anjinho has asked the commission to respond to the appeal by Nov. 4 at the latest. If the EU executive fails to provide a satisfactory response, she will examine the documents herself.
Against this backdrop, the 15 organizations urged the commission to commit to greater transparency, saying journalists routinely face severe delays in obtaining documents, questionable refusals and extensive redactions that render released material largely meaningless.
In some cases, they said, the commission also fails to retain and properly archive crucial documents.
The restrictions have hindered reporting on issues of major public interest, including how EU member states spent billions of euros in post-COVID recovery funds and cooperation with Israel on arms research, the letter said.
“Around Europe, public debate is being harmed. Stories which should emerge do not. Citizens cannot make important political judgements at critical moments,” it said.
The signatories called on the commission to revoke its December 2024 internal rules of procedure, which they said had made access to documents more difficult, and ensure strict implementation of the regulation on public access to EU documents.
The groups also called for a renewed action plan to improve journalists’ access to information, including implementing recommendations from the European Ombudsman, fully complying with European Court of Justice rulings and strengthening internal procedures for filing and archiving documents.
“The European Commission’s reputation for safeguarding EU democratic values is in peril. At a time when democratic norms are under attack around the world, now is the time to uphold these values,” the letter warned.
The signatories included the Committee to Protect Journalists, EUobserver, the European Federation of Journalists, Follow the Money, Forbidden Stories, the International Federation of Journalists, the International Press Institute, Investigate Europe and PEN International.

U.S. Navy finalizes Lockheed order for F-35 power and cooling upgrades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:47:21 UTC
16:47:21 KST

- The U.S. Navy added $13.3 million and 50,000 labor hours to a Lockheed Martin order for F135 Engine Core Upgrade integration and power and cooling work.
- The modification definitizes an earlier undefinitized order, moves the F-35’s power and thermal management upgrade into preliminary design, and runs through April 2027.
The U.S. Navy has added $13.3 million and 50,000 labor hours to a Lockheed Martin order covering integration of the F-35’s upgraded F135 engine core and the move of a new power and cooling system for the fighter into preliminary design.
Naval Air Systems Command announced the cost-plus-fixed-fee, level-of-effort modification on Oct. 27, definitizing an undefinitized contract action, which means the government and Lockheed have now agreed on final terms for work that began before the price was settled, and extending the effort to April 2027. No money was obligated at award, and the work, which supports the U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy, U.S. Marine Corps and the F-35 cooperative program partners, was not competed.
The modification sits on a delivery order NAVAIR first issued in fiscal 2025 as a not-to-exceed $107 million undefinitized order, which paid Lockheed to run trade studies and an alternatives assessment of every potential power and thermal management solution for the F-35, along with the integration work needed to fit Pratt & Whitney’s Engine Core Upgrade into Block 4 aircraft. That order was due to finish in December 2026, so the new action pushes completion back four months while shifting part of the effort from study to design as the power and thermal management upgrade enters its preliminary design phase.
Fort Worth, Texas, where Lockheed builds the F-35, accounts for 47% of the work, while Torrance and El Segundo, California, take 19% between them and two sites in Britain, Blackburn and Cheltenham, take 6% each, with the remainder spread across Haltom City, Texas; South Bend, Indiana; Windsor Locks and West Hartford, Connecticut; Rockford, Illinois; and Orlando, Florida.
The engine and cooling work both stem from the amount of heat the F-35’s electronics generate. The F-35 Joint Program Office has said Block 3 jets produce about 30 kilowatts of waste heat, a figure expected to reach 47 kilowatts in Block 4, while the current engine is optimized to absorb about 14 kilowatts. That heat is removed by the Power and Thermal Management System, or PTMS, a Honeywell unit that draws bleed air from the engine and also provides auxiliary and emergency power, engine starting and cabin environmental control, and because the PTMS takes more air from the F135 than its designers planned, the engine runs hotter and wears out faster, raising sustainment costs across the fleet.
Pratt & Whitney’s Engine Core Upgrade, or ECU, redesigns the F135’s core to produce more thrust, supply more bleed air and electrical power, and restore the engine life lost to heat, while the separate Power Thermal Management Upgrade, or PTMU, will replace or enlarge the cooling system that uses that air. In October 2024, the Joint Program Office named Lockheed the lead systems integrator for the PTMU after concluding that no other company could manage the integration, and the order modified this week is the contract vehicle for that role.
Honeywell, which builds the current PTMS, unveiled a near-term cooling option called P40 in September that would raise capacity from about 32 kilowatts to 40 kilowatts through software changes and liquid-cooling modifications, with no airframe changes and fielding planned for 2029 or 2030, and the company says the architecture could later grow to 62 kilowatts or more. Collins Aerospace, a sister company of Pratt & Whitney within RTX, is competing with a new design called the Enhanced Power and Cooling System, and the two companies have said that pairing it with the ECU would yield about a 7% gain in range and thrust along with double the cooling capacity, figures that come from the manufacturers. The modification does not say which approach Lockheed’s trade studies favored or whether preliminary design will cover one solution or several, and the government has not announced a PTMU selection.
The Pentagon chose in March 2023 to upgrade the F135 instead of re-engining the F-35 with an adaptive-cycle design from the Adaptive Engine Transition Program, citing cost and the difficulty of integrating a new engine into the short-takeoff F-35B and carrier-based F-35C. Pratt & Whitney then completed the ECU’s preliminary design review in July 2024 and later that year received a contract worth up to $1.3 billion for design maturation, rig testing and aircraft integration through March 2028.
In late August, the Navy added a modification worth up to $240.8 million to move the ECU into engineering and manufacturing development and buy long-lead hardware for a spare test engine, and Pratt & Whitney completed the upgrade’s risk reduction design review on Sept. 15. The company describes the ECU as a drop-in replacement core that can be installed on new engines or retrofitted at F135 depots, and John Sneden, the U.S. Air Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for propulsion, said in July that ground testing is planned for late 2027 and flight testing for around 2030, later than the 2029 fielding date Pratt had cited in 2024.
Lockheed’s share of the integration covers the aircraft side of the engine change, since a new core alters bleed-air flow, electrical power extraction, engine controls and heat loads, each of which affects the airframe’s fuel, cooling and mission systems. The engine and cooling upgrades also have to be timed together, because the extra cooling capacity Block 4 needs depends on both programs delivering.
The Government Accountability Office has warned of integration risks to the ECU timeline, and the Block 4 upgrade, which carries the new sensors and weapons responsible for much of the added heat, has slipped repeatedly. The fiscal 2027 budget request seeks $317.5 million for F-35 propulsion work, up from about $121 million in 2026, with much of the increase meant to accelerate the ECU and PTMU.
