Zimbabwe’s platinum boom: Where is the wealth?
The metal is generating billions, but mining communities say basic services have failed to keep pace.
Mimosa, Zimbabwe – Zimbabwe’s platinum industry is generating billions of dollars, but residents in mining communities say roads, schools, water and other basic services have failed to keep pace with the wealth extracted from beneath their land.
Platinum prices hit an all-time high of $2,923 an ounce on January 26 during a broader precious metals rally and continued concerns over the platinum supply, according to the World Platinum Investment Council.
For Zimbabwe, home to the world’s second largest known deposits of platinum group metals (PGMs) after South Africa, the price surge offers an opportunity to increase revenue from a sector central to the economy. Mining accounts for about 75 percent of the country’s exports and about 14.5 percent of its gross domestic product, according to the International Trade Administration in the United States.
The mining sector generated a record $8.5bn in export earnings in 2025, up from $5.9bn the previous year, according to John Musekiwa, then-president of the Chamber of Mines of Zimbabwe. He said the increase was driven by strong output and favourable prices, particularly for gold and PGMs.
But in communities surrounding some of the country’s biggest platinum operations, residents said the wealth extracted from beneath their land has not translated into adequate roads, schools, water supplies and other basic services.
In Mhondoro-Ngezi, one of Zimbabwe’s major platinum-producing areas, that tension is visible on the ground.
A rich mineral belt, struggling communities
The Great Dyke, a geological formation stretching across central Zimbabwe, contains extensive deposits of PGMs. Zimplats operates mines, concentrators and processing facilities in the Mhondoro-Ngezi district there.
Inside the mining complex, ore is processed in modern facilities, and heavy trucks move between mines and plants. Outside, residents of Turf, Mamina, Murambwa and nearby villages said infrastructure has struggled to keep pace with the area’s growth.
Ernest Denhere, headman of Denhere village in Ward 3, said mining companies should leave a lasting legacy in the communities where they operate.
“We call upon Zimplats and other mines to build a road from Kadoma/Kwekwe to Turf, Benhura, Mamina, Murambwa and Kadhani, linking to the Harare-Masvingo highways,” Denhere said.
Ward 3 Councillor Emmah Chikwai said some children travel long distances to reach secondary school.
“Children from Jompani, Majoki, Maleti and Makwavarara walk between 15km and 25km [9 to 15.5 miles] to reach Musinambi Secondary School,” she said. “My appeal is for the mines to assist in setting up a satellite secondary school in Makwavarara.”
Schools, water and livelihoods under pressure
During a September 7 visit, Al Jazeera saw pupils at Turf Primary School learning under trees as rising enrolment strained the school’s facilities.
Nearby, women and young men searched through piles of waste for plastic they could sell. Cattle and goats moved among the rubbish.
For Sakina Lice, collecting plastic is how she supports her family.
“I have 11 children and nine grandchildren. Picking up plastics is the only way I survive. When I resell them, I can make maybe $20 a month,” she said.
“I am the breadwinner. My husband is late, so it is just hand to mouth. My wish is for the mine to empower women, so we can start projects and support our families.”
Residents also raised concerns about the Ngwazani River, about 100 metres (330ft) from the dump site, alleging that sewage from the mining area has entered the waterway and affected its use for household needs and small gardens.
Edson Mabure, whose family was relocated as mining activities expanded, said the river has become a problem for residents in his new community.
“Our village was where the mine is today, so we were relocated. From our new village, I cross the Ngwazani River, which is now flooded with sewage coming from the mine,” he said.
“Since the mine started operating, there is nothing tangible that has been done to leave a lasting legacy for the community. I don’t know whether the responsibility lies with the council or Zimplats.”
Agnes Handidikundiona, whom Al Jazeera met crossing the river with her children, said residents once relied on it for household activities and gardens.
“We are facing a serious challenge because the water is no longer clean,” she said. “Before the sewage spill, we used to use this water for domestic purposes, such as washing clothes and watering our nutritional gardens.”
She said flooding also has prevented some children from reaching school.
“Children from many villages cross here to go to school. Sometimes when the river is flooded, they cannot go to school. We need a footbridge here,” she said.
Ward 11 Councillor Nhomboka Kurebwa Javangwe said the area’s population has increased as mine workers and their families have moved in.
He said Zimplats has built classrooms and houses but demand continues to outstrip available facilities. He called for the company to build and operate a primary school.
Javangwe also said local councillors have limited direct access to the company.
“We do not have direct access to the mine to raise the concerns of our people,” he said, adding that only the council chairperson was authorised to meet with Zimplats officials.
Mines point to community investment
The same concerns are being raised in other platinum-producing areas.
In Shurugwi, home to the Unki Platinum Mine, residents have called for more investment in local infrastructure.
“I call upon Unki to consider assisting with classroom blocks for schools, water and sanitation, and roads in Shurugwi town,” said Bulle Madzitire, chairman of the Shurugwi Residents Association.
In nearby Zvishavane, Kamino Simango, chairman of the Zvishavane Residents Association, said the Mimosa Platinum Mine should focus more on infrastructure benefitting the wider community.
Unki told Al Jazeera that it has invested an average of $1.5m a year in community development over the past five years, covering education, healthcare, water and sanitation, agriculture and infrastructure.
Its public relations manager, Evelyn Mawimba, said the mine has built 63 boreholes, supported 32 schools through its STEP-UP programme and contributed $2.75m towards land purchases and development of the Impali housing estate.
Unki also pays about $130,000 a year in municipal levies to the Shurugwi Town Council and contributes about $850,000 annually to the Tongogara Rural District Council, Mawimba said.
Mimosa did not respond to Al Jazeera’s questions despite several attempts to contact the company.
Al Jazeera also contacted the chairperson of the Mhondoro-Ngezi Rural District Council, Alderman Ephraim Pepukai Chengeta, about Zimplats’s contributions and development plans. He promised to respond but did not return calls or messages. The council’s chief executive officer, Itai A Mawonde, asked for the questions in writing.
Zimplats’s head of corporate affairs, Hama Saburi, also said he would respond but did not do so by publication.
For residents of Zimbabwe’s platinum belt, the demands are straightforward: better roads, schools, water and other services in communities living alongside some of the country’s most valuable mines.
“What is beneath our land speaks volumes,” Denhere said. “We need to see a lasting legacy for our communities.”

‘Nobody heard us’ – why Gen Z are leading protests across Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:06:07 UTC
16:06:07 KST

‘Nobody heard us’ – why Gen Zs are leading protests across Europe
BELGRADE/MILAN/BRUSSELS/TIRANA – Maya Gourdel, a 19-year-old student in Brussels, sits at a desk writing slogans against those running her country: “If we burn, you burn with us!”
The slogan, taken from the 2012 film The Hunger Games that has been adopted as a symbol by many youth movements globally, reflects the anger, frustration and desire for change driving Gen Z-led protests around Europe.
From the suburbs of Paris to the squares of Belgrade, thousands have taken to the streets.
The demands are various but often overlapping – frustrations with shabby schooling facilities, perceived lack of economic opportunity, cost of living, corruption, housing and a sense of not being listened to.
At times, those protests triggered violence – with thousands of shops in France alone being damaged or looted in recent weeks – and police firing stun grenades and water cannons.
In October, they also brought real change – student-led protests culminated in the toppling in an election of Serbia’s long-time leader Aleksandar Vucic after nearly two years of demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism.
“Waking up, the first thing we felt was certainly a sense of relief and freedom,” said student protester Stasa Piletic. “Personally, I feel a sense of victory. I feel that we finally moved from protests to responsibility.”
‘An explosion of rage’
Chiara, a 21-year-old student in protest-hit Milan, believes “it’s vital to take part in people’s spontaneous movements born from an explosion of rage that made collective action possible”.
“I think the worst damage this ruling class has done to my generation is stealing even the ability to imagine a future, to dream,” she said.
She said Italian students were confronting a reality of schools without enough teachers and crumbling buildings.
“And all of this with the prospect of an underpaid job which we didn’t qualify for and the prospect of living in a tiny, overpriced house, probably away from our city, which we didn’t want to live in.”
Protests led by Gen Zs have caused ructions globally as the generation born roughly between 1997 and 2012 found its voice, from Bangladesh in 2024 and Nepal in 2025, to India in 2026. Now Europe has become a focal point.
Rising prices and the cost of living are a concern for 40% of 16-30-year-olds, according to a European Union survey published in 2025.
Among the 92.7 million people in the EU who faced the risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2025, the highest risk was recorded for young adults aged 18-24 years, at 26.3%, while the lowest was recorded for adults aged 65 years or over, at 18.8%.
Younger people are also wary of shouldering the financial burden of an older generation that tends to vote in greater numbers. People over 60 in France make up a quarter of the population but own 60% of France’s wealth, according to the OFCE think tank.
French pensions are by far the biggest public expense, on track to reach 14% of economic output, as the population ages and voters resist raising the retirement age or reducing benefits.
That is still less than Greece or Italy, which spend the largest proportion of national income on public pensions among OECD countries, at around 16% of GDP, according to OECD figures in 2025.
But it is much more than Australia, Chile, Iceland, Ireland or South Korea, which spent less than 4% of GDP on public pensions, according to the OECD.
‘Young people in Europe are united’
Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris, has been protesting against “deplorable” conditions and staff shortages at his school.
“There used to be rats,” he said. Students were evacuated in 2025 when a roof collapsed on the courtyard, though no one was hurt, he said.
Protests showed “that young people in Europe are united”, he said, adding, “we all agree on one point: That young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren’t listened to enough.”
A French government report in October said pension spending had risen by 2.5 percentage points of GDP between 2000 and 2023 while that for education had declined 0.5.
It also showed 32% of the education ministry’s budget went towards pensions, crowding out money for other areas.
Gourdel, too, has been protesting for better conditions in schools in Belgium.
“We tried to do it passively. Nobody heard us. It’s only when people started to burn trash or that kind of stuff that the media and cameras started showing us,” she said.
The protests are still spreading, with a demonstration planned in Germany over cost of living, inequality, war and the state of schools.
Unrest has also hit Albania, where student-led demonstrations against Prime Minister Edi Rama’s government, fuelled by anger over perceived corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, engulfed Tirana and spread to other cities.
“Our Prime Minister spent 130 days not listening to us,” said Xyke Kurti, a 19-year-old architecture student.
“If you ask a student in Albania, ‘where do you see your future?’ Everyone says ‘outside this country’,” she said, arguing that at home, even if you have talent, someone with “connections is always going to beat you”.
Serbia’s student movement did what demonstrators in other European capitals can only dream of.
Now, though, comes the gritty business of governing – something neither the students nor their candidates have any experience of.
Luka Stojakovic, another protester, brushes that aside. “We have seen where people with political experience have brought us.” REUTERS

“The father was treated really badly. I thought, but I wasn’t involved,” Trump added. “That’s Brazil. It’s a different country.”

“You know, it’s pretty close, which was very well,” Trump added. “Because I think when the endorsement went out, it helped him a lot, but I actually heard he did pretty well. It might be winning or tie.”

Japan eyes $6B in private investment in Bangladesh as premiers hold talks in Tokyo

SM Najmus Sakib
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Japan is eyeing private investment of up to 1 trillion yen (approximately $6 billion) in Bangladesh over the next five years as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi hosted her Bangladeshi counterpart, Tarique Rahman, in Tokyo on Tuesday.
Rahman is on his first visit to Japan since being elected in February.
In a joint statement, Takaichi and Rahman welcomed Bangladesh’s efforts to promote foreign direct investment, citing “a projection of upcoming private investment from Japan to Bangladesh up to one trillion yen with two hundred thousand jobs to be created in Bangladesh by the investment from Japan in the next five years.”
The two leaders also agreed to expand cooperation in energy security and supply chains, according to the statement.
Earlier, the two prime ministers addressed a joint news conference.
“Japan will strongly support Bangladesh’s autonomy and resilience,” Takaichi told Rahman, according to Kyodo News. She added that Japan “looks forward to contributing to regional peace and prosperity.”
“The partnership between Bangladesh and Japan has been built on decades of friendship, trust, and mutual respect. Today, we have an opportunity to take this relationship to new heights. I warmly invite Japanese investors, businesses, and financial institutions to explore the opportunities Bangladesh has to offer and be part of our next phase of growth,” Rahman said.
Bangladesh is seeking investment and low-interest loans from Japan as it faces economic hardship, particularly following conflicts in the Middle East.
The two sides reaffirmed their commitment to “further enhance bilateral security cooperation” amid an “increasingly uncertain geopolitical environment,” the statement said.
They also welcomed the signing and entry into force of an agreement concerning the transfer of defense equipment and technology.
 
Safe repatriation of Rohingya
On the Rohingya issue, the joint statement said Takaichi and Rahman remain “concerned by the worsening crisis in Myanmar and its impact on regional security, displacement of all people, including the Rohingya, and the increase in transnational crimes.”
They shared the view that the “ultimate solution to the Rohingya crisis is to realize a voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable return of the displaced persons, including the Rohingya to Myanmar,” it added.
Takaichi and Rahman reiterated their commitment to promoting sustainable peace, security and stability in the Middle East.
They emphasized the need for early de-escalation, as well as the “urgent and full re-opening of the Strait of Hormuz and the safe, secure and unimpeded transit of all vessels… without any additional costs,” the statement said.
They also recognized the strategic importance of maintaining peace and stability in the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait for global energy security and the uninterrupted flow of goods.
Japan is Bangladesh’s largest bilateral development partner and a major export destination, with trade between the countries totaling around $4 billion.
The two countries upgraded ties to a strategic partnership in 2023. In their joint statement, the prime ministers highlighted the development of economic cooperation under the partnership in infrastructure, energy, human resource development, trade and investment.
Earlier this month, the two countries signed an agreement to begin recruiting Bangladeshi workers starting next April, offering new opportunities for Bangladeshi workers in Japan with legal protections.

edible sculptures and snap-button metal armatures activate philip johnson’s wolfhouse in NY

edible sculptures and snap-button metal armatures activate philip johnson’s wolfhouse in NY
the project brings together moving image, edible sculpture, and site-specific interventions, exploring the relationships between memory, landscape, architecture, and the experience of place.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
NO.29 STUDIO STAGES SITE-SPECIFIC EDIBLE SCULPTURES AT Wolfhouse
Presented on October 10th, 2026, at Wolfhouse, a 1949 modernist residence designed by Philip Johnson in Newburgh, New York, Island on Land – A Landscape in Five States is a site-specific exhibition by artists Lang Lang (founder of studio No.29) and Xie Peng. Developed as a spatial translation of Lang’s 2024 experimental short film of the same name, the project merged moving images, ephemeral edible sculptures, and modular metal and acrylic structures across the home’s interior rooms, exterior terrace, and grounds.
ALUMINUM ARMATURES AND ACRYLIC STANDS MAP FIVE FILM CHAPTERS
The installation by No.29 studio mapped five thematic fragments from the film into physical works that juxtaposed durable industrial hardware with biodegradable, consumable media. Indoors, Black Pearls, textured chocolate spheres filled with grape jelly and jasmine cream, sat within spiral spherical recesses on The Panel, a mirrored stainless steel tray reflecting the room as pieces were removed. A Drop Within, a translucent sphere with a deep-red core, was supported by The Stands, an assembly of circular acrylic panels and curved metal joints fastened with fashion-derived snap buttons instead of threaded hardware.
TRANSIENT EDIBLE MEDIA CONTRASTS MODERNIST ARCHITECTURAL SPACE
On the exterior patio framing views of the Hudson River, Red Soil combined buckwheat, fig, and chocolate terrain atop The Table, a two-panel aluminum surface joined with snap fasteners and red steel stabilization rods. White Trace incorporated rice-paper vessels holding watermelon and perilla syrups, set into circular acrylic cutouts on a folding, reconfigurable aluminum screen termed The Partition. Dispersed across the landscape, A Quiet Turn positioned biodegradable door handles directly on the turf. The non-linear sequence allowed attendees to navigate the estate freely, consuming the perishable elements while the fabricated armatures remained.

name: Island on Land – A Landscape in Five States
designer: Studio No.29 | @__no29__
lead designer: Lang Lang and Xie Peng

Bangladesh prime minister hails meeting with Japanese counterpart as step toward stronger ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:56:06 UTC
15:56:06 KST

SM Najmus Sakib
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Wednesday called a meeting with his Japanese counterpart an important step forward in strengthening the strategic partnership between the two nations.
Rahman is currently on a four-day visit to Japan.
"Today, I had a highly productive summit meeting with Prime Minister @takaichi_sanae, where we reaffirmed our shared commitment to democracy, the rule of law, economic development, and a peaceful, stable and prosperous Indo-Pacific," he said on US social media platform X.
"A significant outcome of our summit was our shared commitment to advance the Bay of Bengal Industrial Growth Belt (BIG-B) initiative into a new framework for shared prosperity," he added.
The BIG-B initiative will focus on developing energy, deep-sea ports, industrial infrastructure, technology, and regional connectivity, strengthening Bangladesh’s position as a bridge between South and Southeast Asia.
He also proposed establishing a Bangladesh-Japan Tech Park to advance cooperation in artificial intelligence and advanced technologies.
He also discussed cooperation in space science and satellite engineering as well as Japanese technical and financial support for high-speed rail connectivity.
Rahman also thanked Japan for continued humanitarian assistance to the Rohingya population and called for its sustained engagement in securing their voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable return to Myanmar.
Bangladesh is hosting about 1.2 million Rohingya on its southeastern coast, with most of them fleeing Myanmar military crackdown in August 2017.
Japan is Bangladesh’s largest bilateral development partner and a major export destination, with trade between the countries totaling around $4 billion.
Rahman was sworn in as Bangladesh’s prime minister in February, following his party's victory in the country’s first general election since the 2024 student-led uprising that toppled former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina.

Putin Spends 90 Minutes Discussing History With Finnish and Norwegian Leaders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:55:16 UTC
15:55:16 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin spent most of a 90-minute phone call with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre discussing medieval Slavic history and Moscow’s stated reasons for its war against Ukraine, rather than an immediate ceasefire, the Financial Times reported, citing three sources familiar with the conversation.
Stubb told Finnish media that the call on October 27, which had initially been expected to last less than 30 minutes, continued for an hour and a half.
According to the Financial Times, Putin delivered a lengthy monologue about what the Kremlin describes as the “initial reasons for the conflict,” while the prospect of an immediate ceasefire, which Ukraine has demanded as a starting point for peace negotiations, received little attention.
One source told the newspaper that Stubb and Støre chose not to interrupt Putin during his historical digressions so they could assess how seriously he was approaching dialogue with Europe.
The conversation was the first between Putin and a leader from among Ukraine’s European allies since July 2025, when he spoke with French President Emmanuel Macron.
The October 27 call came as diplomatic efforts to end Russia’s war against Ukraine continued, with trilateral talks involving Ukraine, Russia and the United States expected to take place in Abu Dhabi in November.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the Finnish and Norwegian leaders had discussed measures to de-escalate the war with Putin, particularly those involving Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Stubb described the conversation as “frank and substantive.”
The Kremlin’s account said Putin had reminded the Nordic leaders of what Moscow calls the “root causes” of the war.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen expressed skepticism about the call’s potential outcome, saying it had reportedly not been coordinated with other European countries. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, however, confirmed that the conversation had been coordinated with Kyiv.
The two Nordic leaders later briefed Zelensky on their discussion. The Ukrainian president said: “I am grateful for the detailed briefing and for their active support for our diplomacy and the peace efforts we are pursuing together with all our partners.”
Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen said Finland would not seek to mediate in the war because it supports Ukraine. Speaking at a press conference in Helsinki alongside her Ukrainian and Norwegian counterparts, she said Finland was not looking to improve relations with Russia but wanted to advance efforts to secure peace.
“Finland is not seeking a role to mediate in this war because we are and will remain on the side of Ukraine,” Valtonen said.
She also accused Russia of continuing to escalate the conflict and stressed Finland’s support for both Ukraine and the US-led peace process.
“Unfortunately, Russia has not ended its war, but they keep escalating. So what we are doing, we are supporting not only Ukraine but also the US-led peace process to finding an end to this killing, not only the senseless killing of soldiers at the battlefield, but specifically also the civilians who suffer in their homes, in the Ukrainian cities and elsewhere,” she said.
Putin has previously invoked Russian and Ukrainian history to justify Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, including during a 2024 interview with US host Tucker Carlson.
He reportedly delivered a similar historical lecture to US President Donald Trump during their August 2025 summit in Alaska. The speech included references to medieval Rus princes, including Rurik and Yaroslav the Wise, as well as 17th-century Cossack leader Bohdan Khmelnytskyi. Western historians have repeatedly challenged Putin’s selective historical narratives and distortions, which they say are used to justify Moscow’s actions.
The latest phone call followed an October 20 meeting in Oslo involving Ukrainian, European and US officials. Stubb and Støre stressed that they had not spoken on behalf of Europe as a whole.
The call prompted mixed reactions among European leaders. A European Commission spokesperson told the Kyiv Independent that the EU remained committed to ending the war and securing a lasting peace.
“On the EU side, we are adamantly committed not just to putting an end to the war but to achieve peace that will be just and sustainable. That is our aim and that is the stance we are defending in the ongoing talks,” the spokesperson said.
A senior EU official told the Kyiv Independent that another round of talks was expected to take place in Europe before the planned Abu Dhabi meeting, following mixed messages from Kyiv that had suggested peace negotiations would be held in Brussels during the week.

Unknown

Russia-Africa Summit: Putin hosts leaders from across the continent (As it happened)
Moscow is hosting the third Russia-Africa Summit on Wednesday and Thursday, bringing together leaders and government delegations from 48 African countries for talks on political and economic cooperation.
The agenda covers trade, energy, agriculture, mining, education, healthcare, and artificial intelligence, as well as business cooperation through BRICS.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and African Union chair Evariste Ndayishimiye addressed the summit’s plenary session, while talks between Russian and African officials have covered investment, infrastructure, and economic ties. A series of agreements have also been signed with major African regional organizations.
The gathering follows previous summits in Sochi in 2019 and St. Petersburg in 2023, which helped lay the groundwork for closer relations between Russia and the continent.
The event comes as African governments push for greater influence in international affairs and more diverse economic partnerships against a backdrop of geopolitical tensions. Russia’s expanding ties with the continent have drawn Western criticism, while Moscow has accused Western governments of pressuring African states to stay away from the summit.

Malaysia will still lose tens of billions of ringgit to the 1MDB scandal even after further overseas asset recoveries, its second finance minister said on Wednesday, as disgraced former prime minister Najib Razak prepares to move to house arrest.
Najib has been imprisoned since 2022 following his conviction for corruption and money laundering tied to SRC International, a former subsidiary of 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB). Australian inflation spikes to 4.3 pct
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:49:16 CST
15:49:16 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Australia's annual rate of inflation spiked to a six-month high of 4.3 percent in September, according to official data released on Wednesday.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) said that the consumer price index rose by 4.3 percent in the 12 months to September, up from 4.0 percent in August and the highest figure since March.
It said that the annual trimmed mean, a measure of underlying inflation preferred by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), rose from 3.5 percent in August to 3.6 percent in September.
Economists from the Commonwealth Bank of Australia, the nation's largest bank, had forecast that headline inflation would rise to 4.2 percent in September.
Rachael McCririck, head of prices statistics at the ABS, said that a 5.2 percent rise in housing prices year-on-year was the biggest contributor to annual inflation in September, followed by transport prices, which rose by 8.7 percent due to higher fuel prices.
"On a monthly basis, Automotive fuel prices rose 9.4 percent in September, compared to a rise of 14.8 percent in August. This was driven by higher world oil prices," McCririck said.
The data was released ahead of the RBA Monetary Policy Board's next meeting to consider interest rates at the start of November.
At its previous meeting late in September, the board voted unanimously to raise the cash rate target by 0.25 percentage points for the fourth time in 2026 to a 15-year high of 4.6 percent, citing the inflationary impacts of the conflict in the Middle East.
The Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported that the chances of another rate hike in November rose from 60 percent to 79 percent following the release of the latest inflation data. ■

Interview: China's economy shows resilience, vitality, says Kyrgyz economist
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:49:15 CST
15:49:15 KST

BISHKEK, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- China's economy is demonstrating resilience and vitality through positive development trends despite various challenges, Kyrgyz economist Iskender Sharsheev told Xinhua.
In the first three quarters of 2026, China's gross domestic product (GDP) grew 4.6 percent year on year, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics. In the third quarter, China's GDP expanded 4.5 percent year on year, up from 4.3 percent in the previous quarter.
"Stable economic growth points to the country's new achievements in high-quality development," Sharsheev said, adding that the growth is driven by favorable trends in high-tech manufacturing, services and exports.
He also highlighted the strong performance of China's foreign trade in the first three quarters of 2026. The country's total imports and exports rose by 18.8 percent year on year, according the National Bureau of Statistics. During the same period, trade with countries participating in the China-proposed Belt and Road Initiative surged 17.1 percent.
"These results in China's foreign trade are driven by strong demand for its products from advanced sectors, including integrated circuits, electric vehicles and lithium batteries, as well as by market diversification, resilient industrial and supply chains, and the determined implementation of a policy of high-quality opening-up," the economist said.
For Kyrgyzstan, a country along the Belt and Road, China's expanding foreign trade presents significant opportunities to increase exports of agricultural products and mineral resources, as well as transit services, Sharsheev said.
It also helps attract Chinese investment in infrastructure, logistics and processing industries, while strengthening Kyrgyzstan's role as a regional transport hub, he added.
Effectively leveraging these opportunities could help Kyrgyzstan create jobs, boost foreign exchange earnings and speed up its economic modernization, he said.
"Foreign trade continues to provide strong support for the industrial sector. The Chinese government has expressed confidence in achieving these goals and retains considerable policy space to introduce targeted stimulus measures. Together, these factors provide a solid foundation for China to meet its year-end economic targets," Sharsheev added. ■

S. Korea's August births hit 7-year high amid shifting mindset toward childbirth
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:49:14 CST
15:49:14 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's births hit the highest for the month of August in seven years amid shifting social mindset toward childbirth, statistical ministry data showed Wednesday.
The number of newborn babies rose 13.0 percent from a year earlier to 23,703 in August, marking the largest number of births for any August since 2019, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics.
The newborns continued to rise in double digits since January, keeping an upward trajectory for 26 straight months since July 2024.
For the first eight months of 2026, a total of 193,783 babies were born, up 14.5 percent from a year earlier.
The total fertility rate, or the number of children a woman is expected to bear during life, added 0.09 over the year to 0.87 in August.
The positive trend was fueled by shifting cultural mindsets toward childbirth, a growing population in their 30s, and a recent increase in marriages. ■

WASHINGTON, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- The United States has told several Gulf countries to prepare for a brief but intense military campaign against Iran after the U.S. midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday, citing people briefed on the conversations.

Israel has also drawn up plans and identified targets for a possible new attack, the Journal reported.
U.S. President Donald Trump has not made a final decision but is leaning toward a major attack targeting Iranian infrastructure and nuclear sites, the report said.
Trump could also seek a deal with Iran. Last week, he said the United States might launch another "little Epic Fury," referring to the U.S. and Israeli bombing campaign in the spring, or Iran could agree to a deal.
The president has said he won't attack Iran before the midterms. ■

‘BJP wins through foul means’: Akhilesh alleges MLC poll fraud, warns of 2027 defeat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:44:43 UTC
15:44:43 KST

Akhilesh alleges conspiracy to defeat SP candidate in UP MLC polls, targets BJP
NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party supremo Akhilesh Yadav on Wednesday accused the Bharatiya Janata Party of electoral malpractice in the Uttar Pradesh Legislative Council (MLC) elections, alleging that irregularities during counting were part of a conspiracy to defeat SP candidate Sanjayan Tripathi.In a post on X, Akhilesh alleged that BJP leaders, their associates and officials had colluded to manipulate the counting process. He claimed that the alleged treatment of Tripathi had angered teachers and members of his community, and vowed that the SP would fight "injustice and harassment."
"The corrupt BJP leaders, their conspiratorial associates and complicit officials have stooped to every possible low to win the MLC elections. The conspiracy to defeat Dr Sanjayan Tripathi has been exposed before everyone. The reason for defeating Dr Sanjayan Tripathi through vote-counting irregularities is not merely that he is an SP candidate; the main reason behind it is “Haata nahi bhaata” (he is not acceptable to them). In matters of politics, the BJP has sunk to the lowest depths. After such massive fraud, the public has realised that the BJP has, in fact, lost every seat," he wrote.
"BJP leaders win not through votes, but through foul means," former UP CM added.Targeting the BJP over its alleged treatment of teachers, the SP chief said the incident had left a deep impression on Tripathi's community and teachers across the state.“The way Sanjayan Tripathi has been harassed is being witnessed by his entire community. Neither his community nor any teacher in the state will forget Dr. Tripathi's tears,” the SP chief said, alleging that teachers had received nothing but humiliation from the BJP government.Akhilesh also linked the controversy to the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections, claiming that teachers would remember the alleged mistreatment when they vote.“Every teacher will always remember the despicable conspiracy to make teachers do the unwanted task of collecting fodder, and will fulfil their “guru resolve” by defeating the BJP in the 2027 assembly elections,” he wrote.Taking another swipe at the ruling party, Akhilesh said its alleged electoral tactics would not succeed across the state."The BJP's “400 BC” (a pun on char sau beesi, meaning fraud or deceit) will not work across all 403 seats," he further said.Reiterating his support for Tripathi, the SP chief added, "We stand with Sanjayan Tripathi and against every injustice and act of harassment inflicted upon him and his community. We stand united against the BJP and will continue to do so."
SP candidates allege irregularities in MLC counting
The remarks came amid allegations of irregularities during the counting of votes for the Gorakhpur-Faizabad Division Teachers' constituency. SP candidate Sanjayan Tripathi and independent candidate Rajeev Yadav boycotted the counting process, accusing administrative officials and the election observer of favouring the BJP candidate.Speaking to news agency ANI, Tripathi alleged that the counting trend changed abruptly after the first three rounds, when independent candidate Rajeev Yadav was leading by around 450 votes.“We have boycotted the vote-counting process. Everything was proceeding smoothly for the first three rounds of counting; independent candidate Rajiv Yadav was leading by approximately 450 votes. Suddenly, the counting began to shift entirely in favour of the BJP candidate; the trend changed abruptly, making it appear as though the outcome had been predetermined. Consequently, we decided to boycott the process,” Tripathi said.He also alleged police misconduct and claimed that the authorities were determined to ensure the ruling party's candidate won.A day earlier, Akhilesh had urged Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to take immediate cognisance of the alleged irregularities and ensure transparency in the counting process. He had accused officials of delaying the announcement of round-wise results and warned that the SP would launch a movement and file a case against the Election Commission if any foul play was detected.Similar allegations were raised by SP candidate Danish Akhtar over the results in the Bareilly-Moradabad Teachers' constituency. Akhtar alleged irregularities in the electoral rolls and voting process, claiming that 30 per cent of the names on the electoral roll were fraudulent. He also accused the Election Commission of failing to act despite receiving evidence and repeated representations.
SP claims lead in Lucknow constituency
Meanwhile, in Lucknow, Ram Singh Rana, an SP agent for party candidate Kanti Singh, claimed on Wednesday that the party was maintaining its lead during counting. He alleged that BJP candidate Avnish Singh had repeatedly attempted to disrupt the process.“We have been steadily increasing our lead since yesterday, and it continues to grow. The opposition candidate from the BJP made several attempts to misuse power, but the Samajwadi youth did not bow down; they stood firm and remained unafraid--even when there were lathi-charges during the night, and chairs were smashed,” Rana said.
Rana alleged that the opposition had tried to halt the counting process four or five times and that SP workers had faced harassment throughout the night."The opposition tried to halt the process four or five times, but no one gave in or felt intimidated. We have maintained our momentum and are moving toward victory. We faced harassment all night long. EXPLAINER – What to expect from Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:44:41 UTC
15:44:41 KST

Elena Teslova
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
- Twenty-two countries will be represented by heads of state, according to the Kremlin
- Participants are expected to adopt a 2027-2029 action plan and a declaration on cooperation on the use of artificial intelligence
From grain supplies and nuclear energy to education, technology and new trade routes, Russia and African countries are seeking to expand cooperation as leaders gather in Moscow for the third Russia-Africa Summit starting Wednesday.
Delegations from 48 of Africa’s 54 countries have confirmed participation in the two-day summit, with 22 represented by heads of state, according to Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, the current African Union chair, will co-chair the gathering.
The program includes summit sessions, bilateral meetings and talks with leaders of African regional organizations, alongside the Russia-Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum.
Among the leaders that Putin is scheduled to meet are Egypt’s Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and Ethiopia’s Abiy Ahmed.
 
What is on the agenda?
Trade and investment are expected to be among the central issues, alongside energy, agriculture, infrastructure, food security, science, technology, education and humanitarian cooperation.
Trade between Russia and African countries exceeded $27 billion in 2025, according to Ushakov. That compares with around $16.8 billion in 2019, when the first Russia-Africa Summit was held in Sochi.
Transport and logistics are also on the agenda, with both sides discussing ways to expand trade routes, improve connections and increase the range of goods exchanged.
Participants are expected to adopt a final declaration and a Russia-Africa Partnership Forum action plan covering 2027-2029.
A separate declaration on cooperation in the civilian use of artificial intelligence is also planned, along with intergovernmental and interagency agreements in several sectors.
 
Energy and food security
Energy remains one of the most developed areas of Russian-African cooperation.
One of the largest projects is Egypt’s El Dabaa nuclear power plant, being constructed by Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom.
The summit forum also includes discussions on nuclear energy, conventional power generation, renewable energy, mining and development of energy infrastructure.
Several African states are seeking additional electricity-generation capacity as demand grows with population increases and industrial development.
Similarly, agriculture has become another major part of the relationship.
Russia is an important supplier of wheat and fertilizers to several African countries.
After the 2023 summit in St. Petersburg, Moscow delivered 200,000 metric tons of grain free of charge to Burkina Faso, Zimbabwe, Mali, Somalia, the Central African Republic and Eritrea, fulfilling a commitment announced by Putin.
This year’s talks are expected to cover grain and fertilizer supplies as well as agricultural technology, food processing and logistics.
 
What has changed since Sochi?
The first Russia-Africa Summit took place in Sochi in October 2019.
The second was held in St. Petersburg in July 2023, when participating countries adopted a declaration setting priorities for political, economic, security and humanitarian cooperation.
Leaders also agreed to hold the summit every three years. Between summits, Russia and African countries have developed a ministerial-level format.
The first ministerial conference was held in Sochi in 2024, followed by a second meeting in Cairo in December 2025, where preparations for the Moscow summit were discussed.
The Moscow gathering will now review implementation of those earlier agreements while setting priorities through 2029.

Prime Minister Mark Carney (R), and Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, U.A.E. talk during a signing ceremony on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. (The Canadian Press via AP)
Canada signed a trade pact with the United Arab Emirates on Oct. 27 to expand access for its exporters as Ottawa seeks to diversify trade beyond the United States.
Once fully implemented, the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) will reduce or eliminate tariffs on more than 99 percent of current Canadian exports to the UAE, the Canadian prime minister’s office said.
It is expected to enter into force in 2027.
The deal will improve access for Canadian pulses and canola, industrial machinery, power generation equipment and aerospace products.
It also aims to reduce non-tariff barriers and expand access for goods and services in sectors including forestry, seafood and engineering.
Prime Minister Mark Carney has pledged to double exports to markets outside the United States over the next decade.
U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs and the breakdown of trade talks with Washington have prompted Ottawa to pursue agreements across Asia, Europe and the Middle East.
Canadian International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu and UAE Foreign Trade Minister Thani Al Zeyoudi signed the pact in Ottawa at a ceremony attended by Carney and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
“We see considerable potential for our private sector,” Al Zeyoudi said, citing export opportunities and investment in logistics, communications, advanced technology and manufacturing.
The UAE is Canada’s largest export market in the Middle East.
Two-way merchandise trade totaled C$3.5 billion ($2.48 billion) in 2025, according to Canadian government figures.
The two countries also signed preliminary agreements on energy, diplomatic and defense cooperation. 
The UAE last year pledged up to $50 billion in investment in Canada.

Eurozone banks tighten lending as demand weakens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:40:30 UTC
15:40:30 KST

Eurozone banks tightened standards for company loans and consumer credit in the third quarter as higher interest rates weakened borrowing demand, a European Central Bank survey showed on Oct. 27.
On a weighted basis, the share of banks tightening criteria for company loans exceeded the share easing them by 9 percentage points, up from 7 points in the previous quarter.
The corresponding figure for consumer credit was 14 points.
Banks cited higher perceived risks and reduced risk tolerance, with some pointing to geopolitical uncertainty and energy market developments.
Mortgage approval criteria were broadly unchanged, but the survey’s housing loan demand indicator fell to its lowest level since the third quarter of 2023. Higher rates, weaker consumer confidence and a poorer housing outlook weighed on demand.
Banks expect further tightening across all loan categories in the final quarter, alongside weaker demand for mortgages and consumer credit. Demand from companies is expected to remain broadly unchanged.
The survey covered 159 banks and was conducted between Sept. 21 and Oct. 6.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Central Bank Governor Yang Chin-long (楊金龍) said Wednesday that domestic banks have enough money to meet rising loan demand despite growing pressure on their funds.
Speaking at a legislative hearing, Yang dismissed concerns about a nationwide funding shortage. He said strong demand from businesses and investors had made loans harder to obtain for some borrowers, but the banking system remained stable, CNA reported.
Taiwanese banks had an average liquidity coverage ratio of 120.57% at the end of August, above the required 100% but down from 128.79% a year earlier. The ratio measures whether banks hold enough readily available assets to cover expected cash outflows over 30 days, per Economic Daily News.
The artificial intelligence boom has driven factory expansion and increased demand for business loans. Strong stock market activity has also encouraged more borrowing, putting additional pressure on banks, per CTEE.
Yang said changes in banks' deposits had contributed to the decline in liquidity ratios. Large companies can withdraw substantial deposits at short notice, making them less dependable than deposits spread across smaller customers, per Liberty Times.
Banks have responded by seeking more stable deposits, issuing bonds, and adjusting their lending practices. However, they must also keep enough liquid assets to meet regulatory requirements rather than lend out all their available funds.
Taiwan's problem, Yang said, was not a lack of money but how banks distribute their funds. Loans increasingly favor stronger industries, particularly technology companies, while smaller businesses and traditional manufacturers may find borrowing more difficult.

====================================================================================================

The next phase of military rule in Egypt is here
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:36:59 UTC
15:36:59 KST

The next phase of military rule in Egypt is here
El-Sisi’s announcement that he will not run for a fourth term may signal a new leadership arrangement.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi surprised observers when he recently announced his intention to leave office after his third presidential term ends in April 2030.
El-Sisi had been widely suspected of moving to amend the Egyptian constitution to allow him to serve another term, or possibly indefinitely.
But speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy, el-Sisi insisted that his departure was a settled matter and that “no one would tamper with” the constitution.
So what is behind the decision? There has been much speculation that el-Sisi may use this declaration to rally popular support for a fourth term or preempt a move by the military against him. But there is also the possibility that he is setting up the next phase of military rule in Egypt.
It is important to point out first that voluntarily leaving power is a risky proposition for any authoritarian leader.
In el-Sisi’s case, his 2030 departure would leave open the possibility that a future Egyptian government could seek to use him as a scapegoat for the country’s problems, possibly even holding him to account for alleged crimes committed during his presidency.
El-Sisi led a coup in 2013 against Egypt’s first democratically elected president, Mohamed Morsi, which was accompanied by massacres and the jailing of tens of thousands of politicians, activists, and journalists.
El-Sisi’s economic record has also been the subject of criticism, with detractors accusing him and his government of corruption, poor fiscal policy and lavish spending on vanity projects. Egypt’s debt stands at 81 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), with interest payments alone exceeding combined spending on healthcare, education, wages and subsidies. Meanwhile, the Egyptian pound has lost more than 80 percent of its value against the US dollar since 2014, while cumulative inflation exceeds 460 percent.
In this context, el-Sisi’s announcement that he plans to step down in 2030 was rather unexpected. Some have speculated that he has no intention of actually leaving office and could go back on his statement, as he has done before.
In 2013, following Morsi’s overthrow, el-Sisi denied that he would run for president.
After telling the media in 2017 that he was committed to “preserving [the constitution’s] two four-year terms and not changing it”, he helped lead the drive to amend the constitution in 2019.
A judicial source told Mada Masr last week that el-Sisi’s announcement left open the door for a “popular call” for the president to remain in office.
A second possibility is that with this move, el-Sisi may be attempting to preempt a possible military intervention, which could become more likely if the economy continues to falter.
In 2011, the military responded to popular protests against former President Hosni Mubarak by forcing him to step down.
The army could attempt to defuse public anger by presenting el-Sisi as a scapegoat, forcibly removing him from power, and replacing him with someone who can preserve a measure of stability as well as secure its vast economic interests.
In that context, a member of parliament said recently that he has heard el-Sisi say in private meetings that he would rather step down than wait for the military to force him out.
But a third and much more likely possibility deserves particular attention: el-Sisi may be preparing to leave the presidency while ensuring that Egypt’s military-dominated political system survives his departure.
It is perhaps not coincidental that during the announcement, he cited Article 200 of the constitution, which gives the armed forces an extraordinary role in Egyptian politics.
The article, amended in 2019, makes the military responsible for maintaining the country’s “democracy” and the “gains, rights and freedoms” of the Egyptian people.
According to el-Sisi, the aim of the article is “to protect the Egyptian state from any attempt to infiltrate it or allow people to take it over who cannot handle the responsibility of this country or who do not even understand the meaning of ‘state’”.
Article 200, combined with Article 234 — which requires that a president secure approval from the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces before appointing a defence minister — gives the military significant control over Egyptian political life.
El-Sisi’s vision for the selection of Egypt’s next president gives the military an outsized role. His proposal includes setting up a committee of experts to draft legislation for selecting hundreds of highly educated Egyptians to undergo specialised training at the Egyptian Military Academy.
Applicants, el-Sisi proposes, should hold doctoral degrees, be between 40 and 50 years of age, and be prepared to spend 30 months at the academy learning about the Egyptian state.
The programme would also train future ministers, governors and members of parliament.
Combined with Articles 200 and 234, this proposed mechanism seems intended to preserve the military’s dominance long after el-Sisi leaves office. It could be favourable to him as well.
A genuinely independent, civilian president could seek to investigate massacres overseen by el-Sisi, allegations of corruption, or other alleged crimes. A transition process closely managed by the military is highly unlikely to yield such a result.
The open question now is how an increasingly frustrated and critical Egyptian public will respond to a political process managed by the military that effectively wipes out the need for a popular mandate.
For now, el-Sisi and the military appear determined to shape Egypt’s political future. But the people may have the last word.

Experts defer to AI in decision-making, Anthropic study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:33:19 UTC
15:33:19 KST

Experts defer to AI in decision-making, Anthropic study finds
Professional analysts chose options that matched AI assistant’s preference 86 percent of the time, research finds.
Experts using AI overwhelmingly defer to the technology when making decisions, research by Claude creator Anthropic suggests.
In a research paper published on Tuesday, Anthropic said it asked 50 professional analysts to advise a fictional farming cooperative to determine whether experts make decisions themselves when using AI.
Anthropic said the analysts were tasked with assessing whether a fictitious advisory program for the co-op’s members was working effectively and should be expanded.
Participants were asked to make four choices between two defensible options before making a final policy recommendation.
Unbeknownst to the analysts, Anthropic directed each participant’s AI assistant to lean towards a particular decision to measure whether the analyst’s decision-making was being influenced.
Analysts chose options that matched the AI assistant’s preference 86 percent of the time, compared with a 50/50 outcome that would be expected if they were not influenced, according to the study.
Participants that had a preference before consulting their AI assistant changed their decision 60 percent of the time in cases where the agent disagreed.
While 77 percent of analysts used their AI assistant’s arguments when asked to explain their decision, only 15 percent credited AI as the source of their thinking, according to Anthropic.
Anthropic said the study had some limitations, including that it involved just one task and used AI assistants that had been deliberately set to have a preference.
Anthropic researchers Amaç Herdagdelen, Hailey Joren, and Alex Tamkin said humans’ tendency to defer to AI may be “hard to identify, even for the experts themselves”.
The researchers said their findings raised the possibility that AI’s “priors” could shape consequential policy decisions, including in AI safety.
“If human judgement is to remain a meaningful check as more work is performed with AI, oversight of these decisions has to look at how they get made: Surfacing key decision points as the work proceeds and helping experts articulate the assumptions and values they would otherwise leave unstated,” they wrote in the study.
“A process that lets experts discover their preferences may matter for empowerment as much as the decision itself.”
Anthropic, which is preparing for an IPO valued at up to $2 trillion, and its rivals are at the centre of intense public debate about how to manage the potential dangers of frontier AI.
While AI proponents believe the technology will usher in revolutionary gains in productivity, the rapid pace of its development has prompted widespread concerns about potential negative effects on society, including mass job losses and cyberattacks.

A Chinese investigative blogger who exposed telecoms fraud and other illegal activity was killed by criminals hired on social media, according to media reports, prompting calls for heavier punishment for the perpetrators.
The body of Wu Kai, who used the name “Huijian” on social media and had written for years about telecoms fraud in Southeast Asia, was discovered in southern China in November 2024. His death and details of the case were revealed this week.
In August 2024, Wu accused Liu Ren – a central figure in a conglomerate masterminded by Chinese tycoon Chen Zhi – of being a casino loan shark, beating someone to death, extorting protection fees from shops, operating telecoms fraud compounds and engaging in armed transnational crimes, according to a Jiemian News report on Tuesday.
Liu was extradited from Cambodia to China in June this year. A police statement at the time said he had been ordered by Chen in 2016 to found a group called Jinbei, which operated telecoms fraud compounds in Cambodia and carried out fraud involving “extremely large amounts” of money starting in 2020.

Kengo Kuma & Associates’ Water Culture House to Open in Copenhagen on December 5, 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Designed by Kengo Kuma & Associates in collaboration with Cornelius Vöge Atelier for Architecture and Vilhelm Lauritzen Architects, KAI Water Culture House is set to open on December 5, 2026, on Papirøen (Paper Island) in Copenhagen, Denmark. The 5,800 m² public facility combines ten indoor and outdoor pools, wellness facilities, cultural spaces, and access to Copenhagen Harbour. Comprising five brick towers above a glazed base, the project brings together swimming, recreation, and cultural programming as part of the ongoing transformation of the city's waterfront.
The building's five brick towers are shaped in relation to the pools beneath them, creating distinct interior spaces while establishing a varied roofline. Constructed using approximately 300,000 handmade bricks, the towers contrast with the glazed lower structure, where windows frame views of the harbour and bring natural light into the building. A central feature is the Valley Pool, an outdoor pool positioned between the towers on the first floor, allowing visitors to swim under open skies. An outdoor onsen pool on the same level overlooks the harbour, extending the relationship between the building's interior programme and its waterfront setting.
The pools accommodate different activities across multiple levels. The ground floor contains a 25-metre fitness pool, a teaching pool, and three children's play pools, while the first floor includes a therapy pool, a hot pool, a cold plunge pool, and the two outdoor pools. The facility also incorporates three saunas, a steam bath, and a heated stone. Beyond the building, designated swimming and dipping zones are planned along a timber boardwalk, with views toward the Royal Danish Playhouse and Opera Park. These outdoor harbour-bathing facilities are expected to open in early 2027, after the building's initial opening.
Related Article
Copenhagen Architecture City Guide: 44 Projects Defining the Capital of Human-Scale Design
The project originated in 2015, when the City of Copenhagen invited residents to submit ideas for a cultural and leisure facility on Paper Island. The competition received 160 proposals, many of which called for a swimming facility that could also support relaxation and community activities. An international architectural competition followed in spring 2017, which Kengo Kuma & Associates won. Cornelius Vöge Atelier for Architecture collaborated on the project through the concept design stage, while Vilhelm Lauritzen Architects served as executive architects from detailed design through completion. Developed by the Paper Island Water Culture House Foundation in partnership with the City of Copenhagen, with support from the Nordea Foundation, KAI forms part of the wider transformation of Copenhagen's harbour into a setting for public recreation and cultural use.
Copenhagen's recent architectural developments reflect the city's continued focus on public life and its relationship with the built and natural environment. Named the world's most liveable city for the second consecutive year in the 2026 Global Liveability Index, the Danish capital is also preparing for the second Copenhagen Architecture Biennial, which will take place from September 9 to October 15, 2027, under the theme "Elements," exploring architecture's relationship with fire, earth, air, and water. Meanwhile, Danish practice AART has won the competition for Rigets Skatkammer (The Royal Treasury), a 1,300 m² underground extension to Rosenborg Castle that will add exhibition space beneath the historic moat while partially restoring the water surrounding the Renaissance castle.

"I think with Russia we're making a lot of progress with Russia-Ukraine. There'll be a meeting set up very soon," he said.

Freight development, fleet productivity, service quality, top priorities of railways
TEHRAN- The CEO of the Railways listed the development of international rail transport, an increase in the movement of export cargo, faster wagon turnaround, improved safety, and higher quality passenger services as the company’s priorities.
According to an IRNA report from the Railways, Jabbar Ali Zakeri, at a meeting of the High Committee for the Railway Transport Graph, emphasized the need to improve passenger services, especially on routes leading to holy Mashhad, and described providing the required fleet capacity and increasing readiness to offer satisfactory services to pilgrims and passengers as among the Railways’ priorities.
He considered supplying the wagons needed by cargo owners, removing obstacles to international and export freight transport, and reducing wagon dwell times essential for increasing productivity in the freight sector, and stressed the optimal use of locomotive capacity and the formation of heavy freight trains on routes with adequate capacity and suitable technical conditions.
The deputy minister of Roads and Urban Development also described securing infrastructure and ensuring safe train movement as essential, and stressed strengthening cooperation between the railway police and security guard, increasing patrolling along the lines, and countering the theft of railway equipment.
In another part of the meeting, Zakeri presented certificates of appreciation to two Railways athletes who brought honor to the organization on the world stage: Kaveh Riahi, an employee of the General Directorate of Safety and holder of first place in world weightlifting competitions, and Davood Hadavand, employed at the Tehran Railway General Directorate and holder of third place in world wrestling competitions.
He described support for athletes, the development of public and professional sport, and the expansion of sports programs as effective in increasing organizational vitality, and stressed continued support for the participation of Railways athletes in national and international competitions.
Further, Mirhasan Mousavi, Deputy CEO of the Railways, referring to passengers’ welcome for passenger trains, emphasized increasing fleet readiness and carrying out locomotive overhauls precisely in order to improve service quality on high-traffic routes.
He described increasing the share of rail transport in passenger movement as one of the Railways’ priorities, and listed reduced fuel consumption, improved travel safety, fewer road accidents and less air pollution, and better service quality as benefits of developing this sector.
Later in the meeting, the directors general of Railway North 2, West, Yazd, and Hormozgan, and the director of Khavar Sharq, presented reports on plans to increase fleet productivity, identify regional capacities, attract new cargoes, and strengthen the share of rail transport in freight movement.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc was projected to win 56 seats in the 120-member Knesset, five short of a governing majority, as 49.7% of votes were counted in Israel's parliamentary elections, Israeli media reported Wednesday.
The opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot was projected to secure 49 seats, while predominantly Arab parties were expected to win the remaining 15, according to Israeli daily Yedioth Ahronoth, citing the Central Elections Committee.
Neither major bloc was projected to reach the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.
The Arab parties could play a decisive role in government formation, as their combined 15 seats would give Eisenkot's bloc a majority of 64 if they agreed to support it.
Among individual parties, Netanyahu's Likud led with a projected 27 seats, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar with 21.
The US has told several Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a “short, intense military campaign” against Iran after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people briefed on the conversations.
The messages, conveyed through diplomatic and military channels, are among growing signs that the US and Israel are preparing a new round of heavy combat operations to weaken Iran and push it toward negotiations, according to the report.
The US military is moving a Patriot missile defense system from Texas to the region and has moved troops from bases where they were vulnerable, while US forces are restocking munitions and preparing bombers and fighter jets for strikes, the newspaper said, citing officials.
Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova said a US-brokered ceasefire in the Moscow-controlled city of Oleshky in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region will remain in place until late Sunday.
Lantratova said in a statement that the agreements regarding the ceasefire in Oleshky are being “fully upheld” and that no ceasefire violations have been recorded by either side as of 5.30 pm Moscow time (1430GMT).
“The ceasefire has been in effect since 4 am Moscow time (0100GMT) … today in areas relevant to the humanitarian mission. It will remain in place until 22:59 on Nov. 1,” said Lantratova.

The Brazilian newspaper O Globo reported, citing family allies, that Bolsonaro arrived on a flight to Miami, where he was received by Eduardo, who allegedly helped coordinate his departure with US authorities.
Eduardo, who lives in Texas, traveled to Florida with his wife and children to welcome his brother and his family, according to the report. Türkiye sets Oct 30 start for interim fund payouts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:22:45 UTC
15:22:45 KST

Interim payments of up to 1 million Turkish Liras to investors in funds undergoing extraordinary liquidation will begin on Oct. 30 through İş Bankası and Ziraat Bankası, Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz said.
Addressing parliament’s Planning and Budget Commission on Oct. 27, Yılmaz said payments would start with the smallest amounts.
He expected this round of payments to be completed around mid-November.
“I can say that a substantial amount will be paid on Friday,” he said.
The Capital Markets Board (SPK) has given money market funds priority under rules issued after the liquidation law was published in the Official Gazette on Oct. 27.
Interim payments will be calculated separately for each fund and cannot exceed either 1 million liras or the investor’s net investment, calculated without inflation adjustment.
Where cash is insufficient, payments are also limited by the value of investors’ holdings: Sept. 16 values apply to money market funds, while other funds use values from the day before the payment calculation.
The SPK can approve a payment order or a minimum payout to reach more investors.
The SPK assigned the liquidation of Tera Portföy’s affected funds to İş Bankası and those of Pusula Portföy and Atlas Portföy to Ziraat Bankası.
Yılmaz said Atlas’s eligibility for ordinary liquidation was still being assessed.
Payments will draw on remaining fund assets, voluntary returns and recovered gains and proceeds from assets placed under judicial restrictions, Yılmaz said.
The new law gives the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) powers to sell assets more quickly.
Under ordinary liquidation procedures, 68 billion liras had already been paid to 71,899 accounts across 93 funds by Oct. 23, Yılmaz said.
He put the remaining net investment under extraordinary liquidation at 125 billion liras.
Interim payments will be deducted from final entitlements, with fund units surrendered only at the final payment stage.
People and institutions identified by the SPK as having participated in market abuse, insider trading or manipulation involving the affected funds will be excluded from payments.

Iran, Belarus ink energy cooperation MOU
TEHRAN- A cooperation memorandum of understanding was signed between Abbas Aliabadi, Iran’s Minister of Energy, and the Belarusian Minister of Energy, aimed at establishing cooperation between the parties in the energy sector for mutual benefit.

According to this report, the main axes of this memorandum include promoting cooperation in sustainable energy development, including in the renewable energy sector; promoting cooperation in contracting and energy infrastructure services; and providing the possibility of exchanging experience, training, and technical support.
Also among the provisions of this memorandum are cooperation in the fields of construction and management of energy infrastructure, electricity distribution and transmission systems, joint participation in seminars, conferences, and exhibitions with the aim of attracting investment in the energy field, technical cooperation and exchange of information on engineering and advisory issues, and exchange of visits by senior officials and technical experts responsible for the development and implementation of energy policy.

The Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade, pointing to the industrial capabilities of the two countries, cited cooperation in the supply of mining machinery as one of the important axes of joint cooperation and called for expanding interactions among active companies in this field.

Also, areas of cooperation for the joint production of urban and intercity buses and trucks with the participation of companies from both countries were discussed.

At the end of the meeting, the two sides emphasized the continuation of consultations, follow-up of agreements, and strengthening of joint cooperation in the industrial, commercial, and transport fields in order to enhance the level of economic relations between Iran and Belarus.

France has deployed an Atlantique 2 maritime patrol aircraft to Romania to conduct surveillance and reconnaissance over the western Black Sea, following a request from Bucharest, the Romanian Ministry of National Defense announced.
The aircraft is operating from Mihail Kogălniceanu Air Base, with its mission focused on detecting threats to navigation and improving the protection of critical infrastructure within Romania’s Exclusive Economic Zone.
The French Navy’s Mediterranean and Black Sea Command sent the aircraft to the region as the security situation deteriorates. According to the Romanian ministry, the deployment is scheduled to run from October 18 to November 6, 2026.
Flight operations are being planned and coordinated with assistance from the "Vice Admiral Ioan Georgescu" Naval Component Command, in cooperation with the Maritime Coordination Centre.
The Atlantique 2 mission supports NATO deterrence operations and highlights the role of allied cooperation, interoperability and responsiveness in maritime surveillance.
The deployment also enables joint training between the Romanian Naval Forces and the French military. Romanian military personnel are taking part in Black Sea flights, joint training exercises and information exchanges with Romanian naval vessels operating at sea.
NATO and French naval support supplements Romania’s own efforts to strengthen surveillance and patrols in the Black Sea. The Romanian Ministry of National Defense said national naval forces had stepped up patrols involving ships, IAR-330 Puma Naval helicopters and autonomous unmanned systems.
The Romanian Naval Hydrographic Directorate "Commander Alexandru Cătâneanu" also issues continuous navigational warnings to mariners about identified hazards and recommended routes. The measures are designed to promote safe navigation, prevent maritime incidents and preserve freedom of movement.
The Romanian Naval Forces continue to track maritime activity within their area of responsibility in the Black Sea, working with national defense and security structures and NATO allies. At least eight cargo ships have been affected over the past three weeks.
At least eight cargo ships were affected off the Romanian and Bulgarian coasts in the three weeks leading up to October 27. Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two Russian drones over Romania’s territorial waters in October. NATO has also announced plans to expand Black Sea surveillance through additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and unmanned aerial vehicles.
France’s aircraft deployment forms part of allied efforts to improve maritime monitoring, safeguard critical infrastructure and maintain freedom of navigation in the Black Sea.
The Romanian Ministry of National Defense said the joint operations with France and NATO complement ongoing Romanian Naval Forces activities, including surveillance, patrolling and efforts to contain threats arising from Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Separately, Romanian Foreign Minister Dan Neculaescu and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot reaffirmed the importance of the two countries’ strategic partnership during a phone call on regional security. Their discussion covered the changing security environment, with particular attention to the Black Sea and its strategic importance for Euro-Atlantic security.
