India evacuates over 180,000 as Cyclone Arnab hits coast
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:15:08 CET
15:15:08 KST

By Jatindra Dash and Rishika Sadam
BHUBANESWAR/HYDERABAD, India, Oct 28 (Reuters) - At least three people were killed, dozens of houses damaged and crops destroyed as a powerful cyclone struck India’s eastern coast from the Bay of Bengal on Wednesday, bringing heavy rain and strong winds, authorities said.
Cyclone Arnab, classified by the India Meteorological Department as a very severe cyclonic storm – the third-highest category on its scale – made landfall in Andhra Pradesh state early on Wednesday, with its centre then moving fully inland, the agency said.
“Andhra Pradesh has been most affected … three people have lost their lives,” Narendra Singh Bundela, a top official at the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), told reporters.
Heavy rain and high winds destroyed at least 180 houses, brought down 220 trees and disrupted power supply in several areas, Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu said in a letter to federal Home Minister Amit Shah, updating him on the situation.
Two of the deaths were caused by a tree falling and electrocution, officials in Naidu’s office told Reuters.
Neighbouring Odisha state was not as badly affected, Bundela said, adding that wind-speeds were expected to reduce as the cyclone moved inland.
More than 180,000 people had been evacuated in the states of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha ahead of the cyclone’s arrival.
Some schools were closed and some train and flight services cancelled along the eastern coast.
Several NDRF and state teams were working in the affected areas, Bundela said, adding that some neighbouring states were also likely to be affected by heavy rain.
Television images showed trees fallen on highways as workers in rain gear worked to clear the road of branches and leaves.
“No one knew whose house the water would rush into next, or whose home would be submerged,” said Nagi, a resident of Andhra’s Kakinada district.
“Trees have fallen, houses have been damaged, and all our belongings, including our books, have been destroyed,” said Nagi, who did not give a last name.
Fishermen along the coast had been advised against going out to sea, and the weather department said it anticipated losses to crops, as well as damage to thatched houses and communication lines.
Winds of 125 kph to 135 kph (77.7 mph to 83.9 mph) and gusts of up to 150 kph are forecast, with a storm surge of 1 metre to 1.5 metres (3.28 feet to 4.92 feet) above normal tide likely to inundate low-lying areas of Andhra Pradesh, it said.
Operations at three Andhra Pradesh airports were suspended, India’s civil aviation ministry said.
NEPAL SUSPENDS TREKKING PERMITS
In neighbouring Nepal, authorities suspended the issuing of trekking permits to high mountain areas for three days because of the risk of rain and blizzards due to the cyclone, Immigration Department information officer Gita Ghimire told Reuters.
This is peak trekking season in Nepal with around 750 hikers getting permits per day.
On Tuesday, Nepal warned tourists against venturing into high-altitude areas due to fears that Arnab could trigger torrential downpours, snowstorms and avalanches in the Himalayan region from Thursday night through Saturday.
Arnab formed over the Bay of Bengal, a major region for tropical cyclones that has spawned deadly storms on India’s east coast.
A super cyclone that killed nearly 10,000 people when it hit Odisha in October 1999 remains one of the country’s deadliest natural disasters.
India, however, has over the years developed early-warning systems and preventive measures to minimise loss of life.
(Reporting by Jatindra Dash in Bhubaneswar, Rishika Sadam in Hyderabad, Gopal Sharma in Kathmandu and Sakshi Dayal in New Delhi; Writing by Chris Thomas and Shilpa Jamkhandikar; Editing by Bill Berkrot, Edwina Gibbs, YP Rajesh and Kate Mayberry)

China’s old-age dependency ratio overtakes children for first time
Italy

15:14:49 KST

HONG KONG, Oct 28 - China is now supporting more people aged 65 and above than children, underscoring the impact of its rapidly ageing population and a declining birth rate.
• Data from China’s National Bureau of Statistics showed the old-age dependency ratio — the non-working-age population compared to the working-age population — was 23.1% in 2025, compared with 22% for children, Chinese state-affiliated media Yicai reported
• The ratio has risen steadily over the years, up from 15% in 2016 to more than 20% in 2021
• There are now more than 223 million people in China aged 65 and above compared with around 213 million children aged 14 and under, the data showed
• China’s population fell for a fourth straight year in 2025, as its birth rate dropped to a record low
• The country’s birth rate has been falling for decades, a result of the one-child policy in place from 1980 to 2015, as well as rapid urbanisation
• Authorities have rolled out a range of measures to encourage marriage and childbearing, including family subsidies, childcare support, and reduced childbirth-related medical costs
• They have also pledged to make urban life more supportive for young people, children and families

Flavio Bolsonaro and family to receive US visas after leaving Brazil, State Department says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:14:21 CET
15:14:21 KST

By Ricardo Brito, Gram Slattery and Luciana Magalhaes
SAO PAULO, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has left the country for the United States after losing Sunday’s presidential election, three sources said, with the US State Department due to grant him and his family entry visas.
Bolsonaro, who has yet to concede to leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, left Brazil after refusing to comply with a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports.
The ruling relates to a money laundering probe in which he denies wrongdoing.
Argentina’s migration department said on Wednesday that Bolsonaro and his family had briefly entered the country’s Misiones province on Tuesday night through a road crossing, with valid travel documents, before boarding a private plane bound for Guayaquil, Ecuador at 11:30 pm local time (0230 GMT).
Argentina cited the flight plan, for the plane operated by air charter company Baires Fly, as the source for the aircraft’s destination. The Ecuadorian foreign ministry did not respond to an emailed request for comment outside regular hours.
The current location of Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters was not immediately clear.
Speaking to reporters late on Tuesday, US President Donald Trump had said that he had heard Bolsonaro was in Argentina.
“The State Department will issue visas to Flavio Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the United States,” a senior State Department official said.
BRAZIL-US RIFT GROWS
Bolsonaro’s departure threatens to deepen a rift between the two most populous nations in the Americas. Lula has accused Washington of colluding with the Bolsonaros to put them back in power, and Reuters reported ahead of Sunday’s election on a US State Department campaign to restore them to office.
Trump told reporters on Wednesday that he would approve of Bolsonaro coming to the United States.
“Well, I would approve. I think they’re fine people. The election was very strange, and I thought it was terrible. It’s gotten bad reviews. You look at what happened to their market”, Trump said.
“I think it’s so terrible to see it. I didn’t take sides, you know. I know them both. I know Lula. I know Flavio a little bit. I know the father very well. The father was treated really badly. I thought, but I wasn’t involved. That’s Brazil. It’s a different country”, he said.
Trump has previously alleged Flavio’s father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, was a victim of judicial persecution in Brazil. The elder Bolsonaro also went to the United States after refusing to concede to Lula in 2022, when former US President Joe Biden was in office. He eventually returned but was later given a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after his supporters stormed government buildings in Brasilia.
On Monday, Trump had said the Brazilian vote “looked like another rigged election.”
Lula, speaking in Brasilia, said he had just heard that Flavio had left the country, and called it shameful, saying he should have stayed in Brazil and proved his innocence.
Bolsonaro had been favored to win Sunday’s presidential election but ended up losing in a shock result.
ORDERED TO HAND OVER PASSPORTS
On Monday, he was given 24 hours to surrender his passports, which were canceled after the deadline lapsed, two sources said. In a court ruling seen by Reuters, the Supreme Court cited the risk of Bolsonaro fleeing Brazil and his “significant financial resources” in ordering his passports seized.
Bolsonaro, who loses his immunity from prosecution when his Senate term ends in February, had said on Monday he had no plans to flee.
“I have never thought about leaving the country,” he said. “I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me.”
His departure appeared to have caught his campaign manager off guard.
“We are surprised by the news because, just yesterday, we discussed the need for Flavio — given the 60 million votes he received — to take on this role as leader of the opposition,” Senator Rogerio Marinho told reporters.
FOLLOWING FATHER’S PATH
Although Bolsonaro has yet to officially concede defeat — saying on Sunday he would seek the annulment of the result over alleged voter irregularities — his Liberal Party said on Monday it acknowledged Lula’s victory.
Eduardo Bolsonaro, Bolsonaro’s younger brother who lives in the United States, said ahead of the vote that an election loss would require a move.
“If my brother does not win, I’m in favor that he would leave the country,” he told podcaster Steven Crowder this month.
(Reporting by Ricardo Brito and Luciana Magalhaes; Additional reporting by Lucinda Elliot, Brendan O’Boyle, Oliver Griffin, Simon Lewis, Chandni Shah and Shivani Tanna in Bengaluru; Editing by Gabriel Stargardter, Aurora Ellis and Raju Gopalakrishnan)

‘Working our fingers to the bone’: Can the UK save its struggling high streets?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:05:27 UTC
15:05:27 KST

‘Working our fingers to the bone’: Can the UK save its struggling high streets?
Small business owners in Britain may get some tax relief in Wednesday’s budget, but they say it will not be enough.
Birmingham, United Kingdom – Taking the reins of a family business can be a source of immense pride, but it also comes with enormous pressures.
When Supreet Suri’s father started a photography business in Birmingham 40 years ago, his hard work paid off and he expanded to four locations around the city.
Today, the family has just one shop, in a prime location in the city’s Kings Heath High Street. But Suri is now considering relocating.
The reason: It’s too expensive to continue the business there.
When Suri moved the business to its current site, it gave it greater visibility – but also much higher running costs.
“We are at a point now where we are seriously considering how do we get out of this space purely to reduce costs,” he tells Al Jazeera.
Despite having a loyal customer base, Suri says the financial rewards are increasingly difficult to find.
“We’re sort of working our fingers to the bone, and that’s the side that people don’t see.”
Living ‘month to month’
Suri’s experience reflects a broader struggle on Britain’s high streets as the government presents its budget on Wednesday, with attention focused on whether further relief from business rates could help smaller businesses.
Business rates are a property-based tax paid by businesses occupying commercial premises, although some smaller properties already qualify for relief.
For Suri, however, rates are only part of the problem.
There is also the rent, VAT – a type of sales tax – wages, pensions, the rising cost of energy and specialist materials, which are all eating into his earnings. Refilling one of his professional printers with ink, he says, costs about 2,000 pounds ($2,664).
“I pay myself less than the minimum wage [of 12.21 pounds ($16.26) per hour]”, he says when asked how much he earns. “When I say that I live month to month, I literally mean that.”
Another challenge Suri and other independent business owners face is competition from online retailers, which now account for 28 percent of UK retail sales.
King’s Heath high street faces the same challenges as many of Britain’s main commercial thoroughfares: a fight to remain relevant in an age where big businesses, higher taxes and online shopping are squeezing out independent retailers.
While small business owners on the high street face steeper costs, customers increasingly expect prices comparable to those online, even when they are paying for a specialist, personalised service.
“People come to me wanting the quality that we provide, but they want me to match online pricing, which I simply can’t do,” Suri says.
He understands that the cost-of-living crisis he is struggling with also affects his customers.
“You can’t blame the customer or the consumer for not being able to support your business all of the time,” he says, pointing to household living costs.
Decline of the high street
The pressures on retailers come as many customers are feeling increasingly despondent about the state of their high streets.
Boarded-up shopfronts are a more common sight. Pawnbrokers, betting shops, vape outlets, charity stores and big-chain retailers have moved into high street locations that small business owners can no longer afford. Nearly 14 percent of high street retail units are estimated to be vacant.
For many who once regularly used their local high street, this new reality has become a symptom of decline and depression, even putting them off going there in the first place.
“Years ago, you used to come and have a good look, whatever the weather,” one Birmingham shopper tells Al Jazeera. “But it’s just the same up here all the time now.”
Another says shopping online is increasingly preferable. “It’s more convenient as well. Sometimes you come out here and there’s no inspiration.”
Yet the same shopper says they want more distinctive local businesses and adds that the government should make it easier for entrepreneurs to open them.
A struggle to survive
These challenges go well beyond Birmingham.
At a parliamentary inquiry into revitalising Britain’s high streets earlier this month, the chief executive of the British Independent Retailers Association, Andrew Goodacre, argued that recent business rate reforms had failed to deliver the intended benefits for smaller retailers.
He told members of parliament that some independent shops are facing higher bills, even as a large supermarket near his home stood to pay substantially less.
The inquiry heard another troubling argument that legitimate businesses may also face unfair competition from operators which evade taxes. Politicians heard how some central London souvenir shops allegedly use successive limited companies to avoid paying tax, enabling them to pay rents that compliant businesses could not afford.
The evidence highlights the importance of enforcement alongside tax reform, and warnings that a cut in business rates alone will not stem the deterioration of Britain’s high streets.
That warning is echoed by Suri, who says a reduction in rates would be welcome but not enough.
“That’s a small step in the right direction,” he says. “But if the intention really is to help the high streets thrive, there’s a lot of change that needs to be made.”
His challenge to the UK’s Chancellor of the Exchequer is to spend a month or two running a real high street business and experience the pressures first-hand.
For a family business that has survived four decades, the question now is whether it can afford another year in the place it once hoped to grow.
“If [the government] makes it easier to actually run an independent business successfully, that’s the first domino in a positive effect that could really help our country.”

India’s southern state of Andhra Pradesh evacuated thousands of residents on Wednesday ahead of Cyclone Arnab’s landfall along the southeastern coast, where it brought heavy rainfall and powerful winds.
The Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority said the landfall process had remained stationary for two hours.
“The chance of completely crossing the shore by afternoon. Strong gusty winds and rains continue along the shore. People should remain vigilant even today,” the authority said on X.
Authorities in Andhra Pradesh shifted 84,396 people to 290 relief shelters, while a total of 2,199 shelters were designated across the state, All India Radio reported.
In neighbouring Odisha state, another 48,000 were moved to safer areas, according to All India Radio.
The cyclone, which began making landfall early on Wednesday, caused widespread disruption, with strong winds uprooting trees and damaging local infrastructure, the broadcaster said.
Authorities in Andhra Pradesh and the eastern state of Odisha also ordered school closures as a precautionary measure. Fishing activities were suspended, while rescue teams were kept on standby to respond to emergencies.
The administration of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands also ordered schools to remain closed for two days beginning on Tuesday.
India’s Meteorological Department said a deep depression over the east-central and southeastern Bay of Bengal had moved westward and intensified into Cyclone Arnab.

NEW YORK, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- U.S. President Donald Trump announced plans on Tuesday to roll back regulations aimed at curbing methane emissions from oil and gas operations, arguing that the move would reduce costs and boost domestic energy production.
"Tonight, I'm officially terminating Biden's expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers 45 billion dollars," Trump said at a campaign rally in Lubbock, Texas.
The move would "unlock vast quantities of Texas natural gas" and allow the production of an additional 210 million barrels of oil, Trump said.
The announcement came amid rising fuel prices driven by the U.S. war with Iran, as Trump seeks to ease energy costs ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, the proposed rollback of Biden-era regulations would eliminate a program for identifying and addressing major methane leaks, ease requirements for low-producing oil and gas wells, and relax restrictions on routine flaring of natural gas at oil wells.
The United States is the world's leading emitter of methane from its oil and gas sector, followed by Russia, according to the International Energy Agency. Texas is by far the leading fossil fuel-producing state in the United States.
Methane, the main component of natural gas, is the second-largest cause of global warming after carbon dioxide. It is estimated to be responsible for nearly a third of global warming observed today. ■

Column: Understanding the strengths of China's governance model
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:01:57 CST
15:01:57 KST

by Denis Simon
As China continues on its development path, a range of complex issues will require sustained attention. The good news is that the track record of the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the Chinese government demonstrates a number of institutional strengths and development achievements for dealing with these challenges.
To better grasp the capacity of the Chinese government and the CPC to handle the challenges it is confronting, I would like to emphasize three main themes: long-term strategic planning, governance capacity and policy implementation, and the relationship between economic development and improvements in people's livelihoods.
STRENGTH OF CHINA'S GOVERNANCE MODEL
I believe one of the most important strengths of China's governance model is its ability to combine long-term strategic vision with the capacity to mobilize resources and implement policies on a national scale.
One challenge facing many governments today, particularly in developing countries, is the difficulty of maintaining policy continuity. Electoral cycles, political polarization, competing institutional interests, and short-term political calculations can make it difficult to sustain development strategies over a decade or longer. China has developed an institutional approach that places considerable emphasis on long-term planning, policy coordination, and continuity of national development objectives.
The five-year planning system is an important illustration. It allows the government to establish priorities, coordinate national and local development strategies, mobilize public and private resources, and adjust policies as circumstances change. China's experience in infrastructure development, poverty reduction, industrial upgrading, and technological advancement demonstrates the potential benefits of this approach.
I would identify five lessons that may be relevant to political leaders in developing countries: First, the importance of long-term strategic planning. Governments need to look beyond immediate political and economic pressures and develop a coherent national development vision.
Second, the importance of state capacity. Having good policies is not enough. Governments must possess the administrative institutions, professional personnel, financial resources, and organizational capabilities to translate policy objectives into tangible results. China's experience demonstrates the importance of connecting central strategic direction with implementation at provincial, municipal, and grassroots levels.
Third, the ability to mobilize resources around national priorities. Developing countries often face severe resource constraints. China's experience illustrates how governments can coordinate public investment, private-sector participation, financial institutions, and local development initiatives to advance major national objectives.
Fourth, the importance of pragmatism and policy experimentation. One particularly interesting aspect of China's reform experience has been its willingness to experiment with policies at the local level, evaluate results, and expand successful approaches. The establishment of special economic zones is a prominent example. This suggests that effective governance does not require every policy to be perfect from the beginning. It requires institutional learning and the willingness to correct mistakes.
Fifth, the importance of maintaining social stability while pursuing economic transformation. Development requires a reasonably predictable political, social, and economic environment. Governments must address inequality, unemployment, regional disparities, and public concerns if they hope to sustain public confidence.
However, China's governance model should not be regarded as a universal template that other country can simply copy. Every country has its own political institutions, historical circumstances, social structures, and development challenges. Different countries may draw useful insights from one another's development experiences.
Therefore, the most productive international discussion should focus less on competing political labels and more on identifying practical approaches that improve government effectiveness, strengthen accountability, deliver public services, and create opportunities for economic development.
CORE REASON CPC MAINTAINS LONG-TERM GOVERNING VITALITY
In my view, the fundamental reason is the ability of the Communist Party of China (CPC) to maintain a strong organizational structure while continuously adapting its governing priorities to China's changing economic and social circumstances.
The CPC's longevity cannot be explained simply by its size or organizational reach. Its membership of more than 100 million gives it an extraordinary organizational presence, but size alone does not guarantee governing effectiveness. What matters is how that organization functions and whether it can continue to deliver results.
I would highlight three interconnected factors. First, the CPC has developed a distinctive capacity for long-term strategic thinking. It has consistently emphasized national development objectives that extend beyond immediate economic or political considerations. The ability to maintain continuity in major national priorities, while adjusting implementation to changing circumstances, is an important institutional advantage.
Second, the Party has demonstrated a considerable capacity for adaptation. Since the beginning of reform and opening-up, China has undergone enormous transformations in its economic structure, social composition, technological capabilities, and international position.
The CPC has chosen to adjust its governing approaches to accommodate these changes. The transformation from a predominantly agricultural economy into a major industrial and technological power required not only economic reform but also significant changes in governance, administration and policymaking.
Third, the Party has placed considerable emphasis on organizational discipline, cadre development, and the ability to translate central policy decisions into action throughout the country. This capacity for coordination and implementation is an important source of institutional strength.
I would add one further consideration: the ultimate test of a ruling party's vitality is whether it retains the capacity to recognize problems, correct mistakes, respond to changing public expectations, and maintain public confidence. No political organization can remain effective simply by relying on its historical achievements. China's economic and social circumstances today are very different from those of 20 or even 10 years ago. The expectations of younger generations, the challenges of an aging population, the pressures of economic restructuring, and the demands of technological innovation all require new governing capabilities.
CPC'S PEOPLE-CENTERED PHILOSOPHY OF DEVELOPMENT
I consider the people-centered philosophy of development one of the most important aspects of the CPC's governing approach, particularly because it connects national development objectives with the everyday concerns of ordinary citizens. One of the most significant achievements of China's reform and development experience has been the transformation of living conditions for an enormous proportion of its population.
Consider poverty alleviation. China's achievement in lifting hundreds of millions of people out of extreme poverty is historically significant. It demonstrates what can be accomplished when poverty reduction becomes a sustained national priority, supported by targeted policies, substantial resource mobilization, infrastructure investment, and local implementation.
But the importance of a people-centered philosophy of development should not be measured exclusively by poverty reduction. It also should be reflected in the quality and accessibility of public services, including education, healthcare, employment opportunities, affordable housing, pensions, and social protection.
China has made substantial progress in expanding educational opportunities, improving rural infrastructure, extending healthcare coverage, and developing social security systems. These achievements have helped create a much stronger foundation for social and economic development.
I also would emphasize an important conceptual point: economic growth and improvements in people's livelihoods should not be treated as separate objectives. They are mutually reinforcing. Economic development creates the resources necessary to improve public services, while better education, healthcare, social protection, and employment opportunities strengthen human capital and support further economic growth.
That said, China's people-centered philosophy of development faces an important new test as China has moved into a substantially different stage of development. The challenges today are no longer simply about lifting people out of poverty or expanding basic infrastructure. They increasingly involve improving the quality of development and ensuring that its benefits are shared more equitably.
My overall assessment is that China's experience demonstrates the importance of placing improvements in people's living standards at the center of national development. But the next stage will require moving beyond the achievements of poverty reduction and basic development toward greater equality of opportunity, higher-quality public services, and more balanced and sustainable growth.
EXPECTATIONS FOR FIFTH PLENARY SESSION
I believe the fifth plenary session of the 20th CPC Central Committee comes at an important moment for China. The country is entering a new phase of development, facing a more complicated international environment and a number of significant domestic economic and social challenges.
The principal focus of the Fifth Plenary Session is on advancing the Party's full and rigorous self-governance. Against this background, I expect the Fifth Plenary Session to deliver an important message: institutional self-renewal is essential to long-term governing capacity.
The CPC has repeatedly emphasized the importance of discipline, combating corruption, and strengthening Party self-governance. I believe this is particularly important at a time when China is confronting more complex economic, technological, and international challenges.
But institutional self-renewal must go beyond disciplinary measures. It should also involve improving the quality of governance, strengthening administrative accountability, encouraging innovation, and ensuring that officials at all levels have both the competence and the incentives to address difficult problems.
An effective governing party must be capable of renewing itself before institutional weaknesses become serious obstacles to development.
Looking ahead, I believe the Fifth Plenary Session could strengthen the CPC's institutional capacity and reinforce the importance of administrative discipline and organizational accountability. It could also send an important signal to the international community about China's approach to governance, economic development, and its role in an increasingly uncertain global environment.
Ultimately, my expectation is that the meeting will demonstrate that China's next stage of modernization requires not only strong political leadership and long-term strategic planning, but also continuous institutional reform, greater policy responsiveness, and a stronger commitment to improving people's livelihoods.
The most important outcome should not simply be another set of policy declarations. It should be a clearer demonstration of how the CPC intends to translate its governing principles into practical results for the benefit of the entire population.
Editor's note: Denis Simon is the former Executive Vice Chancellor of Duke Kunshan University in Jiangsu province. He is also a senior faculty member in the Schwarzman College at Tsinghua University.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.

Department stores capitalized on Chuseok gift set sales, which pushed up food revenue by 13.0 percent, alongside autumn fashion demand that raised sales of women's casual wear by 15.2 percent and men's clothing by 8.7 percent.
Convenience stores logged a 5.9 percent gain in processed food sales, catering to single-person households looking for ready-to-eat meals during the holidays.
Online retail sales also benefited from the holiday surge, with grocery purchase in cyberspace climbing 6.7 percent.
Online demand for services and others, including food delivery, travel and cultural products and e-coupon purchase, advanced 10.6 percent as more consumers utilized digital grocery services. ■

Rome’s mayor rules out ‘Venice-like’ entrance fee for tourists
- Rome mayor Roberto Gualtieri rejects a Venice-style entry fee. He says Rome should protect its historic centre by limiting short-term rentals and keeping real local shops.
- Rome has approved stronger housing rules, but new short-term rental laws are still needed. Gualtieri says Venice’s €5 fee suits its smaller size and many day-trippers.
- Rome had record tourism in 2025, with 22.9 million arrivals and 52.92 million overnight stays. Gualtieri also backs a waste-to-energy plant due in 2029 and plans to seek re-election in 2027.
AI generated
ROME – Rome can best preserve the character of its 3,000-year-old city centre with measures like restricting short-term rentals, rather than by increasing taxes imposed on visitors, mayor Roberto Gualtieri said.
“It would make no sense to introduce here an entry ticket to the city, like they did in Venice,” Gualtieri said in an interview with Bloomberg for the video podcast Quello che il potere non dice.
The Eternal City, a destination since ancient times, has no plan to block access, the mayor said.
Visitors want to experience the city as Romans do, and that requires ensuring historic centre isn’t hollowed out, and tourists have access to local shops and restaurants instead of “fake” ones, he added.
“Tourists will always come to Rome,” Gualtieri said. “There have always been tourists and there always will be.”
This past summer, Rome’s city assembly approved an update of rules covering urban development, a process that took nearly 20 years.
Among the changes backed by Gualtieri were stronger protections for residential housing in the historic centre.
Action is still needed to adopt new regulations that apply to short-term rentals.
Venice has tested measures to control the number of tourists and day-trippers visiting the historic centre, including a €5 (S$7.13) access fee which was trialled this summer.
According to Gualtieri, such a system is better suited to the water city because it is smaller, and a large number of visitors do not stay overnight, so they do not pay room taxes.
Florence and Bologna have also passed new regulations on short-term rentals, such as banning a change of use for non-residential properties in their respective historic centres.
Waste to energy
Gualtieri, a former finance minister and a member of the Democratic Party, won election in 2021, pledging to address chronic overtourism and sluggish garbage collection.
To many Romans’ surprise, he jump-started some projects that had eluded predecessors on the left and the right.
A waste-to-energy plant is moving forward after years of resistance, and Catholic Jubilee and European Union recovery funds were used to promote urban regeneration.
Gualtieri confirmed in the interview that the waste plan will become operational at the end of 2029.
Among his remaining priorities is to discourage what he described as hit-and-run tourism, in which visitors “simply consume and give nothing in return”, he said.
According to a survey released in September by real estate company Brixa, Rome’s city centre has more than 122,000 beds available for overnight stays, compared with the 116,000-plus residents of the area.
The research indicated that the trend of short-term lettings, which has traditionally been confined to the historic centre, is spreading to residential neighbourhoods on the outskirts of the city.
“We cannot intervene on existing properties unless we are granted the power to do so,” Gualtieri said. “So we are equipping ourselves with tools to impose restrictions” on various kinds of properties, he added.
His goal is to keep Rome “a great, open city where people want to come back”.
Better-quality tourism, focused on major cultural events that sometimes take place outside the historic centre, will spur a demand for real Roman experiences, Gualtieri maintains.
Rome attracted a record number of tourists in 2025, according to data supplied by the city.
Arrivals totalled 22.9 million, including 12 million from abroad. Overnight stays totalled 52.92 million, another all-time high.
Gualtieri’s term will end in 2027, and he has been tipped as a possible candidate for a centre-left alliance in Italy’s general election in 2027.
The mayor dismissed such an option during the interview, saying he will seek to run for a second mandate.
There are many long-term projects in the city that he wants to oversee, he said.

Should AI Decide Your Court Case? This Judge Says Yes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

In a few days, judge Geoffrey Vos will retire as Master of the Rolls, the most senior position in England’s civil justice system. As one of his final acts, he’s trying to stoke a debate about whether—and how—judges should be using artificial intelligence.
Under the latest guidance, judges in England are advised to confine their use of AI to administrative tasks, and Vos tells WIRED he uses Microsoft Copilot all the time to locate far-flung documents and summarize large bodies of text. But recently, he visited a court in Shenzhen, China, where civil disputes are already being decided by judges with heavy assistance from AI. Impressed by what he saw, Vos believes that courts across the globe should consider following.
That road is littered with pitfalls. Multiple lawyers have been caught citing case law hallucinated by AI, and in a first for the UK, somebody recently lost their license to practice in part because they misused the technology. Meanwhile, with chatbots as their legal counsel, litigants are flooding the courts with an unprecedented number of claims, some of them bogus.
Yet Vos remains convinced that AI will someday help resolve civil disputes more rapidly and in ways that cost far less. While complicated commercial disputes and sensitive family cases might require a human judge, he believes that personal injury claims, low-value professional negligence cases, and the like could easily be adjudicated by AI.
“What most people desperately want in civil disputes is resolution,” Vos tells WIRED. “The question is, where is the line to be drawn?”
Given his impending retirement, the debate for Vos is largely a philosophical one. But for everyone else in the profession—and for coders, cybersecurity experts, math professors, and a whole host of others—the rules are changing fast.
In October, WIRED met with Vos at his office at the Royal Courts of Justice, London. We discussed the ways that AI is spilling into the courts, the practical and ethical issues it raises, and how the justice system might adapt to serve a new generation raised alongside the technology.
This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
WIRED: You’re just a few days away from retirement. How do you feel about leaving the post at this particular juncture, as AI begins to reshape how law is practiced and justice administered?
GEOFFREY VOS: When I started as a lawyer, we had foolscap paper, typists, and Tipp-Ex. We moved rapidly into word processors, faxes, and eventually computers.
Lawyers are conservative with a lowercase c. But that doesn’t mean that they should be backward-looking or retrogressive. It means they should be adopting change cautiously, with their eyes open.
The legal system is for the people of this country. You can’t be effective in providing access to justice if you’re not on the same technological wavelength. But it’s time to leave it to a new generation of leadership judges.
How have you built AI into your practice to date?
I don’t use it for writing judgments, but I use it for finding things out, navigating large quantities of material, and checking things. It saves me time. I have 11 meetings a day. I know there’s a document created years ago that’s relevant to my meeting—and Copilot finds it in seconds. I do that every day.
In law, isn’t the devil always in the details? Doesn’t confidence in the legal system depend on the understanding that a judge will review and consider every inch of every court submission?
I’m a little more cautious about using it to read papers for my cases, but that’s because I do the most important cases in the system.
People have confidence in our justice system because they believe that our judges have absolute integrity. In order not to lose that integrity, you have to explain how you’re adopting technology and achieve a broad consensus that it is appropriate.
How is AI spilling into the courts right now? Is it changing how litigants and legal professionals behave? What issues is it throwing up?
It’s changing everything remarkably quickly. We see a 10 percent rise in the number of county court cases started every year—and it looks as if this may increase. That’s because everybody who has a legal problem now puts it into Gemini, ChatGPT, or Claude. Ask it to create a particulars of claim, a case, a claim form—it can.
What proportion of these claims are based on sound legal principles, though? How often are people led by a chatbot to mistakenly believe they have a claim?
We don’t have the data. But I think it’s a mistake to assume that just because a claim is created by AI, it’s totally frivolous.
In a way it’s a good problem, because it shows there’s greater access to justice because of technology. One of the problems with justice in the past is that it’s only been available to rich people.
If people have a problem sufficient to bother ChatGPT, they probably genuinely think they have a claim. When you explore their problem in detail, you might find it is actually a bit different, but it may still be a legal problem and may still be reasonable for them to have wanted to bring it to attention.
People are not generally time wasters. They’re not generally trying to make trouble.
What about the opportunity for AI to fabricate evidence on which judges have previously been able to rely—images, video, voice recordings? Where does that leave the courts?
Often, judges have to decide whether a person is telling the truth. That is the most difficult thing to do, because humans are not bad at lying. But judges make these decisions every day. There’s absolutely no difference—in scale or qualitatively—in somebody producing a false image created by AI.
The only reason we’re all getting so excited about deepfakes is because they are so new. But actually, that is the stuff of judging.
But we’re talking about a whole category of evidence that’s now somewhat compromised. Doesn’t that affect a judge’s ability to decide whether somebody is lying?
It was always thus. We always had to decide whether wills were forged, because people used to do that. It’s exactly the same with voice recordings, and video. It’s just an extension of the type of false information that is produced to the court.
People will find out when they produce fake images to the court that they are committing perjury and they will go to prison, just as if they’d forged a will.
I think we need to be cautious about predicting disaster. I’m very optimistic.
You’ve previously described an “inevitable” future where simpler civil cases are adjudicated entirely by AI. Why are you confident that’s where we’re headed?
You need to find a way to deliver justice that is within the cultural grain. That doesn’t mean you just conduct all your cases on TikTok. But if you don’t understand that people are asking LLMs for the answer to almost every question under the sun, including legal questions, you’re likely to get it wrong when you try to devise a process fit for the 21st century.
It’s all about consensus. It will only be possible to ask people to accept algorithmic decision-making if they consent to the process in a particular case, or if society decides through legislation.
When people go to court and get an adverse outcome, even if they regard the outcome as idiosyncratic or even wrong, when it’s delivered in a human way, it can be accepted over time. With AI, we have to be careful; it may be less easy for people to accept an adverse machine-driven decision.
I very much want to see a very open, international discussion about how we should resolve disputes.
I suspect part of the reason people object to trial by AI is because we can’t know precisely how a model has arrived at a decision. What’s to be done about this problem of explainability?
I don’t think it’s about reasoning; it’s about outcomes. The AI can produce very plausible reasoning. You can’t see how it produced that reasoning, but you can see the reasoning it produced, and you can judge the plausibility.
I don’t think you’ll ever do away with human judges. There’s something almost biblical about the human judge; it’s in the human psyche to want to be judged by their fellow man. But that does not mean that in some situations people wouldn’t rather have a quick outcome—even if it’s not a human outcome.
Where would you draw the line?
I don’t think judges are yet in the position to say. It’s a question for society, politicians, and legislation to resolve. That debate is really important.
I think that custody and family cases are one of the areas where essentially human judgment is expected, even by the younger generation. In complex commercial cases, I think that’s also the case. But I think we will whittle away at how commercial cases are decided by using AI to collate information to make the decision-making process better and easier.
We will allow more people access to justice more cheaply and more quickly using technology. That will be an overall good for the economy and for the people we serve.

US President Donald Trump said early Wednesday that his endorsement helped Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu perform better than expected in Israel's parliamentary election, as preliminary results showed his bloc leading but falling short of a governing majority, with less than half of ballot boxes counted.
With 48% of ballot boxes counted as of early Wednesday, Netanyahu's bloc was projected to secure 55 seats, six short of a majority in the 120-member Knesset. The opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, was projected to win 50 seats.

Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 in Gaza since October 2023, most of them women and children, while around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed, according to Palestinian authorities.
In November 2024, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.

The US has told several Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a “short, intense military campaign” against Iran after the November 3 midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing people briefed on the conversations.
The messages, conveyed through diplomatic and military channels, are among growing signs that the US and Israel are preparing a new round of heavy combat operations to weaken Iran and push it towards negotiations, according to the report.
The US military is moving a Patriot missile defence system from Texas to the region and has moved troops from bases where they were vulnerable, while US forces are restocking munitions and preparing bombers and fighter jets for strikes, the newspaper said, citing officials.
An additional aircraft carrier strike group and a Marine expeditionary unit are expected to join roughly 20 US warships in the Middle East next month, it added.
President Donald Trump has not made a final decision but is leaning towards a "large post-election attack" that could target Iranian infrastructure and nuclear sites, the report said, citing people familiar with his thinking.
The White House declined to comment on “sensitive military plans that may or may not exist.”
“President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon,” it said.
Speaking at a campaign rally in Lubbock, Texas on Tuesday, Trump said: “You’ll see Iran in a couple of weeks, if you don’t mind.”
“We obliterated Iran’s nuclear enrichment capacity with Operation Midnight Hammer and Operation Epic Fury and defeated them militarily, financially and otherwise. And it will all end very soon,” he said.
“It could be over whenever I wanted it to be over,” he added.
Trump has previously said that he will not attack Iran before the midterms.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28, prompting Tehran to respond with missile and drone attacks in the region and effectively close the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.
A memorandum of understanding was signed in June to pave the way for a final peace deal, but it collapsed amid disagreements, including over navigation in the strait.

Why India has soured on Trump ahead of US midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:43:40 UTC
14:43:40 KST

Why India has soured on Trump ahead of US midterms
Seven years after Modi backed Trump, analysts say New Delhi may now hope US midterm losses leave the president chastened.
New Delhi, India – Standing next to United States President Donald Trump, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi delivered praise after praise.
“Every time [we meet], he has been the same: warm, friendly, accessible, energetic, and full of wit,” he said of Trump, as they addressed a joint rally in a Houston, Texas, stadium packed with more than 50,000 Indian Americans.
That was in 2019, ahead of the 2020 US presidential vote, when Trump was facing a major electoral test – seeking re-election to a second term. Modi was, in effect, galvanising support for him among the Indian-American community, the wealthiest diaspora in the US.
Modi even borrowed a line from his own successful election campaigns, saying: “Abki baar, Trump sarkaar!”, Hindi for “This time, a Trump government.”
But Trump lost.
Seven years later, as Trump prepares for difficult midterm elections that could see him lose significant numbers in the US Congress, potentially crippling his legislative agenda, New Delhi’s equation with Washington could not be more different.
Far from endorsing Trump, Indian officials have in recent weeks been more direct than ever in their criticism of his administration, amid a series of setbacks to bilateral ties. And many analysts believe the Modi government may now actually prefer a Trump chastened by midterm losses.
Striking a nerve
India has long enjoyed bipartisan support in Washington. Yet traditionally, New Delhi’s strategic community has often felt more comfortable with Republican presidents in power.
It was under Ronald Reagan, as the Cold War wound down, that India and the US reset ties after decades of mistrust amid New Delhi’s strong relationship with Moscow. Then, between 2006 and 2008, under George W Bush, India and the US struck a landmark civil nuclear deal. India was allowed access to global nuclear technology and fuel despite not being a signatory to the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT). Under Bush, India and the US also signed major military pacts, including allowing US ships and planes refuelling and logistical access to Indian bases.
By contrast, New Delhi has often seen US Democratic administrations as more critical of India’s human rights record.
The tradition of friendly ties with US Republican presidents appeared set to continue under Trump, amid visible bonhomie between the US leader and Modi. The Indian prime minister even called Trump “India’s best friend in the White House”.
But Trump 2.0 has been very different, from India’s perspective.
So different that New Delhi has chosen to break with a long-held practice. India usually addresses divisive issues with friendly nations quietly, behind the scenes. But months of tensions on a string of issues have pushed India to adopt a more openly critical tone towards the White House.
Last month, speaking at an event in New York, India’s foreign minister, Minister of External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar, shared a pointed, blunt assessment of the Trump administration: It has been an insensitive partner to India’s concerns over “terrorism”; has warmed to its archrival Pakistan; and has pursued “self-centred” trade policies that have disproportionately hurt the Global South.
“Countries should not be so self-centred that you’re in your own world and take your decision, and say, ‘Well, it was not my intention to make your life difficult’,” he said.
One of the biggest sticking points between both capitals is an elusive trade deal that could bring relief to India, among the worst-hit countries under Trump’s tariff regime.
Earlier this month, India’s finance minister, Minister of Corporate Affairs Nirmala Sitharaman, said that the negotiations had reached a “plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very difficult”.
Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement has also often targeted Indians and Indian Americans, using racist tropes, accusing them of “stealing” jobs in the United States via programmes like the H-1B visa schemes. Anti-Indian rhetoric on US social media is at an all-time high. And early in his second term, Trump sent many undocumented Indian immigrants back home shackled in chains – a visual that stirred outrage in India.
Milan Vaishnav, director of the South Asia programme at the Washington, DC-based Carnegie Endowment for International Peace think tank, said the Indian government “can tolerate genuine policy differences with a US administration”. However, “the attacks on India and Indian Americans coming from this administration, and many of their allies in the media and on social media, have struck a nerve,” he said.
Vaishnav, like other analysts, told Al Jazeera that despite recent criticism coming from New Delhi, “the Modi government has shown admirable restraint in its response”.
‘Brought back distrust’
Since Trump returned to office in 2025, the US-India relationship has been beset by a seemingly never-ending series of crises.
Some of the irritants are: punitive US tariffs and stalled trade negotiations; Washington’s pressure on India to stop buying Russian oil; Trump’s repeated claims that he mediated an India-Pakistan ceasefire in 2025, which New Delhi rejects; closer US ties with Pakistan despite India’s concerns over “terrorism”; higher H-1B specialised worker visa fees in the US, and Trump’s wider immigration crackdown affecting Indian workers.
At one point, India was among the countries facing the worst Trump-imposed tariff rates. After the US Supreme Court in February struck down Trump’s sweeping tariffs on numerous nations, his administration swiftly turned to other tools, including a new 10 percent global tariff.
Last month, Trump signed a law under which the US can impose up to 100 percent tariffs on countries like India that buy Russian oil. However, he paused it to avoid driving up energy prices in the US ahead of November’s midterm elections, while keeping negotiations with Russia over Moscow’s war in Ukraine on track.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who visited India’s financial hub Mumbai this week, but skipped the capital, said in an interview with The Indian Express that “none of these tariffs are meant to punish or harm India”.
Rubio argued that Washington’s “broader foreign policy, unfortunately, involves a war going on between Russia and Ukraine” — and added that “one of the reasons why [Trump paused the tariff] is because he understands that it would have a very detrimental impact on a very important relationship with India”.
But Rubio did not rule out that similar measures would return in a matter of time. “I think the president is trying very hard to balance that… but it will be a challenge”, he remarked.
Praveen Donthi, a senior analyst at the Brussels-based International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera: “Under Trump 2.0, the bipartisan consensus on India seems to have ended in Washington.
“The sentiment [in Washington] seems too strong to be attributed solely to President Trump; it points to the broader American establishment,” Donthi said.
The measures undertaken by the Trump administration “have brought back distrust of the US among the Indian strategic establishment”, he said, referring to Cold War-era tensions.
Can a midterm loss subdue Trump?
The upcoming US midterm elections are crucial for Trump. If he loses control of Congress for the final two years of his presidency, it would give Democrats more power to scrutinise his administration’s policies.
Trump is facing the worst approval ratings of his political career amid record-high gas prices in the US due to the global energy crisis triggered by the US-Israel war on Iran, which began in February this year.
Vaishnav, of Carnegie Endowment, said that “a chastened Trump would be in India’s interests”.
“There are many Democrats on Capitol Hill, not to mention Republicans, who are livid with this administration’s handling of US-India ties,” he said. “While they might have their criticisms of India’s politics, economics, and foreign policy, they genuinely believe in the logic of a strong US-India partnership.”
A Democrat-dominated Congress could have a “moderating impact” on Washington’s foreign policy, he said.
But Michael Kugelman, a Washington-based analyst on South Asia, said he doubts Trump’s foreign policy would be affected by the election results, “at least not when it comes to the question of India”.
Kugelman noted that Trump is entering the last era of his presidency – he cannot legally run for a third term – and “he is going to continue to pursue a policy that he would think could best advance US economic interests” when it comes to dealing with New Delhi.
“If he thinks that could entail threatening additional tariffs on India, then he would do that.”
Crisis Group’s Donthi told Al Jazeera that New Delhi would hope that bilateral relations improve after Trump leaves office, “and that [Washington] can take a more patient, strategic approach”.
But, meanwhile, he said, a weakened Trump might not necessarily bring relief to India, “as there seems to be broader consensus [among Trump-aligned Republicans] on the need to pressure India”.
For New Delhi, that landscape marks a dramatic shift from just a few years ago.
Two years back, days after Trump had won the 2024 election, Foreign Minister Jaishankar said, with a wide smile, that “many countries are nervous about the US today, but let’s be honest — we [India] are not one of them”.
Today, those smiles are gone.

South Korea completes development of indigenous marine attack helicopter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Aamir Latif
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
South Korea has completed development of a domestically produced marine attack helicopter under a 450 billion-won ($337 million) project, with production expected to begin next year, local media reported Wednesday.
The helicopter, designed for multidimensional amphibious operations, is equipped with air-to-ground missiles and other weapons systems, Yonhap News Agency reported, citing the Defense Acquisition Program Administration (DAPA).
Based on a marine variant of the KUH-1 Surion helicopter, the aircraft incorporates additional weapons and systems designed to counter threats from enemy helicopters and drones, according to DAPA.
The project, launched in 2022, has undergone a series of evaluations, including live-fire tests involving turret-mounted machine guns, air-to-ground missiles, and guided and unguided rockets.
The helicopter passed a full combat suitability evaluation in July and received airworthiness certification in August, confirming that it meets the required standards for safe flight.
DAPA plans to begin production of approximately 20 helicopters in 2027.

Football Australia says it is monitoring the security situation in the Middle East ahead of two upcoming Socceroos friendlies.
The Australian team is scheduled to play Qatar in Doha and Jordan in Amman next month as the last outings ahead of January's Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia.
Recent violence in the region has heightened concerns, but FA says it expects the games to go ahead..
The Socceroos are set to forge ahead with plans to play friendlies in the Middle East next month in the face of the increasingly volatile conflict in the region.
Australia is scheduled to face Qatar in Doha on November 14 before taking on Jordan in Amman on November 17 in what will be the Socceroos' final hit-outs before coach Tony Popovic names his squad for January's Asian Cup.
But there are security concerns following violence this month, including a Houthi strike at the Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia, which is hosting the cup.
Last week nine people were gunned down by Syrian militants at an orthodox church in Jordan, one of the more stable countries in the Middle East.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade advises Australians to reconsider their need to travel to Jordan. Qatar is rated as a much safer destination.
As things stand Football Australia (FA) is expecting the games with Qatar and Jordan to go ahead as scheduled.
"Football Australia is closely monitoring the situation in the Middle East ahead of the Socceroos' matches against Qatar and Jordan in November," an FA spokesperson said in a statement to AAP.
"The safety and wellbeing of our players, staff and supporters remains paramount.
"Our experienced security team is actively monitoring developments and providing regular updates, and we will be guided by the advice of our head of security.
"Risk assessment is part of our planning for every national team camp, and it will be a key focus of our preparations for November."
While FA's decision to push on is encouraging, there is still no clear decision on what will happen with January's Asian Cup.
Saudi Arabia has been forced to move a friendly with South Korea to Qatar as part of the flow-on effect of the Riyadh attack, and several Asian Champions League games involving Saudi club sides have been postponed.
A decision is yet to be made as to whether the Asian Cup, which is expected to kick off with the hosts taking on Palestine in Riyadh on January 7, will still take place as scheduled.
Australia's is scheduled to take on Singapore in Khobar on January 9 for its first group game of the tournament.
There is growing concern that the Asian Cup would be delayed by 12 months, with AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa saying a decision may not be made until the end of November.
"If we need to make a decision then we will, but we could move back a year to 2028 if we need to," he said in Zurich this month.
"But at the moment we are monitoring the situation and everything is on schedule."

Safira Amazan asks why decisions are made in English but taken in French
There is a curious asymmetry between English and French: in English, we make decisions; in French, we take them (prendre une décision). At first glance, this looks like a harmless idiomatic difference, the sort of thing language learners simply memorize. But idioms often reveal more than grammar. Languages do not merely label reality; they frame it. Therefore, the verbs attached to abstract ideas can reflect how cultures have historically understood action, responsibility, authority, and thought itself.
A decision is not just a mental event. Depending on the language, it may be something one constructs, assumes, arrives at, or seizes. English frames decision as something produced. To make something implies fabrication, authorship, and agency. We make plans, make promises, make arrangements, make mistakes. To make a decision suggests that the speaker actively brings the outcome into existence.
French approaches the same concept differently. Prendre une décision suggests acquisition rather than fabrication. Even in English, we already use “take” to describe acts of assumption or commitment: we take a train, take responsibility, take a position, take power. Through that lens, the French construction feels less foreign. The decision appears less as something manufactured and more as something one adopts or commits to. The emphasis shifts from creation to assumption.
Neither framing is more rational than the other. They simply encode different conceptual habits. Seen more broadly, this is not just an oddity of idiom but an example of how languages structure abstract thought through metaphor. Cognitive linguists George Lakoff and Mark Johnson famously described this through the theory of conceptual metaphor, arguing that humans routinely understand abstract concepts through embodied physical experience. We “grasp” ideas, “weigh” options, “attack” arguments, and “build” theories. The metaphors vary by language, but the underlying mechanism is strikingly universal.
Consider a few comparisons. German uses eine Entscheidung treffen, literally “to meet” or “to strike” a decision, suggesting precision or impact. Spanish uses tomar una decisión, much like French, emphasizing taking rather than making. Italian follows with prendere una decisione. English stands somewhat apart in its preference for productive creation.
Those patterns are not arbitrary; they are shaped by the historical paths languages have taken. English developed through unusually layered linguistic influence. Its Germanic roots contributed a direct, action-heavy verbal vocabulary, while the Norman Conquest of 1066 introduced sustained Anglo-Norman French influence into English law, administration, and elite discourse over centuries. That hybrid inheritance helps explain why English so comfortably pairs blunt Anglo-Saxon verbs like make, take, and do with abstract Latinate nouns like decision, obligation, authority, and contract.
Even the word decision carries its own historical metaphor. It derives from the Latin decidere, meaning “to cut off” or “to settle by cutting away alternatives.” The original conceptual image is not one of creation at all, but separation. English, however, overlays that inherited abstraction with the distinctly productive verb make.
French followed a different historical path. Because of its stronger continuity with Latin administrative, legal, and intellectual traditions, French became closely associated with centralized governance and codified institutional language. Yet linguistic inheritance alone does not explain why certain framings persist; social structures help reinforce them.
More broadly, culture and institutions shape how linguistic habits become normalized. English-speaking commercial and political traditions have often emphasized individual initiative and agency, a tendency that aligns neatly with expressions like make a decision, make progress, or make history. French administrative and legal traditions, shaped more visibly by centralized state structures and codified systems, have often favored linguistic constructions that suggest assumption, adoption, or formal positioning within an existing framework (prendre ses responsabilités, prendre position).
Language may reflect and reinforce such tendencies, but it would be a mistake to treat language as destiny. Claims about linguistic determinism should be approached cautiously. A French executive is not less decisive than an American CEO because of verb choice. Still, language creates habitual pathways of interpretation. It nudges thought, even if it does not confine it.
That influence appears not only in institutional language but in everyday emotional expression. English speakers fall in love. French speakers tomber amoureux—also “fall”—but other languages conceptualize love differently: as catching something (Russian), entering a condition (Japanese), or undergoing possession (Arabic). Such metaphors matter because they shape how experiences are intuitively framed long before speakers consciously reflect on them.
Perhaps nowhere is this clearer than in legal language, where wording carries direct institutional consequences. Contract law offers a particularly revealing example. In English contract law, a clause is usually treated as a specific contract provision whose meaning evolves through court interpretation, precedent, and the parties’ negotiated allocation of risk. French contract law uses the same term, clause, for a specific contractual provision, but the interpretive approach differs. Because French law emerges from the civil law tradition, contractual provisions are read within a framework more explicitly structured by codified principles, mandatory statutory rules, and doctrinal coherence. English courts generally focus on the objective meaning of the words used, while French law gives greater weight to the parties’ shared intention and the purpose behind the provision, a distinction explored in comparative analyses such as Performance of Another’s Obligation: French and English Law Contrasted, by Simon Whittaker. The terminology overlaps, but the legal architecture surrounding that terminology does not. Shared vocabulary does not guarantee shared interpretation.
Contract law proposes an especially concrete reminder of a much broader principle: linguistic equivalence is not always conceptual equivalence. This is the broader lesson of translation. Words do not simply move between languages carrying identical meaning intact. They arrive with different assumptions, institutional histories, and conceptual baggage.
To ask why decisions are made in English but taken in French is really to ask a deeper question: do we imagine human action as creation, selection, or assumption?
Language does not answer that question definitively.
But it often tells us which answer we are most likely to find intuitive.
Safira Amazan is a cross-cultural communication specialist, university lecturer, and general manager of Cultures Communicate at the University of Chicago. She specializes in translation, localization, cultural competence training, and medical interpretation across French, English, Spanish, and Creole languages. She holds a master’s in legal translation and has additional studies in international law.

Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition has secured a parliamentary majority in Israel’s election, according to preliminary results released early Wednesday.
With more than 40 percent of votes counted, Netanyahu’s bloc was projected to win 57 seats, while the opposition was on course for 47, The Times of Israel reported, citing Israel’s election committee.
The two Arab parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, were projected to hold a combined 16 seats, potentially giving them a decisive role in forming the next government.
A majority in Israel’s 120-seat parliament, the Knesset, requires 61 seats.
The figures had already shifted considerably since the count reached 25 percent earlier in the night, and further changes remained possible.
Netanyahu’s Likud party was projected to become the largest party, followed by Yashar!, led by opposition politician Gadi Eisenkot.
Netanyahu ruled out forming a government dependent on support from Arab parties during an overnight speech.
Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas, however, expressed hope Tuesday that his party could help the opposition secure a majority.
Eisenkot said he would work toward forming a united Zionist government.
“The people have voted for change,” he said, adding that “the coalition of failure has lost the people’s trust.”
The election follows three years of regional conflict, beginning with Hamas’ October 7, 2023, attack on Israel.
Israel subsequently launched its war in Gaza, where more than 70,000 people have been killed, according to Gaza’s health authorities.
Israel has also fought in Lebanon, struck targets in Syria and Yemen, and waged war against Iran alongside the United States.

Viking-era Danish coin sells for 136,000 DKK at Copenhagen auction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:31:08 UTC
14:31:08 KST

A Danish coin dating back more than 1,000 years has sold for 18,300 euros, approximately 136,000 DKK, at an auction in Copenhagen.
The coin, associated with Viking king Svend Tveskæg, fetched more than twice its estimated price of 6,000 to 8,000 euros, or roughly 45,000 to 60,000 DKK.
Auction house Stack’s Bowers confirmed the sale on its website following Tuesday’s auction.
The coin is considered the first official Danish coin to feature both the name of a Danish ruler and the country’s name.
Svend Tveskæg was the first ruler to have his name appear on a Danish coin.
“This coin type is considered the first official Danish coin and has an exceptionally great historical significance because it was the first Danish coin that bore both the king’s and the country’s name,” the auction house stated.
However, archaeological discoveries indicate that coins were used in Denmark long before this particular type was produced.
The coin weighs just 1.95 grams and had previously been broken into several pieces before being repaired, according to the auction house.
It belonged to a collection assembled by Danish businessman Lars Emil Bruun, who died in 1923.
Bruun made his fortune as a butter wholesaler, exporting canned butter to markets around the world.
In his will, he stipulated that his extensive coin collection could not be sold until 100 years after his death.
Several other coins from Bruun’s collection were also sold during Tuesday’s auction in Copenhagen.
The auction is scheduled to continue Wednesday, October 28.

Study finds problematic social media use more common among girls
More than one in five girls aged 15 to 21 in a Danish study show signs of problematic social media use, compared with fewer than one in 10 boys, according to research from the Rockwool Foundation, a Danish research foundation.
The study surveyed 8,239 young people about their use of platforms such as Snapchat, TikTok, Instagram and Facebook. Researchers also asked about their well-being and the amount of time they spend on social media.
Based on their answers, participants were classified using an internationally recognized scale for problematic social media use.
The results show that 22.2 percent of the girls surveyed fell into the category, compared with 9.6 percent of the boys.
Nadja Eifler, a PhD student at the Rockwool Foundation, said part of the difference could be explained by the activities young people choose online.
“In the study, we asked specifically about social media such as Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat, so part of the difference between girls and boys may lie in the fact that many boys spend more time on computer games, which is also for many a social activity where you can be in dialogue with friends,” she said.
The study also found a link between problematic social media use and poor well-being, particularly among girls.
“We can clearly see that poor well-being is most widespread among young people with problematic social media use, especially for the girls, where more than half of these young women have low well-being,” Eifler said.
Among girls who did not have problems with social media use, just under four in 10 reported low well-being.
The report recommends looking beyond the number of hours young people spend on social media when assessing whether their use is problematic.
Other warning signs include difficulty reducing use, feeling restless or uneasy when a phone is out of reach, and social media having a negative effect on school or education.
The findings suggest that how young people use social media, and how it affects their daily lives, may be important factors alongside the time they spend online.
ATP’s investment return falls to 1.5 percent after weak quarter
Danish pension provider ATP recorded a negative investment result in the third quarter, reducing its total return for the first nine months of the year to 1.5 percent.
The company announced the figures in a press release on its website but did not disclose the size of the investment loss during the third quarter alone.
ATP’s return stood at 14.5 percent when it published its half-year report a few months earlier. The latest figures show that much of the return earned during the first half of the year was lost in the following three months.
ATP Chief Executive Officer Martin Præstegaard described the period as difficult, pointing to rising interest rates as a key factor behind the weaker result.
“We have had a challenging third quarter, where rising interest rates have affected the result negatively,” he said.
He added that the company had delivered a good investment return during the first half of the year, leaving the overall return positive for the first nine months.
“The interest rate fluctuations do not change the fact that pensioners can count on receiving the pension they are guaranteed, and a robust bonus capacity allows us to increase pensions for all members,” Præstegaard said.
ATP is Denmark’s statutory supplementary pension scheme. Employees who work at least nine hours a week and their employers pay contributions into the scheme. People receiving certain public benefits also contribute to ATP.
Around 5.8 million people are members of the scheme.
ATP provides a guaranteed, lifelong monthly pension payment that supplements the Danish state pension after people stop working.
The company’s investment portfolio accounts for approximately 20 percent of its total assets.
The latest figures cover the first nine months of the year, including the period from July through September, when rising interest rates weighed on investment performance. Despite the decline in the third quarter, ATP said its overall return for the year remained positive.

Danish company Epiq ApS has recalled four electrical products sold at Bilka and Føtex supermarkets because they pose a risk of electric shock.
The recall covers power strips, extension cord sets and a double-socket adapter sold between June 2 and September 18, 2026, the company announced in a press release.

The company has urged customers to “immediately stop using the products” and return them to the store where they were purchased.
