From us, and from the leadership of the nation, he has our full appreciation and praise. We are proud that he is part of our team… part of the story of our nation… and part of what the UAE stands for… a nation of compassion… a nation of peace… and a nation of life," he wrote in a post on X.In an earlier interview with the UAE's state-owned newspaper The National, Machchhar recalled the attack by the co-pilot and said he suffered several blows before he could open the cockpit door.“The first time when I was hit … my thought was something's gone horribly wrong with the aircraft structure, which has fallen on my head. It almost made me fall on my control column. In the next couple of seconds, when the hits kept on coming, (I realised) it was the other person who I thought was supposed to be on the team.”“My immediate action was to free myself from the seat belts. And I tried to just block the blows as much as I could, because the blows were coming on the head… While the first few blows came in, my vision … it was so narrow. I lost a lot. I was just looking (at) outlines,” he told The National.“Immediately, my hand went to the knob which opens the door. And (I was) screaming for my colleagues. I believe that was the first time when I lost consciousness. I fell face down in the cockpit,” he added.Recalling the moment when the aircraft plunged 17,000 feet, Machchhar said, “The scariest thing that I heard and felt was the engines spooling down.”Despite the attack, Machchhar said his love for flying remained unchanged.
“Did my love die for aviation? Not at all. Not at all. I'm just glad that I was able to do my part.”Machchhar managed to unlatch the cockpit door, allowing passengers and off-duty crew members to enter and restrain the co-pilot. The co-pilot had attacked him with an axe in an attempt to bring down the aircraft. A hijacking distress signal was also sent.The flight was diverted to Tabuk, where it made an emergency landing with the help of passengers who helped land the aircraft. All 180 occupants disembarked without injury, according to the account of the incident.Israeli President Isaac Herzog has also announced that he would confer Israel's Presidential Award for Civilian Heroism on Machchhar.

World Insights: COP17 nears conclusion as negotiators make progress but face hurdles
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:30:59 CST
12:30:59 KST

YEREVAN, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- The 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations (UN) Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in the Armenian capital of Yerevan has entered its final stretch.
The conference has adopted 14 decisions and secured more than 1.8 billion U.S. dollars in financial commitments. Yet negotiators remain divided over some of the most contentious issues, including who should bear the cost of protecting nature and how global commitments can be translated into measurable results.
With the conference due to conclude on Friday, the focus has shifted from reaffirming global biodiversity goals to reaching agreement on how to achieve them.
TANGIBLE PROGRESS
The COP17 marks the first global review of progress under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted in 2022 with 23 targets to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.
There are encouraging signs of international cooperation, said Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity, noting that nearly 90 percent of the convention's parties have established national biodiversity targets, while more than 70 percent have submitted national reports.
The negotiations have also yielded concrete results. Parties have adopted 14 decisions under the convention, covering areas such as invasive alien species, biosafety, gender equality and education.
Funding announcements have added to the summit's momentum, with new commitments from governments, philanthropic organizations and other partners.
The Executive Council of the China-initiated Kunming Biodiversity Fund has approved nine biodiversity conservation projects worth roughly 4.5 million dollars for developing nations, Dong Baotong, vice minister of China's Ministry of Ecology and Environment, said Monday.
China has contributed 400 million yuan (60 million dollars) to the fund, which supports biodiversity conservation in developing countries. Schomaker depicted the initiative as an agile instrument for channeling support to where it is needed.
Elsewhere, nine philanthropic organizations pledged 500 million dollars through 2030 for species recovery, while the Global Biodiversity Framework Fund secured over 60 million dollars in new pledges.
These achievements demonstrate that environmental multilateralism is continuing to deliver, even amid profound geopolitical shifts, said Inger Andersen, executive director of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP).
"Nature is not a luxury we protect when economies can afford it," said Andersen. "Nature is what makes economies possible."
OBSTACLES AHEAD
Securing new financial commitments is one thing; establishing a sustainable, long-term funding model for biodiversity conservation is another.
Despite the pledges announced in Yerevan, countries remain divided over who should contribute to international biodiversity finance, how much they should pay and how the funds should be allocated.
Other sticking points include reforming subsidies and incentives that harm nature, arrangements for indigenous peoples and local communities, and aligning biodiversity action with climate commitments and other international obligations.
Andersen said ministers are attending the conference's final week to help break the deadlock, particularly on resource mobilization and the global review.
"Financing the destruction of nature with 30 dollars against every dollar spent restoring it is like paying 30 people to tear down your house for every one hired to rebuild it," Schomaker said, framing the way forward around three priorities: accountability, alignment and acceleration.
According to Schomaker, "accountability" means identifying where countries are falling short through national reporting and scientific evidence, while "acceleration" means stepping up efforts to meet the framework's 2030 targets. "Alignment" may prove the hardest part, requiring governments to ensure that public budgets, private investment, economic policies and financial incentives reinforce rather than undermine biodiversity objectives.
The private sector is already pressing for change. More than 130 businesses and financial institutions have called for faster reform of incentives harmful to biodiversity.
Yet, for companies and investors, uncertainty remains over how global biodiversity targets will translate into national regulations, investment requirements and standards for measuring conservation results. Without clearer and more consistent rules, even a growing willingness to invest in nature may struggle to produce results at scale.
Meanwhile, the environmental pressures driving the negotiations are intensifying. UNEP's latest Emissions Gap Report warns that global warming could reach 2.8 degrees Celsius this century under current policies, with potentially severe consequences for ecosystems and biodiversity.
The United Nations' State of Biodiversity Action report, released ahead of COP17, found that fewer than half of the national biodiversity targets assessed by countries were on track.
Against this backdrop, much now hinges on the proposed "Yerevan Pathway," a document that identifies measurable priorities to address gaps in implementing global biodiversity targets over the next two years.
The conference has already shown that multilateral cooperation can deliver decisions and mobilize resources. Whether it can also resolve the harder questions of financing and implementation will be the real test of its success.
"COP17 will be judged by the long-term results we achieve together after the conference, rather than the number of statements made in Yerevan," said Armenian Environment Minister and COP17 President Hambardzum Matevosyan. ■

WELLINGTON, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's central bank on Wednesday kept the official cash rate unchanged at 2.75 percent, with the monetary policy committee voting 4-3 to hold the rate amid rising inflation risks.
Annual consumer price index inflation eased to 3.7 percent in the September quarter from 4.1 percent in June, coming in lower than expected. However, core inflation measures have risen to around the top of the committee's 1 to 3 percent target band, while price increases have become more broad-based across the economy, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand said in a statement.
The bank expects annual inflation to rise to 4.4 percent in the December quarter, largely reflecting higher fuel prices amid ongoing disruptions in global energy markets. The New Zealand dollar has also fallen by around 3 percent since early September, adding to near-term inflation pressures.
The economy continues to recover, although conditions remain uneven. Export-exposed sectors are benefiting from high commodity prices, strong demand for goods exports and increased tourist numbers, while domestic demand remains subdued outside exporting centers, the statement said.
The committee remains focused on returning inflation to the 2 percent midpoint of its target band over the medium term. It said tighter monetary policy would likely be required, depending on the economic outlook, while warning that prolonged high inflation could affect inflation expectations and price- and wage-setting behavior, making inflation more persistent. ■

Feature: Sixteen years of drills to secure three minutes to safety at rural Chinese school
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:30:25 CST
12:30:25 KST

This file photo taken in March 2026 shows a teacher tutoring students on key points for evacuation during an earthquake drill at Jieduo Township Central Boarding School in Jieduo of Yushu Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, northwest China's Qinghai Province. (Xinhua)
XINING, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Seven-year-old Tenzin Wangso was curled up on his dormitory bed, too frightened to move, when his math teacher Karma Tenzin found him.
The teacher grabbed a quilt, wrapped it around the boy and carried him downstairs to the playground. He then rushed back into the building to make sure no children had been left behind.
A 7.0-magnitude earthquake had struck Baqen County in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region at 10:33 p.m. on Oct. 22, sending strong tremors through neighboring Jieduo Township of Yushu Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture in Qinghai Province in northwest China. Most of the 120 boarding students at the township's rural boarding school were already asleep when the quake hit.
Within about three minutes after the quake struck, all 120 had reached the playground, according to the school's surveillance footage. None was injured.
The school, more than 4,200 meters above sea level on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, had been practicing for such an emergency for 16 years.
Chime Tsering, principal of Jieduo Township Central Boarding School, still remembers the morning of April 14, 2010.
He had arrived as vice principal just a month earlier. Back then, the school consisted of two rows of single-story buildings, one for classrooms and the other for dormitories.
When a 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck Yushu that morning, teachers and students were attending morning study sessions. Nearly 2,700 people died across the region.
"We had no experience dealing with an earthquake. Everyone was terrified," Chime Tsering recalled.
Teachers and students made it to the playground. Subsequent inspections found cracks in both buildings, which were later demolished and rebuilt.
This experience prompted the school to rethink its emergency procedures. As local education authorities called for more earthquake drills, Chime Tsering and his colleagues began working out how to get students to safety.
At first, they simply designated evacuation routes. Early drills took six or seven minutes. As teachers identified problems and revised the procedures, that duration fell to three or four minutes, and eventually to under three.
They also began holding drills at different times of day, including at night, when children would have to be woken and guided out of their dormitories.
Teachers were given specific responsibilities: waking students, directing them at stairwells and guiding them through exits.
The school now holds emergency drills at least once a month, covering both earthquakes and fires, with two or three nighttime exercises each semester. Its most recent earthquake drill was held roughly two weeks before the Oct. 22 quake.
The dormitory building has two designated evacuation routes and the teaching building has three. Each teacher is also assigned a group of 13 students to look after in daily school life, as well as specific rooms or classes to oversee during emergencies.
Karma Tenzin, who has taught math at the school for three years, was grading homework when the tremors began.
"The ground was shaking violently, and the tables and chairs were moving," he said. It was the strongest earthquake he had felt in recent years.
He and other teachers headed for the student dormitories.
Karma Tenzin was responsible for checking five rooms in the boys' dormitory. Moving from one room to the next, he was most worried about younger pupils, who might be slow to react or fall during the evacuation.
Among them was Tenzin Wangso, the first-grader he carried to safety. The boy had started school only in September.
Another teacher, Pema Wanggyal, also carried a first-grader out of the building.
On the playground, children gathered in coats and quilts while teachers checked attendance and comforted those who were frightened.
The school put up temporary tents that night. Parents began collecting their children the next day.
Most of the school buildings had been rebuilt after the 2010 earthquake. They remained largely intact, although fine cracks appeared in some walls.
"Only through repeated practice can we stay calm when something really happens and protect every child," Chime Tsering said.
The school has more than 170 students, most of them children of local herding families. Many live in remote pastoral areas where mobile phone reception is unreliable.
With in-person classes temporarily suspended, teachers began visiting students' homes on Oct. 25 to inform parents of the arrangements and find out whether the children had the equipment and internet access needed for online lessons.
"We have to visit families one by one," Karma Tenzin noted. "We also need to understand their circumstances before deciding how online teaching can be arranged."
For him, the greatest relief was that the drills had worked when they were needed, and that every child had come through the earthquake unharmed. ■

Iran war has cost $47 billion, U.S. military says
The war with Iran has cost the U.S. military at least $47.1 billion as of mid-October, according to a new estimate from U.S. Central Command obtained by CBS News.
The bulk of the war's price tag is the cost of replacing expended munitions, which CENTCOM pegged at around $29 billion, according to the latest estimate, which was provided to lawmakers. The military also tallied $6.1 billion to replace lost equipment and around $11.9 billion in incremental costs like support for American service members.
The estimate does not include the cost of damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East, many of which were targeted by Iranian drones and missiles.
By comparison, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told lawmakers three months ago the war had cost around $37.5 billion, not including damaged U.S. bases.
The Congressional Budget Office said last month the war could cost $2 billion to $3 billion per month for as long as it continues, in part due to the need to replace interceptor missiles to defend against Iranian attacks. That cost could rise during tit-for-tat exchanges between the U.S. and Iran, which were common over the summer but have been quiet in recent weeks.
CBS News has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.
The Iran war will enter its ninth month this week, and the conflict's future is unclear. President Trump has suggested he might restart hostilities with Iran after next month's midterm elections unless Iran agrees to a deal. "We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," he told supporters during a rally in Florida last week.
The Pentagon's inspector general said last month the U.S. is facing "strategic inventory shortfalls" due to the number of munitions expended during the war, leading the Defense Department to work to speed up production. The Trump administration has argued the military isn't facing shortages, with Mr. Trump saying in early September, "we have virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition, far more than we could ever use."
The administration asked Congress to approve tens of billions of dollars in supplemental military funding earlier this year, in part due to the Iran war. That request has not yet passed, and Democrats have pressed Hegseth for a more detailed accounting of the war's cost.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Centers for Disease Control said Tuesday that the health coin incentive program has coincided with increased vaccination against flu, COVID-19, and pneumococcal disease since launching on Oct. 1.
The program awards adults aged 18 and older 450 health coins for flu vaccination, 900 for COVID-19 vaccination, and 600 for pneumococcal vaccination, whether publicly or privately funded, per a press release. One coin is worth NT$1 (US$0.03) and can be redeemed under the program's rules.
The CDC said that, as of Oct. 26, about 2.725 million publicly funded flu vaccine doses had been administered to adults, up approximately 7% from the same period last year. Another 288,000 doses were privately funded, up about 70%.
For COVID-19, approximately 1.176 million publicly funded doses had been administered to adults, up 35% year over year.
Pneumococcal vaccinations also increased. About 104,000 publicly funded doses and 3,000 privately funded doses were administered to adults, representing 3.5 times and 2.4 times the respective totals during the 26 days before the incentive program began.
The CDC also reported that influenza is circulating widely, with influenza A accounting for most infections and the H1N1 subtype making up 93.4% of detected flu viruses.
During the 2026-27 flu season, Taiwan had recorded 391 severe cases and 57 deaths as of Oct. 26. Of the severe cases, 380 involved H1N1, nine involved untyped influenza A, and two involved influenza B.
Of the deaths, 54 involved H1N1 and three involved untyped influenza A, per the press release.
The second phase of publicly funded flu and COVID-19 vaccinations for adults aged 50 to 64 without high-risk chronic conditions is scheduled to begin Nov. 2. Eligible people can receive vaccinations at contracted medical facilities or community vaccination stations organized by local health bureaus.
As temperatures cool, the CDC urged the public to get vaccinated and maintain good hygiene, including washing hands frequently, wearing masks when appropriate, and staying home when sick.
People experiencing warning signs such as shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, bloody sputum, chest pain, altered consciousness, or low blood pressure should seek medical attention promptly. Doctors can assess whether antiviral treatment is appropriate.

Australia providing 'extraordinary' support to ICC staff amid Trump sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
03:10:07 UTC
12:10:07 KST

Australia and other countries supporting ICC amid Trump sanctions
In short:
Australia and other countries are supporting International Criminal Court staff amid ongoing sanctions by the Trump administration, a senior court official says.
ICC deputy prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan said the organisation had received help publicly and through "quiet diplomacy behind closed doors".
She said the ICC was determined to protect staff from the financial implications of US sanctions.
A top International Criminal Court (ICC) official says Australia and other countries are providing "extraordinary" support to help protect the court's staff from the Trump administration's latest sanctions assault, while vowing that the court will not be deterred from pressing on with its work.
ICC deputy prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan, a senior court official who has already been personally sanctioned by the US, is visiting Canberra and Brisbane this week for talks with jurists and officials from across Australia and the Pacific.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has labelled the ICC a "rogue court" and has vowed to demolish it "brick by brick".
The Trump administration has rolled out successive waves of sanctions against the court, including new institutional sanctions designed to cripple the ICC by cutting it off from financial and support services.
The latest sanctions will freeze the court's assets in the US, as well as block financial transactions and IT agreements the ICC has with US companies.
Time to step up
Ms Khan told the ABC that while the sanctions had already created some difficulties, the ICC was heartened that many countries had lent support — some in public and others via "quiet diplomacy behind closed doors".
"I think this is the time when states must step up and support this process [of multilateralism] and support the institutions which are under attack," Ms Khan said.
The deputy prosecutor said the court was determined to protect its staff from the financial impacts of the move, and was adopting new systems to circumvent the sanctions and allow it to keep running.
"We have been working very hard to insulate the court as well as ensuring that our work continues," she said.
"Our main priority is that we continue to serve the victims who come to the court, telling us their stories and wanting their voices to be heard."
The ICC drew furious condemnation from the US and Israel when it announced it would pursue Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant for war crimes and crimes against humanity.
More recently it unsealed arrest warrants for several major Taliban leaders in Afghanistan for their policies persecuting women and girls.
Sanctions effect hard to predict
The latest wave of sanctions announced by the Trump administration on October 9 is meant to target the ICC rather than the large cohort of lawyers and staff who work for it.
The measures include a 180-day grace period before they are fully implemented.
But Ms Khan said the impact of sanctions was unpredictable and the court could not know at this stage how many of its staff might struggle with banking or other services as a result.
"We don't know which institutions will over-comply," she said.
The Australian government copped criticism from international lawyers who accused it of moving "sluggishly" after it joined a statement criticising the most recent sanctions about three days after it was first issued.
But Ms Khan praised the response from Canberra, saying its public statement of support behind the court was valuable.
She said Australian officials in the Netherlands had provided "visible" and "really satisfactory" help to Australians working for the court, including on ensuring they could keep accessing banking and financial services.
The deputy prosecutor said the ICC and other multilateral institutions had to hold the line in the face of growing pressure from the Trump administration and other international forces.
"Multilateralism gives everyone a voice," she said.
"Any attempt … to reverse all the work that has gone behind the rules-based order must be a negative step for the world, and the international community."
She said the court had enormous relevance to the Pacific, pointing to a 2024 proposal by Vanuatu, co-sponsored by Fiji and Samoa, calling for ecocide to be recognised as an independent international crime.

The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
03:02:38 UTC
12:02:38 KST

The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought
- Date:
- October 27, 2026
- Source:
- Yale School of Medicine
- Summary:
- A major new study reveals that autistic children’s brains process faces differently, and those differences may begin earlier than scientists previously thought. Researchers found that brain signals associated with recognizing faces become more specialized as neurotypical children grow older, but show much less change in autistic children. The discovery could help explain why some autistic people have difficulty recognizing faces and reading emotions.
- Share:
A major new study has uncovered important differences in how the brains of autistic children respond to human faces. Published in Nature Mental Health, the research is among the most extensive investigations yet into how face perception works in autism.
Some autistic people tend to look at faces less frequently or make less eye contact. They may also find it more difficult to remember faces or interpret facial expressions compared with neurotypical individuals. Scientists have spent decades investigating the brain activity behind these differences. In the early 2000s, for example, researchers at Yale reported that brain regions responsible for processing faces showed lower activity in autistic individuals than in people without autism.
James McPartland, PhD, Harris Professor in the Child Study Center and director of the Center for Brain and Mind Health, studies how autistic people process faces using electroencephalography (EEG), a technique that records the brain's electrical activity. Previous EEG studies, however, have typically examined signals from limited regions rather than analyzing activity across the entire scalp.
To gain a more complete picture, McPartland and his colleagues conducted a study involving approximately 400 autistic children, examining electrical signals recorded across the scalp. They discovered that brain activity associated with face recognition was less clearly distinguishable in autistic participants. They also identified a striking difference in development: In neurotypical children, the brain's response to faces became more specialized with age, while autistic children did not show the same pattern.
"This is the first time we've leveraged the full volume of very rich information provided by an EEG recording to understand face perception and autism," McPartland says.
How Scientists Discovered Differences in Autistic Brain Activity
McPartland compares traditional approaches to studying face recognition with attempting to understand traffic throughout an entire city by monitoring just one downtown street.
"That's the way most research on face processing so far has worked," McPartland says.
The new approach provides a much broader perspective, similar to observing traffic across an entire city using satellite imagery. To investigate these patterns, the researchers analyzed information collected through the Autism Biomarkers Consortium for Clinical Trials (ABC-CT). The dataset included autistic and neurotypical children across different age groups.
During the experiments, participants viewed pictures of faces and everyday objects while EEG equipment recorded their brain activity. Instead of concentrating on a small number of recording locations, the scientists examined electrical signals from all 128 electrodes positioned around each participant's scalp.
They then applied machine learning techniques to determine whether patterns in the recordings could reveal what each child was viewing.
The results showed that brain activity provided a clearer indication of face viewing in neurotypical children than in autistic children. In other words, the electrical signals associated with seeing faces were less distinguishable in the autistic group.
"The neural activity that we measure at the scalp is just not as distinct in autistic children," says first author Jason Griffin, PhD, assistant professor of psychology at University of Houston. Griffin previously worked as a postdoctoral researcher in McPartland's laboratory.
The researchers also found that the ability to identify what a child was viewing from brain activity improved with age among neurotypical participants. This age related improvement was not observed in autistic children, suggesting that their neural responses to faces develop along a different pattern.
"Their face-specific processing is not following the same trajectory," Griffin says.
Face Recognition Differences May Begin Earlier Than Previously Thought
Beyond identifying differences in brain activity, the study offers new insight into how early those differences emerge during face perception.
Recognizing someone involves multiple stages of neural processing. The sequence begins when visual information enters the eyes and continues as the brain interprets that information until a face is recognized.
Much of the earlier research on autism and face perception has concentrated on a brain signal called the N170. This measurable change in electrical activity typically occurs about 170 milliseconds after a person sees a face. Previous studies have shown that the N170 response tends to occur later in autistic individuals.
By analyzing brain activity over a wider period, the researchers found evidence that differences in face processing begin before this familiar signal appears. This suggests that autism related differences may arise at earlier stages of visual processing than researchers had previously established.
"But when you look at face processing through an approach that's more inclusive of the full temporal range of information, we're seeing that differences in autism occur even earlier," McPartland says.
What the Discovery Could Mean for Autism Diagnosis and Early Support
The findings could eventually influence how researchers approach autism diagnosis and the development of supportive interventions.
Historically, some clinicians attempted to address difficulties with face perception by requiring autistic individuals to maintain eye contact. Research has since shown that forcing eye contact is not an effective solution. A better understanding of how face processing develops in the brain could help identify approaches that are more useful and appropriate.
An ongoing challenge in autism research is separating neurological differences associated with autism itself from changes that may develop through the experience of living with the condition. According to the researchers, the patterns identified in this study suggest that differences in face processing are connected to underlying developmental characteristics of autism rather than simply reflecting accumulated life experiences.
"When we're seeing this expected refinement and specialization in non-autistic people, we're seeing a reduced developmental change in autistic people," McPartland explains.
Because the differences appear during development, the findings also raise the possibility that support aimed at helping autistic children interpret facial emotions could be particularly beneficial when introduced earlier in childhood.
However, the researchers emphasize that autism does not necessarily create difficulties that require intervention. Many neurodivergent people experience little or no impairment related to their autism and may neither need nor want additional support. For others, challenges with recognizing faces or understanding facial expressions can complicate everyday social interactions.
"Imagine navigating life when it's hard for you to perceive the information in another person's face, from navigating a playground to navigating a job interview," McPartland says. "This is one of the critical areas that causes difficulty for many autistic people."
New Brain Signals Could Help Improve Autism Diagnosis
Another potential application involves the search for more objective ways to assess autism. Currently, clinicians diagnose autism primarily by evaluating behavior because reliable biological tests are not yet available for routine diagnosis.
Scientists are investigating several possible biomarkers, which are measurable biological characteristics that could improve diagnostic assessments or help distinguish different groups within the autism spectrum.
The newly identified patterns of face related brain activity could contribute to that effort. By examining how these neural signals differ among individuals, researchers may eventually develop additional diagnostic tools or better identify autistic people who are likely to benefit from particular forms of support, including social skills therapy.
Although more research is necessary before these findings can be used in clinical practice, the study provides a new way to investigate how the autistic brain processes faces and how those responses change throughout childhood.
"This is a first step in introducing a new biomarker," McPartland says.

Materials provided by Yale School of Medicine. Original written by Isabella Backman. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

- Jason W. Griffin, Alan H. Gerber, Kaylee Litson, Susan Faja, Shafali Jeste, Natalia Kleinhans, Geraldine Dawson, Adam Naples, April R. Levin, Sara Jane Webb, Frederick Shic, Catherine Sugar, James Dziura, James C. McPartland. Decoding the temporal dynamics of face-specific neural representations in autism. Nature Mental Health, 2026; 4 (7): 1109 DOI: 10.1038/s44220-026-00672-y

In brief
- Core inflation rose faster than expected, adding to pressure on the Reserve Bank.
- Fresh inflation data has fuelled expectations of another interest rate hike.
Core inflation climbed 1 per cent in Australia over the quarter, with the Reserve Bank governor warning underlying inflation is still too high.
The September quarter increase in the trimmed mean was in line with economists' expectations but exceeded the central bank's forecast of a 0.8 per cent increase.
On an annualised basis, the trimmed mean — a measure of underlying inflation that removes the biggest price swings — rose 3.6 per cent.
Headline inflation was hotter than expected by the market, at 1.3 per cent over the quarter.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers acknowledged inflation is persisting "longer than anyone would like" and citing the war in the Middle East as a major factor.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Markets had upped their bets for a November hike after comments in the past week by the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) deputy governor, Andrew Hauser, and chief economist Sarah Hunter, indicating that inflation remained too high.
At the same time as the data was published by the Australian Bureau of Statistics, RBA governor Michele Bullock was appearing alongside Hauser, Hunter and other top officials at a Senate estimates hearing.
Elevated underlying inflationary pressures were a sign that the labour market was still tight, Bullock said.
"The Monetary Policy Board will meet next week," she said.
"We'll discuss our assessment of the flow of data and how the risks are unfolding. A key question is whether the tightening in monetary policy to date will be sufficient to bring inflation back to target in a reasonable time."
Monthly headline inflation rose 4.3 per cent on an annual basis, up from 4 per cent in the 12 months to August.
"Housing was the largest contributor to annual inflation in September, rising by 5.2 per cent," said Rachael McCririck, ABS head of price statistics.
Transport was the second largest contributor, rising by 8.7 per cent annually, due to higher fuel costs.
Fuel and the war in the Middle East
Speaking to press in Canberra, Treasurer Jim Chalmers issued a small mea culpa.
"We accept our part in the fight against inflation," Chalmers said.
"We take responsibility for government policy when it comes to the fiscal settings and when it comes to managing the budget in a responsible way in the face of this inflation challenge, which is persisting longer than anyone would like."
Chalmers again blamed rising inflation on higher fuel prices driven by the conflict in the Middle East.
"This war in the Middle East has been disastrous for Australians, for cost of living, and for inflation right around the world," he said.
"The point that [Treasury] secretary [Jenny] Wilkinson made today and the point that governor Bullock made today is that global energy prices are much higher than have been assumed. And we know what's driving that."
Speaking to reporters after Chalmers' conference, Opposition treasury spokesperson Tim Wilson said Australian families need the government to get inflation under control.
"There will be a lot of households, family, sitting around the kitchen tables of the nation figuring out — what is left to cut? Small business owners who will take this inflation data as a kick directly at their future opportunity and their hope."

Tanzania: Authorities weaponize counterterrorism laws to restrict civic space amid pervasive impunity over violent election crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

Tanzanian authorities have failed to hold anyone accountable for the violence security forces inflicted on protesters, which left hundreds of people dead and thousands of others injured in the wake of the 2025 general election, Amnesty International said on the first anniversary of the crackdown.
Instead of delivering justice and accountability, authorities have withheld a Commission of Inquiry report from the public and intensified attacks on civic space through the abuse of counterterrorism laws.
Not a single official has been criminally investigated, let alone prosecuted and punished for the excessive force that Tanzanian security forces used against protesters. In fact, the situation has only deteriorated since the crackdown began. In a classic tactic pulled out of the authoritarian playbook, the authorities are increasingly weaponizing counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear,”
Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for East and Southern Africa
The organization has documented how, over the past year, security agencies have committed human rights violations with impunity against government critics, opposition supporters, media organizations, and dissenting members of the ruling party. These include acts that may amount to torture or other ill-treatment, arbitrary arrests, enforced disappearances, abductions, and severe restrictions of freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.
“Not a single official has been criminally investigated, let alone prosecuted and punished for the excessive force that Tanzanian security forces used against protesters. In fact, the situation has only deteriorated since the crackdown began. In a classic tactic pulled out of the authoritarian playbook, the authorities are increasingly weaponizing counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear,” said Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for East and Southern Africa.
Although the Commission of Inquiry report into the 2025 election-related killings was handed over to President Samia Suluhu in April 2026, it has yet to be made public. She has repeatedly alleged that the post-election protests were funded by foreign actors in a bid to overthrow the government.
In August 2026, President Suluhu inaugurated another Commission of Inquiry to identify those who planned, funded, coordinated, or executed the violence, as well as investigate the excessive use of force and the whereabouts of missing persons.
“President Suluhu’s continued refusal to release the Commission of Inquiry report not only entrenches a culture of secrecy, but it also perpetuates impunity,” said Tigere Chagutah.
“It is imperative that this new commission comprehensively address the role of security forces in the election-related crackdown. Its investigations must be thorough, independent, impartial, and transparent. On concluding its mandate, it must ensure its findings are made public immediately.”
President Suluhu’s continued refusal to release the Commission of Inquiry report not only entrenches a culture of secrecy, but it also perpetuates impunity.
Tigere Chagutah
Between 3 and 17 September 2026, Amnesty International interviewed 17 people, including victims of arbitrary arrests, enforced disappearances and abductions, as well as journalists, opposition officials, lawyers, and friends and relatives of the victims of the October 2025 election-related crackdown. Amnesty International also verified charge sheets for those arbitrarily arrested and charged with terrorism in different parts of the country.
Tanzanian authorities did not respond to Amnesty’s request for comment.
Abductions, enforced disappearances and torture or other ill-treatment
Amnesty International documented numerous cases of individuals being abducted by suspected state security officers, held incommunicado, and later charged in court. Some of them remain missing.
Among them is Ibrahim Myovella, a youth leader from the opposition party CHADEMA. He went missing alongside two friends on 18 April 2026, after reporting to Central Iringa police station as per their bail conditions following allegations of involvement in the October 2025 protests. The authorities deny ever holding them.
Also missing is Mashaka Nestory Kindikwa, 37, a former official of the ruling Chama cha Mapinduzi (CCM) who was abducted from his home and led away blindfolded by seven men believed to be security officers on 25 June 2026. The police have denied holding him.
On 20 May 2026, David Djumbe, personal assistant to opposition leader Tundu Lissu, was abducted near his Dar es Salaam home by people believed to be state security officers and subjected to severe beatings which may amount to torture or other ill-treatment. He escaped. Police denied involvement and said they had opened an investigation, but there has been no update on progress or findings.
Stefano Patrick*, 26, who expressed support for protests on Saba Saba Day, a national public holiday commemorating the pivotal moment in Tanzania’s struggle for independence, was arbitrarily arrested on 24 July in Dar es Salaam, and detained for 47 days without being charged in court. He told Amnesty International that during his detention, he was tortured and beaten, while also denied food and water.
He said his interrogators demanded to know who was funding the protests: “I was blindfolded… but I could hear some people crying in the next room. Some officers came to me and said, ‘Can you hear how your friends are crying, if you don’t cooperate, we will kill you,’.
“On the first day, they didn’t give me food. When I asked for water, they urinated on my blindfolded face and said ‘that is the price for those of you opening your mouths to make noise’.
I was blindfolded… but I could hear some people crying in the next room. Some officers came to me and said, ‘Can you hear how your friends are crying, if you don’t cooperate, we will kill you.
Stefano Patrick*
“On the second day, I was taken to Gogoni police station where they beat your legs until they get numb but then insist that you must stand. I saw another person’s legs broken at the police station. Even though I was in trouble, I felt pity for what other people were going through”.
Misuse of counterterrorism laws to target critics
Amnesty International documented the frequent abuse of counterterrorism laws to target opposition supporters and government critics. On 9 July 2026, police spokesman David Misime said 130 people had been arrested for allegedly organizing meetings and preparing and circulating messages that encouraged criminal acts aimed at destabilizing the country. Of these, at least 64 were charged under the Prevention of Terrorism Act, an unbailable offence.
In April 2026, Pendo Jonas Kileo went missing. For two months, the family of the CHADEMA member from Temeke, did not know of her whereabouts. On 27 July, they learned that alongside another CHADEMA member, Kileo had been charged in Temeke District Court with conspiracy to commit terrorist acts as well as participating in terrorist meetings between September 2025 and July 2026.
On 4 July 2026, police arbitrarily arrested university students and CHADEMA student-body members Noah Mwalwange, Gwamaka Mboka, Augustino Wasinyo and Rojas Mpani. They were held at Mbeya Central Police Station until 23 July, when they were charged under the Prevention of Terrorism Act. A source familiar with their case said they were denied access to lawyers, beaten with batons during interrogation, stripped, and forced to record confessions and name CHADEMA leaders as their financiers.
By resorting to terrorism-related charges against its perceived critics, the Tanzanian government is sending a chilling message that it won’t stop at anything in its effort to repress any and all dissenting opinions.
Tigere Chagutah
On 8 July 2026, Melkisedek Kaijage, a political science lecturer at the University of Dodoma, was arrested on allegations of inciting people to participate in Saba Saba protests. He was detained for 17 days on allegations of engaging in sedition, before the charges were later changed to terrorism. These were eventually dropped and he was released on 10 September but must report to the police in Dodoma every month for a year.
In Iringa, three CHADEMA members were arrested ahead of the July 2026 Saba Saba protests. During their three-week detention, they said police told them to sign a pre-written statement before receiving bail. Instead of being bailed, they were taken to court and charged under the Prevention of Terrorism Act.
“By resorting to terrorism-related charges against its perceived critics, the Tanzanian government is sending a chilling message that it won’t stop at anything in its effort to repress any and all dissenting opinions,” said Tigere Chagutah.
“The authorities must end the abuse of counterterrorism laws to stifle freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. They must immediately and unconditionally drop all terrorism charges against those unjustly detained and end harassment of individuals solely for peacefully exercising their human rights.”
Restriction of civic space and violations of press freedom
Over the last year, authorities have adopted numerous tactics to narrow civic space.
They have restricted access to social media sites, such as Club House and X, and deployed large numbers of security forces to intimidate protesters ahead of planned demonstrations on 9 December 2025 and 7 July 2026. On 26 June 2026, the home affairs minister banned political rallies and mass gatherings, further stifling freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.
In February 2026, the Chief Justice issued an order barring lawyers from speaking to the media on cases before the court, violating the rights of lawyers representing their clients, as well as the rights of the media to seek, receive and share information.
Media freedom has also come under increasing and unwarranted pressure.
The authorities must revoke the suspension of Mwanahalisi newspaper, restore access to banned social media platforms, and end censorship of online content. They must also ensure that media outlets are free to operate independently, and that journalists can carry out their legitimate work without fear of reprisals.
Tigere Chagutah
On 2 April 2026, the Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority (TCRA) suspended the online-broadcast licence of Jambo Online TV for 90 days, over content TCRA called unverified and misleading concerning the Commission of Inquiry into the October 2025 general-election unrest. Jambo TV’s licence was reinstated and the station returned to air on 3 July 2026, after the 90-day suspension lapsed.
On 19 August 2026, the Information Services Department suspended Mwanahalisi newspaper’s publishing and distribution licence for six months, over a report that Vice-President Emmanuel Nchimbi had rejected calls to resign.
“The authorities must revoke the suspension of Mwanahalisi newspaper, restore access to banned social media platforms, and end censorship of online content. They must also ensure that media outlets are free to operate independently, and that journalists can carry out their legitimate work without fear of reprisals,” said Tigere Chagutah.

Five key takeaways from Israel’s parliamentary elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
02:53:35 UTC
11:53:35 KST

Five key takeaways from Israel’s parliamentary elections
With more than 76 percent of votes counted, Netanyahu’s bloc holds a slight lead over the opposition but shy of a majority.
Israel’s partial election results show a tight race between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, with neither likely to secure a clear path to a governing majority.
With more than 84 percent of the votes counted by Israel’s Central Elections Committee on Wednesday, Netanyahu’s bloc was on track to win 54 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, Israel’s parliament. Eisenkot’s alliance was set to win 49, and the Arab parties were on track for 17 seats, Israeli media reported.
Tuesday’s vote was largely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership and a response to the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, as well as Israel’s subsequent genocidal war on Gaza.
It also came as Israel’s pogroms in the occupied West Bank have escalated, and amid mounting tensions with several of the country’s neighbours, many of whom it has attacked in the past three years.
Here are five key takeaways from the Israeli elections so far:
Early results show no clear winner
With 84 percent of votes counted in Israel at 12.34am (10:45 GMT) on Wednesday, Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc was on course to secure 54 seats, seven short of a majority in the parliament, according to election commission tallies published by Israeli media.
Eisenkot’s alliance was on track to win 49 seats, while the Arab parties were set to win 17 seats, building on their 2022 performance.
Earlier exit polls had projected a deadlock, with the two main blocs on track for 51 seats each.
The exit polls indicated that Netanyahu’s Likud party – which leads his wider bloc – could emerge as the single largest party with an estimated 27 seats, while Eisenkot’s Yashar party was projected to win 21 seats, according to Channels 12 and 13.
Israelis vote for parties, which then form alliances to create a governing coalition with a prime minister at the helm. No single party has ever won a 61-seat majority.
Released by the major Israeli television networks, exit polls are unofficial indicators of the vote. Preliminary official results are expected on Wednesday and may vary from the exit polls.
Leaders react, predict end to Netanyahu’s reign
Opposition bloc leader Eisenkot said the Israeli public had voted for change and against the incumbent prime minister.
Addressing supporters at his Yashar party headquarters, Eisenkot said, “This will be a new start. A real new start on a new path. The old era is over, and Israel is starting a new era.”
But the prime minister told supporters that his Likud party is dominant and called for the formation of a “national right-wing government”.
“What we’ve seen is that the Likud party is the largest party – nobody can compete with us,” he said. “The second thing that is clear as well is that the right bloc has a majority, and it is a decisive majority.”
He also accused Israeli television channels of trying to discourage his supporters from voting by projecting stronger results for opposition parties.
Far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich told supporters his Religious Zionism party was projected to win seven seats, and pledged to continue the expansion of Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, which are illegal under international law.
Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, meanwhile, praised his Otzma Yehudit party’s performance in a speech to supporters at its headquarters.
“We are very proud of our journey”, Ben-Gvir said. “This party was not even existing on the political landscape.”
The Democrats party leader Yair Golan said on X that voters had “fired the Netanyahu government”, and pledged to work with political partners to form a new administration.
The leader of Ra’am, or the United Arab List, Mansour Abbas said he hopes the final election results will let the opposition bloc and his party hold the 61 seats needed to form a government. The party was projected to win about seven seats.
Record turnout among voters
The Central Elections Committee reported that 77.7 percent of eligible voters participated in the election, the highest turnout since 1999. Turnout was up 7.1 percentage points from 2022, when Netanyahu, who has served as prime minister on and off since 1996, returned to office.
Israel’s military said turnout among soldiers had climbed beyond 68 percent by 5pm local time (15:00 GMT). More than 60,000 Israelis also returned home from abroad to vote.
Polling stations closed at 10pm local time (20:00 GMT), but the official elections body said anyone waiting in line at that time would still be able to vote.
Arab parties as potential tie-breaker
Exit polls and partial results suggested Arab-led parties could win 19 seats, a significant jump from the current 10-seat representation they hold in parliament. That same polling showed Eisenkot and Netanyahu tied at the projected 51 seats each before preliminary official results began trickling in.
Given the 61 seats needed to form a government in Israel, both Eisenkot and Netanyahu’s parties are locked out of the majority without the Arab vote.
Eisenkot and Netanyahu have in the past refused to form a coalition with Arab parties to secure that majority. Netanyahu said the idea of working with Arab leaders would be a “disgrace and a shame“.
Alon Pinkas, a former Israeli ambassador, told Al Jazeera that forming a government could be difficult for both parties because of the promise not to form said coalition.
“There’s a price to pay,” Pinkas said, because the “Arabs can’t be kept outside and only being considered and co-opted when you need their votes”.
What could happen next?
After the vote is finalised, the parties will immediately begin negotiations to try to reach the 61-seat majority.
The bloc with the most votes will have different options to assemble support from smaller parties, including forming a minority government or working with another political leader to alternate as prime minister under a power-sharing arrangement.
Once the final count is in, President Isaac Herzog will speak with party leaders about who they want as prime minister. He will then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.
The person nominated will then have up to 42 days to form a government.
As for the two leading parties unifying to create a majority, voters would “never forgive” Eisenkot if he unites with Netanyahu’s bloc, while sharing power through rotating roles would guarantee “dysfunction”, Pinkas said.
If no government emerges, Netanyahu and his current cabinet will remain as a caretaker government.
If negotiations fail and no coalition can form a government, new elections will be called.
The final vote tally is expected by Friday, and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on November 4.

Netanyahu and rival claim mandate after tight Israel election

- Exit polls showed both blocs on about 51 seats, below the 61 needed, while Arab Israeli parties made strong gains as many voters rejected Netanyahu’s hard-right rule.
- Netanyahu called for a “strong government of the right” and hinted at action against Iran, while Eisenkot urged change, warned against using security for politics, and said he would act “swiftly”.
AI generated
JERUSALEM – Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and rival Gadi Eisenkot each vowed on Oct 28 to form a government after both came up short in the first election since the Oct 7, 2023 attack traumatised the country.
Voters turned out on Oct 27 in the highest numbers in decades to give their verdict on the divisive rule of Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister who has pushed the country sharply to the right and unleashed a wave of wars in response to the Hamas attack.
Exit polls showed Eisenkot, a former military chief and political novice, and his opposition bloc neck and neck with Netanyahu’s hard-right camp, and both well away from the threshold for a majority in Parliament.
The strongest gains came from Arab Israeli parties, whose voters turned out in soaring numbers against Netanyahu, who has relentlessly warned that the minority would dilute the Jewish nationalist direction in which he has taken Israel.
Netanyahu, greeting cheering supporters at a Jerusalem convention centre after 3am, called for a “strong government of the right” and said that the “Jewish and Zionist majority must unite”.
The 77-year-old Prime Minister was unusually brief and did not directly claim victory.
Instead, he listed leaders Israel has killed under his orders and again hinted that he was ready for a third bombing campaign against Iran alongside US President Donald Trump, his close ally.
“Israel has a unique opportunity with our partner President Trump to forever eliminate the existential threat of Iran,” Netanyahu said.
Eisenkot, speaking to his own supporters in Tel Aviv, issued a veiled warning to Netanyahu, who observers say could use a war to push for a unity government. “Netanyahu, don’t you dare use Israel’s security for your political needs,” Eisenkot said.
Addressing Israel’s security establishment, Eisenkot said that they served the state and not Netanyahu, calling him “a caretaker prime minister, without a mandate or the people’s trust”.
‘Public has voted for change’
Eisenkot shares many of Netanyahu’s views on security and has backed the Gaza offensive following Oct 7 that has reduced the territory to rubble.
But Eisenkot has vowed to create a more inclusive atmosphere inside Israel and to rein in extremist settlers in the West Bank who have attacked Palestinians with virtual impunity.
After a turnout of nearly 78%, the highest since 1999, Eisenkot said it would be a mistake to hold a second election and vowed to work “swiftly” to form a government.
“The public has voted for change,” Eisenkot said. “A worthy leader would accept the people’s vote of no confidence and announce his retirement from political life today.”
The three mainstream Israeli television networks in exit polls gave the two blocs each around 51 seats – well below the 61 needed to govern – after initially giving an edge to the opposition.
Israeli Arab lists were projected to win 17 to 18 seats, a sharp gain, with some Israeli Arab communities reporting near-universal turnout driven by outrage to often derogatory rhetoric against them by Netanyahu’s far-right allies.
Key Israeli Arab leader Mansour Abbas said he believed the right had “suffered a major loss” and was open to working with Eisenkot.
But Eisenkot said during the campaign he would not govern with Israeli Arab lawmakers – and Netanyahu again suggested that a government relying on Arab votes would lack legitimacy.
Arab lawmakers could give Eisenkot support in parliamentary votes to maintain a minority government without joining a coalition. If not, Israel could head to new elections.
Itamar Ben-Gvir, a far-right firebrand who according to exit polls did not gain as much as many expected, warned Netanyahu against another option – a unity government with Eisenkot.
“It would be a terrible mistake,” said Ben-Gvir, who champions the expulsion of Palestinians and would likely be excluded from any unity government.
Hebrew University of Jerusalem political scientist Gideon Rahat said Ben-Gvir had succeeded in mobilising votes – of Israeli Arabs. But he said: “Even if Netanyahu lost, that doesn’t mean Eisenkot won.”
Divisive
The election came as Israel looks increasingly isolated on the world stage, driven by the war in Iran and the military campaign in Gaza, soaring settlement construction and violence in the occupied West Bank.
Netanyahu himself faces an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court over Gaza, as well as domestic corruption charges that could land him in prison if he loses power.
Eisenkot is a political novice whose mild manner is the antithesis of the smooth-talking incumbent.
The son of working-class Moroccan Jewish immigrants, Eisenkot would be the first prime minister of Middle Eastern or North African descent.
Before voting, the 66-year-old Eisenkot paid his respects privately at the grave of his son Gal, whose death fighting in Gaza has drawn empathy from many Israelis.
Tens of thousands of Israelis are estimated to have flown in from abroad for an election seen as crucial for their country.
Eilana Zisblit, 55, told AFP she had travelled back from Canada, where she has lived for almost 30 years, to vote for a centre-right party in Eisenkot’s bloc.
“The country is going in a really, really bad direction. Both for Jews and Arabs living in the country, and for Jews living abroad,” she said. The time to act is “now, or the country really won’t survive any more”. AFP

Cyclonic storm Arnab has made landfall along the southeastern coast of India, striking the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam (Puducherry) coasts with sustained wind speeds of 125 to 135 kmph and gusts up to 150 kmph.
NEW DELHI: Cyclonic storm Arnab continued making landfall along the Andhra Pradesh coast on Wednesday morning, bringing heavy rainfall, strong winds and high tides. Trees were uprooted in Visakhapatnam and Odisha’s Malkangiri, while rough seas and gusty winds battered the Kakinada coastline.
The landfall process was expected to continue for around three more hours from 7am, according to reports. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) said the storm was nearly stationary near the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coast early Wednesday, with sustained wind speeds of 120-130 kmph and gusts reaching 145 kmph.
Visuals from Visakhapatnam showed high tides at RK Beach and a tree uprooted near Andhra University’s College of Engineering for Women. In Odisha’s Malkangiri, strong winds and heavy rainfall were also reported.
Heavy rainfall caused waterlogging in several parts of Kakinada, while nearly 6,000 electricity poles were uprooted in Andhra Pradesh’s Konaseema district, damaging power infrastructure. Officials also shifted residents from badly affected areas, including Pagadala Peta, to rehabilitation centres.
A storm surge of 1 metre to 1.5 metres above the astronomical tide was forecast to inundate low-lying areas of Andhra Pradesh over the following three hours before gradually subsiding.
The Andhra Pradesh School Education Department converted 609 schools into rehabilitation centres, accommodating 854 people across the state as of 5.50am on Wednesday, officials said.
Heavy rainfall, red alert in OdishaThe IMD issued a red alert for extremely heavy rainfall at isolated places in Odisha’s Ganjam, Gajapati, Rayagada and Nabarangpur districts. Winds of 60-70 kmph, gusting to 80 kmph, were expected in these areas.
Other southern districts of Odisha were under an orange alert for heavy to very heavy rainfall, accompanied by winds of 50-70 kmph. Wind speeds of 40-70 kmph were expected in Bhubaneswar and Cuttack.IMD scientist Sanjeev Dwivedi warned of possible mudslides and landslides in the Koraput region and advised people to avoid unnecessary travel. Strong winds could damage kutcha houses, thatched roofs and other vulnerable structures.Between 8.30am on October 27 and 4am on October 28, Kannuripalem in Anakapalle district recorded the highest rainfall at 261.5 mm. Vizianagaram recorded 259.74 mm, while Visakhapatnam recorded 259.06 mm during the period.Evacuations, emergency teams deployedAhead of the cyclone, Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu said the state had identified 2,199 cyclone shelters and prepared evacuation plans, prioritising elderly people, children, persons with disabilities and pregnant women. He said 2,360 pregnant women had been moved to medical facilities.“Twelve NDRF and ten SDRF teams have been assigned to the districts, with deployment underway,” the Chief Minister said, adding that police, fire services and medical teams had been mobilised, while the Navy and Coast Guard were ready to assist.
More than 8,400 power restoration personnel had been mobilised, Naidu said. Arrangements were also being made for food, drinking water, medicines and generators, while control rooms were operating round the clock."I appeal to everyone to remain calm, stay alert and cooperate with the authorities. Move immediately to designated shelters when advised. Fishermen must not venture into the sea until official clearance is given," he said.“Keep essential supplies and charged phones ready. Avoid unnecessary travel, beaches, riverbanks, floodwaters and fallen power lines,” he added.The chief minister urged residents to remain in safe shelters until authorities confirmed that the danger had passed and to follow official advisories.

Economic Watch: China, Germany eye broader cooperation in intelligent connected vehicles
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:35:48 CST
11:35:48 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- As electrification, digitalization and artificial intelligence (AI) reshape the global auto industry, how China and Germany can build on their complementary strengths to expand cooperation has become a key question facing both countries' industries.
Last week, the 2026 World Intelligent Connected Vehicles Conference (WICV) was held in Beijing, where government and business representatives from both countries held talks on technology coordination, standards alignment and market access. Both sides agreed that there is a strong need for concrete progress.
China and Germany have long cooperated in the intelligent connected vehicle (ICV) sector. Signed in 2018, their memorandum of understanding on ICVs has served as an important platform for bilateral technical cooperation. Last month, the two sides held a plenary meeting in Berlin, where they exchanged views on practical issues such as vehicle type approval, data recording and vehicle-to-everything communications.
"This is exactly the kind of cooperation we need -- concrete, pragmatic, technology-focused and workable," said Hildegard Müller, president of the German Association of the Automotive Industry.
"China has made remarkable progress in electric mobility and digital technology, while German automakers and suppliers have deep expertise in automotive engineering, systems integration and industrial production. The two countries bring important complementary experience to the automotive industry's transformation," Müller said at the WICV.
She acknowledged that harmonizing standards and regulations is no easy task, but "regulatory differences should not become unnecessary barriers to innovation and market access." The goal, she said, is to build enough common ground for innovation to cross borders and ultimately benefit manufacturers, suppliers and consumers in both countries.
China's push for intelligent connectivity is gaining strong momentum. By the end of August, about 61 million passenger cars were equipped with combined driver assistance systems, some 16 million had 5G terminals, and roughly 2 million carried C-V2X (cellular vehicle-to-everything) direct communication terminals.
The country has also rolled out a series of national standards covering combined driver assistance, automated driving, automatic emergency braking and vehicle cybersecurity, and is scaling up connected-vehicle communications through real-world use.
On the German side, companies are deepening their footprint in China. Milan Nedeljković, chairman of the board of management of BMW AG, said the all-new BMW iX3, produced locally in northeast China's Shenyang, will begin customer deliveries in November.
"This model blends BMW's engineering strength with China's vibrant digital ecosystem," he said. "Intelligent, connected new energy vehicles are at the heart of the automotive industry's transformation and a key driver of China's high-quality development. We are confident in the market's long-term potential."
Chinese automakers, for their part, are stepping up their integration into the German and broader European markets. According to Yin Tongyue, chairman of Chery Holding Group Co., Ltd., Chery has set up R&D centers in Germany as it expands into Europe. Chery's cooperation in Europe, he said, has long moved beyond local manufacturing to leverage local talent and embrace local culture, and has achieved localization across the entire value chain, from R&D and manufacturing to procurement and sales.
"In the early days of reform and opening up, Volkswagen, Audi and Mercedes-Benz set up factories in China, helping to develop the country's market, supply chains and talent pool," Yin said. "Today, as China advances in electrification and intelligent technology, China, too, must learn to share with its peers around the world and move toward an electrified, low-carbon and intelligent era alongside established local automakers."
In intelligent driving, Mercedes-Benz is deepening its partnership with Chinese tech company Momenta. Oliver Thöne, member of the board of management of Mercedes-Benz Group AG and head of the board division Greater China, said Mercedes-Benz offers highway driver assistance in China, with the take-up rate for related features doubling year on year, and is now expanding into urban driver assistance.
"We are also working with Tsinghua University to develop a vision-language AI model, which has been applied to our rear-seat systems and will be deployed globally," he said.
Wang Zhiqin, vice president of the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology, noted that China-Germany automotive cooperation is extending from complete vehicle manufacturing and parts procurement to joint R&D, standards coordination and ecosystem building.
She called on companies from both countries to deepen technological collaboration, conduct joint research and testing in frontier areas, and strengthen cooperation across the ICV supply chain, including in information, communications and software. ■

China, 25 other countries sign UN convention on negotiable cargo documents
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:35:33 CST
11:35:33 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 26, 2026 shows the signing ceremony of the United Nations Convention on Negotiable Cargo Documents in Accra, Ghana. China, Ghana and 24 other countries on Monday became the first signatories to the United Nations Convention on Negotiable Cargo Documents at a signing ceremony in Accra. (Photo by Seth/Xinhua)
ACCRA, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- China, Ghana and 24 other countries on Monday became the first signatories to the United Nations Convention on Negotiable Cargo Documents at a signing ceremony in Accra, capital of Ghana.
Chinese Vice Commerce Minister Jiang Chenghua signed the convention on behalf of the Chinese government at the ceremony.
Jiang said the institutional innovation fills a gap in international rules and provides an international legal framework for financing transactions involving cross-border transport documents.
It will effectively ease the financial pressure on enterprises engaged in international trade, reduce transaction costs in cross-border overland trade, and inject new momentum into the high-quality development of global trade, he added.
China is ready to work with all signatory states to complete their domestic approval procedures as soon as possible, Jiang said, expressing China's hope that more countries will join the convention so that its benefits can reach more nations and contribute to global trade prosperity and the well-being of people around the world.
Anna Joubin-Bret, secretary of the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL), said the convention would help reduce uncertainty, enhance resilience, facilitate trade finance, support trade digitalization and improve the efficiency of international supply chains.
She thanked the Chinese government for bringing the convention project to UNCITRAL. "Since the adoption by the United Nations General Assembly, we have greatly benefited from China's steadfast support to the convention and its efforts to promote the broader understanding of this framework," she said.
Around 400 representatives from more than 60 countries and regions attended the signing ceremony.
Initiated and spearheaded by China, the convention was adopted by the 80th session of the UN General Assembly in December 2025. ■

Mitchell Weiser then threatened to complete Bremen's comeback, but Dortmund regained control in the closing stages.

UN nuclear inspectors see no evidence Iran repaired US-bombed sites

UN nuclear inspectors see no evidence Iran repaired US-bombed sites
NEW YORK – The United Nations nuclear watchdog said it has not detected any efforts by Iran to rebuild nuclear facilities damaged in US and Israeli strikes over the past two years, even as Tehran continues to block inspectors’ access to most of its atomic sites.
“Since June 2025, we have not identified any activity to repair or reconstruct any of the facilities damaged in the military attacks of 2025 and 2026,” International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) director-general Rafael Mariano Grossi told the UN Security Council on Oct 27.
Grossi’s remarks undercut US President Donald Trump’s narrative that launching a new war against Iran in late February was necessary to halt its nuclear weapons ambitions.
The President has repeatedly said he Is weighing renewed strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections.
The assessment echoes a conclusion that former US director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard included in written testimony before a congressional committee earlier in 2026.
She wrote that Iran’s uranium enrichment programme had been “obliterated” in US and Israeli strikes in June 2025, and that there “has been no efforts since then to try to rebuild their enrichment capability”.
At the same time, the IAEA’s ability to assess Iran’s nuclear activities remains constrained by its lack of access to most of the country’s atomic sites.
Grossi reiterated that inspectors have been unable to verify the status of Iran’s nuclear material – including the previously declared 440kg of uranium enriched up to 60% – and called on Tehran to grant renewed access.
“As at today the IAEA has not been able to verify that there has been no diversion of nuclear material required to be safeguarded,” he said.
The Trump administration has repeatedly claimed it had destroyed Iran’s nuclear facilities, but offered little evidence to back up its claims.
Trump started the current war against Iran because he said he needed to stop Iran from having a nuclear weapon, something that most experts said the Islamic Republic was years away from.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has offered other explanations for the war, including that Washington had to act before Israel struck Iran and sparked retaliation against the US.
He’s also said Iran was building up its ballistic missile and drone capability as a conventional “shield” around its nuclear programme. BLOOMBERG

OpenAI plans to buy Google’s chips as part of its AI build-out

- The move is part of OpenAI’s wider push to build AI infrastructure fast. It also plans to use its own chips in 2026, including Jalapeno chips made with Broadcom.
- Google’s TPUs, first built for search, are now a rival to Nvidia’s chips. Oracle will also offer TPUs in its cloud, as Google says AI needs “a diverse range of compute”.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – OpenAI intends to buy artificial intelligence computing chips from Alphabet’s Google, according to a person familiar with the matter, part of broader efforts by the ChatGPT maker to build out its AI infrastructure.
The final terms of any deal are not yet known, according to the person, who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private. OpenAI and Google declined to comment.
The move reflects OpenAI’s multi-pronged bid to quickly add more AI processing power.
The company has already announced plans to start using its own chips to support its artificial intelligence models later in 2026.
It joins a stampede of companies working to develop home-grown AI chips and challenge Nvidia’s dominance in the field.
OpenAI’s in-house Jalapeno chips, developed with Broadcom, were created with help from Google veterans. Richard Ho, who runs the OpenAI internal chip team, was previously involved in the development of Google’s semiconductors – known as tensor processing units, or TPUs.
Google began working on its TPUs more than a decade ago. Initially, the processors were used to speed up the company’s web search engine and improve efficiency.
But the chips soon proved valuable for handling AI work and have emerged in recent years as an alternative to Nvidia’s prized graphics processing units.
Oracle also announced on Oct 27 that TPUs would be available through its cloud-computing infrastructure.
“The next generation of AI will require a diverse range of compute,” Google executive Amin Vahdat said in a statement announcing that deal.
The Information previously reported that OpenAI was planning to buy Google chips. BLOOMBERG

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The ruling DPP is gaining ground ahead of November's local elections, while the opposition KMT faces growing challenges, Japanese political analyst Ogasawara Yoshiyuki said Tuesday.
Ogasawara, an honorary professor at National Tsing Hua University, said the DPP could win races in Chiayi, Changhua County, and Yilan County, CNA reported. He also saw opportunities in New Taipei and Hsinchu County, although the party could lose Penghu County.
Ogasawara identified New Taipei as the most important race in the Nov. 28 elections. He said DPP candidate Su Chiao-hui (蘇巧慧) had steadily gained on KMT candidate Lee Shu-chuan (李四川), drawing level in the spring before taking a narrow lead after September.

In Taipei, Ogasawara said DPP candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) had gained ground since September and was now running neck and neck with incumbent KMT Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安). He said Shen had stronger momentum but cautioned that the race remained too close to call.
Ogasawara linked the DPP's improving prospects to growing public frustration with the KMT's actions in the legislature. He said opposition efforts to block government spending had delayed approval of this year's central government budget until August, a record 266 days late.
He also cited a dispute over cuts and freezes to the Presidential Office's budget, which forced it to cancel orders for mooncakes from workshops employing people with disabilities. Ogasawara said the controversy had fueled criticism that the opposition had gone too far.
Ogasawara said the KMT may have become overconfident after defeating efforts to remove its lawmakers from office in last year's recall votes. However, he said recall votes and regular elections involve different political dynamics.
Meanwhile, Ogasawara said the DPP had shifted its campaign strategy toward local issues and everyday concerns. Rather than focusing on its message of resisting China and defending Taiwan, the party was paying greater attention to voters' daily needs.
